Thyroid function both directions: heat/cold, bowels, palpitations/tremor/sweating/sleep, weight, energy, mood, skin, hair
Cancer questions; the pair: difficulty swallowing? change in voice? plus noisy breathing/lying flat
Risk factors one at a time: radiotherapy to head/neck? occupation now and before, radiation? cancer yourself? thyroid cancer in family? breast cancer? bowel cancer?
The stroke, medications and adherence, reviews, smoking, alcohol, allergies; 'what's been going through your mind since that letter came?' → respond to Trev

STOP the history. Name the kinds of nodule → examination → TSH → branch (uptake scan if fast; ultrasound if normal) → FNA only if suspicious → PATS, safety-net, ring him with the result, check understanding, questions
ask: I do have your results here, and I want to tell you what they show before anything else
Have you ever been told you had a lump or a problem with your thyroid before?
Noticed any swelling in the front of your neck? Pain? Change in the skin?
How do you cope with the weather — heat or cold more than others? Bowels changed? Palpitations, tremor, sweating, trouble sleeping? Weight? Energy, mood, skin, hair?
Lost weight without meaning to? Appetite? Night sweats or fevers? Other lumps, especially above the collarbones?
Two questions I ask everyone with a lump here: any difficulty swallowing? any change in your voice? — ask as a pair; plus noisy breathing or trouble lying flat

Ever had radiotherapy or radiation treatment to your head or neck, at any age? Occupation now and before — worked around radiation? Cancer yourself? Thyroid cancer in the family? Breast cancer? Bowel cancer? — one at a time, never stacked
The stroke: when, what were you left with, medications, taking them every day?, reviews; smoke, alcohol, allergies
What's been going through your mind since that letter came? → 'I'm sorry — that must make this letter very frightening to open'
pefe: Name the kinds first: fluid-filled cyst · overgrown area · inflamed tissue · benign tumour, some of which switch themselves on · a small number are cancers (papillary commonest; follicular, medullary) · very occasionally a cancer from elsewhere
If he asks the odds: 'something like nine in ten are not cancer. I can't promise you which side of that you're on, and I won't pretend I can'

Numbered plan: FIRST examine the neck — size, firmness, tenderness, moves on swallowing, nodes in neck and above the collarbones · SECOND blood test TSH — 'that one test decides what comes next' · THIRD the branch: gland running fast → nuclear (radioiodine uptake) scan, a hot lump is reassuring; TSH normal/low-normal → ultrasound of the neck (what it's made of, how worrying, nearby glands) · FOURTH only if the ultrasound looks suspicious → ultrasound-guided fine-needle sample under local

Wrap: most people are simply watched; bloods here, ultrasound and FNA at a larger centre — PATS; safety-net: grows quickly, voice hoarse, food catching, trouble breathing → sooner or 000; 'I'll ring you myself with the blood result'; check understanding; also address stroke-prevention adherence

Summary to examiner: incidental left nodule on CTA, euthyroid, asymptomatic, no compressive/red-flag features, prior neck irradiation + male + 60; excluding carcinoma; exam → TSH → uptake scan if suppressed or ultrasound with risk stratification → US-guided FNA if indicated; would not repeat CT
fails: No question about swallowing or voice (single-item fail)
Never asking about radiotherapy/radiation — the role-player never volunteers it
Listing tests without saying what you are looking for
Promising it is harmless
Triple-barrelled family cancer question; starting questions cold before the heads-up; ending on the FNA with no safety-net
numbers: Order: examination → TSH → branch → uptake scan (TSH low) or ultrasound (TSH normal/high) → US-guided FNA if indicated
Malignancy ~5–10% of nodules; higher in men, age <20 or >60, after neck irradiation VERIFY · hot = functioning, malignancy uncommon, FNA not routine · cold → ultrasound ± FNA, most still benign

Cytology: Bethesda; FNA cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma → diagnostic hemithyroidectomy · US suspicion: solid hypoechoic, taller-than-wide, irregular margin, microcalcification, extrathyroidal extension, abnormal node
Types: papillary (commonest, best prognosis) · follicular · medullary (MEN 2) · anaplastic · lymphoma · metastasis · syndromes: Cowden (breast), FAP (bowel), MEN 2
Never: CT to characterise · uptake scan with normal TSH · FNA before ultrasound · thyroglobulin as a diagnostic test · blanket reassurance
Clock: heads-up by 0:45 · stop history at 4:40 · last 40 s for understanding, safety-net, follow-up

Variants: TSH suppressed (hot, sweating, 6 kg loss, tremor, loose bowels) → toxic adenoma, nuclear scan not ultrasound, beta-blocker, ECG; recent iodinated contrast — discuss uptake-scan timing with nuclear medicine (Jod–Basedow) · red flags (hoarse 6 wk, food catching, supraclavicular node) → concerned not diagnostic, scan + FNA this week, laryngoscopy, ring him, bring someone · angry patient (letter, 3 weeks, 'cut it out today') → validate, don't defend; surgery risks recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroids, only when tests say so · sibling recall: adrenal incidentaloma — metanephrines, dexamethasone suppression, aldosterone–renin if hypertensive/hypokalaemic; dedicated adrenal CT; never needle before phaeo excluded VERIFY

setting: Your general practice.
stem: James Doherty, a 66-year-old man, presents complaining of nervousness.
Background. He is a known case of atrial fibrillation. He was taking flecainide; his cardiologist changed him to amiodarone four weeks ago. He has come today for his blood test results.
Results handed to you in the room: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (normal, 0.4–4.0) · Free T4 28 pmol/L (high, 10–20) · Free T3 8.9 pmol/L (high, 3.5–6.5).
tasks: Take a focused history
Interpret the investigation results for the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Roughly 4–4:30 history, 1:30 results, 2:00 diagnosis and differentials.

back.dx: Thyrotoxicosis with INAPPROPRIATE TSH secretion — high T4/T3 with a NORMAL TSH. Two diagnoses, in order: (1) TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma; (2) amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction (honest caveat: amiodarone should suppress TSH, and four weeks is early — but TSH can drift back to normal over months, so it stays on the list). The station is built on one mismatch: in thyrotoxicosis the TSH should be suppressed and his is not. Say it to the examiner, and a lay version to the patient. Hidden agenda: wants the amiodarone stopped today; underneath, frightened his heart is getting worse.
plan: Confirm ID; 'I have your results and we'll go through them — first, what do you mean by nervous: stressed and on edge, shaking hands, or racing heart?'
Timing, pattern, impact (4 weeks, since the switch — note it, don't close on it)
AF anchor: how long, adherence, WHY was flecainide changed, side effects, follow-up; complications — racing, chest pain, SOBOE, oedema, TIA/stroke symptoms, anticoagulant
Track 1 thyroid: heat intolerance, bowels, weight loss, sweating, tremor. Track 2 pituitary: headache, blurred vision, side vision, weakness/numbness
Psychiatry + stimulants: mood, sleep, 'I ask everyone — thoughts of harming yourself or anyone else?', home/stress, tea/coffee, alcohol, substances, cold-and-flu tablets

Results in FOUR rungs: gland in the neck makes hormones → yours are high → TSH from the brain controls it → when hormones rise TSH should fall; yours stayed normal — that mismatch is what I must explain. 'Does that make sense so far?'
'Two things on my list' — adenoma (usually not cancer), then amiodarone with the honest caveat. Three ready answers: cancer? stop the tablet? what now? Then the rest of the differentials

Plan: repeat assay on a different platform (ask about biotin), further hormones incl. cortisol, formal visual fields, pituitary MRI, endocrinology; speak to cardiologist yourself; red flags; phone with the repeat result
ask: Can you tell me what you mean by feeling nervous? Stressed and on edge, shaking in your hands, or a racing heart?
How long? Constant or comes and goes? Getting worse? Anything make it better or worse? How is it affecting your day-to-day life?
Why was the flecainide changed? Are you taking the amiodarone regularly, exactly as prescribed?
Still getting racing? Chest pain? Breathless on exertion, ankle swelling? Any weakness/numbness one side, trouble speaking, brief loss of vision? On a blood thinner?
Heat intolerance? Looser/more frequent bowels? Weight loss? Sweating? Shaking hands?
Headaches? Blurred vision, or difficulty seeing to the sides? Weakness or numbness anywhere?
How has your mood been? Your sleep? 'I ask everybody this — any thoughts of harming yourself, or anyone else?'
Who do you live with, any stresses at home or work?
How much tea/coffee? Alcohol? Other substances, cold-and-flu tablets? Any supplements — biotin?
pefe: No examination in this station — results are handed to you

Investigations to name: repeat TFTs on a different assay platform (artefact/biotin), full pituitary hormone profile including MORNING CORTISOL, formal visual field testing, pituitary MRI; endocrinology referral; discuss with cardiologist
To the examiner: 'This is thyrotoxicosis with inappropriate TSH secretion' · 'My first investigation is a repeat assay on a different platform'

Examiner challenge — start carbimazole today? NO: mechanism unknown; if TSH-oma a thionamide lowers T4 and drives TSH higher; if type 2 amiodarone thyroiditis the gland isn't overproducing — thionamide won't help. Repeat assay, involve endocrinology first
fails: Assuming what 'nervous' means and launching a thyroid history without asking
Agreeing 'it's just the tablet' — false reassurance that abandons the normal TSH
Skipping 'why was the flecainide changed?'
Asking mood and sleep but NOT self-harm — marked down hardest
Not asking headache and vision (the pituitary track)
Giving one diagnosis instead of two, in order
Telling him to stop the amiodarone, or not offering to contact the cardiologist
Physiology lecture: drawing the axis, saying 'negative feedback'; jargon without 'in plain English'
numbers: TSH 1.8 normal · fT4 28 · fT3 8.9 both high · 4 weeks on amiodarone — early for drug-induced thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis requires a LOW TSH — except in pituitary disease
Amiodarone thyroid phases: hyper → hypo → normal, over months
Five causes of normal TSH + high T4: assay artefact (biotin), sampling/timing, amiodarone late phase, TSH-secreting adenoma, thyroid hormone resistance
Before any thyroid-directed treatment in pituitary disease: check cortisol first
Five history blocks — block 5 is psychiatry

Variant 1 (early recall): TSH 0.02, 8 months on amiodarone = overt amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis; separate type 1 vs 2 with colour-flow Doppler; endocrine + cardiology together before changing the drug
Variant 2: headaches + clipping door frames = bitemporal field defect → urgent fields, MRI, neurosurgery, cortisol first
Variant 3: high-dose biotin, no symptoms = artefact; stop, wait days, repeat on different platform — VERIFY washout interval
'Is it cancer?' — usually benign, treatable, not what I'm worried about today · 'Stop the tablet?' — no, it holds your rhythm; I'll speak to your cardiologist myself

setting: General practice.
stem: You are a GP. Jenny Alderton, 37, has come in with palpitations and dizziness for three days.
(Version A — shorter stem.)
tasks: Take a focused history (4–5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. 4–5 minutes history, ~30 seconds ECG, remainder diagnosis with a named cause. Ask for vitals before you begin.

back.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response — vitals BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98%: stable but tachycardic. Duration THREE DAYS, CONTINUOUS (>48 h — dictates the whole rhythm-control answer). Hidden clue only if asked about associated symptoms: months of exertional chest tightness and breathlessness up the hill, settling on rest → the named cause is probable ischaemic heart disease, with coffee, alcohol and smoking contributing. Father MI in his fifties. Hidden agenda: 'Is this what my dad had?' and can't afford time off work.
plan: 'Before I begin, could I please have the vital signs?' → name 'tachycardic, irregular, haemodynamically stable' out loud
WIPE, open question, empathy line. Choose PALPITATIONS as the structure — dizziness in one clarifying question (spinning vs faint; actually fainted?)
Characterise: tap it out; sudden/gradual; constant or comes and goes (3 days continuous); triggers; associated chest pain, SOB, sweating, presyncope

Cause sweep, fast: heart (exertional pain — how long?, orthopnoea, PND, oedema, murmur/BP), lungs (cough, fever, pleuritic pain, calf, travel, snoring), thyroid (weight, heat, tremor, bowels, neck lump), habits (coffee, alcohol, smoking, drugs), PMH/meds/allergies/FHx

ECG — all seven steps, no pauses: rate (10-second bypass line), rhythm irregularly irregular, no P waves/fibrillatory baseline, PR not measurable, QRS just over 2 small squares, up-sloping ST V2–V3 not pathological, T waves unremarkable → 'AF with rapid ventricular response'

Name it, explain it plainly, then the CAUSE (arteries — chest tightness uphill; caffeine/alcohol/smoking). Differentials delivered as causes: thyroid, hypertension, valve, peri/myocarditis, PE, hormone tumours; also anxiety, hypoglycaemia, anaemia
Safety-net (chest pain, severe SOB, syncope, one-sided weakness/droop → 000), summary, invite questions, answer 'is this what my dad had?'
ask: Can you tap out on the desk what the beat feels like?
Did it come on suddenly or build up? Constant for the three days, or comes and goes? ★
Does anything set it off — coffee, alcohol, exercise, stress?
With the palpitations — chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, feel like you might black out? ★ (this is where the exertional chest tightness comes out)
The dizziness — spinning, or like you're about to faint? Have you actually fainted?
Breathless lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling? Ever told you have a murmur, high BP, heart problem?
Cough, fever, sharp pain on breathing, calf swelling, long travel? Snore or sleepy in the day?
Weight loss, feeling hot when others don't, tremor, loose bowels, neck lump?
Coffee, alcohol, smoking, other drugs? Other conditions, medications, allergies, heart problems in the family?
pefe: Vitals from the examiner first: BP 118/74, P 128 irregular, RR 16, T 36.6, SpO2 98% RA
ECG seven steps in order: rate → rhythm → P waves → PR → QRS → ST → T; impression AF with RVR

Rate bypass line: 'As the rhythm is irregular, the correct method is to count the QRS complexes across a 10-second strip and multiply by six — may I return to the exact figure?' (ventricular response ~120–140)
If challenged on V2–V3: up-sloping, ramping into the T wave at a fast rate, not horizontal or convex injury; V2–V3 thresholds are higher and vary with age/sex — would not call an infarct
Investigations to name: TSH, echo (pump, valves, clot), FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose and lipids
fails: Taking the dizziness road (vertigo/presyncope/postural drop) and running out of time
Not establishing duration and whether continuous ★
Not eliciting the exertional chest pain ★
Freezing on the rate step — counting boxes, never recovering ★
Over-reading up-sloping ST in V2–V3 as infarct
Giving the label without a named cause ★
Abandoning the systems sweep because you've already guessed AF
numbers: Large square = 0.2 s; 10 seconds = 50 large squares; QRS count × 6
Normal QRS <3 small squares (<120 ms)
ST elevation: ≥1 mm in two contiguous leads; V2–V3 ≥2 mm men ≥40, ≥2.5 mm men <40, ≥1.5 mm women
48 hours = cardioversion safety threshold; unknown duration counts as beyond it
Paroxysmal = self-terminating, usually within 7 days; persistent = beyond 7 days
Her CHA₂DS₂-VA = 0 today (37, no risk factors) — reassess once results back, especially if chest pain is ischaemic

Variant 1 UNSTABLE (BP 84/52, P 165, clammy, chest pain, syncope): stops being counselling — 000/ED, O2 if hypoxic, IV access, troponin/EUC/Mg/FBC, monitoring, urgent synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation
Quitline 13 7848 · 000

setting: General practice.
stem: Same practice. A 55-year-old woman presents with palpitations.

The stem is a full page and already contains the history: heavy coffee, alcohol most nights, some chest pain, and hypertension diagnosed years ago and never followed up. (Version B — long stem; summarised here as the PDF summarises it.)
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan
time: 8 minutes. Management is the predominant assessment area — roughly five minutes for it. Brevity fails this station.

back.dx: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, driven by untreated hypertension (years of high pressure stretching the heart), with coffee and alcohol adding to it. CHA₂DS₂-VA = 1 (hypertension) → discuss, and recommend starting anticoagulation; +1 more if the stem gives diabetes, vascular disease or heart failure → 2, anticoagulate without debate. Age doesn't score until 65. Duration unknown/long = treat as >48 h.
plan: ECG seven steps, no pauses: 10-second rate line → irregularly irregular → no P waves → PR not measurable → QRS narrow-ish → up-sloping ST V2–V3 not pathological → T unremarkable → 'AF with RVR'

Diagnosis plainly: irregular because the electrical signals are disorganised, top chambers quiver; then the CAUSE — untreated blood pressure, plus coffee and alcohol. Differentials as causes: thyroid, valve, peri/myocarditis, PE, hormone tumours; anxiety, hypoglycaemia, anaemia excluded
Signpost: three parts — find the cause, protect from stroke, treat the beat
Pillar 1: TSH + echo (pump, valves, clot inside); FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose, lipids; treat the BP; cut coffee and alcohol, stop smoking (Quitline), diet, exercise

Pillar 2: clot → stroke; name CHA₂DS₂-VA and the thresholds (0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 give); hers = 1 for hypertension → recommend starting; warfarin (regular tests) vs DOAC e.g. apixaban — echo decides: valve problem → warfarin

Pillar 3: rate control first (beta blocker); rhythm — BOTH duration pathways: <48 h cardiovert now; >48 h or unknown → rate control, anticoagulate, TOE OR 3 weeks anticoagulation, then cardiovert, continue ≥4 weeks after; electrical (sedation, controlled shock) vs pharmacological — echo decides
Safety-net (chest pain, severe SOB, syncope, one-sided weakness/droop → 000); summary; cardiologist; questions
ask: (History is in the stem) Confirm duration if not stated — 'I've no idea' counts as >48 h
'Is it alright if I go through the three parts in turn?'
'What questions do you have for me?'
pefe: ECG interpretation as MED-03
Pillar 1 investigations: TSH, transthoracic echo, FBE, EUC, LFT, fasting glucose, lipids
If pressed on the echo: TTE gives EF, valves, chamber size but cannot reliably exclude LEFT ATRIAL APPENDAGE thrombus — early cardioversion needs a TOE
Warfarin vs DOAC decided by the echo (valvular AF → warfarin)
fails: Finishing management in under two minutes ★
Not naming CHA₂DS₂-VA and the thresholds — you name it for the examiner's score sheet ★
Not naming TSH and echo, or omitting risk-factor modification ★
Not naming rate control, or not explaining the 48-hour rule WITH the reason (pushing a clot out → stroke) ★
Giving only one duration pathway — give both
Label without a cause (untreated hypertension) ★
Saying 'it's about clotting' without the score — the folklore trap
numbers: CHA₂DS₂-VA: 0 none · 1 consider · ≥2 give. Age ≥75 = 2; prior stroke/TIA = 2; age 65–74 = 1; hypertension 1. Australian version drops the female-sex point — say which score you're using
48 h threshold; 3 weeks anticoagulation before cardioversion, ≥4 weeks after
Metoprolol 25–50 mg BD · apixaban 5 mg BD · warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 — VERIFY
Opportunistic AF screening from age 65
Variant 3 'never felt it, you found it on my pulse' — common; assume >48 h; same careful order

Variant 4 refuses the blood thinner (mother bruised on warfarin) — DOACs don't need tests and are more predictable; her decision, but make it with the full picture: the harm prevented is a stroke; go through the numbers together; can change her mind anytime
Quitline 13 7848 · 000

setting: General practice.
stem: You are the doctor in a general practice. Ray Docherty, 62, has come in with chest pain for the past two to three months. It comes on when he walks up the hill to the shops and settles when he stops.
Vitals: T 36.6 · HR 96 · BP 132/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · BMI 27.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
Outline your investigations and initial management
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · examination 1:00 · diagnosis and differentials 1:30 · investigations and management 1:15 · close 0:15.

back.dx: Stable typical angina BECAUSE OF iron-deficiency anaemia BECAUSE OF a bleeding NSAID ulcer — a three-link chain. Findings: pale, conjunctival pallor · P 96 regular, no postural drop · soft ejection systolic FLOW murmur · chest clear · mild epigastric tenderness · PR: MELAENA · ECG sinus tachycardia, no acute ischaemia · BSL 5.4. Hidden: black tarry offensive stools for a month (only if asked); supermarket ibuprofen most days for 8 months for his knees (only if asked about OTC painkillers after 'nothing really, just a blood pressure tablet'). Agenda: brother's bypass at 64; once melaena surfaces, fear of cancer.
plan: 'May I have his vital signs, including a postural BP?' → open question → acknowledge → signpost: 'questions that might seem unrelated to your chest — they matter'
Characterise: site/radiation, character, provoked/relieved, duration, REST OR NIGHT PAIN, crescendo, associated sweating/nausea/SOB/palpitations → typical and stable
CV risk factors; other chest pain groups in one sweep (fever/viral, leaning forward, travel/calf, haemoptysis, injury/pressing, rash, heartburn)
ANAEMIA BLOCK: tired, more breathless doing usual things, dizzy, palpitations, told you look pale

UPPER GI BLOCK — the pivot: dyspepsia and relation to food; BLACK OR TARRY MOTIONS → characterise (how long, sticky, offensive) and exclude iron/bismuth; haematemesis/coffee grounds; dysphagia; weight/appetite; bowel habit/fresh blood; family GI cancer

Meds asked twice: 'what medications?' then 'anything for pain or joints — including bought at the chemist or supermarket? Ibuprofen, Nurofen, Voltaren, aspirin? How much, how long?' Previous ulcer/H. pylori; allergies; concerns
PEFE box by box incl. PR with consent + chaperone → 'pallor, flow murmur and melaena fit together'
Chain in three linked steps; differentials incl. honest malignancy; Ix and Mx; the aspirin conflict said out loud; safety-net
ask: Where exactly, does it go anywhere, what's it like — heavy, tight, sharp, burning?
What brings it on and what makes it go? How long does it last?
Do you ever get it at rest, or at night, or does it wake you? ★ Is it coming on with less effort than it used to?
Smoking, BP, diabetes, cholesterol; family heart attacks/strokes and at what age; activity; alcohol
More tired than usual? More breathless doing things you used to manage? Dizzy? Palpitations? Anyone said you look pale?
Any indigestion, burning or gnawing upper tummy pain — related to eating?
Have you noticed your bowel motions turning black or tarry? ★ Sticky, offensive? How long? Iron tablets or Pepto-Bismol?
Vomited blood or coffee grounds? Difficulty swallowing? Weight loss/appetite? Bowel habit or fresh blood? Family bowel or stomach cancer?
What medications are you on? … Anything at all for pain or your joints, including bought over the counter? ★ Ever had an ulcer or Helicobacter treatment?
Anything in particular you're worried about?
pefe: General: pale? conjunctival/palmar pallor, glossitis, angular stomatitis, koilonychia
Vitals: pulse rate and rhythm, BP lying and standing
CVS: heart sounds, murmurs (soft ESM = flow murmur in anaemia — say you'd confirm with echo; keep AS open), JVP, oedema, heart failure signs
Respiratory: air entry, added sounds
Abdomen: epigastric tenderness, masses, organomegaly
'With his consent and a chaperone, may I perform a rectal examination — melaena or mass?' ★
Office tests: ECG, BSL, urine dipstick
fails: Closing on coronary disease on 'exertional pain in a 62-year-old' and running on autopilot
Not asking rest/night pain — what grades it stable rather than ACS
Never asking the five anaemia questions; attributing all breathlessness to angina
Hearing 'black stools' and moving on without characterising/excluding iron and bismuth
Accepting 'no medications' — never asking about OTC painkillers ★
Not requesting the rectal examination ★
Calling the murmur aortic stenosis outright
'It's just the anti-inflammatories' — never naming malignancy honestly
Telling him to keep taking the ibuprofen, or never addressing it ★
Starting aspirin, or omitting it silently, instead of naming the conflict
Ordering cardiac stress testing while still anaemic
numbers: Chain: NSAID → ulcer → chronic blood loss → iron-deficiency anaemia → reduced O2 delivery + increased cardiac work → angina
Bloods: FBC (microcytic hypochromic), iron studies (low ferritin), UEC (urea raised in upper GI bleed), LFT, coags, group and hold/cross-match, ECG ± troponin
Scopes: gastroscopy + H. pylori testing; colonoscopy too — iron deficiency in an older adult warrants both tracts

Treatment order: stop NSAID → PPI → iron → transfuse only if symptomatic at rest/compromised (restrictive threshold, slightly higher in cardiac disease — discuss with senior, don't commit to a number) → eradicate H. pylori → GTN spray for episodes → cardiac functional testing AFTER Hb recovers
Knees: paracetamol + topical anti-inflammatory gel + physio
Aspirin: defer; decide jointly with cardiology and gastroenterology with gastroprotection in place
'Is this ACS?' — no: purely exertional, relieved by rest, no rest/night pain, no acute ECG change; low threshold for troponin if anything changes
Safety-net: rest pain that doesn't settle, haematemesis, worsening melaena, faint → ED

setting: Emergency Department.
stem: Alan Prosser, 58, presents to the Emergency Department with central chest pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward, with a flu-like illness a week ago.
Vitals: T 37.2 · HR 88 · BP 128/76 · RR 18 · SpO2 97%.
ECG handed to you: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No PR depression, no widespread concave elevation.
tasks: Take a history (4–6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG
Explain the diagnosis and immediate management
time: 8 minutes. The history sounds like pericarditis; the ECG overrides it.

back.dx: Acute INFERIOR STEMI — territorial ST elevation (II, III, aVF) with reciprocal change (I, aVL) = infarct, whatever the story. Pericarditis history + infarct ECG: treat the infarct. Name the mismatch to the examiner: this is exactly why ECG and troponin are part of the pericarditis work-up. Obtain V4R for right ventricular involvement → if RV involved, NO nitrates, give fluid (preload dependent).
plan: Vitals; open question; characterise the pain (positional, pleuritic?, viral prodrome), risk factors, other chest pain groups briefly

ECG aloud: 'Rate 88, sinus, normal axis. ST elevation in II, III, aVF — the inferior leads — with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No widespread elevation, no PR depression. Territorial pattern with reciprocal change = acute inferior STEMI, not pericarditis. I would obtain right-sided leads.'
To the examiner: acknowledge the history suggested pericarditis; the ECG overrides it; treating as infarct
To the patient: tracing shows something more serious — an artery supplying your heart is blocked, a heart attack; the pain didn't feel typical but the tracing is clear; acting now, calling cardiology

Immediate management: resus area, monitoring, O2 only if hypoxic, IV access, aspirin 300 mg chewed, second antiplatelet + anticoagulation per protocol, analgesia; reperfusion — primary PCI if prompt, otherwise thrombolysis + urgent transfer; V4R → avoid nitrates/give fluid if RV; watch for arrhythmia and heart block
Rural SA: thrombolyse here after checking contraindications, simultaneous MedSTAR retrieval to a PCI centre, discuss with receiving cardiologist while treating
ask: Where is the pain, what's it like, does it change with position — worse lying flat, better leaning forward?
Any flu-like illness recently? Fever?
Sweating, nausea, breathlessness? Any pain on exertion before this?
Smoking, BP, diabetes, cholesterol, family history
Any bleeding history, recent surgery, stroke, anticoagulants (thrombolysis contraindications)
pefe: ECG in order: rate → rhythm → axis → ST by territory → reciprocal change → PR segment → impression
Right-sided leads (V4R) for RV involvement
Troponin; continuous monitoring

Variant — the ECG really IS pericarditis: widespread concave ST elevation across territories with PR depression and no reciprocal change → still send troponin and arrange echo (exclude infarction and effusion); treat with NSAID plus colchicine
fails: Calling it pericarditis because the history fits — territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change is an infarct ★
Not obtaining right-sided leads / giving nitrates to an RV infarct
Delaying reperfusion to complete the history
Not naming the history–ECG mismatch to the examiner
Reassuring the patient it's 'just inflammation'
numbers: Inferior leads II, III, aVF; reciprocal I and aVL; V4R for RV involvement
Pericarditis pattern: widespread concave STE + PR depression, no reciprocal change
Aspirin 300 mg chewed; second antiplatelet and anticoagulant per local protocol — VERIFY
Primary PCI if it can be delivered promptly; otherwise thrombolysis and urgent transfer
MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — retrieval to a PCI centre (RAH/FMC); country hospital without a cath lab thrombolyses first
RV infarct: preload dependent — fluids, no nitrates

setting: General practice.
stem: Jenny Hollis, 58, presents to your general practice with palpitations.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 150 · BP 124/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · alert and comfortable.
The ECG you will be handed: rate 150 · regular R-R intervals · no visible P waves · PR not measurable · narrow QRS · ST segments normal.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · ECG 1:00 · diagnosis 0:45 · differentials 1:30 · plan and close 0:45.

back.dx: Supraventricular tachycardia — regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 with no visible P waves (the single deflection between QRSs is the T wave, not a P). Stable. Two planted findings you must earn: EIGHT cups of coffee a day (only the number if asked how much; 'a fair bit' if asked vaguely) and blood pressure once found raised and never followed up (only if asked about BP/PMH). Positional trigger: standing quickly or bending. She refuses to tap the rhythm — ask once, accept, move on. Agenda: neighbour died of a heart attack last year — 'is it a heart attack?' whatever you've said.
plan: Vitals INCLUDING RHYTHM ('you don't know that yet' — accept); state stable; open question; acknowledge
BOX 1: what do you mean — fast, irregular, missing a beat? Tap it out? (refusal → move on)
BOX 2: onset, constant vs episodic, how long and how it stops, first time, worsening
BOX 3: better/worse; standing/bending/lying; exertion vs rest; situation
GROUP 1 full CV block: chest pain/SOB/nausea/sweating; dizzy/syncope; oedema/orthopnoea/pillows; murmur/valve/heart attack; FHx; BP/sugar/lipids (→ untreated BP); smoking/alcohol; fever/viral illness
Groups 2–4: cough/wheeze; calves/travel/clots; heat intolerance/weight loss/diarrhoea/tremor; STIMULANTS QUANTIFIED — cups per day; drugs; puffers; nasal sprays; takeaway/MSG
Groups 5–8: stress/mood/fear of dying; tiredness/exertional SOB; headache/sweats/tremor; missed meals/diabetes drugs; LMP/flushes; allergies; concerns
ECG seven steps → 'regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150, no visible P waves — SVT'
Name it, define it plainly, give the reason (coffee); address the heart-attack fear with reasons; differentials BY SYSTEM; plan incl. BP follow-up and referral; safety-net
ask: May I have her vital signs — BP, pulse rate and the rhythm if available, RR, sats, temperature?
Can you describe what you mean by palpitations — fast, irregular, or missing a beat? Could you tap it out on the desk?
When did it start? All the time or comes and goes? How long, how does it stop? First time? Getting more frequent?
Do you notice it more when you stand up, bend forward or lie down? ★ Worse on exertion — and at rest as well? ★ Any particular place or situation?

Chest pain, SOB, nausea, sweating? Dizzy, ever fainted? Leg swelling, breathless lying flat, how many pillows? Murmur, valve, heart attack? Family heart attacks/strokes? High BP, sugar, fats? ★ Smoke, alcohol? Fever or flu-like illness?
Cough, wheeze? Calf swelling/pain, long travel, previous clots?
Weather preference — hot weather hard to tolerate? Weight loss? Diarrhoea, tremor?
How many cups of coffee, tea or energy drink a day? ★ Recreational drugs? Asthma puffers or nasal decongestant sprays? Salty takeaway before it started?
Stress at home/work? Mood? During an episode, did you ever feel you were going to die?
Unusually tired or breathless on exertion? Headaches, sweating episodes, hand tremor? Missed meals, diabetes treatment? Last period, hot flushes?
Allergies? Other conditions or medications? Anything in particular you're worried about?
pefe: ECG seven steps: rate (two large squares → 150) → regular? (equal R-R) → P waves? (only one deflection between QRSs = T wave; P buried in QRS) → PR not measurable → QRS ~1.5 squares, narrow → ST normal → impression
If your nerve goes: DESCRIBE — 'a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 without visible P waves' earns most of the mark
Bloods: FBC, electrolytes with Mg and Ca, TFTs, glucose ± troponin ± metanephrines
Stable: modified Valsalva → adenosine 6 mg rapid push with flush, then 12 mg, monitored, per protocol with senior — VERIFY; long term: cut stimulants, teach vagal manoeuvres, EP referral for ablation
Unstable (hypotension, ischaemic pain, heart failure, altered conscious state): stop the history — resus, monitoring, O2 if hypoxic, IV, senior help, synchronised DC cardioversion with sedation
fails: Not asking for the rhythm with the vitals
Being derailed by the refusal to tap
Skipping exertion vs rest
Skipping the full CV block / missing the untreated hypertension
Accepting 'a bit' of coffee — not quantifying cups per day ★
Pointing at the T wave, calling it a P, reporting sinus tachycardia ★
Differentials given as a list of other arrhythmias — fail ★ (they are causes of palpitations, by system)
Not addressing 'is it a heart attack?' with reasons
Never returning to the blood pressure in the plan ★
numbers: Three exploring boxes: describe ± tap · onset/episodic/first time/worsening · position/exertion vs rest/situation

Eight groups: CV (ischaemia, HF, valvular, cardiomyopathy, peri/myocarditis, risk factors) · respiratory (PE, COPD) · thyroid · stimulants · psychogenic · anaemia · phaeochromocytoma · hypoglycaemia; plus menopause and fever
Stimulant list: coffee, tea, energy drinks, alcohol, nicotine, illicit stimulants, salbutamol puffers, nasal decongestants, MSG
Phaeo triad: headache, sweating, palpitations
Broad-complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise
'SVT or PSVT?' — paroxysmal describes the episodic pattern; report SVT; AVNRT commonest mechanism
'Do I have to give up coffee completely?' — cut down substantially; 8 cups may be enough on its own
Variant — ECG is AF instead: irregularly irregular, no P, fibrillatory baseline, ~130 → plan changes: rate/rhythm control, echo, TFTs, stroke risk assessment (AF carries stroke risk SVT does not)
Variant — situational only ('when I present at work') → social anxiety, but complete the organic screen and ECG first
Safety-net: chest pain, faint/black out, breathless → back straight away

Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 10 minutes. Same shape as MED-07. The stated fear is named and answered BEFORE the differentials.

back.dx: Supraventricular tachycardia in a 27-year-old, driven by a stimulant combination — coffee, a pack of cigarettes a day, five glasses of wine most nights. The general rule this version teaches: whenever the stem states a concern about a specific condition (heart attack here; brain tumour in a headache case; cancer in a weight-loss case) you name it and address it with reasons before the patient asks again — never a bare reassurance.
plan: Vitals incl. rhythm; open; acknowledge the fear early
BOX 1 adapted: 'what do you mean by being aware of your heartbeat — do you simply feel it, or is it faster, or irregular?' Then boxes 2–3

Differentials by system; the stimulant conversation — each alone can set it off, together much more likely; offer help with smoking and drinking; plan, referral, safety-net

setting: General practice.
stem: Raymond Doyle, 68, attends your general practice with three days of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. He describes his heart 'racing steadily, not jumping about'. He has hypertension on perindopril, BMI 33, and drinks around 30 standard drinks a week. An ECG has been performed and is available.
Observations: BP 128/76 · PR 148 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 96% RA · Temp 36.5 °C · no chest pain, alert and well perfused.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Give your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Outline your management
time: 8 minutes, no history. Two-minute plan: stable? → 150 regular = flutter 2:1 → sawtooth leads → 3 days = outside 48 h → rate · rhythm · ANTICOAGULATE · ablate · drivers → drivers in the stem (BP, alcohol, BMI → OSA) plus TFTs.

back.dx: Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 AV block — ventricular rate ~150, metronomically regular, no discrete P waves, continuous sawtooth baseline with no isoelectric segment, negative in II, III, aVF and positive in V1, atrial rate ~300, two flutter waves per QRS, narrow QRS, no acute ischaemia (flutter waves distort ST). Stable. The two things they are testing: do you name the rhythm rather than stopping at 'SVT', and do you anticoagulate. Failing to anticoagulate is a fail regardless of the total.
plan: Say STABLE out loud before interpreting: BP, HR, RR, sats, temp + chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest → 'so I can work through this rather than proceed to immediate cardioversion'
ECG read-out: rate, regular, no P, sawtooth, leads, atrial ~300, 2:1, narrow QRS, no ischaemia → 'typical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction'

'Why not sinus tach?' — sinus is a response and needs a driver (afebrile, comfortable, perfused); sinus varies with respiration, this is metronomic at ~150; if unsure, increase AV block with vagal manoeuvre/adenosine under continuous ECG — diagnostic, not therapeutic

Two SEPARATE lists: differentials of the rhythm (sinus tach, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia, AF with very rapid response) · causes of the flutter by system (CV: HTN, IHD, HF, valve, recent cardiac surgery; RS: PE, COPD, OSA; endocrine: thyrotoxicosis; drugs/lifestyle: alcohol, caffeine, stimulants, obesity)

To the patient: loop and filter → tired heart (breathless) → clot → stroke → blood thinner. Answer '300? should I be dead?' · 'stroke?' · 'shock it today?' (WHY it must wait) · 'from the drinking?' (honest, with the number: 30 vs limit of 10)

Management five things: rate (beta-blocker; or verapamil/diltiazem; never both; flutter less responsive than AF) · stroke prevention (score + bleeding risk; scores for HTN and age → DOAC; ASPIRIN IS NOT STROKE PREVENTION) · rhythm (outside 48 h → 3 weeks anticoag or TOE, then ≥4 weeks after) · CTI ablation early, curative · drivers (BP, alcohol, weight, OSA screen). Ix: FBC, electrolytes incl. Mg, renal, TFTs, CXR, TTE
ask: (No history task) If examiner allows: chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest; alcohol with a number; snoring/witnessed apnoeas
pefe: ECG: rate ~150 regular · no discrete P · sawtooth, no isoelectric segment · negative II, III, aVF, positive V1 · atrial ~300 · 2 waves per QRS · narrow QRS · no acute ischaemic change
Say unprompted: 'Aspirin is not stroke prevention.' 'Adenosine unmasks, it does not terminate.'
Investigations: FBC, electrolytes incl. magnesium, renal function, TFTs, CXR, transthoracic echo

Examiner's five questions, in order: why not sinus tach? · would adenosine treat this? · 3 days — cardiovert today? · is aspirin enough? · how does this differ from AF? (give four divergences — regular vs irregularly irregular, sawtooth vs fibrillatory baseline, atrial ~300 vs 400–600, rate control harder / CTI ablation curative — and state anticoagulation is IDENTICAL)
fails: Not stating haemodynamic stability out loud before interpreting ★
'Sinus tachycardia at 150' or 'SVT' without going further ★ (identify 2:1 block)
Not anticoagulating / not naming a risk score ★ — fail regardless
Not stating aspirin is not stroke prevention ★
Not applying the 48-hour rule (3 weeks or TOE, then 4 weeks) ★
Saying 'not today' without explaining WHY cardioversion must wait
Combining beta-blocker with verapamil/diltiazem
Blurring rhythm differentials with causes
Vague 'do you drink?' — address alcohol with a number
numbers: Atrial rate ~300; 2:1 → 150; 3:1 → 100; variable block gives an irregular response but the sawtooth still distinguishes it from AF
Alcohol 30 standard drinks/week vs recommended limit of 10
Rate control: beta-blocker first line; verapamil/diltiazem if unsuitable; never both
Anticoagulation on the score (HTN + age) → DOAC; bleeding risk assessed; anticoagulation continues after successful ablation if the score says so (AF may follow)
48 h rule: 3 weeks therapeutic anticoag or TOE before cardioversion, ≥4 weeks after
CTI ablation: curative, high success, low complications — raise early, not as last resort

Variant 1 UNSTABLE (BP 78/44, clammy, ischaemic pain): urgent synchronised DC cardioversion with sedation, senior help, anticoagulate around it — 48 h rule does not delay cardioversion in an unstable patient
Variant 2 variable block: rate 110 irregular, sawtooth visible — still flutter
Variant 3 1:1 after flecainide (rate 215, clammy): Class Ic slows the atrial rate so it conducts 1:1 → immediate cardioversion; never flecainide for flutter without an AV nodal blocker
Variant 4 broad complex regular at 150: VT until proven otherwise
Variant 5 day 4 post-CABG: common; correct K/Mg, rate control, exclude sepsis/PE, anticoag decision with the surgical team
Variant 6 refuses anticoagulation (brother bled into brain): respect, correct the misconception (DOACs lower intracranial bleed risk than warfarin), don't push today, review this week

setting: Emergency Department.
stem: Your next patient is a 35-year-old woman who has presented to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath and chest pain.
Vitals: T 37.4 °C · HR 104 · BP 118/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% on room air · alert.
tasks: Take a relevant history — six minutes
You will be given the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
State your investigations
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · interpret findings 0:45 · diagnosis and reasons 1:00 · differentials 1:30 · investigations 0:30 · close 0:15. Originally an online case — findings arrive on a card, or request them.

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism from a left calf DVT after a two-day car drive Queensland → Melbourne, on a COMBINED pill (Levlen), smoker, mother had a post-op DVT. Findings: anxious, mildly breathless · HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 94%, T 37.4 · loud P2 · left parasternal systolic murmur (TR from RV strain) · dullness and reduced breath sounds left base (infarction + small effusion, NOT pneumonia) · left calf swollen and tender · abdomen soft. Hidden agenda: father died of a heart attack at 52 — 'is this a heart attack?' early and again. Choose CHEST PAIN as the lead complaint out loud; fold breathlessness in with three questions.
plan: Vitals → 'stable but tachycardic, tachypnoeic, mildly hypoxic' → open question → acknowledge → 'I'd like to start with the chest pain, then come back to your breathing'
Full pain analysis incl. BETTER/WORSE — breathing, moving, position, pressing (worse on inspiration and cough)
Breathlessness in three: what do you mean · better/worse · cough, noisy breathing, haemoptysis; dizziness/faint
CVS group: sweating/nausea/racing; smoking/BP/DM/lipids/FHx; fever/viral, leaning forward; orthopnoea/pillows/leg swelling (→ FOLLOW UP the leg: one or both, painful, when); blackouts
RS group — the turn: chest injury; LONG TRAVEL OR LONG PERIODS SITTING STILL (open form, not flights); calf swelling/pain/redness; fevers/chills/phlegm; weight loss/lumps
COST-VMPF immediately: Contraceptive pill BY NAME · Overweight · Surgery/injury/admission · Trauma · Varicose veins · Menstrual/pregnancy · Previous clot · Family history
Finish the sweep: reflux, chest wall, rash, stress; SADMA, PMH, allergies; concerns (the father)

Interpret findings OUT LOUD (P2/murmur = RV strain; basal dullness = infarction/effusion; calf = source; fever from the clot) → diagnosis plain, three reasons, honest answer to the fear → two differentials explained then the rest NAMED → investigations in priority order → stop the combined pill + alternative contraception → safety-net, summary
ask: Where exactly? When and how — sudden or gradual? Sharp, dull, heavy, burning? Travel anywhere? Out of ten?
Anything makes it better or worse — breathing, moving, position, pressing on it? ★
What do you mean by shortness of breath? Better or worse? Cough, noisy breathing, wheeze, coughed up blood? Dizzy or faint?

Sweating, nausea, racing, dizziness with the pain? Smoke? BP, diabetes, cholesterol, family heart disease? Fever or flu-like illness — better leaning forward? Breathless lying flat, pillows, leg swelling? Ever blacked out?
Any injury to your chest? Any long travel or long periods sitting still recently? ★ Any swelling, pain or redness in your legs, especially the calf? ★ Fevers, chills, phlegm? Weight loss, lumps?
Are you on a contraceptive pill — and do you know its name? ★ Overweight? Operations, injuries, admissions? Varicose veins? LMP — any chance you're pregnant? Family clots? Previous clot yourself?
Heartburn/acid, related to eating? Worse on moving or pressing the chest wall? Rash? Stress? Conditions, medications, allergies? Alcohol, drugs?
Is there anything you're worried about?
pefe: If you must request: general appearance and work of breathing; vitals incl. sats and temp; trachea; expansion, percussion, auscultation; heart sounds incl. P2 and any murmur; JVP; BOTH CALVES for swelling, tenderness, asymmetry (the request candidates forget)

Interpret, don't recite: loud P2 + LLSE systolic murmur = raised pulmonary pressure with TR from RV strain; basal dullness = pulmonary infarction with small effusion; swollen tender calf = the source; low-grade fever is caused by the clot

Investigations in priority order: CTPA first → V/Q if contrast allergy, renal impairment or pregnancy → D-dimer rule-out only when suspicion is low (not here) → ECG → bloods: FBC, renal function (guides DOAC choice/dose), LFT (if warfarin considered), coags, troponin → β-hCG → CXR → leg Doppler
Anticoagulate before imaging with high suspicion and no bleeding contraindication
fails: Trying to run both complaint structures — not naming a lead
Skipping better/worse (the highest-yield chest pain question)
Filing 'leg swelling' under heart failure and not following it up
Asking only about flights — immobility is the risk
Accepting 'the pill' without the name (combined must stop; POP need not)
Converting basal dullness + 37.4 into pneumonia
Explaining two differentials beautifully and never naming the rest
Undifferentiated shopping-list investigations (FBC, ESR, CRP, TFTs…) — lead with CTPA
'Probably a muscle strain' or 'just anxiety' — fail
Not stopping the combined pill / leaving her without alternative contraception
numbers: Wells (PE): DVT signs · PE most likely · HR >100 · immobilisation/surgery within 4 weeks · previous VTE · haemoptysis · malignancy; two-level >4 = PE likely → image

PERC (low suspicion only, all 8 negative): age <50 · HR <100 · SpO2 ≥95% · no haemoptysis · no oestrogen · no previous VTE · no unilateral leg swelling · no surgery/trauma needing hospitalisation in 4 weeks
ECG: sinus tachycardia commonest; RV strain, RBBB, T inversion V1–V4; S1Q3T3 uncommon
Treatment: apixaban 10 mg BD 7 days then 5 mg BD; or rivaroxaban 15 mg BD 21 days then 20 mg daily — VERIFY; pregnancy: LMWH (no DOAC, no warfarin)
Duration: at least 3 months if provoked; longer/indefinite if unprovoked or recurrent
Massive PE (SBP <90, syncope, arrest): stop history, resus, high-flow O2, large-bore IV, cautious fluids, senior/ICU, bedside echo for RV strain, thrombolysis; embolectomy if contraindicated/fails
Murmur location: 4th–5th ICS, lower left sternal edge (TR)
Variant 1 recall (raised JVP, soft murmur, swollen ankle): unilateral after immobility = DVT; JVP from RV strain; bilateral oedema + orthopnoea + S3 would point to HF
Variant 2 pregnant: V/Q or perfusion scan to limit breast radiation; LMWH; obstetrics involved
Three reasons to the patient: swollen painful calf · sharp pain worse on breathing in with breathlessness · right-heart strain on examination

setting: Emergency department.
stem: You are the doctor in the emergency department. James Okafor, 22, has presented with sudden onset chest pain that started while he was exercising today. He is already on oxygen when you enter the cubicle.
Information available: HR 98 · BP 122/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% · T 36.8 °C · alert and orientated.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Version A: at about five minutes a chest X-ray is provided — explain the X-ray to the patient. Version B: ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History stops at 5:00 (the X-ray appears at the prompt whether or not you've finished) · X-ray or PEFE 60–75 s · diagnosis 30–40 s · everything left goes on differentials — the block candidates lose.

back.dx: Primary spontaneous LEFT pneumothorax, no tension — tall slim 22-year-old, daily vaper (since 18, occasional cannabis), rowing machine, no knock. Pain: left, can point to one spot, sudden, sharp stab, 4/10, constant, no radiation, MUCH WORSE ON DEEP BREATH, leaning forward and rest/activity make no difference. PEFE (Version B): trachea midline · reduced expansion L · hyper-resonant L · absent breath sounds L · reduced vocal resonance L · JVP normal, apex undisplaced, no murmur · no calf asymmetry · ECG pending. Hidden agenda: 'Is it my heart? People my age drop dead' — and a Bali trip in three weeks with a learn-to-dive course. The station in one line: say 'pleuritic' out loud, run the whole structure anyway, name the trachea, protect the last two minutes.
plan: Four vitals (BP, pulse, RR, temp) or the online closed statement; WIPE; open question; empathy ONCE, properly
SOCRATES in full — 'is it an area, or can you point to one spot?' — then the THREE named modifiers: deep breath? rest vs activity? leaning forward?
Say the conclusion aloud: 'sharp, well-localised, sudden, worse on breathing in — we call that pleuritic; it points me towards your lungs rather than your heart. I still need to check both.'

CVS block in FULL: SOB/sweating/nausea; BP/DM/lipids/smoking/FHx; cocaine/amphetamines; fever/flu, leaning forward; orthopnoea/PND/oedema/congenital; ever fainted, esp. on exercise; FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH (ask here, not at the end)

Respiratory: calves, travel, immobility, family clots, haemoptysis; WHAT EXERCISE and any knock/tackle; previous pneumothorax self/family; smoke/vape/cannabis; fever/cough/phlegm; 'unlikely at your age but I ask everyone' weight loss/lumps/night sweats
GI (heartburn, waterbrash, food), MSK (rash, pressing, twisting), psych (stress, mood); SADMA, PMH, allergies, concerns

BELL — X-ray script, six steps, 60–75 s, trachea named even though normal; answer 'am I going to be alright?' with two reasons (trachea central, BP normal) then finish. Version B: PEFE by named items, interpret the card aloud

Diagnosis 30–40 s plain → three reasons (sharp, pleuritic, X-ray/PEFE) → HCM, PE, infection each with a reason → the rest as a rapid list → drain, admit, repeat X-ray, stop vaping, no flying until healed, no diving ever without surgery, safety-net
ask: Where exactly — an area, or can you point to one spot? When, what were you doing, sudden or gradual? Sharp/dull/heavy/tight/burning? Go anywhere? Out of ten? Constant or waves, worse?
Anything better or worse? Specifically — does a deep breath make it worse? Change with rest or activity? Does leaning forward help? ★

SOB, sweating, nausea? BP/diabetes/cholesterol? Smoke? Family heart disease? Cocaine or amphetamines? Fever/chills/flu-like illness? Breathless walking/lying flat, wake at night, ankle swelling, born with a heart condition? Ever fainted, especially during exercise?
Any family history of sudden cardiac death — anyone who died suddenly and young, during sport or in their sleep? ★
Calf swelling/pain? Long flights/car trips, surgery, immobility? Clotting problems in the family? Coughed up blood?
What exercise were you actually doing — and did you take any knock or tackle to the chest? ★
Ever had a collapsed lung, or anyone in the family? Smoke, vape, cannabis? Fever, cough, coloured phlegm? Weight loss, lumps, night sweats?
Tummy pain, vomiting, heartburn, sour fluid? Related to food? Rash on the chest, worse on pressing or twisting? Stress at home or uni, mood? Medications, allergies, past history, operations?
What are you worried it might be?
pefe: X-ray six lines: (1) 'This is the X-ray of your chest' (2) three shades — white bone, grey soft tissue, black air (3) landmarks — heart, spine, WINDPIPE and whether it's central (4) normal side — markings to the edge, sharp angle at the base (5) abnormal side — lung edge visible, no markings beyond it, air in the space (6) 'that's a pneumothorax'. The finding is ABSENT MARKINGS beyond a visible pleural edge, not blackness — trace apex to costophrenic angle for the subtle apical one

Poor paper film: 'The print quality makes fine detail difficult — clinically your symptoms and examination point to a left pneumothorax, and that's what I can see at the edge; I'd review the digital image'

Version B PEFE by name: general appearance/distress/cyanosis/drowsy; vitals on air and on O2; expansion symmetrical? TRACHEA midline or deviated? bruising/focal tenderness? percussion resonant/hyper-resonant/dull? breath sounds present and equal, added sounds, rub? vocal resonance? JVP, apex, S1/S2, murmurs; abdomen; oedema and calf asymmetry; ECG?

Interpret aloud: reduced expansion + hyper-resonance + absent breath sounds + reduced vocal resonance on the left, trachea midline, BP normal = left pneumothorax without tension; hyper-resonance = air (dull would be fluid/consolidation/haemothorax)
fails: Shortcutting to lung questions once 'pleuritic' is reached — the structure is the mark
Never acknowledging the fear, or sympathising after every answer and reaching 5:00 with half a history
Asking only the open 'better or worse?' and accepting 'nothing really'
Leaving sudden cardiac death to the end and running out of time
Not asking what exercise / any knock (separates spontaneous from traumatic)
Skipping malignancy or psychogenic questions because he's 22
Not commenting on the trachea (Version B: not asking 'midline or deviated?' — the pass-or-fail question) ★
Radiology language to a frightened 22-year-old
Accepting 'air entry reduced on the left' as the whole examination — expansion, trachea, percussion, vocal resonance are four separate marks
The beautiful 40-second physiology explanation that eats the differential time; never finishing the list ★
Tension variant: 'I'd get an urgent chest X-ray to confirm' — the sentence that fails the station ★
numbers: Signs: reduced expansion · hyper-resonant · absent breath sounds · reduced vocal resonance · trachea midline. Dull instead → effusion, consolidation, haemothorax

Tension = hypotension + trachea deviated AWAY + distended neck veins → clinical diagnosis, no imaging: needle decompression 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line (2nd ICS MCL traditional alternative), then intercostal catheter — decompression is temporising
Drain: safe triangle, 5th ICS anterior to mid-axillary line, small-bore 8–14 Fr; symptomatic or unstable → intervene; otherwise conservative/ambulatory with review
Recurrence ~30%, mostly within 1–2 years; vaping/smoking cessation is the single best prevention
Flying: not until resolved, typically a week beyond; diving: never without definitive surgery

Variant 2 HCM: central tightness on running, eased on stopping, near-syncope, uncle died in sleep at 38, NOT pleuritic → ECG + echo; autosomal dominant, commonest cause of SCD in young athletes; ESM louder on standing/Valsalva, softer on squatting (opposite of AS); ECG LVH, deep narrow Q, TWI; cardiology, no competitive sport, avoid dehydration/nitrates/diuretics, screen first-degree relatives

Variant 3 traumatic haemopneumothorax: tackle, bruising, focal rib tenderness, DULL base → large-bore IV, G&H/cross-match, FBE, coags, erect CXR ± CT, large-bore tube, surgeons early (ongoing drain loss = theatre), check flail segment and sub-diaphragmatic injury

Variant 4 pericarditis: two days, central, better leaning forward, worse flat, post-viral, febrile, rub with resonant chest → ECG (saddle STE, PR depression), troponin, inflammatory markers, echo for effusion; NSAID + colchicine, exercise restriction
Safety-net: more breathless, worse pain, faint, racing heart, blue lips/fingers → 000

setting: Emergency Department.
stem: Your next patient is a 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset chest tightness and shortness of breath that began while watching a movie at home. He has had similar episodes before and was told nothing was wrong. His parents are separated, he lives alone, works as an accountant, and has been under stress.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 96 · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 99% RA · alert, anxious.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the pathophysiology of the condition
time: 10 minutes. History 6:00 · diagnosis 1:00 · differentials 1:15 · pathophysiology 1:15 · management and close 0:30.

back.dx: Panic attack → PANIC DISORDER with agoraphobic avoidance (Daniel Pike, 25). Peak within 5–10 minutes, settled over half an hour; pounding heart, sweating, dizziness, trembling, PERIORAL AND FINGER TINGLING (hyperventilation fingerprint), derealisation. Five or six attacks over three months, mostly out of the blue (desk, train, supermarket queue); two prior ED visits with normal tests. Three key questions make the diagnosis: fear of dying? worried about another? changed behaviour? (stopped cinema, drives instead of train). Also: 5–6 coffees + energy drinks; 'I'm generally an anxious person' (bait for GAD — screen by criteria, don't relabel). The trap: the psychosocial stem is bait — run a CHEST PAIN history and reach the psychogenic bucket LAST. Hidden agenda: convinced doctors keep missing a heart problem; privately frightened he's going mad.
plan: Vitals → open question → acknowledge the 'nothing wrong' frustration explicitly → signpost: tightness, then breathing, then rule out important causes
Full pain analysis INCLUDING 'how long did it take to reach its worst?' and how it settled
Breathlessness in three questions
CVS + RS sweep (note the tingling — use it later); GI, MSK/rash; caffeine/energy drinks QUANTIFIED, drugs, alcohol, recently stopped anything; thyroid symptoms
ANNOUNCE the negative organic screen out loud, then ask permission to move to the episodes
Characterise: how many, over what period, out of the blue or triggered, what was happening in the film, trembling/choking/unreal
THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS verbatim → agoraphobia screen → GAD by criteria → stressors → mood → self-harm

Diagnosis: attack, then disorder; 'your symptoms are real'; 'not in your head — in your body' → differentials of CHEST PAIN with why each is less likely (still do ECG, TFTs) → pathophysiology (alarm system, adrenaline, over-breathing/CO2, vicious cycle; peaks ~10 min, not dangerous) → CBT, MHTP, SSRI low and slow if needed, no benzos, cut caffeine, limit tests, safety-net
ask: Where exactly? When and how quickly? How long did it take to reach its worst? ★ Tight/sharp/heavy/burning? Travel? Out of ten? Better or worse — breathing, moving, position, pressing? How long, how did it settle?
What do you mean by shortness of breath? Better/worse? Cough, noisy breathing, wheeze?

Sweating, nausea, racing, dizziness with it? Smoke, BP, DM, lipids, family heart disease? Fever/flu, better leaning forward? Flat/pillows/leg swelling, ever fainted esp. exercise? Long travel/sitting still, calf swelling/pain, haemoptysis? Chest injury? Fevers, chills, phlegm, weight loss, lumps?
Abdominal pain, vomiting, acid/heartburn, related to eating? Worse on moving or pressing? Rash?
How much coffee or energy drink a day? ★ Recreational drugs, alcohol? Recently stopped anything? Weight loss, feeling hot, tremor, loose bowels?
'I've asked about your heart, lungs, stomach and chest wall and haven't found anything pointing that way — now I'd like to ask about the episodes themselves. Is that all right?' ★
How many, over what period? Out of the blue or a trigger? What was happening in the film? Trembling, choking, things not quite real?
During the attack, did you feel you were going to die — were you afraid of dying? ★
Since then, have you been worried about having another attack? ★
Have you changed any routines or behaviour because of that worry? ★

Places you avoid — public transport, crowds, queues, shopping centres, far from home alone? Apart from the attacks, excessive hard-to-control worry about everyday things — how long? Restless, tired, irritable, tense, poor sleep? What's been happening at home and work? Mood? Thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn't worth living?
pefe: No examination task. Investigations: ECG · FBC, electrolytes/renal, TFTs, glucose · drug screen if indicated — then STOP; 'I don't want to keep repeating tests, because that feeds the worry'

Differentials of the COMPLAINT, each with why it's less likely: ACS/angina (25, no risk factors, non-exertional, no radiation — still ECG) · PE (no travel, no calf, no haemoptysis, sats normal) · pneumothorax (no injury, normal exam/sats) · pericarditis (no viral illness, no positional change) · arrhythmia (possible — ECG) · reflux/ulcer (no heartburn, no meal relation) · chest wall (pressing doesn't reproduce) · thyrotoxicosis and caffeine (bloods) · GAD possible alongside — the attacks define it

Technical pathophysiology if asked: amygdala/sympathetic activation → catecholamine surge (tachycardia, ↑CO, sweating, tremor); hyperventilation → hypocapnia, respiratory alkalosis → cerebral vasoconstriction (light-headedness, derealisation), ↓ionised Ca (perioral/peripheral paraesthesiae, carpopedal spasm); catastrophic misinterpretation → positive feedback; conditioned anticipatory anxiety and avoidance → panic disorder → agoraphobia
fails: Taking a psychiatric history instead of a chest pain history because you recognised the recall ★
Not acknowledging the 'nothing wrong' frustration
Skipping time-to-peak
Hearing the tingling and moving on
Omitting caffeine/stimulants and thyroid rows
Not announcing the negative organic screen before switching
Saying 'probably anxiety' without the three key questions ★
Relabelling as GAD on 'I'm an anxious person'
'It's just anxiety' / 'there's nothing wrong' / 'try to relax' — marked communication failures ★
Differentials given as a list of anxiety disorders
Prescribing benzodiazepines; repeating investigations
numbers: Panic attack: abrupt surge peaking within minutes (typically <10), ≥4 of 13 symptoms, characteristically fear of dying/losing control
Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month of worry about further attacks OR maladaptive behaviour change
Agoraphobia: fear/avoidance of ≥2 of public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues/crowds, outside home alone; typically 6 months
GAD: excessive hard-to-control worry about multiple matters ≥6 months with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, tension, sleep disturbance — discrete attacks not a core feature
Organic mimics: arrhythmia · thyrotoxicosis · hypoglycaemia · asthma · stimulant use or withdrawal

Management: validate → CBT first line → Mental Health Treatment Plan → SSRI if needed, start low go slow, warn of early worsening → avoid benzodiazepines (dependence, safety behaviour reinforcing avoidance) → cut caffeine/alcohol/stimulants → follow-up
'Will I have to take tablets forever?' — CBT is first line; medication only if needed and reviewed
Variant 1 lifelong worrier: panic disorder primary, possible comorbid GAD — name and treat the attacks first, same approach helps both
Variant 2 snake scene, lifelong fear: specific phobia — triggered attack, similar therapy
Variant 3 organic swap: pleuritic pain, 16-hour drive, right calf ache, SpO2 93% → Wells, CTPA, treat as PE until proven otherwise

setting: You are the doctor working in the Emergency Department.
stem: Jack Mitchell, 40 years old, has presented complaining of chest pain for the last two days. He is a known case of schizophrenia.
Vital signs available from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient
Explain your initial management to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Roughly six minutes of history; diagnosis and management share the last two minutes.

back.dx: Stable angina (ischaemic heart disease) in a man whose cardiometabolic risk is driven by risperidone — central heaviness to the neck, 6/10, brought on by walking and stairs, settles in a few minutes with rest, NEVER at rest, longest episode five minutes. Vitals normal (BP 138/86, PR 82, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98%). Risk load: father MI at 50, pack a day since 20, 6–8 beers most nights, takeaway diet, no exercise, 20 kg gain on risperidone, nobody has checked lipids or sugar in years. Discriminating question: 'do you ever get this pain when you are resting?' — that answer is the diagnosis. Version B: a voice at night and 'people are giving me this pain' — validate, gently decline the belief, carry on. Hidden agenda: frightened of dying like his father; frightened of being dismissed as 'in my head again'.
plan: Vitals from the examiner BEFORE greeting; intro, name, confidentiality statement (unless risk of harm to you or someone else)
'Tell me more about this pain' — silence; empathy line
SOCRATES as one fluent run; then the discriminator out loud: pain at rest? longest episode?
Signpost, then four schizophrenia questions: when diagnosed, treatment, taking it regularly, side effects (weight, postural dizziness, tremor, dry mouth), GP/psychiatrist follow-up
Three-question screen in order: harm to self or others → hear/see/feel things others don't → anyone trying to harm or control you. Version B: one sentence of validation, note it, move on
CVS risk factors as one continuous run: family MI/stroke, BP/cholesterol/diabetes, smoking, alcohol, drugs, diet, exercise
System sweep in one breath: ACS features, pericarditis, heart failure, PE, chest injury/cough, weight loss/lumps, GORD, MSK/rash; other conditions, meds, allergies
Diagnosis: name it, plain-words mechanism, THREE reasons (pain character, risk factors, the antipsychotic); five-second differential insurance line

Management in three headings: find it (ECG + troponin now, stress test ± echo) · protect the heart (aspirin, statin, GTN, Quitline, alcohol, diet, walking) · fix the cause (do NOT stop risperidone; speak to psychiatrist re switch e.g. aripiprazole, mental health review) · 000 safety-net · summary, questions
ask: Before I begin, could I have Jack's vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?
Everything we talk about stays between you and me — unless there's a risk of harm to you or to someone else. Is that alright?
Jack, tell me more about this pain. → 'I'm sorry to hear that, and I completely understand your concern. I'll do my best to find the cause today.'
Point to exactly where? Sharp, burning, or a heaviness? Out of ten? Travel anywhere? Comes and goes or constant? Brings it on? Makes it better?
★ This next question is important: do you ever get this pain when you are resting — sitting still, or lying in bed at night? And what's the longest one has lasted?

I saw you have schizophrenia — can I ask a few quick questions? It may actually be relevant to your chest pain. When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Able to take it regularly? Side effects — weight gain, dizzy on standing, shaky hands, dry mouth? See your GP and psychiatrist regularly?

★ I ask everyone this: any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else? Do you ever hear, see or feel things other people don't? Do you ever feel anyone is trying to harm you, or controlling you?
Version B reply: 'That sounds frightening, and I can hear how distressing it is. I don't see it the same way you do — but I have no doubt the pain is real, and I'm taking it seriously.'

Anyone in the family had a heart attack or stroke? Ever told high BP, cholesterol or diabetes? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol — how much a week? Recreational drugs? What do you usually eat in a day? Any regular exercise?

With the pain: sweating, SOB, nausea, racing heart? Fever or recent flu-like illness, worse lying flat / better sitting forward? Breathless lying down at night, leg swelling? Long travel, calf pain or swelling? Chest injury, cough, phlegm? Weight loss, appetite, lumps? Tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste, related to eating? Rash, worse on pressing or moving? Other conditions, medications, allergies?
pefe: No examination task. Ask for vitals only — treat 'just a history station' as the trap; he could be infarcting

Diagnosis to patient: 'ischaemic heart disease — stable angina. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart has narrowed, not blocked. When you walk the heart needs more oxygen than the narrowed tube can deliver — that shortage is the heaviness. When you rest it settles.' No atherosclerosis / ischaemia / stenosis

Three reasons: character of the pain (central, heavy, to the neck, exertional, relieved by rest) · risk factors (father at 50, smoking, weight, diet) · the medication he takes for schizophrenia raises heart risk
Differential insurance line (5 s): 'no sign you're having a heart attack, though we'll check; I also thought about inflammation around the heart, a clot on the lung and reflux — they don't fit'

Management: FIND — ECG now, troponin (pain new within 48 h), exercise stress ECG (treadmill, faster and steeper every 3 min) often with echo; CT coronary angiography increasingly first-line locally · PROTECT — aspirin, statin, GTN spray for pain, stop smoking (Quitline 13 7848), cut alcohol, diet, build to 30 min walking most days · FIX THE CAUSE — risperidone raises weight, cholesterol, sugar and heart risk; 'I won't change it and you mustn't stop it — stopping suddenly can make you unwell'; speak with psychiatrist about switching (e.g. aripiprazole) + mental health review
Safety-net: pain at rest, >10 min, or with sweating/vomiting/breathlessness → 000, don't drive. Summary + invite questions
If the examiner challenges investigations: ECG + serial hs-troponin to exclude ACS because symptoms are new; functional testing (stress ECG/echo) establishes stable angina; CTCA per local pathway
fails: Never asking about pain at rest and episode duration ★
Omitting the harm-to-self / harm-to-others question ★
Saying the pain is stress, anxiety or part of his illness ('it's in my head again')
Stopping or promising to stop the risperidone; changing it yourself rather than via the psychiatrist
Chasing a full MSE after the delusion and abandoning the chest pain; colluding with or arguing against the belief
Skipping vitals; skipping diet and exercise; giving the diagnosis with no reasons; MONA / aspirin-plus-troponin as the whole plan; no stress test named
numbers: 6 min history · ~1 min diagnosis · ~1 min management · 4 questions per known condition · 3 psych screen questions · 3 reasons · 3–4 differentials in 5 s
Stress ECG positive: ST depression ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping; Bruce protocol increments every 3 min VERIFY

Aspirin 100 mg daily (300 mg stat if ACS) · atorvastatin 40–80 mg nocte · metoprolol 25–50 mg BD · GTN 400 microg SL q5 min up to 3, 000 if pain persists 10 min after first dose · 150 min moderate activity/week VERIFY

Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring: baseline, 3 months, then at least annually · premature FHx: first-degree male <55, female <65 (father 50) · life-expectancy gap in severe mental illness 15–20 years, mostly cardiovascular

Variant 1 pain at rest, woke him at 3 am, 30 min → no longer stable angina: ECG within 10 min, IV access, serial hs-troponin, aspirin 300 mg chewed, GTN, analgesia, monitor, urgent cardiology — manage as ACS, keep him in

Variant 2 'everyone would be better off without me' → stop, explore ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors; same-day mental health assessment; still finish the chest-pain thread

Variant 3 'take me off the tablets' / refuses treadmill → don't stop; speak to psychiatrist; respect refusal, explore the worry, still start heart protection · Variant 4 clozapine + fever → clozapine myocarditis (first 2 months): troponin, CRP, ECG, echo, psychiatry + cardiology before any further dose
Quitline 13 7848 · Ambulance 000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450
