setting: You are the doctor on duty at a rural hospital.
stem: Bernard Hollis, 68, has attended with two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness following an episode of gastroenteritis last week. He has chronic kidney disease stage 4 and takes ramipril, spironolactone, metformin and atorvastatin. His blood results have just returned and are on the desk.
K⁺ 7.2 · Na⁺ 134 · urea 24.1 · creatinine 312 · eGFR 16 · HCO₃ 16 · corrected Ca 2.18. BP 104/62 · PR 52.
tasks: Interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner
State the likely causes
Outline your immediate management
Explain the situation to the patient
time: 8 minutes. The ECG is only handed over if you ask for it.

back.dx: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes — AKI on CKD 4 (prerenal from gastroenteritis), ACE inhibitor + spironolactone, metabolic acidosis; hidden ibuprofen for his knee (only if you ask about NSAIDs). ECG (must be requested): rate 52, P waves flattened/low amplitude, PR prolonged, QRS broad ~130 ms without bundle-branch morphology, tall narrow-based symmetrical peaked T waves in mid-precordial leads. The station is decided by your FIRST sentence: monitor + 12-lead ECG immediately, and 'was the sample haemolysed?' — before you finish reading the panel.
plan: Reading time
Write five things: ECG + monitor now, ask haemolysis · PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE · doses · stop ramipril/spironolactone/NSAIDs/trimethoprim · four causes
First sentence
'The potassium is 7.2 — severe. I'd attach cardiac monitoring and get a 12-lead ECG immediately, and check whether the sample was haemolysed'
ECG

Rate · P · PR · QRS · T, in that order → 'changes of severe hyperkalaemia, needs treatment now'. If asked 'ischaemic T waves?' — hyperacute T waves are broad-based and asymmetrical; the flat P, long PR and wide QRS make hyperkalaemia the explanation
Biochemistry
Creatinine 312 / eGFR 16 = advanced renal impairment; urea 24 with prerenal pattern = AKI on CKD; HCO₃ 16 = metabolic acidosis shifting K⁺ out of cells; mild hyponatraemia fits volume depletion
Causes
Four at once: CKD 4 baseline · AKI on top (gastro, poor intake) · ramipril + spironolactone additive · acidosis. Then ask: OTC NSAIDs, recent trimethoprim, potassium salt substitutes
Management

Three jobs: PROTECT calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–3 min on the monitor, repeat at 5 min if ECG unchanged, lasts 30–60 min, does NOT lower K⁺ · SHIFT 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL 50% glucose IV over 15–30 min, hourly BGL for ≥6 h unprompted, plus salbutamol 10–20 mg neb; consider bicarbonate given HCO₃ 16 (weak evidence) · REMOVE oliguric, eGFR 16 → haemodialysis is definitive, renal team + retrieval now. Withhold ramipril and spironolactone, cautious volume, recheck K⁺ at 1–2 h
Patient

Explain the effect, never the number: 'a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be … upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart … calcium protects the heart while the rest works … two of your tablets hold potassium in — stopping both today, don't restart until reviewed'. Answer heart attack / my fault / Adelaide honestly; offer to call someone
ask: ★ Examiner, before I go through these in full — the potassium is 7.2, which is in the severe range. I would attach cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately, and I would check whether the sample was reported as haemolysed.

Examiner's three questions after management, in order: 'Does the calcium lower his potassium?' → No — stabilises the myocardium, serum level unchanged, must always be given alongside something that shifts or removes K⁺, never instead. 'Commonest complication of your treatment?' → hypoglycaemia from insulin, often delayed, hence hourly BGL for 6 h. 'ECG had been normal — would you still treat?' → yes, K⁺ 7.2 is treated on the level; a normal ECG is not permission to wait

To the patient: 'Am I going to have a heart attack?' → 'Not a heart attack in the usual sense — this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery. I don't want to understate it — at this level the rhythm can become dangerous, which is why you're on a monitor and I'm treating you now. It is very treatable.'

'Is it something I did? I couldn't keep anything down.' → 'You have not done anything wrong. Being unwell and dehydrated strained kidneys that were already struggling, and two of your tablets hold potassium in — that combination caused this.'

'Do I have to go to Adelaide?' → 'Possibly. If the potassium doesn't come down with treatment, dialysis is the most effective way to remove it and that means transferring you. I'm arranging that conversation now so we aren't delayed. Is there someone you'd like me to call?'
If he looks blank at '7.2 — is that bad?' you have quoted the number instead of the effect — restart in lay terms
pefe: No history or examination task — results, causes, management, explanation
Investigations to name: 12-lead ECG + continuous monitoring first; haemolysis check; repeat K⁺ at 1–2 h; VBG/ABG; urine output; BGL hourly ×6 h; consider digoxin level if relevant
Drugs to stop: ramipril, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim; hold metformin with eGFR 16 and acute illness VERIFY

Version B run (K⁺ 6.1, well 44-year-old woman, pre-procedure bloods): order of operations — ECG and observations FIRST, ask about haemolysis/delayed processing/platelet and white cell counts, THEN repeat with wide-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet or fist clenching, prompt transport — THEN conclude pseudohyperkalaemia; do not treat and do not cancel the procedure until a clean result; if repeat high, it's real → renal function, medications, adrenal causes
SA: renal team and MedSTAR retrieval early rather than after failed medical therapy; PATS for the transfer; family call
fails: Not asking for an ECG and monitoring in the first response — a fail regardless of the total ★
Calcium gluconate without dose and route; or not stating that calcium does NOT lower potassium ★
No hourly glucose monitoring, unprompted ★
Not withholding ramipril and spironolactone ★
Naming one cause and stopping; reading the whole panel before asking for the ECG; quoting '7.2' at the patient; false reassurance on the heart-attack question
Not naming dialysis as definitive here; not involving renal / retrieval early
numbers: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–3 min, repeat at 5 min, protects 30–60 min · insulin 10 u short-acting + 50 mL 50% glucose over 15–30 min, hourly BGL ≥6 h · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb (additive) · sodium bicarbonate considered when acidotic, weak evidence · dialysis definitive VERIFY
Severe ≥6.5 or any ECG change; moderate 6.0–6.4 (Version B 6.1) VERIFY · recheck K⁺ 1–2 h
ECG sequence: peaked T → flat P → long PR → wide QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole
Four causes here: CKD 4 · AKI on CKD (urea 24, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, prerenal) · ACEi + spironolactone · acidosis HCO₃ 16 · plus hidden ibuprofen

Variant 1 sine wave K⁺ 8.4, drowsy, hypotensive = peri-arrest: calcium immediately and repeated, insulin–dextrose and salbutamol simultaneously, call for help + arrest trolley, emergency dialysis · Variant 2 digoxin toxicity K⁺ 6.4, nausea, yellow-green vision: hyperkalaemia marks severity → digoxin-specific antibody fragments definitive; avoid reflex calcium, discuss with toxicology · Variant 3 DKA K⁺ 5.9, glucose 28, pH 7.12: total body K⁺ depleted, follow DKA protocol, replace K⁺ once <5.5 and passing urine · Variant 4 well dialysis patient K⁺ 6.9, normal ECG, dialysis tomorrow: chronic tolerance, not permission to wait — monitor, treat medically, bring dialysis forward · Variant 5 angry patient ('your tablets nearly killed me'): validate, both tablets prescribed for good reasons, kidneys took a hit, they need reviewing when things change
Pass guide: 17/22 items and all five starred · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Poisons Information 13 11 26 · TIS National 131 450

setting: You are an HMO in a metropolitan emergency department.
stem: A 52-year-old man has presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath that started one hour ago. The pain began while he was chopping wood.
Vital signs: BP 135/85 · pulse 78 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on room air · T 36.8°C. He has no history of bleeding disorders.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes. About one minute on the ECG, then the management. No history taking, no physical examination.

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI — ST elevation in I, aVL and V2–V6 with reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF; most likely proximal LAD; sinus rhythm ~65–70, normal axis, normal PR, narrow QRS, no established Q waves. Treat as time-critical: primary PCI within 90 min (metro). James Whitfield, self-employed builder, smoker 15/day, untreated BP, father died of MI at 58, no bleeding problems, no sildenafil. Hidden agenda: terrified of dying like his father; money — two jobs booked, no income if he stops. Discriminating behaviour: 'six things, one at a time' — every drug with dose and route, the sildenafil question attached to the nitrate, oxygen refused with the 92% threshold, PCI translated.
plan: Park the patient in one sentence: 'I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly — I've been asked to look at your heart tracing with my examiner first, give me one minute.' If 'am I having a heart attack?' → 'that's exactly what I'm checking and I'll tell you straight away'

ECG in fixed order: details/date/calibration → rate → rhythm → axis → PR → QRS → ST segments (elevation V2–V6, I, aVL; reciprocal III, aVF) → no Q waves → impression anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

Say 'heart attack' plainly with plain-words mechanism; 'I've already let the cardiac team know'; acknowledge the father. Then: (1) aspirin 300 mg chewed + clopidogrel 600 mg (2) GTN 400 microg SL q5 min ×3 — ask Viagra/Cialis in last 24 h FIRST, say the other contraindications (3) IV access (4) troponin + FBC/UEC/lipids/coags — 'we are not waiting for it'; morphine 2.5–5 mg IV, ondansetron 4–8 mg IV

(5) oxygen only if SpO2 <92%, repeat ECG 1–2 hourly (6) PCI within 90 min: fine tube from wrist/groin, dye, balloon or stent — translate every word; cardiology consent. 'Are you cutting my chest open?' → no, a needle puncture at the wrist

'Am I going to die?' — no false promise: serious, caught early, treatment works well, I'm staying with you. Offer to call Karen. Ask for concerns (money → social work). One-line summary. If time remains: DAPT 12 months then aspirin, statin, ACEi, beta-blocker, cardiac rehab, smoking, driving — never drift into history taking
ask: Hello James — I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. Give me one minute with my examiner and I'll come straight back with the plan.

Examiner, this is a 12-lead ECG; I'd confirm patient details, date and calibration. Rate ~65–70 (R–R about 4½ large squares). Regular, P before every QRS — sinus. Axis normal. PR normal and constant, QRS narrow. ST elevation V2–V6 and I, aVL — ≥1 mm limb, ≥2 mm V2–V3; reciprocal ST depression III and aVF. No established Q waves. Impression: acute anterolateral STEMI, likely proximal LAD, time-critical.

The tracing shows that you are having a heart attack. One of the blood tubes supplying your heart muscle has become blocked by a clot, so part of that muscle isn't getting blood and oxygen — that's the pain. It is serious. It is also very treatable and we're starting right now. I've already let the cardiac team know.
There are six things I'm going to do in the next few minutes. Let me take them one at a time.

★ Before I give you the spray — one question I have to ask everybody: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours? ('why?' → together they can drop your blood pressure dangerously low)
How long for the blood test? → 'It doesn't change what we do today — we're not waiting for it. The tracing is enough to act on; waiting would cost you heart muscle.'
Shouldn't I be on oxygen? → 'It's 97% which is good; extra oxygen doesn't help and can narrow the heart arteries — if it falls below 92% I'll start it.'

Am I going to die? → 'I'm not going to pretend this isn't serious — it is. But you got here fast, we've caught it early, and the treatment works well. I'm going to stay with you.' Is there anyone you'd like me to call? Any questions or concerns?

ECG: ST elevation I, aVL, V2–V6; reciprocal depression III, aVF; sinus ~65–70; normal axis; narrow QRS; no Q waves → anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD
Investigations: ECG within 10 min of arrival, repeat 1–2 hourly; troponin (named, then discounted as a reason to wait), FBC, UEC, lipids, coags; continuous monitoring

Reperfusion Version A: primary PCI — target 90 min, acceptable if reachable within 120 min of first medical contact; translate 'percutaneous coronary intervention' → fine tube from the wrist, dye, ballooning, stent = tiny metal scaffold; awake but comfortable; cardiology consents

Long-term if time allows: aspirin + clopidogrel 12 months then aspirin 100 mg lifelong, atorvastatin 40–80 mg / rosuvastatin 20–40 mg, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker once stable, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking (Quitline 13 7848), diet, activity, driving restrictions VERIFY

Summary: 'your tracing shows a heart attack; aspirin and clopidogrel to stop the clot growing, a spray and morphine for the pain, and the cardiac team is preparing to reopen the artery within the hour. I'll be right here.'

'I'll give you a blood thinner' — any drug without dose and route scores nothing ★

Implying you will wait for the troponin; putting a normoxic patient on oxygen; three minutes on the ECG

setting: You are an HMO in a rural hospital. Your closest tertiary centre is 400 km away.
stem: A 55-year-old man has been brought in by ambulance complaining of chest pain that started suddenly one hour ago while he was working. He is a known hypertensive.

The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner or the medical student
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management
time: 8 minutes. About one minute on the ECG; the diagnosis is a separately marked task here. No history taking, no physical examination.

back.dx: Acute anterolateral STEMI (ST elevation I, aVL, V2–V6; reciprocal depression III, aVF; sinus, narrow QRS, no Q waves) — 400 km from PCI, so fibrinolysis is the reperfusion strategy: alteplase or tenecteplase with enoxaparin, after the FOUR bleeding questions, then transfer for angiography at 3–24 h. Same six steps as the metro version; task 2f is replaced entirely. Hidden agenda as before: father died of MI at 58; self-employed, money. Harder run: bleeding ulcer admission last week → do NOT lyse unilaterally; escalate to cardiology + retrieval and keep treating everything else.

ECG in fixed order → acute anterolateral STEMI, proximal LAD, time-critical

Reperfusion: 'nearest hospital that can physically reopen it is 400 km — four hours. If we can't get you there within two hours, waiting does more harm than travelling does good. So we treat you here with a clot-dissolving medicine through the drip.' Four bleeding questions in ten seconds → alteplase bolus then infusion over 60–90 min (or tenecteplase single bolus) + enoxaparin; monitor for reperfusion arrhythmias; repeat ECG and troponin; cardiology re transfer for angiogram in the next day or so

'Four hours? Can't you fly me?' → retrieval is being arranged, but the medicine can be given now and now is what matters. 'What if it doesn't work?' → straight to transfer for the procedure; I'll know within ~90 min. Am I going to die / call Karen / concerns / summary

Six things, one at a time — drug, dose, route every time
★ Before the spray: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours?

★ Four bleeding questions, ten seconds: 'Any bleeding in the brain, stroke or brain tumour? Any bleeding disorder, or bleeding anywhere now? Any stomach ulcer or bleeding from the bowel? Any major surgery or serious head injury in the last three months?'

'Good — nothing there that stops us. So: alteplase, a starting dose into the vein followed by a drip over the next hour to hour and a half, and a second blood thinner called enoxaparin alongside it. You'll stay on the monitor because the rhythm can misbehave as the artery opens; we'll repeat the tracing and blood test, and I'll be speaking with the cardiac team about transferring you for an angiogram in the next day or so.'
Is there anyone you'd like me to call? Any questions or concerns? → summary

setting: You are the Hospital Medical Officer in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan Australian hospital.
stem: James Whitfield, a 55-year-old man, has presented with the sudden onset of central chest pain that began approximately 20 minutes ago. He is anxious and says his father died of a heart attack.
BP 124/78 · pulse 98 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 98% room air · temp 37.8 °C · BGL 5.6 (exact vitals vary between recalls — the pattern is stable with a low-grade fever).
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will be shown an ECG — give the examiner your overall impression and the key features that support it
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Version A — the ECG is handed over after the history (mini-bell / prompt at about 4 minutes in the face-to-face format). Stop the history when the bell goes.

back.dx: Acute pericarditis, most likely viral — the case that looks exactly like an MI until the last SOCRATES question. Central, crushing, sudden, 20 min, constant, 7/10, to left arm and jaw … then BETTER LEANING FORWARD, worse lying flat, sharper on deep breath, flu ten days ago, feverish and tired, no CV risk factors (never smoked, clear check-up). The role-player sits leaning forward clutching his chest — look at him. ECG: rate ~100, sinus, normal PR/QRS, concave ST elevation I, II, V2–V6 (crosses territories), no reciprocal depression except aVR, PR depression. Discriminating behaviour: finish SOCRATES before opening the differential; never say 'definitely not a heart attack' before the troponin.
plan: Vitals from examiner → 'haemodynamically stable'; wash; intro, confirm name; open question; acknowledge the father's death — 'I'll come back to that'; signpost + consent
SOCRATES to the end — the box is sealed until E: 'anything make it worse? better? — I notice you're sitting forward holding your chest, is it easier like that? and lying flat? deep breath or cough?'
Associated + prodrome: cold/flu in last 1–2 weeks, feverish, tired

Kill list in one block: MUST ASK CVS (exertional pain before today, sweating/nausea/doom, tearing to back, arms different, palpitations, blackouts, oedema, orthopnoea/PND) · MUST ASK resp (sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf pain/swelling, travel/surgery/immobility, fever/cough/sweats/weight loss) · GI (burning, meals, acid, forceful vomiting before pain, black stools) · MSK/skin (injury, lifting, tender on pressing, rash/burning skin) · psych (stress, panic, tingling)
SADMA (cocaine/amphetamines; anticoagulants), PMHx (DM/HTN/lipids, previous MI, cardiac surgery, autoimmune, cancer, TB, HIV, renal), FHx with age, ICE 'what are you most worried this might be?'
Bell → excuse yourself → ECG in seven steps → impression in four words: widespread · doesn't match a territory · no reciprocal · concave (+ PR depression)

Diagnosis in plain words + THREE reasons (leans forward, recent flu — most are viral, the tracing) · honest troponin line · long DDx one clause each, killers first · plan: troponin, CXR, echo, FBE/ESR/CRP, admit, colchicine + NSAID, no strenuous exercise · safety-net · summary · questions
ask: Examiner, before I begin — may I have the vital signs: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?
That sounds very frightening and I can see you're uncomfortable. I'm going to take a history and then examine you so I can come to a diagnosis and make a plan — is that okay?
Where exactly? When — sudden or gradual? Sharp, dull, crushing, tight? Move anywhere? Constant or comes and goes? Out of ten?

★ Anything make it worse? Anything make it better? — 'I notice you're sitting forward and holding your chest — is the pain easier when you lean forward like that? And what happens if you lie flat?' Does it change with a deep breath or cough?
★ Any cold or flu-like symptoms in the last week or two? Felt feverish or unusually tired?

Exertional chest pain before today? Sweating, nausea, a feeling of doom? Tearing pain through to the back? Pain different in each arm? Palpitations? Blackouts? Leg swelling? Breathless lying flat or waking at night?
Sudden breathlessness? Coughing up blood? Calf pain or swelling? Long flights, car trips, surgery, time in bed? Fever, productive cough, night sweats, weight loss?

Burning pain, worse lying down or after meals? Acid coming up? Forceful vomiting before the pain? Black stools? Injury, heavy lifting? Tender when pressed? Rash or blistering? Stress, panic, tingling?

Smoke? Alcohol? Cocaine or amphetamines? Regular medicines — any blood thinners? Allergies? Diabetes, BP, cholesterol, previous heart problems or surgery, autoimmune disease, cancer, TB, HIV, kidney problems? Family — heart attack or sudden death, and at what age? What are you most worried this might be?

'So it's definitely not a heart attack?' → 'It looks much more like pericarditis — but the two can look very similar and I won't tell you a heart attack is excluded until the troponin blood test is back. That test is the main reason I'd like to keep you in hospital.'
pefe: ECG read-out, fixed order: rate ~100 → regular → P before every QRS → PR normal → QRS normal → ST: 'more than 1 mm limb, more than 2 mm chest — elevation in I, II, V2–V6; concave; no reciprocal depression apart from aVR which I disregard; PR segment depression' → 'overall impression acute pericarditis: widespread, doesn't match a single coronary territory, concave, no reciprocal changes'
aVR pearl: it looks from the opposite direction, so ST depression and PR elevation in aVR are expected, not the reciprocal change of infarction

Explain: 'the heart sits inside a thin covering, a bit like a sac; in pericarditis that covering becomes inflamed and that is the pain'. Three reasons: better leaning forward/worse flat · flu ten days ago and most cases are viral · the tracing shows the changes of this condition, not a heart attack

DDx to patient, one clause each: heart attack (tracing pattern; confirm with troponin) · clot on the lung (no leg swelling, travel, surgery; sats normal) · tear in the main blood vessel (not tearing, not to the back) · collapsed lung (no injury, equal breath sounds) · then in one sweep: tear in the food pipe, heart failure, tight valve, chest infection, growth in the lung, reflux, ulcer, shingles, chest-wall cartilage, stress

Investigations: ECG · troponin (essential — raised = myopericarditis) · echo (effusion, tamponade) · CXR · FBE, ESR, CRP · UEC/LFT/BGL baseline before colchicine/NSAID · cultures if febrile and unwell. Managed in hospital because you need the troponin now

Treatment: colchicine + NSAID — ibuprofen 400–600 mg TDS with food until symptoms settle and CRP normalises then taper (aspirin 600–900 mg TDS if post-MI), plus gastric protection; colchicine 0.5 mg BD (0.5 mg daily if <70 kg or poorly tolerated) for 3 months VERIFY; no steroids first-line (recurrence); restrict strenuous exercise; admit, serial troponin, cardiology; GP in a week, repeat CRP; complete the colchicine course

Safety-net: pain much worse or different, increasing SOB, faint/dizzy/blackout, palpitations, high fever, leg or abdominal swelling → back immediately. Tamponade in the station: 'stop, call for help, MET call, IV fluids, urgent bedside echo, cardiology for pericardiocentesis'
fails: Diagnosing MI at 'radiates to the left arm' — never asking relieving factors ★
Omitting the troponin; saying 'it's definitely not a heart attack' ★
Not looking at the patient leaning forward; being put off by the pleuritic quality; being talked out of it by risk factors
A one-word ECG answer; not saying the four words (widespread, no territory, no reciprocal, concave)
Two differentials only, or over-explaining each; talking over the mini-bell; skipping vitals
No safety-net, no summary, jargon
numbers: ST elevation significant: >1 mm limb leads, >2 mm chest leads · pericarditis ECG: widespread concave elevation + PR depression, aVR reversed, no reciprocal · MI: territorial, convex, reciprocal depression

Pericarditis vs MI: posture (better forward / none) · pleuritic (often / no) · prodrome (viral, fever / exertional, diaphoresis) · rub (yes / S4, failure) · troponin (normal unless myopericarditis / rise and fall)
Causes: viral commonest · autoimmune (SLE, RA) · bacterial/TB · post-MI (early or Dressler) · uraemia · malignancy · radiotherapy · post-cardiac surgery · trauma · drugs
Colchicine 0.5 mg BD × 3 months (0.5 mg daily if <70 kg) · ibuprofen 400–600 mg TDS with PPI · aspirin 600–900 mg TDS if post-MI · no steroids first-line VERIFY

Tamponade = Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg fall on inspiration → MET call, fluids, echo, pericardiocentesis · myopericarditis = raised troponin, arrhythmia, poor LV → admit, cardiology, no exercise · purulent = high fever, rigors → cultures, IV antibiotics, drainage

★ Anything make it better? I notice you're sitting forward holding your chest — is it easier like that? What about lying flat? Deep breath or cough?

One-breath PEFE if short of time: 'Examiner — general appearance and vitals; cardiovascular inspection, palpation and auscultation, and specifically is there a pericardial friction rub; respiratory air entry and added sounds; lower limbs for oedema.' The rub must survive the compression

setting: General practice / outpatient clinic.
stem: Lily, a 50-year-old woman, presents with on-and-off chest pain. Her father had a heart attack recently. She is worried she is having a heart attack too.
An ECG has already been done — it will be handed to you approximately 4–5 minutes into the station. Vital signs are provided on request.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Interpret the ECG to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses, including an explicit response to her concern about a heart attack
time: 8 minutes. 0:00–1:00 stability, WIPE, acknowledge the fear · 1:00–5:00 history · 5:00–6:00 ECG read and explained to her · 6:00–7:15 diagnosis, reasons, her concern, management · 7:15–8:00 rapid differential list, summary.

back.dx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease — months of on/off burning retrosternal + epigastric pain, 4–5/10, not progressive, doesn't wake her, no radiation, worse lying down, better leaning forward (the planted pericarditis red herring), 'not sure' about food (deliberately vague — keep asking), acid brash YES, water brash YES, regurgitation sometimes; 3–4 coffees a day, a drink most nights, regular ibuprofen for her knee (the modifiable cause); no CV risk factors; father's MI at 78 (ask the age); no alarm features. ECG completely normal (BP 128/78, PR 76, RR 16, SpO2 99%, T 36.7). Discriminating behaviours: ask acid brash and water brash by name; call the ECG normal with confidence; de-escalate her fear with TWO named reasons, never the ECG alone.
plan: Vitals → wash → intro, confirm name/DOB → purpose + consent → comfort → open question → she volunteers the fear → structured reassuring statement (names the emotion, names the dad, gives a plan, promises to return, asks permission)
SOCRATES incl. the night-waking red flag (chronic pain) — probe all three axes: activity/rest, position, food; don't accept 'not sure'
Cardiac symptom screen (all negative) → every risk factor: HTN, DM, lipids, smoking, alcohol, weight, activity, FHx + 'how old was your father?'
Other CVS (pericarditis — fever/viral/pleuritic; AS; HF; dissection; arrhythmia) → respiratory (pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, cancer screen doubles as GI alarm screen)

GI block — where it's decided: abdominal pain/N&V → ★ acid or bitter taste? ★ mouth filling with saliva? regurgitation on bending? cough/hoarse/wheeze → alarm features: food sticking, painful swallowing, weight loss, black tarry sticky stools, vomiting blood → PUD discriminators (to the back, dull ache, night pain) → biliary → GORD risks: coffee, spicy/fatty/late meals → ★ medications incl. OTC → rash, worse on pressing/moving, mood/stress; SADMA, PMHx, allergies
ECG: read systematically, then to Lily in plain words with the honest limit ('one normal tracing doesn't rule out heart disease forever — it's one piece')

Four moves: name it → explain the valve → reasons (burning, posture, acid/water brash, coffee/alcohol/ibuprofen) → her concern: two reasons + offer CV risk check → management → safety-net → rapid DDx list → summary
ask: Lily, I completely understand how frightening chest pain can be, especially after what happened to your dad. Let me ask a few questions, then I'll look at your heart tracing. We'll work out the cause together, and I promise I'll come back to your concern. Is that alright?

Where exactly — point with one finger? Sudden or gradual, when? Burning, crushing, tight, sharp, tearing? Travel anywhere — arm, jaw, neck, back? Constant or on and off, getting worse? Does it ever wake you from sleep? Worse? Better — antacids, peppermint? Out of ten?
Walking uphill or stairs — and settles with rest? Lying flat, bending, leaning forward? After meals, before, large or late meals? (all three axes, every time)
SOB, nausea/vomiting, sweating, palpitations, dizziness, blackouts, ankle swelling, orthopnoea, PND, exercise tolerance?

High blood pressure? Blood sugar? Cholesterol? Smoke, ever? Alcohol per week? Weight? How active? Heart disease in the family — ★ how old was your father when it happened? ('it matters most under 55')

Fever or viral illness, sharp pain worse on deep breath? Chest pain, breathlessness or blackouts on exertion? Pillows, PND, ankle swelling? Sudden tearing pain to the back? Racing or skipping? Cough, sputum, fever? Sudden SOB, haemoptysis, calf pain, travel, surgery, pill/HRT, previous clot, cancer? Weight loss, appetite, night sweats, hoarse voice, neck lumps?

★ Do you get an acidic or bitter taste at the back of your mouth? ★ Have you noticed your mouth suddenly filling with saliva? Does food or fluid come back up when you bend or lie down? Chronic dry cough, hoarse in the morning, wheeze at night?
★ Does food ever stick? Hurt to swallow? Weight loss without trying? Bowel motions black, tarry and sticky like tar? Vomited blood? Persistent vomiting? Family history of stomach or food-pipe cancer?

Pain through to the back, or a deep dull ache rather than burning? Right upper tummy pain after fatty meals, yellow eyes, pale stools? Tea/coffee — how much? Spicy, fatty, fried, chocolate, late meals? ★ Any medications at all, including over the counter or from the pharmacy? Rash or blistering? Worse when you move, twist or press? Mood, stress at home or work?
pefe: ECG to the examiner/yourself: details, calibration → rate ~75 → regular → P before every QRS, sinus → PR normal → QRS normal, no Q waves → no ST elevation or depression in any territory → T waves normal → QTc normal → 'a completely normal ECG'. Don't over-read mild concave ST elevation in V5–V6 (benign early repolarisation) as pericarditis

ECG to Lily: 'this is a tracing of your heart's electrical activity. The good news is it's completely normal — rate about 75, rhythm regular and coming from the right place, and importantly none of the changes we'd expect if the heart muscle wasn't getting enough blood or you were having a heart attack. One honest thing: a normal tracing today doesn't rule out heart disease forever — it's one piece of the picture'

Diagnosis: 'reflux — a valve between food pipe and stomach that keeps acid where it belongs; when it doesn't close properly acid comes back up and the food pipe, which isn't built for acid, gets irritated — that's the burning'. Reasons: burning quality · posture (acid moves up when gravity isn't helping) · acid taste + mouth filling with saliva are quite specific · coffee, alcohol, ibuprofen

Her concern — two reasons: (1) tracing normal (2) more important — character doesn't fit heart pain (heavy/crushing, on exertion, eases with rest, to arm/jaw) vs hers (burning, months, not activity-related, changes with position). 'That said, because of your dad I'd like to check your overall heart risk properly — bloods and BP' = partnership

Management: STOP the ibuprofen (paracetamol; look at the knee) · lifestyle: cut coffee, reduce alcohol, avoid provoking foods/chocolate/peppermint/fizzy drinks, smaller meals, nothing within 3 h of lying down, head of bed up 15–20 cm on blocks, weight, loose clothing · antacid/alginate PRN · PPI once daily 30–60 min before breakfast for 4–8 weeks then step down (esomeprazole 20 mg / pantoprazole 20–40 mg / omeprazole 20 mg) VERIFY · FBC, H. pylori (UBT or stool antigen — withhold PPI 2 weeks) VERIFY, lipids, HbA1c, UEC for absolute CV risk · review 4–6 weeks; no response or alarm features → endoscopy
Examination to state: CVS, resp, abdomen incl. epigastric tenderness, chest-wall palpation, skin for zoster, BMI, BP

DDx list to Lily briskly: heart (tracing normal, pain doesn't fit) · sac around the heart (no fever/viral) · stomach ulcer (possible with ibuprofen — usually to the back, dull ache) · clot on lung, collapsed lung, chest infection (no sudden SOB, cough, fever) · gallbladder · chest-wall muscle/joint · shingles (no rash) · stress/anxiety. 'Reflux fits best'
fails: Never asking the reflux questions — acid brash and water brash ★
Reassuring on the ECG alone; 'there's nothing wrong with your heart' / 'it's just reflux' ★
Abandoning the structure — jumping to GI on 'burning', or locking onto pericarditis on 'better leaning forward'
Not asking the father's age; skipping alarm features in a 50-year-old; missing the OTC ibuprofen
Over-reading a normal ECG as pericarditis; not addressing her stated concern explicitly
Jargon (GORD, retrosternal, melaena); no ambulance threshold; running out of time before the differentials
numbers: Premature CVD: first-degree male <55, female <65 · father 78 = not premature · 'melaena' → 'black, tarry, sticky, like tar'
Two-axis rule: tracks with meals and posture → oesophagus; tracks with exertion and rest → heart. Radiation: arm → cardiac; jaw shared; epigastrium → oesophageal
PPI trial 4–8 weeks then step down · H. pylori test off PPI 2 weeks · review 4–6 weeks · endoscopy if alarm features, new onset >50 with persistent symptoms, or failed PPI VERIFY
Drugs that worsen reflux: NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, anticholinergics, doxycycline, potassium supplements
Safety-net: exertional pain, to arm/jaw, sweating, SOB, faint → 000, don't drive · food sticking, vomiting blood, black tarry stools → urgent review · not better in 4–6 weeks → come back
Version B (28-year-old man, 6-min history, squeezing pain to the jaw, relieved by peppermint tea) is MED-20 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450

Normal ECG. The recall that caused panic: candidates who never ran the GI block were left with 'an MI with no MI symptoms' and froze. setting: Emergency department, Australian metropolitan hospital. You are the ED junior doctor.
stem: James, a 49-year-old man, has brought himself to ED with severe central chest pain that started 30 minutes ago.
Vital signs are available from the examiner on request. An ECG will be provided after the history.
tasks: Take a focused history — 5 minutes. A warning bell sounds at 5 minutes
Interpret the ECG to the examiner — step by step, out loud, in a fixed order
Explain your likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient in plain language
time: 8 minutes. History 5:00 (bell) · ECG ~1:00 · explanation ~2:00.

back.dx: Acute inferior STEMI — super-typical pain: central area not a point, 7–8/10, tightening/crushing, 30 min constant, to jaw and left shoulder, worse walking better resting AND at rest now; SOB, sweating, nausea; four discriminators all negative (breathing, position, eating, movement). KEY POINT of every chest-pain station: the five risk factors — dad and uncle MI, hypertension + cholesterol on tablets, 15/day for 25 years, beers at weekends, overweight. Vitals: BP 128/76, pulse 52 (bradycardia is a clue — RCA supplies SA/AV nodes), RR 18, T 36.8, SpO2 97%. ECG: rate ~50, regular sinus, PR normal, QRS wide (esp. chest leads — bundle branch, describe and move on), ST elevation II, III, aVF (III and aVF marked), reciprocal depression I and aVL, plus depression V2–V4 (possible posterior extension), no ST elevation in V1 (no RV clue).
plan: Vitals from examiner ('stable though bradycardic') → wash → intro, name/DOB → consent → open question → acknowledgement line

SICORA: site (point or area?) → intensity → character (crushing or sharp?) → onset/course → radiation → aggravating/relieving; if 'haven't noticed' → 'does activity make it worse and rest better?' → 'pain at rest right now?'
Four discriminators every time: deep breath? leaning forward? eating? movement/pressing?

Systems screen 1–2 questions each in fixed order: CVS (SOB/sweat/nausea/palpitations; fever/flu/leaning forward; orthopnoea/pillows/oedema; syncope on exertion) → resp (calf, travel, clots; trauma; fever/cough/noisy breathing; weight/appetite/lumps/haemoptysis) → GI (abdo pain/vomiting; acid taste/saliva; meals) → MSK/skin (movement/pressing; rash) → psych (stress, mood)
★ KEY POINT — five risk factors: FHx heart attack/stroke · sugar/BP/fats · smoking amount and years · alcohol · overweight
Recreational drugs (cocaine/amphetamines) · medications incl. sildenafil · allergies · 'anything else you'd like to tell me?'

Bell → ECG seven steps → impression → to patient: name it, one sentence, three reasons (typical pain, risk factors, ECG) → reason 1–2 DDx then rapid list, life-threatening first → what happens now, safety-net, summary
ask: Examiner, before I begin I'd like the patient's vital signs please: BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation.
I understand how concerning chest pain can be, James. Let me ask you a few questions, I'll try to find the cause and make the best plan for you, and I'll address your concerns as quickly as I can.

Where is the pain — a point you can put a finger on, or an area? One to ten? Crushing, or sharp? When exactly did it start — constant or on and off since, getting worse? Does it travel anywhere? Anything make it better or worse? → ★ Does activity make it worse and rest make it better? ★ Do you have pain at rest right now?
Is it related to breathing — deep breath worse? To position — leaning forward better? To eating? Worse on movement or pressing on the chest?
Any SOB? Sweating? Nausea? Racing heart? Fever, chills, flu-like symptoms? Breathless lying flat, how many pillows, leg swelling? Ever fainted, especially with exercise?

Calf swelling or pain? Long travel, family history of clots? Chest injury? Fever, cough, noisy breathing? Weight loss, appetite, lumps, coughed up blood? Tummy pain, vomiting? Acidic or bitter taste, sudden saliva? Related to eating? Rash? Stress at home or work, mood?
★ Family history of heart attacks or strokes? Past history of high sugar, high blood pressure or high fats in the blood? Smoke — how much, how long? Alcohol — how much? Are you currently overweight?
Recreational drugs? Any medications — including anything like Viagra? Allergies? Anything else you'd like to tell me today?
'Am I going to be alright?' → 'I understand this is frightening. You came in early and we have a well-established treatment pathway that we're starting right now' — then the three reasons
pefe: Seven-step ECG, never the impression first: 1 rate (300 ÷ large squares → ~50) 2 rhythm regular 3 P waves → sinus 4 PR < 1 large square 5 QRS — 'wide, particularly in the praecordial leads' 6 ST elevation — name every lead and the territory: II, III, aVF = inferior 7 look deliberately at the opposite territory: reciprocal depression I and aVL; also V2–V4 · extra step for inferior MI: 'is there ST elevation in V1?' — QR pattern but no elevation → no RV clue · THEN 'acute inferior STEMI'
Don't open with 'I'd check the name and date' — if at all, say it last

Diagnosis script: 'most likely a myocardial infarction — the same as a heart attack. One of the blood tubes of your heart has become blocked so the muscle isn't getting enough oxygen, and that's the pain.' Three reasons: typical pain (central, to jaw and shoulder, worse with activity) · risk factors (family, BP, cholesterol, smoking) · the ECG shows the changes

DDx: reason the first one or two (pericarditis — no fever/flu; PE — no travel; pneumothorax — no injury) then list: aortic dissection, oesophageal rupture; heart failure, narrowed valve; chest infection, growth in the lung; reflux, stomach ulcer; rib-joint inflammation, shingles; panic attack. Life-threatening first. When the bell goes mid-sentence: finish the phrase, 'that's my list of differentials', stop

Management if extended: resus bay, monitor, defib to bedside, IV ×2, ECG within 10 min (repeat; V4R for inferior), aspirin 300 mg chewed, titrated IV opioid + antiemetic, nitrate only if BP adequate and no RV infarct/PDE-5 inhibitor, oxygen only if hypoxic, activate STEMI pathway + cardiology NOW — troponin never delays reperfusion; PCI within targets else fibrinolysis; CCU, not for discharge; DAPT, statin, beta-blocker, ACEi; cardiac rehab; screen family

One-line lay DDx: pericarditis 'inflammation of the covering of your heart' · pneumothorax 'a collection of air in the chest' · PE 'a clot in your lungs' · dissection 'a tear in the main blood tube of your body' · rupture 'a tear in your food pipe' · HF 'your heart isn't pumping normally' · GORD 'stomach acid irritating your food pipe' · shingles 'reactivation of the chickenpox virus' · costochondritis 'inflammation of the rib joints' · AS 'a narrowed heart valve'
fails: Skipping cardiovascular risk factors — the single commonest reason candidates fail the MI case ★
Not checking haemodynamic stability before the first question ★
Jumping to the ECG impression; not naming reciprocal changes
Narrow cardiac-only differential; over-explaining two differentials and no list when the bell rings
'Don't worry, I'm sure it's nothing'; talking over the bell; no plan or safety-net sentence
numbers: Rate = 300 ÷ large squares · PR normal < 1 large square (200 ms) · QRS narrow < 3 small squares (120 ms) · significant ST elevation >1 mm limb, >2 mm chest VERIFY
Territories: inferior II, III, aVF ↔ reciprocal I, aVL, check V1/V4R for RV · anterolateral I, aVL, V1–V6 ↔ reciprocal III, aVF ± II · pericarditis widespread concave, NO reciprocal, aVR depressed
Inferior MI: RCA → SA/AV node → bradycardia/heart block · RV infarct = preload dependent → no nitrates, give fluids · ST depression V1–V4 may be posterior extension → V7–V9
Aspirin 300 mg chewed · ECG within 10 min · no routine oxygen if normoxic · nitrate contraindications: hypotension, RV infarct, PDE-5 inhibitor within 24–48 h VERIFY
DDx order: MI · pericarditis · PE · pneumothorax · dissection · oesophageal rupture → HF, AS → pneumonia, lung cancer → GORD, PUD → costochondritis, shingles → panic

Model paragraph: 'technically difficult, but rate, rhythm, P waves, PR and QRS are normal. ST elevation of about one small square in I and aVL, and across V2–V6. SADMA, PMHx (DM, cancer, HIV, autoimmune, transplant, renal), FHx, who's at home, 'what were you most worried this might be?' (heart attack — address it first later)

Does it come on when you exert yourself? Spread to jaw, neck, left arm? Sweating, nausea, faint? Shortness of breath, coughing blood? Calf swelling or pain, long flights, surgery, time in bed? ★ You had the flu — is it worse lying flat and better sitting forward? Heartburn, related to eating, difficulty swallowing? Injury, heavy lifting, hard coughing?
Noticed any rash or blisters on that area? ★ What do you do for work — children or healthcare? ★ Contact with anyone pregnant, any newborns or young children, anyone with a weak immune system?

★ 'Some questions may seem unrelated' — lost weight without trying? Drenching night sweats? Lumps in neck, armpits or groin? Unusual bruising or bleeding? Persistent fevers? More tired than usual? Drinking or passing urine more? Known diabetes? Steroids, chemotherapy, arthritis or bowel-disease drugs, injections affecting the immune system? 'I ask everyone — anything in your background that might affect your immune system, such as blood-borne virus risk?' Chickenpox as a child? Shingles before? Vaccinated? Rash near the eye, forehead, tip of nose, eye pain, vision change? Ear pain, hearing, dizziness, facial weakness?
Smoke, alcohol, drugs, medications, allergies? Past conditions? Family — heart disease, clots, cancer? Who's at home? What were you most worried this might be?

'Is it cancer?' → 'I can't tell you today and I don't want to alarm you. These symptoms need proper investigation rather than ignoring. Some causes are straightforward — diabetes, a recent infection. Others involve the blood or lymph glands, and those are the ones I want to find or rule out, because finding them early matters.'

'No rash' answer: 'The absence of a rash does not exclude shingles — the pain typically precedes the rash by a few days. My provisional diagnosis remains herpes zoster, and I would warn him a rash is likely over the next 2–3 days and review within 48–72 h so antivirals start inside the window'

Explain: heart worry first → 'shingles — when you had chickenpox the virus went to sleep in the nerve roots near your spine; years later it can wake up and travel along one nerve — that's why the pain is a band on one side that stops dead in the middle, and why the skin is so sensitive. Management: 1 antiviral — famciclovir 500 mg TDS × 7 days (or valaciclovir 1 g TDS × 7, or aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7); within 72 h of rash if immunocompetent, any duration if immunocompromised; renal dose adjustment VERIFY 2 analgesia — not paracetamol alone: regular paracetamol + NSAID, paracetamol/codeine for breakthrough with constipation advice, early amitriptyline/gabapentin/pregabalin if severe 3 skin — cool compresses, calamine, clean/dry, loose clothing, non-adherent dressing, don't scratch 4 contacts — until every blister has crusted avoid pregnant women who haven't had chickenpox, newborns, unvaccinated young children, immunosuppressed; cover, hand-wash, no shared towels; 'the fluid gives chickenpox, not shingles' · off work while lesions can't be covered, medical certificate, check childcare requirements · notifiable in SA (say you'll comply) VERIFY · review 2–3 days · Shingrix once recovered if eligible (NIP ≥65, ATSI ≥50, immunocompromised ≥18) VERIFY

PHN warning: 'the rash settles but the nerve pain can outlast it — come back, there are specific medicines'

No contact advice, no occupation question, no notification; exposing the chest without consent/chaperone offer
'It's only a rash'; jargon (herpes zoster, dermatomal, dorsal root ganglion) untranslated; no PHN warning, no review date

Famciclovir 500 mg 8-hourly × 7 · valaciclovir 1 g 8-hourly × 7 · aciclovir 800 mg five times daily × 7 · reduce in renal impairment · IV aciclovir if disseminated/immunocompromised VERIFY

setting: You are a general practitioner.
stem: Your next patient is Margaret Doyle, 65, who was admitted two weeks ago with pneumonia, treated with antibiotics, discharged, and is now well. She has a permanent pacemaker for a bradyarrhythmia and uses CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea. She plans to travel interstate in two weeks. Two chest X-rays are available: the admission film and a repeat film taken this week.
Observations: T 36.6 °C · P 72 regular · BP 128/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% room air.
tasks: Explain the two chest X-rays to the patient
Take a relevant focused history
Counsel her about the risks of travelling and advise her accordingly
time: 8 minutes. 0:30 films · 1:30 pneumonia box · 2:30 pacemaker/CPAP · 3:45 risk factors/SADMA · 4:30 the trip · 5:15 verdict and counselling · 7:30 summary and safety-net.

back.dx: Fit to travel — resolved right middle lobe pneumonia (admission film: dense white patch right mid-zone, pacemaker box with two leads; this week's film: cleared, sharp heart border), symptoms settled, SpO2 97%. Two things she will NOT volunteer: CPAP only two nights a week (mask digs into her nose) and ten cigarettes a day for forty years. 'Somac' = pantoprazole — say it. Cairns, ten days, three-hour flight, staying with sister Anne — and a beginner scuba dive is booked (surfaces only if you ask what she'll do). Discriminating behaviours: hold the verdict until the history is done; ask 'how many nights a week' not 'do you use it'; ask what she plans to do; letter + written red flags because she'll be 2,500 km away.
plan: WIPE, confirm name; open question; agenda: films → recovery, heart and sleep apnoea, the trip → clear answer + something in writing

Films: three colours → heart, spine, windpipe → normal left lung first → right mid-zone white patch → NAME the pacemaker → second film: black again, sharp heart border → 'cleared completely' → 'I think the answer will be yes — let me check a few things first'
Box 1 pneumonia: admitted/discharged, days of antibiotics and finished?, cough, sputum, BLOOD, SOB walking/lying flat, fever/chills/sweats, chest pain, appetite and WEIGHT
Box 2: pacemaker — when, last check, tablets, racing/fluttering, dizzy spells/blackouts; CPAP — 'how many nights a week do you actually use it?' → two → acknowledge, flag you'll come back
Box 3: asthma/emphysema, diabetes, kidney/liver, cancer, steroids, stroke/memory/choking; medications (Somac = pantoprazole); flu and pneumonia vaccines; smoke — how much; alcohol; occupation
Box 4: where, when, how long; flying or driving; who with, staying with whom; WHAT will you do; insurance, enough medication

Verdict: yes — 'no rule that you must wait a set time after a pneumonia'. Letter (admission, antibiotics, pacemaker, CPAP settings). Red flags + 000 + tell your sister. No scuba (snorkelling fine; formal dive medical if she insists, later). CPAP: consequences, mask refit/nasal pillows/humidifier, sleep service referral, take it on the plane. Smoking: ask-advise-assess-assist-arrange in 90 s, Quitline 13 7848, NRT. Flu vaccine today, check pneumococcal and COVID. Tropical advice, flight advice
Summary in one breath; 'have I missed anything you were worried about?'
ask: 'On an X-ray there are really only three colours: white is bone, grey is soft tissue like heart and muscle, black is air. Here is your heart, your spine, your windpipe down the middle. Your left lung is completely black — normal. Compare the right: a dense white patch here in the middle — that's where the infection was. And this box with two wires into your heart is your pacemaker, correctly placed, wires intact.'

'Second film — same colours, same landmarks, same pacemaker — but the area that was white is black again, and the heart edge is sharp. Your pneumonia has cleared completely. I think the answer will be yes; before I commit, let me ask about your recovery, your heart and sleep apnoea, and the trip.'

When admitted, when home? Days of antibiotics — finished? Still coughing, bringing anything up? ★ Any blood in it? Breathless walking or lying flat? Fever, chills, night sweats since? Chest pain? Appetite and weight?

Pacemaker — when put in, last checked? Any heart tablets, taken daily? Racing, fluttering, funny beating? Dizzy spells or blackouts? ★ 'And the sleep apnoea — how many nights a week do you actually use the CPAP?' → 'Thank you for being honest — I want to come back to that, there are things we can do about the mask'

Asthma or emphysema? Diabetes, kidney, liver, cancer? Steroid tablets? Stroke, memory trouble, choking on food or drink? What medications? ('Somac is pantoprazole — that settles acid') Flu and pneumonia vaccinations up to date? ★ Do you smoke, how much? Alcohol? What did you do for work?
★ Where are you going, when, how long? Flying or driving? Who with, staying with whom? What are you planning to do while you're there? Travel insurance, enough of your medications?
'Yes, you can make this trip. Symptoms settled, oxygen normal, repeat film clear — there is no rule you must wait a set time after a pneumonia; what matters is that you've recovered, and you have.'

'One thing I'd steer you away from: the scuba dive. Diving puts the lungs under pressure and so soon after a pneumonia there's a real risk of lung injury. Snorkelling on the surface is fine. If you genuinely want to dive you need a formal dive medical first — and I'd rather that waited.'
pefe: No examination task. If the examiner asks for a doctor-level read: erect PA films; admission — right middle lobe consolidation with loss of the right heart border, dual-chamber pacemaker in situ with leads in the right atrium and right ventricle, no effusion; repeat — resolution of consolidation, right heart border restored
The letter: admission dates, antibiotic given, pacemaker (model/date), CPAP settings, medications, allergies, GP contact; hand over to any doctor in Cairns

Red flags, written: cough returning or worsening · more breathless · fever or chills · chest pain · coughing up blood · feeling faint → see a doctor; severe → 000; tell Anne so she can act if you can't

CPAP counselling: two nights a week = the discomfort without the benefit; untreated OSA → repeated overnight desaturation, higher BP, strain on a heart that already needs a pacemaker, more chest infections; fixes — different mask size, nasal pillows, humidifier; refer back to the sleep service for a refit; take the machine on the plane (airlines carry it as medical equipment — noted in the letter)

Smoking, 90 seconds: 'I won't lecture you, but at ten a day smoking is the biggest single thing making another pneumonia likely — and the one thing we can change. Have you thought about stopping?' → Quitline 13 7848 (they ring you back), nicotine patch + lozenge/gum, review a fortnight after she's home. Never moralise; if she says 'after the trip', accept it as a start

Vaccines and travel: influenza today (adjuvanted from 65), check pneumococcal (funded at 70; from 50 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander; earlier with risk conditions) and COVID booster; up there — avoid coughs and crowded indoor places while the lungs finish healing, repellent, don't drink from creeks, wet season keep cuts covered and out of mud; on the flight drink water and walk about
SA: Country Health Connect for the sleep-service referral pathway if rural; healthdirect 1800 022 222; TIS 131 450
fails: Answering 'yes, off you go' after the films and losing the history — or never giving a clear verdict at all ★
Accepting 'yes I've got the machine' — never asking how many nights ★
Never asking about smoking, or not quantifying it
Not asking what she'll do on the trip — the dive advice is the only patient-specific advice in the station
Safety-net with nothing written; no letter; no red flags; no 000

Starting the film with the abnormality; not naming the pacemaker; not comparing the two films; turning smoking into a full cessation consult; lecturing (she becomes defensive: 'I've heard all this before')
numbers: Quitline 13 7848 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450 · 000

Radiographic clearance normally 4–6 weeks · repeat film at 6 weeks in smokers over 50 · CURB-65 and SMART-COP ≥3 are severity tools at presentation, NOT travel tools · cabin altitude equivalent 1,500–2,500 m VERIFY
Influenza annually, adjuvanted from 65 · pneumococcal funded at 70 (50 for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults; earlier with risk conditions) VERIFY current NIP
Long-term PPI is a modest pneumonia risk factor · OSA untreated → hypertension, arrhythmia, higher infection risk · CPAP adherence target ≥4 h/night on ≥70% of nights VERIFY

Variant 1 examiner: 'what is her risk score?' → 'there is no validated risk score for travel after pneumonia; I assessed her under four headings — complete resolution, comorbidity control, ongoing risk factors, demands of the trip — and she is fit, with two modifiable risks addressed'

Variant 2 still symptomatic, shadow not cleared: 'my advice is different from what you hoped' — persistent cough and incomplete clearance at 65 with a smoking history → bloods and CT chest before travel to be certain nothing sits behind the infection; postpone a few weeks; book the scan this week
Variant 3 overseas: destination vaccines, food/water, mosquitoes, insurance with declared pre-existing conditions, medications in hand luggage with a letter, nearest reliable facility

setting: General practice.
stem: Jenny Alcott, 60, has been brought to your practice. She has been breathless for two months and has been coughing up red / pink sputum.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 5 minutes)
A chest X-ray is provided at 5 minutes — explain it to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient
time: 8 minutes. History 5 min · film ≤1 min · diagnosis, reasoning and differentials 2 min.

back.dx: Small right pleural effusion secondary to lung cancer — two months of progressive exertional breathlessness ('can't get enough air'), now some breathlessness at rest, pink/streaky red sputum five or six times in a fortnight (a few drops, no clots), dry cough, 5 kg weight loss since Easter, poor appetite, very tired; retired aged-care nurse; smoked ten years in her twenties; no asbestos, no fevers/sweats/travel, one pillow, no oedema. Film: blunted right costophrenic angle, sharp left angle, trachea central. DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: 'pleural effusion' is a sign, not a diagnosis — name the finding, then name the cause as 'a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung', justified from her own findings.
plan: Vitals — REACT to SpO2 91%: 'her saturations are low, so I'd keep her oxygen on while we talk'. WIPE, open question, acknowledge the fear, promise a process

Beat one (90 s): describe the breathlessness (air in / tightness / not enough air), duration, constant, worse?, modifiers → 'does rest help — are you ever breathless at rest?' → sputum: how many times, pink or red, streaks/clots, how much → cough, wheeze
Beat two (70 s): CANCER BLOCK FIRST — weight loss quantified, appetite, lumps, previous cancer, occupation now AND before, asbestos, arm numbness/eyelid/face (Pancoast)

Beat three: chest pain/palpitations/dizziness; family atopy; smoke now OR EVER; childhood chest infections; fever, sore throat, night sweats, travel, TB contact; pillows, leg swelling; rash, joints; tiredness; SADMA only if spare
Film in ≤1 min: three colours → heart, spine, airway central → normal LEFT side first, sharp angle → right angle missing, filled in → 'fluid around the lung — a pleural effusion'

'Breathlessness can have a number of causes — but in your case I have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung' → three reasons (weight loss, blood in sputum, fluid on the film) → pause, acknowledge, support person → differential list → plan (bloods, CT, US-guided pleural tap, urgent respiratory referral) → safety-net → teach-back
ask: Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature? → acknowledge the low saturation
'I'm so sorry to hear that, and I understand how worrying it must be. Let me ask a few questions, then I'll go through your chest X-ray with you, find the cause and make the best plan.'

Is it difficulty getting the breath in, tightness, or not enough air? How long? Constant or on and off? Worse? Better or worse with anything? ★ 'You've said it's worse walking — does rest make it better? Are you ever breathless at rest, sitting still?'
The pink phlegm — how many times? Pink or frankly red? Streaks or clots? A few drops, a teaspoon, or more? Cough with it? Noisy breathing or wheeze?

★ Cancer block: lost weight without trying — how much, over what period? Appetite? Lumps or bumps? Ever had cancer before? Occupation now — and before that? Asbestos? Numbness or weakness in the arm, anyone comment on your eyelid or face?
Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ 'Do you smoke now, or have you ever smoked?' Recurrent chest infections as a child?
Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose? Night sweats, overseas travel, TB contact? Breathless lying flat — how many pillows? Leg swelling? Rashes, joint pains? Unusually tired?

Film: 'This is an X-ray of your chest. Three colours — white is bone, grey soft tissue, black is air. This big shadow is your heart, down the centre your spine, this line your main airway, sitting nicely central. Start with the normal side: on your left the lung is dark and there's a sharp angle at the bottom where lung meets chest wall. On your right that sharp angle is missing — filled in. That happens when fluid collects around the lung — we call it a pleural effusion.'
pefe: No examination task. If examiner wants a doctor-level read: erect PA, adequate inspiration and penetration, no rotation; blunting of the right costophrenic angle with a meniscus; trachea and mediastinum central; no pneumothorax; no focal bony lesion — small right pleural effusion. Never say this to the patient
Speak in HER sides — the patient's right is on the image left; the marker R sits over her right

Diagnosis: 'I do have a concern about the possibility of a cancer in the lung. I want to explain why, because it isn't a guess: you've been losing weight without trying, you've been coughing up what I believe is blood, and your X-ray shows fluid around the lung. I can't tell you today that that's what it is — but I'm not going to wait either.' → 'I can see that's a shock, I'm sorry to be telling you this today. Take a moment. Is there someone you'd like with you? I'll write everything down.'

Differentials, spoken: infection in the chest including TB (no fevers, sweats, travel) · heart not pumping well (one pillow, no ankle swelling) · liver or kidney problems, underactive thyroid · asthma · smoking damage · scarring from dusts at work · repeated chest infections · low in blood

Plan: FBE, UEC, LFT, TFT; CT chest; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration by a specialist (protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S, pH) — 'tells us what the fluid is and often what's causing it; draining some will help your breathing'; urgent respiratory referral; review in a few days regardless; safety-net — much more breathless, more blood, chest pain, fever → straight to hospital

Version B (James Whitlock, 70): massive LEFT effusion with mediastinal shift to the right — 'a large white shadow covering most of the lung, pressing it upward, and your heart has been pushed across'; answer = primary lung cancer OR metastatic prostate cancer (name both, say you can't separate them from the film), third differential occupational lung disease incl. mesothelioma (boilermaker, asbestos) → see MED-26
SA: urgent respiratory referral RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; Aboriginal Liaison Officer if relevant; TIS 131 450
fails: Never saying 'pleural effusion' on the film; or stopping at 'fluid in your lung' without naming the CAUSE ★
Cancer block left to the end 'if there's time'; weight loss not quantified; haemoptysis not characterised; 'do you smoke?' without 'ever' ★
'You have lung cancer' as a verdict — or 'probably nothing serious' as false reassurance; ploughing from the word cancer straight into the list without a pause
Omitting the rest-breathlessness question; forgetting pillows (HF) or travel (TB)
Jargon on the film (costophrenic, opacification); reversing her sides; film over a minute; not reacting to SpO2 91%
Skipping the differential list after naming cancer; no plan, no safety-net
numbers: Film script ≤1 min: three colours → three landmarks → normal side → abnormal side → NAME IT · white = bone, grey = soft tissue, black = air · heart, spine, trachea
Fluid visible ~200 mL on PA, ~50 mL lateral · white-out: shift AWAY = effusion, TOWARDS = collapse, none = consolidation VERIFY

Exudate: cancer, infection/empyema, TB, infarct, connective tissue · transudate: heart failure, liver failure, nephrotic, hypothyroidism · Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, fluid LDH >⅔ ULN VERIFY
Signs: reduced expansion, stony dull, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting · cytology ×3 VERIFY

Four beats: complaint 90 s · cancer block 70 s · sweep 2 min · film + diagnosis + list + plan 3 min · self-check when the film appears: weight quantified, haemoptysis, previous cancer, occupation before, smoking ever

Variant B 'just tell me straight — is it cancer?' → 'I don't know yet — I need the scan and a sample of the fluid. But I won't pretend: cancer is the thing I'm most concerned about, which is why I'm arranging things urgently. You'll hear it from me as soon as I know' · Variant C 78 F, four pillows, oedema, bilateral small effusions, big heart → heart failure, not the cancer recall
Four questions for any named past condition: when · treatment · follow-up · complications

Clarify the TRUE duration; describe, constant, progression, modifiers; rest question + breathless at rest; cough, wheeze

Chest pain, racing heart, dizziness? Family asthma, eczema, hay fever? ★ 'Do you smoke now, or have you ever smoked?' → pack a day 30 years, stopped 5 years ago. Childhood chest infections? Fevers, chills, sore throat, runny nose? Night sweats, travel, TB contact? Lying flat — pillows? Leg swelling? Rashes, joints? Tired?

Film: 'Three colours — white bone, grey soft tissue, black air. Heart, spine, main airway. On your right the lung is dark and healthy with a sharp angle at the bottom — normal. On your left there's a large white shadow covering most of the lung, pressing it upward, and your heart has been pushed across a little away from that side. That white area is fluid collecting around the lung — a pleural effusion.'

'James, breathlessness can have a number of causes. But in your case my main concern is the possibility of a cancer in the lung — or a spread of your prostate cancer to the lung. It isn't a guess: you've lost around four kilos without trying, you have a previous cancer, you smoked heavily for thirty years, and your X-ray shows a large collection of fluid. From the X-ray alone I can't tell which of those two it is — both are genuinely possible. That's what the next tests are for.'

'The other thing high on my list, because you were a boilermaker, is a lung condition caused by dust and asbestos — scarring, or a specific cancer of the lining of the lung. Beyond that: infection including TB; the heart not pumping well; smoking damage; asthma; repeated chest infections; being low in blood.'
pefe: No examination task. Doctor-level read if asked: near-complete opacification of the left hemithorax with a meniscus superiorly, mediastinal shift to the right, right lung clear, no visible rib lesion — massive left pleural effusion

If challenged on the boilermaker: 'boilermaking was a high asbestos-exposure trade in Australia, so alongside dust-related interstitial disease I'd specifically consider mesothelioma, asbestosis and benign pleural plaques — a unilateral effusion in that occupational context raises mesothelioma until excluded; it also has occupational compensation implications (ReturnToWorkSA / asbestos-related disease claims)'

Plan: bloods incl. FBE, UEC, LFT, PSA; CT chest ± abdomen/pelvis; ultrasound-guided pleural aspiration (protein, LDH, cytology ×3, MC&S) and therapeutic drainage ≤1–1.5 L per sitting; urgent respiratory referral; multidisciplinary lung cancer / urology input; safety-net — much more breathless, haemoptysis, chest pain, fever → hospital; support person (his wife); written summary

Role-player behaviour: understates; if you rush past the cancer word without acknowledgement he looks away and gives short answers; if you use jargon he asks 'sorry, what does that mean?'; near the end asks 'what else could it be?' / 'is it the cancer come back?'
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if he deteriorates in a regional setting; PATS for tertiary appointments; RFDS; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20; TIS 131 450
fails: Naming only one cancer — not saying both primary lung and metastatic prostate, or not saying you can't separate them ★
Taking 'I don't smoke', 'I'm retired', 'a bit' at face value — missing 30 pack-years, the boilermaker, the 4 kg ★
Prostate cancer dropped and not followed by the four questions and bone pain
Accepting 'last week' from the stem; omitting the rest question; omitting haemoptysis because it wasn't in the stem
Not saying 'pleural effusion'; jargon; reversing sides; film over a minute; not describing the mediastinal shift
No occupational lung disease in the differential; no pause after bad news; no plan or safety-net
numbers: Version B: 70 M · 3 months · 3–4 kg loss · prostate cancer 6 years · 30 pack-years · boilermaker · massive left effusion with shift · answer = both cancers + occupational third
White-out with shift AWAY = effusion; TOWARDS = collapse; no shift = consolidation · massive effusion = >⅔ hemithorax VERIFY
Mesothelioma latency 20–40 years after asbestos · boilermaking, shipbuilding, lagging, Wittenoom = high-exposure history VERIFY
Four questions for a named past cancer: when · treatment · follow-up · complications/spread — then bone pain for prostate
Light's criteria: protein ratio >0.5 · LDH ratio >0.6 · fluid LDH >⅔ ULN · cytology ×3 · drain ≤1–1.5 L per sitting VERIFY
Calibrated phrase: 'a concern about the possibility of' — never 'you have cancer', never 'probably nothing'
Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · TIS 131 450

setting: General practice.
stem: Gerald Munro, 60, presents with shortness of breath for three months. The previous doctor has already requested a full blood count, thyroid, liver and renal function — all normal. Spirometry has also been requested and will be given to you.
Spirometry: FEV1 predicted 2.60 L, pre-bronchodilator 1.35 (52%), post 1.37 (53%) · FVC predicted 3.35, pre 2.50, post 2.54 · FEV1/FVC predicted 0.83, measured 0.54.
tasks: Take a history and rule out your differentials
Interpret the spirometry — to the examiner face-to-face, to the patient online
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
time: 8 minutes. History 5 · chart 1.5 · explanation 1.5.

back.dx: Moderate COPD — 40 pack-years ('gave it up two years back' — you must ask 'did you ever?'), three months of progressive exertional air hunger (stops at the top of the drive), not at rest, morning cough with clear phlegm; fitter at the works forty years with asbestos in the old sheds (ask occupation); no red flags, one pillow, no oedema, one BP tablet; father had emphysema. Chart: ratio 0.54 vs predicted 0.83 → obstructive; FEV1 1.35 → 1.37 = 20 mL, 1.5% → not reversible (<200 mL and <12%) → COPD not asthma; post-BD ratio <0.70 confirms; post-BD FEV1 53% = moderate. The examiner marks the WORKINGS: 'step one, the ratio measured against predicted…'. Hidden agenda: he blames himself and is frightened of ending up like his father.
plan: Vitals even though it's 'three months'; intro; 'how can I help?'; acknowledge the frustration of a pile of normal bloods and no answer; agenda
Heart or lung: tightness vs difficulty getting air in; duration; constant; worse?; better/worse; at rest?; cough, wheeze, phlegm
Cancer and occupation: weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, haemoptysis, previous cancer; occupation now and before; dust, fumes, stone, asbestos, mask

'Do you smoke, or did you?' → 'did you ever? how much, how long?' → say '40 pack-years' aloud; chest pain, palpitations, dizziness; pillows, ankle swelling; childhood infections; atopy/family asthma; fevers, sweats, travel, TB; joints, rashes; tiredness, bleeding; medications, allergies, FHx (father — emphysema)

Chart: FIVE SECONDS OF SILENCE → name the columns → step 1 ratio vs predicted → obstructive → step 2 FEV1 pre vs post (never the ratio again) → 0.02 L = 20 mL, 1.5% → below both thresholds → COPD → post-BD ratio <0.70 confirms → 53% = moderate

Diagnosis with TWO reasons (40 pack-years; airway narrowing that barely moved with Ventolin) → 'is it going to get worse?' honest: doesn't reverse, slope is in our hands, stopped smoking already, inhalers, pulmonary rehab, vaccines → differentials with one reason each (~8) → plan and summary to examiner
ask: Before I start, could I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?

Tell me about the breathlessness — is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in? How long, constant or comes and goes, getting worse? What makes it better or worse — and are you short of breath at rest as well? Cough, wheeze, noisy breathing, phlegm?
★ Lost weight without trying? Appetite? Lumps or bumps, night sweats? Have you coughed up any blood? Any previous cancer?
★ What is your occupation, and what did you do before that? Worked with dust, fumes or stone? Asbestos? Mask or respirator?
★ Do you smoke, or did you? → 'gave it up' → 'And before that — how much, and for how long?' → 'That's forty pack-years, which is important and I'll come back to it'

Chest pain on exertion, palpitations, dizziness? Worse lying flat — how many pillows? Ankle swelling? Childhood chest infections or repeated pneumonias? Hay fever, eczema, asthma in the family? Fevers, sweats, travel, TB contact? Joint pains, rashes? Tiredness, bleeding? Medications incl. anything long-term? Allergies? Family history?

Chart to the examiner: 'Before I interpret this, let me orientate myself to what I've been given: pre- and post-bronchodilator columns, predicted values, percentage predicted in brackets, and all three values I need — FEV1, FVC and the ratio. Step one, the ratio measured against predicted: 0.54 against 0.83 — decreased, so an obstructive pattern; obstruction is now certain. Step two, because the ratio is decreased, I compare FEV1 before and after the bronchodilator — the predicted values and the ratio are no longer relevant. 1.35 to 1.37 litres: 0.02 litres, that is 20 millilitres, about 1.5 per cent. Under 200 mL and under 12 per cent — no significant reversibility, so COPD rather than asthma. Post-bronchodilator ratio remains below 0.70, which confirms COPD; post-bronchodilator FEV1 53 per cent predicted = moderate airflow limitation.'

To the patient (online): 'Three numbers — total air you can blow out, air in the first second, and the ratio. Your ratio is lower than expected for your age and height — narrowing in your airways. We gave you a puff of Ventolin and repeated it; your numbers barely moved, about 20 millilitres. Asthma usually improves a lot with that puffer, this hasn't. So the pattern fits COPD.'
pefe: No examination task

Diagnosis: 'most likely COPD — chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. In plain terms your lungs have been damaged by many years of smoking. Two reasons: a pack a day for forty years, the single biggest cause; and your breathing test shows narrowing that barely improved with the puffer — that pattern points to COPD rather than asthma'

'Is it going to get worse?' → 'I'll be honest: COPD doesn't reverse. But how fast it progresses is very much in our hands — the biggest thing is you've already stopped smoking, which changes the slope more than any tablet. Inhalers make day-to-day breathing easier, pulmonary rehabilitation genuinely improves what people can do, vaccinations keep you out of hospital'

Differentials, one reason each: lung cancer (no weight loss, no haemoptysis — still CXR) · IHD and heart failure (no chest pain, no oedema, sleeps flat) · asthma (puffer test) · interstitial lung disease from asbestos (HRCT, keep an eye) · bronchiectasis · infections incl. TB · sarcoidosis · anaemia (FBC normal)

Summary to examiner: CXR; consider HRCT for the asbestos history; reinforce abstinence; inhaled bronchodilator (LAMA first-line; LAMA/LABA if still symptomatic); pulmonary rehabilitation; influenza, pneumococcal, COVID vaccination; written COPD action plan; review; Lung Foundation resources VERIFY
SA: pulmonary rehab via Country Health Connect / local hospital; Quitline 13 7848 (already quit — relapse prevention); PATS for respiratory review; TIS 131 450
fails: Reading numbers out and appending a guess — 'ratio 0.54, FEV1 1.35, I think COPD' ★
Comparing the ratio pre and post bronchodilator instead of FEV1 ★
Quoting one threshold, or getting the units wrong (0.02 L is 20 mL, not 0.02 mL) ★
Not asking 'did you ever smoke?' — missing 40 pack-years ★
Dropping the cancer questions / haemoptysis because the bloods were normal ★
Not pausing to read the chart layout; naming the pattern not the disease; fewer than six differentials; breezy 'nothing to worry about' ('my father died of this'); jargon ('you've lost me, doc')
numbers: Three values only: FEV1 · FVC · FEV1/FVC · % predicted = measured ÷ predicted × 100 · reversibility = (post − pre) ÷ pre × 100 · significant = ≥200 mL AND ≥12% · bronchodilator repeated after 10–15 min VERIFY

This chart: ratio 0.54 vs 0.83 · FEV1 1.35 → 1.37 L = 20 mL, 1.5% · post-BD ratio <0.70 = COPD · severity on post-BD FEV1 %: ≥80 mild · 50–79 moderate · 30–49 severe · <30 very severe → 53% moderate VERIFY (GOLD)
Pack-years = packs/day × years: 1 × 40 = 40 · FeNO ≥40 ppb supports asthma · mesothelioma latency 20–40 years VERIFY

Variant 1 restrictive (45-yo stonemason, engineered benchtops): ratio 0.90 vs 0.79 = increased → not obstructive; FEV1 and FVC both ~half predicted → restrictive; confirm with lung volumes and gas transfer, HRCT; ILD/silicosis; notify SafeWork SA, ReturnToWorkSA claim, screen co-workers; engineered stone prohibited nationally VERIFY
Variant 2 reversible: FEV1 3.00 → 3.70 = 700 mL, 23% → exceeds both thresholds → asthma

Variant 3 spirometry pending, CXR handed over: flattened hemidiaphragms, hyperlucent fields, long narrow tubular heart, >6 anterior ribs above the diaphragm → hyperinflation, emphysema/COPD — describe first, don't just say 'COPD'
Variant 4 normal chart: doesn't exclude asthma (normal between episodes) → FeNO or bronchial challenge; revisit cardiac and non-respiratory causes
