★ 'Do you have any weather preference — are you intolerant of cold or of heat?' → 'Thank you, that is helpful. Let me ask a few more about that.'

★ 'Has your skin been dry?' / ★ 'Have you been constipated?' / ★ 'Have you had any weight gain?' / ★ 'Any hair loss — and have you noticed the outer part of your eyebrows thinning?' / ★ 'Any puffiness of your eyelids, face or legs?' / 'Has your voice become hoarse? Any swelling in your neck or difficulty swallowing?'
★ 'When was your last period? Are they regular? Any hot flushes?'

★ 'I would like to perform a thyroid examination — asking her permission to expose the neck and remove any scarf, and offering a chaperone.' / ★ 'What is the relaxation phase of the ankle reflex?' / 'Can she rise from a chair without using her arms?' / 'Pemberton's sign, given the goitre' / 'Is that sugar random or fasting?'

★ 'Most likely you have hypothyroidism. The gland in the front of your neck is underactive and is not making enough of its hormone.' / ★ 'The reasons I have come to this today are your own answers and what I found when I examined you…'

★ 'I considered menopause — it can cause exactly this at your age, but it is less likely in you because your periods are regular and you have no hot flushes.' / 'Anaemia — less likely, no breathlessness or palpitations on exertion, periods not heavy, but I will still check.' / 'Depression — less likely, your mood is reasonable and you still enjoy things.'

'The main test is called TSH, which measures how hard your body is having to push the gland.' / 'Will I be on tablets forever?' → 'Usually yes — one tablet a day, inexpensive, and most people feel like themselves again.' / 'Will the weight come off?' → 'Some usually does — a lot is fluid — but treating the thyroid does not usually take off all the weight on its own; it should give you back the energy to be active.'
Never say to the patient: TSH unexplained, euthyroid, myxoedema, Woltman sign, or 'your metabolism is slow' without the plain-English version
pefe: Examiner: dressed warmly; dry, coarse skin; no pallor/jaundice/rash · T normal, ★ pulse 60 regular, BP 110/70 · ★ diffusely enlarged thyroid, moves on swallowing, no nodules, non-tender, percussion resonant (no retrosternal extension) · no lymphadenopathy · HS normal, chest clear · no hepatosplenomegaly · ★ reflexes present with delayed relaxation phase · power normal · Pemberton negative · random BSL normal, dipstick normal

If asked what you are looking for mid-thyroid exam: 'a swelling that moves upwards on swallowing — thyroid rather than node or cyst; diffuse vs nodular — a discrete nodule changes the pathway to ultrasound; percussion for retrosternal extension'
Variant — single firm nodule: thyroid ultrasound ± FNA by sonographic features and size; still TSH first (suppressed TSH → functioning nodule) VERIFY
Variant — periods stopped 8 months ago with hot flushes: menopause moves to the top, but they overlap and coexist — still check TSH before attributing everything to menopause
Variant — lithium or amiodarone: both cause hypothyroidism; check TSH (lithium: renal function and level too); discuss with the prescriber rather than stopping it
Variant — pregnant or planning: requirement rises, targets tighter — urgent TSH, start/increase early, obstetric team, monitor more often VERIFY

Bloods: TSH first → free T4 if abnormal → TPO antibodies for cause; high TSH + low fT4 = primary; high TSH + normal fT4 = subclinical · plus FBE, ferritin, HbA1c, coeliac serology, UEC, LFT · levothyroxine ~1.6 µg/kg/day full replacement, start 25–50 µg if older or cardiac VERIFY · empty stomach, separate from calcium/iron by ~4 h · recheck TSH 6–8 weeks · SA: TIS 131 450 · PATS >100 km VERIFY

setting: General practice. You are the GP. The patient attends alone. Version 1 — she stopped the prednisolone abruptly.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago (some versions: giant cell arteritis; Version 3: sarcoidosis). She attends today concerned about tiredness and, separately, loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes — 7 + 1, the longest history and shortest close in the cluster. Acknowledge the concern · both complaints explored, weight loss quantified (how much, over how long) · the steroid block and the hinge question 'abruptly, or reduced gradually?' · follow the dog into the mood · adrenal features (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving) and steroid-diabetes questions · malignancy red flags and the THREE screening programs · rest of the mnemonic, postmenopausal bleeding, geriatric screen · 60-second answer: name, two-sentence explanation, reasons, then the list fast.

back.dx: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (not crisis — stable, talking) after abrupt cessation of prednisolone four months into PMR treatment: six weeks of profound fatigue, 5–6 kg unintentional weight loss, poor appetite, nausea, abdominal pain, loose bowels, postural light-headedness; stopped the tablet abruptly six weeks ago after her dog died, nobody told her to taper, missed follow-up; no PMR/GCA relapse features; mood flat since the bereavement (grief; screen, not diagnose). Reasons: tired, weight loss, abrupt cessation after four months, GI features. Differentials (the list is the mark): malignancy — leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel (no lumps, screening up to date); depression/adjustment disorder after the loss; relapse of PMR/GCA; steroid-induced diabetes; thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, other autoimmune, medications, heart failure, OSA. Plan: morning cortisol today (short Synacthen if needed), restart prednisolone with a proper taper, steroid card, sick-day rules, emergency advice, mood review next week. Handle 'is it my fault?' without blame.
plan: Intro, 'how would you like me to address you?'; ★ acknowledge the concern in one line; permission to proceed

Tired: feverish / low energy / sleepy → no energy · 6 weeks · constant · worse · nothing helps · can't do housework · ★ weight: 'how many kilograms, and over what period?' → 5–6 kg in 6 weeks, not trying

★ Steroid block: when diagnosed · what treatment · 'are you taking it regularly?' → stopped · why? → the dog · ★ 'did you stop it abruptly, or reduce the dose gradually?' → just stopped · side effects (weight gain) · follow-up (missed) · relapse: shoulder/hip stiffness; GCA: headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change
★ 'I'm so sorry about your dog — how are you coping?' · mood · anhedonia (three questions, twenty seconds)
★ Adrenal features: nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, postural dizziness, salt craving · steroid-diabetes: polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections
Malignancy: appetite, lumps, night sweats, family cancer · ★ three screening programs: mammogram, cervical screening test, bowel cancer kit

Rest of the mnemonic briskly: tanning/jaundice, heat/cold, exertional dyspnoea/palpitations, joints/rash, fever/travel, bowel change/blood, cough, smoking, snoring, occupation, other meds/OTC, allergies · ★ 'when did your periods stop — any bleeding since?' · geriatric screen: memory, who do you live with, support, falls, who cooks (lives alone, husband died 3 years ago, son in Perth, 'toast mostly') · 'what are you worried about?' (sister — cancer)

★ 60 s: 'adrenal insufficiency — on long-term steroids the adrenal gland stops working; stop suddenly and it can't restart straight away'; reasons; ★ the list, read fast; 'bloods today incl. morning cortisol, restart the steroid with a plan to reduce slowly, a card, sick-day rules; vomiting, very dizzy or confused = ambulance; see you next week about your mood'
ask: 'When you say tired — feverish, low in energy, or sleepy?' / ★ 'How many kilograms, and over what period?'
'When were you diagnosed? What treatment? Are you taking it regularly?' → 'Can I ask why you stopped?' → ★ 'Did you stop it abruptly, or did you reduce the dose gradually?'
'Any shoulder or hip stiffness? Any headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on chewing, or change in your vision?'
★ 'I'm so sorry about your dog. How are you coping with that?' → 'How has your mood been? Still enjoying the things you used to?'
★ 'Any nausea or vomiting? Tummy pain? Diarrhoea? Dizziness when you stand? Craving salty food?' / 'Because you've been on steroids — more urine, thirstier, recurrent infections?'
★ 'Are you up to date with your mammogram, cervical screening test and bowel kit?' / ★ 'When did your periods stop — have you had any bleeding since?'
'How's your memory? Who do you live with? Enough support? Any falls? Who does the cooking?'

★ 'When you take steroids for a long time the adrenal gland stops working; if you stop suddenly it can't restart straight away.' / 'My reasons are that you're tired, you've lost weight, you stopped your prednisolone abruptly after four months, and you've had nausea, tummy pain and loose bowels.'

'So it's my fault for stopping the tablets?' → ★ 'No — nobody explained that these tablets have to be reduced slowly rather than stopped, and that's something we should have made much clearer. It's very treatable.'
★ 'If you start vomiting, become very dizzy or confused — that's an emergency, call an ambulance.'

setting: General practice. You are the GP. Version 2 of the steroid station — she is still taking the prednisolone. Stem reconstructed from the variant section.
stem: Samantha (Sam) Doyle, 60, was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica four months ago and remains on prednisolone. She attends today concerned about tiredness and loss of weight.
tasks: Take a relevant history (7 minutes)
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses (1 minute)
time: 8 minutes, 7 + 1. Identical spine to MED-63 — the steroid block comes back clean (compliant, followed up, no relapse, no side effects). Say nothing about the recall; work down the mnemonic until you reach mood, then complete the depression criteria and the safety question. Do NOT do a full psychiatric history — plan the case from the complaint, not the outcome.

back.dx: Major depressive disorder presenting as tiredness and weight loss in a bereaved 60-year-old widow living alone: low mood, anhedonia, middle-of-the-night waking, poor appetite with weight loss, poor concentration, guilt/worthlessness, fatigue — five or more of nine features over more than two weeks; no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. Steroid history clean (taking it, tapering as planned, follow-up kept, no relapse). Differentials — the same broad list: malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma, breast, bowel — no lumps, screening up to date), adrenal insufficiency (excluded — never stopped), PMR/GCA relapse, steroid-induced diabetes, thyroid, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications (steroid-induced mood change), heart failure, OSA. The one exception to 'no full psychiatric history' is the safety question — never omit it. If challenged: 'I approached this as undifferentiated tiredness and screened organic causes first; having reached a mood disorder I would complete a full mental state assessment at a dedicated follow-up.'

Tired defined, explored; ★ weight loss quantified (amount, period)

Then the list fast; bloods today to exclude organic causes; dedicated follow-up for a full assessment and treatment plan; safety net.

'I did consider other things — because of the weight loss, cancers such as leukaemia, lymphoma, breast and bowel, but no lumps and your screening is up to date; a relapse of the polymyalgia; the steroid affecting your mood or your sugar; thyroid disease, anaemia, haemochromatosis, hepatitis, coeliac disease, other autoimmune conditions, heart failure and sleep apnoea.'

time: 8 minutes. Four reasons: dry cough for three weeks; low-grade rather than high fever; aches, night sweats and exhaustion; and the antibiotic failure points towards, not away from, this — plus right-sided chest signs. Differentials in two announced groups. Group 1, other causes of persistent cough: typical bacterial pneumonia (chesty cough, high fever, would have responded), tuberculosis (taken seriously — three weeks of cough with night sweats; no weight loss or haemoptysis; CXR and sputum settle it), lung cancer (CXR in any adult with cough >3 weeks, never-smoker or not). Group 2, travel-acquired infections: Q fever, leptospirosis, melioidosis, mosquito-borne viruses — Ross River fits the aches. Then the negative screen: anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, hepatitis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications, mood, OSA. Do not blame the previous doctor. Plan: CXR today, bloods, sputum, atypical PCR swab, travel serology; doxycycline 100 mg bd 5–7 days (macrolide if pregnant or <8 y); review 48 h; named red flags.

setting: Regional general practice, Wallaroo, South Australia. You are the GP. Booked for routine BP monitoring with the practice nurse; nurse's note: BP 135/85, he has asked to see you because he has been feeling tired.
stem: James Corrigan, 40, has known hypertension on perindopril for six months. He attended for routine blood pressure monitoring with the practice nurse (BP 135/85 mmHg) and has asked for a consultation because he has been feeling tired lately.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
No management or investigations task — do not drift into either

Acknowledge, contract · sleepy vs low energy — get the fork right in the first minute · H to D in ~90 s · C: the heart-failure screen you must be HEARD to do (clarify the ambiguous night-waking) · O: snoring/witnessed apnoeas, the sleep probe, weight, alcohol, ★ occupation → ★ sleepy at the wheel · hidden cardiac worry · plain-English diagnosis reasoned from his answers · BP link · three reasoned differentials then the list · non-blanket driving advice, safety net.

Reasons drawn from his own answers. BP link: OSA is a recognised cause of hypertension resistant to tablets (nocturnal sympathetic surges); treating the OSA may do more than another tablet. Differentials reasoned: heart failure (no chest pain, one pillow, no oedema — the arousals settle in seconds), lymphoma/leukaemia (no weight loss, lumps, sweats), infections — EBV, COVID, hepatitis, HIV (no fever, travel, risk); then hypothyroidism, diabetes, anaemia, haemochromatosis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications/alcohol, depression, shift work. Driving: no blanket ban, no blanket reassurance — 'I am not taking anything off you today'; do not drive sleepy; sleep study; commercial standards stricter (Austroads), specialist opinion and evidence of treatment; hidden worry is his father's MI at 58.

'I can't afford to stop. I'll push through.' → 'I don't want you to lose your income. setting: Your general practice. Face-to-face station. The role-player is in the room even though there is no history-taking task. Notice on the door: findings are given only if you ask for them specifically.
stem: Mary Whitfield, a 40-year-old woman, has presented complaining of feeling tired, weight loss over the last few months, night sweats and loss of appetite.
tasks: Ask the examiner for the findings of the physical examination you would perform
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Request your further investigations
time: 8 minutes (2 reading). Greet the patient first, then turn to the examiner. Frame the examination in one sentence · general, vitals (temperature first), hands, face/mouth · ★ all lymph node chains, then the four node characters · thyroid with the reason · bone tenderness · chest · abdomen — name splenomegaly · bedside tests · examination gate 5:10 · turn to her, warning shot, say the word lymphoma · reasons from your findings, not her stem · differentials by group · investigations in order — FBE, film, excisional biopsy, PET-CT — then the rest.

back.dx: Lymphoma (Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) presenting with B symptoms: four months of fatigue, ~7 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, anorexia, generalised pruritus; examination — pallor, thin and unwell, T 37.8, HR 96, scratch marks, ecchymoses, conjunctival pallor, two to three rubbery, fixed, non-tender cervical nodes (largest ~3 cm, skin normal), bone tenderness, splenomegaly 4 cm, thyroid normal, chest clear. Clubbing is present but is NOT a lymphoma sign — it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on the list (say so). Reasons to the patient led by your findings: rubbery, fixed, non-tender neck glands (infection glands are tender and mobile), enlarged spleen, scratch marks from the itch — plus her B symptoms. Differentials by group: other cancers — leukaemia (ecchymoses, bone tenderness), lung/bowel/breast; infections — TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis (some need consent); hyperthyroidism (explains fatigue, sweats, weight loss; thyroid normal today). Investigations in order of priority: FBE, blood film today, excisional node biopsy (architecture, not FNA cells), PET-CT staging (or CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis); then LDH, ESR/CRP, HIV and syphilis serology with consent, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma serology, IGRA + CXR, TSH. Febrile neutropenia = emergency: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour.
plan: Gel; ★ greet the patient first ('I've been asked to examine you and then talk you through what I think — give me a moment with the examiner'); ★ frame: 'a general examination with a focus on the haematological system, looking for a cause of B symptoms — general appearance, hands, face and mouth, all lymph node groups and thyroid, chest, abdomen, bedside tests'

General: cachexia, pallor, jaundice, rash · ★ vitals, temperature first, then HR, BP, RR, SpO2 · hands: clubbing, scratch marks, ecchymoses, joint swelling → ★ 'pruritus is a recognised feature of lymphoma' · ★ 'clubbing is not a lymphoma sign, so it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on my list' · face/mouth: conjunctival pallor, gum hypertrophy/bleeding, tonsils

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains over the whole body — cervical and supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal' → two to three cervical nodes → ★ 'consistency? mobile or fixed? tender? overlying skin? — I ask about tenderness to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy' → rubbery, fixed, non-tender, 3 cm → 'that is a malignant pattern'; ask anyway if the examiner deflects

Thyroid with the reason (hyperthyroidism explains tiredness, sweating, weight loss): mass, size, nodularity, tenderness, retrosternal percussion · ★ bone tenderness sternum/spine/long bones · chest: air entry, added sounds, S1 S2, murmur · abdomen: inspection, tenderness, masses, ★ 'specifically hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?' → spleen 4 cm · bedside BSL, dipstick — ★ stop asking at 5:10

Turn the chair fully, lower the voice, eye contact: ★ 'I have finished examining you, and I am afraid I have found some things that concern me. Is it alright if I go through them?' [pause] ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' — say the word, stop, let it land

★ Reasons led by findings: rubbery, fixed, non-sore neck glands vs infection glands; enlarged spleen; scratch marks — then her tiredness, weight loss, sweats. 'Am I going to die?' → no number you cannot stand behind; many lymphomas respond very well; not yet a diagnosis until a gland is sampled

★ Differentials by group: other cancers (leukaemia; lung/bowel/breast less likely), infections (TB, HIV, syphilis, EBV/CMV/toxoplasma — 'some need a blood test and your permission'), overactive thyroid; 'why HIV?' answered

★ To the examiner, in order and slowly: FBE · blood film today · excisional biopsy of a cervical node ('lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture; an aspirate gives cells without architecture') · PET-CT staging (or CT N/C/A/P) · then LDH, ESR, CRP; HIV and syphilis with consent; EBV/CMV/toxoplasma; IGRA + CXR; TSH · febrile neutropenia answer if asked · safety net to Mary (fever, breathlessness, face/neck swelling, bleeding → hospital; specialist phoned; results by phone; someone with you; Cancer Council SA 13 11 20)

★ 'A full lymph node examination, all chains, over the whole body.' → ★ 'Consistency? Mobile or fixed? Tender? And the overlying skin?' / ★ 'I am asking about tenderness because I want to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy.'
'Pruritus is a recognised feature of lymphoma.' / ★ 'Clubbing is not a lymphoma sign, so it keeps an intrathoracic malignancy on my list.' CORRECTION
★ 'Specifically, is there hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?' — 'any masses?' gets 'no'
★ 'I am afraid I have found some things that concern me.' → ★ 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.'

★ 'Glands from an infection are usually tender and mobile; yours are rubbery, they do not move under my fingers, and they are not sore. I also found your spleen — an organ on the left side of your abdomen — is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks from the itching.'
'Why HIV?' → 'Because HIV can cause swollen glands, weight loss and sweats, and it is treatable. I test for it in anyone with this picture. I'd need your consent, and the result stays confidential.'

★ 'My investigations in order of priority: one, full blood examination; two, a blood film today; three, an excisional biopsy of one of the cervical nodes — lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture, so an aspirate is not enough; four, PET-CT to stage.' Then the rest.

'If she rings tonight with a fever of 39?' → 'A medical emergency until proven otherwise — present immediately; blood cultures and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour; haematology involved; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval is needed.'

ask: 'Before we look at them — can I ask what prompted the test in the first place?'
'Any dizziness, confusion, memory trouble, headaches, tiredness, or any change in your walking or balance?'
★ 'Can you tell me every medicine you take — prescribed, bought over the counter, and anything herbal?'
'Your blood test shows a low sodium level. Sodium is a mineral, or a salt, that your body keeps in careful balance in the blood.'

'The most likely cause is a condition called SIADH — the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH. ADH is a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Your body makes more of it than it should, so you hold on to extra water, and that extra water dilutes the salt in your blood.'
'In your case the most likely trigger is your medication — both citalopram and carbamazepine are recognised causes, and that is a side effect rather than anything you have done wrong.'

'There are other things that can cause SIADH and I've looked for them: certain cancers, particularly of the lung, and lymphoma — your chest X-ray is normal; infections of the chest or the lining of the brain; and problems inside the head such as a bleed or an injury — your brain scan is normal.'

'Causes outside SIADH: losing fluid through vomiting, diarrhoea or not drinking enough; fluid tablets; an underactive thyroid, which your test has ruled out; and heart, liver or kidney problems, which your results and examination don't support.'

★ 'Should I stop them?' → 'Not today. We confirm it first, then I talk to whoever prescribes them — stopping an antidepressant suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms, and stopping carbamazepine suddenly can bring on seizures. We plan the change together.'
'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you get a bad headache, become confused or unusually drowsy, start vomiting, or have any fitting.'

stem: Mr John Whitfield, 60, known end-stage kidney disease on maintenance haemodialysis, attends for his scheduled session. He has had several days of palpitations and diarrhoea. back.dx: Acute kidney injury on end-stage kidney disease with hyperkalaemia (K 5.9 with ECG changes = treat as severe) — multifactorial: (1) perindopril dose increased by the GP last week (he can't say which tablet; deduce it from pharmacology — of perindopril, hydrochlorothiazide, erythropoietin, the ACE inhibitor is the one that raises potassium), (2) missed Monday's dialysis — a session's worth of potassium not removed, (3) four days of watery diarrhoea with poor intake and postural dizziness — volume depletion. eGFR 10–12 (baseline ESKD); VBG no significant acidosis → reduced clearance and retention, not a transcellular shift. 'You have hyperkalaemia' is a laboratory state, not a diagnosis — the commonest fail. Explain: 'your kidneys have taken a sudden knock on top of the long-standing damage — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease'; three reasons stacked; potassium controls the heart's electrical rhythm, hence the palpitations. Plan: cardiac monitor, dialysis brought forward to today, hold the perindopril, letter to the GP, don't stop anything else alone. Handle 'my GP did this to me' by explaining the monitoring gap (UEC 1–2 weeks after any ACE-i dose change), not the person.

Four differential buckets, numbered, in plain English: (1) not enough in — restricted diet; (2) losing it through the bowel — vomiting, diarrhoea, laxatives (name tablets, powders, teas); (3) losing extra through the kidneys — a tablet like his, or 'a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium' (primary aldosteronism: cramps, weakness, polyuria, resistant BP); (4) shift into cells — some asthma puffers, insulin, and 'a rare adrenaline-producing tumour' (phaeo triad: headache + sweating + palpitations, patients go pale, not flushed). back.dx: Excessive vitamin D supplementation (4 × 1000 IU = 4000 IU/day for six weeks, started because his mother has osteoporosis with two fractures this year) → probable hypercalcaemia → polydipsia. Ten days of constant worsening thirst, 4–5 L/day up from 2, no polyuria, nocturnal drinking not voiding, bowels sluggish this last week; no weight loss, vision change, infections; no bone pain, fatigue, sweats, bruising; no headache/vision loss; no heat intolerance, loose bowels, palpitations, tremor; no stones, nausea; lifestyle unremarkable. Four-link chain in plain words: vitamin D helps you absorb calcium → too much pushes blood calcium up → high calcium makes the kidneys pass out more water → your body feels that as thirst; the word is hypercalcaemia. Differentials, each with why less likely: diabetes (no polyuria/weight loss; finger-prick today anyway), overactive thyroid, a brain problem with the water-balance hormone (DI), a bone-marrow condition that raises calcium (myeloma — asked bone pain, tiredness, infections), everyday causes (coffee, alcohol, salt, heat). Honest uncertainty: no blood test yet, so no declared 'vitamin D poisoning'. Plan: stop the capsules today, bring the bottle in, BSL now, bloods for calcium, UEC, 25-OH vitamin D, glucose, TSH; drink to thirst 2–3 L; review when results back, phone sooner if needed. Separate him from his mother: her dose was worked out for her bones and her blood test — his wasn't; do not change her treatment.

Calcium was 'high last year'; she was told to stop her multivitamin and cut dairy — chronicity makes malignancy less likely but does not exclude it, and diet was never the driver (correct the science kindly without attacking the colleague). Only positive symptom: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk'. Malignancy screen clean (weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, breast/mammogram clear last year, cough, smoking, haematuria); mother had breast cancer at 60 — the hidden agenda; ask ICE before you explain. Explain: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, different job — keep blood calcium right; one is overworking, pulling calcium from bone; the hormone is raised, which confirms it; not cancer, not the thyroid tablets, not diet. Differentials named: cancers (blood, breast, lung, kidney), vitamin D/calcium antacid excess, fluid tablets, lithium, overactive thyroid (excluded), sarcoid/TB. Refer endocrinology (age <50 → surgery will be discussed, their decision with her); hydrate; do not restrict dairy; safety-net.

pefe: Role-player: Janine, 45, teacher's aide 4 days/week, husband, two teenagers, 40-min drive; levothyroxine 100 µg, never misses; stopped multivitamin last year on advice; Gaviscon ~monthly; no BP/fluid/mood tablets; never smoked, 2 wines Friday; mammogram last year clear; mother breast cancer at 60, alive. Only positive: 'a bit more thirsty, I keep a bottle on my desk' — given only if asked. Brisk, impatient at first; guarded during cancer questions; after the breast question asks 'why are you asking all this?' every time; if you read the total calcium as normal: 'so there's nothing wrong then?'; asks 'is it my thyroid tablets?' and 'will I need an operation?'; if falsely reassured before tests: 'how can you be sure?'. Hidden agenda released on ICE, else volunteered at ~7 min as you summarise

Examiner returns: PTH elevated · 25-OH vitamin D normal · phosphate low-normal · eGFR 88 · full examination normal · everything else normal. Examiner challenges: 'Why not image the parathyroids?' → 'the diagnosis is biochemical; sestamibi/ultrasound are for the surgeon to localise, not to diagnose' · 'Avoid dairy?' → 'no; severe restriction can worsen bone loss; hydration matters more' · 'Frusemide?' → 'only for overload during rehydration; not a routine calcium-lowering treatment'

Version B — high-dose health-food vitamin D for 8 months + calcium antacids most nights: examiner gives PTH suppressed <1.0, 25-OH D 310, eGFR 74, PO4 normal → 'a low parathyroid hormone tells me the gland is behaving and being switched off — the extra calcium is coming from somewhere else; your vitamin D is ~4× target — the supplement, probably with the antacids (milk–alkali)' → stop both today, hydrate, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ suppressed PTH is the MALIGNANCY arm — still complete CXR and bloods · corrected Ca 2.88

Variant C — 62, corrected Ca 3.15, 6 kg loss since Christmas, night-waking low back ache, worn out; Hb 96, creatinine 148, PTH suppressed, ESR 88 → 'myeloma until proved otherwise': SPEP, serum FLC, urine Bence-Jones, film, LDH, whole-body low-dose CT or MRI spine (not plain films); IV normal saline now; urgent haematology; ★ ask about cord compression (numbness, leg weakness, bladder/bowel) — same-day emergency; warning-shot register, 'today rather than next week'

Variant D — 58 on indapamide + lithium, corrected 2.72, asymptomatic: switch the thiazide to another antihypertensive, recheck 2–4 weeks; ★ do NOT stop lithium unilaterally — speak with the psychiatrist, decide together; check PTH (lithium can make the glands overactive) · Variant E — 28M, Ca 2.70 pre-employment, father and sister 'high calcium', PTH mildly raised: FHH — 24-h urine calcium and Ca:Cr clearance ratio (<0.01 supports), CaSR gene testing; these patients are harmed by parathyroid surgery
SA: endocrinology referral (RAH/FMC/Lyell McEwin); PATS for travel; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 only if a Version B/C patient needs retrieval; TIS 131 450
fails: Saying 'your calcium is actually normal' because you read the total line ★
PTH not first in the investigation list, or a flat list with no BECAUSE ★
Never asking a single cancer question; abandoning the malignancy screen because it was 'high last year' ★
Falsely reassuring ('it's definitely nothing') before any tests; or finishing on the diagnosis with no differentials, plan or safety-net ★
Jargon: 'PTH-dependent hypercalcaemia secondary to a parathyroid adenoma'
Endorsing the dairy restriction to avoid contradicting a colleague; asking 'any other medications?' and accepting 'no' without naming thiazide and lithium by use
Skipping ICE so the mother's cancer lands at minute seven; stopping the supplement in Version B and declaring the case closed; stopping lithium unilaterally in Variant D
numbers: Corrected Ca = total + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L) · here total 2.56, albumin 31, corrected 2.78 · reference 2.10–2.60 · mild <3.0 · moderate 3.0–3.5 · severe >3.5
Top three: PTH · 25-OH vitamin D + phosphate · UEC/eGFR · causes 1 and 2: hyperparathyroidism, then malignancy · adenoma ~85% of primary disease
Surgery triggers: age <50 · Ca >0.25 above upper limit · eGFR <60 · urine Ca >10 mmol/day · stones · T-score ≤−2.5 · FHH: Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01 · ECG: short QT
Severe: saline 4–6 L/24 h · zoledronic acid 4 mg IV over ≥15 min after rehydration · calcitonin 4 units/kg SC/IM 12-hourly · prednisolone 20–40 mg/day if vitamin D–mediated VERIFY

Timing: 0:00 WIPE/name it · 0:30 why/before · 1:00 symptoms · 1:45 malignancy · 2:45 drugs etc + ICE · 4:15 explain · 5:15 ranked ix · 6:15 dx/DDx/plan · cut the thyroid block, never the malignancy block · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: Suburban general practice; you are the GP. Vitals (including BSL) on request. 9-minute station. RECALL NOTE: the source recording verifies the stem and history; later tasks follow the standard three-task shape.
stem: Marianne Kovac, 50, presents with two days of nausea and vomiting on a week of feeling weak, tired and lethargic. She is holding a vomit bag. Known hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Current medications: perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings and investigations you want
Explain the most likely diagnosis and outline your immediate management
time: 9 minutes: 40 s opening · 4 min history · 1.5 min examination/investigations · 2 min explanation · 45 s safety-net and close. The diagnosis is on the medication list — the marks are for what you ask AFTER you've worked it out: ★ obs incl. BSL · acknowledge the bag, offer water · vomit content · ★ 'when did you start the PAINKILLER, who started it' + OTC/chemist separately · ★ cardiac screen unprompted · abdomen/melaena · ★ urine output, uraemic symptoms · fluid status FIRST · investigations by analyte incl. ECG and troponin · ★ diagnosis by name · triple whammy in plain English · stop, hold, ★ transfer today, no driving · teach-back.

back.dx: Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease (stage 2 — eGFR 45 → 22, creatinine roughly doubled) with hyperkalaemia (K 6.3 + peaked T waves, narrow QRS → treat as severe) and metabolic acidosis (HCO3 18) — the 'triple whammy': NSAID (constricts the afferent arteriole) + ACE inhibitor (dilates the efferent) + thiazide (lowers circulating volume), in a woman with baseline CKD. Ibuprofen 400 mg tds for three weeks for a knee — self-bought at the chemist, then scripted by a locum who didn't have her record; she doesn't call it a medication. Uraemic symptoms: much less urine, postural dizziness, metallic taste; examination — dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft, no bladder, no asterixis. BSL 5.4 removes DKA at the door; troponin normal and cardiac screen negative (nausea + lethargy without chest pain is a recognised MI presentation in women and CKD). Explain: 'your kidneys were working at about half strength and have taken a sudden extra hit — an acute injury on chronic kidney disease; waste products build up and cause the sickness and exhaustion'; mechanism of the three drugs in plain words; 'you can buy it anywhere' → 'that's exactly why it catches people out'. Plan: ibuprofen stops today and never again without checking; hold (not stop forever) perindopril and the thiazide while unwell; ★ ED today for fluids and potassium treatment — ring ahead, results with her, don't drive; repeat UEC 48–72 h; paracetamol + physiotherapy for the knee; letter to usual GP, flag on file. Hidden agenda: mother died on dialysis — 'not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off'.
plan: ★ 'Examiner — BP, pulse, RR, saturations, temperature AND blood sugar?' → 142/86, 72 reg, 16, 98%, afebrile, BSL 5.4 → 'stable, afebrile, normal sugar — a diabetic emergency is unlikely from the outset'
WIPE, 'how would you like me to address you?' · open · ★ 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?' (the vomit bag is marked)

Symptom package in one block: onset (tiredness 1 week, vomiting 2 days), worse, better/worse · 'tired — low energy, sleepy, or breathless?' · frequency 4–5/day · ★ 'what does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?' (UGI bleed vs obstruction; she's on an NSAID) · keeping anything down?

Background: when diagnosed CKD (5 y, 'about half') and HTN (10 y), what for them → perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' · adherence · ★ 'and when did you start the PAINKILLER — who started it, and what was it for?' → ibuprofen ~3 weeks, knee, self-bought then locum script · ★ 'did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?' → 'it's only ibuprofen' (don't correct now; save it) · 'anything from the chemist, or herbal?'

★ Cardiac screen, unprompted, 10 s: 'a few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious — chest/arm/jaw/back discomfort, exertional SOB, cold sweats (clammy yesterday), palpitations, blackouts'
Abdomen: pain/where, bowels, ★ black/tarry stools, fevers, jaundice · ★ urine output 'more, less or the same?' → much less · dizzy standing (yes) · confusion, hiccups, itch, ★ metallic taste (yes)

★ Examination — fluid status FIRST: postural BP, mucosa, JVP, cap refill; abdomen (tenderness, guarding, organomegaly, palpable bladder); cardiorespiratory; pallor, pigmentation, oedema, asterixis → dry, postural drop 20, JVP not seen, soft abdomen, no bladder, no asterixis

★ Investigations by name: ECG now (hyperkalaemia AND ischaemia) · UEC/eGFR vs baseline — specifically K, Na, bicarbonate · VBG · troponin · FBE, Ca, PO4, Mg, LFT, lipase, urinalysis → eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, peaked T narrow QRS · 'why a troponin with no chest pain?' answered · read back: stage 2 AKI on CKD; K moderate by number, severe by ECG; acidosis shifts K out of cells

★ Diagnosis by name · 'will I need dialysis? my mother died on dialysis' → pause, acknowledge, honest answer · mechanism: three medicines, three directions — painkiller narrows the vessel in, perindopril widens the vessel out, fluid tablet lowers the circulating volume — 'the triple whammy' · 'you can buy it anywhere' → exactly why it catches people out · 'the locum's fault?' → missing record, not the person; letter to usual GP

Plan: 1 ibuprofen stops today, never that class without checking · 2 hold perindopril and the fluid tablet — temporary, don't stop anything else alone · 3 ★ ED today (K affects the heart's rhythm; can't keep fluids down) — ring ahead, results with her · ★ don't drive · red flags en route: chest pain, palpitations, faint, weak muscles → ambulance · repeat UEC 2–3 days · paracetamol + physio for the knee · ★ teach-back · 'anything still worrying you?'
ask: ★ 'Could I have her observations — including a blood sugar?' / 'I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?'
'When you say tired — low in energy, sleepy, or breathless when you move about?' / ★ 'What does the vomit look like — any blood, or anything green?'
★ 'When did you start the painkiller, and who started it for you?' / 'Anything from the chemist, or anything herbal?' / 'Did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?'
★ 'A few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious. Any discomfort or tightness in the chest, arm, jaw or back?'
★ 'How much urine have you passed in the last day — more, less, or the same?' / 'Any confusion, hiccups, itch or a metallic taste?'

★ 'I'd like her fluid status first — postural blood pressure, mucous membranes, JVP and capillary refill.' / 'Why a troponin with no chest pain?' → 'Because nausea and lethargy without chest pain is a recognised presentation of infarction in women and in chronic kidney disease.'
★ 'Her eGFR has halved from 45 to 22, which meets criteria for a stage 2 acute kidney injury.' / ★ 'The potassium is 6.3, and with ECG changes I treat that as severe regardless of the number.'

★ 'Your kidneys have taken a sudden extra hit on top of the long-standing damage — an acute kidney injury on top of chronic kidney disease.' / 'Will I need dialysis?' → 'Not today, and in most cases like yours this is reversible once we take the pressure off — that's exactly why we're acting now.'

★ 'Each of these medicines is sensible on its own. Together, with kidneys like yours, they're too much — in Australia we call it the triple whammy.' / 'But it's only ibuprofen — you can buy it anywhere' → 'You can — and that's exactly why it catches people out. Being sold without a prescription doesn't make it harmless for your kidneys.'

★ 'The painkiller stops today. The other two we hold while you're unwell — that's temporary.' / ★ 'I'm sending you to the emergency department today. Please don't drive.' / 'Could you tell me back what you'll say when you get to the hospital?'
pefe: Role-player: Marianne, 50, school administrator, husband, two grown children; HTN 10 y, CKD 5 y ('about half'), never dialysed; perindopril + 'a fluid tablet' never missed; ibuprofen 400 mg tds ~3 weeks for right knee (self-bought, then locum script; usual GP on leave) — not thought of as a medication; never smoked, wine most weekends; mother died on dialysis. 'What medications?' → 'perindopril and a fluid tablet' and STOP; ibuprofen only for 'painkillers', 'from the chemist', 'over the counter'. Slow, flat, retching; withdraws if not offered water; defensive once 'it's only ibuprofen'; 'is this the locum's fault?'; pushes back once on hospital 'can't I stop the tablets and come back Friday?' — agrees only if you hold firm with a reason; 'sorry — what does that mean?' at jargon; hidden agenda dialysis/mother in the last two minutes unless asked

Examiner returns: BP 142/86, PR 72, RR 16, SpO2 98, T 36.6, BSL 5.4 · dry mucosa, postural drop 20 systolic, JVP not visible, abdomen soft non-tender, no palpable bladder, HS dual, chest clear, no pallor/oedema/asterixis · eGFR 22 (baseline 45), creatinine ~×2, K 6.3, HCO3 18, troponin normal, ECG peaked T narrow QRS

Variant A — prevention: visiting gout patient on perindopril + a fluid tablet demands indomethacin → 'I can treat that today — before I write anything, what else are you on, any kidney trouble? …an anti-inflammatory is the one thing I don't want to give you: those three together can shut the kidneys down within days' → colchicine or short prednisolone, check UEC while here VERIFY TG gout dosing/renal cautions

Variant B — ECG: ST elevation II, III, aVF → 'inferior STEMI presenting as nausea and lethargy without chest pain — ambulance now, aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, activate the acute coronary pathway; the renal picture is real but no longer the priority' ★ continuing the triple-whammy talk = automatic fail

Variant C — coffee-ground vomit + black sticky stools: NSAID upper GI bleed contributing to the AKI → ambulance now, bloods, fluids, PPI, endoscopy · Variant D — refuses (daughter's wedding Saturday): honest risk statement, 'I'd be failing you if I sent you home; may only be hours on a drip'; if still declines: document discussion and specific risks, confirm capacity, written red flags, same-day repeat bloods, defined review, can change her mind any time — never simply agree
SA: ED (nearest regional/metropolitan); MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval; PATS; TIS 131 450; recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping, 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i
fails: Asking only 'what medications are you on?' — walking past the ibuprofen ★
No cardiac screen without being prompted ★
'High potassium' as the diagnosis instead of AKI on CKD; not explaining the three-drug combination in her words ★
Sending her home to 'come back Friday' with K 6.3 and ECG changes; letting her drive ★
Continuing to discuss the triple whammy after an ischaemic ECG (Variant B) ★
Ignoring the vomit bag; asking only how many times, never what the vomit looked like; never asking about urine output or black stools
'Renal function tests' with no analyte; stopping perindopril and the thiazide forever rather than holding; blaming the locum; deflecting the dialysis fear; no alternative for the knee; no teach-back
numbers: Triple whammy = diuretic + NSAID + ACE-i/ARB · here eGFR 45 → 22 · creatinine ~×2 · K 6.3 · HCO3 18 · troponin normal · peaked T, narrow QRS
AKI staging: stage 1 creatinine ×1.5 · stage 2 ×2 · stage 3 ×3 or dialysis VERIFY against current KDIGO wording · K mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · any ECG change = severe
Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–5 min · insulin–dextrose 10 units in 50 mL 50% glucose over 15–30 min, onset ~15 min, 4–6 h, BSL hourly × 6 h · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb
Recheck UEC 48–72 h after stopping the drugs · 1–2 weeks after restarting an ACE-i · aldosterone rule: hypoaldosteronism → high K; hyperaldosteronism → low K
Timing: 40 s · 4 min · 1.5 min · 2 min · 45 s (9-minute station) · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

setting: General practice in Kadina, regional South Australia; you are the GP registrar. A results card is handed to you. Expect a prompt at 5 minutes covering tasks 1 and 2.
stem: Mr Colin Whitfield, 58, semi-retired farm contractor, returns for the results of blood tests taken a fortnight ago when he attended feeling tired. Hypothyroidism for six years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medication recorded. BP 138/82, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.7; he looks well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 15 (10–20), total calcium 2.58 (2.15–2.60), albumin 28 (low), corrected calcium 2.82 (HIGH), phosphate 0.68 (low, 0.75–1.50), creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE and LFT normal, PTH sent — result not yet available.
tasks: Explain these blood results in language he can understand
Take a focused, relevant history
Give your most likely diagnosis and your differentials
Explain what happens next
time: 8 minutes: results 90 s MAXIMUM (signpost → thyroid in one breath → ★ calcium in four sentences: straight reading normal, stuck to a protein, protein low, corrected is high → check understanding → permission) · history 3½ min in seven blocks: tiredness · ★ stones · bones · groans · moans · ★ cancer · drugs incl. OTC · family/alcohol · ★ ICE before the diagnosis · transition line · four glands, one overactive, usually benign, 'I'm not going to promise you that today' · ★ say the word PTH and what high and low each mean · rest of workup, referral, PATS · fluids, don't cut dairy, avoid diuretics/supplements · safety-net · summary · 'have I missed anything?'

back.dx: Primary hyperparathyroidism with end-organ disease — corrected calcium 2.82 (total 2.58 + 0.02 × (40 − 28)), phosphate 0.68 low (PTH wastes phosphate — read the whole panel), TSH/T4 normal (dose right, no change), FBE/LFT normal; PTH pending — 'I've already sent that sample, so we won't lose any time'. History: six months of tiredness; ★ renal colic three years ago (overnight at Wallaroo) + nocturia ×2 + thirst; hip ache ('forty years on tractors'); constipation new this year; 'I've been flat' — name low mood as part of the illness, not a weakness; malignancy block clean (weight steady, never smoked, no sweats/lumps/cough); thyroxine only, 'doesn't hold with vitamins'; no FHx of calcium/stones/neck surgery (FHH, MEN 1); beers Friday, more at harvest (explains the low albumin); diet plenty of milk and cheese. Hidden agenda: brother Wayne died of bowel cancer at 55 last year — ask ICE before you explain, then build the explanation around it. Explain: one of four small neck glands behind the thyroid, different job, slightly overactive, pushing calcium out of bone — fits the stone, constipation, thirst, feeling flat; usually benign and treatable; honest middle — 'a couple of other things can raise calcium, one is a cancer somewhere else, which I know you've worried about since your brother'; what makes it less likely: weight steady, never smoked, normal FBE/LFT, no bone pain or lumps. ★ PTH: high → the gland, common, treatable; low → calcium from somewhere else → CXR and further bloods. Workup: vitamin D, magnesium, renal function, 24-h urine calcium, DXA, renal ultrasound (stone history); PTH confirms → endocrinology in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse; neck scan only to plan surgery, not to diagnose; some need the gland out, some are watched — decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bone scan. Meanwhile 2–3 L fluids, more in the heat; don't cut dairy; avoid fluid tablets and calcium/vitamin D supplements; safety-net; ring him with the PTH; review two weeks.
plan: WIPE, DOB · ★ signpost: 'Most of them are reassuring, but there is one I want to go through properly with you — and then I'll need to ask you some questions. Is that alright?' · 'the wife reckoned you'd only get me back in if something was up' → one sentence of acknowledgement, then proceed

Thyroid in one breath: 'the TSH tells us whether you're on the right dose — normal, well controlled, T4 normal too, no change to your thyroxine' · 'what's TSH stand for?' → do not take the invitation; one line and move

★ Calcium in four sentences: 'we measured a mineral called calcium; the straight reading came back normal — but it isn't reliable on its own, because a large part of the calcium is stuck to a protein, and your protein is low, so the reading understates it; we do a calculation that corrects for the protein — and once we do, your calcium is high' · 'so is it normal or isn't it?' → 'the corrected number is the one we go on' · ★ 'is that making sense so far?' · 'not an emergency, you look well, but it needs explaining — may I ask some questions?'

Tiredness — two sentences, not two minutes (6 months, done by lunchtime) · ★ stones: 'ever passed a kidney stone, severe back/side pain?' (3 y ago, Wallaroo) · 'passing more urine, up at night?' (×2, thirsty) · bones: aches, fragility fracture, height loss (hips) · groans: constipation (new this year), indigestion/ulcer, nausea/vomiting · moans: mood, memory, concentration, sleep ('flat') → 'that can be part of this picture — not you being difficult'

★ Cancer block: 'questions I ask everyone with a high calcium' — weight, night sweats/fevers/lumps, cough/haemoptysis, smoking → all clean · drugs incl. OTC: fluid tablets, lithium, calcium/vitamin D, antacids, vitamin A/multivitamins → thyroxine only · FHx: high calcium, stones, parathyroid/neck operation, pituitary/pancreas tumour → no · alcohol (Friday beers, more at harvest) · home/work

★ ICE before the diagnosis: 'what did you think might be causing the tiredness? anything you've been particularly worried about?' → brother, bowel cancer, 55 → 'I'm sorry about your brother — and I'm glad you told me, because it changes how I explain the next bit' · ★ transition line: 'I've got what I need. Let me tell you what I think is going on and what I'd like to do about it'

Diagnosis: 'one of four small glands in your neck — the parathyroid glands, behind your thyroid but a completely different job — has become slightly overactive and is pushing calcium out of your bones into your blood; that fits the kidney stone, the constipation, the thirst and feeling flat; usually a benign growth, not a cancer, treatable' · 'but you can't be sure' → ★ 'not today, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise' — the honest middle; why cancer is less likely (weight, never smoked, FBE/LFT normal, no bone pain/lumps); 'I want to prove it rather than assume it'

★ 'There is one blood test that separates those two possibilities, and it's called PTH. If it's high, it's the gland — common and treatable. If it's low, the calcium is coming from somewhere else and I'd look for a cause in the chest and the bones with a chest x-ray and further blood tests. I've already sent that sample' · alongside: vitamin D, magnesium, kidney function, 24-h urine calcium, bone density scan, renal ultrasound (stone) · PTH confirms → endocrinologist in Adelaide, PATS via the practice nurse · 'an operation?' → some do, some are watched; decided with the specialist on calcium, kidneys, bones; neck scan is for surgical planning, not diagnosis

Meanwhile: 2–3 L/day, more in the heat on the property · ★ 'don't cut down on dairy — people assume they should and it makes it worse' · avoid fluid tablets, no calcium/vitamin D supplement without checking · ★ safety-net: very thirsty, vomiting, confused/drowsy, passing much more urine → straight back or ED · 'I'll ring you myself when the PTH is back; see you in two weeks either way' · summary · ★ 'have I missed anything you wanted to ask?'
ask: ★ 'Most of them are reassuring, but there is one I want to go through properly with you.' / 'The main test we look at is the TSH — that tells us whether you're on the right dose. Yours is normal, which means your thyroid is well controlled on your current tablet.'

★ 'We also measured a mineral in your blood called calcium. The straight calcium level came back in the normal range — but that measurement isn't reliable on its own, because a large part of the calcium in your blood is stuck to a protein, and if that protein is low, as yours is, the reading comes out falsely low. So we do a calculation that corrects for the protein — and once we do that, your calcium is high.'

'Hang on — so is it normal or isn't it?' → 'The first number is normal. The corrected number — the one that actually reflects what's in your body — is high. It's the corrected one we go on.' / ★ 'Is that making sense so far?' / 'Is it alright if I ask you some questions to work out which cause it is?'
★ 'Have you ever passed a kidney stone, or had severe pain in the back or side? Any passing more urine than usual, or getting up at night to go?'
'How has your mood been? Any trouble with memory or concentration?' → 'Thank you for telling me — that can be part of this picture, and it's not you being difficult.'

★ 'Now some questions I ask everyone with a high calcium. Has your weight changed without trying? Any night sweats, fevers or lumps? Any cough, or coughing blood? Do you or did you smoke?' / 'What tablets are you on, including anything over the counter — fluid tablets, lithium, calcium or vitamin D, indigestion powders?'

★ 'What did you think might be causing the tiredness? Is there anything you're especially worried about?' (before the diagnosis) / 'I've got what I need. Let me tell you what I think is going on and what I'd like to do about it.'

★ 'One of four small glands in your neck — the parathyroid glands, which sit behind your thyroid but do a completely different job — has become slightly overactive, and it's pushing calcium out of your bones into your blood.' / ★ 'It is usually a benign growth, and it is treatable — but I'm not going to promise you that today, because a couple of other things can raise calcium, and one of those is a cancer somewhere else, which I know is what you've been worrying about since your brother.'

★ 'There is one blood test that separates those two possibilities, and it's called PTH — the hormone those neck glands make. If it's high, it's the gland. If it's low, the calcium is coming from somewhere else and I'd look for a cause in the chest and the bones.' / 'Would I need an operation?' → 'Some people do and some are safely watched with regular blood tests. That decision depends on your calcium, your kidneys and your bone scan, and it's made with the specialist.'

★ 'Keep your fluids up — two to three litres a day, more on hot days out on the property — and don't cut down on dairy; people assume they should and it actually makes it worse.' / ★ 'If you become very thirsty, start vomiting, get confused or drowsy, or you're passing much more urine, don't wait for the appointment — come straight back or go to the emergency department.' / 'I'll ring you myself when the result is back. Have I missed anything you wanted to ask?'
pefe: Role-player: Colin, 58, property 20 min outside Kadina, wife Denise, two adult children in Adelaide; seeding/harvest for three neighbours; understated, dry, minimising, watches your face. Levothyroxine only, no supplements ('don't hold with vitamins'), never smoked, 4–5 beers Friday/more at harvest, plenty of milk and cheese. Father MI at 70, mother 84 arthritis, brother Wayne died at 55 of bowel cancer last year. Does not hand over the stone unless asked about stones/urine; constipation only if asked about bowels. Pushes 'so is it normal or isn't it?' once; asks 'is it dangerous?', 'would I need an operation?'; if you lecture physiology: 'you've lost me'; if you use 'cancer' without warning: two-second silence; ★ if you say his calcium is normal he thanks you and stands up to leave — let them fail. stem: James Whitlock, 27: runny nose for two weeks, getting worse. Known hay fever; mother has asthma. Examination: afebrile, clear watery discharge, enlarged swollen inferior turbinates, respiratory examination normal.

back.dx: Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound congestion from two weeks of xylometazoline — Otrivin — 3–4 times a day, both nostrils) on a background of allergic rhinitis. Pattern: brilliant for the first few days, now lasts an hour, nose worse than before he started. Treatment history: antihistamine tablets helped eyes not nose; a steroid spray WORKED but he stopped it because of cost (saving for a house) and switched to Otrivin — so the plan is to restart that drug cheaply, not invent a new one. Explain: decongestant squeezes the vessels in the lining — beautiful for 3–5 days, then the lining becomes reliant, each dose wears off into more swelling; three reasons — two weeks, helped then stopped, swollen with clear discharge and no fever (not infection). Long-term ladder by name: saline → antihistamine (oral cetirizine/loratadine/fexofenadine for eyes, or intranasal azelastine for the nose) → ★ mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily, preventer not rescue, no immediate relief, up to 2 weeks → Dymista 1 spray bd (bitter) → montelukast if asthma. Five-step technique. Allergen measures. Allergy testing (specific IgE or skin prick) BEFORE immunotherapy (SC or SL, 3–5 years, allergy clinic in Adelaide, PATS). Review 2 weeks not 6, bring the spray.

stem: James Coulter, 25, warehouse storeperson, has come in with a sore throat and is asking you for antibiotics. time: 8 minutes. Surface the antibiotic request in the first minute and defer it fairly · ★ one side or both · ENT screen · ★ red-flag block · ★ cough (present — a viral feature and a Centor feature) · gut/spleen, sexual health · ★ rheumatic fever / ATSI named · read the card, name the four features that make it viral · ★ diagnosis + bucketed differential with reasoning to the examiner · ★ reassure before you refuse; two honest options with benefits and harms; elicit his values; recommend · ★ solve the real problem — medical certificate · analgesia doses · safety-net with named red flags · check-back. He pushes for antibiotics three times.

To the examiner — most likely viral pharyngitis/tonsillitis; differentials in order of what you would not miss: bacterial streptococcal tonsillitis; peritonsillar abscess; epiglottitis/deep neck space infection; infectious mononucleosis with splenomegaly; gonococcal/chlamydial pharyngitis; scarlet fever; laryngitis and sinusitis with PND; pneumonia; and in a different patient, drug-induced agranulocytosis or head and neck malignancy. Counselling: reassure first ('this will settle by itself — even bacterial ones do; that's why we're careful, not automatic'); two options — symptoms alone, or symptoms + antibiotic: benefit ~1 day; harms — up to 1 in 10 side effects, resistance, EBV rash with amoxicillin; 'what matters most to you?' → recommend no antibiotic; ★ medical certificate solves the real need (hidden agenda: casual, no sick leave, behind on rent); paracetamol 1 g qid, ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food, fluids, salt-water gargle, rest, cut smoking; safety-net: can't swallow saliva/drooling, noisy breathing, voice change, neck swelling/stiffness, rash, not improving 5–7 days; teach-back. setting: General practice, regional South Australia. No observations supplied. Prompt at 4 minutes to move to examination; a photograph is handed over when you ask for Horner's syndrome. Indirect laryngoscopy is unavailable.
stem: Margaret Ellis, 45, primary school teacher, presents with a change in her voice — hoarseness.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately 4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the further investigations you would arrange
time: 8 minutes, four tasks — lost on time far more than knowledge. 0:00 short open + agenda · 0:25 ★ timing and pattern: constant, 'does voice rest help?', 'same all day or worse by evening?' — two months is a red flag on its own · 1:15 infection, airway red flags, overuse tested and DISCARDED out loud ('I'm a teacher' is the red herring) · 2:00 cancer screen throat → oesophagus → thyroid → ★ lung: cough, haemoptysis, SOB, shoulder pain, ★ pack-years aloud · ★ the two Pancoast questions (hand numbness ulnar side; droopy eyelid) · 3:20 reflux, myasthenia, hypothyroid, neck surgery, ★ 'steroid inhalers or puffers' by class, alcohol, FHx, ICE · 4:00 examination by component with targets — Horner's, C8–T1 · ★ basal signs = effusion secondary to the apex · 5:20 warning shot, pause, plain words, two reasons · differentials in three buckets · 6:50 ★ three numbered investigations · ownership of the result, safety-net, Quitline.

back.dx: Pancoast (apical lung) tumour with left recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, left Horner's syndrome, C8–T1 lower brachial plexus involvement and a secondary left pleural effusion. Two months of constant, slowly worsening hoarseness, no better with two weeks' voice rest at Easter, same morning and night (kills overuse); dry cough three months, puffed on stairs, left shoulder ache 'blamed on marking', couple of kilos lost; 20/day since 20 = 25 pack-years; ★ left hand numb along the ulnar edge, husband said her eye 'looked lazy in a photo'. Examination: not cachectic, no neck mass, T 36.8, throat/nose/nodes/thyroid normal; left lower zone — reduced expansion, dullness, absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance (effusion); photograph — partial ptosis, miosis (ask about anhidrosis) = left Horner's → sympathetic chain → lung apex; C8–T1 weakness and sensory loss. Resolve the apparent contradiction before the examiner asks: an apical mass produces no chest signs itself; the basal signs are an effusion caused by it. To her: 'a growth in the upper part of your left lung — a lung cancer; can't be certain today' + two reasons (hoarseness/cough/smoking; fluid around the lung with eye and hand changes fitting a growth at the top pressing on nerves). Never 'Pancoast', 'Horner's', 'pleural effusion' to the patient. Differentials in three buckets with a why: infections (no fever, too long), strain (rest didn't help), growths — cords, thyroid, oesophagus, lung; rarer — reflux, hypothyroid, myasthenia, inhaled steroids. Investigations: 1 CXR today · 2 urgent ENT laryngoscopy · 3 CT chest + biopsy (then PET-CT, MRI thoracic inlet, TFTs, bloods). Own the result: call her personally, see her this week, bring her husband; safety-net; Quitline once, no lecture; Cancer Council 13 11 20. Hidden agenda: mother died of lung cancer at 58 — why she waited.

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Initial observations supplied. Findings from the examiner on request. History closes at 3:00 — this station is scored in the second half.
stem: Mr Jason Whitfield, 28, warehouse team leader, presents with a three-day sore throat. He told the receptionist he needs something to fix it fast because he cannot afford to miss work. T 37.4, HR 78, RR 14, BP 124/76, SpO2 99% on air.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Ask the examiner for your examination findings
Explain the likely diagnosis and your management to the patient
Address the patient's concerns
time: 8 minutes: 0:00 greet, ★ agenda question up front, signpost · 0:45 history — course, cough/coryza/hoarseness, fever/nodes, ★ signposted red-flag sweep (saliva, drinking, muffled voice, mouth opening, one-sided, breathing, neck stiffness/rigors), ★ rheumatic fever + ATSI + medications (thyroid/mental health/arthritis), ICE and impact · 3:00 named findings from the examiner · 3:30 diagnosis in plain English — viral and why; never 'just a virus' · 4:30 ★ solve the work problem FIRST — certificate, employer letter, modified duties · 5:15 analgesia doses, fluids, rest · ★ three pillars (no benefit · harm · resistance) · 'how does that sit with you?' · 7:00 six named safety-net symptoms, destination, review 3–4 days, teach-back. He pushes three times; the 'just in case' script is a fail.

back.dx: Viral pharyngitis: three days, 6/10, bilateral, dry cough and runny/blocked nose from the start, voice normal, swallows and drinks fine, felt warm the first night only, no red flags, no rheumatic fever/ATSI risk, no meds (paracetamol irregularly), no allergies. Examiner: T 37.4, pharynx and tonsils erythematous without exudate, uvula midline, no lymphadenopathy, no trismus, normal voice, no rash, spleen not palpable — Centor 0–1. Explain: 'everything points to a virus — the same family that causes a cold: red inflamed throat but no pus, no swollen glands, normal temperature; the cough and blocked nose actually tell me it's viral; settles over 3–5 days, throat last to go' — and ★ 'viral doesn't mean mild; these can knock you flat.' Hidden agenda: short-staffed, supervisor questioning his reliability, frightened of losing the team-leader role — solve it BEFORE antibiotics: medical certificate, a short letter to the employer (unwell, infectious, rest gets him back faster), or duties away from the team; the register softens and the antibiotic request loses its force. Symptomatic: paracetamol 1 g qid max 4 g, ibuprofen 200–400 mg tds with food, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges. Three pillars: wouldn't work (kills bacteria, not a virus — not a day shorter); can harm (~1 in 10 diarrhoea/rash; amoxicillin-clavulanate hepatitis/jaundice); costs later (resistance when he genuinely needs one). 'Last time I was better in two days' → validate natural history, never criticise the prior GP ('every throat is different'). No 'just in case' script — offer review in 3 days and name what would change your mind. Safety-net six symptoms + destination + review 3–4 days + teach-back.
plan: WIPE · ★ 'before we get into it — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today? I'd rather know now' → 'antibiotics' (push 1) → 'fair enough — I might well be able to help with that; can I ask a few questions first so I know what we're dealing with?'
Course: onset, better/worse, /10 · cough, blocked nose, hoarseness (cough + coryza = viral evidence) · fever/shakes, neck lumps

★ Signposted: 'a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious' — swallow saliva? managing to drink? voice muffled? mouth opens fully? much worse on one side? trouble/noisy breathing? neck stiffness, shakes and shivers? → all no

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone with a sore throat' — rheumatic fever or heart-valve problem? Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? regular medications — thyroid, mental health, arthritis? allergies? · ICE + impact: 'how's it affecting you day to day, and what were you worried it might be?' → work, short-staffed, team falls apart

★ 'Examiner, may I have my findings: temperature and observations; the tonsils and whether there is exudate; asymmetry or deviation of the uvula; anterior cervical nodes; trismus or a muffled voice; any rash; and whether the spleen is palpable' → viral picture

'Everything points to a virus…' with the four features · 'it should settle over three to five days, the throat can be the last thing to go' · 'so it's just a cold?' → ★ 'it's a viral infection, and viral doesn't mean mild — it can floor you for a few days' · 'does that make sense so far?'

★ 'Now, you mentioned work, and I want to deal with that first because I suspect that's the bit really weighing on you' — certificate for the days he needs; a short letter to the employer; or duties away from the team while infectious — 'which would be most useful?' → register softens

Analgesia with doses, fluids, rest, gargles/lozenges · ★ three pillars, signposted: 'you asked about antibiotics and I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no' — 1 wouldn't work · 2 can harm · 3 costs later · push 2 'better in two days last time' → natural history, no criticism · push 3 'some to have on hand?' → ★ no script; review in three days and what would change my mind

★ 'How does that sit with you?' · safety-net: can't swallow saliva/drooling; muffled voice/can't open mouth; much worse on one side; high fever with shakes; dizzy/can't keep fluids down; short of breath → back or ED · not clearly improving 3–4 days → book back · ★ 'could you tell me back the ones you'd act on?'
ask: ★ 'Before we start — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today?' / 'I might well be able to help with that. Can I ask a few questions first?'

★ 'I'm going to ask a few quick questions to make sure this isn't something more serious.' / ★ 'Can you swallow your own saliva? Has your voice changed? Can you open your mouth fully? Is it much worse on one side?'

★ 'A couple of routine background questions I ask everyone — have you ever been told you had rheumatic fever? Do you identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander? Any regular medications — anything for thyroid, mental health or arthritis?'
★ 'Examiner, may I have my findings — observations, tonsils and exudate, uvular position, cervical nodes, trismus or voice change, rash, and spleen?'

'Everything points to a virus — the same family of bugs that causes a cold. Your throat is red and inflamed, but there's no pus on the tonsils, no swollen glands, and your temperature is normal. The cough and the blocked nose actually help me here.' / ★ 'Viral doesn't mean mild. These can knock you flat for a few days.'

★ 'Let me deal with work first, because I think that's the real worry.' / 'I can write you a medical certificate, and a letter to your employer if that would help — or we could ask about duties away from the team while you're infectious. Which would be most useful?'

★ 'I want to give you a proper answer rather than just saying no. First, they wouldn't work — antibiotics kill bacteria; they do nothing to a virus. Second, they can do harm — around one in ten get diarrhoea or a rash, and occasionally they inflame the liver. Third, they cost you later — every unnecessary course makes the bacteria more resistant, so next time you genuinely need one it's less likely to work.'

'Last time I was better in two days' → 'That's a really common experience and it makes sense — most sore throats settle in about that time either way, so it's hard to tell what did the work. If I thought an antibiotic would get you back to work faster, I'd write it right now.' (never criticise the previous prescriber)

'Some to have on hand, just in case?' → 'I'd rather see you again in three days than give you a script to hold. What would change my mind is pus on the tonsils, swollen glands, a real fever, or the cough disappearing — if any of that happens, I'll treat it.'

★ 'How does that sit with you — is there anything about it you're not comfortable with?' / 'Come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you can't swallow your saliva or start drooling; your voice goes muffled or you can't open your mouth; the pain gets much worse on one side; a high fever with shakes; dizzy or can't keep fluids down; or short of breath. Otherwise if not clearly better in three to four days, book back in.' / ★ 'Could you tell me back the ones you'd act on?'
pefe: Role-player: Jason, 28, team leader at a produce distribution centre outside Renmark; partner, child of three; non-smoker, 4–5 beers weekends; paracetamol irregularly; no PMHx; not ATSI; grew up in Adelaide. Blunt, impatient, not rude. Three pushes: opening line; 'better in two days last time' (defensive if you criticise 'my GP for years'); 'some on hand in case?' — accepts a script with thanks then marks a fail. If work is solved first: drops to one push, 'oh — that'd actually help a lot'. 'Just a virus' → 'it doesn't feel like just anything, mate'. If never asked about concerns: at ~7 min, flat, 'so what am I supposed to tell work?'

Examiner: T 37.4, other obs normal · pharynx/tonsils erythematous, no exudate · uvula midline, no asymmetry · no cervical lymphadenopathy · no trismus, normal voice · no rash · spleen not palpable · Centor 0–1

Variant 1 — findings turn bacterial (exudate both tonsils, tender anterior nodes, T 38.5, no cough; Centor 4): 'bacterial rather than viral' — and the Australian nuance: still not automatic antibiotics in a healthy adult (shortens ~1 day); treat if very unwell, scarlet-fever rash, or high ARF risk; symptomatic + review 3 days · Variant 2 — scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue): treat — phenoxymethylpenicillin bd 10 full days; not infectious after ~24 h of treatment

Variant 3 — 19-year-old Aboriginal man, exudative tonsillitis, 38.6, grew up in a remote community: high ARF risk → treat 'to protect the heart, not the throat': swab, phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg bd 10 days (or single IM benzathine benzylpenicillin); Closing the Gap PBS; Aboriginal Liaison Officer/ACCHS follow-up with permission; ARF/RHD notifiable in SA VERIFY

Variant 4 — 34F, 4 days sore throat + fevers, 'something for an overactive thyroid' → ★ carbimazole: agranulocytosis warning sign — FBE today, stop carbimazole until the result, phone the endocrinologist; low neutrophils = febrile neutropenia → urgent assessment, cultures, empirical antibiotics. Treating as viral = automatic fail
SA: medical certificate; employer letter; ACCHS/Closing the Gap where relevant; SA Health notification for ARF/RHD; TIS 131 450; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

An antibiotic prescribed to end the argument — including a 'just in case' script ★
Agranulocytosis (carbimazole) or quinsy missed in a variant ★
No safety-netting — 'come back if it gets worse' without the six symptoms, destination and review date ★
Skipping rheumatic fever and medication questions because it 'looks viral'; not naming uvular deviation and trismus in the examiner request
'Just a cold'; criticising the previous prescriber; the certificate as an afterthought; announcing the plan instead of 'how does that sit with you?'
