setting: General practice, Kadina, Yorke Peninsula. Vitals on the card. Examination findings from the examiner (Version A: all normal; Version B: boggy pale mucosa). Online variant adds a mechanism explanation task.
stem: Ms Denise Harmer, 45, part-time office worker at a grain-handling depot: blocked and runny nose, continuously for the past six months. T 36.6, BP 122/78, HR 72, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA, BMI 26; afebrile, systemically well.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (approximately 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Online variant: explain the mechanism of the condition in lay terms
time: 8 minutes: 6 history → 20 s PEFE → 90 s explanation. 0:00 frustration line + early ICE · timing, ★ 'one nostril or both?' (say the answer back), CCVO — colour, consistency, volume, odour, blood · better/worse, ★ season AND place, impact · atopic package — nose, eyes, chest, skin + personal/family atopy · triggers ×4 — home, work, ★ drugs incl. nasal sprays by name and duration, smoke · ★ signposted sinusitis screen · ★ signposted malignancy screen — do NOT reassure before it · PEFE by component; 'normal' doesn't change the diagnosis · hay fever + three reasons + two differentials excluded · mechanism in four plain sentences · plan, safety-net, summary.

back.dx: Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) — perennial (cat on the bed, dust mite in an older fully carpeted house, grain dust at the depot, partner smoking indoors) with a spring pollen flare; persistent and moderate–severe by ARIA (sleep, work, taste, embarrassment). Six months, intermittent weeks, ★ bilateral, clear watery copious discharge, no smell, no blood; worse in spring, worse at home in the mornings and in bed; chemist antihistamines help for hours. Atopic package: itchy nose, sneezing fits, red streaming eyes, itchy throat, no chest symptoms (harder version: night cough, puffed at netball → asthma), childhood eczema, sister asthma, mother hay fever. Occasional decongestant spray ('not really a medication') — a week here and there: counsel the 5-day limit, stop it. Two exclusions signposted and clean: chronic rhinosinusitis (no facial pain/pressure, fever, PND, upper toothache, smell loss) and sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy (no epistaxis, weight loss, neck lumps, unilateral ear blockage, diplopia, facial numbness). Hidden agenda: aunt had 'a growth in her nose' — surfaces at the red-flag questions; reassure with the specific negatives, after the screen. PEFE normal → 'a normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, polyp or growth; hay fever is diagnosed on the story'. Three reasons: clear watery bilateral discharge; the travelling symptoms (sneeze, itch, eyes); trigger exposure + family atopy. 'Why all year?' → perennial (mite, cat) plus seasonal (pollen). Mechanism: allergen → mast cell → histamine → inflammation and leaky dilated vessels → blockage and watery discharge (two waves: early histamine = itch/sneeze/run, antihistamines work; late inflammatory cells = blockage, needs the steroid, 1–2 weeks). Plan: cat out of the bedroom, mite covers, hot-wash bedding, lift/vacuum the carpet, recirculate on pollen days; mometasone 2 sprays each nostril daily (technique, 2 weeks); cetirizine 10 mg; eye drops; stop the decongestant; smoke-free home, Quitline; review 4–6 weeks with the spray; escalate to combination spray or testing/immunotherapy if uncontrolled.
plan: WIPE · ★ 'I'm very sorry you've been having such a difficult time — six months is a long while, and being told it's a cold each time must be frustrating. I'll ask some questions to find the cause, then we'll make the best plan. Is that all right?' · ★ 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' (she deflects — note it, move on)

Timing: constant or comes and goes, worse · ★ 'one nostril, or both?' → both → ★ 'that's reassuring — a one-sided blockage would make me look for a different set of causes' · CCVO: clear or green/yellow; watery or thick; a lot or a little; smell; blood
Better/worse · ★ 'a particular time of year?' (spring) · ★ 'a particular place — home, work, outdoors?' (home, mornings, bed) · impact — sleep, work, concentration, taste, embarrassment

Atopic package, four addresses: nose — itch, sneezing · eyes — itchy/red/watery · throat itch · chest — cough at night/exercise, wheeze, SOB · skin — eczema · own allergies · family asthma/eczema/hay fever

Triggers ×4: home — pets (cat on the bed), carpets/bedding/curtains, dust, damp/mould (older carpeted house 8 months) · work — grain dust, harvest · ★ 'any medications, including over the counter — any nasal sprays, which one, how long?' → 'a spray, not really a medication' → pursue: decongestant, a week here and there · smoke — partner indoors

★ Signposted sinusitis screen: 'to make sure this isn't a sinus infection, because that's treated quite differently' — headaches; pain/pressure cheeks, forehead, behind the eyes, bending forward; fevers; PND; upper toothache; smell → all no

★ Signposted malignancy screen: 'questions I ask everybody with a blocked nose this long, to be sure I'm not missing anything serious' — nosebleeds, weight/appetite, neck lumps, unusual tiredness, one ear blocked/muffled, double vision, facial numbness → all no → 'why are you asking — could it be cancer? my aunt had a growth' → thank her, validate, reassure WITH the negatives (bilateral, clear, no blood, no bleeds, weight stable, no lumps, hearing normal) · close: PMHx/surgery/nasal injury, alcohol, anything else

PEFE by component: general/vitals · external nose, sinus tenderness · anterior rhinoscopy — mucosa, turbinates, septum, polyp/mass, discharge · oropharynx — PND, cobblestoning · eyes — conjunctival injection · otoscopy — effusion · neck nodes · chest — wheeze → 'all normal' → ★ rescue sentence

'Has anyone mentioned hay fever before?' · allergic rhinitis named · three reasons · two differentials (sinusitis — why not; growth — what I checked) · 'why all year?' → perennial + seasonal · mechanism in four sentences if asked · management, stop the decongestant, Quitline for the partner, review 4–6 weeks with the spray · safety-net: one-sided, nosebleeds, thick/coloured/bloody, facial pain/fever, smell loss, one ear, neck lump, weight loss · summary, questions
ask: ★ 'I'm very sorry to hear you've been having such a difficult time with this. I'll ask you some questions to try to find the cause, and then we'll make the best management plan for you. Is that all right with you?' / 'Before I start — was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'
★ 'Is the blocking and the discharge coming from one nostril, or both?' → 'Both sides — that's reassuring, because a one-sided blockage would make me look for a different set of causes.'
'Is it clear, or green or yellow? Watery, or thick and sticky? A lot or a little? Any bad smell? Any blood?' / 'Is there a particular time of year, or a particular place, that makes it worse?'

'These conditions often travel together — so let me ask about your eyes, your chest and your skin.' / ★ 'Any nasal sprays — which one, and for how long?' ('that's not really a medication, is it?' → 'it certainly counts')

★ 'I'd like to ask a few questions to make sure this isn't a sinus infection, because that's treated quite differently.' / ★ 'And a few questions I ask everybody with a blocked nose this long, to be sure I'm not missing anything serious.'

'Do you think it could be cancer? My aunt had a growth in her nose' → 'Thank you for telling me — I'm glad you have, because it explains why you've been so worried, and it's exactly what those questions were for. Nothing you've told me points that way: it's on both sides, the discharge is clear with no blood, no nosebleeds, your weight and appetite are unchanged, no lumps, hearing normal. Let me examine you and then I'll tell you what I think.'
★ 'A normal examination doesn't change my diagnosis — it reassures me there's no infection, no polyp and no growth. Hay fever is diagnosed on the story.'

★ 'Most likely you have allergic rhinitis, which most people know as hay fever. Three reasons: the discharge is clear, watery and from both sides; you have the symptoms that travel with it — sneezing, itchy nose, red watery eyes; and you're around the common triggers — a cat on your bed, an older carpeted house full of dust mite, grain dust at work, smoke in the house — with hay fever and asthma in the family.' / 'Yours is year-round from the cat and the dust mite, with a spring flare from pollen.'

Mechanism: ★ 'An allergen activates a mast cell, which releases histamine, which causes inflammation and widens the small blood vessels in the lining of your nose — that swelling and leaking is the blockage and the watery discharge, and it's why antihistamines help.' / 'Why don't antihistamines fix the blockage?' → 'Two waves — the first is histamine, itch and sneeze; the second, hours later, is inflammatory cells arriving, which causes the blockage; that's what the steroid spray is for, and why it takes a week or two.'

★ 'Use it every day, not just on bad days — aim it outwards towards your ear, don't sniff hard, and give it up to two weeks.' / 'Can I ask you to stop the decongestant spray? Used more than about five days it makes the blockage worse.' / ★ 'Come back sooner if it becomes one-sided, nosebleeds, coloured or bloody discharge, facial pain or fever, loss of smell, one ear blocking, or a lump in your neck.'

Frustrated and clipped — softens if the six months is acknowledged; if not, three-word answers and 'is this going to be another cold, then?' (also pushes once at ~4 min). Withholds cat, carpet, depot dust, smoking partner, family history and the spray unless asked directly. Hidden agenda: aunt's nasal growth — deflects if asked in the first two minutes; reveals at the red-flag questions ('why are you asking all that?'); if reassured before the screen: 'how can you know that already?'

PEFE Version A: all normal · Version B: nasal mucosa swollen, boggy and pale bilaterally with clear watery secretions; everything else normal → 'the classic appearance in allergic rhinitis; no polyp, mass or purulent discharge — against sinusitis and against anything sinister'

Variant 2 — 'it's the left one really; a bit of blood on the tissue': STOP the hay-fever line. Complete red flags (ear, neck lumps, facial numbness, diplopia, weight) → ★ 'because this is one side only with some blood I'm not treating it as hay fever — a one-sided blocked nose in an adult needs a specialist to look inside with a camera; urgent ENT, nasendoscopy ± scan; Adelaide, PATS today'. Examiner 'why not treat and review in 6 weeks?' → unilateral obstruction + epistaxis in an adult is a red flag for sinonasal/nasopharyngeal malignancy; a therapeutic trial delays diagnosis; nasendoscopy isn't available to me in GP

Variant 3 — decongestant every day for four months, wears off in an hour: rhinitis medicamentosa on top — rebound explained, stop it, ★ warn 1–2 weeks worse, INCS started at the same time, review 2 weeks not 6 (cross-ref MED-77) · Variant 4 — night cough + puffed at netball in spring: asthma in the same allergic family → spirometry, reliever + written action plan, thunderstorm asthma advice

Examiner: 'why not simply an antihistamine?' → persistent, moderate–severe by ARIA (sleep and work), obstruction dominant; antihistamines control early-phase itch/sneeze; obstruction is late-phase inflammation → INCS first-line regularly, antihistamine added for itch/eyes · 'allergy testing?' → not routinely — clinical diagnosis, triggers evident; skin prick or specific IgE if the trigger is unclear, avoidance decisions depend on it, or uncontrolled and considering immunotherapy (clinical immunology, Adelaide)

stem: Jane Whitmore, 30, has come in feeling unwell. She reports there has been an incident at work. No further detail is given. T 38.1, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card

time: 8 minutes: 0:00 open + concern · 0:30 'unwell' in four questions · ★ 1:15 'you mentioned an incident at work — tell me more' · say the exposure back ('urine and faeces') · ★ four exposure questions: PPE · fluid in eyes/mouth · incident report · head injury · 2:15 three infection groups: hepatitis (jaundice, RUQ pain, nausea, dark urine/pale stools) · gastroenteritis (diarrhoea loose vs watery, blood, fever/chills) · leptospirosis (rash, nodes, calf pain, red eyes) · ★ 4:15 PTSD screen — coping, mood, sleep, nightmares, avoidance · 5:00 the rest fast incl. hepatitis vaccination · examination by name incl. urine dipstick and calves · diagnosis with reasons · differential with named organisms + leptospirosis + psychological · safety-net, notification, teach-back.

back.dx: Version A — acute viral hepatitis (A or E) after falling chest-deep into sewage five days ago while sampling for the water utility (full PPE; doesn't know if fluid entered mouth/eyes; incident report filed; no head injury): five days of fever, aches, night sweats, anorexia, RUQ pain, mild nausea, no diarrhoea; card — no jaundice yet, T 38.1, tender hepatomegaly, RUQ tenderness, no splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness, ★ urine dipstick bilirubin positive (bilirubinuria precedes visible jaundice — the point of the card). Explain: 'acute hepatitis — inflammation of the liver — most probably hepatitis A or a close relative, hepatitis E; both picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage; not yellow yet but the pigment is already building up in the urine'; settles over weeks, doesn't become chronic; infectious via the bowel — handwashing, household vaccination. Version B card (no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, mild lower abdominal tenderness, dipstick normal; history of loose stools 4–5/day, lower abdominal pain) → gastroenteritis, said cleanly: 'not hepatitis' — no hedging with 'might be early hepatitis'. Differentials aloud: sewage-borne — gastroenteritis viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), bacterial (Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter), protozoal (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba); leptospirosis (rat urine; no calf pain/red eyes but treatable — test); liver abscess (needs ultrasound); PTSD/adjustment reaction (replaying it, two dreams, hasn't been back down); further down EBV, CMV, HIV, syphilis, travel infections, lymphoma/leukaemia, thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, coeliac, autoimmune ('cancer?' → 'not worried about that here — it's on the list I work through'). Plan: LFTs, clotting, hepatitis and leptospirosis serology, liver ultrasound; rest, fluids, no alcohol; notify hepatitis A; vaccinate household (3-year-old son); employer letter — off work while infectious; ReturnToWorkSA; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids down, turning yellow; review 2 days, talk about the dreams properly then.

time: 8 minutes. ★ 'Is my patient haemodynamically stable?' · define unwell · rash: redness/blisters/bruising, where it started, spread (not 'worse'), itch/pain, ★ blanches? · fever, travel · ★ 'do you use condoms?' → the hinge — 90 s of sexual history, no apologising: stable partner, multiple, ★ male/female/both, ★ oral/vaginal/anal ('tells me which sites to swab'), previous STI, alcohol/drugs · four rapid screens incl. ★ genital sores/ulcers now OR in the past months (the chancre) · meningism ×4 · immunisations, antibiotics · closing sweep — night sweats, lumps, new medications · findings aloud + ★ palms/soles, spleen, mouth · name HIV and syphilis with reasons · pause after the news · grouped differentials · ★ name the HIV test and seek consent · three-site swabs · contact tracing anonymised · safety-net.

back.dx: HIV seroconversion illness ± secondary syphilis. Eight days of fever, chills, aches, headaches, exhaustion (sick twice), mild early sore throat; two days of a flat red blotchy non-itchy non-painful ★ blanching rash chest → back and upper arms; lumps in neck and axillae, night sweats, appetite down, weight steady. Sexual history: MSM, several casual partners in six months, no stable partner, never condoms, oral and anal insertive and receptive, never diagnosed, alcohol involved, never injected, no travel. ★ Hidden detail: a small painless penile sore ~two months ago that healed alone — the primary chancre, given only to a specific sores/ulcers question. Findings: febrile, generalised lymphadenopathy, ★ lesions on the palms (ask), no splenomegaly, mouth clear. To Ben: 'I'm concerned about a sexually transmitted infection — specifically HIV, or syphilis, or possibly both'; reasons from history (MSM, no condoms, casual partners; eight days of fever/aches/headache/exhaustion, spreading rash) and examination (fever, glands everywhere, rash on the palms — characteristic of syphilis; the painless sore fits); 'they look identical at this stage, which is exactly why we test for both'. Long silence → 'Am I going to die?' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' (uncle died of AIDS in the 90s) → HIV today is not that illness: treatment, normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible; syphilis cured with an injection; don't promise a result you don't have. Differentials grouped: meningococcal (unlikely — blanching, no meningism) · other STIs (herpes, mpox, disseminated gonococcal) · rash viruses (EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, measles) · travel (dengue, Ross River — no travel) · infective endocarditis · leukaemia/lymphoma · drug reaction (nothing new). Plan: bloods today — ★ 'one of them is for HIV and I need your permission for that specifically' — syphilis (treponemal EIA + RPR), hepatitis, FBE; swabs throat, anorectal, first-pass urine; sexual health clinic referral; phone with results; partner notification anonymised via the clinic; safety-net non-blanching rash, headache with stiff neck/photophobia, much worse → 000/ED.

Temperature measured? chills? paracetamol? · travel (none) · sexually active? · ★ 'do you use condoms?' → pause → 'no, not really' → everything now pivots

'Thanks for being straight with me. A few questions about your sex life — routine when someone's unwell with a rash, and it stays between us. Okay?' → stable partner? · multiple? · ★ 'male, female or both?' → men · ★ 'oral, anal, or both — I ask because it tells me which sites to swab' → both, both ways · previous STI? · alcohol/drugs?

★ 'Are your partners male, female, or both?' / ★ 'What kind of sex do you have — oral, vaginal, anal? I ask because it tells me which sites to swab.' / 'Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? Has any of it happened when you'd been drinking or using drugs?'

'So he is febrile with generalised lymphadenopathy and every other system normal. ★ Can I confirm whether there is rash on the palms or soles, whether there is splenomegaly, and whether there is any oral ulceration?'

'Ben, I'm concerned about the possibility of a sexually transmitted infection — specifically HIV, the human immunodeficiency virus, or syphilis, or possibly both. From your history: you have sex with men, you don't use condoms, several casual partners; eight days of fever, aches, headaches and exhaustion, and a rash that spread from your chest. On examination: a fever, enlarged glands all over, and the rash involves your palms, which is quite characteristic of syphilis. That painless sore two months ago fits too.' / ★ 'I can't tell which of these it is by looking at you, which is exactly why we test for both.'

'Am I going to die?' → (two-second pause) 'That's a lot to hear. What's going through your mind?' → 'HIV today is not the illness it was in the nineties. With treatment, people live a normal life span and cannot pass it on. And syphilis is cured with an injection. But I don't want to promise you a result I don't have — let's test and find out.'

'The most serious one I considered is meningococcal disease — but your rash fades when pressed and you've no neck stiffness or light sensitivity, so I think that's unlikely. Then other STIs — herpes, mpox, a spread-out form of gonorrhoea; the rash viruses — glandular fever, CMV, toxoplasmosis, measles; travel infections like dengue and Ross River, much less likely with no travel; infective endocarditis; blood cancers such as leukaemia and lymphoma; and a medication reaction, but you haven't started anything new.'

★ 'Some blood tests today — one of them is for HIV, and I need your permission for that specifically — plus syphilis, hepatitis and a blood count. And swabs from your throat, your back passage and a urine sample, because we swab every site.' / ★ 'The clinic can notify your partners anonymously — your name does not have to go anywhere. You won't have to make those calls yourself.'

'If that rash stops fading when you press it, or you get a bad headache with a stiff neck or light hurting your eyes, or you feel much worse — call 000 or go straight to emergency.' / Non-blanching variant: 'I'm going to stop and act on something — that rash doesn't fade, and with your fever and headache that could be meningococcal disease. I'm giving you an antibiotic injection now and calling an ambulance. I'm not waiting for tests, because waiting is the risk.'

setting: General practice. Examination card at six minutes — three versions: (1) hepatitis card, (2) HIV seroconversion card (scripted here), (3) endocarditis card. Six minutes of history.
stem: Gary, 26, attends alone feeling unwell. He has recently returned from an overseas trip in South-East Asia, and used heroin while he was away.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
You will be given a physical examination card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the fear in one sentence · ★ signpost three blocks: the unwellness, the trip, the heroin · define, time, impact · ★ full travel history A B C D E F G S (don't accept 'just fun with mates'); write down 'no sex overseas' · ★ heroin in three steps IN ORDER: open question → route → shared needles · ★ three BBV boxes every time: hepatitis · HIV · injection/endocarditis · ★ go BACK for the sexual history ('ever been sexually active?') · ★ guilt ×3 → mood, anhedonia, self-harm, use since · card — interrogate for jaundice, organomegaly, murmur, injection sites, dipstick · name the version's diagnosis with reasons · grouped differentials · ★ HIV test named, consent · malaria films · harm reduction · confidentiality with the notification caveat · safety-net.

back.dx: Version 2 — HIV seroconversion illness: a week of no energy and fever, constant, worsening, bed-bound two days; three weeks in Indonesia, back two weeks; one night injected heroin — first ever use — one needle shared between the group, none since; street food nightly; pre-travel GP gave a hepatitis shot; no bites, sick contacts, animals, tattoos, transfusion; 'no sex overseas' — but ever sexually active: yes, never condoms, multiple partners at times, women. HIV box positive: sore throat, chest rash, fever/chills, drenching night sweats, some weight loss, neck lumps; hepatitis box negative; injection box negative. Card: T 38.2, morbilliform rash, generalised lymphadenopathy, exudative tonsillitis; on request — no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly, no murmur, injection sites unremarkable, dipstick negative. EBV is the trap answer — say it is the closest mimic. Explain: 'I'm concerned you contracted HIV when you shared that needle — the first stage, seroconversion illness, causes exactly this: fever, sore throat, rash, glands, night sweats, exhaustion — it looks like flu and is very commonly missed'; reasons — the route, the symptoms, the findings. 'I've ruined my life over one stupid night' → pause, 'what's going through your mind?' → concern not result; treatment today — normal lifespan, undetectable = untransmissible. Differentials: EBV/CMV/toxoplasma · hepatitis B and C ('your shot covers A and B; no vaccine for C — curable with tablets 8–12 weeks') · infective endocarditis (no murmur, reassuring) · malaria, dengue, typhoid (films) · syphilis · leukaemia/lymphoma · depression/anxiety. Plan: ★ HIV test with specific permission (4th-gen Ag/Ab ± RNA, repeat 6 weeks), HBV/HCV, syphilis, EBV, LFT, FBE, thick/thin films ×3; sexual health referral; confidentiality honest — notifiable, contacts traced sensitively, name not given; NSP and take-home naloxone 'not because I assume you'll use again'; mood review next week; safety-net confusion/drowsiness, jaundice, chest pain/SOB → ED/000.

setting: General practice, Kadina. Nine-minute station. He coughs harshly and repeatedly throughout — the acting is data. Observations from the examiner include the fifth vital sign. Two headings: infection, and malignancy.
stem: Jack Mullins, 30, has come in feeling unwell and feverish. He is a known case of HIV and stopped his antiretroviral medication six months ago.
tasks: Take a history from the patient (about 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings, or read them from the card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 9 minutes: 0:00 ★ all five observations incl. SpO2 · one empathic sentence · ★ 'I can hear that cough' · unwell and fever explored separately · 1:30 HIV history — diagnosed when, ★ why stopped (no moralising), follow-up, complications · 2:15 ★ signposted whole-body infection screen (breadth not depth; characterise the cough in three questions) incl. sexual history despite HIV, injecting, chest pain · 4:45 ★ open the malignancy heading — weight, appetite, lumps, sweats, mouth ulcers/patches, purple marks, haemoptysis, smoking, asbestos, moles · mood · 5:45 examination in one run incl. vocal resonance and a full node survey · ★ the white patch — painful? scrapes off? colour? where? · ★ 'normal chest but febrile, tachypnoeic, hypoxic — in advanced HIV a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia' · 7:00 pneumonia named and reasoned · opportunistic infection as a concern not a diagnosis · ★ the cancers named honestly, reaction contained · other infections individually · restart ART · safety-net.

back.dx: Pneumonia in a man with untreated HIV (ART stopped six months ago — felt well, tablets nauseated him, long trip to Adelaide; no specialist review for a year; no prior complications), with opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis, TB) and malignancy on the list. Three to four days feverish with rigors, worsening, paracetamol useless; dry cough; new exertional breathlessness on stairs; everything else negative; smokes 10/day; mood flat. Examiner: alert, no rash/jaundice, mildly dehydrated; T 38.0, HR 104, BP 118/74, RR 24, ★ SpO2 92% RA; ★ a white patch in the mouth — scrapes off, on tongue and buccal mucosa (candidiasis — but describe before naming: Kaposi = violaceous, raised, hard palate, doesn't scrape; OHL = white, corrugated, lateral tongue, doesn't scrape); no lymphadenopathy; ★ respiratory examination entirely normal; HS dual; abdomen and dipstick normal. To the examiner: 'although the chest is normal he is febrile, tachypnoeic and hypoxic — in advanced HIV there isn't enough immune function to produce consolidation, crackles or an effusion, so a normal chest does not exclude pneumonia — the same principle as febrile neutropenia'. To Jack: 'the most likely thing is a pneumonia — fever, cough, unwell, Panadol not helping; on examination your oxygen is low and you're breathing fast — your lungs aren't picking up oxygen properly, even though listening sounded normal'; 'but my chest sounded fine?' → 'the low oxygen tells me more than my stethoscope does'. Opportunistic concern named (Pneumocystis, TB) alongside common causes (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma) — don't call it Pneumocystis with no CD4, viral load, white cells or film. ★ 'HIV also raises the risk of certain cancers, and I have to be honest with you': lung cancer (cough, smoker), Kaposi sarcoma (the patch — exclude), lymphoma, leukaemia → he is shaken → contain: 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer; I'm telling you what I have to rule out; the most likely explanation today is still an infection'. Other infections named individually (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, sinusitis; gastroenteritis; hepatitis; syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea; meningitis; cellulitis); then low mood/adjustment, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, OSA. Plan: send in today — CXR, bloods incl. CD4/viral load, start treatment; reconnect with the HIV team; ★ restarting ART is one of the most important things we do — and look at what made it hard last time. 'Is this because I stopped my tablets?' — hidden agenda at ~7 min.
plan: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have his observations — BP, pulse, RR, temperature AND oxygen saturation?' → 118/74, 104, 24, 38.0, 92% · 'Hello Jack, I'm sorry to hear you've not been well — let's work out what's going on together' · ★ 'I can hear that cough — we'll come to it'
Unwell: sleepy/low energy/feverish? duration (3–4 days), constant, worse, better/worse · fever block: measured? chills? (yes) taken anything, helped? (Panadol, nothing)

HIV: 'when were you diagnosed? (5 y) I know you've stopped your medication — can you tell me what led to that? (felt fine, nausea, long trip to Adelaide) — no judgement here · regular follow-up? (not for a year) · any complications before? (never)'

★ 'I'm going to run through the whole body fairly quickly, area by area — most of these will be a simple no, and that's what I'm hoping for': sore throat/coryza/facial/ear pain · ★ cough — dry or chesty? SOB? noisy breathing? (dry; puffed on the stairs — three questions, keep going) · nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain/diarrhoea · dysuria/frequency · headache/stiff neck/photophobia · ★ sexual health (active in 3 months? condoms? discharge/rash/ulcers/scrotal pain) — despite HIV · jaundice/dark urine/pale stools · rash, hot painful skin · travel · ★ recreational drugs, ever injected? chest pain/palpitations (endocarditis) · animals

★ Malignancy heading: 'a few more — weight loss without trying? appetite? lumps or bumps? night sweats? ulcers or patches in your mouth? new purple or red marks on your skin? ever coughed up blood? do you smoke? (10/day) what work — asbestos? new or changing moles?' · if time: 'how has your mood been?' (flat)

setting: General practice, Moonta. EXAMINATION-FIRST station — no history taking. Findings from the examiner for four minutes; the results card is handed over at exactly four minutes; then you explain results, diagnosis and differentials to Jane.
stem: Jane Whitmore, 40, has come in feeling unwell — tired and nauseated, no fever. She has recently returned from a trip to the Philippines. No sexual activity overseas, no mosquito bites, no needle exposures. Appendicectomy ten years ago.
tasks: Begin with a physical examination, asking the examiner for the findings — there is no history taking
At four minutes you are given the investigation results; explain them to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 minutes: ★ 0:00 GREET JANE FIRST — name, role, what will happen, when I'll be back, is that all right (15 s) · 0:20 examination as one run across the differentials, not at the liver: general (jaundice) · four vitals · throat, ears · thyroid, full node survey · chest · heart · abdomen → 'hepatomegaly' → ★ don't accept it: span, tender?, border, shifting dullness, scratch marks, bruising, bowel sounds · DRE · ★ 'with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone' pelvic · ★ two office tests: dipstick (bilirubin) and ★ pregnancy test · 4:00 turn back to Jane, acknowledge the wait · results in three sentences (test → plain English → meaning), under a minute, no numbers, no abbreviations · 5:30 'most likely' hepatitis A + reasons incl. bilirubin in the urine · 6:30 differentials — ★ TRAVEL FIRST, then liver/abdominal incl. cancer, then pregnancy, then the generic tiredness list · plan, notification, hygiene, alcohol, safety-net.

back.dx: Acute hepatitis A (most likely — confirmatory anti-HAV IgM pending): three weeks in the Philippines with relatives, home cooking and street food, back a fortnight; a week tired, nauseated, off food, afebrile; husband noticed yellow eyes two days ago. Examination: alert, ★ jaundiced, no rash/pallor, mildly dehydrated; BP 120/80, HR 88, RR 12, T 36.9; throat/ears/thyroid/nodes normal; chest clear; HS dual; abdomen not distended, ★ hepatomegaly 3 cm, non-tender, smooth regular border, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no scratch marks/bruising, bowel sounds normal; DRE and pelvic normal; ★ dipstick bilirubin positive, urobilinogen raised; ★ pregnancy test negative. Results card: WCC 13.2, bilirubin 68, ALT 780, AST 640, ALP 130, GGT 110, INR 1.1, albumin 38, HBV and HCV negative — hepatocellular pattern (to the examiner). Explain in three beats each: FBC — white cells, immune cells, raised = fighting infection/inflammation · liver test — enzymes raised = inflammation in the liver · hepatitis B and C negative. 'Damaged?' → 'inflamed rather than damaged; the two numbers that measure how well it's doing its job are normal today'. Diagnosis 'most likely', never certain: enlarged liver, jaundice, bilirubin in the urine ('made by the liver, normally never reaches the urine — finding it there tells me the problem is in your liver'), raised enzymes, B and C negative, recent travel, nausea; spreads via contaminated food/water. Settles over 2–8 weeks, no specific treatment, never chronic, lifelong immunity. Differentials in the order the case demands: (1) travel — malaria, dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis E, EBV, HIV, TB; (2) liver/abdominal — hepatitis B/C (negative), autoimmune hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, gallstones/cholangitis, ★ cancer of the liver or pancreas ('particularly because your liver was not tender'); (3) pregnancy (tested, negative); (4) anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, lymphoma/leukaemia, autoimmune, depression, heart failure, OSA. Plan: anti-HAV IgM, liver ultrasound, review this week; no alcohol, check before any medication (paracetamol at reduced dose VERIFY); handwashing, don't prepare food for others, don't share towels; notify — household vaccinated (within 14 days VERIFY); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, worsening jaundice, can't keep fluids down. Hidden agenda: sister died of pancreatic cancer — tearful at the word cancer; name it, proportion it, say what resolves it.
plan: ★ 'No questions, thank you. — Hello Jane, I'm Dr [name], one of the doctors here, and I'll be looking after you today. setting: General practice. Vitals in the stem. Examination findings on screen/card when asked. Five minutes of history. No management task — but a plan and a safety-net still earn marks.
stem: Ben Alderton, 25, has come in feeling unwell. He attends a sauna regularly with friends, and his friends have similar symptoms. He is currently taking PrEP. T 38.4, HR 96, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.

You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: 8 minutes. Acknowledge the worry · 'unwell' in four questions · ★ open the sauna: how often, ★ 'what do your friends have?', what do you do there (sex) · ★ three water infections: Legionella (cough, SOB, fever, diarrhoea, confusion) · hepatitis A (abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine/pale stools) · Pseudomonas (itchy spots under swimwear) · ★ PrEP block, three separate marks: adherence · 3-monthly screening · hepatitis A/B vaccination · ★ normalise once, then the full sexual history (partners, number, gender, condoms, practices, previous STI, alcohol/drugs) — don't stop to counsel · STI symptoms incl. ulcers, discharge, scrotum, back passage · the rest · examination by name incl. throat, nodes, palms/soles, genitals, dipstick · acute viral hepatitis WITHOUT guessing the subtype · differentials by exposure: sauna ×3 + crypto, STIs with ★ HIV high on the list despite PrEP · ★ three-site swabs · confidentiality accurately · vaccinate · 3-monthly reviews · safety-net.

back.dx: Acute viral hepatitis (subtype deliberately not guessed — A via faecal-oral including sexual transmission between men, or B/C via sex) in an MSM on PrEP: a week of fever, anorexia, upper abdominal pain, vomiting, partner says he looks yellow, urine darker; no cough/SOB/diarrhoea/confusion (Legionella less likely), no rash (Pseudomonas less likely). Sauna 2–3×/week, same group, a couple of friends off work with unknown symptoms; 'we have sex there as well' (say it back: both a water exposure and a sexual exposure). PrEP: misses the odd dose when he stays out; last review two months ago but ★ never screened for STIs; doesn't know if he's had hepatitis A/B vaccines. Sexual history: no stable partner, several partners, all men, no condoms, oral and anal, never diagnosed, sometimes after drinks. No STI symptoms. Card: jaundiced, T 38.4, tender hepatomegaly span >13 cm, no splenomegaly, chest clear, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no genital/perianal lesions or discharge, dipstick bilirubin positive. Differentials grouped by exposure: sauna — Legionella (warm-water spray; no cough/SOB), Pseudomonas folliculitis (no rash), cryptosporidium (chlorine-resistant; no diarrhoea); STIs — ★ HIV high on the list ('PrEP is very effective but not absolute, and it depends on taking it consistently — you miss doses; one blood test'), syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea and chlamydia (throat and rectum often asymptomatic — urine alone misses them); then EBV/CMV, travel, lymphoma/leukaemia, depression, thyroid/diabetes/anaemia/coeliac. Plan: LFT + clotting, full hepatitis panel, HIV (4th-gen ± RNA), syphilis; ★ swabs throat, anorectal, first-pass urine; rest, fluids, no alcohol, no shared food preparation, no sex until results; hepatitis A/B vaccination if not covered; PrEP reviews back to 3-monthly with a full screen; confidentiality accurate (notifiable as a case, not a name; partner notification anonymised; cousin in town → flag the file, results to a chosen number); safety-net confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, can't keep fluids, worsening jaundice; review 2 days; teach-back.

setting: General practice, Wallaroo. Four tasks in eight minutes — examination begins at 4:00, management at 7:00. Observations from the examiner at the door (online: 'I'm taking you through to the treatment room to check your observations').
stem: Mary Ellis, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has come in because she has been feeling unwell for the past few days. First pregnancy; antenatal care so far uncomplicated.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings (2 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
time: 8 minutes: observations first, one sentence · empathic sentence · ★ offer the word FEVERISH — she won't volunteer it · fever block: measured, chills, medication · urinary upper and lower: dysuria, frequency, haematuria, nausea/vomiting, ★ flank pain — site and radiation only · sexual health with a permission sentence · other infection: throat, cough, headache/neck, travel · ★ pregnancy-specific: vision, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia) · thirst and polyuria separately (GDM) · jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP) · palpitations/SOB (anaemia) · obstetric close — tightenings, fluid/bleeding, movements · ★ allergies BEFORE naming an antibiotic · 4:00 examination as one run: findings not regions, four vitals again, ★ fundal height, uterine tenderness, fetal heart · ★ 'is there any renal angle tenderness?' · dipstick — leucocytes and nitrites · 6:00 pyelonephritis with reasons; the baby question in one sentence; differentials LISTED not explained · 7:00 ★ ED today, admission, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, culture first.

back.dx: Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks: 3–4 days hot and shivery with rigors last night, worsening, paracetamol useless; dysuria and frequency, no visible haematuria; vomited 3–4 times; right flank/back pain radiating to the groin (Version B: low central suprapubic pain — the diagnosis is unchanged when renal angle tenderness is positive). Pregnancy-specific screen negative: no visual blurring, swelling, headache (pre-eclampsia); no thirst/polyuria (GDM); no jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch (cholestasis/AFLP); no palpitations/SOB (anaemia); no tightenings, fluid, bleeding; baby moving; pregnancy vitamins only; no allergies. Examiner: alert, flushed, mildly dehydrated; BP 110/70, HR 108, RR 18, ★ T 38.7; throat/chest/heart normal; mild suprapubic tenderness, no RUQ tenderness, no organomegaly; ★ fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, uterus non-tender, FHR 145; ★ right renal angle tenderness POSITIVE; dipstick leucocytes +++, nitrites +, blood ++, protein trace. To Mary: 'pyelonephritis — an infection in your kidney: burning, going more often, fever, vomiting, tender over your kidney, urine test showing infection'; 'dangerous for the baby?' → 'it can be, which is exactly why we treat it properly and quickly — today is the best thing for both of you'. Differentials LISTED in 25 s: pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, other infections (STIs incl. herpes and HIV, throat, chest, meningitis), the liver conditions of pregnancy (cholestasis, acute fatty liver), appendicitis, renal stone, anaemia. Management, the four things first: ★ ED today, expect admission, IV antibiotics + IV fluids ('too serious to treat with tablets at home'), MSU for culture before antibiotics; then oral switch once afebrile 24–48 h, 10–14 days total, test-of-cure culture 1–2 weeks after, obstetric team checks the baby; 'do I have to go?' → sepsis and preterm labour risks; 'safe for the baby?' → yes, well-studied antibiotics. Safety-net: worse, shaking chills, can't keep fluids down, tightenings, bleeding, fluid, reduced movements → straight back.

setting: General practice, regional South Australia. Counselling station — the assessment is already done and summarised in the stem; no history task. 'Can I get temazepam?' arrives when you ask for her concerns at the start, or at minute seven if you never ask. Cross-reference MED-57 (sleep history version).
stem: Jane Miller, 17, Year 12 student, presenting with tiredness over two to three months. Your completed assessment: recent examinations with considerable stress; bed after 1 am, up at 6:30; easy-going personality; mood normal, no anxiety disorder; three to four cups of coffee every night while studying. No weight loss, fever, night sweats, lumps or travel; no snoring or witnessed apnoeas; no medications, alcohol or drugs; periods regular and not heavy. Examination and vital signs normal.
tasks: Explain your assessment to the patient — diagnosis and cause of the tiredness (about 3 minutes)
Counsel her regarding your management plan
Answer the patient's questions
time: 8 minutes. 30 s: open question, empathy, ★ 'anything you were hoping we'd sort out today?' (the temazepam line — park it explicitly), ★ 'is it all right if I explain what I think, then we make a plan together?' · Task 1, four blocks, three minutes: NAME it (sleep restriction) · DEFINE it (8–10 h needed; she gets ~5) · REASON it (exam trigger, pattern persisting, caffeine) · SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED · teach-back · Task 2, eight headings one sentence each: hygiene · diary · ★ CBT-I first line · caffeine · relaxation · lifestyle · named organisation · review 4 weeks + conditional bloods/sleep study · Task 3, ★ VALIDATE → DECLINE with ≥2 reasons → SUBSTITUTE (not second best) → CONTRACT (four weeks, a date) · safety-net incl. mood/self-harm · driving.

back.dx: Chronic insufficient sleep — behaviourally induced sleep restriction — in a 17-year-old: ~5 hours on school nights (bed 1–2 am, up 6:30), studies and scrolls in bed, 3–4 instant coffees each evening (last ~11 pm, ~380 mg, half still circulating at bedtime), set off by exam stress and persisting after it; catches up to midday at weekends and feels much better (the pattern that says 'not enough sleep', not blood or thyroid); mood normal, no self-harm, no snoring/apnoeas/sleep attacks. 'Nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease'. Management aim: improve quantity and quality of sleep — (1) sleep hygiene: fixed bed and wake time seven days, bed for sleep only (no phone/laptop/study/TV), dark quiet cool, out of bed if not asleep in 20–30 min, warm shower/milk; (2) sleep diary two weeks (bedtime, sleep onset, hours, quality/10); (3) ★ CBT-I — first line in Australia, more effective than hypnotics and durable — psychologist referral or Australian online programmes; cognitive half (the 'if I don't sleep I'll fail' worry) + behavioural half (stimulus control, relaxation, time-in-bed matching); (4) caffeine: half-life ~5 h, nothing after early afternoon, cut the total, expect a headache; (5) relaxation — mindfulness, breathing, PMR, yoga; (6) lifestyle — daytime exercise, regular meals, no alcohol/smoking/vaping, screens off; (7) named: Sleep Health Foundation fact sheets, headspace (12–25); (8) review 4 weeks with the diary → if no better TSH, FBE, ferritin → sleep study if another disorder is suggested. Temazepam: validate (exhausted, worked for a friend) → decline with reasons (dependence/tolerance/withdrawal, next-day drowsiness for driving and study, not recommended under 18, doesn't fix the cause) → substitute (CBT-I works better and lasts) → contract (four weeks, then we look together). 'Just a few for exams?' → exam time is when grogginess costs most; two weeks is enough to start dependence. 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I'm not doing the thing that helps for two weeks and causes a problem for two years — everything else starts today.' Safety-net: mood drops, hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, sudden daytime sleep attacks, snoring/apnoeas → sooner. Driving: don't drive sleepy, pull over (P-plater).
plan: 'Hello Jane, how have you been feeling since we last spoke?' · 'I'm sorry — that sounds miserable, especially in Year 12' · ★ 'before I start explaining — anything you were hoping we'd sort out today, or anything you've been worried about?' → temazepam → 'a really good question and I'll answer it properly — can I first tell you what I think is going on?' · ★ 'is it all right if I explain, and then we make a plan together?'

1A NAME: 'the most likely cause is a sleep problem — there are breathing types like sleep apnoea, body-clock types, nightmare disorders; yours is sleep restriction, or sleep deprivation — your sleep itself is fine, there just isn't enough of it'
1B DEFINE: 'enough good-quality sleep is a basic requirement — concentration, memory, mood, appetite, immune system; at your age eight to ten hours; bed after one, up at half six, is about five'

1C REASON: 'it started when your exams started — stressed, up late; sleep problems are often triggered by a stressful stretch and keep going after it, because the pattern is set; and three or four coffees in the evening is still working at bedtime' · 'I'm fine on weekends' → 'that's exactly what we see when the problem is not enough sleep rather than something in the blood or thyroid'

1D EXCLUDED: 'no weight loss, fevers, sweats, lumps, travel; normal periods; no snoring or breathing pauses; mood fine; normal examination — that's what lets me be confident' · 'nothing wrong with me?' → 'there is something wrong — it just isn't a disease' · 'anaemic? mum said bloods' → not needed now; bloods at review if no better · teach-back: 'if a friend asked tonight what the doctor said?'

Aim stated · 2A hygiene, the specifics · 2B diary two weeks · 2C ★ 'CBT for insomnia — in Australia first line, more effective than sleeping tablets, keeps working after you stop; psychologist, or an Australian online programme' · 'what would they do?' → cognitive half / behavioural half

2D caffeine: 'the big one for you — hangs around five hours; nothing caffeinated after early afternoon; cut the total; expect a headache' (defensive 'I need it' → no lecture) · 2E relaxation · 2F lifestyle · 2G ★ Sleep Health Foundation, headspace — named · 2H review 4 weeks with the diary → bloods (thyroid, FBE, iron) → sleep study if indicated

Safety-net: mood drops, hopeless, thoughts of harming yourself, sudden daytime sleep attacks, snoring/breathing pauses → come sooner · ★ 'don't drive when you feel sleepy — pull over' · summary in one breath · 'anything I've missed?'
ask: ★ 'Is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd sort out today?' / ★ 'Is it all right if I explain what I think is going on, and then we make a plan together?'

★ 'In your case I think it's sleep restriction — your sleep is fine, there just isn't enough of it.' / 'Someone your age needs eight to ten hours.' / 'These problems are often triggered by stress and then keep going after the stress has passed.'

★ 'I've looked for the other causes and not found them — that's what lets me be confident.' / 'So there's nothing wrong with me?' → 'There is something wrong — it just isn't a disease. Not getting enough sleep is a real problem with real effects and a real treatment. I'm not dismissing it.'
'Bed for sleep only. If you're not asleep in twenty to thirty minutes, get up, do something boring in dim light, and come back when you feel sleepy.'

★ 'CBT for insomnia is first line — more effective than sleeping tablets, and it keeps working after you stop.' / 'What will the psychologist actually do?' → 'Two halves. The cognitive half works on the thoughts that keep it going — the "if I don't sleep I'll fail" worry that itself keeps you awake. The behavioural half teaches stimulus control, relaxation, and matching your time in bed to the sleep you're actually getting.'
'Caffeine hangs around about five hours, so four cups in the evening is half still circulating at bedtime. Nothing with caffeine after early afternoon.'

★ 'I can see why you're asking — you're exhausted and you've heard it worked for someone else. But I don't think a sleeping tablet is the right answer for you. It helps for a short time, but it comes with real problems. The main one is dependence — your body gets used to it, it stops working at the same dose, we end up increasing it, and if you try to stop you get withdrawal: worse sleep than before, anxiety, shakiness. There's next-day drowsiness, which matters for driving and study, and these tablets aren't recommended at your age. And most importantly — it doesn't fix the cause.'

★ 'What I'm offering instead isn't second best. The psychological treatment works better than the tablets do, and it keeps working after you finish.' / ★ 'Give me four weeks with the diary and the plan. Come back and we'll look at it together — and if it hasn't worked we think again, properly, not by reaching for a tablet.'

'Just a few, to get through exams?' → 'Exam time is exactly when the next-day grogginess would cost you most, and two weeks is long enough to start the dependence problem. What I can do this week is get the diary going, fix the coffee, and get you a psychology appointment quickly.' / 'So you're not going to help me?' → 'I am helping you — I'm just not doing the thing that would help for two weeks and cause a problem for two years. back.dx: Cardiac (exertional) syncope from aortic stenosis. 'Out cold', <1 min, witnessed by his wife, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, not confused after (shaken only), grazed elbow, no head strike. ★ Walking up the driveway with the shopping (exertion), ★ no warning at all, prior light-headedness twice on the golf course walking uphill, months of chest tightness and breathlessness on hills 'put down to age' — the AS triad. No meds, none stopped; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: no postural drop, pulse regular slow-rising (ask: low volume? heave? thrill?), ESM RUSE radiating to the carotids, soft S2, neuro normal, glucose 5.6, ECG SR with LVH. To Bill: 'not a trip — a blackout from the heart rather than a simple faint: no warning (faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating), and it happened on exertion; a murmur — a narrowed, stiff valve, the door blood leaves the heart through; on exertion the body asks for more blood, the valve can't let enough through, the brain briefly goes short'. Differentials: arrhythmia (still needs excluding), cardiomyopathy, PE, stroke/seizure. Plan: admit to a monitored bed, bloods, echo, cardiology; if severe → valve replacement, works very well. ★ 'Please don't drive until the specialists have assessed you' (Austroads; SA Registrar of Motor Vehicles; notification duty) · no heights, machinery, swimming alone · 000 if recurrent, chest pain, palpitations, severe SOB. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law's stroke; 'can I drive home and come back tomorrow?' — always asked.

'What you had wasn't a trip — you blacked out, and I think the blackout came from your heart rather than being a simple faint. Two things point me there: you had no warning at all — simple faints almost always give a few seconds of dizziness or sweating first — and it happened while you were exerting yourself.'

'There's a murmur — an extra sound — which suggests one of the valves has become narrowed and stiff. That valve is the door blood leaves your heart through. When you exert yourself your body asks for more blood, the narrowed valve can't let enough through, your brain briefly goes short, and you black out. It also explains the chest tightness and breathlessness on hills.'

'Is it serious?' → 'I want to be straight with you: blacking out with this kind of valve problem is serious, and it's treatable. I'd like to admit you today to a bed with heart monitoring, do bloods, and arrange an echo to see exactly how narrow that valve is. If it's significantly narrowed the treatment is to repair or replace it, which works very well.'

back.dx: Vasovagal (reflex) syncope — third episode, each with a textbook trigger and a prodrome: (1) jumped out of bed to answer the phone, (2) the sight of blood, (3) today after 1–2 hours standing still in a hot, packed, exciting parade — blurry vision and light-headedness first, 30 s LOC, went floppy (no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence), tired but oriented after, 'white as a sheet', hip bruise. Chronic headaches on Nurofen (distractor): no morning vomiting, weight loss, nocturnal/positional worsening; fundoscopy normal → refer to GP, medication-overuse flagged. No palpitations, chest pain, SOB; periods regular; no alcohol/drugs; no FHx sudden death. PEFE: BP 120/80 sitting → 94/62 standing (drop 26/18 — name it), pulse 82 reg, neuro/fundi/CVS/RS/abdo normal. Explain: nerves overactive → vessels in the legs widen → blood pools → brain short for seconds → lying flat fixes it. Three reasons: setting (hot, prolonged standing, crowd, excitement); earlier episodes fit classic triggers; clear prodrome. Postural drop = supporting evidence, not the diagnosis (postural hypotension causes dizziness/near-fainting more than true LOC; reflex syncope produces a transient drop). Differentials by system: cardiac (arrhythmia — no palpitations; HOCM — no chest pain/SOB/FHx, had a warning; valve/ischaemia), brain (seizure — friends' account; SOL, bleed, meningitis), chemistry (glucose, sodium), blood (anaemia — periods), drugs/alcohol/medications, panic. Management: lie down legs up or head between knees at the warning; counter-pressure; fluids in heat; don't skip meals; keep calves moving; FBC + pregnancy test today; caution heights/swimming alone; GP 1–2 weeks (headaches, ibuprofen frequency); driving — a triggered, prodromal, standing faint generally doesn't restrict; tell the GP if the pattern changes; return if no warning, supine, exertional, or chest pain/palpitations first. Hidden agenda: brain tumour fear from googling the headaches; the licence.

back.dx: Congenital long QT syndrome: three syncopal episodes over months, each while seated doing nothing (class, home, class), ~1 min, complete LOC, no jerking/tongue bite/incontinence, ★ never any warning ('I'm fine, then I'm on the floor'), not confused after, not pale, no injury; everything else negative — no chest pain/palpitations/SOB, no medications (none for acne/allergies/nausea/mood), no alcohol/drugs, no stress, no PMHx; ★ mother used to faint when younger and still does sometimes; no sudden deaths, drownings, cot deaths or congenital deafness. Vitals: pulse 50 (bradycardia — note it). ECG in seven steps: rate ~50 (six large squares), regular, P before every QRS → sinus bradycardia, PR normal, QRS normal, ST no elevation/depression, T waves and QT → ★ 'examiner, could you tell me what the QTc is?' → 0.54 s = 540 ms — markedly prolonged (expect <~460 in a girl; >500 high risk) → sinus bradycardia with a significantly prolonged QTc — long QT syndrome. Never try to measure it silently on a laminated tracing (paper-folding unavailable, Bazett under time pressure unrealistic — candidates default to sinus bradycardia/sick sinus and fail; a correct differential does not rescue a wrong primary diagnosis). To Lily: 'after each beat the electrical system takes longer than it should to reset; sometimes it tips the heart into a fast, disorganised rhythm — the heart can't pump, blood doesn't reach the brain, you black out, then it settles, which is why you wake up fine'. Three reasons: the QT on the tracing; mum's fainting (a version runs in families); no warning (cause in the heart, not a simple faint). 'Could I die?' → honest: taken seriously, occasionally dangerous — hence not home; very treatable; finding it today is good news; a tablet (beta blocker) greatly reduces the chance; a list of medicines to avoid. Differentials across systems: other rhythms (too slow, block), muscle/valve, seizure, brain, glucose/salts, PE, reflex/orthostatic (seated, no warning), panic last. Plan: admit on a monitor, K/Mg/Ca/TSH/glucose, paediatric cardiology today, beta blocker likely, QT-prolonging drug list (antibiotics, antiemetics); ★ when mum arrives — with Lily's permission — mum needs an ECG today; screen parents and siblings; sport — defer to the specialists (type-dependent), hold competitive sport, no swimming (some forms triggered by exercise and swimming).

Examiner won't give it: 'The QT runs from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave, measured in lead II. My assessment: the corrected QT is prolonged; with recurrent syncope without prodrome and a family history, long QT syndrome.'

ECG: rate ~70, regular sinus, PR normal, QRS narrow, axis normal, ★ ST elevation II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression aVL and I (reciprocal change = infarction, not pericarditis/early repolarisation), no Q waves, T upright; examine V1–V3 for posterior extension; ★ right-sided leads (V4R) before any nitrate → 'acute inferior STEMI — a time-critical emergency' (RCA ~80%; ST III > II favours RCA). 'Am I going to die?' → serious and very treatable; the safest thing is what we're doing now. Differential: hypoglycaemia (skipped breakfast, hours of walking — may still be part of it), hyperglycaemia/DKA, arrhythmia/valve, PE, TIA, seizure, electrolytes, dehydration, anaemia, medication — the tracing puts MI at the top. Action: ★ aspirin 300 mg chewed, IV access, monitor with a defibrillator available, oxygen only if SpO2 <93%, V4R before nitrates, ★ 000 to a PCI-capable centre, ECG transmitted ahead, stay with her; no party; ★ no driving today or until cleared (~2 weeks after successful PCI); call the husband; car stays.

back.dx: Pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise — provoked by post-operative immobilisation, day 1 after TKR (syncope occurs in ~1 in 7 PE presentations and suggests a central clot with RV strain). Complete LOC ('there's a gap', last memory reaching for the rail), unwitnessed, found a few minutes later, first ever; had just passed urine, not straining, not standing long, bathroom not hot, knee sore but no worse; ★ no warning; no chest pain/palpitations; nobody saw shaking; 'white as a sheet'; muddled ~1 min then himself; grazed elbow, shoulder took the impact, 'I don't think I hit my head' (if he clipped the sink and is on enoxaparin → CT head too); ★ entirely negative respiratory and calf screen — do NOT downgrade PE (that is the designed reaction); no CNS/GI/fever; oxycodone at midnight, paracetamol; ★ nightly abdominal injection, name unknown, ★ one dose missed on the day of surgery; perindopril restarted this morning; nil by mouth pre-op, eaten little; no previous VTE/cancer/travel/FHx; ex-smoker 20/day quit 10 y; BP tablet only. Vitals: HR 104, SpO2 94%, postural drop 118/74 → 104/66. To John, lead with the dangerous diagnosis: 'the thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs; the reason isn't your symptoms, it's your situation — major knee surgery yesterday, hardly able to move that leg; blood clots in the deep veins and a piece travels to the lungs; it can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all; even though your breathing is fine I'm not prepared to leave that untested'. Then: vasovagal (pain, toilet, first stand after surgery — may well be it), peri-operative MI (days 0–3, can be quiet), orthostatic hypotension (surgical blood loss + opioids), rhythm, glucose, salts. 'But I feel fine' → 'a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does; treatable, very treatable early; the scan takes twenty minutes'. Investigations tied to differentials: bedside — lying/standing obs, continuous sats and cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, BSL, oxygen to 94–98%, two large-bore cannulae; PE — ★ urgent CTPA after renal function and contrast allergy (V/Q if contrast contraindicated); ★ no D-dimer (raised in virtually everyone a day after surgery, wouldn't change management); MI — ECG + serial troponin; bleeding — FBE, coags, group and hold, wound and drains; metabolic — UEC (also for contrast), Ca, Mg; CXR (collapse/effusion/pneumothorax); CT head if head strike or persistent confusion; bedside echo for RV strain if hypotensive; discuss empirical anticoagulation with orthopaedics while awaiting the scan; bed rest, supervised mobilisation, mechanical prophylaxis; escalate to the registrar now; MET if he deteriorates; ★ 'press the buzzer before you get up'. Hidden agenda: home Friday — wife Margaret has early dementia; social work either way.

'Did it happen while you were passing urine or opening your bowels, or straining? Was the bathroom hot?' / ★ 'Did you get any warning?' / ★ 'Did you hit your head?'

★ 'Have you had a blood-thinning injection since the operation — do you know which one, and have any doses been missed?' / 'What have they been giving you for pain — anything strong like morphine or oxycodone, or a nerve tablet such as pregabalin? Were your usual blood-pressure tablets restarted this morning?'

'Have you ever had a clot in the leg or the lung? Any cancer? Long flights or drives? Anyone in the family with clotting problems, or died suddenly and young?' / ★ 'Is there anything you have been particularly worried about?'

★ 'Everything you've told me is reassuring, and I want to be honest about where that leaves us. The thing I am most concerned about is a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood tubes of your lungs. The reason I am concerned is not your symptoms — it is your situation. You had major knee surgery yesterday and you have hardly been able to move that leg; when the legs stay still, blood can clot in the deep veins, and a piece can travel to the lungs. That can cause exactly this sort of blackout, sometimes with no chest symptoms at all. So even though your breathing is fine, I am not prepared to leave that untested.'

'But I feel fine — how can it be a clot?' → 'I know, and that's a good sign. But a clot in the lung doesn't always announce itself — sometimes a blackout is the only thing it does. It is treatable, and very treatable when we find it early, which is exactly what I'm trying to do. The scan takes about twenty minutes and we'll know today.'

'A simple faint — a vasovagal faint — is common when people are in pain, or straining on the toilet, or standing up for the first time after an operation, and that may well be what happened. Heart attacks are more common in the first few days after a big operation and can be surprisingly quiet, so I want to check that. Low blood pressure from blood loss during surgery, together with the strong painkillers, can also drop you when you stand.' / 'A simple faint is a diagnosis I can only make after ruling out the dangerous ones.'

★ 'For pulmonary embolism, which is my leading diagnosis: an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram, after checking renal function and contrast allergy — a V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated.' / ★ 'I would not order a D-dimer, because it is elevated in virtually every patient a day after major surgery and would not change my management either way.'

'For myocardial infarction: the ECG plus serial troponin. For bleeding and anaemia: full blood examination, coagulation profile, group and hold, and inspection of the wound and drains. For metabolic causes: urea, electrolytes and creatinine — which I also need before contrast — plus calcium and magnesium. A chest X-ray; a CT head if he struck his head or remains confused; a bedside echo looking for right ventricular strain if he becomes hypotensive.' / 'I'd discuss empirical anticoagulation with the orthopaedic team while awaiting the scan, escalate to my registrar now, and call a MET if he deteriorates.'

'Am I still getting home Friday? My wife's not well' → 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear how much it matters. I can't promise, but I'll make sure the team knows about your wife and that social work is involved either way.' / ★ 'Please press the buzzer before you get up — do not walk to the toilet on your own.'

setting: Suburban GP, South Australia. Vitals on the door (all normal, no postural drop). You do not examine — findings are supplied only for what you NAME; ask for nystagmus and Dix–Hallpike by name or the station never discloses them. History hard-stops at 5:00. stem: James Whitfield, 60, has come in complaining of dizziness. Reception note: 'dizzy spells, 5 days'. HR 78 reg · BP 132/80 sitting, 128/78 standing · RR 14 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.7 · BGL 5.8 · GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings you require
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan to the patient

back.dx: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (posterior canal) — Version A. True spinning ('like six beers'), bursts of 20–30 s, completely normal between, ★ set off by rolling over in bed, getting up, looking up to the top shelf; settles lying still; no LOC, no falls (grabbed the bedpost); all five ear questions negative; all nine brain questions negative; no CVS symptoms; perindopril 5 mg × 6 y unchanged, 2–3 beers Friday, ex-smoker at 40; widowed, lives alone, drives grandson to school Thursdays. Hidden agenda: brother's stroke at 62 — he will not volunteer it unless asked concerns; if never asked he interrupts at ~6 min 'is this a stroke?'. PEFE: positional nystagmus present, Dix–Hallpike positive, everything else normal → 'that combination is what lets me call this peripheral and benign'. Reassurance without reasons = 'but how do you know?' and a lost mark.

(nothing noticed) → ★ 'does a change of position — rolling over in bed — set it off?' → 'now you say it, every time' · exertional onset = cardiac story, not vestibular
★ Ear ×5 as a named block: hearing change/loss either side · nausea/vomiting · ringing/buzzing · pain/discharge · cold or flu in recent weeks → all negative = permission to say 'benign'

ask: 'Before I begin, may I confirm the patient is haemodynamically stable?' / 'Was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'

★ 'Dizziness means different things to different people. Do you mean a spinning sensation — the room going round, or you going round? Or light-headed as if you're about to faint? Or off-balance and unsteady on your feet?' / 'Any fainting or blacking out, even for a second? … And any falls?'
'When you get an episode, how long does it last? Is it there all the time or does it come and go?' / ★ 'Does a change of position — for instance rolling over in bed — set it off?'

★ 'A few questions about your ears: any change in your hearing on either side? Any nausea or vomiting with the spells? Any ringing, buzzing or roaring? Any pain or discharge? A cold or flu-like illness in the last few weeks?'

'Any slurred speech? Double or blurred vision? Weakness in the arms or legs? Numbness or pins and needles? Trouble with balance or walking between the spells? Any recent knocks to the head or falls? Any headache — particularly vomiting first thing in the morning — or weight loss? Flashing lights or sensitivity to light? Any fever?'
★ To examiner: 'specifically, is there any nystagmus — present or absent, in which direction, and does it fatigue?' / 'As a special test I'd like to perform the Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre.'

★ 'You have a condition called benign positional vertigo. It happens because of a disruption of the normal fluid circulation in the balance organ of your inner ear, so when you move your head your brain briefly gets a false signal that you're spinning.' / ★ 'There are two reasons I'm saying that. First, true spinning brought on by changing position and lasting under a minute is very characteristic. Second — and just as important — I've looked specifically for the serious causes and they aren't there.'

'A stroke affecting the balance centres almost always causes constant dizziness rather than short bursts, and nearly always brings something else with it — slurred speech, double vision, weakness, or being unable to walk. You have none of those.' / scan: 'this is diagnosed by the story and the positional test, not by a scan — where I would arrange one is if you developed hearing loss on one side, any of the warning signs, or didn't improve as expected.'

★ 'The main treatment isn't a tablet — it's a manoeuvre I can do right now. I need to warn you it will make you feel very dizzy for a few seconds and possibly a bit sick — that's expected and it passes. It fixes it in about eight out of ten people. Are you happy for me to go ahead?' / 'Only a couple of days of the anti-sickness tablet — taking it longer actually slows your recovery.'

★ 'While you're still having attacks you shouldn't drive — including the school run. Don't drive straight home after the manoeuvre today. Here in South Australia doctors have a legal duty to notify the licensing authority about anyone who isn't safe to drive, so I'd much rather we sort this out together and get you back behind the wheel quickly.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or call an ambulance, if you get slurred speech, weakness or numbness down one side, double vision, trouble swallowing, a severe headache or new neck pain, hearing loss or ringing in one ear, if the dizziness becomes constant instead of coming in bursts, or you can't walk without help.' / 'What will you do if you get any of those warning signs?'

back.dx: Multifactorial acute falls — FOUR causes, numbered: (1) symptomatic UTI (48 h frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria; suprapubic tenderness; nitrites + leucocytes) — the reason he is rushing at night; (2) postural hypotension 120/80 → 94/60 (26 systolic), likely from reduced intake + infection, no meds; (3) hypoglycaemia border — capillary glucose exactly 4.0 after skipping dinner ('cooking for one's a nuisance, I go to bed early'); (4) the situation — woken from sleep, drowsy, dark hallway, toilet at the far end, hurrying because he can't hold on. Nothing points to stroke: never blacked out, awake the whole way down, speech/vision/strength/sensation normal. Hidden agenda: brother's stroke at 68 — if never asked he interrupts the explanation with 'is this a stroke?'. Naming only the UTI is the single commonest fail.

Head strike with hospital attendance: establish imaging, anticoagulation, symptoms since (subdural). Do not lecture; be straight; do NOT advise abrupt cessation; thiamine BEFORE any glucose.

back.dx: Multifactorial falls driven by uncontrolled type 2 diabetes — THREE causes: (1) diabetic sensory neuropathy (glove-and-stocking, volunteered); (2) osteoarthritis of both knees (tender, reduced ROM — only found if you ask about joint pain and then palpate); (3) diabetic retinopathy with reduced acuity (only found if you request fundoscopy by name — he never mentioned his eyes). Underneath: random glucose 15 (>11.1), metformin 'when I remember', no check-ups. No LOC, no postural drop, TUG prolonged. Three falls in three unrelated settings with no trigger = accumulated risk factors, not one mechanism. Naming one cause = fail with the right diagnosis.

★ 'Falls usually have multiple reasons — and in your case I've found three. Number one — you have a condition called diabetic sensory neuropathy. The high sugar levels have damaged the nerves in your legs, which is why you get the numbness. When you can't feel your feet properly, that increases your risk of falling. Number two — osteoarthritis in your knees, the wear and tear we expect at your age; it causes pain and stiffness, and that increases your risk of falling too. Number three — when I looked into your eyes I found diabetic retinopathy; not seeing clearly also increases the risk of falls. And underneath all three, your sugar isn't well controlled.'

'There are other things that increase the risk of falls, and I've checked for them — around the home, joint pain, numbness, vision or hearing, needing to rush to the toilet, and medications or alcohol. There are also conditions that can make someone collapse, which I've considered and think less likely — seizures, brain tumours or mini-strokes; irregular rhythms, ischaemic heart disease or a narrowed valve; a drop in blood pressure on standing; low sugar; salt imbalance; simple fainting — because you've never lost consciousness, your rhythm and heart sounds are normal, and your blood pressure doesn't drop when you stand.'

The reason I've gone looking for every contributing cause is that most of them can be improved — your sugars, your knees, your glasses, your footwear, your home. plan: 'I'm Dr —, one of the doctors here in Emergency. Are you Mrs Harper — Denise? Do you mind if I pull up a chair?' · ★ 'before we start on the plaster — how's the pain right now, out of ten?' (3/10) · ★ 'is there anything in particular worrying you about going home with this on?' → pause, 'not really' → note it

★ 'I'd like to cover five things: what you've actually broken, how to look after the plaster, the warning signs that would bring you straight back, the plan over the next six weeks, and one important thing about your bones. I'll stop at each so you can ask.'

(1) 'You've broken the end of the radius just above the wrist; the broken end has tipped slightly backwards — a Colles' fracture. The pieces are lined up well, so plaster rather than an operation. The plaster holds the ends still so the bone can knit, about six weeks. Thumb left out deliberately — a scaphoid would have the thumb wrapped in.'

(2) SWELLING: 'the plaster can't stretch, so we keep the swelling down three ways — arm up (sling by day; at night forearm on pillows, ★ hand above the heart), ice on top of the plaster in a bag/thin towel 15–20 min every 2–3 h for the first days, and ★ keep the fingers moving — full fist, straighten, every hour awake; moving them pumps the swelling out' · DRY: 'plaster of Paris goes soft if wet — two plastic bags taped to skin for showers, no baths/swimming for six weeks; if damp, hairdryer on ★ COOL only — never warm; you can burn skin you can't see' (sister's wet cast → 'hers may have been fibreglass; yours is plaster') · CLEAN: 'nothing down inside — no needles, pens, coat hangers; cool air for the itch; no powder/lotion/oil; don't trim the edges — ring us; rest it on something soft for a day or two while it hardens' · itch is normal — a fixed burning pain in one spot is a pressure sore · MOVING: 'fingers, elbow, shoulder all free and I want them used — the wrist is the only thing that stays still' · ★ 'let's get the rings off — if the fingers swell overnight a ring turns into a tourniquet'

(3) ★ 'Two things would make me want to see you straight away. First, if the plaster becomes too tight: pain getting worse rather than better, painkillers stop touching it, fingers numb or tingly, pale, blue or cold, can't move them or it hurts to straighten them — ★ come straight back here to Emergency, don't wait for the clinic; we can split the plaster in two minutes and that fixes it. Second, the skin underneath: fever, a bad smell, ooze or staining through the plaster, or a burning rubbing pain in one fixed spot — ★ same day, us or your GP. I'll write both lists down.' ('would I need a new one?' → 're-do once the swelling settles; splitting costs nothing, a tight plaster can cost you the use of your hand')

(4) Plan: ★ 'fracture clinic in one week with another X-ray — these occasionally slip in the first week or two and it's far easier to fix early; if it's holding, plaster stays until about six weeks and comes off at the clinic, not at home' · distance → PATS, coordinate the film locally VERIFY · ★ 'expect a stiff wrist and weaker arm when it comes off — normal, not a complication — I'll arrange physiotherapy / hand therapy; a couple of months of exercises to get movement and grip back' · 'will it go back to normal?' → honest

(5) ★ 'The most important part: you broke this bone falling from standing height, on the flat. A healthy bone at your age shouldn't break from a fall like that. We call that a minimal-trauma fracture — a signal the bone may be thinner than it should be: osteoporosis. I'd like to arrange a bone-density scan, a DEXA, and some blood tests, and your GP will go through the results. If the bones are thin there are very good treatments, and starting now substantially cuts the chance of the next fracture — which could be a hip. Is that something you'd be happy for me to organise?' ('my mother had a hip' → 'all the more worth doing — it runs in families')
