Summary: thinned bones from the steroids and your chest condition, low vitamin D, and falls we can do something about. Anything I haven't covered?'
ask: 'I'd like to go through them with you, ask you a few questions, then we'll make a plan together.' / 'Before we start — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd cover?'

★ 'It gives us two scores. The T-score compares your bone density with a healthy young adult of the same sex; the Z-score compares you with someone your own age. I'm going to use your T-score, because that's the one we make the diagnosis on.' / ★ 'Because they sit between minus one and minus two-and-a-half, you have a condition called osteopenia. That means your bones have thinned — it's the stage before osteoporosis, when bones become fragile and break easily. So it's a warning, not a disaster.'

★ 'Thin bones don't make you fall — but they turn a fall into a broken bone. That's why we're going to work on both.' / 'Your blood count, sugars, kidneys, liver and thyroid are all normal, which rules out most of the other causes of thinning bones. The one thing that isn't: your vitamin D is low, at 30, when it should be above 50.'

★ 'When you fall, do you black out completely, or are you aware the whole time?' / ★ 'Have you ever broken a bone — even years ago, and even if it seemed minor at the time?' (if yes: 'which bone, and was it a big injury or a simple trip?')

★ 'Do you have dairy products regularly — milk, cheese, yoghurt? Roughly how much in a day? How much time do you spend outdoors in the sun in a normal week? What sort of exercise do you manage — and does your breathing limit what you can do? And how much alcohol in a week?' / ★ 'How many flare-ups in the last twelve months, were you admitted, and how many days of prednisolone do you take each time?'

★ 'The main cause is the steroid medication. There are two kinds: the steroid in your puffer, which is a small amount but not nothing, and more importantly the prednisolone tablets you take with every flare-up. On top of that, COPD itself thins bones — through the inflammation, and because it stops you being as active.' / ★ 'Please don't stop anything. We manage the risk; we don't abandon the treatment.' / ★ 'Next flare-up, take the prednisolone for five days, not eight — five days is what the guidelines recommend.'

★ 'Because you've never broken a bone, and this is osteopenia rather than osteoporosis, I'm not starting a bone tablet today. I'll put your details into a fracture risk calculator, and if it comes back high I'll recommend treatment — a weekly tablet, or a six-monthly injection. Either way I'd send you to the dentist first.' / 'Injection? what sort?' → one sentence: 'a six-monthly injection under the skin — the important thing is having it on time.' / 'Food first — three to four serves of dairy; we only add tablets if you can't manage that.'

★ 'For the falls: I'll refer you to a falls clinic. They'll check your vision and hearing, a physiotherapist will work on your balance and strength, and an occupational therapist will come to the house — starting with that hallway rug. We'll review your medications, including the fluid tablet, since that light-headedness on standing may be part of it. And I'd suggest a personal alarm.' / 'So I'm not going to end up in a home?' → ★ 'That's the opposite of what I'm aiming for. Everything on this list is designed to keep you safe in your own house.'

Variant 1 (wrist from the dog lead): ★ 'That's important and it changes what I'd recommend. Breaking a wrist from a simple trip is a minimal trauma fracture — when someone's had one, we start treatment at −1.5 rather than waiting for −2.5. Your spine is −2.1, so I'd start treatment now, alongside the vitamin D, the calcium and the falls plan.' / Variant 2 (hip 18 months ago): 'A broken hip from a simple fall tells me more than the scan does — we treat whatever the reading, so I'd start now and I won't need a calculator.' / Variant 3 (mid-back pain, lost height): 'Losing height with new back pain can mean a small crack in a spine bone — I'd like an X-ray of your back; if it shows what I suspect, we treat regardless of the scan.'

Version B (Symbicort, still smoking, no falls, family hip fracture, vit D 37): 'You haven't had a fall, and I want to keep it that way — so I'm still going to refer you for a falls assessment.' / 'You're on Symbicort — already a steroid and a long-acting reliever. With four flare-ups a year I'd add a third, tiotropium, and refer you to a respiratory specialist for spirometry. The most important thing is the smoking: the patches didn't work — there are two tablets, varenicline or bupropion, and I'd combine either with Quitline 13 7848 and counselling, because the combination works far better than any alone.'
pefe: Role-player: Ben Hartley, 55, married to Denise (works Tue/Thu), daughter 10 min away; retired early from the grain silo; single-storey, two front steps, long hallway with a rug. COPD 8 y; budesonide most days (forgets some mornings); 3–4 exacerbations/yr, prednisolone 8 d each, no admissions; quit smoking 5 y ago after 30 pack-years — proud. Three mechanical trips, no LOC, last over the hall rug with his daughter there; no injury. Fluid tablet for BP; no sedatives; glasses 4 y old; knees ache on stairs; light-headed on standing (never mentioned); milk in tea only; indoors; wine most nights; two coffees. Friendly, anxious, short sentences. 'How is your diet?' → 'pretty good, I reckon' — make them ask dairy. Numbers read at him → 'I don't know what that means'. 'Osteoporosis' → 'that's what my mother had'. Never volunteers fracture history. Pushes once: 'should I stop the puffer then?'. setting: General practice, Wallaroo SA. NO history taking — one rapport line, one agenda question, then the film; the examiner stops you if you start asking questions (you may respond to what she volunteers). 'Immediate' = the fracture; 'long-term' = the bone. Two problems, in order. Hidden agenda: mother's hip fracture and nursing home — released the moment you say 'osteoporosis'.
stem: Jenny Halloran, 72, retired school administrator, lives with her husband. Low back pain for twelve days, sudden onset lifting a bag of shopping from the car boot. Your partner saw her eight days ago, started paracetamol and arranged a thoracolumbar X-ray; she is back for the result. Report: anterior wedge compression deformity L1, ~30% anterior height loss; alignment maintained; posterior cortex and pedicles intact; generalised reduced bone density; no lytic or sclerotic lesion — osteoporotic insufficiency fracture. BP 132/78 · HR 76 · afebrile · BMI 21. Localised thoracolumbar tenderness; legs neurologically normal, normal gait, no saddle numbness, no bladder/bowel disturbance.
tasks: Explain the X-ray findings to the patient
Explain the possible causes of her symptoms and of the fracture
Explain your immediate and long-term management to the patient
time: 8 minutes. 0:00 WIPE, 'how can I help?', ★ three-part agenda, ★ 'has anything in particular been worrying you?' (she says no — ask anyway; it's the only agenda mark available) · 0:30 ★ turn the film to her; three colours (white bone, grey soft tissue, black air); column of blocks — vertebrae · 1:20 ★ 'in one of those blocks, here, I can see a break' — compression/wedge, front squashes, back stays → wedge vs the square ones; 'is it actually broken?' → YES, then bound it (cord not involved, back wall intact, legs working, no operation/plaster) · ★ 'but I only picked up a bag' → THE HINGE: 'a healthy bone would not break doing that — the bone was already weak' · 2:30 ★ osteoporosis named AND translated (honeycomb) · six causes in order: age · menopause/oestrogen · calcium/dairy · vitamin D/sun · exercise · conditions and medicines (steroids, long-term PPI) · reflect back what she offers (PPI 6 y, no milk) — don't turn it into a history · 3:50 mother's hip → acknowledge, honest about risk, no false reassurance, reason for hope · 4:00 ★ 'two things, in order' · 4:20 FRACTURE: regular paracetamol 1 g qid ± short stronger course + aperient; ★ NOT bed rest; physio; orthopaedic opinion (brace sometimes; procedure rarely — their call) · 5:15 BONE: DEXA, vit D, Ca, bloods — ★ 'not waiting for those to start' · options, not an order: weekly tablet / yearly infusion / 6-monthly injection — let her choose · ★ dentist first · size ONJ/AFF honestly · 6:20 non-drug: 3–4 dairy serves (food first), vit D + sensible sun, ★ supervised exercise (exercise physiologist), cut wine/coffee, ★ falls clinic ('the next bone is likely your hip') · 7:15 review 1–2 wk, DEXA 2 y, reading, ★ neuro safety-net (leg weakness/numbness, saddle numbness, urinary trouble), summary, 'anything I've missed?'

back.dx: Osteoporotic L1 anterior wedge compression fracture (~30% anterior height loss, Genant grade 2) from lifting a bag of shopping — minimal trauma → treat regardless of DEXA. Two halves: the fracture (analgesia, keep moving, physio, orthopaedic opinion) then the bone (DEXA/vit D/Ca/bloods as a baseline not a gate; antiresorptive by her choice after a dental check; calcium, vitamin D, supervised exercise; falls prevention). She volunteers: pantoprazole 6 y, dislikes milk, black tea, cheese repeats; walks to the letterbox; two wines most nights, 3–4 coffees; periods stopped at 51; hysterectomy at 48 with ovaries left; a wrist fracture 10 y ago tripping on a step (a prior minimal-trauma fracture — name it back). Mother: osteoporosis, hip at 78, never home, nursing home. Bed rest is a scripted invitation and an automatic fail.
plan: 'Good morning Mrs Halloran — Jenny? How can I help you today?' → back pain, here for the result, a bit worried · ★ 'I do have the X-ray and I have an answer. I'd like to do three things: go through the picture with you, explain why it has happened, and talk about what we do about it — today and longer term. Please stop me at any point.' · ★ 'Before I start — has anything in particular been on your mind?' → 'no, not really'

★ Pick the film up, turn it to her: 'On any X-ray there are really only three colours. White is bone, grey is soft tissue and muscle, black is air. Today we're only interested in the white. This white column is your spine — built out of little blocks of bone stacked on each other; each block is a vertebra. Can you see them?' → 'like a row of bricks'

★ 'And in one of those blocks, here, I can see a break.' → 'actually broken?' → 'Yes. It's called a compression fracture, or a wedge fracture. It happens when the bone has become weak and fragile — so weak that even a small strain like lifting a bag is enough for the block to squash down and collapse at the front. When the front squashes and the back stays put, the block stops being a square and becomes a wedge — see it there, next to the square ones above and below?' · bound the fear: 'the spinal cord is not involved, the back wall is intact, your legs are working — this is not a break that needs an operation or a plaster' · 'does that make sense so far?'

★ 'But I only picked up a bag of shopping' → 'That is exactly the point — the most important thing I'll say today. A healthy bone would not break from lifting a bag of shopping. The fact that yours did tells us the bone itself is the problem. Can I explain why?'

★ 'The main cause is osteoporosis — which simply means the bones have become thin, weak and fragile. Picture the inside of a bone as a honeycomb: in osteoporosis the walls thin out and the spaces get bigger. There's usually more than one reason:' AGE · ★ MENOPAUSE — 'once the periods stop the drop in oestrogen speeds bone loss up a lot — the main reason women get this more than men' · CALCIUM/dairy · VITAMIN D/sunlight · EXERCISE ('if we don't use it we lose it') · ★ CONDITIONS AND MEDICINES — steroid tablets, long-term stomach-acid tablets · she offers PPI + no milk → ★ 'that's really useful — both are on my list and both are things we can do something about' (do NOT start asking smoking/menopause questions; 'that's something I'd want to check today')

Mother's hip surfaces ('am I going to end up like that?') → ★ 'Thank you for telling me — I can hear that it frightens you. I'm not going to pretend the risk is nothing. But your mother's generation mostly didn't get offered treatment for this, and you are being offered it today. Treatment makes the bone stronger and lowers the chance of the next fracture — and a big part of what I'll suggest is aimed at making sure you don't have that fall in the first place.'

★ 'Two things to sort out, in order. First, the broken bone itself: pain relief taken REGULARLY — paracetamol 1 g four times a day, not just when it hurts; if that isn't holding it, something stronger for a few days with something for your bowels alongside. Rest when the pain demands it, but ★ NOT bed rest — lying in bed makes the bone thinner and you weaker; I want you up and doing as much of your normal day as the pain allows. Physiotherapy for the pain and your posture. And I'll refer you to the orthopaedic team for their opinion — sometimes a brace in the early weeks; very occasionally a procedure, but that's uncommon and their call.' ('flat on my back for a fortnight?' → 'I'd push back on that — it's one of the few things that would make this worse')

★ 'Second, and the bigger job, the bone. A bone density scan — a DEXA, ten minutes on a couch; vitamin D and calcium; other bloods to make sure nothing else is driving it. But I'm not waiting for those before we start: because you've already broken a bone in your spine from something as small as lifting a bag, that on its own tells me the bone needs treating. The scan is a starting point to measure against, not permission to begin.'

★ Options, her view: weekly alendronate (first thing, full glass of plain water, upright, nothing else 30 min; indigestion) · yearly zoledronic acid infusion (fluey/achy a day or two after the first) · 6-monthly denosumab injection (very effective, nothing daily — but ★ must not be late; protection drops away quickly) → 'I already rattle with tablets' → injection, on a recall · ★ 'please see your dentist first — teeth out or implant work, get it done now; these medicines carry a small risk of a jaw-healing problem' ('my friend got a rotten jaw' → ONJ is real, rare at osteoporosis doses, far more common at cancer doses; the fracture risk without treatment is much higher) · 'is it for life?' → duration 5 / 3 / indefinite years VERIFY

'The medicine is only half of it': ★ calcium 3–4 dairy serves/day (glass of milk, tub of yoghurt, matchbox of cheese) — sheet of non-milk calcium foods; supplement only if she can't · vitamin D checked + sensible sun avoiding midday · ★ exercise, supervised — exercise physiologist, not a gym alone with a fractured spine · cut alcohol and coffee; smoking · ★ FALLS: 'if you fall now, the next bone is likely to be your hip' → falls clinic — OT home visit (rugs — the hall runner, lighting, bathroom), physio for balance

'Review in a week or two for the pain; repeat the bone scan in about two years; reading on osteoporosis and calcium-rich foods.' · ★ 'Come back sooner, or go straight to hospital, if the pain becomes severe and doesn't settle, or you notice any weakness, numbness or pins and needles in your legs, numbness around the back passage, or trouble passing urine.' · summary in five: wedge fracture · thin bone/osteoporosis · fracture plan · bone plan (injection after dentist + Ca/vit D/exercise) · falls clinic · 'have I missed anything you wanted to ask?' ('will it mend? will I go bent over?' → heals over weeks; treatment + exercise + posture work reduce further collapse)

Pain 5/10, worse rising from a chair and turning in bed, easier lying still; legs fine. Composed, polite, anxious; tearful ONCE about her mother; if told 'don't worry, that won't happen to you' → goes quiet, short answers for the rest. Says 'no, not really' to the agenda question; releases the mother when you say 'osteoporosis' (blurts at ~6 min otherwise). Pushes: 'but I only picked up a bag of shopping' (early), 'my neighbour said flat on my back for a fortnight' (~5 min — you must say no), 'I already rattle with tablets' (offer injection/infusion, don't argue), 'my friend got a rotten jaw', 'I've got a wobbly molar the dentist wants out' (→ get it done first), 'will I need an operation?', 'that's the bit I'd want — it was a rug that did for Mum'. If you start a history: brief answer then 'but what does the X-ray show, doctor?'

Film/report: L1 anterior wedge, ~30% anterior height loss (Genant 2: 25–40%; grade 1 20–25%; grade 3 >40%; ≥20% defines a vertebral fracture), alignment maintained, posterior cortex and pedicles intact, generalised osteopenia, no lytic/sclerotic lesion. Commonest sites T12/L1; above T5 think malignancy. Exam: localised thoracolumbar tenderness, neuro normal, no saddle anaesthesia/sphincter symptoms. Red flags for a non-osteoporotic cause: age <50 with no risk, fracture above T5, posterior element involvement, lytic/sclerotic lesion, weight loss/fever/night pain, known cancer → MRI whole spine, SPEP/UEP, Ca, ALP, FBE, ESR, PSA

Variants: B — second fracture on prednisolone (PMR) with alendronate 'not suiting' → name the pattern (bone still losing ground, plan not working), steroid + PPI contribution, write to the rheumatologist re lowest dose, review PPI need, ★ ask why the alendronate stopped, switch to zoledronic/denosumab ('take the remembering out of it'), not re-prescribe blindly · C — film not osteoporotic (bone 'eaten away') → don't guess; MRI whole spine + bloods this week; 'is it cancer?' → 'it's one of the things I have to rule out, and that is exactly why I'm not waiting' · D — refuses treatment (ONJ fear) → acknowledge, size it, do the rest, keep the door open · E — 'my right leg has been giving way and I couldn't feel the toilet seat' → ★ stop: cord compression/cauda equina until proven otherwise — urgent MRI, speak to the hospital now, don't drive, same day; NOT the osteoporosis speech

★ 'Marion, the lump in your groin is a hernia, and a loop of bowel has become trapped and strangled in it. That is why your tummy hurts and why you are vomiting.' / 'A hernia is a weak spot in the muscle wall that bowel pushes through. If the neck of that opening tightens, the bowel is trapped and its blood supply is squeezed off.'

'But I've had it for years and nobody worried about it' → 'That's right — and while it was going back in, it was safe. What has changed is that it stopped going back and became sore. That is the point at which it becomes an emergency, and you were right to come in.'

★ 'You need an operation today … I am not going to send you for a scan first, because the examination has already told me what I need to know and waiting risks the bowel.' / 'Will I lose part of my bowel?' → 'Possibly. The surgeon will free the trapped loop and see whether it recovers its colour. If it does, they repair the weak spot and that is the end of it. If it doesn't, they remove that short segment and join the ends. Either way, doing this today is what protects the bowel.'
pefe: Role-player: Marion, 55, office at a farm supply store in Kadina, married, three grown children; one BP tablet, no allergies, never had an operation, non-smoker, occasional wine. Stoic, apologetic ('don't want to make a fuss'), frightened by the vomiting but downplays. Mentions the groin lump ONLY if asked directly about a lump/swelling/hernia; reveals it stopped reducing and is sore ONLY if asked whether it's behaving normally lately or whether it's tender/reducible. Doesn't volunteer flatus. Once told surgery today: anxious, asks about her bowel

Hernia vocabulary: reducible (safe) → irreducible/incarcerated (trapped, not yet ischaemic) → strangulated (blood supply compromised — tender, tense, overlying erythema, systemic upset, obstruction) · femoral hernias (below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, commoner in women) strangulate more often · never attempt forceful reduction of a tender irreducible hernia · management: NBM, IV fluids, NG, analgesia, antiemetic, bloods + cross-match, antibiotics if strangulation suspected, urgent theatre — resection if non-viable; imaging only if the diagnosis is genuinely unclear and the patient is stable

back.dx: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — most likely an embolus from atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular pulse, 'my heart flutters, they mentioned it once') on a background of chronic mesenteric ischaemia (months of post-prandial pain, food fear, ~6 kg weight loss) that may now have thrombosed. Pain 10/10, constant, generalised, with a soft, only mildly tender abdomen; dark stools (mucosal sloughing). Three things push towards ischaemia over obstruction: pain out of proportion, an embolic source, and chronic post-prandial pain with weight loss. If that clot travels to an artery feeding the bowel, the bowel is starved of blood — which hurts a great deal even though there is little to feel from outside.'

★ 'Three things push me towards a blocked blood supply rather than a blocked bowel. First, the pain is out of proportion — he describes ten out of ten and the abdomen is soft. Second, his pulse is irregularly irregular, which is a source of clot. Third, he has had post-prandial pain and weight loss for months, so there may already be a narrowed artery that has now thrombosed. pefe: Role-player (reconstructed): Reg, 60; constant unbearable generalised pain, 10/10, three days; heart flutters, someone once mentioned an irregular beat; dark motions; months of post-prandial pain, eating less, ~6 kg lost; barely flinches on examination
PEFE: soft abdomen, mild tenderness only, bowel sounds present, pulse irregularly irregular, no groin lump, dark stool on the glove

Acute mesenteric ischaemia: SMA embolus (AF, recent MI, valve) ~50%; SMA thrombosis on chronic atherosclerosis (post-prandial pain, food fear, weight loss = 'intestinal angina'); non-occlusive (low flow, vasopressors); mesenteric venous thrombosis (hypercoagulable). Early: pain out of proportion, soft abdomen, gut emptying (vomiting/diarrhoea); late: peritonitis, bloody stool, sepsis, acidosis. Lactate/VBG (normal early does not exclude), leucocytosis, amylase; CT angiography (arterial + venous phase) is the test — plain CT misses it. Management: resuscitation, NBM, IV heparin VERIFY, antibiotics, urgent vascular/surgical review — embolectomy/endovascular revascularisation ± laparotomy with resection of non-viable bowel, second look. Mortality high, rises with delay

Distinguish ischaemic colitis (older, low-flow/anticoagulated, crampy LEFT-sided pain, bloody diarrhoea, thumbprinting on AXR, usually supportive care) from small bowel ischaemia (CTA, surgery). Dark stool DDx: melaena (upper GI bleed), iron, bismuth — probe
SA: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — vascular surgery is metropolitan; do not wait for the scan to call · TIS 131 450

Not probing the dark stool; not requesting DRE stool colour
Ordering a plain CT or AXR instead of CT angiography; waiting for the scan before calling surgery/vascular; treating as SBO with drip-and-suck alone
No lactate; no anticoagulation discussion; no acknowledgement of the severity to the patient

Erythema nodosum causes: IBD and sarcoidosis first; then streptococcal infection, TB, drugs (OCP, sulfonamides), pregnancy, idiopathic. Extra-intestinal IBD: EN, pyoderma, aphthous ulcers, uveitis/episcleritis, arthritis/spondylitis, PSC, clubbing. Crohn vs UC: Crohn — mouth to anus, skip lesions, perianal disease, strictures/fistulae, transmural; UC — rectum upward, continuous, bloody diarrhoea. Paediatric Crohn induction: exclusive enteral nutrition first line; UC: 5-ASA; steroids/immunomodulators/biologics per specialist; growth monitoring; bone health; vaccination before immunosuppression

Faecal calprotectin distinguishes inflammatory from functional (normal makes IBD very unlikely — harder variant: otherwise well teen with normal bloods and calprotectin → functional named, with exclusion criteria said aloud). IBS: no alarm features, generally <50, no nocturnal symptoms. Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA) while eating gluten. Stool MCS, C. difficile, Giardia

Ask the examiner for the examination findings

back.dx: Coeliac disease — gluten-related bloating and discomfort for months, steatorrhoea (bulky, pale, offensive, floats, needs two flushes = fat malabsorption), iron deficiency anaemia unresponsive to oral iron, tiredness. Explain: gluten (wheat, barley, rye) triggers the immune system to attack the small bowel lining; the finger-like villi flatten so fat and iron aren't absorbed — greasy stools and iron tablets that don't work. Order: serology → gastroscopy with biopsies → diet. Lifelong, manageable; first-degree relatives ~1 in 10 → test them (including future children).

So the order is: blood test, then a gastroscopy with small biopsies, and only then the diet — which will be lifelong, and which a dietitian will help you with.'

'Gluten — a protein in wheat, barley and rye — triggers your immune system to attack the lining of your small bowel. The tiny finger-like folds that absorb food get flattened, so you don't absorb fat or iron properly. That is why the stools are greasy and why the iron tablets haven't worked.'

'It's a lifelong condition, but it's completely manageable, and people who stick to the diet feel entirely well. Yes, it is for life — even small amounts of gluten keep the damage going. It does run in families, so your first-degree relatives should be tested, and that will include any children. Coeliac Australia is genuinely useful for the practical side.'

Already gluten-free before testing: 'I can't pretend the tests are valid on a gluten-free diet — either a supervised gluten challenge, roughly four slices of bread a day for six weeks VERIFY, before we test, or I refer you for specialist advice.'

setting: Regional SA general practice. Six-minute history, then diagnosis with reasons and differentials SPOKEN to the examiner (writing it down does not score — single-item fail). Same stem, two versions: A — IBS (bloating eases after defecation, alternating stool, work stress); B — coeliac (worse after pizza/bread, steatorrhoea, iron-deficiency anaemia pre-explained as 'heavy periods', dermatitis herpetiformis on the elbows, sister with 'something to do with gluten').
stem: Jenny Walker, 25, administration officer, complains of bloating. T 36.7 · P 72 · BP 112/70 · RR 14 · BMI 21. Well and comfortable.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give the examiner your differential diagnoses
time: 6 min history. Intro, acknowledge, consent (bowels and periods), ★ concerns in the first minute (aunt with bowel cancer) · ★ DEFINE 'bloated': burping / more wind / tummy actually swollen · timing: how long, constant vs comes and goes, worse time of day, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' · triggers: better/worse, ★ 'worse after eating — any food that sets it off?' (A: eases after the toilet — Rome IV bait, don't close; B: pizza and bread — only when food is named) · GI screen: N/V, pain, ★ constipation or diarrhoea must be answered, fever · ★ red flags by 4:10: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness (B: 'anaemic — they said it's my heavy periods'), blood/dark stools, lasting habit change, FHx bowel/ovarian cancer · ★ ovarian and obstruction: early satiety, urinary frequency, FHx ovarian/breast, previous surgery, groin lump, ★ passing wind normally · ★ diet: dairy; ★ 'greasy, bulky, float, stick to the pan, hard to flush?' (B: yes to all, flushes twice, thought normal) · infection/motility: travel/camping, meds incl supplements (★ iron tablets), diabetes, cold intolerance · IBD/IBS: joints, mouth ulcers, eyes, ★ rashes (B: itchy blistery rash on elbows), alternating stools, relief with defecation · ★ periods by 5:00: LMP, regular, ★ pregnancy possible, home/work stress · stop at 6:00 → speak the diagnosis in full sentences → DDx by group, IBS last.

back.dx: Version A — irritable bowel syndrome: recurrent discomfort related to defecation with a change in stool form (Rome IV), a clear work stressor, and a positive diagnosis of exclusion — no weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, mass, family history, dietary trigger, travel, not pregnant. Version B — coeliac disease: gluten-related symptoms, steatorrhoea, iron-deficiency anaemia 'I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded', itchy blistery elbow rash (dermatitis herpetiformis), sister with a gluten problem; second contributor — oral iron itself causes bloating, cramping and constipation. Discriminating behaviour in B: challenge the 'heavy periods' explanation and ask stool character directly.
plan: 'Am I speaking with Jenny? What's brought you along?' → 'that sounds uncomfortable and I'm glad you came in — I'll ask about your bowels and your periods, is that all right? ★ Before I start, was there anything in particular you were worried it might be?' (aunt — bowel cancer)
★ 'When you say bloated, can you describe it — are you burping a lot, passing more wind, or does your tummy actually look and feel swollen?' → swollen and windy

How long (A 6 mo / B ~1 y), comes and goes, getting worse, worse time of day, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (no) · ★ 'anything that makes it better or worse — in particular worse after eating, any food that sets it off?' (A: eases after the toilet; B: 'not really' → name food → pizza and bread)
GI screen: nausea/vomiting, tummy pain (crampy), ★ 'constipation or diarrhoea?' (A alternates / B loose and pale), fever

★ 'I ask everybody these next questions, just to be safe': weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness (B: anaemic, heavy periods, iron tablets → ★ 'low iron can also mean the bowel isn't absorbing properly'), blood/dark stools, lasting habit change, FHx bowel or ovarian cancer (aunt)

★ Ovarian/obstruction: 'do you get full very quickly after a small amount?', urinary frequency, FHx ovarian/breast, previous abdominal surgery, groin lump, ★ 'passing wind normally?' · ★ diet: dairy; 'are your stools greasy or bulky — do they float, stick to the pan, or need flushing twice?' (B: yes) · FHx coeliac (sister) · travel/camping · meds incl OTC/supplements (iron) · diabetes, cold intolerance · joints, mouth ulcers, eyes, ★ rashes (elbows) · alternating stools, relief with defecation
★ Periods: LMP, regular (B heavy), ★ 'any chance you could be pregnant?' · who's at home, how's work (A: awful since the restructure) · smoking/alcohol/drugs · summarise

★ Aloud to the examiner — A: 'My most likely diagnosis is irritable bowel syndrome. She meets Rome IV criteria — recurrent abdominal discomfort related to defecation with a change in stool form — and there is a clear stressor. I say this as a positive diagnosis of exclusion: no weight loss, no bleeding, no anaemia, no nocturnal symptoms, no mass, no family history, no dietary trigger, no travel, and she is not pregnant.' B: 'coeliac disease — gluten-related symptoms, steatorrhoeic stools, an iron deficiency anaemia I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded, an itchy elbow rash consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis, and a sister with a gluten problem; a second contributor is the oral iron.' · DDx by group: malignancy (bowel; ★ ovarian — presents exactly like this) · obstruction (adhesions, hernia, volvulus, constipation — normal flatus, no surgery) · dietary (coeliac, lactose) · infection (giardia, post-infectious) · motility (drugs, diabetic enteropathy, hypothyroidism) · IBD · functional — IBS last, a diagnosis of exclusion · exclude pregnancy
ask: ★ 'When you say bloated, can you describe it for me? Is it that you're burping a lot, or passing more wind than usual, or is it that your tummy actually looks and feels swollen?' / ★ 'Does it ever wake you at night?'

★ 'I ask everybody these next questions, just to be safe. Any weight loss without trying? Change in appetite? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired? Any blood or very dark stools? Any lasting change in bowel habit? Family history of bowel or ovarian cancer?'

★ 'Do you get full very quickly, after only a small amount of food? Any change in how often you pass urine? Have you ever had surgery on your tummy? Any lump or swelling in your groin? Are you passing wind normally?'

★ 'Heavy periods may well be part of it, but low iron can also mean the bowel isn't absorbing properly — are your stools greasy or bulky? Do they float, stick to the pan, or need flushing twice?' / 'Any rashes — particularly an itchy rash on the elbows or knees?'
★ 'When was your last period, are they regular, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?'

★ To examiner (A): 'My most likely diagnosis is irritable bowel syndrome … I say this as a positive diagnosis of exclusion …' / (B): 'My most likely diagnosis is coeliac disease. The symptoms are gluten-related, the stools are steatorrhoeic, and there is an iron deficiency anaemia that I do not accept as menstrual until malabsorption is excluded. She also describes an itchy rash on her elbows, which would be dermatitis herpetiformis. A genuine second contributor is her oral iron supplement.'

'In any woman with persistent bloating I would want to exclude ovarian cancer.' / 'I place irritable bowel syndrome last because it is a diagnosis of exclusion.' / B to patient: 'Please keep eating gluten until we've tested you — stopping it makes the tests come back falsely normal. Blood test today; if positive, a camera test with a small biopsy; then a dietitian, iron, vitamin D and bone checks, and testing for your sister and close relatives.'

Variant — already gluten-free: 'the blood test only works while you're eating gluten — I'd ask you to go back onto a normal diet for about six weeks before we test; a wrong answer here would follow you for life.' / 'Isn't this just IBS?' → 'It might be — but you have two things that don't fit it: stools that suggest you're not absorbing fat, and low iron. I'd rather check than assume.' / Ovarian version (she is 52): 'bloating, early fullness and passing urine more often can occasionally come from the ovaries — a pelvic ultrasound and a CA-125; not telling you it's sinister, telling you it's something I always check for.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Walker, 25, council depot admin, lives with partner, non-smoker, 4–6 SD/week, never had surgery; polite, self-conscious, braced for 'it's nothing'. Volunteers nothing; 'not really' to the general trigger question — pizza/bread only when food is named; stool character only when asked directly (flushes twice, thought it normal); offers the anaemia readily, always with 'they said it's my heavy periods'; sister's gluten problem and the elbow rash only if asked. Pushes at ~4 min 'do you think it's serious?'; volunteers the aunt's bowel cancer at 5:30 if concerns never asked. If told to stop gluten before testing: 'I'll start tonight' — marks an error

No examination in the standard station (piloted variant: 5 min history → examination → diagnosis). Version A key positives: bloating settles after defecation, alternating hard/loose, work stress. Version B: worse after pizza/bread, greasy bulky floating stools, iron-deficiency anaemia on iron tablets, itchy blistery rash on elbows, sister 'something to do with gluten', periods regular but heavy

Rome IV IBS: recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week in the last 3 months, onset ≥6 months ago, with ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form; no alarm features. Four meanings of 'bloating' → four differential groups (aerophagia/burping; flatulence — diet, lactose, coeliac, SIBO; distension — constipation, ascites, mass, obstruction; sensation — functional). Ovarian symptom index: persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary frequency — >12 times a month, new onset → USS + CA-125 (mainly >50). Red-flag age for new bowel symptoms: >50

Coeliac: ~1 in 70; first-degree relatives ~1 in 10; tTG-IgA + total IgA while eating gluten; gluten challenge ~4 slices/day × 6 weeks VERIFY; biopsy confirmation; dermatitis herpetiformis = coeliac until proven otherwise; oral iron side effects — bloating, cramping, constipation, dark stools. IBS management (A): explain positively, reassure with the exclusion list, low-FODMAP trial with a dietitian, fibre/psyllium, stress management/CBT, antispasmodics, review; investigate minimally (FBE, CRP, coeliac serology, ± calprotectin)
Timing: red flags by 4:10 · periods by 5:00 · stop at 6:00 · SA: Country Health Connect dietitian · Coeliac Australia · Cancer Council 13 11 20 (the aunt)
fails: ★ Not speaking the diagnosis aloud in full sentences (nodding/writing = single-item fail)
Opening with 'how long?' and never defining the bloating; closing early on the Rome IV bait in A
Accepting 'they said it's my heavy periods' — the whole station in B; 'are your bowels normal?' instead of naming the four stool descriptors
Omitting the ovarian block because she's 25; forgetting flatus; leaving periods/pregnancy to the last 30 seconds and never reaching them
A medication history that misses the iron tablets; missing the elbow rash; telling her to stop gluten before testing
Differentials as a flat list; IBS placed first
numbers: Rome IV: pain ≥1 day/week · last 3 months · onset ≥6 months · 2 of 3 features · red-flag age >50 · ovarian symptoms >12/month
Coeliac 1 in 70 · relatives 1 in 10 · gluten challenge ~4 slices/day × 6 wk VERIFY · tTG-IgA + total IgA · biopsy

setting: Regional SA general practice. Six-minute history, then diagnosis with reasons and differentials spoken to the examiner. Rare recall. The whole case turns on one exchange: the general aggravating-factor question gets 'no, not really' — the dairy trigger appears only when food is named, and then dairy is named. If the examiner says 'the group calls this abdominal migraine', don't just agree.
stem: Daniel Roberts, 20, apprentice diesel mechanic, complains of abdominal pain. T 36.6 · P 68 · BP 118/74 · RR 14 · BMI 23. Well.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Tell the examiner your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons
Give the examiner your differential diagnoses
time: 6 min. Intro, acknowledge, consent (pain, bowels, diet), concerns ('my mate reckons it's an ulcer') · ★ 'point to it with one finger' (vague periumbilical → small bowel), character (dull, crampy), radiation, /10 (3–4) · onset (6 mo), ★ episode duration (1–2 h), worse?, ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (never) · ★ 'anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ DO NOT ACCEPT: 'what about food — dairy like milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? bread or pasta? fatty or fried meals?' → milk and ice-cream, an hour after, every time · ★ dose: small amount or big serve? hard cheese? · GI screen: N/V, ★ bloating/wind (lots, after dairy), ★ bowels (alternate), fever · ★ red flags 'I ask everybody': weight, appetite, tiredness, blood/mucus, fever/sweats · ★ IBD screen: mouth ulcers, joints, eyes, shin lumps, perianal pain/discharge, FHx Crohn/UC · ★ coeliac despite the dairy answer: bread/pasta/beer, greasy/pale/floating/hard-to-flush stools, FHx · infection/upper GI/surgical: travel/camping/tank water, reflux, NSAIDs, previous surgery, groin lump, ★ passing wind · IBS/social: relief with defecation, FHx bowel/cancer (mum's migraines), home/work stress ('honestly none'), smoking, alcohol, drugs · dairy named by 4:25, stop at 6:00 → speak the diagnosis → DDx by group.

back.dx: Lactose intolerance — reproducible bloating, wind, cramping and loose stools 30 min–2 h after milk and ice-cream (a milkshake is worst; cheese on toast is fine — dose-dependent), well between exposures, no red flags, no nocturnal symptoms, bread fine. IBS placed below it (stools alternate, but a reproducible food trigger takes precedence and IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion). Still exclude coeliac (causes secondary lactose intolerance) and IBD (must-not-miss at 20). Explain: enzyme (lactase) shortage, not an allergy — depends on the amount. Plan: FBE, iron, CRP, coeliac serology (while eating gluten); 2–4 week lactose exclusion then structured rechallenge to find his limit; dietitian for calcium/vitamin D; safety-net.
plan: Intro · 'months is a long time to put up with that — I'll ask about the pain, your bowels and your diet, then tell you what I think; anything you were worried about?' → ulcer

★ 'Where exactly — can you point with one finger?' (circles the umbilicus) · what does it feel like (dull, crampy) · moves anywhere (no) · /10 at worst (3–4) · when (6 mo) · ★ each bout (1–2 h) · worse? · ★ 'does it ever wake you at night?' (never)

★ 'Is there anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ 'can I ask more specifically about food — is it worse after dairy, so milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? What about bread or pasta? Fatty or fried meals?' → 'actually — yeah. Milk and ice-cream. About an hour after, every time. Bread's fine.' → ★ 'does a small amount do it, or only a big serve? how about hard cheese?' → milkshake worst; cheese on toast fine

GI screen: N/V (no) · ★ bloating/wind (loads, after dairy) · ★ bowels (constipated ↔ loose) · fever · ★ 'these next ones I ask everybody': weight loss, appetite, tiredness, blood/mucus, fevers/night sweats · ★ IBD: mouth ulcers, joints, eyes, shin lumps, perianal pain/discharge, FHx Crohn/colitis → all no

★ Coeliac anyway: 'worse after bread, pasta or beer? stools ever greasy, bulky, pale, floating, hard to flush? family history?' → no · travel/camping/tank water · reflux/heartburn · ★ anti-inflammatories · previous surgery, groin lump · ★ passing wind normally

IBS/social: relief with defecation (not particularly) · FHx bowel problems/cancer (mum — migraines) · home/apprenticeship stress ('honestly, no stress') · smoking (social), alcohol (5–6 beers weekend), drugs · summarise

★ Aloud: 'My most likely diagnosis is lactose intolerance. His symptoms are reproducibly triggered within an hour or two of dairy, with bloating, wind and cramping, and he is well between exposures. I place irritable bowel syndrome below it: his stools do alternate, but IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and a reproducible food trigger takes precedence. I would still exclude coeliac disease, because it causes secondary lactose intolerance, and inflammatory bowel disease, the must-not-miss diagnosis at his age.' · DDx by group: dietary/malabsorptive (lactose, coeliac, other carbohydrate intolerance) · inflammatory (Crohn, UC — no blood, nocturnal, weight loss, extra-intestinal features) · infective (giardia — no travel/tank water) · upper GI (PUD, functional dyspepsia, gallstones, chronic pancreatitis) · structural/surgical (constipation, hernia, adhesions) · functional (IBS, abdominal migraine — both require no better explanation, and here one exists)
ask: ★ 'Where exactly is the pain — can you point to it with one finger?' / ★ 'Does it ever wake you at night?' / 'How long does each bout last?'

★ 'Is there anything that makes it better or worse?' → 'no, not really' → ★ 'What about food? Is it worse after any particular food — dairy like milk, cheese, yoghurt or ice-cream? Bread or pasta? Fatty or fried meals?' / 'How soon afterwards, and does a small amount do it? How about hard cheese?'

★ 'These next ones I ask everybody. Any weight loss without trying? Change in appetite? Unusually tired? Any blood or mucus in your stool? Any mouth ulcers, joint pains, sore eyes, or tender red lumps on your shins? Any pain or discharge around the back passage? Anyone in the family with Crohn disease or colitis?'

★ 'Is it worse after bread, pasta or beer? Are your stools ever greasy, bulky, pale, floating or hard to flush?' / 'Any anti-inflammatory tablets? Any previous surgery, or a lump in your groin? Are you passing wind normally?'

★ To examiner: 'My most likely diagnosis is lactose intolerance … I place irritable bowel syndrome below it … I would still exclude coeliac disease, because it causes secondary lactose intolerance, and inflammatory bowel disease, which is the must-not-miss diagnosis at his age.'

To patient: ★ 'Your bowel is short of an enzyme called lactase, which normally breaks down a sugar called lactose in dairy foods. Without enough of it, the sugar passes through undigested, pulls water into the bowel and is fermented by the bacteria there — that produces the gas, bloating, cramping and loose motions an hour or so after dairy.' / 'So I'm allergic to milk?' → ★ 'Not quite — an allergy is the immune system reacting, and even a tiny amount causes trouble. This is an enzyme shortage, so it depends on the amount: a milkshake floors you, a bit of cheese may be fine.'

'Blood tests — full blood count, iron, an inflammation marker and a coeliac screen, because coeliac disease can cause exactly this as a knock-on effect. Then cut lactose out completely for two to four weeks, and if it settles bring it back gradually to find your limit. A dietitian so you don't lose calcium — that matters for your bones at your age. Come back sooner if you see blood, lose weight, get fevers, or the pain wakes you at night.'

Examiner 'isn't this abdominal migraine?' → ★ 'I did consider it. Abdominal migraine requires discrete episodes of midline pain with complete wellness between them, usually with anorexia, nausea or pallor, and critically the final criterion is that the pain is not better accounted for by another disorder. Here it is — there is a reproducible dairy trigger. The family history of migraine is background rather than evidence.' / 'My mate said it's an ulcer' → 'ulcers give burning pain higher up, often at night or when hungry, linked to anti-inflammatories or Helicobacter — none of that fits; yours is tied to dairy.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel Roberts, 20, second-year apprentice diesel mechanic, lives with parents, social smoker, 5–6 beers on the weekend, no meds; laid back, brief, volunteers nothing, genuinely believes nothing makes it worse. 'No, not really' flatly to the general question — reveals dairy ONLY when milk/cheese/ice-cream is named; if never named, never revealed and the station fails. 'Honestly, there's no stress.' Mum's migraines only if family history asked. Pushes at ~4 min 'is it something serious?'. Marks an error if told to stop all dairy without calcium/bones/dietitian

No examination. Positives: periumbilical dull crampy pain 3–4/10, 1–2 h bouts, 6 months, never at night; reproducible after milk/ice-cream within an hour; bloating, wind, alternating stools; all red flags, IBD, coeliac, infection, surgical screens negative

Lactose intolerance: primary (adult-type hypolactasia — common in East Asian, Aboriginal, African, Mediterranean ancestry), secondary (coeliac, gastroenteritis, Crohn, giardia), congenital (rare). Onset 30 min–2 h after lactose. Hydrogen breath test: rise ≥20 ppm over baseline after 25–50 g lactose VERIFY; exclusion/rechallenge is the pragmatic GP test. Most tolerate ~12–15 g lactose/day (≈1 cup milk) in divided doses; hard cheese and yoghurt low-lactose; lactase enzyme drops/lactose-free milk; calcium 1000 mg/day + vitamin D VERIFY. IBS Rome IV: pain ≥1 day/week over 3 months, onset ≥6 months, 2 of 3. Abdominal migraine (Rome IV): paroxysmal midline pain ≥1 h, complete wellness between, ≥2 of anorexia/nausea/vomiting/headache/photophobia/pallor, not better explained

Harder version with red flags (blood, weight loss, night pain): 'not features I put down to a food intolerance' → FBE/CRP/iron, faecal calprotectin, gastroenterology for colonoscopy — 'these are the symptoms we don't sit on'

setting: ED. Door sheet: WCC raised, lipase markedly raised, AST/ALT 2–3× ULN, bilirubin normal. Three versions, one patient: A — twelve drinks on Saturday; B1 — known hypertriglyceridaemia (father too); B2 (the 2025 case) — semaglutide six months, 3 kg intentional loss, previous cholecystectomy. Four automatic fails: no cardiac question/ECG; mild transaminase rise called a second disease; weight loss treated as a red flag without asking intent; pancreatitis named with no cause sought.
stem: Steph Corrigan, 25, presents with severe epigastric pain since last night and repeated vomiting. Results: WCC raised · lipase markedly raised · AST and ALT 2–3× upper limit · bilirubin normal.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the results and your diagnosis
Give your differentials and management
time: 8 min. Stability (118/72, 104, 20, 37.4, 98%) · intro, ★ analgesia first, open · pain: where, /10 (9), ★ three epigastric add-ons — 'through to your back?' (yes), 'sitting forward or curling up help?' (a bit), 'what does food do?' (worse, not eating) · vomits ×5–6, bilious, blood?, bloating/wind/D/C/fever · ★ six cause questions in order: alcohol (standard drinks/week, heavy session?) · gallstones/gallbladder surgery (cholecystectomy 4 y) · medicines — NSAIDs, steroids, diuretics, ★ 'any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity?' · cholesterol/triglycerides/FHx, calcium · ERCP/trauma · viral illness · ★ cardiac: chest pain/tightness, SOB, sweating, jaw/arm — 'I would like an ECG' · red flags: weight loss → ★ 'was that on purpose?' (yes — the injection), appetite, dysphagia, haematemesis/melaena, lumps, FHx · urinary · SADMA · summarise · explain each result in plain words · dx + CAUSE · DDx · management spoken: admit, fluids (the single most important treatment), analgesia, antiemetic, USS, lipids + Ca, early feeding, no routine antibiotics, stop the GLP-1 and report the reaction.

back.dx: Acute pancreatitis — 9/10 epigastric pain boring through to the back, eased sitting forward, food makes it worse, bilious vomiting ×5–6, lipase markedly raised. Cause by version: A alcohol (twelve drinks Saturday); B1 severe hypertriglyceridaemia (inherited — father); B2 semaglutide — no alcohol, no lipid disorder, gallbladder out four years ago (choledocholithiasis still possible — look), pancreatitis is a recognised uncommon effect of GLP-1 agonists → stop it, report it, 'you haven't done anything wrong'. Mildly raised AST/ALT are expected with pancreatitis and prompt a gallstone look, not a second disease; normal bilirubin suggests the main duct isn't blocked. 3 kg loss was intentional — a therapeutic effect, not a red flag.
plan: ★ 'Examiner, may I confirm she is haemodynamically stable — BP, HR, RR, T, sats?' · 'I'm Dr —, am I speaking with Steph? You look like you're in a lot of pain — would you like something for it before we start? Tell me what's been happening.'

'Show me where. Out of ten? Sharp, or deep and boring? ★ Does it go through to your back? ★ Does sitting forward or curling up make any difference? ★ And what does food do to it — better, worse, no change?' → 9, through to the back, forward helps, hasn't eaten

★ Six causes: 'alcohol — standard drinks in a usual week, any heavy session in the last few days?' · 'ever told you have gallstones, or had surgery on your gallbladder?' (out 4 y) · 'anti-inflammatories, steroids, water tablets? ★ any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity?' (Ozempic 6 months) · 'high cholesterol or triglycerides — anyone in the family? calcium/parathyroid?' · 'recent camera test of the bile duct, injury to the tummy?' · 'recent viral illness?'

★ Cardiac: chest pain/tightness, SOB, sweating, jaw/arm, cough/fever → 'I would like an ECG' · red flags: 'any weight loss?' → 3 kg → ★ 'was that on purpose?' → yes → 'that's the treatment working, not a warning sign' · appetite, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena, lumps, FHx GI cancer · urinary · smoking, drugs, meds, allergies, PMHx/ops · summarise back

★ Results in plain words: lipase — 'an enzyme your pancreas makes; when it's inflamed it leaks into the blood; yours is very high — with this pain, the pancreas is inflamed' · WCC — 'your body's response to inflammation, not necessarily infection' · AST/ALT — 'liver tests only slightly up; expected with pancreatitis, not a separate liver problem — but it makes me want to check for a gallstone' · bilirubin normal — 'reassuring; the main bile tube isn't blocked at the moment'

★ Dx + cause: A 'acute pancreatitis, most likely caused by alcohol' (without moralising; offer help) · B1 'caused by very high triglycerides — high enough to inflame the pancreas directly; inherited — family should be checked' · B2 'the most likely trigger is the weight-loss injection, and we should stop it' → 'but why? I don't drink, no gallbladder' → 'the two commonest causes don't fit; stones can still form in the duct, so we'll look; the injection can, uncommonly, inflame the pancreas — I can't prove it today but it's high on my list' → 'have I done something wrong?' → 'not at all — an uncommon reaction to a medicine used properly' · DDx: duct stone, perforated ulcer (abdomen not rigid), cholecystitis (no gallbladder), MI (ECG)

★ Management: 'you need to come into hospital: rest the gut, a drip and plenty of fluids — the single most important treatment; strong pain relief; anti-nausea; ultrasound of the bile ducts; more bloods including cholesterol and calcium; regular review over 48 h; ★ eating again as soon as you can tolerate it — starving for days is old practice; ★ no antibiotics unless a specific infection' · B2: stop semaglutide, report the adverse reaction (TGA), discuss a safer option later · B1: fasting, sometimes insulin infusion, then fibrate, low-fat diet, no alcohol · A: alcohol conversation · rural → MedSTAR if severe
ask: ★ 'Does the pain go through to your back? Does sitting forward or curling up make any difference? And what does food do to it — better, worse, or no change?'

★ 'Alcohol — how much in a usual week, in standard drinks, and any heavy session in the last few days? Have you ever been told you have gallstones, or had surgery on your gallbladder? Any anti-inflammatories, steroids or water tablets? Any injections for weight loss or diabetes — Ozempic, Wegovy, Trulicity? High cholesterol or triglycerides — anyone in the family? Any recent camera test of the bile duct, or injury? Any recent viral illness?'

Dysphagia logic: oropharyngeal (difficulty initiating, cough/choke, nasal regurgitation — neuro/muscular, pharyngeal pouch) vs oesophageal (sticks after swallowing — throat vs chest); solids only, progressive = mechanical obstruction (cancer, stricture, extrinsic compression); solids and liquids from the start, intermittent = motility (achalasia, spasm, scleroderma); odynophagia = infection (candida, HSV, CMV), pill oesophagitis, ulcerated tumour. Six differential groups: cancers (oesophageal, oropharyngeal, thyroid, lung/mediastinal) · strictures/reflux (peptic, Schatzki, eosinophilic oesophagitis in the young) · infection · neurological motility (stroke, MS, MND, myasthenia, Parkinson's, diabetic neuropathy) · autoimmune (scleroderma, Sjögren) · medications (bisphosphonates, doxycycline, NSAIDs, KCl; anticholinergics)

Oesophageal cancer risks: adenocarcinoma — GORD/Barrett's, obesity, male; SCC — smoking, alcohol, achalasia, caustic injury. First investigation: gastroscopy with biopsy (Category 1, urgent VERIFY timeframe); barium swallow first only for suspected pharyngeal pouch; CT/PET for staging after tissue; MDT. Peptic stricture: endoscopic dilatation + long-term PPI, biopsy the stricture

SA: Category 1 referral to an Adelaide upper GI unit · PATS travel/accommodation started at this visit · Country Health Connect · dietitian · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if she obstructs completely or aspirates · TIS 131 450

Cholangitis: Charcot's triad (pain, fever/rigors, jaundice) → Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension + confusion (severe). Tokyo criteria (systemic inflammation + cholestasis + imaging). Causes: choledocholithiasis (commonest), strictures, malignancy, post-ERCP, stents. Management: sepsis bundle — two large-bore IVs, cultures, lactate, ★ IV antibiotics within 1 h (e.g. amoxicillin + gentamicin ± metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam/ceftriaxone + metronidazole VERIFY TG), fluids (30 mL/kg if hypotensive), analgesia, antiemetic, NBM, monitor urine output; USS (dilated CBD, stones); ★ biliary decompression — ERCP with sphincterotomy/stent within 24 h (urgent if severe/not improving), PTC or surgery if ERCP fails; correct coagulopathy (vitamin K); cholecystectomy same admission after recovery. Beware paracetamol dosing in liver dysfunction; no NSAIDs if renal impairment

Cholecystitis vs cholangitis: both Murphy +; cholangitis has jaundice + obstructive LFTs + higher fever/rigors; cholecystitis fever 38–38.5, no jaundice (unless Mirizzi), treated with antibiotics + early cholecystectomy. Gallstone pancreatitis: raised lipase (his is normal). Hepatitis: ALT dominant. Liver abscess: fever, tender hepatomegaly, imaging

★ 'I've specifically checked for the things that would worry me, and they're not there.' / ★ 'Come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you develop a fever, blood in the stool, severe pain, or you feel faint.' / 'Was there anything you were particularly worried about today?'

Gastroenteritis version (recent travel, street food): 'Most likely you have a condition called gastroenteritis — an infection in your bowel. Three reasons: you've just come back from overseas; you ate street food, an important risk factor for a food-borne infection; and watery diarrhoea coming on over a few days with cramping fits an infection. I'm not going to guess the exact bug — knowing which doesn't change what we do first.' / DDx: 'because you've travelled — typhoid, malaria, bacterial infections, which is why I asked about mosquito bites; hepatitis A; inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, dairy intolerance, medication side effects, an overactive thyroid, irritable bowel — and I always think about bowel cancer in anyone with a change in their bowels.'

Loperamide avoided in bloody/febrile diarrhoea and suspected C. difficile. Travel DDx: typhoid, malaria (fever + travel = malaria until excluded), hepatitis A/E, amoebiasis, giardia, cholera

Skipping the cancer red-flag block because the history is five days; 'my dad had bowel cancer' without asking the age

setting: Regional SA general practice. Version F of the master diarrhoea station (2025 chronic recall; stem reconstructed). The role-player is instructed to describe leaking-fear isolation — acknowledge it explicitly, it is an approach mark in plain sight. The coeliac trap: telling her to start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy is a scripted examiner challenge.
stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with diarrhoea for six months.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Same master structure as MED-136. Six months → ★ 'how is this affecting your day-to-day life?' → 'I don't leave the house, stopped work, don't shop — frightened of leaking' → ★ 'that must be incredibly isolating; thank you for telling me — that's exactly what I need to know' · nocturnal (no) · ★ CCCVO → 'greasy, they float, hard to flush, smell awful' → ★ immediately: weight loss (5 kg over 6 months, not trying), family history, gluten relationship, iron/anaemia symptoms · bloating, cramps · red flags (no blood, no FHx) · IBD ×4 · lactose · meds · thyroid · sexual, stress · dx coeliac with reasons → ★ 'keep eating gluten normally until the blood test is done' → DDx: bowel cancer (weight loss — unlikely, no bleeding/FHx, but always considered), IBD, infection (giardia), medications, hyperthyroidism, IBS (diagnosis of exclusion, not with weight loss and steatorrhoea).

back.dx: Coeliac disease — six months of chronic diarrhoea with steatorrhoea (greasy, floating, hard to flush, offensive), 5 kg unintentional weight loss, bloating, no blood, not nocturnal; disabling fear of incontinence. Confirm with tTG-IgA + total IgA while still eating gluten, then gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, then a lifelong gluten-free diet with a dietitian; check FBE, iron, B12, folate, vitamin D, Ca, LFT, TSH; screen first-degree relatives; DEXA if long-standing. Also send stool MCS/OCP (giardia), calprotectin, and keep bowel cancer, IBD, hyperthyroidism and medication causes on the list.
plan: Identity, open ('six months') · ★ 'six months is a long time — how is it affecting your day-to-day life?' → isolation → ★ acknowledge it

Timing: constant vs intermittent, worse, ★ nocturnal (no) · ★ CCCVO: count, consistency, blood (no), bulky, ★ 'greasy? float? stick to the pan? hard to flush? offensive?' → yes to all → ★ 'have you lost weight?' (5 kg, not trying) · ★ 'worse after bread, pasta, cereal? tried cutting anything out? eating gluten now?' · FHx coeliac/bowel disease

General GI: nausea, ★ bloating, wind, constipation before, cramps, fever · red flags: appetite, lumps, tiredness (anaemia symptoms — SOB, dizziness), blood, FHx bowel cancer (age), screening · IBD ×4 (mouth ulcers, joints, eyes, rash incl elbows) · lactose · ★ meds incl chemist (iron?), PPIs, metformin, laxatives · thyroid (heat, palpitations, weight) · travel/tank water (giardia) · sexual · stress/mood (isolation) · summarise

Impact: fear of faecal incontinence is disabling — name it, plan for it (continence nurse, products, GP mental health plan if mood affected) · SA: Country Health Connect dietitian · Continence Foundation helpline 1800 33 00 66

Hearing 'floats, hard to flush' and not immediately asking weight loss and family history; calling six months of steatorrhoea with weight loss IBS
Not asking impact, or not acknowledging the isolation when it is handed to you
No cancer named in the differential with the reason it's unlikely; no deficiency work-up; no dietitian/family screening

Steatorrhoea DDx: coeliac · pancreatic insufficiency · giardia · SIBO · Crohn's · Continence Foundation 1800 33 00 66

setting: Cruise ship berthed in Sydney after sailing from New Zealand; you are the ship's medical officer. A different task set: four-minute focused history, then an assessment — directed to the examiner — of whether this patient can be released home. He is furious about being held on board. The 2025 finding: a cannula-site infection photograph handed over on request, which does not by itself prevent discharge.
stem: A 40-year-old man on a cruise ship berthed in Sydney has been diagnosed with norovirus gastroenteritis. He is insisting on being discharged home.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Perform an assessment, directed to the examiner, of whether this patient can be released home
time: 8 min. ★ Opening for the approach marks: 'I can hear how frustrating this is — I'd be frustrated too; can I ask what's making you so keen to get home? There may be something I can help with. Whatever you tell me stays between us.' (cat alone at home → 'we can almost certainly arrange for someone to look in on her') · ★ 'when did it start? is it still going? if it has stopped — when was the last symptom?' (the exclusion criterion is time since the last symptom) · count, consistency, ★ blood (would change the diagnosis) · fever/chills, abdominal pain, N/V, dizziness (must be asymptomatic, not just diarrhoea-free) · ★ 'eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?' · ★ immunocompromise: diabetes, cancer, steroids, chemo · ★ 'what treatment did you receive on board?' → IV fluids → the cannula · ★ occupation: food handler, childcare, healthcare (changes the exclusion period, public health duty) · to examiner: appearance/dehydration, vitals incl postural BP, full abdominal examination, ★ 'look at the cannula site' → photo: erythema, swelling, purulent discharge · ★ release criteria stated: no diarrhoea/vomiting for 48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no dehydration, normal abdomen → release, remove cannula, oral flucloxacillin, mark the edge, GP 48 h / ED if fever or spreading.

back.dx: Resolved norovirus gastroenteritis meeting exclusion criteria for release (symptom-free ≥48 h, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration, normal abdominal examination) — plus a peripheral cannula-site infection (erythema, swelling, purulent discharge at the insertion point) from the IV fluids given on board: remove the cannula, oral flucloxacillin as for a skin and soft tissue infection, mark the margin, GP review in 48 h, ED if fever, spreading redness or unwell. IV antibiotics only for systemic features (high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness) — he has none. Not a reason to keep him on board.
plan: 'I'm furious, stuck in the harbour' → ★ 'I can hear how frustrating this is, and I'd be frustrated too — being held on board past your disembarkation date is really hard. Can I ask what's making you so keen to get home? There may be something I can help with. Whatever you tell me stays between us.' → cat alone → 'that's a real worry — we can almost certainly arrange for someone to look in on her today. Let me ask a few questions and then I'll tell you exactly where we stand.'

★ 'When did it start? Is it still going? If it has stopped — when exactly was your last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting?' · count, consistency, ★ blood · 'fever or chills? tummy pain? nausea? dizziness?' · ★ 'are you eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?'

★ 'Any medical conditions or medications affecting your immune system — diabetes, cancer, steroids, chemotherapy?' · ★ 'what treatment did you receive on board?' → IV fluids via a cannula (still in? sore?) · ★ 'what do you do for work — food handling, childcare, healthcare?' · anyone else in the cabin unwell · meds, allergies (penicillin) · who's at home

★ 'Examiner, before I decide about release I'd like: general appearance — does he look well, any evidence of dehydration? Vital signs — temperature, pulse, BP including a postural BP, respiratory rate. A full abdominal examination, because I would not release anyone with abdominal tenderness. And I'd like to look at the cannula site, since he had intravenous fluids on board.' → photo: erythema, swelling, purulent discharge at the insertion point → describe it

★ 'My criteria for release are: no diarrhoea and no vomiting for 48 hours, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration and a normal abdominal examination — he meets them.' · challenge 'would you still release him with that cannula site?' → ★ 'Yes. He meets the exclusion criteria for norovirus. The cannula site needs treatment, but that is oral antibiotics I can prescribe, and there is no reason to keep him on board to give it. I would remove the cannula, start flucloxacillin, mark the edge of the redness, and ask him to see his own GP in 48 hours or attend an emergency department if he develops fever, spreading redness or feels unwell. IV antibiotics would be indicated only for systemic features — high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, drowsiness — and he has none.' · public health: notify the ship's outbreak log/port health; hand hygiene (soap and water — alcohol gel is less effective against norovirus), stay off food handling for 48 h after symptoms; the cat

★ 'When did it start? Is it still going? If it has stopped, when was the last time you had any diarrhoea or vomiting?' / 'Are you eating and drinking normally and keeping it down?' / 'Any conditions or medicines affecting your immune system?' / 'What treatment did you receive on board?' / 'What do you do for work — do you handle food, or work in childcare or healthcare?'

★ To examiner: 'General appearance and any evidence of dehydration; temperature, pulse, blood pressure including a postural blood pressure, and respiratory rate; a full abdominal examination; and I would like to look at the cannula site, since he tells me he had intravenous fluids on board.'

★ 'My criteria for release are: no diarrhoea and no vomiting for 48 hours, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no clinical dehydration and a normal abdominal examination.' / ★ 'Yes, I would still release him … I would remove the cannula, start flucloxacillin, mark the edge of the redness, and ask him to see his own GP in 48 hours or attend an emergency department if he develops fever, spreading redness or feels unwell.'

Examiner hands over the cannula-site photo on request

Photo: peripheral cannula site with erythema, swelling and purulent discharge at the insertion point — phlebitis/cellulitis. Management: remove cannula, swab, oral flucloxacillin 500 mg qid 5–7 d (cefalexin/clindamycin if allergic) VERIFY TG, mark margin, review 48 h; IV/admission if systemic features, spreading, or purulent thrombophlebitis with a cord

Norovirus: incubation 12–48 h; symptoms 24–72 h; highly infectious; shedding continues after symptoms — exclusion 48 h symptom-free (some services 48–72 h VERIFY SA Health/national guidance); food handlers, childcare and healthcare workers excluded 48 h after symptoms resolve; soap and water hand hygiene; bleach-based cleaning; outbreak reporting (ships: port health/Department of Agriculture and state health); prolonged/severe in the immunocompromised, elderly, infants

Discharge criteria in any gastroenteritis: symptom-free window, afebrile, tolerating oral intake, no dehydration (postural BP), normal abdomen, safe home situation, not a public-health risk; document the shared decision
fails: Arguing with the angry passenger or lecturing him; never asking why he wants to get home
Not asking when the last symptom was — the single exclusion criterion; not asking about oral intake or immunocompromise
Not asking what treatment he had (missing the cannula), or not asking to look at the site
Keeping him on board for IV antibiotics for a localised cannula infection; or ignoring it entirely
Not stating the release criteria explicitly to the examiner; forgetting occupation/public-health duty

Cannula infection: remove, flucloxacillin 500 mg qid 5–7 d VERIFY, mark margin, GP 48 h · IV only if systemic
Soap and water (alcohol gel less effective) · food handlers excluded 48 h post-symptoms · port/state health notification

setting: General practice. Within the first minute he volunteers that he is gay and his male partner has the same symptoms — every candidate received that without digging. Reorder the consultation: sexual history to the front. Three traps in task 2: avoiding the word HIV; testing without consent and a pre-test discussion; saying 'PrEP protects you, so it can't be HIV' (untrue — the reassurance trap the case is built to catch).
stem: Michael Reid, 32, presents with diarrhoea for two weeks. 'I'm gay, and my boyfriend has exactly the same thing.'
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: 8 min. Identity, open → disclosure → ★ 'thank you for telling me that so openly — it's directly relevant. I'd like to ask about your bowels, and also about your sexual health, because that may well be part of what's going on. Everything is confidential. Is that all right?' · ★ PrEP first: on it? every day, missed doses? since when, who prescribes? ★ 'last HIV/STI check and did you get the results?' (a month ago, never got them → 'I'll retrieve them today — not the same as a negative') · ★ three boxes — partners (stable? multiple? male/female/both), practices (condoms? oral/anal? receptive/insertive?), risk (previous STIs — chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis; sex under alcohol/drugs; sex work) · say it back · ★ seroconversion: fevers/night sweats, sore throat, glands, rash, mouth ulcers, myalgia · ★ anorectal: pain, discharge, tenesmus, bleeding · generic structure at pace: timing, CCCVO, general GI, travel/contacts, hepatitis + hep A/B vaccination, IBD/coeliac/lactose, other meds, thyroid, red flags · summarise · ★ name HIV as the condition to exclude, reasons, PrEP not absolute, grouped DDx (PrEP side effect, proctitis — chlamydia/gonorrhoea/LGV, enteric STIs — shigella/giardia, hepatitis A, general causes), ★ consent + pre-test discussion (window, repeat 6 and 12 weeks, result in person), three-site STI screen, ★ partner in for the same tests.

back.dx: Acute HIV infection to be excluded — two weeks of watery diarrhoea 4–5/day in a man on PrEP with ~fortnightly missed doses, a fluey illness with sore throat, fever, myalgia and a chest rash two weeks ago, persistent cervical lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers, some anal discharge; risk profile: open relationship, several male partners, condomless receptive anal sex, chlamydia ×2, gonorrhoea, syphilis, chemsex; last screen a month ago with results never seen. Most probable diagnoses are a PrEP side effect or a sexually transmitted enteric infection/proctitis — HIV is first as the diagnosis I most need to exclude because the consequence of missing it is greatest and the seroconversion picture fits. PrEP substantially reduces but does not eliminate risk; breakthrough is described.
plan: Identity, 'what's brought you in?' → disclosure → ★ 'thank you for telling me that so openly — it's directly relevant, so I'd like to ask about your sexual health now rather than later. Everything you tell me here is confidential.'

★ 'Are you taking PrEP? every day, without missing doses? since when, who prescribes it? ★ when was your last HIV and STI check, and did you get the results?' → ~a year; misses one a fortnight; a month ago, never told → 'I'll look those up today — a test you haven't had a result for isn't the same as a negative'

★ Partners: 'stable relationship? ever multiple partners? male, female or both?' · practices: 'condoms? oral, anal or both? receptive, insertive or both?' · risk: 'ever diagnosed with an STI? sex under the influence of alcohol or drugs? ever paid for sex?' → open relationship, several men, no condoms with the boyfriend, mostly receptive, chlamydia ×2/gonorrhoea/syphilis, parties · say it back without flinching

Timing/CCCVO: 2 wk, constant, 4–5/day, watery, no blood, not nocturnal · general GI: nausea, cramps, no constipation, felt feverish · ★ 'alongside the diarrhoea — fevers or night sweats? sore throat? swollen glands? rash? mouth ulcers? aching muscles?' → sore throat + fluey 2 wk ago, neck glands up, chest rash · ★ 'pain in the back passage? discharge? needing to go when there's nothing there? bleeding?' → some discharge

Travel/contacts (none; just the partner) · hepatitis symptoms; ★ 'vaccinated against hepatitis A and B?' (not sure) · IBD ×4 (mouth ulcers yes), greasy stools, dairy · other meds/chemist, thyroid · red flags: weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness (bit), blood, FHx · ★ summarise back the whole picture

★ 'Thank you for being so open — I want to be straight with you. The most serious condition I need to rule out is an HIV infection. I'm not telling you that you have it; it's the thing I most need to exclude, and I want to explain why: diarrhoea can be one of the first symptoms of HIV in the first weeks after someone catches it — often with fever, sore throat, swollen glands and a rash, which is close to what you've described; and the risk factors line up. ★ You're taking PrEP, which is genuinely very good protection — but it isn't one hundred per cent, and it works best taken every single day. It lowers the risk a lot; it doesn't remove it.' · 'but I'm on PrEP — I thought I couldn't get it' → hold the line · DDx grouped: the PrEP itself (nausea, loose stools) · proctitis — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, LGV, herpes · enteric STIs — shigella, giardia · hepatitis A · general: IBD, coeliac, lactose, thyroid, IBS; bowel cancer very unlikely at 32

★ Consent: 'I'd like to do a blood test for HIV today — it looks for the virus and your body's response. There's a window in the first weeks where it can be negative even if someone has been infected, so if it's negative I'll repeat it at six and twelve weeks. The result comes back to me and I'll give it to you in person. It's confidential. Are you happy for me to do that?' · 'how long? will anyone find out?' → answered · three-site screen (anorectal, pharyngeal, urine NAAT), syphilis serology, hepatitis serology/vaccination, stool MCS/PCR (shigella, giardia, campylobacter), UEC (PrEP), FBE · ★ 'I'd like your partner to come in too — he needs the same tests' · partner notification support; do not stop PrEP without advice; SHINE SA/Clinic 275
ask: ★ 'Thank you for telling me that — it's directly relevant, so I'd like to ask about your sexual health now rather than later. Everything you tell me here is confidential.' / ★ 'Are you taking PrEP? And are you taking it every day, without missing doses? When was your last HIV and STI check, and did you get the results?' / 'A test you haven't had a result for isn't the same as a negative.'

★ 'Are you in a stable relationship? Have you ever had multiple partners? Are your partners male, female or both? Do you use condoms? What kind of sex do you practise — oral, anal or both — receptive, insertive or both? Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? Have you ever had sex under the influence of alcohol or drugs? Ever paid for sex?'

★ 'Alongside the diarrhoea, have you had any fevers or night sweats? A sore throat? Swollen glands? Any rash? Mouth ulcers? Aching muscles?' / 'Any pain in the back passage? Any discharge? Any feeling that you need to go when there's nothing there? Any bleeding?' / 'Are you vaccinated against hepatitis A and B?'

★ 'The most serious condition I need to rule out is an HIV infection. I'm not telling you that you have it. I'm telling you it's the thing I most need to exclude, and I want to explain why.' / ★ 'Diarrhoea can be one of the first symptoms, in the first few weeks after someone catches it.' / ★ 'PrEP is very good protection, but it isn't absolute, and it works best taken every day.'

★ 'I'd like to do a blood test for HIV today … There's a window early on when the test can be negative, so I'd repeat it at six and twelve weeks. The result comes back to me and I'll give it to you in person. It's confidential. Are you happy for me to do that?' / ★ 'I'd like your partner to come in as well — he needs the same tests.'

Examiner 'he's adherent — is HIV really top?' → ★ 'I would not put it at the top as the most probable diagnosis — that is a PrEP side effect or a sexually transmissible enteric infection. I put HIV first as the condition I most need to exclude, because the consequence of missing it is the greatest and the seroconversion picture fits. PrEP substantially reduces risk but does not eliminate it, particularly with intermittent missed doses, and breakthrough infection is described. Testing costs him one blood test.' / 'Should I tell my partner?' → 'He should be tested and he needs to know he may have been exposed. You don't have to do that alone — there are services that notify partners anonymously, and I can help with the conversation. stem: A 40-year-old man presents with diarrhoea for three days — watery stools six times a day with abdominal cramps, no blood, no travel. Recent bronchitis treated with amoxicillin for five days. Examination: dry mucous membranes, vital signs within normal limits, abdominal examination normal.

back.dx: Pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile toxin-mediated colitis) 'may have' — three days of profuse watery diarrhoea 6–7/day with cramps starting ~10 days after a five-day amoxicillin course for bronchitis; no blood, no travel, mild dehydration, normal obs and abdomen. Second (and more common): plain antibiotic-associated diarrhoea — settles alone; a stool toxin test tells them apart, and only the first needs specific treatment. Management: stop the antibiotic (chest infection settled), oral vancomycin 125 mg qid 10 days if confirmed (metronidazole alternative for non-severe VERIFY), oral rehydration, no loperamide (prolongs toxin contact, toxic megacolon risk), soap-and-water hand hygiene and bleach cleaning (spores resist alcohol gel), red flags, review 2–3 days.
