plan: 'I'm Dr —; can I confirm your name and date of birth? ★ 'I'm concerned you may have a condition called pseudomembranous colitis. Your bowel normally has a large population of harmless bacteria living in balance. When you take an antibiotic, it doesn't only kill the bug causing your chest infection — it disturbs that balance. One particular bug, Clostridioides difficile, can take over and overgrow. That bug produces a toxin — a poison — and it is the toxin that inflames the lining of the bowel and causes the diarrhoea and cramps. It's called pseudomembranous because with a camera we'd see whitish patches on the lining.' · 'is that serious? do I need hospital?' → non-severe form, treatable as an outpatient if the plan is followed

★ 'The other possibility — and the more common one — is simply that the antibiotic itself has loosened your bowels. That settles by itself. The difference matters, because the first needs specific treatment and the second doesn't, and a stool test tells us which it is.' · DDx with reasons from the stem: food/travel infection (no travel, no eating out, nobody unwell), IBD (no blood/mucus, not nocturnal, only 3 days), coeliac (not greasy/floating), dairy (no link), thyroid (no weight loss/heat), other medications (I'll check — Somac), bowel cancer (at 40 with no bleeding, weight loss or FHx — very unlikely; it stays on the list with any habit change)

Fissure: painful passing a motion? constipated? straining? blood on paper? · haemorrhoids: lumps before? reducible? painless bleeding in the past? · abscess: red/swollen? pus? had this before? · ★ pilonidal: 'exactly in the midline between the cheeks? ever noticed a small hole or pit there? hair coming out? long sitting or driving?' · proctitis/prostatitis: dysuria, frequency, penile or anal discharge, tenesmus, sexually active/condoms · IBD: bloody diarrhoea/mucus, joints, eyes, rash, mouth ulcers · host: itch, rash, warts, blisters; ★ diabetic? immune-suppressing medicines? smoking (10/day)

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — unwell or septic? vital signs including temperature; abdomen — tenderness, guarding, masses; groins — inguinal lymphadenopathy' → uncomfortable, not septic, T 38.1, HR 96, BP normal, abdomen soft, groins normal · ★ 'I would like to examine the perianal area, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection — skin changes: redness, rash, a visible fissure, skin tags? lumps or swellings: their site relative to the anal verge and to the midline, colour, whether they look fluctuant, any punctum or opening? any discharge or bleeding?' → photo handed over → ★ 'Describing what I can see: an erythematous, indurated swelling immediately lateral to the anal verge, with what appears to be a fluctuant centre and surrounding cellulitis. No midline pit, no visible fissure, no purple thrombosed pile at the verge.' · ★ 'Given that appearance and the degree of pain, I would not proceed with a digital rectal examination — it would be extremely painful and would not change management; full assessment would be under anaesthesia.'

★ 'Mr Keane, most likely you have a perianal abscess — an infection right next to the back passage that has formed a pocket of pus. It starts in one of the tiny glands inside the back passage and tracks outwards to just under the skin — which is why it's so painful and why sitting is unbearable. I'm saying that because of where it is — immediately beside the back passage rather than up in the crease — because of the fever and shivers, and because of what I can see: red, swollen, and it looks like it has pus underneath.' · DDx with reasons: pilonidal abscess (crease, midline, ingrown hair — not midline); thrombosed pile (purple lump at the opening, no fever); anal fissure (pain specifically with motions); proctitis; Crohn's disease (if this ever recurs); anal cancer — always considered with any lump, nothing here suggests it

★ 'The important thing is that antibiotics on their own won't fix this — they can't get into a pocket of pus. It has to be opened and drained: a small operation, usually under a general anaesthetic, and it needs to happen today. I'm arranging for you to go to hospital and I'll speak to the surgical team myself. Strong pain relief now; nothing to eat or drink in case they take you to theatre. I'd add antibiotics if the redness is spreading, or if someone is diabetic or immune-suppressed.' · 'can't you just give me antibiotics? we're seeding' → hold firm, acknowledge · ★ 'one thing to know in advance: in around a third of people a small tunnel can form afterwards between the bowel and the skin — a fistula. If you notice ongoing discharge after it heals, come back — that's treatable too.' · smoking, hygiene, sitz baths after drainage, review
ask: ★ 'I can see you're in a lot of pain — I'll be quick, and I'll get you something for it.' / ★ 'I'll need to ask about a fairly private area. Is that all right?' / ★ 'Is it immediately beside your back passage, or higher up, between the cheeks of your bottom?' / ★ 'Is the lump coming out of the back passage, or is it beside it?'

★ 'Is it worse when you open your bowels, or when you sit?' / ★ 'Any fevers or chills?' / 'Is it exactly in the midline between the cheeks? Have you ever noticed a small hole or pit there, or hair coming out of it? Do you sit or drive for long periods?' / 'Are you diabetic, or on any medicines affecting your immune system?'

★ To examiner: 'I would like to examine the perianal area, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection — any skin changes: redness, rash, a visible fissure, skin tags? Any lumps or swellings: their site relative to the anal verge and to the midline, colour, whether they look fluctuant, any punctum or opening? Any discharge or bleeding?' / ★ 'Describing what I can see: an erythematous, indurated swelling immediately lateral to the anal verge, with what appears to be a fluctuant centre and surrounding cellulitis. There is no midline pit and no visible fissure.' / ★ 'Given that appearance I would not proceed with a digital examination — it would be very painful and would not change management.'

★ 'A perianal abscess is an infection beside the back passage that has formed a pocket of pus. It starts in one of the tiny glands inside the back passage, and the infection tracks outwards to just under the skin.' / ★ 'Antibiotics on their own won't clear a pocket of pus — they can't get into it. This needs to be opened and drained, and that needs to happen today.' / ★ 'In about a third of people a small tunnel forms afterwards between the bowel and the skin. If you get ongoing discharge once this heals, come back — that's treatable too.'

Pilonidal version (midline, a pit that weeps for years, truck driver): 'Most likely a pilonidal abscess — some call it a hair cyst. In the crease between the cheeks a hair grows inwards and makes a small pit that traps hair and debris; when it gets infected and fills with pus we call it an abscess. It needs draining now; later you may need an operation to remove the pit, otherwise it tends to come back — hygiene and hair removal help. The wound is often left open to heal from the bottom up, so district nursing for a while.' / Fistula version (months of offensive expressible discharge, an abscess drained a year ago; photo — external opening with granulation tissue, induration, no cellulitis): 'A fistula is a small tunnel between the inside of the bowel and the skin near the back passage — what leaks out is bowel content, which is why it's offensive and keeps coming back; it very often follows an abscess. A surgeon maps the tunnel, usually under anaesthetic, sometimes with an MRI first, then lays it open or places a soft drainage stitch called a seton. I'd also check for Crohn's disease.'

Examiner challenges: 'oral antibiotics and review?' → 'Antibiotics do not penetrate a collection of pus; the definitive treatment is incision and drainage. Antibiotics as an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression or valvular heart disease.' / 'perianal vs pilonidal?' → 'Site. Perianal — immediately adjacent to the anal verge, from an infected anal gland at the dentate line. Pilonidal — midline of the natal cleft in hair-bearing skin, from a midline pit with ingrown hair, typically pointing slightly off the midline.' / 'three abscesses in two years?' → 'raises Crohn disease — ask about diarrhoea, blood, weight loss, mouth ulcers; colonoscopy and pelvic MRI with gastroenterology; check for diabetes and immunosuppression.' / 'diabetic, 39.5, tachycardic, dusky skin' → 'Fournier's gangrene — a surgical emergency: resuscitate, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately, cultures and lactate, urgent surgical debridement — immediate MedSTAR retrieval on 1300 13 12 33.' / 'irregular ulcerated bleeding lesion' → 'anal cancer — usually squamous cell, HPV-associated: urgent specialist referral for examination and biopsy, examine the inguinal nodes, offer HIV testing with consent.'
pefe: Role-player: Tom Keane, 35, farm hand near Maitland, partner; lies on his side throughout, winces; 8/10 throbbing constant pain, worse each day, sitting unbearable, no sleep; hot and shivery since yesterday; no pus/discharge/bleeding; can't push it anywhere; first episode; 10 cigs/day; not diabetic; all other blocks negative. Vague 'where?' → 'on my bum' — the precise site only with the two options. Stoic, embarrassed, terser if pain unacknowledged; irritated by compound questions. Hidden: nearly didn't come; cancer fear — 'it's not cancer, is it?' if asked concerns. Pushback once: 'can't you just give me antibiotics? we're in the middle of seeding'

Examiner: uncomfortable, not septic; T 38.1, HR 96, BP normal; abdomen soft; groins normal. Photo on requesting inspection: perianal abscess (erythematous indurated fluctuant swelling lateral to the verge with cellulitis). If DRE requested: 'the patient will not tolerate it.' If inspection never requested: 'the examination is unremarkable' and nothing else. Variants: pilonidal (midline pit, Figures 4/5), fistula (external opening with granulation, Figure 6), thrombosed pile (36 h sudden severe pain, purple lump at the verge, years of painless bleeding, no fever, Figure 7)

Numbers: perianal abscess → fistula ~1/3 · thrombosed external pile — excise within ~72 h · fissure posterior midline ~90% · antibiotics adjunct only (cellulitis, diabetes, immunosuppression, valvular disease) VERIFY · Goodsall's rule: anterior external openings track radially; posterior openings curve to the posterior midline (horseshoe); exception — anterior >3 cm from the anus behaves posteriorly · Fournier's gangrene — necrotising perineal infection, diabetes/immunosuppression · anal cancer — HPV-related SCC; consider HIV testing

Abscess management: I&D under GA (or LA if small and superficial), swab/culture, packing/sitz baths, analgesia, review for fistula; MRI pelvis/EUA for complex or recurrent; seton or fistulotomy for fistula (sphincter-preserving where needed); pilonidal — I&D then definitive excision/flap, hygiene, hair removal, district nursing for an open wound
SA: surgical referral same day (Yorke and Northern LHN/Adelaide) · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for Fournier's · TIS 131 450

★ Accepting 'on my bum' — never offering the two site options; not asking whether the lump comes out of the anus or sits beside it
★ Consent and chaperone not said before inspection; naming the photograph without describing it; attempting a digital examination (or not explaining why you won't)
★ Prescribing antibiotics and arranging review — an abscess is drained; caving to 'can't you just give me antibiotics?'
No fistula warning/follow-up; no diabetes/immunosuppression questions; anal cancer never on the list

setting: Regional SA general practice. Six-minute history, then diagnosis with reasons, then differentials — no examination task. Same stem, two versions: A — constipation only, every red flag negative → diverticulitis, with the reassurance coming AFTER the stated negatives; B — weight loss and rectal bleeding when probed → 'I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer'. Differentials must come from at least three groups (GI, KUB, hernia, genital, other), each with a reason.
stem: Gary Nolan, 50, presents with pain in the left lower abdomen for one month. BP 128/78 · HR 78 · RR 16 · T 36.8.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis with reasons
Explain your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. Identity, open → 'I can hear this has been worrying you, and a month is a long time' (make it land) · 'in pain now — want something?' · pain without pausing for a story: show me · ★ '1 to 10, ten the worst pain you've ever felt, one the least' (anchors in the same breath) · sharp/dull (dull ache, 5) · when, first time, constant, worse · ★ 'has it ever woken you at night?' (B: yes) · radiation · food/position · impact · GI general six: N/V, bloating, ★ wind, diarrhoea, ★ constipation, fever → 'constipated for years' → ★ probe: how long, hard stools, painful/difficult · ★ 3:30 'these next ones are the important warning-sign questions': weight loss → ★ how many kilos / over what period / on purpose? (B: 5 kg, 2 months, no) · appetite (B: down) · lumps · ★ blood in motions or black tarry (B: bright red — 'thought it was piles') · change in habit · FHx bowel cancer · ★ screening kit ('on the bench') · KUB three: burning, frequency, haematuria · ★ groin lump · ★ scrotal swelling/redness/pain · rash, injury, palpitations · smoking (pack/day 30 y), alcohol, drugs, meds, allergies, ★ operations · summarise · A: negatives first then diverticulitis · B: 'I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer' — warning, pause, four reasons · DDx across groups with reasons · plan.

back.dx: Version A — diverticulitis: a month of constant dull LIF pain 5/10 in a 50-year-old with years of constipation and hard stools, no night pain, and every red flag negative (no weight loss, no bleeding, no habit change, no FHx). Version B — 'concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer': the same pain but it wakes him, 5 kg unintentional loss over two months, appetite down, bright red rectal bleeding he attributed to piles, age 50, a screening kit on the bench, pack-a-day smoker. Diverticulitis fits the constipation and site but not the weight loss or bleeding. Hidden agenda: brother-in-law died of bowel cancer three years ago.
plan: 'Am I speaking with Gary? How can I help?' → 'a month, not getting better, worried' → ★ 'I can hear this has been worrying you, and a month is a long time to put up with pain. I'll ask some questions, then explain what I think and what we do next. Are you in any pain right now — would you like something for it?'

Pain: 'show me where' (LIF) · ★ 'on a scale of one to ten, ten being the worst pain you've ever felt, one the least — how bad?' (5) · sharp or dull (dull ache) · when, first time, constant, worse · ★ 'has it ever woken you at night?' (A no / B a couple of times) · travel · food/position · 'how is it affecting day to day?' (still working)

GI six: nausea/vomiting, bloating, passing wind, diarrhoea, ★ constipation, fever → 'constipated for years' → ★ 'tell me more — how long? are the stools hard? painful or difficult to pass?' (years; hard and stony; hard to push out, not painful)

★ 'These next ones are the important warning-sign questions. Any weight loss?' (B: pause… 'a bit') → ★ 'how many kilos? over what period? on purpose — dieting or exercise?' (5 kg, ~2 months, no) · appetite (a bit down) · lumps · ★ 'blood in your bowel motions, or black tarry motions?' (bright red — 'thought it was piles') · change in habit · FHx bowel cancer (no) · ★ 'have you done your bowel screening test?' (kit on the bench)

KUB: burning, frequency, haematuria · ★ 'any lump or swelling in your groin?' · ★ 'any swelling, redness or pain in your scrotum?' · rash on the tummy, injury, racing heart · smoking (pack/day, 30 y), alcohol (few beers weekends), drugs, meds, allergies, ★ operations on the abdomen (none) · PMHx (BP mentioned once), FHx · ★ summarise: 'a month of constant dull pain low on the left, years of constipation with hard stools, five kilos you didn't intend, some bright red blood; waterworks and groin clear — anything missed?' · concerns → brother-in-law

B: ★ 'Gary, during our conversation I was thinking about a number of conditions, and I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer. Let me tell you why.' [pause — let it land] · 'cancer? are you serious?' → 'that's a frightening word and I'm sorry to raise it. I'm not saying you have it — I'm saying it must be ruled out, and there is a clear way to do that. My reasons: a month of pain that isn't settling; five kilos of weight loss you didn't intend; blood in your bowel motions; and your age' (+ the unreturned kit) · A: ★ negatives first: 'before I tell you what I think this is, I want to be clear about what I have ruled out — not losing weight, no blood, habit unchanged, no family history. That's genuinely reassuring, and it's why I'm comfortable calling this diverticulitis: small pouches form in the wall of the large bowel, usually from long-standing constipation pushing on the wall, and one has become inflamed.'

★ DDx across groups, each with a reason: bowel — cancer (why I asked the warning signs) / diverticulitis (fits site and constipation, not weight loss or bleeding) / impacted constipation / obstruction · waterworks — UTI or ureteric stone (no burning, frequency, haematuria) · groin — hernia (no swelling) · genital — epididymo-orchitis (no swelling/redness) · lower — shingles, injury, mesenteric ischaemia · B plan: examine including the back passage, bloods (FBE/iron), ★ urgent colonoscopy, do the kit anyway; ED if severe pain, heavy bleeding, vomiting, faint; bring his wife for results · A plan: analgesia, fluids, soft diet during the flare (hold fibre until settled, then reintroduce), CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast to confirm, ± antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 bd 5 d VERIFY — uncomplicated diverticulitis often managed without), review 48–72 h, colonoscopy 6–8 weeks after resolution; ED if worse, fever/shakes, vomiting, dizzy

How long has that been going on? Are the stools hard? Is it painful or difficult to pass them?'

Any weight loss? … How many kilos, over what period, and was it intentional?' / ★ 'Any blood in your bowel motions, or any black tarry motions?' / 'Have you done your bowel screening test?' / ★ 'Have you noticed any lump or swelling in your groin? Any swelling, redness or pain in your scrotum?' / 'Any operations on your abdomen?'

★ B: 'Gary, during our conversation I was thinking about a number of conditions, and I am concerned about the possibility of a bowel cancer. Let me tell you why I'm thinking that.' [pause] / 'That's a frightening word and I'm sorry to raise it. I'm not saying you have it — I'm saying it must be ruled out, and there is a clear way to do that. My reasons: a month of pain that isn't settling, five kilos of weight loss you didn't intend, blood in your bowel motions, and your age.'

★ A: 'Before I tell you what I think this is, I want to be clear about what I have ruled out. You are not losing weight, there is no blood in your bowel motions, your habit hasn't changed and there is no family history. That is genuinely reassuring, and it is why I am comfortable calling this diverticulitis. Small pouches form in the wall of the large bowel, usually from long-standing constipation pushing on the wall. In your case one has become inflamed.'

'Diverticulitis — inflamed pouches in the bowel wall — fits the constipation and the site but not the weight loss or bleeding. Constipation becoming impacted. A hernia in the groin, but there's no swelling. Urinary causes, but no burning, frequency or blood. An infection in the testicle, but nothing there either.' / 'What happens next: I'll examine you including the back passage, do bloods including a check for anaemia, and refer you urgently for a colonoscopy. Please do that kit on the bench too. If you get severe pain, heavy bleeding, vomiting or feel faint, go straight to the emergency department. Would you like to bring someone when we get the results?'
pefe: Role-player: Gary Nolan, 50, fitter and turner at the Wallaroo grain terminal, married, two adult kids; pack/day since his twenties, 4–5 beers weekends; no meds/allergies/operations; BP mentioned once. Practical, gruff, plays it down, came because his wife made him; opens up if warm, monosyllabic if tick-boxy. Hand low on the left; 'I don't know how to answer that' if the 1–10 anchors aren't given. B: pauses at weight loss — 'yeah… a bit' — number only if asked; bright red blood 'thought it was piles'; kit on the bench. Hidden: brother-in-law died of bowel cancer 3 y ago — only if concerns asked; last minute 'it's not cancer, is it?'

No examination task. Vitals 128/78 · 78 · 16 · 36.8. A: constipation only, all red flags negative. B: night waking, 5 kg/2 months unintentional, appetite down, bright red PR blood, unreturned kit. Version C (Jimmy Rahman, adhesional SBO with a LIF twist) = MED-146

Diverticulitis: LIF pain, fever, change in habit, ± PR bleeding; CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast confirms (uncomplicated vs complicated — abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction); uncomplicated — analgesia (avoid NSAIDs), clear fluids/soft diet during the flare, antibiotics not routinely required in immunocompetent uncomplicated disease VERIFY TG (amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg bd 5 d if used), review 48–72 h; complicated/systemically unwell/immunosuppressed/comorbid → admit, IV antibiotics; colonoscopy 6–8 weeks after resolution to exclude malignancy (first episode); long-term fibre; recurrent → surgical opinion. Red flags for ED: worsening pain, fever/rigors, vomiting, peritonism, dizziness

Colorectal cancer: age ≥50, weight loss, PR bleeding, habit change, iron-deficiency anaemia → Category 1 colonoscopy (~30 d VERIFY); iFOBT 2-yearly 45–74 (opt-in 45–49 since July 2024). Blood attributed to 'piles' is a classic delay. Automatic fails from the source: ★ a benign label without asking red flags · ★ 'nasty growth' or refusing to name cancer · ★ stating a physical finding never requested

time: 8 min. back.dx: Adhesional small bowel obstruction — LIF pain, 'normal' bowels on the surface but no motion for 3–4 days and no flatus for ~2, appendicectomy ten years ago; PEFE: appendicectomy scar, LIF tenderness with guarding and rebound, absent bowel sounds, empty rectum, groin and scrotum normal. 'I know the pain is on the left and I did think about diverticulitis. Two things don't fit: you haven't passed wind or opened your bowels for several days, and I couldn't hear any bowel sounds and the back passage was empty — that tells me the bowel is blocked rather than inflamed. The most likely cause is bands of scar tissue from your appendix operation.' Hospital today: NBM, IV fluids, NG, analgesia, antiemetic, bloods, erect/supine AXR then CT, surgical team; many settle, operate if strangulating.

GI six: nausea/vomiting (colour, green?), bloating, wind, diarrhoea, constipation, fever → 'my bowel motions are completely normal' → ★ 'that's helpful — can I ask it a slightly different way: when did you last open your bowels? and when did you last pass wind?' → 'now that you say it — three or four days; no wind for a couple of days'

Warning signs: weight, appetite, lumps, blood/melaena, habit, FHx, screening (all negative) · KUB three · ★ groin lump · ★ scrotum · rash, injury, palpitations · smoking, alcohol, drugs, meds, allergies · ★ 'any operations on your abdomen?' → appendix ~10 years ago (keep it — it is the cause) · summarise

★ Examiner, each named: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydration, pallor · all four vitals incl temperature · inspection — movement with respiration, scars, Cullen or Grey Turner · superficial and deep palpation — tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, masses · percussion tenderness · auscultation — bowel sounds present, absent or high-pitched · groin and scrotum — lump, swelling, redness, tenderness · DRE — is the rectum full or empty · urine dipstick' → alert, well perfused, obs normal, appendicectomy scar, LIF tenderness with guarding and rebound, no mass, no percussion tenderness, bowel sounds absent, groin/scrotum normal, rectum empty, dipstick negative

★ 'Jimmy, your bowel is blocked — the condition is called a small bowel obstruction. Four reasons: you haven't passed wind or opened your bowels for several days; you had your appendix out ten years ago; I could not hear any bowel sounds; and the back passage was empty. Your small bowel is blocked by bands of scar tissue that form after an operation on the tummy.' · ★ refuse the momentum: 'I know the pain is on the left and I did think about diverticulitis — two things don't fit …' · DDx by group: bowel — diverticulitis, cancer (warning signs asked), impaction; KUB — UTI/stone (no burning/frequency/haematuria, dipstick clear); groin — hernia (none); genital — epididymo-orchitis (normal); other — mesenteric ischaemia, shingles

'This needs hospital today. Stop food and drink, a drip for fluids, a small tube through the nose into the stomach to take the pressure off, something for pain and nausea, bloods and an X-ray of the abdomen — erect and supine — then a CT, and the surgical team will see you. Many settle without an operation; if the bowel is being strangled we operate.' · harder variant: vomiting + no flatus + a week of 'constipation' = obstruction; a tender irreducible groin lump = strangulated hernia — emergency, not a clinic letter · rural → MedSTAR if strangulation suspected

★ 'James, before I tell you what I think, I want to be honest that there's a limit to what I can be sure of over the phone, because I can't examine you. From what you've told me I have two concerns. That means either you're very dehydrated, or your kidneys have stopped working properly — and the blood pressure tablet you've kept taking can make that worse when you're dehydrated. back.dx: Hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by a return to alcohol (beer cans hidden in the cupboard) and constipation — a few weeks of fluctuating, worsening forgetfulness (glasses, whether she's eaten; recognises him), day–night sleep reversal, intermittent confusion, in a woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis who has stopped specialist follow-up and may not be taking her tablets; also easy bruising, an enlarging abdomen (ascites), poor intake; no fever, no jaundice, no bleeding, no oliguria. Two differential groups: (1) other cirrhosis complications — spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatorenal and hepatopulmonary syndromes, variceal bleeding; (2) other causes of confusion in an older person — infection (chest/urine), medications/withdrawal, intracranial (subdural after a fall, stroke, tumour), dementia (Alzheimer's, Lewy body), electrolytes/glucose. Usually treatable and often reversible once the trigger is corrected: lactulose, assessment (bloods, abdominal examination, ascitic tap to exclude SBP), alcohol support.

Never volunteers the beer cans — only to a direct alcohol question ('the notes say she stopped, so I won't ask' → silence). Volunteers the bigger tummy casually mid-answer. ~6 min voice cracks: 'is she losing her mind, doctor?'; end: 'she won't come in — what do I do?'. No examination. Findings by proxy: fluctuating forgetfulness with intact recognition, sleep reversal, intermittent confusion, easy bruising, abdominal distension (ascites), constipation, poor intake, low mood, no falls; non-adherence, lost to follow-up; hidden alcohol

Hepatic encephalopathy: West Haven grades 1–4 (sleep reversal/subtle → lethargy/disorientation → somnolence/confusion → coma); asterixis, fetor; ammonia not required for diagnosis. Six precipitants: alcohol, infection (SBP, UTI, chest), medications (sedatives, opioids, diuretics), constipation, GI bleeding, dehydration/electrolytes (also hypokalaemia, TIPS, HCC). Treatment: identify/treat the trigger; lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day; rifaximin for recurrence VERIFY; avoid sedatives; nutrition (don't restrict protein); thiamine. SBP: ascitic neutrophils ≥250/mm³ → IV ceftriaxone VERIFY, albumin, prophylaxis. HCC surveillance 6-monthly USS ± AFP. Standard drink 10 g; NHMRC ≤10/week. Cirrhosis follow-up: 6-monthly, varices screening, vaccinations

I understand this may be shocking — I wish I had better news' → water, tissues, silence → 'my team and I are here to support you' · history — ★ four cancer questions: when diagnosed (2 y), treatment (operation; told no chemo/RT), ★ follow-up (never went back — say it back without blame), complications · red flags: weight (6 kg), appetite, lumps, tiredness, cough, bone pain · liver: jaundice (eyes a bit yellow), itch, dark urine, pale stools · ★ 'do you have enough support at home?' ★ 'Can you tell me a little more about yesterday — what were you told?' → 'something in my liver; they said metastasis — what does that actually mean?' → ★ 'Metastasis means a cancer that started in one part of the body has spread to another part. In your case I think it is most likely that the bowel cancer you were treated for has spread to your liver.' → [quiet] → ★ 'Before we go further, would you like anyone to be with you while we talk about this? Its purpose would be to slow things down and keep you feeling better for longer.' → 'is palliative care giving up?' → 'No — it's active care focused on you living as well as possible for as long as possible.'

★ Step 4 — plan ahead: 'I'd also recommend we make an advance care directive — a document recording what treatment you would and wouldn't want — and that you choose someone as your substitute decision-maker in case there comes a time when you can't tell us yourself. Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses
time: 8 min. Vitals · intro, open → 'just here for my results' → ★ the bridge: 'I do have them and I'll go through them — before I do, may I ask a few questions so the results make more sense? then we'll look at them together' · symptoms: jaundice, itch, dark urine, pale stools · red flags: weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness, FHx cancer · ★ alcohol done properly: 'do you drink?' → 'a drink most nights — restaurant, goes with the job' → ★ 'what do you drink, roughly how much on those nights, how many nights a week?' → a bottle of wine, every night → ★ 'how long at that level?' → 20 years → ★ convert aloud without judgement: 'a bottle is about 7–8 standard drinks, so roughly fifty a week; the recommended maximum is ten — I'm not saying that to make you feel bad, it's directly relevant to the result' · ABP FIT NO SEX: antibiotics, transfusions/tattoos/piercings/IVDU/travel/food, occupation/needle-stick, sexual, ★ regular/OTC/herbal/gym supplements · fatty-meal pain, operations · ★ fever · PEFE named: jaundice, cachexia, scratch marks, oedema, ★ stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema); temperature; abdomen — distension, scars, tenderness, ★ hepatomegaly/splenomegaly, ★ shifting dullness; dipstick bilirubin → all normal · results explained: enzymes leak when the liver is irritated — mildly up; ★ one more than twice the other = alcohol · alcoholic hepatitis → cirrhosis if continued; ★ largely reversible now · three reasons · DDx: fatty liver, viral B/C, drugs/herbal, autoimmune, iron/copper, gallstones, cancers · ★ don't stop suddenly alone — supported withdrawal, thiamine, bloods, USS, review 2 weeks, safety-net, 'how do you feel about it?'

back.dx: Alcoholic hepatitis (alcohol-related liver disease, early) — asymptomatic 40-year-old restaurant owner drinking a bottle of wine every night for ~20 years (≈7.7 SD/night ≈ 54/week vs NHMRC ≤10), with a mild transaminase rise (<5× ULN) and AST:ALT ≈2.4 (>2 favours alcohol), raised GGT, normal examination (no stigmata, no hepatomegaly, no ascites, no jaundice). Three reasons: amount and duration; exclusion of viral risk factors, medications, gallbladder symptoms, travel, family history; the test pattern — mild rise with ratio >2 (a viral hepatitis would give a far larger rise). Still test: hepatitis B/C serology, iron studies, autoimmune screen, lipids/glucose, USS; stage with FIB-4 ± elastography. Largely reversible if the alcohol stops — supported reduction (withdrawal can be dangerous after 20 years), thiamine, brief intervention, review in a fortnight. Hidden agenda: his wife has been saying he drinks too much.
plan: 'May I have his vital signs?' → normal · 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with James? how can I help?' → 'just here for my blood results' → ★ 'thank you for coming in for them. I do have your results here and I will go through them with you. Before I do, may I ask a few questions so the results make more sense when we get to them? Then we'll look at them together.'
Symptoms: yellowing of skin/eyes, itching, dark urine, pale stools → none · red flags: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness (works 14-hour days), FHx bowel/liver/pancreas/stomach cancer → none

★ 'Do you drink alcohol?' → 'a drink most nights — I own a restaurant, it goes with the job' → ★ 'that's helpful — can I ask a bit more precisely: what do you drink, roughly how much on those nights, and how many nights a week?' → 'if I'm honest, a bottle of wine, most nights — probably every night' → 'thank you for being straight with me — that helps a great deal' → ★ 'and how long have you been drinking at that sort of level?' → 20 years · ★ 'so that we're working with the same picture: a bottle of wine is about seven to eight standard drinks, so that's roughly fifty in a week. The recommended maximum for a healthy adult is ten a week. I'm not saying that to make you feel bad — it's directly relevant to the result I'm about to show you.' → 'I didn't realise it added up like that' · morning shakes/sweats, previous attempts to cut down, CAGE

ABP FIT NO SEX: recent antibiotics · transfusions, tattoos, piercings, injected drugs, travel, unusual food · occupation, needle-stick risk · sexually active, condoms (married, monogamous) · ★ regular medications including over-the-counter, herbal or gym supplements (none) · fatty-meal pain, operations (none) · ★ fever or chills (no) · concerns → 'my wife says I drink too much — is that what this is?'

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — jaundice, cachexia, scratch marks, oedema, ★ any stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider naevi or palmar erythema · vital signs, particularly temperature · abdomen — inspection for distension and scars; superficial and deep palpation for tenderness and masses, specifically ★ hepatomegaly and splenomegaly; percussion for ★ shifting dullness; auscultation · office test — urine dipstick for bilirubin' → no jaundice, no stigmata, afebrile, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no shifting dullness, dipstick normal → 'the examination is normal, which is reassuring'

★ Results: 'Let me show you what we found. We measured your liver enzymes — chemicals that leak out of liver cells when the liver is irritated. Yours are up, but only mildly. There's a second thing I look at: the relationship between two of those enzymes. In your case one is more than twice the other, and that particular pattern is very characteristic of alcohol. The condition is alcoholic hepatitis — inflammation of the liver caused by drinking. In the long run, if the inflammation continues, it leads to scarring — cirrhosis — and at that point the liver stops working properly. The important part is that at this stage it is largely reversible if the alcohol stops.' · 'is my liver damaged?' → 'a warning rather than a catastrophe; at the stage you're at, largely reversible — that's genuinely good news' · ★ three reasons: amount and duration; the other causes ruled out; the pattern — mild rise with ratio above two, where a virus gives a far larger rise

DDx: 'I'll test for them — fatty liver from cholesterol and weight can look identical on this test; viral hepatitis B and C; medications including over-the-counter and herbal; autoimmune inflammation; inherited conditions such as iron overload or a copper problem; gallstone disease and blocked drainage tubes; and cancers of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas — though no weight loss and no family history' · ★ 'the most useful thing I can offer today is help to stop. Because you've been drinking heavily for a long time, I don't want you to stop suddenly on your own — withdrawal can be dangerous. Let's plan it together, and I can involve a service that supports people through it.' → thiamine, bloods (hepatitis B/C, iron studies, autoimmune screen, lipids, glucose, FBE/platelets, INR), USS, review in a fortnight · ★ safety-net: yellow, tummy swelling, bruising/bleeding, vomiting blood/black stools, confusion → sooner · 'how do you feel about what we've discussed?' → 'I can try — hard with the restaurant' → practical plan; summary

DDx: PID (previous chlamydia, tender exam — stays on the list), appendicitis (no migration, not off food, special tests negative), ovarian cyst torsion/rupture, UTI/stone (no burning, dipstick clear), hernia. 'Each month an egg grows inside a small sac on the ovary. Around day 14 that sac bursts to release the egg, and a little fluid and blood escape into the tummy — in some women that stings for a day or two. That is mid-cycle pain. If the egg is fertilised it should travel down the tube and settle in the womb. If it settles in the tube instead, that is an ectopic pregnancy.'

Version B (Mittelschmerz — LMP exactly 14 days ago, regular 28-day cycle, two previous identical self-limiting episodes, mild pain settling with rest and paracetamol, no vomiting): 'The most likely explanation is mid-cycle pain — Mittelschmerz — pain from releasing an egg: your last period was exactly 14 days ago, which is when the egg is released; the pain is mild and settles with rest and simple painkillers; you've had the same thing before and it went away; and the warning signs are all absent. But I want to be careful: the single most important thing in any woman with lower tummy pain is to be sure she is not pregnant, so if I could do one test today it would be a urine pregnancy test. If that's negative and it settles over the next day or two as before, no further tests are needed.' / Ruptured-ectopic variant (pale, tachycardic, shoulder-tip pain): 'two large-bore cannulae, fluids, cross-match, call the surgical or gynaecology team — and in a country hospital, MedSTAR' — say the sequence aloud; the history no longer matters

USS malignant features: wall >3 mm, thick septations, solid/papillary components, bilateral, ascites, Doppler flow; RMI = U × M × CA-125 (M 1 premenopausal, 3 postmenopausal; refer >200 VERIFY); CA-125 raised in only ~half of early-stage disease — not a screening test; shifting dullness detects ~1.5 L. Management: gynaecological oncology MDT, CT C/A/P, surgical staging/debulking ± platinum chemotherapy; genetic testing (BRCA) with implications for family; no percutaneous biopsy of a resectable ovarian mass (spillage/upstaging); image-guided biopsy of omental/peritoneal disease only under specialist direction when neoadjuvant chemotherapy is planned

back.dx: Ureteric colic — an obstructing stone (Version B: at the vesicoureteric junction, the last centimetre before the bladder): sudden 9/10 sharp right flank pain this morning, in waves, migrating to the groin, pacing, vomited once, now improved; stinging, frequency, pink urine, urgency, some dribbling; father had stones twice; hot shed, drinks almost no water; afebrile. PEFE: settled, T 36.8, mild right-sided tenderness, no peritonism/mass, BS normal, right renal angle tender, groin and scrotum normal, dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace. Three reasons: flank-to-groin path, waves, blood in the urine. The fork: loin tenderness + haematuria could mean pyelonephritis — no fever, no nitrites, no leucocytes → no infection → not hospital today. Investigations: non-contrast CT KUB (site and size), urine MCS (no infection behind the block), UEC/eGFR (kidney function changes the plan). Management by size: ≤5 mm — home, NSAID first (± opioid), antiemetic, tamsulosin, strain the urine, normal fluids (don't force), review 2–3 days; >7 mm — urology (ureteroscopy + laser for a low stone, ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving). Long term: 2.5–3 L/day, low salt, normal calcium/dairy, stone analysis, metabolic work-up. Hidden agenda: uncle died of bladder cancer at 58.
plan: 'I'm Dr —; am I speaking with James? I'm glad it has eased. I'll ask a series of questions to work out what caused it.' · 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs, in particular his temperature?' → afebrile, stable

★ 'Where exactly did it start — point with one finger? … And where is it now?' (high right flank → right groin) · 'how bad at its worst, out of ten? (9) sharp, dull, cramping? (sharp, stabbing) when did it start — suddenly? (2 h ago, instant) ★ there all the time, or coming and going in waves? (waves) travel — back, groin, testicles? (groin, top of the leg) anything better or worse — moving, lying still, eating? painkillers?' (nothing; couldn't sit still; two Panadol did nothing)
GI: nausea/vomiting (once), appetite (off), bowels, bloating/wind · ★ 'and have you had any fevers, chills or shaking episodes?' → no → 'good — that matters more here than you'd think'

★ Pivot: 'the way you've described that — one side, coming in waves, travelling to your groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks next.' → 'burning or stinging? (a bit) passing urine more often? (a lot) ★ any blood — pink, red or tea-coloured?' → 'pink this morning — that's really why I came' (tense) → 'thank you for telling me — important, we'll come back to it' · 'dribbling at the end, trouble starting? sudden urges you can't hold? up at night? passing normal amounts? ★ have you, or anyone in your family, ever had a kidney stone?' (dad, twice, about my age)

'Two quick ones — yellowing of the eyes or skin, pale stools, cramping after fatty food? any lump in your groin, or pain/swelling in your testicles?' (no) · if the clock allows: smoking (10/day), alcohol, meds/allergies, gout/high calcium, operations/kidney surgery, one kidney?, ★ 'how much fluid do you drink in a day?' ('hardly any water — hot in that shed') · ★ 4:00 HARD STOP: 'before I examine you — was there something in particular you were worried this might be?' → [pause] 'my uncle died of bladder cancer at 58 — when I saw the blood I thought, that's it' → ★ 'thank you for telling me. That must have been a frightening morning. I can't promise you anything before I've examined you and done a scan, but I will tell you honestly what I think, and we will not leave that question hanging.'

★ Examiner: 'general appearance — distress, restlessness, dehydration, pallor, jaundice · vital signs, temperature first · full abdominal examination — inspection for distension and scars; palpation superficial then deep for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound, organomegaly and any pulsatile mass; percussion for tenderness and a distended bladder; auscultation for bowel sounds and renal bruits · inguinal region, external genitalia, digital rectal examination · ★ as a special test — renal angle tenderness on both sides · ★ as an office test — a urine dipstick' → uncomfortable but settled; T 36.8; abdomen soft, mild right-sided tenderness, no guarding/rebound, no mass, BS normal; right renal angle tender; groin/scrotum normal; dipstick blood ++, nitrites −, leucocytes −, protein trace

★ 'James, I think you have what we call a ureteric colic — most people say a kidney stone. A small stone has formed in your kidney and started moving down the narrow tube that carries urine to your bladder. It presses on the wall of that tube and blocks it, and that is what causes the pain. Three things point to it: where the pain is — it started in your flank and travelled toward your groin, exactly the path that tube takes; it comes in waves, which is typical; and there's blood in your urine, which happens as the stone scrapes its way down.' · ★ discriminating sentence: 'I also want to be clear about something. You're tender over your kidney and there's blood in your urine, and those can suggest a kidney infection. But you have no fever, and your dipstick shows no nitrites and no white cells, so there's no sign of infection — and that's important, because a stone with an infection would mean hospital today.' · ★ the cancer worry: 'I can't rule anything out until the scan is back, and I won't pretend otherwise. But blood in the urine with this exact pattern of pain, at forty, with your father's history, points strongly to a stone. The scan will settle it.' · DDx by group: kidney/bladder — pyelonephritis, less likely a growth; liver/gallbladder (right-sided) — gallstones, inflammation, hepatitis; bowel — appendicitis, inflammation, rarely a growth; groin/testicle — hernia, torsion/epididymitis (excluded); the main abdominal blood vessel — very unlikely at forty

★ 'Three tests. One, a special CT scan of the kidneys, ureters and bladder without dye — the best test we have; it shows me where the stone is and how big. Two, your urine to the laboratory for culture, because I want to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage. Three, a blood test — UEC — to check your kidney function, because if the kidney is struggling that changes what I recommend.' (pushed: FBE/CRP if infection suspected, cultures if febrile, calcium/urate if recurrent; ultrasound if pregnant) · ★ safety-net: 'come straight back, or go to the emergency department, if you get a fever or shakes, if the pain becomes uncontrollable despite the tablets, if you stop passing urine, or if you're vomiting so much you can't keep fluids down' · analgesia now (NSAID) · summary: 'sudden severe colicky right pain, flank to groin, blood in the urine, no fever — most likely a kidney stone on the move; scan, check for infection and kidney function, then decide together how to get it out. What questions do you have?' ('how long? work? will it happen again?')

'I have your scan here — let me take you through what it shows, then what it means, then what we do' · ★ orient: 'this is a slice through your lower tummy, looking from your feet upward; these bright white shapes either side are your hip bones; this big grey circle in the middle is your bladder' → 'two narrow tubes carry urine from your kidneys into the bladder — the ureters. This small bright dot is a stone, sitting in one of those tubes right where it joins your bladder — the vesicoureteric junction, or simply the last centimetre before the bladder' · dx: 'a kidney stone on the move — I can see it, and your story fits exactly' · ★ the fork before 4:15: 'what we do next depends on how big the stone is. But before any of that, two things: I need to be certain there's no infection sitting behind the blockage — urine for culture; a stone and an infection together is the one combination that means hospital the same day. And a blood test for kidney function, because that changes what I recommend.' · ★ small (≤5 mm): home — NSAID first (ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food / indometacin 100 mg PR), oxycodone 5 mg if inadequate, ondansetron, tamsulosin 400 mcg daily (light-headed on standing — get up slowly) VERIFY, ★ strain the urine and catch the stone, ★ drink normally — don't force water, review 2–3 days · ★ large (>7 mm): urology — ureteroscopy + laser (suits a low stone), ESWL, PCNL for large renal stones, stent if the kidney needs relieving; analgesia and tamsulosin meanwhile · long term: 2.5–3 L/day especially in the heat, low salt, ★ keep dairy/calcium normal ('cutting calcium out makes stones more likely'), stone analysis, blood/urine tests · safety-net · 'how big is it?' → 'the report doesn't give a measurement and I'm not going to guess from the picture — so here are both possibilities'

Variant 1 (T 38.7, rigor, HR 118, BP 96/58, nitrites + leucocytes +): ★ 'This changes things completely — an obstructing stone with evidence of infection is an infected obstructed kidney, a urological emergency. James, the picture has changed: a stone blocking the tube with signs of infection behind it; antibiotics alone will not fix it — the blockage has to be relieved. Hospital today: IV fluids, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, urgent urological decompression — a stent up the tube or a drain through the back into the kidney — and from here that means MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33.' / Variant 3 ('just give me the Endone'): 'I'm not going to leave you in pain. The most effective drug for this particular pain is actually an anti-inflammatory, so I'll start there; if that isn't enough I'll add something stronger — a short course, and you must not drive or operate the forklift on it.' / Variant 4 (24 weeks pregnant): ultrasound not CT; paracetamol ± opioid, no NSAIDs; obstetrics + urology early; UTI commoner and more serious VERIFY / Variant 5 (solitary kidney, anuria, creatinine 210): 'size is irrelevant — an obstructing stone in a solitary kidney with a rising creatinine needs urology today for decompression.'

The nurses tell me you haven't passed water since your operation.' → 'bursting, nothing happens' → 'that is a horrible feeling and I'm sorry you've been sitting with it. Can I explain what I think is going on, go through the risks, and then you decide? ★ Is there anything worrying you before I start?' → brother's nursing-home catheter infection → 'thank you for telling me — I want to come back to that properly at the risks'

Indication: 'your bladder has filled up but can't empty. That's very common after bowel surgery — the anaesthetic, the strong pain relief you're pressing, and lying flat all switch off the signal that lets the bladder squeeze. The scan shows nearly 800 mL — about three cups. If we leave it, the bladder muscle can be stretched and damaged, and the pressure can back up to the kidneys.' · 'can I just have another go, standing?' → 'reasonable — standing genuinely helps some people. My honest view: at three cups and eight hours, waiting isn't safe, and the longer we leave it the harder it is for the bladder to recover. Better pain relief and fifteen minutes at the sink with the tap running — but if nothing comes, I'd want to drain it. Could you live with that?' → 'let's just do it'

'A catheter is a soft, thin, flexible tube — about the thickness of a drinking straw. It goes in through the opening at the tip of the penis, along the water pipe, and into the bladder, so the urine drains into a bag. A tiny balloon near the end is filled with a little sterile water once it's inside so it can't fall out. You stay awake; the only anaesthetic is a numbing jelly.' · ★ 'To do it I need to uncover you from the waist down — only for the minute or two it takes, with a sheet over you the rest of the time. Curtain and door closed. I'd also like one of the nurses in the room with us — routine for this, there for your comfort as much as mine. Would you prefer a male or a female nurse? Is there anyone you'd like asked to step out?' → male; wife outside → 'I'll ask her myself so it doesn't come from you'

★ Contraindication screen: 'a few quick safety questions. Any injury to your pelvis or the area between your legs — a fall, a straddle injury? Any blood at the tip? Ever had a catheter before, or an operation on the prostate or the water pipe? Ever told the water pipe is narrowed? Any allergies — latex in particular? And has anything changed in the feeling around your bottom or in your legs since the anaesthetic?' → no to all (excludes urethral injury and cauda equina aloud)

★ Risks and alternatives: 'the common things — it can sting going in, a little blood in the urine for a day, a feeling of needing to go even though the bladder is empty. The one I most want you to know about is infection — the risk climbs for every day the tube stays in, so we check every morning whether it can come out. Less commonly it can graze the water pipe. Rarely people react to the material. And occasionally it won't pass — then I stop and ask the urology team rather than force it. The alternatives are to wait a bit longer with better pain relief and privacy, or, if it can't go in, a tube through the skin above the pubic bone by the specialists. Doing nothing isn't safe at this volume.' · brother → ★ 'that's real, and it's the risk I'd worry about most too — nursing-home catheters stay in for months; yours: sterile insertion, a sealed drainage system, a review every morning, out the moment you're walking — a day or two, not weeks' · ★ teach-back: 'if you were telling your wife what we're about to do, what would you say?' → 'tube to drain the bladder, small infection risk, out in a day or two' → 'exactly. Any questions? ★ Are you happy for me to go ahead? Thank you — I'll write in your notes that we've discussed the reasons, the risks and the alternatives, that a nurse was present, and that you agreed.'

Steps — 'three parts: getting everything ready, passing the tube, finishing up; I'll talk you through and you can stop me' · (1) Ready: clean the trolley, collect, check every packet sealed and in date; clean hands, apron, gloves; open a sterile pack — 'the inside of that wrapper becomes a clean working surface nothing unsterile is allowed to touch'; drop in the tube, bag, syringe, cleaning fluid without touching; clean hands again, sterile gloves · paper sheet with a small opening; hold the penis with a swab, ease the foreskin back, clean around the opening with sterile salty water, fresh swab each time, working outwards; ★ numbing jelly into the opening, pinch closed, ★ wait three to five minutes — deliberate

(2) Passing: 'hold the penis upright at a right angle with a little stretch — straightens the water pipe; feed the tube in slowly. About two-thirds of the way there's a muscle ring guarding the bladder; when I reach it I lower the penis towards your toes with steady, gentle pressure until it slips past. Pressure, not pain. I never force it' ('if it doesn't go?' → 'I stop and ask urology — forcing is how the pipe gets damaged') · ★ 'I push the tube all the way in, right up to where it splits in two, even after urine starts coming — because the little balloon sits back from the tip, and if I blew it up too early it would be inside the water pipe. Once I can see urine draining, and only then, I fill the balloon with sterile water — the exact amount is printed on the tube, about two teaspoons. Then pull back gently until it sits snugly.' · (3) Finish: closed drainage bag below the bladder; ★ 'I make sure the foreskin is pulled back forward — if it's left back it can swell'; tape to the thigh with slack; clean up and cover; measure and chart the volume; daily review — out once walking and off the morphine, then a trial without it; safety-net: fever/shakes, back pain, no urine in the bag for four hours, heavy bleeding → nurses

★ Equipment: 'this one — a two-way Foley catheter: two ports at the funnel end, one to drain and one to fill the balloon. The three-way beside it has a third channel for washing the bladder out — only for heavy bleeding with clots or after prostate surgery; Mr Whitfield has simple retention with clear urine, so two-way. ★ Fourteen French — French is the circumference in millimetres, so a little under 5 mm across; 12–16 is the adult male range and 14 is the routine choice for clear urine — the smallest that drains reliably; bigger causes more urethral trauma without draining clear urine faster; the green funnel confirms the size. From the pack: sterile drape as the working surface, gallipot for sterile sodium chloride, gauze swabs and plastic forceps for cleaning, the fenestrated drape. I add sterile gloves, apron and eye protection, a 2% lignocaine gel syringe, ★ a 10 mL syringe of sterile water — not saline, which crystallises in the inflation channel so the balloon may not deflate — a closed drainage bag and a securing device. I confirm the balloon volume printed on the catheter, and check the expiry date and integrity of every package before opening.' · 'why not bigger?' → 'size is chosen by what has to pass through the lumen, not the size of the patient' · close: 'I'll get the nurse and the trolley. If at any point you want me to stop, say stop and I stop.'

★ 'A two-way Foley, fourteen French … The three-way has a third channel for irrigation, which I'd use only for heavy haematuria with clots or after prostate surgery.' / ★ 'Ten millilitres of sterile water — not saline. Saline can crystallise inside the inflation channel, and then the balloon may not deflate when we come to remove the catheter.' / 'Size is chosen by what has to pass through the lumen, not by the size of the patient.'

Variants: refuses with capacity ('one more hour on my own') → 'It's your decision and I'll respect it. Can I tell you what worries me about waiting, then we agree a time limit? If nothing has come by six, will you let me drain it? I'll write down that we've discussed this and what you decided.' / blood at the meatus after a ladder fall → 'I'm not passing a tube through the water pipe: that spot of blood suggests the pipe itself may be injured and a tube could make it worse. I'll get urology now — they may drain the bladder through the skin above the pubic bone and do a dye X-ray of the pipe first.' / Version B (explain to a medical student — jargon permitted): 'aseptic non-touch technique; meatal cleaning with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride, single stroke per swab, working outwards; instil 2% lignocaine gel, occlude, dwell 3–5 min; insert to the hub — the balloon lies proximal to the tip — confirm urine, then inflate with the labelled volume of sterile water; reposition the prepuce.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitfield, 55; hemicolectomy this morning, PCA; heavy bursting suprapubic pressure 6/10, constant urge; polite, gruff, embarrassed, avoids eye contact at the genital mention; three agendas in order — fix the pressure, one more try on his own, brother's catheter infection. Jargon → 'sorry doc, you've lost me'; 'I'm going to put in a catheter' unexplained → 'and what does that actually involve?'; no privacy/chaperone by ~4 min → 'you're not doing this here with the curtain open, are you?'; no risks → 'is it going to get infected? my brother's did'; never volunteers agreement unless asked; digs in if the extra hour is refused without an offer. Background if asked: up twice a night, slow stream for a year; never catheterised; no prostate surgery; no stricture; no trauma; no blood at the tip; legs normal ('why — should they not?'); no latex allergy; BP tablet only. Asks: 'will it hurt? be straight', 'will I be knocked out?', 'how long am I stuck with it?', 'how soon will I feel better?'

Findings given: bladder palpable, scan 780 mL; HR 96, BP 138/84, afebrile; pain 6/10. Trolley: two-way and three-way Foley catheters of various sizes, catheter pack, lignocaine gel, syringes, sterile water and saline ampoules, drainage bags, securing device, gloves

Numbers: 14 Fr default adult male (12–16); funnel colours 12 white, 14 green, 16 orange, 18 red, 20 yellow, 22 purple; Fr ÷ 3 = mm outer diameter; male catheter 40–45 cm; three-way 20–22 Fr for irrigation; balloon 10 mL sterile water (volume printed); lignocaine 2% gel 6–11 mL, dwell 3–5 min VERIFY; hand rub 20–30 s, soap and water 40–60 s; residual 780 mL — >1000 mL → hourly output, U&E; post-obstructive diuresis >200 mL/h × 2 h or >3 L/24 h VERIFY. CAUTI risk ~3–7%/catheter day; contraindications — suspected urethral injury (blood at the meatus, perineal haematoma, high-riding prostate), known stricture/false passage; relative — recent urethral/prostate surgery (contact the surgeon); alternatives — suprapubic catheter (urology), intermittent catheterisation; post-op retention risk — anaesthesia, opioids, anticholinergics, pelvic/anorectal surgery, BPH, IV fluids

Aftercare: closed system below bladder level, secure, daily necessity review, TWOC when mobile and off opioids (consider tamsulosin before TWOC if BPH VERIFY), measure residual, document; safety-net — fever/rigors, loin pain, no drainage 4 h, frank haematuria/clots, bypassing, pain · TIS 131 450 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)

setting: Telephone station — MO on duty, no patient, a desk and a phone; the ward nurse is calling. Four tasks, but resuscitation outranks the printed order: say 'I am treating this as sepsis' and give four instructions with a read-back before listing bloods. Cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within the hour (don't let specimens delay past ~45 min); ask what the penicillin allergy actually was before naming a drug. Automatic fails: accepting oral trimethoprim; never treating as sepsis; antibiotics before cultures with no caveat; never saying 'catheter-associated'; naming a drug without asking about the allergy.
stem: Mr Trevor Nolan, 60, known BPH, attended ED two days ago in acute urinary retention; catheterised, catheter removed yesterday. Today he has re-presented exhausted and feverish. T 39.5 · BP 80/50 · tachycardic · saturations low. The ward nurse has telephoned to discuss him.
tasks: Explain your diagnosis to the nurse
Discuss the investigations you require
Discuss your immediate management
Discuss the long-term management (may be held back — offer it once the first three are complete)
time: 8 min. 'Dr —, MO on duty — am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' · 'tell me in your own words what's happened, and his full observations — ★ respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output, allergies' (RR 26, sats 91%, HR 122, 'a bit vague', no urine since morning, penicillin allergy) · ★ dx in both halves, causally: 'a catheter-associated urinary tract infection — seeded when he was catheterised two days ago — that has progressed to sepsis; with 80/50 he may be in septic shock — I'll know once we see the response to fluid'; four reasons: instrumented 48 h ago, 39.5, hypotensive/tachycardic, hypoxic/drowsy · 'we've got oral trimethoprim' → ★ no — 'oral isn't enough, absorption unreliable in shock' · ★ sepsis door first: (1) oxygen to 92–96% (2) two large-bore cannulae (3) 500 mL crystalloid over 15 min then repeat BP and tell me the number (4) obs every 15 min + bladder scan (retention again?) → ★ 'can you read those four back to me?' · investigations in two buckets, before antibiotics: urine MCS — midstream or from the sampling port of a NEW catheter, never the bag; bloods — two sets of blood cultures separate sites, FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, coags, ★ VBG with lactate, BSL, group and hold; bedside — ECG, CXR ('I won't assume the urine is the only source') · 'no urine since morning' → bladder scan first (620 mL) → recatheterise, specimen from the new catheter, relieves obstruction · ★ 'before I name a drug — what does the chart say about allergies, and what actually happened?' (rash as a teenager → cephalosporin reasonable: IV ceftriaxone; or gentamicin + amoxicillin if no allergy; immediate reaction → no beta-lactams, gentamicin + advice) · within the hour, narrow at 48 h · continuous monitoring, hourly obs, strict fluid balance, hourly urine · ★ 'I'm walking down now and I'll call the registrar myself' · ring me if BP doesn't come up, more confused, stops passing urine · long term: 7 days (10–14 if slow), IV→oral when afebrile, narrow; the prostate — alpha blocker, 5-ARI, urology (TURP) — fewer catheters prevent the next one; no prophylactic antibiotics at insertion/removal · summary, 'anything worrying you I haven't covered?'

back.dx: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (catheterised 48 h ago for retention, removed yesterday — within the 48-hour definition) that has progressed to sepsis, possibly septic shock (T 39.5, BP 80/50 → MAP 60, HR 122, RR 26, SpO2 91% RA, vague/drowsy, no urine since morning — bladder scan 620 mL = retention again). Sepsis bundle by phone: oxygen 92–96%, two large-bore IVs, 500 mL crystalloid bolus over 15 min (repeat towards 20 mL/kg with reassessment), obs q15 min, bladder scan → recatheterise (aseptically) and take the urine from the new catheter's port; cultures (urine MCS, two sets blood cultures), FBE/UEC/CRP/LFT/coags/VBG+lactate/BSL/G&H, ECG, CXR; IV antibiotics within 60 min — gentamicin (weight/renal-dosed loading) + amoxicillin, or ceftriaxone if delayed-rash penicillin allergy; avoid all beta-lactams and seek advice if immediate hypersensitivity; escalate — walk down, call the registrar, ICU if not fluid-responsive. Long term: 7 days (10–14 if delayed response), IV→oral when afebrile, narrow at 48 h; treat the BPH (tamsulosin ± finasteride, urology/TURP) — fewer catheters is the single best prevention; no antibiotic prophylaxis at insertion/removal.
plan: Pick up, sit, pen ready: 'Hello, Dr —, medical officer on duty. Am I speaking with the nurse looking after Mr Nolan? May I take your name?' → Jane · 'I've read his notes — could you tell me in your own words what's happened, and give me his full observations, ★ including respiratory rate, conscious state, urine output and allergies?' → 39.5, 80/50, HR 122, RR 26, sats 91% air, 'a bit vague', little urine, penicillin allergy → 'thank you — particularly the respiratory rate and that he's vague'

★ 'Here is what I think is going on. Mr Nolan has a catheter-associated urinary tract infection — an infection seeded when he was catheterised two days ago — and that infection has progressed to sepsis. With a blood pressure of 80 over 50 he may already be in septic shock; I'll know that once we see whether he responds to fluid. Four things: instrumented 48 hours ago; temperature 39.5; hypotensive and tachycardic; hypoxic and drowsy — a systemic picture, not a bladder one.' · 'we've got oral trimethoprim — shall I start it?' → ★ 'No — oral is not enough and absorption is unreliable when someone is shocked.'

★ Sepsis door: 'Before we talk about tests, I am treating this as sepsis and I want a few things started now. One — oxygen, titrate to saturations of 92 to 96. Two — two large-bore cannulae. Three — 500 mL of balanced crystalloid over 15 minutes, then repeat his blood pressure and tell me the number (saline is fine if that's what you have). Four — observations every 15 minutes, and a bladder scan — I need to know whether he's in retention again. ★ Can you read those four back to me?'

★ Investigations, two buckets, before antibiotics: 'urine — a sample for microscopy, culture and sensitivity; midstream if he can, and if we recatheterise him, from the sampling port of the new catheter, never from the bag. Bloods — two sets of blood cultures from separate sites, FBE, UEC, CRP, LFT, coagulation, ★ a venous gas with a lactate, a blood sugar, and a group and hold. Bedside — an ECG and a chest X-ray, because I don't want to assume the urine is the only source' (cannula site, chest, wounds asked) · 'he hasn't passed urine since this morning' → 'then bladder scan first (620 mL). If there's urine he can't pass — catheterise, take the specimen from the new catheter; that also relieves the obstruction. Don't let the urine hold the antibiotics past about 45 minutes.'

★ 'Before I name a drug — the chart says penicillin allergy. What actually happened?' → 'a rash as a teenager' → 'that's a delayed rash, not an immediate reaction — a cephalosporin is reasonable: please prepare IV ceftriaxone at therapeutic dose; I'll confirm the choice and dose against the guideline when I'm with you. I want it in within the hour, and we'll narrow it when the cultures come back at about 48 hours.' (no allergy → gentamicin loading dose by weight/renal function + IV amoxicillin; 'lips swelled, couldn't breathe' → avoid all beta-lactams, gentamicin + on-call physician/ID advice, flag the allergy) · 'what dose?' → 'IV, empirical, therapeutic dosing, checked against the guideline' (never invent a number) · 'continuous monitoring, hourly observations, strict fluid balance and hourly urine measurement. ★ I am walking down now, and I will call the registrar myself. Ring me immediately if his blood pressure doesn't come up after that fluid, if he becomes more confused, or if he stops passing urine.' ('ICU?' → if not fluid-responsive — vasopressors; discuss with the registrar/ICU)

Long term, offered: 'once he's stable — two threads. The infection: seven days of antibiotics if he responds promptly, 10–14 if delayed; IV to oral once afebrile and tolerating intake; narrow when sensitivities return. The prostate — the part that stops it happening again: review anything worsening his outflow, an alpha blocker such as tamsulosin 400 mcg daily, finasteride or a combination if the gland is large; urology for a TURP or a newer endoscopic procedure if medical treatment fails or he re-obstructs. If we treat his prostate properly he shouldn't need catheterising again — and fewer catheters is the single best way to prevent this infection.' (no prophylactic antibiotics at insertion/removal/change) · ★ 'Thanks Jane. To summarise: oxygen, fluids, cultures, antibiotics within the hour, obs every 15 minutes. I'm on my way down and the registrar is being called. Anything you're worried about that I haven't covered?'

I will use gentamicin and take advice from the on-call physician or infectious diseases on the second agent before we give it. Please make sure the allergy is flagged properly in the chart.'

Pushes once early: offers oral trimethoprim (accepting it = fail, uncorrected). Pushes at the antibiotic: 'what dose?' — notes a confidently invented number. Anxious at 4 min if nothing started: 'is there anything you want me to start? he doesn't look well.' At 6 min if never asked: 'the notes say he's allergic to penicillin — does that matter?' 'A rash as a teenager' — or, if you've coped well, 'his lips swelled and he couldn't breathe'. Won't read back unless asked. Bladder scan if asked: 620 mL. Observations: T 39.5 · BP 80/50 (MAP 60; target ≥65) · HR 122 · RR 26 · SpO2 91% RA · vague · anuric since morning · bladder 620 mL. Catheter-associated = catheter in situ or removed within 48 h. Sepsis red flags: hypotension, RR ≥22, altered mentation (qSOFA ≥2), lactate >2, oliguria

Sepsis bundle (Sepsis Kills/SA Health VERIFY): oxygen to 92–96%, IV access, cultures (blood ×2 + urine + relevant sites) before antibiotics, lactate, IV antibiotics within 60 min, fluids 500 mL boluses to 20–30 mL/kg reassessing, hourly urine output, escalate (MET criteria); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if MAP <65 after fluid → ICU. Empirical urosepsis antibiotics VERIFY TG: gentamicin 4–7 mg/kg IV loading (renal/weight-adjusted, ideal body weight, single dose then review) + amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly; delayed non-severe penicillin rash → ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily acceptable; immediate hypersensitivity → no beta-lactams, gentamicin ± advice (e.g. ciprofloxacin); narrow at 48 h; duration 7 d (10–14 if slow/complicated); no post-treatment culture unless prostatitis; catheter removal if colonised; source control — relieve retention (recatheterise), exclude abscess/obstructing stone (USS/CT if not improving 48–72 h)

Long term BPH: tamsulosin 400 mcg daily; finasteride 5 mg daily (up to 6 months; halves PSA); combination; urology — TURP/laser/UroLift/Rezum; TWOC planning with alpha blocker; no antibiotic prophylaxis at catheter insertion/removal/change VERIFY. Telephone conduct: identify both ends, structured handover (ISBAR), closed-loop read-back, state you are attending and escalating, document · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 (rural)

stem: James Corrigan, 60, presents with erectile dysfunction for a number of months. T2DM diagnosed 5 years ago; MI 4 years ago. Medications: metformin, atenolol. HbA1c 8%. BP today 150/90.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the possible causes to him
Discuss further interventions
time: 8 min. Intro, confidentiality → 'things aren't working downstairs' → ★ acknowledge + normalise + warning shot: 'not easy to bring up; common; a medical problem; in most men we find the reason. I need to ask some quite personal questions — about erections, intercourse and masturbation — I ask every man with this problem; tell me if anything's uncomfortable' · ★ define and grade: how long (6 mo), every time, worse · 'getting and keeping an erection, or finishing sooner than you'd like?' · 'able to start intercourse, or does it go before that?' ★ Causes, without blame: 'James, erections depend on healthy blood vessels — blood has to flow in quickly and be held there; anything that damages small vessels affects it. First and biggest, your diabetes: your recent test was 8% where we aim for around 7, and missing doses will be part of that. Over years, high sugar damages the small blood vessels and later the nerves — the numbness in your feet tells me that damage has already started elsewhere. Second, one of your tablets — atenolol is known to cause this in some men. Third, your heart attack: the arteries that supply an erection are much smaller than the ones in the heart, so they often show trouble first. I also thought about hormones — a low testosterone level, which I'll test; thyroid; the penis itself — a curvature — or the prostate; nerve or spinal causes; and stress and mood, which are both a cause and a consequence. This is a physical, treatable problem — not a failing on your part.' · 'so it's my fault for skipping the tablets' → ★ 'No — the metformin upset your stomach, and that's a real side effect, not a character flaw. There are ways around it, and that's a problem we can solve together.'

setting: General practice counselling station. The history and examination are done; the dipstick is in the stem. Four tasks: diagnosis with reasons (say cystitis, say bladder, name and exclude pyelonephritis, urethritis and prostatitis even though nobody asked), investigations (urine MCS before the first tablet — every man, every time — plus how to collect it), immediate management (nitrofurantoin SEVEN days, not three or five; the penicillin allergy is a distractor), long-term (reason first, stage one only). Critical errors: antibiotics without MCS; no further investigation advised.

back.dx: Acute uncomplicated cystitis in a man — two days of dysuria and frequency, afebrile, no discharge, no flank/suprapubic pain, normal abdomen and DRE; dipstick nitrites positive + leucocytes + trace blood. Excluded aloud: pyelonephritis (no fever, vomiting, loin pain), urethritis (no discharge; one wife, fifteen years), prostatitis (DRE normal). Culture first (every man), treat today: nitrofurantoin 100 mg qid for 7 days (male regimen; not a penicillin — allergy irrelevant; trimethoprim 300 mg daily or cefalexin second line VERIFY), paracetamol, avoid urinary alkalinisers, normal fluids, review if no better at 48 h; same-day/ED for fever, rigors, vomiting, loin pain. Long term, staged: UEC + BSL today; renal/bladder/prostate ultrasound with post-void residual in 2–4 weeks; CT/urology only if abnormal or recurrent; no PSA during infection (falsely high). Hidden agenda: 'is this something I've caught? would I have to tell my wife?'
