★ 'The condition you have is called cystitis — a urine infection in the bladder. Bacteria have got into the bladder and inflamed the wall, and that inflammation causes the stinging and the need to go so often. Three reasons I'm confident: your symptoms; the urine test — leucocytes, white blood cells your immune system sends where there's infection, and nitrites, a chemical the bacteria themselves make — that's the important one; and the examination, which was normal.' · ★ 'I also considered and ruled out three things: pyelonephritis — infection travelled up to the kidney — you'd have a high temperature, vomiting, and pain in the back or side; urethritis — inflammation of the tube urine comes out through, usually sexually transmitted — the give-away is discharge, and you have none; and prostatitis — infection of the gland below the bladder — the internal examination was normal.'

★ The worry: 'which brings me to your question. What you have isn't usually sexually transmitted — but one condition can look similar, so with your permission I'd like to ask a few personal questions I ask everyone. Is that alright?' → 'just my wife, fifteen years; no discharge, no sores, never had an infection' → 'that, with no discharge, makes a sexually transmitted infection very unlikely — this isn't something you've caught. I'd rather have asked than assumed.'

★ 'One test I need today: another urine sample, to the laboratory for microscopy, culture and sensitivity — they look at it under the microscope, grow the bug to identify it, and tell us which antibiotic will kill it. In a man I do this every time, because urine infections are uncommon in men.' · 'another one? do I wait for the result?' → ★ 'No — you'll get the antibiotic today. But I need the sample before the first tablet, because once the antibiotic is in, the test can't tell us which bug it was.' · ★ how: 'a midstream sample — wash your hands; clean the tip of the penis, foreskin back if you have one; start passing urine into the toilet and let the first part go; then mid-stream hold the jar in the flow until about half full; finish in the toilet; close and label it; drop it at the pathology centre today. Does that make sense?'

★ 'I'm starting the antibiotic today — nitrofurantoin, four times a day for seven days; the seven days is the bit to remember, because men are treated longer than women. Take it with food; don't be alarmed if your urine goes brown — that's the drug, harmless. You mentioned a penicillin allergy — nitrofurantoin isn't a penicillin, so that's not a problem. If the culture shows the bug isn't sensitive, we'll change it. Paracetamol for the discomfort. ★ Leave the Ural-type sachets alone this week — they make the urine less acidic and that stops nitrofurantoin working properly. Drink normally, and don't hold on when you need to go.' ('can I drink on it?' — alcohol not contraindicated but sensible to limit; 'what if it doesn't work?' → next line) · ★ 'Two things bring you back sooner: no improvement after 48 hours; or fever, shakes, vomiting or pain in your back or side — that means it's gone up to the kidney, and I want you seen the same day or at the emergency department.'

★ Long term — reason before what: 'One more thing. Urine infections aren't common in men — in women they're routine; in men the plumbing normally protects you, so when one does happen it's worth a look, particularly if it happens again. I'm not expecting to find anything sinister. So, in stages: today, with the urine, your kidney function and blood sugar. In a few weeks, once this settles, an ultrasound of the kidneys, bladder and prostate — no needles, no radiation: you drink so the bladder is full, they scan, you empty it, they scan again to see what's left behind. Only if that shows something would we go further — a CT, or a urologist. Most men never need that. Does that sound reasonable?' · 'a scan? for a water infection? is it serious?' → ★ 'I can hear that, and most of the time this is straightforward. If something simple is behind it — a small stone, or the bladder not emptying fully — finding it now saves you having this again and again. No needles, no radiation. Only if it shows something would we go further. If you'd rather start with just the urine and blood test today, that's reasonable too — but I'd want to see you after the treatment either way. What would you prefer?' · 'dad had prostate trouble — can I have the blood test?' → 'not today — an infection pushes the result up; let this settle, then a proper conversation'

★ Recap: 'cystitis — an infection in the bladder. Urine sample today before the first tablet. Nitrofurantoin four times daily for seven days. Back if you're no better in 48 hours, sooner with fever or back pain. Bloods today, ultrasound in a few weeks, and I'll see you after the treatment. Anything I haven't covered?'

It's one we're required to notify to SA Health — routine, your name handled confidentially — and recent partners need to be told so they can be tested; that can be done anonymously, and I can do it for you.' / Variant C ('my wife can't find out — please'): 'That sounds like the thing you're most frightened of. Tell me what you're afraid would happen.' [listen] 'I won't contact anyone without your agreement. For some infections we do have to let partners know so they can be treated, but it can be done anonymously — she'd be told she's been in contact, not by whom. And whatever you decide, she needs testing for her own health. Let's work out together how that could happen.' (neither absolute secrecy nor threatened disclosure)
pefe: Role-player: James Petrakis, 57, shearing contractor, Yorke Peninsula; divorced 3 y, two sons in Adelaide, lives alone; smokes 10/day, weekend beers, BP tablet, no allergies; never tested for HIV, never an STI. Embarrassed, avoids eye contact, 'awkward'. Relaxes with the confidentiality/permission line; without it — one-word answers, 'is that really relevant?' once. Volunteers only 'something on my penis'; blisters only if asked what it looked like at the start; condoms 'most of the time' → 'not always, if I'm honest' only if pushed. Hidden (looking at the floor, ~5 min if concerns not asked): 'I've just started seeing someone properly — Marie — have I given her something?' and 'my brother had a thing cut off his face — is this cancer?'. Told herpes → 'is it curable?' — 'yes' accepted and marked down

Photo: multiple shallow ulcers, scalloped irregular margins, erythematous base, no induration, no raised everted edge (if already eroded — the history rescues you). T 37.6, tender bilateral inguinal nodes by history. Variant photos: indurated painless ulcer (syphilis); non-healing bleeding ulcer/mass (SCC)

Genital ulcer logic: painful — herpes, chancroid; painless — syphilis, SCC, warts, LGV (buboes); itchy — dermatitis, candida, scabies; nodes — herpes tender, syphilis non-tender rubbery, LGV buboes. Biopsy threshold: ulcer >4 weeks or failing treatment. Treatment VERIFY TG: first-episode herpes — valaciclovir 500 mg bd 5–10 days (or aciclovir/famciclovir); recurrences — episodic or suppressive therapy; early syphilis — benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g (2.4 MU) IM stat; LGV — doxycycline 100 mg bd 21 d; chancroid — azithromycin/ceftriaxone. Testing: lesion swab HSV PCR (+ syphilis PCR), first-pass urine (first 20 mL, ≥20 min since last void) NAAT chlamydia/gonorrhoea, syphilis serology (repeat at 6 and 12 weeks if early), HIV (repeat at window), hepatitis B ± C. Notifiable in SA: syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, HIV, donovanosis — herpes is not. Gonorrhoea causes discharge, not ulcers; LGV is a chlamydial serovar. Herpes counselling: asymptomatic shedding, disclosure to partners, condoms reduce but don't eliminate transmission, suppressive therapy reduces transmission ~50%, avoid sex during outbreaks, first-episode urinary retention (sacral radiculitis) and meningitis are the safety-net items; psychological support

Penile SCC: >50, uncircumcised, HPV, smoking, phimosis, lichen sclerosus; non-healing ulcer/mass, bleeding, hard inguinal nodes → biopsy + urology (Adelaide, PATS) · SA: SHINE SA · Adelaide Sexual Health Centre (Clinic 275) · ACCHS · letthemknow.org.au · TIS 131 450

setting: ED, regional SA hospital. Three tasks, eight minutes: focused history (3 min) → examination findings from the examiner → results card explained to the patient, then the plan. Timing discipline: history 3:00 · examination 1:30 · results 2:00 · plan 1:00 · summary 0:30. Single-item fail: asking to remove the pressure bandage. The station turns on a bloody gauze on the elbow when the bite is on the leg — name the drip/needle site in the bleeding question.
stem: Nick Tanner, 25, brought in by ambulance after a snake bite to the right calf on his property this afternoon. Pressure immobilisation bandage and splint applied; IV cannula in place. Alert and talking. T 36.8 · HR 96 · BP 122/76 · RR 18 · SpO2 98% · GCS 15.
Results card: INR 4.1 (0.9–1.2) · aPTT 62 s (25–35) · WCC 16.4 · Hb 141 · platelets 178 · CK 90 (<200) · Na 139, K 4.2, urea 5.1, creatinine 78 — normal.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (3 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
The examiner hands you the investigation results — explain them to the patient
time: 8 min. 'Before I start, could I have his vital signs and conscious state?' → 'stable — I'll take a focused history' · 'Hello Nick, I'm Dr —; I can see you've had a real fright — what happened?' → ★ honest reassurance without false comfort: 'you did exactly the right thing; you're in safe hands; quick specific questions, then examination, then your bloods' (never 'most bites are harmless') · the bite ×4: where exactly, ★ what time, ★ what did you do straight afterwards (bandage, still, 000; not washed/cut), did you see it — colour/size, one bite or more ('should we have brought it in?' → never go back for a snake; photo from a distance) · ★ four systems as headings — bite site: pain/swelling, groin tenderness · ★ clotting: new bruises/rash; 'bleeding from your nose or gums, blood in your urine — or oozing from the drip site or where they've put needles in?' → 'they took the drip out — it kept bleeding; that's the dressing on my elbow' → look, name it: systemic bleeding · nerves: headache/dizziness, ★ droopy eyelids/double vision, speech/swallowing/breathing · muscles: aching/weakness back, shoulders, thighs · kidneys: passed urine? colour? · collapse/faint; nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, sweating · 30 s: last tetanus (10 y — defer until clotting normal), ★ blood thinners, allergies, previous antivenom, PMHx/asthma/family bleeding, smoking/alcohol · ★ 'anything in particular you're worried about?' (uncle nearly died from a brown snake; truck to Adelaide tomorrow) · examiner: appearance/conscious state, bruising/petechiae, repeat vitals + postural, ★ bite site through the bandage window (fang marks, swelling, ooze) + ★ swab for the venom detection kit before cleaning, draining nodes, limb perfusion/compartments, ★ bleeding survey (cannula site, needle sites, gums, nose), ★ full neuro (cranial nerves — ptosis, eye movements, pupils; power, reflexes; single-breath count, head lift), CVS/resp/abdo, dipstick, BSL, ECG → say the cannula finding aloud; bandage stays on · results: four things venom does → INR (normal ~1, his 4 → why he bled), aPTT (different clotting factors, also high), WCC (reaction, not infection — no antibiotics), ★ normal CK and renal named and what they exclude, normal neuro · plan ×6: swab/VDK, antivenom (monovalent if identified, polyvalent if not) slowly with a doctor at the bedside — allergic reaction risk, bandage on until antivenom ready, observe ≥12 h with repeat bloods/fluids/analgesia, tetanus when clotting normal, ★ serum sickness warning · 'truck tomorrow?' → no · summary + first-aid reminder.

back.dx: Systemic envenoming with venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy after a probable brown snake bite (brownish, ~1.5 m; Yorke Peninsula) — bitten ~3 pm on the right calf, textbook first aid (pressure immobilisation bandage, splint, kept still, 000, nothing washed/cut), two puncture marks with mild swelling, tender right inguinal nodes, oozing from the left antecubital cannula site (systemic bleeding), queasy in the ambulance; no neurotoxicity (normal cranial nerves, power, single-breath count), no myotoxicity (CK 90, no myalgia), no renal impairment (creatinine 78, dipstick negative, normal-coloured urine); INR 4.1, aPTT 62, WCC 16.4 (venom reaction, not infection), platelets normal. Antivenom is indicated (laboratory evidence of systemic envenoming): venom detection kit swab from the bite site before cleaning; monovalent (brown) if identified, polyvalent (or tiger + brown) if not; one vial IV diluted over 15–30 min, doctor at the bedside, adrenaline drawn up, no routine premedication; bandage stays on until antivenom is ready at the bedside; observe ≥12 h with repeat coags/FBE/UEC/CK at 1 h after bandage removal, 6 h and 12 h; tetanus booster deferred until the coagulopathy resolves; serum sickness warning (4–14 days, oral prednisolone). No driving tomorrow.
plan: 'Before I begin, could I have the vital signs — BP, pulse, RR, saturations, temperature and conscious state?' → 122/76, 96, 18, 98%, 36.8, GCS 15 → 'haemodynamically stable, so I'll take a focused history' · 'Hello Nick, I'm Dr —, one of the emergency doctors. I can see you've had a real fright — can you tell me what happened?' → paddock, struck the leg, mate bandaged it, 000; 'am I going to be all right?' → ★ 'That sounds frightening, and you did exactly the right thing getting straight here. You're in safe hands — we will do everything necessary to look after you. I need to ask some quick, specific questions, then check a few things and go through your blood tests. Is that all right?'

The bite: 'where exactly did it bite you? (right calf above the ankle) ★ what time? (about 3 — two hours ago) ★ what did you do straight afterwards? (sat still, mate bandaged the whole leg, splinted, rang the ambulance — nothing washed, cut or sucked) → 'that was textbook first aid' · did you see the snake — colour, size? (glimpse; brownish; ~1.5 m) one bite or more?' · 'should we have brought it in?' → ★ 'No — never go back for a snake; that's how people get bitten a second time. A description or a photo from a safe distance is plenty.'

★ Four systems, headings aloud: 'the bite site — pain or swelling there, or in your groin?' (stings; groin tender) · 'your clotting — any new bruises or rash? ★ any bleeding from your nose or gums, blood in your urine — or any oozing from the drip site or where they've put needles in?' → 'they had to take the drip out — it kept bleeding; that's the bandage on my elbow' → [lean in, look] ★ 'thank you — that's very important. Bleeding from the drip site suggests the venom is already affecting the way your blood clots. I'll come back to that.' · 'your nerves — headache or dizziness? droopy eyelids or double vision? trouble with speech, swallowing or breathing?' (no) · 'your muscles — aching or weakness in your back, shoulders or thighs?' (no) · 'your kidneys — passed urine since? changed colour or gone dark?' (normal) · 'did you faint or nearly black out? nausea, vomiting, tummy pain, sweating?' (queasy in the ambulance)

30 s: 'last tetanus injection?' (school — ~10 y) · ★ 'any blood thinners — warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, aspirin — or regular medicines?' (none) · allergies; ever had antivenom? (no) · medical problems, asthma, family bleeding problems; smoking/alcohol · ★ 'before I move on — is there anything in particular you're worried about?' → 'my uncle nearly died from a brown snake when I was a kid' → 'thank you for telling me — I can see why you're frightened. We've got you here early, we have the antidote, and I'll keep you informed at every step.'

★ Examiner, box by box: 'general appearance and conscious state — alert or drowsy, pallor, sweating, bruising or petechiae anywhere · repeat vital signs incl a postural BP · ★ the bite site through the bandage window — fang marks, swelling, redness, oozing — and I would swab the site for the venom detection kit before anything is cleaned · draining lymph nodes — tender or enlarged · limb perfusion — distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, any tense compartment · ★ bleeding survey — the cannula site, previous needle sites, gums and nose · ★ full neurological examination — cranial nerves especially ptosis, eye movements and pupils; tone, power, reflexes and sensation upper and lower limbs; a single-breath count and head lift for respiratory muscle strength · cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination · office tests — urine dipstick, blood glucose and ECG' → alert, anxious, no rash; obs as given, no postural drop; two puncture marks right calf, mild swelling/redness, no ooze at the site; right inguinal nodes tender; perfusion normal, compartments soft; ★ left antecubital cannula site oozing, dressing blood-stained; neuro entirely normal; heart/chest/abdomen normal; dipstick negative, BSL 5.6, ECG sinus → ★ 'Thank you — oozing from the cannula site tells me this is systemic bleeding, not a local wound problem. That makes envenoming with a coagulopathy very likely. I'd keep the pressure bandage on until we have antivenom ready at the bedside.'

Results → ★ 'Nick, I have your blood results and I'd like to go through them one at a time — some are abnormal; stop me any time. Snake venom can affect four things: the clotting of your blood, your nerves, your muscles, and your kidneys. We test for all four. In your case, it's the clotting.' · ★ 'The first test is the INR — it measures how long your blood takes to clot. Normally it sits around one. Yours is four, so your blood is taking much longer than it should — and that's exactly why you bled from the drip site.' ('could I bleed anywhere? dangerous?' → 'it does mean a higher risk of bleeding, which is why you're staying with us and why we're starting the antidote — but we can treat it') · 'The aPTT is another clotting test — a different set of clotting factors — also high, the same picture. Your white cell count is up — white cells are part of your immune system, and the number often rises as a reaction to the bite; on its own it isn't a worry' ('infected? antibiotics?' → 'no — a reaction to the venom, not an infection; snake bites very rarely get infected and we don't routinely give antibiotics') · ★ 'Now the good news: the creatine kinase — the test for muscle damage — is normal, and your kidney tests are normal, so there's no sign of damage to your muscles or kidneys. Your examination was normal, so no sign the venom has affected your nerves either.'

★ Plan: 'One — we swab the bite to run through a venom detection kit, which tells us which type of snake. Two — because your clotting is affected, you do need the antivenom: if we identify the snake we use the specific antidote; if not, a broader one covering the main dangerous Australian snakes. Three — we give it slowly through the drip with a doctor at the bedside, because a small number of people have an allergic reaction, and we're ready for that. Four — the bandage stays on until the antivenom is ready at the bedside. Five — you stay here overnight, at least twelve hours, repeat bloods, fluids and pain relief, close watching. Six — you're due a tetanus booster; we'll give it once your clotting is back to normal — an injection into muscle could bleed at the moment. ★ And for later: in the week or two after antivenom some people get a flu-like illness — fever, rash, aching joints — serum sickness; treatable with a short course of steroid tablets, so come back if it happens.' · 'truck to Adelaide tomorrow?' → 'not tomorrow — overnight at least, clotting normal and feeling well before you drive; I'll give you a certificate' · ★ summary: 'a snake bite affecting your blood's clotting, muscles and kidneys fine, antivenom and overnight monitoring, then tetanus and follow-up. And next time — bandage firmly over the whole limb, keep still, ring triple zero, and don't go looking for the snake. Anything I've missed?'
ask: ★ 'Before I begin, could I have his vital signs and conscious state?' / ★ 'You did exactly the right thing coming straight in. You're in safe hands — we'll do everything necessary to look after you.' / 'Some of these questions will sound odd — they're the ones that matter most after a snake bite.'

★ 'Any bleeding from your nose or gums, blood in your urine, or oozing from the drip site or any needle site?' / ★ 'The bite was on your leg — can I ask what the dressing on your elbow is for?' / ★ 'Bleeding from the drip site tells me the venom is already affecting the way your blood clots.' / ★ 'Please never go back for a snake — that's how people get bitten a second time. A description or a photo from a safe distance is all we need.'

★ 'Snake venom can affect four things: your blood's clotting, your nerves, your muscles and your kidneys. We test for all four.' / ★ 'The INR measures how long your blood takes to clot. Normally it's about one; yours is four, so your blood is taking much longer than it should.' / ★ 'The aPTT checks a different group of clotting factors — it's also high, which fits the same picture.' / ★ 'Your white cell count is up as a reaction to the bite — it doesn't mean an infection.' / ★ 'The muscle test and the kidney tests are normal, so there's no sign of damage there.'

★ 'We'll swab the bite to find out which snake it was, so we can use the specific antivenom; if we can't identify it, we use a broader one that covers the main dangerous Australian snakes.' / ★ 'In the fortnight after antivenom, if you get fever, a rash and aching joints, come straight back — that's serum sickness and it's easily treated.'

Examiner challenge on premedication/indication → ★ 'I would give antivenom for clinical or laboratory evidence of systemic envenoming, without routine premedication, but fully prepared to treat anaphylaxis — and I'd confirm the approach with the clinical toxicologist through the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.' / Variant 1 (tiger snake — 'eyes heavy, everything doubling, thighs aching, urine like Coke'): 'the drooping and double vision mean the venom is affecting the nerves that control your eye muscles, and that can go on to the muscles you breathe with — I'm moving you somewhere we can watch your breathing closely and starting the antivenom now. The dark urine isn't blood — it's a protein released when muscle breaks down, and it can block the kidneys, so fluids through the drip and repeat kidney tests' → single-breath count and head lift, urgent antivenom, ICU early, MedSTAR / Variant 2 (well, wants to leave — 'tests normal, bus to catch'): 'I'm pleased your first tests are normal. The difficulty is that the effects can appear hours later — a normal test now doesn't tell us you're in the clear. We repeat at six and twelve hours; if all normal and you're well, you can go. I can't keep you against your will, but leaving now would be genuinely dangerous, and I'd be failing you if I didn't say so. Can we ring someone about the bus?' / Variant 3 (apixaban): 'two reasons to bleed rather than one — extra careful, hold the next dose, haematologist with the toxicologist'

stem: Liam Petrides, 19, first-year university student. Two weeks of sore throat, fevers and profound fatigue. Amoxicillin five days ago from another clinic; widespread itchy rash three days later, stopped. T 37.9 · HR 88 · BP 118/70. Looks exhausted.

Explain the diagnosis and results
Give management advice and answer questions
time: 8 min. 'Am I speaking with Liam? You look like you've had a rough couple of weeks. Results are back — a few questions first, then the results, then what happens next. ★ Before I start — what's worrying you most?' (exams in three weeks; 'allergic to penicillin now') · ★ two emergencies in 30 s: 'can you swallow your own saliva and drink normally? any noisy breathing at night?' · 'any pain in the upper left of your tummy, or at the tip of your left shoulder? any knock there?' · jaundice/dark urine · ★ the rash characterised: how long after the tablets (3 d), what/where (flat red itchy blotches, chest/back/arms), ★ lip/face swelling, wheeze, tight chest (no), ★ blistering, peeling, mouth/eye ulcers (no), still there (fading) · red flags: weight loss, drenching sweats, bruising/bleeding, other lumps · contacts (housemate sore throat) · ★ 'routine questions about sexual health — I ask everyone who presents like this, because a few infections look exactly the same: new partners recently? condoms?' (someone new three weeks ago, unprotected) · tattoos/piercings/IVDU · alcohol (few beers — more if out), sport (social footy — training Tuesday), lifting, uni/exams · dx: glandular fever — EBV — plain English · ★ results one at a time: atypical lymphocytes explained BEFORE he worries ('sounds alarming and it isn't'), mild transaminitis (no alcohol, recheck), ★ EBNA negative = current (appears 6–12 weeks) · ★ un-label the allergy: amoxicillin–EBV rash, not allergy; lifelong harm of the label; record it precisely; what to tell future doctors; allergy testing if ever critical · ★ spleen: no contact sport/heavy lifting ≥4 weeks from onset — reason (rupture), light exercise fine, warning signs (LUQ/left shoulder-tip pain, faint → ambulance, don't drive), ★ teach-back; hold under two pushes · fatigue honest (no date), no alcohol while LFTs up, transmission (saliva; no exclusion from uni), ★ certificate + special consideration/deferral · ★ HIV test offered as routine + STI screen; confidentiality; review 2 weeks; 'two things you'll remember?'

back.dx: Acute EBV infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) with an amoxicillin-associated exanthem — NOT a penicillin allergy — and mild transaminitis: two weeks of pharyngitis, fever, profound fatigue; lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes; ALT 180/AST 145; VCA IgM + / VCA IgG + / EBNA − (EBNA appears 6–12 weeks — its absence means current infection); GAS negative. Rash three days after amoxicillin — flat red itchy macules chest/back/arms, no urticaria, angio-oedema, wheeze, blistering or mucosal involvement, fading. Safety: airway fine (swallowing saliva, no stridor), no LUQ/shoulder-tip pain, no jaundice. Unprotected sex with a new partner three weeks ago → offer HIV (seroconversion mimics IM) and STI screening as routine. Management: un-label the allergy precisely on the record; no contact sport or heavy lifting for at least four weeks from symptom onset and not while exhausted (splenic rupture — usually someone who felt better and went back early), with shoulder-tip/faint warning and teach-back; honest fatigue timeline (throat/fever 1–2 weeks; exhaustion weeks to months; no treatment shortens it; pushing through prolongs it — graded return); no alcohol while LFTs deranged, recheck in 2 weeks; saliva transmission — no kissing/shared drinks while symptomatic, no exclusion from uni; medical certificate + special consideration/deferred exams; steroids only for airway obstruction, severe haemolysis or thrombocytopenia; not notifiable.
plan: 'Good morning, I'm Dr —, one of the GPs. Am I speaking with Liam? You look like you've had a rough couple of weeks. Your results are back and I can tell you what's going on — a few more questions first, then the results properly, then what happens next. ★ Before I start — what's worrying you most?' → 'exams in three weeks and I've done nothing; and the other doctor said I'm allergic to penicillin now' → 'I'll come to both — and I've got something useful to say about the penicillin'

★ Safety: 'can you swallow your own saliva and drink normally? any noisy breathing, especially at night?' (sore, manages; no) · 'any pain in the upper left of your tummy, or at the tip of your left shoulder? any knock or injury there?' (no) · 'any yellowing of your eyes, or dark urine?' (no)

★ The rash: 'how long after starting the tablets did it come up? what did it look like, and where? ★ any swelling of your lips or face, wheeze or tight chest? ★ any blistering, peeling, or ulcers in your mouth or eyes? is it still there?' → 3 days after; flat red itchy blotches — chest, back, arms; no swelling/wheeze; no blisters; fading

Red flags: weight loss, drenching night sweats, easy bruising/bleeding, lumps elsewhere (no) · 'anyone around you unwell?' (housemate sore throat) · ★ 'Can I ask some routine questions about sexual health — I ask everyone who presents like this, because a few infections look exactly the same. Any new partners recently, and do you use condoms?' → (awkward) 'someone new about three weeks ago — we didn't use anything' → 'thanks for telling me — useful, I'll come back to it' · tattoos, piercings, injecting (no) · alcohol (few beers weekends → 'a fair bit if we're out') · 'do you play sport — what kind? heavy lifting at work or the gym?' (social footy — training Tuesday) · 'how's this affecting uni — anything coming up?' (exams in three weeks)

★ 'The good news is we know what this is, and it isn't anything sinister. You've got glandular fever — infectious mononucleosis. It's caused by a very common virus, Epstein-Barr. Most people catch it at some point; as a small child you barely notice; catching it as a young adult gives you this — the throat, the fevers, the swollen glands, and above all the flattening exhaustion.' ('the kissing disease?' — yes, spread in saliva) · ★ results one at a time: 'your blood count shows a lot of lymphocytes — a type of white cell — and they look "atypical" down the microscope. That sounds alarming, and it isn't: it's the classic appearance of a body fighting this virus' ('atypical? sounds like cancer' → 'no — which is why I wanted to explain it rather than let you read it') · 'your liver tests are mildly raised — very common with glandular fever; the virus irritates the liver a bit; it settles, and it's why I'll ask you to lay off alcohol' ('my liver? I'm nineteen') · ★ 'the specific virus test confirms it: three parts — two positive, and one called EBNA which is negative. That negative one is the most useful, because EBNA only appears six to twelve weeks after you catch the virus — so its absence tells us this is current, not something from years ago' · throat swab: no strep

★ Un-label: 'Now the rash, because I gather you've been told you're allergic to penicillin — and I don't think you are. There's a well-recognised effect where people who have glandular fever and take amoxicillin come out in exactly this sort of widespread rash. It's caused by the infection, not by an allergy — it's so typical it can actually help make the diagnosis. Once the glandular fever has gone, you can almost always take penicillins normally. This matters more than it sounds: if "penicillin allergy" goes on your record, for the rest of your life you'd be given second-choice antibiotics — often less effective, more side effects, sometimes a drip instead of tablets. So I'm going to record it precisely as an amoxicillin rash in the setting of glandular fever, not a true allergy. If a doctor ever asks, say that rather than just "I'm allergic". If it's ever critical, an allergy specialist can test you properly.' ('so am I allergic or not? he was pretty definite' → 'almost certainly not, once this has passed')

★ Spleen: 'One part I need you to take seriously — the only genuinely dangerous bit. This virus makes the spleen swell — an organ under your ribs on the left. Enlarged, it's fragile, and a knock can rupture it: serious internal bleeding, emergency surgery. It's uncommon, but when it happens it's usually someone who felt better and went back early. So: no contact sport, no heavy lifting, nothing where you could take a hit to the abdomen, for at least four weeks from when this started — and I won't clear you while you're still this exhausted. Light exercise as you tolerate is fine.' → 'four weeks? training's Tuesday — it's only social' → hold: 'I know, and I'm sorry. Social footy still involves people running into you, and honestly you're too exhausted to play well anyway. Running and light gym as you tolerate is fine.' → pushes again → hold, same reason, offer a review at four weeks and a note to the club · ★ 'the warning: sudden severe pain in the upper left of your tummy, or at the tip of your left shoulder, or feeling faint — call an ambulance, don't drive yourself. Can you tell me back what you'd do?'

★ Four practical things: 'the tiredness — I'll be straight rather than optimistic: throat and fevers usually settle in one to two weeks; the exhaustion drags — several weeks for most, a few months for some; no treatment shortens it, and pushing through tends to prolong it; a gradual stepped return works best' ('give me a number' → weeks to months; no date promised) · 'alcohol: none while your liver tests are up — a few weeks at least, and I'll recheck' · 'passing it on: saliva — no kissing, don't share drinks, cutlery or a toothbrush while symptomatic; but you don't need to stay away from uni — it's shed for months, so isolating achieves nothing' · ★ 'exams: I can write a medical certificate with the dates and how it's affected you, and support special consideration or a deferred exam — would that help?' (relieved) · ★ 'One last thing — I ask this of everyone who presents the way you have; it isn't about anything you've told me. A small number of infections cause exactly this picture — fever, sore throat, swollen glands, a rash — and one is the early stage of HIV. Uncommon, very treatable when found early, a simple blood test; I'd like to include it when we recheck your liver — is that alright? And since you mentioned a new partner, sensible to check the others too. Everything stays confidential.' ('do you think I've got HIV?' → no — routine; 'can my parents find out?' → 'no — you're nineteen; it's your record and your result') · review 2 weeks, sooner if worse; 'what are the two things you'll remember?' → 'no footy four weeks; not actually allergic to penicillin'
ask: ★ 'You look like you've had a rough couple of weeks.' / ★ 'Before I start — what's worrying you most?' / ★ 'Can you swallow your own saliva and drink normally? Any noisy breathing at night?' / ★ 'Any pain in the upper left of your tummy, or at the tip of your left shoulder?' / ★ 'Any swelling of your lips or face, any wheeze, any blistering or peeling?'

★ 'Can I ask some routine questions about sexual health — I ask everyone who presents like this, because a few infections look exactly the same.' / ★ 'You've got glandular fever — infectious mononucleosis, caused by Epstein-Barr virus.' / ★ 'They look "atypical" down the microscope. That sounds alarming and it isn't — it's the classic appearance of fighting this virus.' / ★ 'EBNA only appears six to twelve weeks after you catch it — so its absence tells us this is current.'

★ 'I don't think you're allergic to penicillin.' / ★ 'That rash is caused by the infection, not by an allergy — it's so typical it can help make the diagnosis.' / ★ 'If a doctor ever asks, say it was a rash with glandular fever, rather than just "I'm allergic".'

★ 'No contact sport, no heavy lifting, for at least four weeks from when this started.' / ★ 'Sudden severe pain in the upper left of your tummy or at the tip of your left shoulder — call an ambulance.' / 'Can you tell me back what you'd do?' / ★ 'The exhaustion drags — weeks for most people, a few months for some. Pushing through tends to prolong it.'

★ 'I ask everyone with these symptoms, because one of the infections that looks exactly like this is early HIV.' / 'Do you think I've got HIV?' → 'No — it's routine; a positive glandular fever test doesn't rule anything else out, and the consequences of missing HIV early are enormous, whereas found early it's a manageable condition with a normal life expectancy.' / 'Can my parents find out?' → 'No — you're nineteen, it's your record and your result.'

Version B (grand final in three weeks — 'you have to clear me'): 'I understand what that means to you, and I'm not going to pretend this isn't a blow. But I can't clear you, and I'd be doing you harm if I did … it's the specific way young, fit people occasionally die from glandular fever, and it almost always happens to someone who felt better and went back early. What I can do: light running and non-contact conditioning as your energy allows; review at four weeks from onset; if symptom-free and well, we talk about a graded return; I'll write to your club so this isn't on you to explain. And if you play anyway — know the signs: sudden severe pain in the upper left of your abdomen or the tip of your left shoulder, or feeling faint — ambulance.' / Version C (can't swallow spit, easier sitting forward): 'that changes things and I need to act now — your tonsils are swollen enough to be narrowing your airway, the one part of this illness that can become an emergency. Hospital today, ENT team; you'll likely need corticosteroids — one of the few situations we use them — and they'll want to watch you. Don't drive; someone to take you, or an ambulance?' / Version E (four months on, bloods normal): 'a prolonged period of fatigue after glandular fever is well recognised; normal bloods are genuinely reassuring — the acute infection has resolved; it doesn't mean the tiredness is imagined. I'd check iron studies, thyroid, and screen for low mood. Then a graded, paced return — a level you can sustain on a bad day, hold it a week, increase slightly; boom-and-bust keeps people stuck; regular review — you shouldn't be running this alone.'
pefe: Role-player: Liam Petrides, 19, first-year engineering, share house in Adelaide, from Port Lincoln; two bottle-shop shifts a week; social football (training Tuesday, missed two weeks); slept through a lecture sitting up; amoxicillin from a bulk-billing clinic 5 days ago → flat red itchy blotches 3 days later, no swelling/wheeze/blisters/ulcers, fading; told 'allergic — write it on forms'. Can swallow/drink, no breathing trouble, no LUQ/shoulder pain, no jaundice, no weight loss/sweats/bruising; housemate had a sore throat. Hidden: unprotected sex with a new partner ~3 weeks ago (only if asked; awkward); drinks more than he first admits. Real concern: exams in three weeks — frightened of failing first year. Flat, tired, blunt; perks up with practical solutions. Key hinges: 'atypical? that sounds like cancer'; 'so am I allergic or not? he was pretty definite'; pushes TWICE on footy ('training's Tuesday — it's only social'); 'give me a number — weeks? months?'; 'is that a promise?' if a date is given; 'should I be staying away from people?'; relieved at a certificate/deferral; 'do you think I've got HIV?' then 'can my parents find out?'; teach-back: 'no footy four weeks, and I'm not actually allergic to penicillin'

Vitals: T 37.9, HR 88, BP 118/70. Results: FBE lymphocytosis + atypical lymphocytes · ALT 180 / AST 145 / bili normal · EBV VCA IgM +, VCA IgG +, EBNA IgG − · throat swab GAS negative. No examination task (would expect pharyngitis/exudate, cervical lymphadenopathy, ± splenomegaly ~50%, ± hepatomegaly, palatal petechiae)

IM: peak 15–25; incubation 4–6 weeks; VCA IgM +/IgG +/EBNA − = acute (EBNA appears 6–12 weeks; heterophile/monospot may be falsely negative in the first week and in children); splenomegaly ~50%; rupture risk highest first 3–4 weeks — no contact sport/heavy lifting ≥4 weeks from onset (guidance 3–8 weeks VERIFY), USS if athlete/uncertain; transaminitis common — avoid alcohol until normal, recheck; amoxicillin/ampicillin rash 80–90% — NOT allergy (document 'amoxicillin rash with EBV'); if GAS proven use phenoxymethylpenicillin; steroids only for airway obstruction, severe haemolytic anaemia, severe thrombocytopenia; supportive — fluids, analgesia, rest; saliva shedding for months — no exclusion from school/work/uni; not notifiable; complications — airway obstruction, splenic rupture, hepatitis, haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, neurological (GBS, encephalitis), chronic fatigue in a minority. DDx: streptococcal pharyngitis, CMV, ★ acute HIV seroconversion, toxoplasmosis, hepatitis A/B, lymphoma/leukaemia (persistent nodes, cytopenias) — always offer HIV
SA: medical certificate; university special consideration/deferred exams; headspace 1800 650 890 if mood low; SHINE SA for STI screen; TIS 131 450
fails: Going straight to the results without asking his concern; omitting the airway (swallowing/noisy breathing) and spleen (LUQ/shoulder-tip) questions
Reassuring about the rash before excluding urticaria/angio-oedema/wheeze and blistering/mucosal involvement
Skipping the sexual history because EBV is positive; ★ never offering an HIV test, or offering it accusingly
Saying 'atypical lymphocytes' without explaining it; ★ leaving 'penicillin allergy' on the record 'to be safe'

★ Clearing him for contact sport or caving after two pushes; restriction without the reason; no teach-back; promising a recovery date; routine steroids; telling him to isolate from uni; no certificate/deferral offer

ALT 180 / AST 145 → no alcohol, recheck 2 wk · amoxicillin rash 80–90%, not allergy · steroids only: airway, severe haemolysis, severe thrombocytopenia · not notifiable · always offer HIV

setting: Telehealth from general practice, Wallaroo; you cannot examine her and nobody else is in the house. The stem looks like a COPD exacerbation and tempts you into prednisolone + amoxicillin — it is not: the comorbidities make her eligible for an oral antiviral, and the ABSENCE of increased breathlessness removes the exacerbation treatment. Don't ask for vital signs she can't give. Time split: history to 4:35 · diagnosis · antiviral, reliever, sick-day rules by 7:35 · safety-net with teach-back.
stem: Mrs Barbara Quinn, 65, retired teacher aide, lives alone. Sore throat and productive cough for three days, worsening, more phlegm; no shortness of breath. COVID-19 test positive today. Known diabetes, COPD and hypertension.
tasks: Take a history
Explain your diagnosis
Explain your immediate management
time: 8 min. 'Is that Barbara Quinn? Dr — from the practice. Date of birth and address? Good time, somewhere you can talk? If we get cut off I'll ring you straight back. Tell me what's been happening' → ★ acknowledge the fear (positive test, alone) · cough ×6: when/worse, dry or chesty, ★ colour + changed?, blood, ★ more than usual?, smell · throat: ★ one side or both, ★ difficulty swallowing, ★ drooling/managing saliva, voice, mouth opening · ★ breathlessness — the disposition questions: SOB? ★ 'worse than your usual?', ★ normal daily activities (kitchen, shower), ★ breathless sitting still, wheeze/rattle, chest pain, haemoptysis · systems: N/V/D, keeping fluids down (off food, drinking tea), fever, aches, headache, dizziness, rash · COVID before? ★ vaccinations and date (~2 y) · ★ puffers (Seretide, Ventolin) · ★ 'what are you taking for the diabetes?' → metformin + ★ empagliflozin; BP — fluid tablet + another · reviews, control, checking sugars (not lately) · ★ who's at home / who could get to you tonight (nobody; Val next door; daughter in Adelaide) · concerns → 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' · ★ two diagnoses in two sentences: COVID-19 lower respiratory tract infection + viral exacerbation of COPD · ★ antiviral FIRST: eligible (COPD + diabetes, 65), within 5 days (day 3), molnupiravir 4 capsules bd × 5 days, nausea, interaction check, script sent, delivery, subsidised · reliever: salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4h; continue Seretide · ★ the two refusals with reasons: no antibiotics (virus; trigger = breathing worse + phlegm change), no prednisolone (not more breathless; sugars) — 'if your breathing changes, both decisions change' · ★ sick-day rules: stop empagliflozin (ketoacidosis) and metformin until eating/drinking; test sugars more often; hold the diuretic if dry; no NSAIDs, paracetamol fine · ★ escalation: breathless at rest/worse than usual, can't do normal activities, chest pain, haemoptysis, confused/drowsy, can't keep fluids down → 000; healthdirect 1800 022 222 overnight; Val today; 'I'll ring you tomorrow'; ★ teach-back: 'tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance'.

back.dx: COVID-19 lower respiratory tract infection causing a viral exacerbation of COPD in a 65-year-old living alone with COPD, type 2 diabetes and hypertension — day 3 of sore throat (bilateral, swallowing ok, no drooling) and worsening productive cough with increased volume of whitish-yellow sputum (baseline colour), mild fever, off food but drinking, ★ no increase in breathlessness from baseline, no rest dyspnoea, no functional decline, no haemoptysis or chest pain; last COVID vaccine ~2 years ago; Seretide + Ventolin; metformin + empagliflozin; a diuretic + another antihypertensive; not checking sugars. Immediate management: oral antiviral today (eligible — 65 with two risk factors, within the five-day window): molnupiravir 800 mg (4 capsules) bd × 5 days (nausea; not in pregnancy) — or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir if no interactions VERIFY — script to the pharmacy with delivery; salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer every 3–4 h, continue the preventer; no antibiotics (confirmed viral; exacerbation antibiotic criteria not met — needs increased dyspnoea plus sputum volume/purulence), no corticosteroids (no increased dyspnoea; hyperglycaemia) — both decisions change if breathing changes; diabetes sick-day plan: withhold empagliflozin (euglycaemic ketoacidosis risk) and metformin until eating and drinking normally, monitor glucose more often, hold the diuretic if dehydrated, no NSAIDs; escalation criteria with 000/healthdirect, neighbour check today, GP phone review in 24 h; teach-back. Hidden agenda: husband Ron died of pneumonia in hospital — she fears admission.
plan: 'Good morning, is that Barbara Quinn? I'm Dr — from the practice. Can I confirm your date of birth and address? Is this a good time, and are you somewhere you can talk? If we get cut off I'll ring you straight back. Tell me what's been happening.' → cough 3 days, worse, more phlegm, test positive this morning, 'a bit frightened — on my own here' → ★ 'I can hear how worrying this is, especially with the test coming back positive today and you being on your own. Let me ask some questions so I can work out the safest plan, then I'll tell you exactly what we're going to do.'

Cough ×6: 'when did it start, is it getting worse? dry or bringing something up? what colour, and has the colour changed? any blood? bringing up more than usual? any bad smell?' → 3 d, worse each day; chesty; whitish/a bit yellow — always like that; no blood; definitely more; no smell · throat: ★ 'one side or both? any difficulty swallowing? any drooling or trouble managing your own saliva? voice changed? can you open your mouth normally?' → both; hurts but goes down; no drooling; croaky from coughing

★ Breathlessness: 'are you short of breath? ★ is it worse than your usual? ★ can you do your normal daily activities — getting to the kitchen, showering? ★ are you breathless sitting still? any wheezing or rattling? chest pain? blood coughed up?' → no more than usual (puffed on stairs, always); managing the same as last week; not at rest; a rattle when coughing; no pain/blood · systems: 'nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea — keeping fluids down? fever, aches, headache, dizziness? rash?' → off food, drinking tea; a bit hot yesterday; no rash

'Had COVID before? ★ vaccinations — when was the last one?' (once, 2 y ago; jab ~2 y) · ★ 'what puffers are you on for your chest, and are you using them?' (Seretide bd, Ventolin prn) · ★ 'what are you taking for the diabetes and the blood pressure?' → metformin and ★ 'one called empagliflozin'; a fluid tablet and another · 'seeing your GP/specialist regularly — sugar and BP usually well controlled? checking your sugars?' (not lately) · ★ 'who's at home with you? who could get to you quickly if you got worse tonight?' → nobody; Val next door looks in; daughter in Adelaide · 'anything worrying you?' → 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' → acknowledge; honest: the plan is to keep her safe at home with clear triggers

★ 'Barbara, your test confirms COVID-19, and from what you've described it has gone down into your chest — a lower respiratory tract infection. COVID is a virus, and for most people it settles by itself. There's a second part: because you have COPD, your airways are already narrowed, and the inflammation this virus causes makes that narrowing worse — so you're also having a flare-up of your COPD. That's why the cough and phlegm have picked up. Does that make sense?' ('is it pneumonia? will I end up in hospital?' → no signs of that today; the plan is built to keep you out of hospital, and clear triggers if that changes)

★ Antiviral first: 'The most important thing today: because you have COPD and diabetes you're at higher risk of becoming seriously unwell with COVID, and that makes you eligible for an antiviral tablet. It works best started early — within the first five days — and you're on day three, so I want to start it today. Four capsules twice a day for five days; the commonest side effect is a bit of nausea. I'll check it against your other tablets, send the script to the pharmacy now and arrange delivery so you don't leave the house. It's subsidised because you qualify.' · 'Second — increase your blue Ventolin: four to eight puffs through a spacer, repeat every three to four hours if you need it. Keep the Seretide as normal.' · ★ 'Two things I'm deliberately not doing. I'm not giving antibiotics: we know this is a virus, and antibiotics do nothing to a virus — the trigger for antibiotics with your chest is when your breathing gets worse as well as the phlegm increasing or changing colour, and your breathing hasn't changed. And I'm not giving steroid tablets — those are for when a flare-up makes you significantly more breathless, and they push your sugars up, which with diabetes and an infection isn't a trade I want to make today. If your breathing changes, both of those decisions change.' ('my old doctor always gave me antibiotics' → hold; 'couldn't I have some in case?' → hold, promise the review)

★ Sick-day rules: 'Because you're on empagliflozin and metformin and you're off your food, stop both until you're eating and drinking normally — empagliflozin in particular can cause a dangerous build-up of acid if you're not eating. Keep your fluids up, and test your sugar more often than usual, not less — illness pushes it up even when you're not eating. If you get dehydrated, hold the fluid tablet too; no anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen — paracetamol is fine.' · ★ 'Now, when to worry: ring us straight away, or call an ambulance on 000, if you become breathless at rest or more breathless than your usual, if you can't do your normal activities, if you get chest pain, cough up blood, become confused or drowsy, or can't keep fluids down. Overnight, healthdirect is 1800 022 222. Can Val look in on you today? I'll ring you myself tomorrow.' · ★ 'Before we finish — tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance.' (correct the one she gets slightly wrong) · isolation: stay home, mask if anyone comes in, keep away from the elderly/immunosuppressed; Val leaves things at the door · booster when recovered
ask: ★ 'If we get cut off, I'll ring you straight back on this number.' / ★ 'I can hear how worrying this is, especially with you being on your own.' / ★ 'Has the colour changed, and are you bringing up more than usual?' / ★ 'Is the throat sore on one side or both? Any difficulty swallowing? Any drooling?'

★ 'Is the breathlessness worse than your usual?' / ★ 'Can you do today what you could do last week?' / ★ 'Can you finish a whole sentence without stopping for breath?' / 'What are you taking for the diabetes — which tablets exactly?' / 'Who's at home with you? Who could get to you quickly if you got worse tonight?'

★ 'You have COVID, and because of your COPD it has tipped you into a flare-up.' / ★ 'Because you have COPD and diabetes, you are eligible for an antiviral, and it works best within the first five days.' / ★ 'Antibiotics do nothing to a virus, and taking them when you don't need them stops them working when you do.' / ★ 'The trigger is when your breathing gets worse as well as the phlegm changing.'

★ 'Stop the empagliflozin and metformin until you're eating and drinking normally.' / ★ 'Test your sugar more often, not less — illness pushes it up.' / ★ 'Tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance.'

Variant A (day 7): 'Because you're a week in, the antiviral tablets have passed the window where they help — they only work in the first five days, when the virus is still multiplying. That doesn't leave us with nothing: it means we watch you more closely instead. I want to speak to you every day for the next three days, and I want you to be very clear about when to call an ambulance.' / Variant B (breathless at rest): stop counselling — 'your breathing has changed and I don't want to manage this over the phone. I'm arranging an ambulance to take you to hospital now to check your oxygen and your chest properly. I know that's not what you wanted to hear — can you tell me what worries you most about going in? … I'll ring the department myself and let them know you're coming and why.' / Variant C (one-sided throat, drooling): 'that pattern suggests a collection of pus behind the tonsil — antibiotics alone won't clear it, it needs to be drained; emergency department today.' / Variant D (third demand for antibiotics): 'Here's what I'll do instead: a script to hold, and you start it only if two things happen — your breathing gets worse AND the phlegm increases or changes colour. Write those two down. And I'm ringing you tomorrow. Does that feel fair?' / Variant E (grandchildren): 'not while you're infectious — stay home; mask and open windows if anyone must come in; keep away from the elderly or immunosuppressed; I'll give you the current SA Health advice on how long.'
pefe: Role-player: Barbara Quinn, 65, retired teacher aide, widowed, alone in Wallaroo; daughter Kylie in Adelaide; neighbour Val looks in most days; ex-smoker 15 y; COPD (Seretide bd, Ventolin prn), T2DM (metformin + empagliflozin), hypertension (a fluid tablet + one she can't name); COVID once 2 y ago; last vaccine ~2 y. Anxious, polite, short sentences (breathy from coughing but finishes them). Pushes twice on antibiotics ('my old doctor always gave me antibiotics' → 'couldn't I just have some in case?'). Withholds empagliflozin unless diabetes tablets are asked by name; 'I haven't got anything like that here' to BP/oxygen requests. Hidden: 'I don't want to go into hospital — my Ron went in with his chest and never came home' (~6 min if concerns not asked). Repeats the plan back with one thing slightly wrong so you correct it

No observations obtainable. History positives: day 3, increased sputum volume, baseline colour, bilateral sore throat without dysphagia/drooling, mild fever, off food but drinking; negatives: no increase in dyspnoea, no rest dyspnoea, no functional decline, no haemoptysis, chest pain, unilateral throat, vomiting → no red flags for emergency assessment

Antiviral eligibility (PBS, VERIFY current): ≥70; 50–69 with ≥2 risk factors; Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander ≥30 with ≥1; ≥18 immunocompromised; within 5 days of symptom onset. Molnupiravir 800 mg (4 × 200 mg capsules) bd × 5 days (40 capsules) — nausea, not in pregnancy; nirmatrelvir/ritonavir 300/100 mg bd × 5 days — many interactions (statins, anticoagulants, some antihypertensives), renal dosing VERIFY. COPD exacerbation (Anthonisen): increased dyspnoea + sputum volume + sputum purulence — antibiotics if ≥2 including purulence, or ventilatory support: amoxicillin 500 mg tds × 5 d or doxycycline VERIFY; prednisolone 30–50 mg × 5 days for significant dyspnoea; salbutamol 4–8 puffs via spacer q3–4h; escalation — rest dyspnoea, SpO2 <92%, confusion, inability to complete sentences, cyanosis. Diabetes sick-day rules: withhold SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA), metformin (lactic acidosis), ACEi/ARB/diuretics if dehydrated, NSAIDs; check BGL 2–4-hourly, ketones if available; insulin adjusted not stopped. COVID booster: 65–74 recommended 12-monthly, eligible 6-monthly VERIFY; isolation per SA Health advice (stay home while symptomatic, mask if leaving, avoid high-risk settings ≥7 days VERIFY)

Telehealth conduct: identity + two identifiers, consent, call-back plan, don't request unobtainable observations, escalation criteria, teach-back, documented review · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · 000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450
fails: Opening with 'can I have her vital signs?' on a phone to a woman alone at home

Hearing 'more phlegm' and starting antibiotics; accepting 'I do get short of breath' without 'worse than your usual?' (in COPD the answer is always yes); skipping the throat red flags (one side, drooling)

★ 'Jenny, thank you — that helps a lot, and I don't think this is just stress. The most likely explanation is a condition called hyperthyroidism. There's a small butterfly-shaped gland at the front of your neck called the thyroid, and its job is to set the pace your body runs at. Yours is producing too much hormone, so everything is running fast. That fits what you've told me: feeling anxious and on edge, not being able to bear the heat, looser bowels, sweating through your clothes, your heart racing, and — the one that convinces me most — losing weight even though you're eating more. Those together point to the thyroid rather than to nerves. Your mother having a thyroid problem fits too — it can run in families.' · 'so it's not all in my head? is it cancer?' → 'it's not in your head, and the great majority of the time it isn't cancer — usually the gland becoming overactive, which is very treatable. ★ DDx, each with a because: 'anxiety conditions — generalised anxiety, panic attacks, phobias, post-traumatic stress — and low mood or an adjustment reaction: but no particular trigger, no panic attacks, your mood is reasonable and you're still enjoying your garden. Thyroiditis — inflammation of the same gland: but no neck pain, no fever, no recent viral illness. The menopause, which overlaps a lot at your age: but menopause doesn't usually cause weight loss or a racing heart. A rare adrenal tumour called a phaeochromocytoma — episodes of headache, sweating and palpitations with high blood pressure: that pattern isn't there. Heart rhythm problems like atrial fibrillation or SVT — we'll check with a tracing. And stimulants — caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, some medicines — two coffees wouldn't do this.' · ★ close the loop: 'a blood test for your thyroid, a full blood count and a heart tracing today, and I'll examine your neck, your eyes and your pulse before you go. Management: stable → vagal manoeuvres (modified Valsalva — strain 15 s then legs raised; carotid massage if no bruit) → adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with flush, then 12 mg (warn about the horrible transient feeling; caution asthma; monitor, record the strip) → verapamil/diltiazem if no pre-excitation VERIFY; unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered mentation, heart failure) → synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation. setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — the framework every CVS station is built on. Regional SA general practice; you are the resident. 8 minutes (2 reading): 1 min WIPE · 1½ min peripheral signs · 3½ min praecordium · 2 min presenting. If you're not at the chest by 2:30 you're behind. There is NOTHING to find and the examiner will not invent findings — every mark is for sequence, accuracy and completeness inside the time. Reaching the bell with the praecordium unfinished is the failure mode.
stem: Ben Whitmore, 46, grain handler from the Yorke Peninsula, well. His employer requires a cardiovascular check before a supervised return-to-fitness programme. Triage: BP 124/78 · HR 88 · RR 14 · T 36.6 · SpO2 98%. Bed at 45°, gown open at the front; a timer and three BP devices on the trolley.
tasks: Perform a cardiovascular examination with running commentary (6 minutes)
Report your findings to the examiner
Give your diagnosis and differential diagnoses (2 minutes)
time: WIPE: intro, 'I've been asked to examine your heart — look, feel, listen; chest exposed; ★ any chest pain at the moment? ★ sit forward — I'm making sure the bed is at 45 degrees — lie back; happy to go ahead? wash hands' · peripheries 90 s: general appearance (comfortable, no central cyanosis, no cachexia, ★ no Marfan features) → hands (tar, xanthomata, ★ nails together — no clubbing; splinters, Osler, Janeway) → ★ pulse: rhythm named before rate, 15 s × 4 → 'may I measure the BP — palpatory then auscultatory' → face (arcus, xanthelasma), mouth (central cyanosis, high-arched palate) → ★ 'turn your head to your left — no raised JVP at 45°' · ★ examiner snaps 'why the hands? move on' → 'of course, Examiner — moving to the pulse' (next stop is the NECK, not the chest) · praecordium: second consent → inspection (apex, pectus, scars) → ★ apex (palm — 'I cannot feel the apex beat'; no mimed counting) → ★ heave (HEEL of hand, left sternal edge) → ★ thrills (PADS, four areas named) → auscultation: bell at mitral, diaphragm × 4, ★ carotids (fifth spot) → 'to complete': lung bases, liver from the RIF, ankles · present: position first, sequence in order, 'in summary a normal cardiovascular examination', 'to complete I would…' · differentials by system.

back.dx: Normal cardiovascular examination — no clinical evidence of valvular disease, heart failure or endocarditis; asymptomatic, fit for a supervised programme. Differentials by system (buckets, not a flat valve list): cardiac — occult valvular disease or cardiomyopathy (echo if any symptom or murmur), ischaemic heart disease (ECG + absolute CV risk calculation); respiratory — airways disease (spirometry); endocrine/metabolic — undiagnosed diabetes, dyslipidaemia, thyroid disease; drug-related — alcohol, stimulants, anabolic agents (ask directly given the programme).
plan: Gel, patient's right. 'Hi Ben, I'm Dr —, one of the doctors here. Name and date of birth? I've been asked to examine your heart today — I'll look at your chest, feel your chest, and listen with my stethoscope. I'll need your chest exposed. ★ Any chest pain at the moment? — Could you sit forward a moment while I make sure the head of the bed is at 45 degrees… and lie back. Happy for me to go ahead? I'll just wash my hands.' (say the 45° words even if the bed is already there)

'On general appearance Ben is comfortable at rest, no central cyanosis, no cachexia, no features of Marfan syndrome. — May I see your hands? — No tar staining, no xanthomata. Nails together like this for me — no clubbing. No splinter haemorrhages, no Osler nodes, no Janeway lesions. — Taking the pulse now… Examiner, the pulse is regular… rate 88. May I measure the blood pressure? Palpatory first, then auscultatory.' → 'auscultatory only / put the cuff on — 124 over 78' → cuff correctly (artery marker over the brachial) · ★ if snapped at: 'Of course, Examiner. Moving to the pulse.'

'No corneal arcus, no xanthelasma. Ben, open your mouth and lift your tongue — no central cyanosis, no high-arched palate. Now turn your head and look over to your left — Examiner, I cannot see a raised JVP at 45 degrees.' ('what are you looking at?' → 'a vein in the neck that acts like a pressure gauge for the right side of the heart — sitting you at this angle lets me read it')

★ 'Ben, I'm going to look at and feel your chest now — is that alright?' → 'On inspection: no visible apex beat, no pectus carinatum or excavatum, no scars. — I'm feeling for the apex beat… Examiner, I cannot feel the apex beat. — Heel of my hand on the left sternal edge for a parasternal heave… no parasternal heave. — Pads of my fingers for thrills: mitral… tricuspid… pulmonary… aortic — no palpable thrills at any of the four areas.'

'Auscultating now — bell on the mitral… diaphragm on the mitral… tricuspid… pulmonary… aortic. S1 and S2 normal, no added sounds, no murmurs. — And the carotids… no bruits.' · 'everything alright, doc?' → 'All normal so far, Ben — let me finish and I'll talk you through it properly.' (one sentence, keep examining)

'To complete, I'm listening at both lung bases — no bibasal crepitations. Palpating from the right lower quadrant up — no hepatomegaly. And inspecting the ankles — no peripheral oedema.' · behind at 5:00 → straight to auscultation, then 'to complete I would examine the lung bases, liver and ankles' — never abandon auscultation for the abdomen

★ Present (40 s): 'I examined Ben at 45 degrees. General appearance — comfortable, no cyanosis, cachexia or Marfanoid features. Hands — no clubbing or stigmata of endocarditis. Pulse 88 regular; BP 124/78. No arcus or xanthelasma; JVP not raised. Praecordium — no scars or deformity; apex not palpable; no heave; no thrills; S1 and S2 normal with no added sounds or murmurs; no carotid bruits. In summary, a normal cardiovascular examination. To complete I would examine the lung bases, liver and ankles.' → 'My examination today is entirely normal — no clinical evidence of valvular disease, heart failure or endocarditis; Ben is fit for a supervised programme. Differentials by system: cardiac — occult valvular disease or cardiomyopathy, so an echo if any symptom or murmur, and ischaemic heart disease — ECG and an absolute cardiovascular risk calculation; respiratory — airways disease, spirometry; endocrine — diabetes, dyslipidaemia, thyroid; drugs — alcohol, stimulants, anabolic agents, asked directly.' · last 30 s to Ben: 'everything I examined today was normal — heart sounds normal, blood pressure normal, nothing that would stop you starting the programme'

Technique numbers: 45° · pulse 15 s × 4 (ceiling 30 s; 60 s if irregular) · re-inflate 20–30 mmHg above palpated systolic · Korotkoff I systolic, V diastolic · cuff bladder 80% of arm circumference / 40% width · JVP ≤3 cm above the sternal angle; abdominojugular hold 10 s · apex 5th ICS mid-clavicular · manubriosternal angle = 2nd ICS · 3 palpation steps (apex, heave, thrills) · 5 auscultation spots (mitral bell + diaphragm, tricuspid, pulmonary, aortic, carotids) · thrill = murmur ≥4/6

Where the real cases diverge: murmur station (PE-02) adds Marfan/endocarditis packages and the three manoeuvres, stops at the chest; hypertension station (PE-04) adds fundoscopy and end-organ assessment, radio-radial/radiofemoral delay in the secondary-cause version; heart-failure station (PE-03) adds S3, lung bases, liver, abdominojugular reflux, oedema and the discharge conversation. Global rating: clear fail — praecordium unfinished, or heave and thrills both missing; borderline — all steps but rushed/disorganised or position never mentioned; pass — ordered, named, unhurried, 90 s left to present; excellent — plus graceful recovery from the interruption and a system-bucketed differential

Inventing an apex beat — counting rib spaces after feeling nothing; palm/heel/pads confused

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION. General practice; referral from an insurance medical examiner. Two tasks; the task EXCLUDES the abdomen and lower limb. Split: 45 s WIPE · 60 s peripheries · 75 s inspect/palpate · 3 min auscultation with manoeuvres · 90 s explaining. There is no murmur and nobody will give you one — the three manoeuvres, performed with commentary, and explaining a normal examination to a worried man are the entire mark sheet. Do NOT attempt radio-radial delay ('stick to your task').
stem: James Corrigan, 40, self-employed builder, looks well and faintly worried. Referred after an insurance medical at which the examining doctor heard a murmur. James had a fever on the day of that check.
tasks: Perform a murmur examination, excluding the abdomen and the lower limb
Explain your diagnosis and your findings to the patient
time: WIPE with the positions clause: 'I'll look, feel and listen — ★ and towards the end I'll ask you to move into a few different positions while I listen; chest exposed, lying at 45°; any chest pain? happy to start?' · 'is it serious?' → park in one sentence · peripheries 60 s: ★ Marfan named; hands — ★ splinters/Osler/Janeway/clubbing → examiner 'why the hands? skip it' → ★ 'of course — moving to the pulse… regular, 84; BP — palpatory then auscultatory' (→ 'auscultatory only' → 118/74) → ★ JVP still done · neck, inspection, apex ('cannot feel'), heave (heel), thrills (pads ×4) — no abdominojugular reflux, carotids come at the aortic step · ★ manoeuvres announced before each: MITRAL — bell, diaphragm; 'roll onto your left side, breathe out and hold' — still no murmur — 'into the axilla — nothing radiating' · TRICUSPID — diaphragm; ★ Valsalva: 'pinch your nose and blow out with your mouth closed, like popping your ears' (demonstrate on yourself, don't explain) · PULMONARY · AORTIC — 'lean forward, breathe all the way out and hold' — no murmur → carotids right, left — no bruits · explain: ★ 'I listened very carefully and could not hear any murmur at all' → flow murmur from the fever → ★ echo anyway → red flags (fevers, night sweats, weight loss, breathlessness) · his three questions: heart fine? insurance? dad's valve?

back.dx: Normal murmur examination — no murmur at rest or on any manoeuvre; most likely a physiological flow murmur from the fever on the day of the insurance check (a fast, hard-pumping heart moving blood through normal valves). Plan: echocardiogram to be certain (father had a valve replaced — one more reason to scan rather than reassure), letter to the insurer once the echo is back, no work restriction, safety-net for endocarditis/rheumatic disease (fevers, night sweats, weight loss, breathlessness). Must not miss: endocarditis (fever at the time of a new murmur — if still febrile, three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics + urgent echo), rheumatic heart disease.
plan: 'Hi James, I'm Dr —. I understand the doctor at your insurance check heard a murmur and asked you to see me. I've been asked to examine your heart today. I'll look at your chest, feel your chest, and listen with my stethoscope — ★ and towards the end I'll ask you to move into a few different positions while I listen. I'll need your chest exposed, and I need you lying at 45 degrees. Any chest pain right now? Happy for me to start?' · 'is it something serious?' → ★ 'That's exactly what I'm here to sort out. Let me examine you properly first and then I'll tell you what I find.'

'Examiner, on general appearance no features of Marfan syndrome, no central cyanosis, no cachexia. — James, may I see your hands? — No splinter haemorrhages, no Osler nodes, no Janeway lesions, no clubbing.' → 'why are you doing the hands? skip it' → ★ 'Of course, Examiner. Moving to the pulse… regular, rate 84. May I check the blood pressure? Palpatory then auscultatory.' → 'auscultatory only' → 'thank you… 118 over 74' (no radio-radial delay — that is the hypertension station)

'James, turn your head and look to your left — Examiner, no raised JVP at 45 degrees. — James, I'm going to look at and feel your chest now, is that alright? On inspection, no visible apex beat, no pectus deformity, no scars. I cannot feel the apex beat. Heel of my hand at the left sternal edge — no parasternal heave. Pads of my fingers: mitral… tricuspid… pulmonary… aortic — no palpable thrills.' (no abdominojugular reflux; carotids later)

★ MITRAL: 'Bell on the mitral valve… now the diaphragm… S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs. I'd like to perform the mitral manoeuvre. James, roll onto your left side for me — and breathe out and hold — still no murmur. And into the axilla — nothing radiating to the axilla.' (stethoscope stays on the chest as he rolls)

★ TRICUSPID: 'Diaphragm at the tricuspid area… normal. I'd like to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre. James, pinch your nose and blow out with your mouth closed — like popping your ears on a plane.' → 'sorry, like what?' → [pinch your own nose, mime the effort] 'Like this — nose pinched, blow out with your mouth shut.' → 'Thank you. No murmur.'

★ PULMONARY, AORTIC, CAROTIDS: 'Pulmonary… normal. Aortic… normal. I'd like to perform the aortic manoeuvre — James, lean forward for me, breathe all the way out and hold — no murmur. And the carotids, right… left… no bruits.' · at 5:00 with one manoeuvre done → abandon the pulmonary valve, never the manoeuvres · bell before the aortic manoeuvre → 'I would complete by listening at the aortic area with the patient leaning forward in expiration, and auscultating both carotids'

★ 'James, the good news first — I listened very carefully today and I could not hear any murmur at all. The most likely explanation is the fever you had on the day of that check. When we have a fever the heart pumps faster and harder, and blood moving quickly through completely normal valves can make an extra sound — a flow murmur. It settles when the fever settles, and that fits exactly with what I found today. Even so, I'd like to arrange an echocardiogram — an ultrasound scan of the heart, painless, no needles — which looks directly at the valves so we can be certain there's nothing I can't hear. And if you develop fevers, night sweats, weight loss or any breathlessness before that scan, I want to see you straight away.' · 'so my heart's fine?' → yes on today's examination, echo to be certain · 'will this affect my insurance?' → 'I can't speak for the insurer, but I can write to them once the scan is back — a normal echo is the strongest thing you can give them' · 'do I need to stop working?' → 'nothing I found today gives me any reason to stop you working' · 'my dad had a valve replaced — is this that?' → 'worth knowing — one more reason to do the scan rather than just reassure you' · spare seconds → narrate the manoeuvres back (mitral valve when you rolled left, aortic when you leaned forward, heart muscle for the Valsalva) · close: 'normal examination today, most likely a harmless murmur from the fever, an echo to be certain, and back sooner if any warning signs — I'll write to you and the insurer once the scan is back'

pefe: Role-player: James Corrigan, 40, self-employed builder (no income protection if he stops); insurance medical six weeks ago with a cold and fever that week; 'the insurance doctor said he heard something in my heart'; completely well since; preoccupied with insurance and work. Never smoked, six beers a weekend, no meds; no sore throats/joint pains/rashes/dental work; father had a valve replaced in his sixties (doesn't know which). Nothing to find. Asks 'is it something serious?' early (marks counselling now); 'sorry — like what?' on the Valsalva (should be demonstrated, not explained); never asked to roll/lean/Valsalva → fail, says nothing; abdomen or ankles examined → marks it (excluded by the task). Three questions at the end in order: 'so my heart's fine?', 'will this affect my insurance?', 'my dad had a valve replaced — is this that?'. Second examiner: 'why are you doing the hands? skip it'; 'auscultatory only' → 118/74

Manoeuvre logic: left lateral + bell + expiration = mitral stenosis (and accentuates MR radiating to the axilla) · Valsalva — HOCM and MVP louder, everything else softer · lean forward + diaphragm + expiration = aortic regurgitation · handgrip — louder in regurgitant lesions, softer in AS and HOCM · AS radiates to the carotids, MR to the axilla · bell first at the mitral · pulse 15 s × 4 · 3 palpation steps · 5 auscultation spots · 3 manoeuvres. Flow murmur: soft, early/mid-systolic, no radiation, normal S2, disappears with resolution of fever/anaemia/pregnancy. Echo: TTE; TOE if endocarditis suspected. Endocarditis — Duke criteria; blood cultures ×3 from separate sites over ≥1 h before antibiotics VERIFY

Global rating: clear fail — fewer than two manoeuvres, or no explanation of the normal result; borderline — manoeuvres silent/hurried, or reassurance with no mechanism and no echo; pass — three manoeuvres named and performed, complete, honest explanation with mechanism, plan and safety net; excellent — plus absorbing the interruption and narrating the manoeuvres back

Examining the abdomen or lower limb — excluded by the task; wasting time on abdominojugular reflux
