There is guarding; there is no rigidity.' · the skip, spoken in full: 'I am stopping superficial palpation here, skipping deep palpation and rebound and skipping percussion, because they would add nothing and cause unnecessary pain' · what still costs her nothing: auscultate, request groins, request DRE with consent and chaperone, and offer a PELVIC examination with consent and chaperone, naming all the bimanual items · diagnosis with reasons → causes as rupture / progressed obstruction / ischaemia / pancreatitis → plan.

back.dx: Generalised peritonitis — she was unable to cough and had severe tenderness with guarding in three separate quadrants on LIGHT palpation (guarding present, rigidity absent); on the verbal pelvic examination, cervical motion tenderness with bilateral adnexal tenderness. Causes, grouped: rupture — perforated peptic ulcer (she takes ibuprofen most days), perforated appendix or diverticulum, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, and in a woman a ruptured ovarian cyst, tubo-ovarian abscess or, if younger, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy; obstruction that has progressed — tumour, strangulated hernia, faecal impaction; then mesenteric ischaemia and acute pancreatitis. Plan: nil by mouth, two large-bore cannulae, bloods with lactate and beta-hCG, fluid resuscitation, adequate analgesia, erect chest X-ray and CT abdomen and pelvis, surgical referral now; at a rural SA site start all of that and call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 while the workup runs.
plan: Gloves on. 'Good morning, Examiner. Before I begin, may I have the vital signs, please — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → 'BP 104/62, pulse 112, RR 22, temperature 37.9' (or 'all observations are stable' / 'assume they are normal'). Say what you heard: 'Thank you — she is tachycardic at 112 with a soft blood pressure; I will keep that in mind as I examine her.' Move to the patient's right side.

WIPE: 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors in the emergency department. Can I check your name and date of birth? Thank you, Jane. I've been asked to examine your tummy — I'll look at it, gently feel it, gently tap on it, and at the end listen with my stethoscope. I'll need to see the whole tummy, so could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? You can stay lying as you are. Let me wash my hands — and before I start, are you in pain now? Would you like something for it?' → 'the nurse gave me morphine twenty minutes ago, it hasn't touched it' → 'I'm sorry — I'll ask her to review that as soon as we finish.' → 'you do it' → ask, then act: 'Of course. Is it all right if I lower your trousers a little so I can see the whole tummy?'

Peripheral survey — do not skip it: 'Examiner, on general appearance she is alert but in obvious pain and distress, lying very still, guarding her abdomen. No pallor. Jane, may I see your hands? Capillary refill under two seconds, skin turgor normal, no pale palmar creases, no cold peripheries, radial pulse of good volume. Face — no sunken eyes, no dry mucous membranes. Look up for me — no conjunctival pallor.' ('skip the peripheries' → stop mid-sentence and move on.)

Inspection, exposing xiphisternum to below the umbilicus: 'No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no visible masses, no redness. Bending down to look across the abdomen — movement with respiration is shallow and symmetrical.' Then the cough: 'Jane, could you give me a cough, and tell me if it hurts and where?' → 'I can't. I really can't.' → 'That's absolutely fine, don't force it. Examiner — she is unable to cough, which in itself suggests significant peritonism. The stem does not localise the pain, so I will begin superficial palpation in one corner and work across.'

The scream and the recovery script. Lightest touch, left upper quadrant → 'AAH! Don't — please don't!' → 'Jane, I am so sorry. I did not realise you were in that much pain. Would you like some more pain relief before I go on? I do need to feel your tummy once or maybe twice more, so that I can understand what is happening inside. I know it hurts, and I will be as gentle as I can. Is that all right?' → '...Alright. Be quick.' (Ask 'shall I continue?' without explaining and she hands it back: 'It's your call, doctor.')

Switch maps OUT LOUD and test three quadrants: 'Examiner, given the severity I am going to assess by quadrant rather than by nine regions. Second quadrant -' (scream) '- tender. Third quadrant -' (scream) '- tender again. I am not going to test the fourth, because I am now confident this is generalised and I do not want to cause unnecessary pain. There is guarding; there is no rigidity.'

The skip, spoken in full: 'Examiner — on that basis I am stopping superficial palpation here. I am skipping deep palpation and rebound tenderness, and I am skipping percussion, because they would add nothing and would cause unnecessary pain. I will continue with the rest of the examination.'

What still costs her nothing: 'Jane, I'm just going to listen with my stethoscope — this won't hurt. Examiner, bowel sounds are present. I would like to inspect the inguinal regions for hernias' → 'normal'; 'a digital rectal examination, with consent and a chaperone' → 'normal'; 'and as this is a woman with lower abdominal pain, a pelvic examination, with consent and a chaperone: on inspection — bleeding, discharge, rash or swelling? On speculum — bleeding or discharge from the cervix, tissue at the os, is the vaginal wall normal? On bimanual — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexal masses or tenderness? And a urine dipstick.' → CMT present, uterus normal size, bilateral adnexal tenderness, dipstick negative.

Diagnosis with reasons, then grouped causes, then plan (see dx). Examiner probes and the answers: 'why no pulsatile mass?' → 'the aorta lies deep and I cannot reach it without a deep palpation this patient cannot tolerate — I would exclude an aneurysm with a bedside ultrasound.' 'Why no shifting dullness if you think there is free blood?' → 'both shifting dullness and a fluid thrill require percussion, and percussion here would be uninterpretable as well as painful.' 'Would you do the appendicitis tests?' → 'no — once peritonism is generalised, localising it to the appendix does not change the management, which is theatre.' Her worry, if it surfaces: 'Am I going to need an operation? My husband's at home on his own.'

Variants: Version A (localised, mild-moderate) — everything unchanged; at the tender area press, hold, WARN, release in one movement, then percuss for tenderness, auscultate, groins, rectum, and finish with the special test matching the quadrant: 'tenderness in the right lower quadrant, rebound negative, tenderness on percussion — that is localised peritonitis.' / Version B (localised, screams on DEEP palpation) — correct to proceed to deep palpation, because that pain is necessary; still take rebound on that single press: 'severe tenderness with rebound in the right upper quadrant. I am going to skip percussion, because peritonism is already established and percussion would only add pain.' The Version-B error is asking her permission to move from superficial to deep — she will say 'it's your call' and you lose both the mark and the time.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Hollis, 52, retired teacher. Sudden severe pain across the WHOLE abdomen three hours ago while watching television, 10/10, unmoved since; no vomiting; bowels opened normally yesterday; ibuprofen most days for her knees and occasional indigestion (Gaviscon); periods stopped four years ago; no operations; rarely drinks, never smoked. Frightened and exhausted, not difficult — lies very still, knees slightly drawn up, breathing shallowly. Asked to cough: 'I can't' (pushed twice: 'I really can't, it's too sore'). Screams loudly and immediately at the FIRST touch anywhere; screams again on the second and third quadrant, tensing the abdominal muscles — that tensing is the guarding. Apologise + explain + ask → 'Alright. Be quick.' Ask without explaining → 'It's your call, doctor. I don't know.' Asked to expose → 'you do it' the first time. 'At my age? No' to pregnancy. If nobody asks her worry: 'Am I going to need an operation? My husband's at home on his own.'

Numbers and technique: capillary refill under 2 s — postural drop >=20 mmHg systolic or >=10 mmHg diastolic — normal liver span 8-12 cm (not tested here) — bowel sounds listened for 2-3 minutes before being called absent VERIFY — THREE quadrants before the word generalised — WIPE in 30-45 s — diagnosis spoken by 7:00. Rebound is press, hold, warn, release in one movement — never lift off and come back to test it separately, that is the same pain inflicted twice.

Four scored domains, only one of which is knowledge: (1) choice and technique of examination — below 4 here and the station fails whatever else you do; (2) accuracy — a press-and-yelp is not a Murphy sign and a shallow prod is not deep palpation; (3) approach to the patient — consent, warning, apology, offer of analgesia, stopping when you have what you need; (4) diagnosis and differentials — structured, by system, delivered before the bell.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. The fever at the door chooses the diagnosis, and the Murphy sign is the scored moment: out, press, IN — in that order, or the role-player is briefed to give you nothing. Look for jaundice TWICE (general appearance, then sclerae). Palpate for the liver EDGE but do not drift into the chronic liver disease station — no liver span here. Automatic fails: taking the temperature and not reacting to it; refusing to go on to deep palpation because superficial hurt; pressing first and then asking for a breath out; leaving out the ECG and the respiratory examination in upper abdominal pain.

Common variant: a 45-year-old woman, same history, with mild scleral jaundice.

back.dx: Acute cholecystitis — right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right scapula, fever 38.4 with tachycardia, RUQ guarding with positive rebound, a positive Murphy sign, and no jaundice. Differentials by system: biliary — biliary colic, ascending cholangitis; gastrointestinal — pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, perforation, hepatitis; cardiorespiratory — inferior myocardial infarction, right lower lobe pneumonia, pulmonary embolism; urinary — right pyelonephritis, renal colic. Investigations: ECG, bloods with LFTs and lipase, FBC/CRP, right upper quadrant ultrasound; expect raised WCC and CRP with normal or mildly deranged LFTs — a markedly raised bilirubin and ALP point to a stone in the common bile duct or cholangitis, a raised lipase to pancreatitis. Management: nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, IV antibiotics and surgical referral for cholecystectomy VERIFY TG; rural SA — discuss transfer with the receiving unit and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if unwell.
plan: Gloves on. 'Examiner, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → '118/74, pulse 104, RR 18, temperature 38.4.' → 'Thank you — he is febrile at 38.4 and mildly tachycardic, which makes an inflammatory or infective cause more likely than simple biliary colic.' (Taking the numbers and moving on loses the mark: the fever is the fact that chooses the diagnosis.)

WIPE: name and date of birth, the four steps, 'I'll need to see the whole tummy — could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? Let me wash my hands. Are you in pain now — would you like something for it?' → 'It's bad. They gave me something twenty minutes ago.'

Jaundice twice, and the peripheries: 'Examiner — on general appearance he is alert, in obvious pain, lying still, NOT JAUNDICED and not pale. Jake, may I see your hands? Capillary refill under two seconds, turgor normal, no pale palmar creases, no cold peripheries, pulse of good volume. Could you look up for me? No conjunctival pallor, and NO SCLERAL ICTERUS.'

Inspection and cough: 'No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no masses, no redness. Bending down — the abdomen moves symmetrically with respiration. Jake, could you cough for me and tell me where it hurts?' → 'Ah! Up here, under my right ribs.'

Superficial then deep — do not stop: 'I'll feel your tummy very gently, starting on the far side. Tell me the moment it hurts.' → 'ooh, there. That's sore.' → 'Examiner — mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant on superficial palpation, with guarding and no rigidity. Jake, I need to press a bit deeper now to feel underneath. Tell me if it hurts.' → he SCREAMS → 'I'm so sorry. I'm keeping my hand exactly where it is for a second... now I'm taking it away. Tell me if you get a stab of pain.' → 'Ow! Yes, that was worse.' → 'Severe tenderness with guarding and positive rebound in the right upper quadrant. I'm going to skip percussion, as localised peritonism is established and percussion would only add pain.'

Liver edge — not a span: 'Starting in the right iliac fossa and moving up towards the costal margin on each expiration — the liver edge is not palpable and there is no palpable gallbladder.' Then 'auscultating below the umbilicus — bowel sounds are present. I'd like to inspect the inguinal regions for hernias' → 'normal' — 'and a digital rectal examination, with consent and a chaperone' → 'skip that.' (Percussing a liver span here costs you the minute you need for Murphy and the differentials.)

THE MURPHY SIGN, in three named steps: 'Jake, one more test. I'll ask you to breathe all the way out, then I'll press in under your right ribs, then I'll ask you to take a deep breath in. It may be uncomfortable — is that all right? ... Breathe all the way out for me... and out... good. Pressing in under the ribs now... and take a deep breath in.' → he starts to inhale, catches his breath and stops: 'Ah — ! No, I can't.' → 'Thank you, I'm sorry. Examiner — Murphy sign is positive: he arrested inspiration as the gallbladder descended on to my fingers. Repeating the manoeuvre on the left produces no pain, so the sign is specific.'

The two offers, then the explanation: 'Examiner, given the site of the pain I would also like an ECG, because an inferior myocardial infarction can present as upper abdominal pain, and I would like to examine the respiratory system for a right lower lobe pneumonia.' → 'Jake, I think your gallbladder is inflamed — that's a small bag under your liver that stores bile to help digest fat. If a small stone blocks its outlet the bag gets inflamed and infected. That fits everything: pain after a meal, the temperature, and catching your breath when I pressed. I'd like blood tests and an ultrasound. You'll need antibiotics through a drip and most likely an operation to take the gallbladder out.' → 'Do I have to have the operation?' → 'The surgical team will discuss it, but a gallbladder that has made one stone usually makes more, so removing it is the usual advice — you can live perfectly well without it.'
Present: most likely acute cholecystitis, with the system-grouped differential list and the investigations (see dx).

'I'm keeping my hand exactly where it is — now I'm taking it away.' / 'I am going to skip percussion, and this is why.' / 'Moving up from the right iliac fossa on each expiration — the liver edge is not palpable.'

The Murphy lines: 'Breathe all the way out... pressing in... now take a deep breath in.' / 'Murphy sign is positive — he arrested inspiration.' / 'Repeating on the left produces no pain, so the sign is specific.' / 'Given the site of the pain I would also like an ECG and to examine the respiratory system.'

Variants: jaundiced and rigoring → 'RUQ pain, fever with rigors and scleral icterus — that is Charcot triad, and my diagnosis is ascending cholangitis. He is also hypotensive and confused, which makes this Reynolds pentad. I would resuscitate, take blood cultures, start IV antibiotics and arrange urgent biliary drainage by ERCP — antibiotics alone will not treat an obstructed, infected biliary tree.' / settled and afebrile with a negative Murphy → 'more consistent with biliary colic: outpatient ultrasound, dietary advice about fatty food, and referral for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.' / 'how can the abdominal examination be normal in a myocardial infarction?' → 'because the pain is referred — visceral afferents from the inferior wall enter the cord at the same levels as upper abdominal structures, so the patient localises it to the epigastrium even though nothing in the abdomen is inflamed. That is why a soft, non-tender abdomen does not reassure me and why I want the ECG.' / 'what would you expect on the bloods?' → raised WCC and CRP with normal or mildly deranged LFTs; markedly raised bilirubin and ALP → CBD stone or cholangitis; raised lipase → pancreatitis.
pefe: Role-player: Jake Morrissey, 35, diesel mechanic. Fish and chips last night, severe pain under the right ribs an hour later, constant, 8/10, radiating to the right shoulder blade; vomited once; hot and shivery; two or three milder episodes this year after big meals, always settling in a couple of hours; four or five beers on a Friday, non-smoker, no medicines, allergies or operations. In real pain, slightly impatient, not hostile. Coughs, winces, points under the right ribs. Superficial RUQ: 'ooh, that's sore', nothing elsewhere. Deep RUQ: SCREAMS and says stop, tensing the muscles. On release: 'ow — that was worse.' THE MURPHY IS THE KEY MOMENT — he reacts ONLY if you ask him to breathe out first, then press, then ask him to breathe in; if you simply press and ask if it hurts he says 'yes' and nothing more. Repeat on the left → 'no, that's fine.' Worry near the end: 'Am I going to need an operation? I've got work on Monday.'

Numbers: gallbladder wall over 3 mm on ultrasound — common bile duct over 6 mm VERIFY — biliary colic settles in 1-6 hours; cholecystitis is constant beyond six hours with fever — Charcot triad is three (RUQ pain, fever/rigors, jaundice), Reynolds pentad is five (plus hypotension and confusion) — Murphy done by 6:30, diagnosis started by 7:00. Three biliary syndromes to keep separate: biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, ascending cholangitis.

Scored behaviours: asked for the temperature and commented on the fever — jaundice commented on TWICE — proceeded to deep palpation despite superficial tenderness — rebound taken in a single movement — percussion skipped OUT LOUD with a reason — liver edge palpated and no span measured — groins and rectum requested — Murphy in the correct order with the left-sided control — ECG and respiratory examination offered — plain-language explanation plus a system-grouped list.
fails: ★ Taking the vitals and not reacting to the fever — it is the fact that chooses the diagnosis
★ Reporting jaundice only once; the sclerae are a separate observation and yellowing appears there first
Stopping at superficial palpation because it hurt — mild superficial tenderness is a reason to continue to deep palpation, not to stop; or lifting off and coming back to test rebound separately
Murphy performed in the wrong order (press first, then ask for a breath out) — the gallbladder has to be out of reach before your hand goes in; and never testing the left side to show specificity
Drifting into a liver span and the chronic liver disease examination; leaving out the ECG and the respiratory examination in upper abdominal pain

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED, VERSION A of the RLQ-pain-in-a-woman document: the pregnancy-positive version. The pelvic examination is the station, and the UTERINE SIZE is the single fact that separates an ectopic pregnancy from an intrauterine pregnancy with a separate adnexal problem — read the findings back before you commit. Automatic fails: never offering a pelvic examination in a woman with lower abdominal pain; never asking for a urine pregnancy test; hearing 'uterus enlarged, about ten weeks' and still saying ectopic; spending the last minute on Rovsing and obturator and reaching the bell without a diagnosis.
stem: Emergency department. A 27-year-old woman with pain in the right lower abdomen for one week — intermittent at first, now constant, 6/10. Nauseated, vomited twice. A home urine pregnancy test was weakly positive. BP 110/70 with no postural drop — HR 80 — RR 12 — T 36.5. The pelvic examination will be given to you verbally if you ask for it.

Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: DOOR: vitals INCLUDING temperature (fever moves PID up the list) · WIPE, expose ('you do it' → 'is it all right if I lower your trousers a little?'), wash, offer analgesia · peripheral survey and inspection in 40 s: general appearance, CRT, turgor, palmar creases, peripheries, pulse volume, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, conjunctival pallor; Cullen and Grey Turner by name, scars, distension, masses, bend down and look across · cough → she localises to the RLQ · superficial palpation of all nine regions starting away from the pain: no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity → deep palpation: RLQ tenderness → rebound in ONE movement (press, hold, WARN, release) → Version A: rebound NEGATIVE · percussion for tenderness, auscultate below the umbilicus, groins, DRE with consent and chaperone (tender? stool? blood on the glove?) · THE PELVIC EXAMINATION, unprompted, with consent and a chaperone: inspection / speculum / bimanual naming all four items (cervical motion tenderness, uterine SIZE, uterine tenderness and contour, adnexal masses and tenderness) + urine pregnancy test and dipstick · read the findings back, then commit: normal-sized uterus + CMT + adnexal tenderness + positive test = ectopic; uterus enlarged to ten weeks = intrauterine pregnancy with a separate adnexal problem · four-bucket differential (GI / O&G / KUB / MSK) · special tests only if time remains.

back.dx: Findings set 1 — inspection and speculum normal, cervical motion tenderness POSITIVE, uterus NORMAL SIZE, right adnexal tenderness, urine pregnancy test positive: ectopic pregnancy. 'The pregnancy is not where it should be.' Serum beta-hCG, urgent transvaginal ultrasound, gynaecology now. Findings set 2 — CMT negative, uterus ENLARGED to about ten weeks, right adnexal tenderness, test positive: an intrauterine pregnancy with a SEPARATE adnexal problem — ovarian cyst, haemorrhagic cyst or its rupture, ovarian torsion, salpingitis, and rarely a heterotopic pregnancy; urgent ultrasound and gynaecology review. Four-bucket differential: gastrointestinal — appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, mesenteric adenitis, strangulated hernia, bowel cancer in an older patient; obstetric and gynaecological — ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ovarian cyst or rupture, pelvic inflammatory disease; urinary — ureteric colic, urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis; musculoskeletal — septic arthritis of the hip, rectus sheath haematoma. If she is shocked with a positive test and peritonism: treat as a ruptured ectopic — two large cannulae, bloods with cross-match, fluid resuscitation, massive transfusion protocol if needed, gynaecology and theatre now, no delay for ultrasound; rural SA — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 while resuscitating.
plan: 'Examiner, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?' → '110/70, no postural drop, pulse 80, RR 12, temperature 36.5.' → 'Thank you — she is afebrile and haemodynamically stable.' (Not asking for the temperature is the trap: fever moves pelvic inflammatory disease up the list.)

WIPE: name and date of birth, the four steps, 'I'll need to see the whole tummy, so could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? Stay lying as you are. Let me wash my hands. Are you in pain now — would you like something for it?' → 'You'll have to do the clothes' → 'Of course. Is it all right if I lower your trousers a little so I can see the whole tummy?'

Peripheral survey and inspection (four scored steps, forty seconds — do not rush it to get to the pelvis): 'Alert, in mild discomfort, not pale, not jaundiced. Hands — capillary refill under two seconds, turgor normal, no pale palmar creases, no cold peripheries, pulse of good volume. Face — no sunken eyes, no dry mucous membranes, no conjunctival pallor. Abdomen — no Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no masses, no redness. Bending down — it moves symmetrically with respiration.'

Cough, then palpation: 'Jane, could you cough for me and tell me if you feel any pain, and where?' → 'Yes — down here on the right.' → 'I'll feel your tummy very gently now, starting away from the sore side.' → 'Superficial palpation of all nine regions: no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity.' → 'I'll press a little deeper this time.' → 'Ah — yes, that's sore.' → rebound in ONE movement: 'I'm going to keep my hand exactly where it is... and now take it away — tell me if you get a stab of pain.' → Version A: 'No, that's alright' = rebound negative.

'Jane, I'll tap gently over the sore area — tell me if it hurts. Examiner — tenderness on percussion of the right lower quadrant is present/absent. Auscultating below the umbilicus — bowel sounds are present. I would like to inspect the inguinal regions for hernias' → 'normal' — 'and a digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone — is it tender, can I feel stool, and is there blood on the glove?' (Asking is the mark; a 'skip that' does not excuse never having asked.)

THE PELVIC EXAMINATION, offered unprompted: 'Examiner, as this is a woman with lower abdominal pain I would like to perform a pelvic examination, with the patient's consent and with a chaperone present. On inspection — any bleeding, discharge, rash, swelling or mass? On speculum — any bleeding or discharge from the cervix, any tissue at the os, is the vaginal wall normal? On bimanual — is there cervical motion tenderness? What is the SIZE of the uterus, is it tender, and is the contour regular? And in the adnexae — masses or tenderness? Finally, a urine pregnancy test and a urine dipstick, please.'

READ THE FINDINGS BACK before committing. Set 1: 'CMT positive, uterus normal size, right adnexal tenderness, pregnancy test positive — my most likely diagnosis is an ectopic pregnancy: the pregnancy is not where it should be. Serum beta-hCG, urgent transvaginal ultrasound, and I would involve gynaecology now.' Set 2: 'the uterus is enlarged to about ten weeks, so this is an intrauterine pregnancy with a separate adnexal problem — most likely an ovarian cyst, a haemorrhagic cyst or its rupture, ovarian torsion or salpingitis, and rarely a heterotopic pregnancy. Urgent ultrasound and gynaecology review.'

The four-bucket differential (see dx), then her worry if it has not surfaced: 'Doctor, is the baby all right?' → answer honestly and without abandoning the plan. Special tests (Rovsing, obturator) ONLY if time remains — if the bell goes here in Version A you have lost the diagnosis, and nobody fails an ectopic station for omitting an obturator sign.

back.dx: Acute appendicitis — pain that began periumbilically and migrated to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, RLQ tenderness on deep palpation with POSITIVE rebound and tenderness on percussion, Rovsing positive and obturator positive; pelvic examination and urine pregnancy test normal/negative, which is what allows the diagnosis to stand. Explain in plain language: the appendix is a small pouch where the small bowel joins the large bowel, low down on the right; it hurt when I pressed there, it hurt more when I let go, and both extra tests brought the pain back to that spot. Usual treatment is an operation to remove it — bloods, imaging, and the surgical team to see her now. Four-bucket differential: gastrointestinal — inflammatory bowel disease, mesenteric adenitis, strangulated hernia, bowel cancer in an older patient; obstetric and gynaecological — ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ovarian cyst or rupture, pelvic inflammatory disease; urinary — ureteric colic, urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis; musculoskeletal — septic arthritis of the hip, rectus sheath haematoma. Rural SA: if theatre is not available on site, keep her nil by mouth, cannulate, analgese, discuss with the receiving surgical unit and arrange transfer (MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33), PATS for the family's follow-up travel.

Tell me if you feel any pain, and where.' → 'Yes — but it hurts over on the right.' → 'Examiner, Rovsing sign is positive.' → 'I'm now going to bend your right hip and knee and gently move your ankle outwards. Is that all right?' → 'Ooh. That hurts, down low.' → 'Obturator sign is positive.'

Explain and present: 'Jane, I think you most likely have appendicitis... The reasons are that it hurt when I pressed there, it hurt more when I let go, and both of the extra tests I did brought the pain back to that spot. The usual treatment is an operation to take it out.' → 'Will I need surgery today?' → 'Most likely, yes. I'll take some blood tests and arrange a scan, and I'm going to ask the surgical team to see you now.' Then the four-bucket differential to the examiner (see dx).

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — medical outpatient clinic. This is NOT an acute abdomen: the whole point of the station is the examination the acute abdomen station forbids. Differentials for the liver disease: viral hepatitis B or C, fatty liver disease, haemochromatosis, autoimmune liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma. Differentials for the ascites itself: malignancy, right heart failure, nephrotic syndrome. Plan: bloods including coagulation profile and albumin, DIAGNOSTIC ascitic tap for cell count, culture and cytology, ultrasound with Doppler, endoscopic variceal screening, salt restriction with spironolactone and frusemide VERIFY TG, and referral for alcohol support — abrupt unsupported cessation is dangerous, so assess withdrawal risk first. plan: 'May I have his vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' → 'all within normal limits, afebrile.' WIPE: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. I've been asked to examine your tummy today. I'll start by looking at your hands and your face, then I'll look at your tummy, gently feel it, gently tap on it, and listen with my stethoscope. I'll need to see you from the CHEST down to the HIPS, so could you take your shirt off and lower your trousers a little? Let me wash my hands. Are you in any pain?' → 'No pain. It's just the size of it — my ankles have gone up too.'

Hands and the flap: 'Leukonychia is present; no clubbing; palmar erythema; a Dupuytren contracture of the right ring finger; no pale palmar creases. Could you hold both arms straight out, bend your hands back at the wrists as if stopping traffic, and spread your fingers? Hold that for me.' HOLD 15-30 SECONDS. 'Examiner, after thirty seconds there is no flapping tremor.' → 'what does a flap indicate?' → 'hepatic encephalopathy; I would hold the position fifteen to thirty seconds. It is not specific to the liver — it also occurs in carbon dioxide retention and in uraemia.'

Arms, face, chest (do not spend more than three minutes here — everything after this is worth more): 'No bruising or scratch marks; I count six spider naevi over the upper chest and arms, which is more than the five that can be normal, and they blanch from the centre. Could you lift both arms above your head?' → 'that's hard work, they feel heavy' → 'there is proximal weakness, consistent with an alcohol-related proximal myopathy.' 'Look up — there is scleral icterus; no conjunctival pallor; no xanthelasma. Feeling in front of and below both ears — bilateral parotid enlargement. Open your mouth and put your tongue out — no glossitis, no fetor hepaticus. Chest — gynaecomastia and loss of body hair. Left supraclavicular fossa — no lymphadenopathy.'

Abdomen: 'The abdomen is distended with fullness in the flanks, the umbilicus is everted, and there are dilated veins radiating from it — caput medusae. No scars. Bending down to look across — it moves symmetrically with respiration. Superficial palpation of all nine regions — soft, no tenderness, no guarding. Deep palpation — no discrete masses.'

THE LIVER SPAN: 'Could you take some deep breaths in and out for me? Starting in the right iliac fossa and moving up towards the costal margin on each expiration, using the radial border of my index finger — the liver edge is palpable three centimetres below the costal margin, firm, smooth, non-tender, with a regular edge. Now percussing downwards from above the nipple in the mid-clavicular line for the upper border — resonant... resonant... dull, at the fifth intercostal space. Measuring between the two, the liver span is fifteen centimetres — enlarged; normal is eight to twelve.' If you cannot feel the edge, SAY SO and still give a number: 'the liver edge is not palpable below the costal margin, so I will take the costal margin as my lower border and measure from there.'

Spleen and kidneys: 'Palpating for the spleen FROM THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA towards the left costal margin on expiration — the spleen is palpable two centimetres below the left costal margin. I'll roll him towards me into the right lateral position and feel again to confirm. Percussing Castell's point in the lowest left intercostal space in the anterior axillary line — it becomes dull on inspiration, supporting splenomegaly. Ballotting both kidneys — not enlarged.' (Starting at the umbilicus means palpating straight over a large spleen.)

THE TWO ASCITES TESTS: 'I'm going to tap on your tummy and then ask you to roll on to your side — is that all right? Percussing from the umbilicus out to the left flank — resonant, resonant, dull here. I'll keep my finger exactly on that spot. Could you roll towards me on to your right side?' WAIT ABOUT THIRTY SECONDS, re-percuss the marked point: 'it is now resonant — shifting dullness is present.' Then: 'one more test — could you place the edge of your own hand firmly down the middle of your tummy? That stops the wave travelling through the fat instead of the fluid. I'll place my hand flat on one side and flick the other... a fluid thrill is present.'

Auscultation and the three offers: 'Bowel sounds present. Listening over the liver and the epigastrium — no bruit. To complete I would examine the legs for pitting oedema, examine the external genitalia for testicular atrophy with consent and a chaperone, perform a digital rectal examination for melaena and haemorrhoids, and formally assess for hepatic encephalopathy.' → 'legs show pitting oedema to the mid-shin.'

Explain, then present: 'The swelling is fluid, not fat or wind — two of the tests I did show that clearly. Fluid builds up when the liver becomes scarred and stiff, so blood can't flow through it easily and the pressure backs up. We call that cirrhosis... The single most important treatment is stopping alcohol completely, because the liver can recover if the damage stops. Stopping suddenly on your own can be dangerous, so I'd like to arrange proper support.' → 'I've tried before.' → 'That's very common, and trying before makes the next attempt more likely to work, not less.' Then the examiner presentation and plan (see dx).

Inside the room: a mannequin torso on the bed and a person seated in a chair. An abdominal X-ray is on the wall or handed to you.

back.dx: Simple (not strangulated) small bowel obstruction, most likely ADHESIONAL from the previous open appendicectomy — absolute constipation with no flatus, bilious vomiting, generalised symmetrical distension, a soft non-tender resonant abdomen, an empty rectum, and a supine film showing centrally placed dilated loops over 3 cm with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the lumen and no rectal gas. Differentials: obstructing malignancy, an obstructed hernia, and in the large bowel a volvulus or faecal impaction. Plan — drip and suck: nil by mouth, IV fluid resuscitation, nasogastric tube, urinary catheter, bloods including a lactate, erect chest X-ray and CT abdomen and pelvis, surgical referral; adhesional obstruction may be given about 48 hours of conservative management if there is no peritonism VERIFY. Operate immediately for: peritonism, fever, tachycardia, a rising lactate, free gas on the erect film, a strangulated hernia, or a caecum beyond about 9 cm. Rural SA: start all of it locally and call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and the receiving unit together; PATS for the family's travel.
plan: 'Examiner, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature? And may I confirm — am I examining the model on the bed, and is this gentleman the patient?' → 'Observations are stable. That is the patient's son. The patient is the mannequin.' (Guessing here is how the whole station goes wrong.)

WIPE to the son: 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors here. Are you Mr Hallam's son? Thank you for coming in, Danny. I've been asked to examine your dad's tummy — I'll look at it, gently feel it, gently tap on it, and listen with my stethoscope at the end. I'll ask you a few questions as I go, because you may know things he hasn't been able to tell us. Is that all right? Examiner — I would confirm the patient's own consent for the examination and for discussing his care with his son. Let me wash my hands.' → 'He has consented. Please continue.'

History while you work: 'When did your dad last open his bowels?' → 'Tuesday.' 'And HAS HE PASSED ANY WIND since then?' → 'No — he said that's what's bothering him.' 'What's the vomiting been like — how often, and what colour?' → 'Six or seven times since yesterday. It's gone green.' 'Has his tummy been swollen?' → 'Like a drum.' 'Any weight loss, or blood in the motions?' → 'No.' 'And what operations has he had?' → 'He had his appendix out when he was young.'

Inspection of the mannequin — do not skip it: 'Exposing from the xiphisternum to below the umbilicus. No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign. There is a RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA SCAR consistent with an open appendicectomy. The abdomen is distended. No visible peristalsis, no obvious mass. Bending down to look across — the distension is symmetrical and generalised.'

Palpation, percussion, auscultation without inventing anything: 'Superficial palpation of all nine regions — no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity. Examiner, is there any tenderness on deep palpation?' → 'No tenderness anywhere.' → 'Deep palpation of all nine regions — no tenderness, no palpable mass. As there is no tenderness, rebound cannot meaningfully be assessed. Percussing all four quadrants — resonant throughout, consistent with gaseous distension, no tenderness on percussion. Auscultating below the umbilicus — bowel sounds are present.' → 'What sort of bowel sounds?' → 'I report them as present or absent. If they were abnormal I would describe the character — high-pitched and tinkling in mechanical obstruction, and absent in ileus or a late, exhausted obstruction.' (Never 'hyperactive'.)

Groins and rectum: 'I would inspect and palpate both inguinal regions and the SCROTUM for a hernia, since an obstructed hernia is a cause I can find at the bedside.' → 'No hernia.' → 'And a digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone — is the rectum empty or loaded, is there a mass, and is there blood on the glove?' → 'The rectum is empty. No mass, no blood.' → 'An empty rectum supports a mechanical obstruction proximally rather than faecal impaction.'

THE FILM: 'This is a supine plain abdominal radiograph of an adult, marked right, and I would confirm the patient's identity and the date. Reviewing systematically — the bowel gas pattern shows multiple dilated loops which are CENTRALLY placed, with mucosal folds crossing the FULL WIDTH of the lumen, so these are valvulae conniventes and this is small bowel. The loops measure over three centimetres. There is no gas in the rectum. There is no free gas and no abnormal calcification. The solid organ outlines, the bones and the lung bases are unremarkable. The appearances are of small bowel obstruction.'

Explain to the son, then present: 'There's a blockage in his bowel, Danny. The loops above it have filled with gas and fluid and swollen up, and there's nothing beyond it. Given he had his appendix out years ago, the most likely reason is scar tissue forming bands that kink the bowel — adhesions. The reassuring part is that his tummy is soft and not tender, which suggests the blood supply is still all right.' → 'Does he need an operation?' → 'Possibly, but not necessarily. First we rest the bowel completely — nothing to eat or drink — put a drip in for fluids, and pass a small tube through his nose into his stomach to drain what's building up. That stops the vomiting and takes the pressure off, and quite often the blockage settles by itself over a day or two. The surgical team will see him; if it doesn't settle, or if we become worried about the blood supply, he'd need surgery and we'd transfer him to Adelaide.' Then the examiner presentation and plan (see dx).

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED. Hydration is a full structured examination in its own right and is scored SEPARATELY from the abdomen. The single most commonly omitted item in the station is the POSTURAL blood pressure — it is not among the routine observations, so 'the observations are stable' never includes it: ask again, specifically. Then choose ONE dominant complaint for the differential list rather than hunting for a single diagnosis that explains all four symptoms, and offer gastroenteritis as a diagnosis of exclusion with the dangerous mimics named first. Automatic fails: accepting 'stable' and never getting a standing pressure; reporting dry LIPS as dry mucous membranes; skipping the abdominal examination because you expect it to be normal.
stem: Version A: Emergency department. A 35-year-old man with abdominal pain, fever, vomiting and diarrhoea for two days; observations in the notes. Lying BP 118/76, pulse 92; standing 96/64, pulse 112 — RR 16 — T 37.8.

Version B (February 2026 recall): Emergency department. A patient with vomiting and diarrhoea. Your ONLY task is to assess hydration status and report your findings — same eight minutes for a quarter of the work.
tasks: Assess his hydration status
Perform a focused abdominal examination
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the examiner
time: DOOR: 'for the hydration assessment may I have the vital signs · and may I have the LYING AND STANDING blood pressures, please?' → fobbed off with 'stable' → ask again: 'may I specifically have the standing blood pressure? A normal lying pressure does not exclude significant volume depletion' → 118/76 lying, 96/64 standing, pulse 92 to 112 = a drop of 22 systolic and 12 diastolic with a compensatory tachycardia · SAY THE TECHNIQUE OUT LOUD: supine rest 5 minutes, systolic by palpation first then auscultation to avoid an auscultatory gap, stand and repeat at ONE and THREE minutes recording the pulse each time, and ask him to say if he feels dizzy · WIPE · hydration items: conscious level, CRT (prolonged at 3 s), skin turgor (the fold tents), pulse volume (low), peripheries warm and dry, sunken eyes, 'could you OPEN YOUR MOUTH for me' · dry mucous membranes and no pooled saliva · charts: fluid balance, urine output, a recorded weight to compare · GRADE it and say what the grade changes: 'moderate dehydration · he needs intravenous rather than oral rehydration' · abdomen in full even though you expect it to be normal: Cullen/Grey Turner, scars, distension, masses, bend down, cough, superficial nine regions, deep (mild generalised crampy discomfort only), no tenderness on percussion, auscultate, groins, DRE with consent and chaperone looking for BLOOD · then 'I will take abdominal pain as the dominant complaint' and the system list.

back.dx: Acute infective gastroenteritis with MODERATE dehydration — postural hypotension (22 systolic / 12 diastolic) with compensatory tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill at 3 seconds, reduced turgor, low-volume pulse, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, negative balance of about 1.5 L and poor urine output; abdomen soft and non-tender with only generalised crampy discomfort, and no blood on the rectal examination. Announce ONE dominant complaint — abdominal pain — then: the two other diagnoses that would explain all four symptoms are appendicitis and inflammatory bowel disease; by system — gastrointestinal: diverticulitis, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, C. difficile colitis, bowel cancer; urinary: pyelonephritis, renal calculus, urinary tract infection; obstetric and gynaecological in a woman: ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian torsion; metabolic: diabetic ketoacidosis. Plan: bloods with a lactate, capillary glucose and ketones, urine dipstick, beta-hCG in a woman, IV sodium chloride 0.9% and an antiemetic; NOT antibiotics routinely; stool sample if blood or mucus, prolonged or severe illness, recent antibiotics or hospital, travel, immunosuppression, or a suspected outbreak. Safety-net: return if unable to keep fluids down, blood, severe or localising pain, or no urine output. Public health: exclusion from food handling until 48 hours symptom-free VERIFY.
plan: 'Examiner, for the hydration assessment may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature? And may I have the lying and standing blood pressures, please?' → '118/76, pulse 92, RR 16, temperature 37.8.' → ASK AGAIN: 'Thank you — may I specifically have the standing blood pressure and standing pulse? A normal lying pressure doesn't exclude significant volume depletion.' → 'Standing, 96/64, pulse 112.' → 'The systolic falls by 22 and the diastolic by 12 with a rise in pulse rate — that is postural hypotension and it indicates significant intravascular volume depletion.'

The technique, spoken (this paragraph is most of the technique mark, and in Version B most of the spare five minutes): 'I would rest him supine for five minutes and take the pressure, taking the systolic by palpation first and then confirming by auscultation so I do not miss an auscultatory gap. I would then stand him and repeat at one minute and at three minutes, recording the pulse each time, and I would ask him to tell me if he feels dizzy.'

WIPE: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. I've been asked to check how dehydrated you are and then to examine your tummy. I'll look at your hands and your face, then look at, feel, tap and listen to your tummy. Could you pull your top up and lower your trousers a little? Let me wash my hands. Are you in pain at the moment — would you like anything for it?' → 'It's just crampy. It comes and goes. I feel awful, though — dizzy when I stand up.'

The hydration examination itself: 'Examiner, he is alert and orientated. May I see your hands? Capillary refill is prolonged at three seconds. Pinching a fold of skin on the forearm — turgor is reduced, the fold tents. The radial pulse is of low volume. The peripheries are warm and dry. Looking at the face — the eyes are sunken. COULD YOU OPEN YOUR MOUTH FOR ME?' → 'It's like sandpaper in there.' → 'The mucous membranes are dry and there is no pooled saliva.' (Dry lips are not dry mucous membranes.)

The charts and the grade: 'Examiner, may I see the fluid balance chart and the urine output, and does he have a recorded weight I can compare?' → 'Negative balance of about a litre and a half. Urine output has been poor. No weight available.' → 'Putting that together — postural hypotension with a compensatory tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, reduced turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output — this is MODERATE dehydration, and he needs intravenous rather than oral rehydration.'

The abdomen in full, despite expecting it to be normal: 'No Cullen sign, no Grey Turner sign, no scars, no distension, no masses. Bending down — it moves symmetrically with respiration. Could you cough for me and tell me if it hurts?' → 'It pulls a bit but it doesn't really hurt.' → 'Superficial palpation of all nine regions, starting away from the pain — soft, no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity. Deep palpation — mild generalised crampy discomfort only, no localised tenderness, no rebound and no masses. No tenderness on percussion. Auscultating below the umbilicus — bowel sounds are present. I would inspect the inguinal regions for hernias, and I would like a digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone, looking in particular for BLOOD on the glove.' → 'Groins normal, rectal normal, no blood.' (Report the normal abdomen as a finding, not apologetically — it is what removes appendicitis, obstruction and diverticulitis from the top of the list.)

Explain: 'The good news is that your tummy is soft and not tender, which makes something surgical like appendicitis much less likely. I think this is most likely a tummy bug — an infection of the gut, usually viral. What does concern me is how much fluid you've lost: your blood pressure dropped when you stood, your mouth is dry and your skin is slow to spring back. I'd like to put a drip in, give you fluid and something for the sickness, and take some blood tests.' → 'How long will I be here?' → 'A few hours at least, until you can keep fluids down and your blood pressure stays up when you stand.' Safety-net in plain words.

Present: 'Rather than looking for one diagnosis that explains all four symptoms, I'll take abdominal pain as the dominant complaint...' then the list and the plan (see dx), ending with 'I would not give antibiotics routinely.'
V-B

VERSION B — filling the spare five minutes, in order and out loud: the full technique for the postural reading; palpatory then auscultatory systolic; readings at one and three minutes with the pulse; symptoms on standing; then EVERY peripheral sign with its normal value stated; then the jugular venous pressure from the sternal angle; then the fluid balance chart, urine output and a weight; then the grading; then what the grade changes. Finish by offering the bedside tests — capillary glucose and ketones, urine dipstick, and a pregnancy test in a woman. Candidates who finish in three minutes and stand in silence lose marks they could have collected.

'Capillary refill is prolonged at three seconds.' / 'Skin turgor is reduced — the fold tents.' / 'Could you open your mouth for me?' / 'May I see the fluid balance chart and the urine output?' / 'This is moderate dehydration, and he needs intravenous rather than oral rehydration.'

'The abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout.' / 'Looking in particular for blood on the glove.' / 'I will take abdominal pain as the dominant complaint.' / 'I would not give antibiotics routinely.'

Examiner probes: 'why can turgor mislead?' → 'skin elasticity falls with age, so an older patient can tent without being dehydrated, and an obese patient can have normal turgor while significantly depleted — I would weight the postural blood pressure, the urine output and the mucous membranes more heavily.' / 'how would you rehydrate?' → 'mild — oral rehydration solution in small frequent volumes; the glucose and sodium content matters, so plain water or soft drink is not equivalent. Moderate to severe, or persistent vomiting — IV sodium chloride 0.9%, with a bolus of about 20 mL/kg if shocked VERIFY, then reassessment. Check electrolytes before adding potassium, and reassess the postural blood pressure and urine output rather than working to a fixed volume.' / 'could this be something else entirely?' → 'three that are easy to miss: diabetic ketoacidosis, which is why I want a capillary glucose and ketones; ectopic pregnancy in any woman, which is why I want a beta-hCG; and in an older patient, sepsis from any source, where the only sign may be confusion and a postural drop.'
pefe: Role-player: Aaron Doyle, 35, shearer. Two days of crampy generalised abdominal pain about 4/10 that moves around, fever, four or five vomits keeping almost nothing down, watery diarrhoea about eight times a day with NO blood; two workmates have the same thing; ate at a roadhouse three days ago; no travel, no recent antibiotics or hospital; has not passed urine since this morning and it was dark; dizzy on standing; very thirsty; no medicines, allergies or operations. Flat and tired, not distressed. VOLUNTEERS the dizziness on standing early — a gift to a candidate who has not thought about the postural blood pressure. Asked to open his mouth: 'it's like sandpaper in there'; if they only look at his lips he says nothing. Coughs — 'it pulls a bit, doesn't really hurt.' No pain on superficial palpation; on deep palpation 'that's just the crampy feeling, nowhere in particular' — never localises, never guards. Worry near the end: 'Do I need to be admitted? I'm meant to be back at work Monday.'

Numbers: postural drop >=20 mmHg systolic or >=10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes VERIFY — capillary refill under 2 s — supine rest 5 minutes before the lying reading — moderate dehydration 5-10% of body weight VERIFY — resuscitation bolus 20 mL/kg of sodium chloride 0.9% VERIFY — C. difficile: oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days VERIFY — exclusion from food handling until 48 hours symptom-free VERIFY. Fourteen hydration items: conscious level, CRT, turgor, pulse volume, peripheries, sunken eyes, mucous membranes, pooled saliva, thirst, postural BP, postural pulse, urine output, fluid balance chart, weight.

Scored behaviours: asked for the STANDING blood pressure — and asked AGAIN when told the observations were stable — described the postural technique fully — reported level of consciousness — CRT, turgor, pulse volume, peripheries — asked him to open his mouth — looked for sunken eyes — asked for the fluid balance chart and urine output — GRADED the dehydration and said what the grade changes — did the whole abdominal examination despite expecting it to be normal — requested groins and a rectal examination mentioning blood — announced ONE dominant complaint before listing differentials — named appendicitis and inflammatory bowel disease near the top — mentioned glucose, ketones and a pregnancy test in a woman — said antibiotics are not routine.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — hospital ward. A normal screening examination with ONE finding that only appears if you actively test for it: hold both arms out, palms up, eyes closed, and WAIT A FULL TEN SECONDS. Miss the drift and you report a normal examination in a man who has had a TIA. 'Basic' means SCREENING — all four limbs, representative roots, gait at the end; it does not mean an exhaustive examination of one limb and it does not mean cranial nerves. The examiner interrupts three times with skip instructions and you must obey INSTANTLY and say what you are omitting. Automatic fails: examining one limb when the task said basic/screening; arguing with or ignoring a skip; unsafe gait assessment; silence — examining with no commentary.
stem: Hospital ward. A 54-year-old man admitted after a brief episode of feeling weak and clumsy down one side, which has now resolved. He is alert and comfortable; vital signs stable.
tasks: Perform a basic neurological physical examination with running commentary
State your findings and where you would localise any abnormality
time: DECLARE (15 s): 'I will perform a screening neurological examination of all four limbs · inspection, tone, power, reflexes, screening sensation and coordination · comparing both sides throughout, and I will assess gait at the end if it is safe' · WIPE 35 s + global look: alert and comfortable, speech fluent, face symmetrical, no tremor or involuntary movement, no mobility aid at the bedside · UPPER LIMBS 95 s: inspection, tone (let your arms go floppy), power C5 abduction / C5-6 elbow flexion / C7 extension / C8 grip / T1 finger abduction, biceps + supinator + triceps · THE TEST THAT MAKES THE STATION 15 s: 'hold both arms straight out in front, palms up, close your eyes' and WAIT TEN SECONDS → right arm pronates and sinks → 'there is a pronator drift of the right arm · an upper motor neuron sign, the only abnormality so far; I will pay particular attention to the right side' · LOWER LIMBS 95 s: inspection, tone + ankle clonus, power L2/3 hip flexion, L3/4 knee extension, L5/S1 knee flexion, L4/5 dorsiflexion, L5 great-toe extension, S1/2 plantarflexion, knee and ankle jerks, PLANTARS ('this may feel unpleasant') · SENSATION 60 s: cotton wool demonstrated on the sternum, C5/C6/C8 and L3/L5/S1 with the escalation rule stated · COORDINATION + GAIT 55 s: finger-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin, ask about falls, walk BESIDE him, watch the turn · SUMMARISE 45 s with explicit negatives, then LOCALISE before diagnosing.

back.dx: Normal screening examination in all four limbs EXCEPT a pronator drift of the right arm — a subtle upper motor neuron sign that formal power testing at 5/5 misses. It localises to the LEFT cerebral hemisphere, most likely the corticospinal pathway, and in a man with a transient episode of right-sided weakness that has resolved, the leading diagnosis is a transient ischaemic attack. Say the localisation BEFORE the diagnosis — the localisation is the mark and the diagnosis follows from it. Plan: time-critical even though he looks well — immediate blood glucose, ECG for atrial fibrillation, urgent same-day assessment on the TIA/stroke pathway with brain and carotid imaging, vascular risk factor assessment (BP, lipids, glucose, smoking), antiplatelet or anticoagulant discussed with the stroke service, and do NOT drive until assessed, documented. Completion: cranial nerves, full sensory testing including vibration and proprioception, cardiovascular examination with pulse, heart sounds and BP in both arms, and cognition/speech. If the drift is ABSENT, do not manufacture a finding: 'this is a normal screening neurological examination — a normal examination does not exclude a TIA, because by definition the deficit has resolved, and the urgency of assessment is unchanged.' That sentence scores as well as finding the drift.
plan: Decode and declare: 'Examiner, I will perform a screening neurological examination of all four limbs — inspection, tone, power, reflexes, screening sensation and coordination — comparing both sides throughout, and I will assess gait at the end if it is safe.' (Silently choosing a scaffold means brevity later reads as omission rather than design.)

WIPE and exposure: 'Hello, I am Dr -, one of the doctors here. I have been asked to examine your nerves — I will look at you, check your arms and legs, test strength, reflexes, sensation and coordination, and then watch you walk. I will need your arms and legs exposed. Please tell me if anything is painful. Is that all right?' Then the global look, which produces no physical act but is free marks: 'alert and comfortable at rest, speech fluent, face symmetrical, no tremor or involuntary movement, no mobility aid at the bedside.'

Upper limbs, ITPR: 'no wasting, fasciculation, abnormal posture or tremor. Please let your arms go floppy — tone is normal and symmetrical at the wrist, elbow and shoulder. Copy me and don't let me move you — shoulder abduction C5, elbow flexion C5/6, elbow extension C7, grip C8, finger abduction T1. Power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical from C5 to T1. Biceps, supinator and triceps reflexes are present and symmetrical.'

THE DRIFT: 'Please hold both arms straight out in front of you, palms facing up, and close your eyes. Hold them there for me.' WAIT THE FULL TEN SECONDS in silence. The right arm slowly pronates and sinks. 'Examiner, there is a pronator drift of the right arm. That is an upper motor neuron sign and it is the only abnormality I have found so far. I will pay particular attention to the right side for the remainder of the examination.' (Two or three seconds and the sign never appears — drift detects the pyramidal weakness that 5/5 power testing misses.)

Lower limbs: 'no wasting, fasciculation or deformity. Please let your legs go floppy — tone is normal, and I am testing for ankle clonus, of which there is none. Hip flexion L2/3, knee extension L3/4, knee flexion L5/S1, dorsiflexion L4/5, great-toe extension L5, plantarflexion S1/2 — power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical. Knee jerks L3/4 and ankle jerks S1/2 present and symmetrical. Plantar responses — this may feel unpleasant — are downgoing bilaterally.' (Dropping the plantars in a possible pyramidal lesion throws away the most informative ten seconds available.)

Screening sensation with the escalation rule: 'This is cotton wool, and this is what it feels like on your breastbone. Now please close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' (C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C8 little finger; L3 medial knee, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot, each compared left with right.) 'Screening light touch is intact and symmetrical in representative dermatomes in all four limbs. Had any point been abnormal I would have mapped it fully — distal to proximal for a sensory level and root by root for a dermatomal pattern — and added vibration and proprioception.' (Never apologise for screening; state the plan and the escalation rule.)

Coordination and gait: 'Touch your nose, then my finger, as quickly and accurately as you can — keep your arm fully straight... now turn your hands over rapidly on your thighs... now the heel of one foot on the opposite knee and run it down the shin. Have you had any falls or dizziness? Good — if you feel safe, please walk to the wall, turn around and walk back; I will walk beside you.' → 'gait is normal, normal base and stride, preserved arm swing, normal turn, no ataxia, foot drop or circumduction.'

Summarise with explicit negatives, LOCALISE, then diagnose, then plan (see dx). Examiner: 'anything you would add to complete your examination?' → cranial nerves, full sensory testing, cardiovascular examination with BP in both arms, cognition and speech.
skips

The three interruptions — obey INSTANTLY, mid-movement if necessary, and state the omission. ~2 min: 'assume the reflexes are normal' → 'Thank you — I will move on to...' ~4 min: 'assume sensation is normal, move on' → 'Thank you — I will omit sensory testing and move to coordination and gait. For completeness I would have screened light touch in representative dermatomes in all four limbs and mapped fully if any point were abnormal.' ~5:30: 'tell me your findings now' → summarise what you have actually done, then say what remains: 'I had not yet assessed gait; I would want to before completing my assessment.' NEVER say 'can I just finish this?'

ask: 'I will perform a screening neurological examination of all four limbs, comparing both sides throughout.' / 'I would wash my hands, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination and obtain consent, ensure appropriate exposure and positioning, and offer a chaperone where appropriate.' / 'The patient is alert and comfortable at rest; speech is fluent and the face is symmetrical.'

'Please let your arms go completely floppy and let me do the work.' / 'Copy me and don't let me move you.' / 'Power is 5 out of 5 and symmetrical from C5 to T1.' / 'Hold both arms out in front, palms up, and close your eyes.' / 'There is a pronator drift on the right — an upper motor neuron sign.' / 'I am testing for ankle clonus.' / 'This may feel a little unpleasant — I am checking the plantar response.'

'I am screening representative dermatomes, and I would map fully if any point were abnormal.' / 'Have you had any falls? I will walk beside you.' / 'This localises to the left cerebral hemisphere.' / 'A normal examination does not exclude a transient ischaemic attack.' / 'I would complete my assessment with cranial nerves, full sensory testing, and a cardiovascular examination.'

Variant B — the GIDDINESS stem ('relevant neurological examination' in a 60-year-old): 'Examiner, given giddiness, the relevant components are cranial nerves with particular attention to nystagmus and eye movements, cerebellar testing in the upper and lower limbs, gait and Romberg, a screening limb examination for focal deficit, and a lying and standing blood pressure. I would also ask whether the giddiness is spinning or light-headedness, because that distinction changes the examination.' Trap: a rote four-limb screen with no coordination, gait or postural BP — 'relevant' is an instruction to CHOOSE, and choosing badly is worse than choosing narrowly.

Variant C — the CONSCIOUS-STATE stem (drowsy patient, formal power impossible): 'I will begin by assessing conscious state using the Glasgow Coma Scale, then pupils, then a limb examination adapted to a patient who cannot cooperate fully.' Score it aloud in components: 'eyes open to voice, E3; confused but using words, V4; localises to a central painful stimulus, M5 — total 12 out of 15, E3 V4 M5.' 'Because power cannot be formally tested I am relying on tone, reflexes, plantar responses and the symmetry of response to a painful stimulus; I would check pupils for size, equality and reaction, and the blood glucose immediately.' Traps: a bare GCS number, and a sternal rub — use a trapezius squeeze or supraorbital pressure and say which. Drift in someone who cannot lift their arms → observe asymmetry of resting posture and of response to a painful stimulus.
pefe: Role-player: Dennis Hale, 54, truck driver admitted overnight. Yesterday afternoon his right arm and leg felt weak and clumsy for about ten minutes, then normal; he feels completely fine and thinks the fuss is unnecessary. Smoker, blood pressure tablets taken 'most days'. Worried about his licence but raises it only if asked what is on his mind: 'Will this stop me driving my truck?' THE ONE ABNORMAL FINDING — if asked to hold both arms out, palms up, eyes closed, the right arm slowly pronates and sinks over about TEN seconds; held only two or three seconds, nothing happens; never asked, the sign never exists and is marked missed. No drift during any other test. The partner also plays the examiner and interrupts three times with skip instructions.

Numbers: MRC 0-5 — GCS 3-15 in three components — more than 3 beats of clonus is sustained — TEN SECONDS is how long you hold a drift — C5-T1 upper limb, L2-S2 lower limb power, L1-S1 lower limb sensation — 128 Hz for vibration — biceps C5/6, triceps C7, knee L3/4, ankle S1/2.

To the patient, never the jargon: 'when you held your arms out with your eyes closed, the right one drifted a little, which suggests the signal from the brain to that arm is not quite getting through as it should.' Avoid in front of the patient: pronator drift, upper motor neuron, pyramidal, dysmetria, plantar response. Licence question — do not promise: there are national medical standards for commercial drivers, you will go through them once he is assessed, and in the meantime he must not drive; VERIFY the commercial-vehicle standards in Austroads before quoting a timeframe.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional general practice. The patient offers you 'my mate reckons it's carpal tunnel' in the first minute; candidates who take the bait start palpating the wrist and testing Tinel and never finish the examination they were asked for. Park it, examine, then explain why the findings do NOT fit a median nerve — naming the SPARED MIDDLE FINGER is the single highest-scoring negative available. Three agreeing findings (power, reflex, dermatome) assemble into one root. Automatic fails: performing carpal tunnel provocation tests instead of the neurological examination; testing sensation by peripheral nerve territory rather than by dermatome; silence; diagnosing without localising, or naming a diagnosis with no differentials.
stem: Regional general practice. A 61-year-old carpenter with six weeks of right-sided neck pain radiating down the arm, tingling in the thumb and index finger, and a grip that feels weaker. Worse looking up or turning his head. Vital signs normal.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination with running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: DECLARE (10 s): 'a full upper limb neurological examination · inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination · comparing both sides at every step' · WIPE 30 s, BOTH arms exposed to the shoulders (you cannot compare through a sleeve) · the carpal tunnel line arrives: 'that is a very reasonable thought and I will come back to it properly once I have examined you · the examination is what will tell us' (do NOT palpate the wrist) · INSPECTION 35 s: thenar and hypothenar wasting, guttering between the metacarpals seen from the DORSUM, fasciculation, posture, tremor, scars · TONE 40 s in more than one plane (wrist flexion/extension AND supination/pronation, elbow, shoulder) + pronator drift held ten seconds · POWER 95 s, MRC graded, side by side movement by movement: C5 abduction 5/5, C5/6 elbow flexion 4/5 RIGHT, C6 wrist extension 4/5 RIGHT, C7 extension, C8 grip, T1 finger abduction all 5/5 · REFLEXES 40 s with both arms positioned identically: biceps and supinator REDUCED on the right, triceps symmetrical; REINFORCE ('clench your teeth when I say') before calling any reflex reduced · SENSATION 75 s BY DERMATOME: C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm → reduced at C6 right, MIDDLE FINGER SPARED · COORDINATION 35 s with the target a full arm's length away · offer to complete: lower limbs and plantars, cervical spine with Spurling, entrapment provocation tests if indicated · assemble three findings into one root, then explain in plain English.

back.dx: Right C6 cervical radiculopathy — three findings that agree with one another: weak elbow flexion and wrist extension at 4/5, reduced right biceps and supinator reflexes, and reduced light touch in the right C6 dermatome, with neck pain worse on looking up. Excluded, each with a reason: carpal tunnel syndrome — the sensory loss is dermatomal with a SPARED middle finger, there is neck pain, and a reflex is depressed; cervical myelopathy — no upper motor neuron signs; Pancoast tumour — no small-muscle wasting and no Horner syndrome. To the patient, no jargon: 'a nerve where it leaves your neck is being pinched; that single nerve supplies the thumb side of your arm and it explains all three things I found.' Plan: bloods for diabetes and thyroid, chest X-ray given forty years of smoking (Pancoast), keep moving and keep working with modified overhead work and heavy lifting, physiotherapy, a letter for the employer and a ReturnToWorkSA pathway if work-related; most settle in 6-12 weeks, surgery considered only if weakness progresses or pain does not settle. (Wrist flexion, extension, SUPINATION and PRONATION, elbow, shoulder, both sides — cogwheeling and spasticity show up in rotation.) 'Tone is normal and symmetrical. Pull me towards you — elbow flexion C5/6 is 4 out of 5 on the right and 5/5 on the left. Cock your wrist back, stop me — wrist extension C6 is 4 out of 5 on the right. Push me away — elbow extension C7 5/5 both sides. Squeeze my two fingers — grip C8 5/5. Spread your fingers — finger abduction T1 5/5.' (Testing one whole arm and then the other makes a 4/5 invisible.)

Triceps C7 is present and symmetrical. Before I call a reflex reduced I will reinforce: please clench your teeth when I say... it remains reduced on the right.' (Position both arms identically or the asymmetry you find will be your own.)

Sensation BY DERMATOME: 'This is cotton wool — this is what it feels like on your breastbone. Now close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' (C5 lateral upper arm, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm, comparing sides.) → 'that one's duller on the right' at the thumb → 'There is reduced light touch over the right thumb and lateral forearm — the C6 dermatome. 'Now turn your hands over rapidly on your thighs. Coordination is normal — no dysmetria, intention tremor or dysdiadochokinesia. Examiner, that completes my upper limb neurological examination. setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — Version A of the lower limb neuro document. The weakness is SUBTLE and grade 4: a candidate who is not actively looking for it records normal power and the station is already lost. Expect a firm press from a 40-year-old man — anything less than firm is a finding. Power gets two full minutes; the bell at six minutes stops you dead, mid-movement. back.dx: Symmetrical proximal lower limb weakness — power reduced at L2, L3 and L4 bilaterally with L5 and S1 preserved, on a background of normal tone, normal reflexes and normal sensation and coordination. Three leading explanations, in order: a SARCOID-related polyradiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy; a CORTICOSTEROID-induced proximal myopathy; and a STATIN-associated myopathy — and they cannot be separated on examination alone. The full ladder for any motor deficit: upper motor neuron — stroke, haemorrhage, tumour, multiple sclerosis; cord and roots — compression, canal stenosis, lumbar radiculopathy; lower motor neuron — peripheral neuropathy, entrapment, traumatic nerve injury; neuromuscular junction — myasthenia; muscle — drug-induced, inflammatory or endocrine myopathy. Plan: bloods including CK and nerve conduction studies to separate neuropathic from myopathic; do NOT tell the patient to stop any medication in the station — 'please do not stop anything on your own; we will decide together.'
plan: ID and gloves BEFORE speaking. 'Hello James, I am Dr -. I have been asked to examine your legs. I will look at both legs, ask you to do some movements, gently tap your knee and ankle with this hammer, and check sensation with cotton wool. I will need both legs fully exposed. Is that alright?' → 'Yes doctor, that's fine.' → 'Thank you. I would wash my hands.'

Inspection, ten seconds: 'Examiner, on inspection of both lower limbs there is no muscle wasting, no fasciculations and no tremor. No abnormal posture, no scars and no skin changes.' → 'anything else on inspection?' → add 'no swelling, no deformity, and the patient is comfortable at rest.'

Tone: 'James, just relax completely and let me move your legs for you.' (Roll the ankle, lift the knee and let it drop, roll the thigh, both sides.) 'Tone at the ankle, knee and hip is normal on both sides.' → 'what would increased tone suggest?' → 'an upper motor neurone lesion.'

POWER — the decisive block: 'I am going to ask you to do some movements. I will place my hands on your leg, and I want you to press against them as hard as you can.' L2, hands on both thighs, 'press up against my hands' → the press is soft → 'Examiner, that press is weaker than I would expect. There is weakness of L2 bilaterally.' L3, knees bent and feet flat, hands on the shins, 'press forward' → 'L3 is also weak, bilaterally.' L4, hands behind the calves, 'pull your heels back towards you' → 'L4 is weak as well, on both sides.' L5, legs straight, hands on the dorsum, and S1 on the soles → 'L5 and S1 power are normal bilaterally.'

Reflexes: forearm under both thighs — 'I am checking the knee reflex, L3 and L4 — present and normal both sides.' Knee bent and foot held in dorsiflexion — 'ankle reflex, S1 and S2 — present and normal, both sides.' → 'what if you could not elicit it?' → 'I would reinforce with the Jendrassik manoeuvre — asking him to clench his teeth or interlock and pull his fingers — before calling it absent.'

Volunteer sensation and coordination: 'Examiner, I would now like to test light touch sensation with cotton wool in each dermatome from L1 to S2, comparing both sides.' → 'sensation is normal, please skip.' → 'Thank you. I would like to check coordination with the heel-shin test.' (Perform supine, both sides.) 'Coordination is normal. If time permits I would complete the examination by assessing his gait, including heel-to-toe walking, and I would ask about a Romberg test.'

BELL — stop dead. Summary: 'no wasting or fasciculation, tone normal, reflexes present and normal, sensation and coordination reported normal. Power is reduced symmetrically at L2, L3 and L4 bilaterally, with L5 and S1 preserved — a PROXIMAL pattern of lower limb weakness.' Then the three causes in order and the ladder (see dx).

To the patient: 'Some of the muscle groups in your hips and thighs are weaker than I would expect. This points either to the nerves supplying those muscles, or to the muscles themselves. I cannot tell you today which of the three it is.' → 'Is it the cholesterol tablet? My friend said those ruin your muscles.' → 'It may be, and that is one of three things on my list — but I do not want to blame it before I have checked. Your sarcoidosis can affect the nerves, the steroid tablets can weaken the big muscles around the hips, and yes, the cholesterol tablet can occasionally affect muscle. PLEASE DO NOT STOP ANYTHING ON YOUR OWN. I will arrange blood tests including a muscle enzyme, and nerve testing, and we will decide together.'
