back.dx: Acute right S1 radiculopathy from an L5/S1 disc protrusion — a lifting injury with radiating leg pain, lower lumbar and paraspinal tenderness, flexion grossly limited, a straight leg raise positive at about 45 degrees with a positive Bragard sign and a positive CROSSED straight leg raise (highly specific for a disc lesion), an ABSENT right ankle jerk against a normal left, and reduced sensation in the right S1 dermatome. Differentials in SIX GROUPS: MECHANICAL — radiculopathy from a disc (working diagnosis), non-specific mechanical back pain, facet arthropathy, spondylolisthesis, canal stenosis, vertebral fracture including osteoporotic and pathological; INFLAMMATORY — the spondyloarthropathies and sacroiliitis; MALIGNANCY — metastatic disease, myeloma, primary bone tumours; INFECTION — discitis, vertebral osteomyelitis, epidural abscess, and herpes zoster which can precede its rash by days; THE NEUROLOGICAL EMERGENCY — cauda equina syndrome, specifically screened for; REFERRED AND VISCERAL — pyelonephritis, renal colic, prostatitis, pancreatitis, and in an older patient a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm. Management: no imaging in the first six weeks without red flags; analgesia, keep moving, physiotherapy, review in a week; most are much better by six weeks, with leg pain taking 6-12 weeks.
plan: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. Is it James? I can see you're in a lot of pain — have you had something for it?' → 'Nurse gave me something.' → 'Good. I'm going to look at your back, gently feel it, ask you to try a couple of movements, and then do some tests on your legs. I'll stop the second you tell me to. I'll need your back uncovered — could you open the gown for me?' → 'Can you do it? I can't really let go.' → 'Of course — MAY I STEP BEHIND YOU AND OPEN IT? Thank you. I'll just clean my hands. Happy for me to start?' (Opening the gown unasked, or giving up and examining through fabric, are both fails — ask, get the yes, act, ten seconds.)

General appearance and the DEFERRED gait: 'on general appearance my patient is in obvious pain and distress, standing in a protective posture, leaning forward onto the desk for support with his hand over his lower back. He is not febrile and there is no obvious weight loss. I would normally assess gait, including heel walking for L4 and L5 and toe walking for S1. Given his pain and the fact that he can barely stand, I am DEFERRING gait — it would distress him without changing my management, and I would reassess once his pain is controlled.'

Inspection in TWO views: 'from behind, the spinous processes are in the midline with no scoliosis. There is no swelling, no redness and no rash, no scars and no muscle wasting. From the side, the lumbar lordosis is preserved — I'm looking for flattening, which would suggest paraspinal spasm.' Then palpation: 'James, I'm going to feel along your back now. Sing out the moment anything is sore. Backs of my fingers at three levels — no local rise in temperature. Now the spinous processes with my THUMBS, from the lower thoracic spine down to the sacrum — tenderness over the lower lumbar spinous processes, no step, no gap. Now the paraspinal muscles, both thumbs at the same level — bilateral spasm and tenderness, worse on the right. Finally the sacroiliac joints, pressing forward and outward — non-tender.'

ONE movement, then the declared omission: 'can you try bending forward for me, as far as is comfortable?' → about five degrees, 'ah — no' → 'flexion is grossly limited by pain. On that basis I am skipping extension, lateral flexion and rotation, because forcing further movement would distress my patient without adding information.' (Pushing him further is a fail; announcing the skip BEFORE attempting one movement tells the examiner you are running a recall.)

THE TRANSFER, narrated: 'James, I need you on the couch for the next part. There's no rush — would you like to take my arm? One step at a time. Sit down first... good... now I'll support your back while you lie down.' (The role-player is briefed to notice a candidate standing in silence, visibly impatient, for the forty seconds this takes — narrating it converts dead time into a communication mark.)

SLR, all THREE parts, with the ANGLE: 'let your right leg go completely floppy and let me do all the work. Tell me the moment you feel anything.' → 'Ah! — there' → 'straight leg raise POSITIVE on the right at approximately 45 degrees — within the 30 to 60 degree range suggesting root irritation. Backing off slightly and dorsiflexing the ankle reproduces the pain — BRAGARD'S sign is positive. Now the left: raising the LEFT leg reproduces the pain in the RIGHT leg — a positive CROSSED straight leg raise, which is highly specific for a disc lesion.' (Asking him to lift his own leg is not a straight leg raise, and 'positive' without a number is not an interpretation.)

THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE SECTION, then reflexes and sensation: 'I'd like to perform a lower limb neurological examination — I CANNOT CALL THIS A RADICULOPATHY WITHOUT DEMONSTRATING A ROOT DEFICIT. No wasting, no fasciculation. Tone and power...' → 'skip those' → 'thank you. Reflexes: the knee jerk, L3 and L4, is present and normal on the right. The ankle jerk, S1 and S2, is ABSENT on the right — and present on the left.' Then sensation with ONE tool: 'this is cotton wool — it feels like this on your chest. Now close your eyes, tell me when you feel it, and tell me whether it feels the SAME ON BOTH SIDES.' L1 groin, L2 mid thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral border of the foot and heel → 'sensation is intact from L1 to L5, with reduced sensation in the S1 dermatome on the right.'

The completion statement WITH the red-flag screen: 'to complete I would ask about saddle numbness, bladder and bowel function and bilateral leg symptoms; if present I would assess anal tone and perianal sensation and treat it as a CAUDA EQUINA EMERGENCY. I would check the plantar responses, and examine the hips and the abdomen including the aorta for referred causes.'

Diagnosis in plain English, thirty seconds: 'one of the nerves that comes out of your spine and runs down your leg is being squeezed. That's why you get pain in your back and pain shooting down your right leg, and why the feeling in the outer edge of your right foot is dulled. The usual reason is a tear in one of the discs — the cushions between the bones — with some of the softer centre pushing out onto the nerve.' → 'So it's a slipped disc? Am I going to need an operation? My dad had his back done and he was never right after.' → acknowledge it, then: 'the great majority settle without any operation — most people are much better within about six weeks, with the leg pain often taking a bit longer. We'll manage the pain, keep you moving, get physio going, and review you next week.' Then the six grouped differentials to the examiner (see dx).

Imaging: NONE in the first six weeks without red flags. Natural history: most better by six weeks, sciatica 6-12 weeks. Reflex hammer in your hand by 5:30. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33. back.dx: Left C6 cervical radiculopathy, most likely from a C5/6 posterolateral disc protrusion, with NO evidence of myelopathy, infection or malignancy: left paraspinal tenderness at C5-C6, restricted left lateral flexion and rotation with pain radiating to the thumb, a positive Spurling manoeuvre reproducing thumb paraesthesia, 4+/5 elbow flexion and wrist extension on the left, reduced left biceps and supinator reflexes, and reduced sensation over the left thumb and lateral forearm — motor, reflex and sensory findings ALL AGREE and localise to one root. The myelopathy screen (Hoffmann, inverted supinator jerk, Lhermitte, clonus) is negative. Differentials given to the PATIENT in groups: nerve — a pinched nerve (working diagnosis), pressure on the cord itself (tested for, normal), a trapped nerve lower down such as at the wrist; joint and bone — wear and tear, arthritis, fracture (no injury, no bony tenderness); muscle — postural strain, very common in her job; infection — spinal infection (afebrile, well); cancer — a growth or spread (no night pain, weight loss, systemic symptoms or bony tenderness); referred pain from the shoulder (her pain comes on moving the NECK). Management: conservative six-week trial, no imaging in the first six weeks without red flags, MRI rather than plain film if needed, simple analgesia, physiotherapy, stay active — rest and a collar make it slower, not faster; review in two weeks.
plan: WIPE: '...I have been asked to examine your neck. That means looking at it, gently feeling it, asking you to move it, and then testing the strength and feeling in your arms. I will need your neck and shoulders exposed — is that all right? Please stay sitting. ARE YOU SORE ANYWHERE IN PARTICULAR, so I can leave that part until last? I will wash my hands, and I will talk the examiner through what I am doing as I go.' → 'It's the left side, and it goes down into my arm.'

THREE views: 'on general inspection Sarah is comfortable at rest, alert and orientated, not distressed, not febrile, and not holding her neck in a protective posture. FROM THE FRONT — no visible masses, no redness, no scars, no thyroid swelling, trachea central. FROM THE SIDE — the normal cervical lordosis is preserved, head not held forward. FROM BEHIND — no scoliosis, no step deformity, no muscle wasting, no swelling or redness.'

Palpation, temperature then tenderness: 'using the backs of both hands I am comparing temperature over the paraspinal regions at three levels — no increase. Now the spinous processes, from the base of the skull down to the upper thoracic spine — C7 is the vertebra prominens and I will go two levels below it. Sarah, tell me if anything is tender. Then the paraspinal muscles and trapezius on both sides. There is mild tenderness over the LEFT paraspinal muscles at C5 to C6, with NO midline bony tenderness and no step. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and the thyroid is not enlarged.' (Midline bony tenderness suggests bone; paraspinal tenderness suggests soft tissue.)

ACTIVE movements only, demonstrated: 'Examiner, I will assess the spine with ACTIVE movements only — I will not move her neck for her. Sarah, copy me please. Tuck your chin to your chest... look up at the ceiling... right ear to right shoulder... and the left... look over your right shoulder... and the left.' → 'That's the one — it shoots down to my thumb.' → PICK IT UP IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you — pain radiating to the thumb corresponds to the C6 NERVE ROOT, and I will test that root specifically. Examiner: flexion and extension are full; left lateral flexion and left rotation are restricted by pain that travels into the left arm; right-sided movements are full and pain free.'

SPURLING, warned first: 'Sarah, I am going to do a test that may briefly bring on your arm symptoms — that is what tells me the diagnosis. I will stop as soon as you tell me to. Is that all right?' Then to the examiner: 'I am performing the Spurling manoeuvre: slight extension, then lateral flexion and rotation TOWARDS the symptomatic left side, then gentle axial compression of about seven kilograms through the vertex for up to ten seconds. This narrows the intervertebral foramen on that side.' → 'Stop — that's exactly the pain, down to my thumb.' → RELEASE IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you, I have my answer and I will stop there. It is positive on the left, reproducing pain and paraesthesia into the left thumb. Local neck pain alone would have been negative. It is highly SPECIFIC but poorly sensitive, so a negative result would not have excluded radiculopathy.'

THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE SECTION: 'because I suspect a nerve root problem, I CANNOT MAKE THAT DIAGNOSIS WITHOUT EXAMINING THE NERVE. I will now perform an upper limb neurological examination, comparing both sides.' Then ITPRSC condensed: 'inspection — no wasting, in particular of the small muscles of the hand, no fasciculation, no scars, no Horner syndrome. Tone normal and symmetrical, no spasticity, no clonus. Power — C5 shoulder abduction 5/5 both sides; C6 elbow flexion and wrist extension 4 plus out of 5 on the left, 5/5 right; C7 elbow extension 5/5; C8 grip 5/5; T1 finger abduction 5/5. Reflexes — left biceps and SUPINATOR reduced compared with the right; triceps equal. Sensation — light touch and pinprick reduced over the left thumb and lateral forearm, normal at the deltoid, middle finger, little finger and medial forearm. Coordination — I would complete with finger-nose testing.' THEN THE LOCALISATION SENTENCE: 'those three findings — motor, reflex and sensory — all agree, and localise to the left C6 nerve root.'

TASK 2 — the myelopathy screen, which is why task 2 exists: 'because radiculopathy and myelopathy present with the same complaint but are managed completely differently, I will now screen for upper motor neurone signs. Hoffmann sign — negative bilaterally. The supinator jerk is not inverted. Sarah, could you tuck your chin to your chest — any electric-shock feeling down your spine? No: Lhermitte sign is negative. There is no clonus.' Then the completion statement: 'to complete I would examine the lower limbs for tone, reflexes and plantar responses and assess gait; examine the shoulder and acromioclavicular joints, because rotator cuff disease refers pain to the neck; palpate the supraclavicular fossae and examine the LUNG APICES, because an apical tumour can produce a C8/T1 pattern with Horner syndrome; and check the peripheral pulses and blood pressure in both arms.' ('Nothing further, thank you' is a wasted mark.)

Tasks 3 and 4 to the patient: nerves leave the spine in the neck and travel into the arm, and one is being pinched where it leaves — usually a disc bulging slightly or wear-and-tear narrowing the tunnel; the nerve involved supplies the THUMB SIDE of the arm, exactly where her symptoms are; THE SPINAL CORD ITSELF IS NOT AFFECTED — checked specifically. Most are much better within six weeks with simple analgesia, physiotherapy and staying active, most never need an operation, and scans at her age nearly always show wear and tear that does not change treatment. Then, when she says 'my mum had a tumour in her spine, so I've been really scared it was that': acknowledge it directly, then give the grouped differentials naming what you looked for and what you found (see dx), and the safety-net: worsening weakness, CLUMSY HANDS (dropping things, trouble with buttons or coins), unsteadiness, bladder or bowel change, fever, or an electric-shock feeling down the spine on neck flexion.

To the patient: neck structures can refer pain into the arm without a nerve being trapped; physiotherapy, workstation changes, keep the neck moving, no scan. THE TRAP: candidates who announced 'radiculopathy' during inspection cannot climb back down — commit only after the findings agree, and 'the examination does not support my initial impression' SCORES while defending a wrong label does not.

VERSION C — MYELOPATHY: brisk biceps and triceps reflexes, an INVERTED SUPINATOR JERK, positive Hoffmann bilaterally, positive Lhermitte, a broad-based unsteady gait and wasting of the small hand muscles → 'this is cervical MYELOPATHY, not a radiculopathy. I would arrange an urgent MRI of the cervical spine and discuss with neurosurgery today. I would NOT refer for cervical manipulation or high-velocity physiotherapy, and I would counsel her about symptoms requiring immediate return' — Royal Adelaide spinal service with PATS support for travel. To the patient: be straight — the problem is pressure on the cord itself, which fits the clumsy hands and unsteadiness; it is more serious than a pinched nerve and needs a scan quickly because early treatment gives a much better result; no neck manipulation, and straight to ED for weaker hands or legs, more unsteadiness, or trouble passing urine. THE FAILURE MODE: eliciting brisk reflexes and a positive Hoffmann, not commenting, then reassuring and referring for physiotherapy — a patient-safety fail regardless of the rest.
pefe: Role-player: Sarah Whitfield, 35, dental assistant in a country town, four days a week with her head held forward over patients; married, one child of six, drives 40 km to work; never smoked, two standard drinks on a Friday, occasional paracetamol, no anticoagulants, one uncomplicated pregnancy. Three weeks of left neck ache shooting down the outside of the arm into the THUMB with pins and needles there; worse looking up, turning left, and at the end of a working day; sometimes wakes her rolling onto that side but she is otherwise completely well; no injury, fever or weight loss; grip normal, nothing dropped, no trouble with buttons or coins, walks normally, no bladder or bowel problems, no imaging. Pleasant and cooperative, winces briefly on left rotation and during Spurling and says 'stop' ONCE — and if not warned first, looks startled: 'what are you doing?' HIDDEN AGENDA, delivered quietly once: 'my mum had a tumour in her spine, so I've been really scared it was that' — if brushed aside she becomes quieter and less forthcoming.

Numbers: range of movement — flexion 45-50, extension 45-70, lateral flexion 45 each, rotation 80 each. Spurling: extension plus ipsilateral side-bend and rotation plus axial load about 7 kg for up to 10 s; roughly 90% specific, 30-60% sensitive. Upper limb tension test about 97% sensitive and poorly specific — a rule-OUT test. Roots: C5 deltoid / shoulder abduction / biceps; C6 thumb / elbow flexion and wrist extension / biceps and supinator; C7 middle finger / elbow extension and wrist flexion / triceps; C8 little finger / grip; T1 medial forearm / finger abduction. LEVEL TO ROOT: C5/6 gives C6, C6/7 gives C7, C7/T1 gives C8. Commonest roots: C7 about 60%, C6 about 20%. Conservative trial six weeks, review at two, most settle in 4-8 weeks. Paracetamol 1 g QID max 4 g/24 h, ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food, amitriptyline 10-25 mg nocte VERIFY. No imaging in the first six weeks without red flags, and MRI rather than plain film.

Scoring checklist: hands washed, introduced, identity confirmed, consented and exposed; asked about a sore spot before touching; general appearance including 'alert'; inspected from front, side AND back; temperature before tenderness; palpated occiput to upper thoracic distinguishing midline from paraspinal; four planes of active movement, demonstrated; WARNED AND CONSENTED before Spurling; correct technique towards the symptomatic side; stopped immediately when asked; interpreted Spurling correctly (specific, not sensitive); performed an upper limb neurological examination INCLUDING the supinator reflex; tested all five landmark dermatomes; named a single root and said the findings agree; screened for myelopathy and said so explicitly; offered lower limbs, gait, shoulder and lung apices; explained without jargon; gave differentials as named groups; addressed the mother directly; gave a specific safety-net; finished within eight minutes.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — rural SA general practice. The case is BUILT so that nothing is tender and every movement is full and painless, which forces you into the special tests — and the examiner is watching three things: whether you perform a correctly executed special test at all, whether you COMPLETE THE PACKAGE rather than stopping at the first positive, and whether you deliver a GROUPED differential list before time runs out. Screen the nerves with two questions in the opening instead of examining them, and your answer to the 'why no neurological examination?' challenge is banked before it is asked. Automatic fails: no special test or one done wrongly; stopping after a positive Cozen's; omitting the medial pair; hurting her by forcing a movement; running a neurological examination instead of the musculoskeletal one.
stem: Rural South Australian general practice. Jane Whitmore, 37, with pain in her right elbow. No history of injury; observations normal. 8 minutes; no history required and no management plan unless the examiner raises it.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination of the elbow, giving a running commentary to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Give your differential diagnoses to the examiner
time: 0:00-0:35 the opening block, verbatim: introduce, explain look-feel-move-special tests, consent, ask for BOTH arms and shoulders uncovered, offer sitting or standing (she will say she'd rather sit · accept in four words and do not react), warn her to report pain, hand hygiene, and THE TWO-QUESTION NEUROLOGICAL SCREEN: 'do you have any neck pain, or any numbness, pins and needles or weakness in the hand?' · 0:35-0:50 general appearance: no pain or distress, no protective posture · 0:50-1:40 INSPECTION led by the CARRYING ANGLE by name (arms by the sides, palms forward), then the generic list, and TURN THE ARM OVER to look at the back · olecranon bursitis, nodules, tophi, psoriatic plaques · 1:40-3:10 PALPATION, four steps, ONE hand: temperature at three levels, capillary refill, radial pulses, then every landmark named aloud · medial epicondyle, olecranon and bursa, ulnar groove, lateral epicondyle, radial head, joint line, biceps tendon, extensor mass, flexor mass → NO tenderness anywhere, said confidently, plus 'that does not exclude an epicondylitis, so I will proceed to the special tests' · 3:10-4:00 MOVEMENT, demonstrated and copied: flexion, extension, supination, pronation, reporting BOTH range and pain, then the stated reason for omitting passive · 4:00-5:10 lateral tests: passive wrist flexion (ER · Extension Resisted so passive flexion), Cozen's, Maudsley's · 5:10-5:50 MEDIAL tests done anyway: reverse Mill's and resisted wrist flexion, both negative · 5:50-6:10 valgus and varus stress with a proper pivot · 6:10-7:00 explain to the patient in five parts · 7:00-8:00 EIGHT grouped differentials.

back.dx: Right LATERAL EPICONDYLITIS (tennis elbow) — pain reproduced BOTH by passively stretching the common extensor origin (passive wrist flexion with the elbow extended and forearm pronated) and by resisted wrist extension (Cozen's) and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's), all localised to the lateral epicondyle, with a full painless range of joint movement, no tenderness, and negative medial and ligamentous tests. Point tenderness is neither sensitive nor specific — the diagnosis rests on two independent provocation tests with a full painless range. EIGHT differential groups, each with a reason: tendon and soft tissue (medial epicondylitis, biceps and triceps tendinopathy — medial tests negative, biceps non-tender); bursal (olecranon bursitis — no swelling); joint (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, psoriatic and gouty arthritis — full painless range, no effusion, nodules, tophi or rash); bone and cartilage (osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, loose body, radial head fracture — no locking, catching or trauma); ligamentous (collateral injury — valgus and varus negative); neurological (cervical radiculopathy, cubital tunnel, and RADIAL TUNNEL syndrome, which mimics tennis elbow but is tender 4-5 cm more distally — no neck pain, no paraesthesiae); infective (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, septic bursitis — afebrile, no warmth) — never omit this one; and referred pain from the shoulder or neck. Management, one sentence unless asked: graded exercise with a physiotherapist rather than rest; no imaging — it is a clinical diagnosis and a scan would not change what happens next; most settle within 6-12 months VERIFY.
plan: The rehearsed opening block: '...Today I've been asked to examine your elbow. For this I'll look at both of your elbows, then feel them, then I'll ask you to do some movements, and I'll finish with a couple of specific tests. Is that all right? I'll need both arms and shoulders uncovered so I can compare sides. We can do this sitting or standing — whichever is more comfortable for you.' → 'I'd rather stay sitting.' → 'That's completely fine — we can do all of it sitting.' (Four words, no visible reaction; candidates who argue or lose their thread here do not recover.) 'Please tell me straight away if anything I do is painful and I'll stop. I've washed my hands. And before I start — DO YOU HAVE ANY NECK PAIN, OR ANY NUMBNESS, PINS AND NEEDLES OR WEAKNESS IN THE HAND?' → 'No, nothing like that.' → 'Examiner, I have screened for neck pain and for hand paraesthesiae, both negative, so I will proceed with a musculoskeletal examination of the elbow, comparing both sides throughout.'

General appearance, two statements, then inspection LED BY THE CARRYING ANGLE: 'a well-looking woman sitting comfortably, not in pain or distress, no protective posture. Jane, could you hold your arms straight down by your sides with your palms facing me? Examiner, I am first assessing the CARRYING ANGLE. It is symmetrical and within the normal range — wider in women than in men — with no cubitus valgus and no cubitus varus.' Then TURN THE ARM OVER: 'looking at both elbows from the front and from behind, comparing sides: no swelling, in particular no localised swelling over the olecranon to suggest a bursitis and no fullness to suggest an effusion; no redness; no rash — specifically no psoriatic plaques over the extensor surface; no bruising or scars; no nodules or tophi; no deformity; no wasting.'

PALPATION, four steps, one hand: 'checking for a local rise in temperature with the backs of my fingers, comparing both sides at three levels — none. Capillary refill under two seconds and equal. Radial pulses present, symmetrical, normal volume, so the proximal supply is intact. Now I'll press gently around the elbow: the medial epicondyle... the olecranon and the olecranon bursa... the ulnar groove... the lateral epicondyle... the radial head... the joint line... the biceps tendon and muscle belly... the extensor mass arising from the lateral epicondyle... and the flexor mass arising from the medial epicondyle.' → nothing hurts → 'Examiner, there is NO tenderness at any point. THAT DOES NOT EXCLUDE AN EPICONDYLITIS, so I will proceed to the special tests.' (The absent tenderness is scripted into the case on purpose — say it confidently and convert it into evidence of reasoning.)

MOVEMENT — name it while she does it, then report range AND pain: 'Jane, copy me and stop if anything hurts. Active elbow flexion... extension... supination, turning the palms up... and pronation, palms down. Examiner, active movements are full and symmetrical, the range is normal and there is no pain on any movement. Because the active range is full and painless I will not repeat these passively, and I'll move to the special tests.'

LATERAL tests — slow down, say the movement word BEFORE your hands move: 'Jane, I'm going to hold your wrist and bend it gently forwards. Tell me what you feel.' → 'that pulls, right on the outside' → 'with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated I am passively flexing the wrist, which STRETCHES the common extensor origin. This reproduces her pain over the lateral epicondyle — positive.' Then 'make a fist and bend your wrist back towards me — hold it, don't let me push it down' → 'resisted wrist extension, COZEN'S test — positive, pain localised to the lateral epicondyle.' Then 'rest your hand flat and lift your middle finger, hold it against me' → 'MAUDSLEY'S test is also positive.'

THE MOMENT THE STATION IS WON — do the MEDIAL pair anyway: 'Jane, I'll turn your palm up now, bend your wrist backwards and straighten your elbow.' → no pain → 'that is the REVERSE MILL'S test — passive wrist extension with the forearm supinated, stretching the common flexor origin — not painful, negative.' Then 'bend your wrist towards you and don't let me pull it up' → 'resisted wrist flexion also negative, so I have no evidence of a medial epicondylitis.' Then ligaments with a proper pivot: 'my palm sits under the elbow with the olecranon in my palm, fingers on the medial collateral and thumb on the lateral; my other hand holds the wrist as the lever. Valgus stress, testing the medial collateral — no pain, no laxity. Varus stress, testing the lateral collateral — no pain, no laxity.' Then the single most valuable line: 'although the lateral tests are positive I have COMPLETED THE MEDIAL TESTS AS WELL and both are negative, which excludes a coexisting medial epicondylitis, and the collateral ligaments are intact.'

Explain to Jane in FIVE parts: name it and give the common name ('lateral epicondylitis — most people know it as tennis elbow, although you certainly don't have to play tennis to get it'); one sentence of anatomy (the muscles that lift the wrist and fingers backwards all start from a small bony bump on the outer elbow, and the tendon there gets overloaded and breaks down); YOUR OWN FINDINGS AS THE REASON ('that's why it hurt in two different ways — once when I stretched those muscles by bending your wrist forwards, and again when I asked you to push against me'); what it is NOT (not arthritis, not an infection, not damaging the joint); and check understanding. 'Do I need a scan?' → a confident NO: 'it's a diagnosis we make from the examination, and a scan wouldn't change what we do next.'

EIGHT grouped differentials with reasons (see dx). The examiner challenge: 'you listed cervical radiculopathy — why did you not perform a neurological examination?' → 'the predominant system here is musculoskeletal — the likely pathology is tendon, bursa, cartilage or joint. I screened for the neurological differentials at the start by asking about neck pain and about numbness or paraesthesiae in the hand, and both were negative. Had either been positive, a focused upper limb neurological examination would have become the appropriate examination and I would have performed it in preference to the special tests.' And: 'there was no tenderness over the lateral epicondyle — does that not go against your diagnosis?' → 'point tenderness is neither sensitive nor specific; the diagnosis rests on two independent provocation tests with a full painless range of movement.' If you arrive here late, DROP THE REASONS and give the eight group names alone.

ask: 'For this I'll look at both of your elbows, then feel them, then ask you to do some movements, and I'll finish with a couple of specific tests.' / 'That's completely fine — we can do all of it sitting.' / 'Do you have any neck pain, or any numbness, pins and needles or weakness in the hand?' / 'I have screened for neck pain and hand paraesthesiae, both negative, so I will proceed with a musculoskeletal examination.'

'I am first assessing the carrying angle... no cubitus valgus and no cubitus varus.' / 'There is no tenderness at any point. That does not exclude an epicondylitis, so I will proceed to the special tests.' / 'Because the active range is full and painless I will not repeat these passively.' / 'Passively flexing the wrist stretches the common extensor origin — this reproduces her pain at the lateral epicondyle, positive.'

'Although the lateral tests are positive I have completed the medial tests as well and both are negative.' / 'Valgus stress tests the medial collateral ligament — no pain and no laxity.' To the patient: 'most people know it as tennis elbow, although you certainly don't have to play tennis to get it' / 'it's not arthritis, it's not an infection, and it isn't damaging the joint itself.' Say 'Cozen's', 'Mill's', 'Maudsley's' — never 'Mulder's', which is a foot sign for Morton's neuroma.

Variant A — MEDIAL EPICONDYLITIS: identical stem, findings flipped — the lateral tests are negative and reverse Mill's plus resisted wrist flexion reproduce pain at the medial epicondyle → 'my provisional diagnosis is a medial epicondylitis — golfer's elbow.' Add and stand out: 'I would also palpate the ulnar groove and check a Tinel's sign there, because cubital tunnel syndrome commonly accompanies a medial epicondylitis and would change my management' VERIFY. The trap is reporting the lateral tests as positive because that is what you rehearsed — LISTEN to what the role-player actually says.

Variant B — THE LOCKING ELBOW (online/remote format, younger thrower or racquet player, locking rather than pain): osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum with or without a loose body — MOVEMENT becomes the important step, with a mechanical block to full extension; the epicondylitis tests are negative but still performed; the extra test is the RADIOCAPITELLAR COMPRESSION test (arm outstretched, support the elbow, take the hand as though shaking it, pronate and supinate while applying axial compression — lateral pain is positive). Here you DO want imaging: AP and lateral radiographs. Do not import this test into the face-to-face pain station. / Variant C — THE HOT SWOLLEN ELBOW: short history, hot red tense swelling over the olecranon, exquisite tenderness, unwilling to move it, fever supplied → STOP: 'I am stopping the examination here. My primary concern is a septic olecranon bursitis, and I must exclude a septic arthritis. Full observations, blood cultures and inflammatory markers, and ASPIRATE for microscopy, culture and crystals BEFORE antibiotics, with urgent orthopaedic discussion' — rural SA: the on-call orthopaedic registrar at the receiving Adelaide hospital, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 if retrieval is needed. Ploughing through Cozen's and Mill's on a septic joint is the trap — which is why temperature is the first thing your hands do.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitmore, 37, well, comfortable and cooperative, sitting in a chair. IF ASKED TO STAND: 'I'd rather stay sitting, if that's all right' — with no explanation, because it is deliberate. Asked about neck pain or hand numbness: 'no, nothing like that — it's just the elbow.' WHEN PRESSED ANYWHERE AROUND THE ELBOW, NOTHING HURTS — this is the most important thing she does, and she gives no tenderness even over the lateral epicondyle. All movements are full, easy and painless. Only FOUR things hurt: passive wrist flexion with the arm straight ('ooh, that pulls, right on the outside of my elbow'), resisted wrist extension ('that's sore too — same spot'), and resisted middle finger extension ('yes, that's sore as well'). Everything else, including passive wrist extension with the palm up and resisted wrist flexion, is fine. After the explanation she asks: 'do I need a scan?'

Numbers and hooks: ER = LATERAL — Extension Resisted, therefore passive flexion. PEFR = MEDIAL — Passive Extension, Flexion Resisted. Carrying angle about 5-15 degrees in men and 10-25 in women VERIFY. Flexion/extension 0-150 / 0. Supination/pronation 80-90 / 75-85. Functional arc 30-130 degrees of flexion. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Radial tunnel syndrome is tender 4-5 cm DISTAL to the lateral epicondyle and also makes Maudsley's positive — mentioning it shows you know the limits of your own test. Recall split: about 9 in 10 lateral, 1 in 10 medial. Natural history: most settle within 6-12 months VERIFY.

Where the marks actually sit: 0:00-4:00 is roughly a third and everyone gets most of it — introduction, inspection, palpation and movement are generic and rehearsed. 4:00-6:10, the special tests, is another third and is where the cohort separates. 6:10-8:00, the explanation and differentials, is the last third and is most commonly lost to the CLOCK rather than to knowledge — which is exactly why the neurological examination is screened with two questions, passive movement is skipped, and power testing is optional. Four starred items, each a fail on its own: passive wrist flexion, Cozen's, reverse Mill's and resisted wrist flexion. A complete, unhurried, correctly performed set of four special tests plus valgus and varus, followed by eight grouped differentials, will pass this station even if everything else is merely competent.
fails: ★ No special test performed, or one done wrongly — this alone fails the station
★ Stopping after a positive Cozen's and never doing the medial pair or the stress tests
Saying 'flexion' while performing extension — it happens because you are talking and moving at the same time; say the movement word BEFORE your hands move

Reciting the generic joint list and never mentioning the carrying angle; never turning the arm over, so bursitis, nodules, tophi and psoriasis are never excluded; being thrown by the absent tenderness

Explaining 'lateral epicondylitis' or 'inflammation of the common extensor origin' to the patient and stopping; giving three differentials and drying up; reaching for an ultrasound, which undermines the point of having done the special tests

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. The general hand framework, run on nodal osteoarthritis. TWO DECISIONS ARE MADE BEHIND THE DOOR: musculoskeletal or neurological (the TASK WORDING decides) and nerves or nerve roots (the SITE OF THE LESION decides) — and you say which, out loud. The pillow, paper, pen and cotton ball on the table are there because you are expected to USE them. Automatic fails: never reaching the functional or special tests; examining the palms only and never turning the hands over; running dermatomes and myotomes when the task said hand examination; performing the three nerve tests without naming which nerve each one tests.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia, 8 minutes. Mrs Denise Fairlie, 58, retired school administrator, with three months of pain and stiffness in both hands, worse by the end of the day, and she has begun dropping cups. No trauma, observations normal, afebrile. On the table beside her: a pillow, a sheet of paper, a pen and a cotton ball.
tasks: Perform a focused hand examination, giving a running commentary to the examiner as you proceed
Report your positive findings and your significant negative findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: 0:00-0:45 WIPE, consent, and BOTH HANDS ON THE PILLOW palms up (examining a hand on a lap loses access and reads as though you have never done this) · general appearance in ten seconds: comfortable, no pain or distress, no protective posture, no sling, no aids, no signs of systemic illness · 0:45-1:45 INSPECTION, palmar AND dorsal · ask her to turn the hands over, because every finding in this case is on the dorsum · and lead with the SPECIFIC finding (Heberden nodes, thumb-base squaring), with the generic list afterwards in one breath · 1:45-3:30 PALPATION, four steps, ONE hand supporting from underneath, zone by zone named aloud: temperature at fingers, palm and wrist; capillary refill; radial pulses; then tenderness through the fingers and IP joints, metacarpals and MCPs, wrist, anatomical snuffbox, radial and ulnar styloids and shafts · 3:30-4:30 MOVEMENT, asked SEPARATELY for fingers, thumb and wrist ('I can't move my hand' does not tell you which), then the stated reason for omitting passive · 4:30-6:00 THE DECLARATION and the neurological screen: 'because this is a DISTAL problem I am screening the three peripheral nerves rather than dermatomes and myotomes' · median (thumb abduction against resistance), ulnar (Froment's with the paper), radial (wrist extension against resistance), all BILATERAL and each NAMED, then one sensory modality at the index pulp, little fingertip and snuffbox · 6:00-7:00 FUNCTION as the special test for this version: grip, pinch, the button, the pen · 7:00-8:00 report positives and SIGNIFICANT negatives, then diagnosis and differentials to the patient, ending with 'what was on your mind when you came in today?'

back.dx: Nodal osteoarthritis of the hands — Heberden nodes at the DIP joints bilaterally, squaring at both thumb bases, tenderness at those same joints, and reduced grip strength. SIGNIFICANT negatives (the ones that exclude the differentials, not every negative): no thenar or hypothenar wasting, no ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonniere deformity, no MCP synovitis, no joint hot or red, and median, ulnar and radial motor and sensory function intact bilaterally. Differentials explained TO THE PATIENT with the reason each is less likely: rheumatoid arthritis — a different disease where the immune system attacks the joints, and it usually hits the knuckles and spares the joints nearest the nails, which is the opposite pattern; psoriatic arthritis — no skin or nail changes; carpal tunnel syndrome — the nerve testing was normal. Plan: X-rays of both hands and bloods to exclude the inflammatory types, hand therapy for grip strengthening and joint protection, simple analgesia, review in six weeks. Safety-net: any joint becoming hot, red and swollen over a day or two, fever, numbness or sudden weakness — same day.
plan: WIPE and USE THE PILLOW: '...I have been asked to examine your hands. I will be looking at your hands, feeling your hands, and asking you to do some movements. I will need both hands uncovered. Is that alright? Please tell me if anything is sore and I will stop. COULD YOU REST BOTH HANDS ON THIS PILLOW FOR ME, PALMS UP TO BEGIN WITH? I will just wash my hands before we start.' (If you cannot see a pillow, ask for one.) Then general appearance: 'comfortable at rest, not in pain and not in distress. No protective posture and no sling. No walking aids and no signs of systemic illness.'

INSPECTION — palms first, then TURN THE HANDS OVER, and lead with the specific: 'now could you turn your hands over for me so I can see the backs? Examiner, inspecting the palmar and then the dorsal aspect of both hands, THE SPECIFIC FINDINGS ARE bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints of both index and middle fingers, consistent with HEBERDEN NODES, and SQUARING at the base of both thumbs. There is no thenar or hypothenar wasting, no ulnar deviation, swan-neck or boutonniere deformity, and no synovitis at the metacarpophalangeal joints. There is no swelling, redness, rash, bruising, scar or nail change.' (Opening with 'no swelling, no redness, no rashes' is the generic error — the named finding comes first and the list goes afterwards in one breath.)

PALPATION, four steps, ONE hand: 'Denise, I am going to feel your hands now — tell me if anything is sore. Examiner, temperature is normal and equal at the fingers, palm and wrist, with no local rise over any joint. Capillary refill under two seconds bilaterally. Radial pulses present and equal with normal volume. I am now palpating for tenderness: the fingers and interphalangeal joints one by one... the metacarpals and metacarpophalangeal joints... the wrist, supporting it from below... the anatomical snuffbox... the radial styloid and shaft, and the ulnar styloid and shaft. There is mild tenderness over the distal interphalangeal joints bilaterally and at the base of both thumbs, with no tenderness elsewhere.' (Grasping the whole hand and squeezing gets you an 'ow' you cannot localise — and in almost every MSK case the point of tenderness IS the diagnosis.)

MOVEMENT, asked separately for each region: 'copy my movements. Make a fist, and open. Spread your fingers, and close them. Now the thumb — out to the side, back in, across the palm, out again, and count your fingers with your thumb. Now the wrist — bend it down, bend it back, tip it towards the thumb, tip it towards the little finger. Examiner, active finger, thumb and wrist movements are full and symmetrical apart from slightly reduced finger flexion and mild discomfort at end-range opposition. SINCE ACTIVE MOVEMENT IS FULL, I AM NOT PERFORMING PASSIVE MOVEMENT.' (Do not presume a finding because a recall said she would not move — ask.)

THE DECLARATION, then the three nerves NAMED: 'Examiner, because this is a DISTAL problem I am screening the three peripheral nerves rather than dermatomes and myotomes. Denise, touch my finger with your thumb and hold it there against me — thumb abduction against resistance is five out of five bilaterally: MEDIAN motor function is intact. Now grip this paper between your thumb and finger and don't let me take it — Froment's sign is negative: ULNAR motor function is intact. Bend both wrists back and stop me pushing them down — wrist extension five out of five bilaterally: RADIAL motor function is intact.' Then one sensory modality: 'this is a piece of cotton wool — it feels like this on your forehead. Now close your eyes and say yes whenever you feel it. Examiner, sensation is intact and symmetrical at the index pulp, the little fingertip and the snuffbox — median, ulnar and radial.' (Motor without resistance is movement, not power; one side only is not a neurological examination; and three tests without naming the nerves cannot be scored.)

FUNCTION — the special test for an arthritis case: 'grip my two fingers as hard as you can. Now pinch this piece of paper between your thumb and index finger. Could you undo this button for me? And pick up this pen and write your name. Examiner, grip strength is reduced bilaterally, pinch grip is preserved, and she completes the button and the pen task slowly but independently. To complete my examination I would examine the elbows and the cervical spine and review the observation chart.' (Reaching for Phalen's and Tinel's here reads as a memorised list rather than clinical reasoning — special tests are case-specific.)

Report POSITIVES and SIGNIFICANT negatives only (see dx — reciting every negative burns the time task 3 needs), then explain to the patient: the knobbly swellings and thumb-base tenderness fit osteoarthritis — wear-and-tear change where the smooth cartilage thins and the body lays down extra bone at the edges, which is what she can feel; then each differential with the reason it is less likely, in plain words. Then ASK: 'what was on your mind when you came in today?' → 'I have my two grandsons two days a week. The little one is eighteen months. I dropped a mug last week and it just went straight through my fingers. What if that's him?' → 'thank you for telling me — osteoarthritis does not cause sudden loss of control, but reduced grip is real and we can work on it': hand therapy for grip strengthening and joint protection, simple analgesia, review in six weeks, and sitting down before picking him up as a sensible precaution rather than a restriction. Safety-net and close.

That takes me away from a peripheral problem in the hand and towards CERVICAL MYELOPATHY — cord compression in the neck. I would examine the lower limbs and the gait, look for Hoffmann's sign, and arrange an urgent MRI of the cervical spine.'

Three months of aching stiff hands worse by the end of the day, morning stiffness about FIFTEEN minutes, both hands with the right slightly worse, no trauma and no swelling that comes and goes; knees ache going downstairs; no pins and needles, no systemic symptoms, no neck pain; her mother had 'terrible hands' and could not open jars. Pleasant and chatty, quieter only if asked what is worrying her. Tenderness given ONLY at the DIP joints of index and middle fingers and both thumb bases, and only if the right spot is pressed — if the whole hand is grabbed she says 'ow' and does NOT localise. Movements all possible with slightly incomplete fist; power normal; sensation normal; grip weak-ish; she can undo the button and write, slowly. HIDDEN AGENDA: she dropped a mug last week and is frightened she will drop the 18-month-old — revealed only to an open question about concerns, otherwise in a small voice at the very end.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice, and often a REAL patient with visible disease. THE ONE THING: say 'I CAN SEE', never 'I am looking for'. Then get to the four objects — a key, a coin, a paperclip and a bottle, set out of the immediate line of sight, and finding them is part of the station. Expect the examiner to cut across you with 'don't tell me what you're looking for — tell me what you see': do not apologise or restart, just point and name one finding. FOUR automatic fails: a generic inspection naming no specific sign; 'I am looking for' instead of 'I can see'; Heberden's and Bouchard's the wrong way round; the four objects never used.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Reg Callaghan, 60, with pain in both hands. No history required. Task 1 about 6.5 minutes, task 2 about 1.5 minutes.
tasks: Perform an examination of the hands, with a running commentary to the examiner
Give the examiner your differential diagnosis
time: SET UP: spot the tray during the WIPE · WIPE with both arms uncovered to the elbow on a pillow and THE PAIN QUESTION before touching several dozen inflamed joints · general appearance · INSPECTION, DORSAL THEN PALMAR, twelve named findings and every one opened with 'I CAN SEE': for osteoarthritis · Heberden's, Bouchard's, thumb-base squaring; for rheumatoid · ulnar deviation, radial deviation at the wrists, Z thumb, swan neck, boutonniere, dactylitis; nails · pitting, ridging, onycholysis, nail-fold vasculitis, splinter haemorrhages; nodules in the hands and AT THE ELBOWS; small muscle wasting; joints swollen but not red; then palms · thenar and hypothenar wasting, Dupuytren's, palmar erythema · PALPATION: temperature, capillary refill, radial pulses, then EVERY joint group supported and SQUEEZED GENTLY for tenderness AND SYNOVITIS · DIPs, PIPs, thumb IP, MCPs one to five, metacarpals, wrist, snuffbox, both styloids · and offer to repeat identically on the other hand · MOVEMENT: thumb (out, in, back, across, touch each fingertip), fingers (fist, open, spread, together), wrist (forward, back, side to side) · FUNCTION, and protect the time for it: grip, then THE FOUR OBJECTS with instruction and NEVER demonstration, then the thumb grind test · then the grouped differential with a leading diagnosis, investigations and referral.

back.dx: RHEUMATOID ARTHRITIS is the leading diagnosis — an MCP and PIP distribution with SPARING OF THE DIPs, ulnar deviation with radial deviation at the wrists, a Z thumb and swan neck deformities, small muscle wasting, boggy soft synovial fullness rather than hard bony nodes, reduced grip with lost lateral (key) grip and lost fine pinch, and a NEGATIVE thumb grind test which argues against first carpometacarpal osteoarthritis. Differentials IN GROUPS: inflammatory arthritis — rheumatoid (leading), psoriatic, gouty, reactive; degenerative — osteoarthritis, less likely because the DIPs and thumb base are spared and the grind test is negative; connective tissue disease — systemic lupus erythematosus and related; neurological and soft tissue causes of hand pain — carpal tunnel syndrome (which rheumatoid predisposes to), De Quervain's tenosynovitis, cervical radiculopathy. Investigations and plan: inflammatory markers, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, X-rays of both hands, URGENT rheumatology referral because outcomes depend on early disease-modifying treatment, analgesia, and occupational therapy for splinting and aids. Distribution rules: OA takes the DIP, PIP and first CMC and SPARES the MCPs; RA takes the MCP, PIP and wrist and SPARES the DIPs.
plan: WIPE, exposure, pillow — and the pain question: 'I've been asked to examine both of your hands. I'll look, gently feel, ask you to do some movements, and then ask you to use a few objects for me. Is that alright? I'll need both arms uncovered to the elbow, resting on this pillow. Before I start — ARE YOUR HANDS SORE NOW, AND IS ANYWHERE ESPECIALLY PAINFUL? I'll be gentle, and tell me if you want me to stop. I'll wash my hands.' → 'They're sore most days. The knuckles are the worst of it, especially first thing.' (Asking about pain before touching dozens of inflamed joints is both scored and basic decency — and it buys you permission to keep going when he winces later.)

INSPECTION, dorsal first, every finding opened with I CAN SEE: 'Reg, may I look at the backs of your hands? Examiner, on the dorsal surfaces of both hands: FOR OSTEOARTHRITIS, I can see no Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes and no squaring of the thumb base. FOR RHEUMATOID, I can see ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints with mild radial deviation at the wrists, a Z deformity of the thumb, and swan neck deformities of the index and middle fingers. There is no boutonniere deformity and no dactylitis. At the nails: no pitting, ridging or onycholysis; no nail-fold changes of rheumatoid vasculitis; no splinter haemorrhages. No rheumatoid nodules in the hands OR AT THE ELBOWS. There is wasting of the small muscles of both hands, and the MCP and PIP joints are swollen but not red. No scars.' Then 'could you turn them over? On the palmar surfaces there is thenar and hypothenar wasting, no Dupuytren's contracture and no palmar erythema.' (Naming a NEGATIVE specific sign — 'no Heberden's nodes' — is not the generic error; naming nothing is.)

THE INTERRUPTION, when it comes: 'don't tell me what you're looking for — tell me what you see.' Do NOT apologise or restart. Point and name one finding immediately: 'I can see ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints.' Then carry straight on through the list. If your mind goes blank on which eponym is which, DESCRIBE THE LOCATION — it is always correct: 'I can see hard, bony swellings at the joints nearest the fingertips, and similar swellings at the middle joints of the index and middle fingers. The knuckles are not involved. That distribution favours osteoarthritis.'

PALPATION and movement: 'Reg, I'm going to feel your hands now — tell me if any joint is sore. Examiner, there is no local rise in temperature, capillary refill is under two seconds, and the radial pulses are present and normal. I am now palpating each joint FOR TENDERNESS AND FOR SYNOVITIS OR EFFUSION, supporting each joint and squeezing gently: the distal interphalangeal joints... the proximal interphalangeal joints... the interphalangeal joint of the thumb... the metacarpophalangeal joints one to five... the metacarpals... the wrist, the snuffbox, and the radial and ulnar styloids. I would repeat this identically on the other hand.' → he winces: 'ooh, that one's tender' → 'sorry Reg, I'll keep it gentle — tell me if it's too much' and KEEP GOING (a palpation abandoned halfway tells the examiner nothing about the distribution, which is the whole point). Report it precisely: 'tenderness with a BOGGY, SOFT FULLNESS at the MCP and PIP joints bilaterally; the distal joints are not tender.' Then movement: 'thumb — out, in, back, across, and touch each fingertip. Fingers — fist, open, spread, together. Wrist — forward, back, side to side.' → 'active movement is globally reduced, most markedly on making a full fist.'

FUNCTION — protect the time for this: 'squeeze two of my fingers as hard as you can, both hands. Examiner, grip strength is reduced bilaterally, and I cannot feel any palmar tendon crepitus. Now I'd like you to use a few things for me. Take this key and TURN IT AS IF YOU WERE OPENING A LOCK... pick up this coin... open this paperclip... unscrew this bottle and do it up again. Try each one with both hands.' → 'Examiner, the patient has abnormalities in the practical functions of the hand — he holds the key WITHIN THE PALM rather than using a lateral grip, cannot open the paperclip, and opens the bottle with the whole hand.' (INSTRUCT, never demonstrate — showing him how to hold the key destroys the test, because the abnormality is the grip he chooses when left to himself.)

The grind test, reported with confidence: 'I am gripping the thumb metacarpal and compressing it towards the wrist while rotating — Reg, is that sore? Examiner, the thumb grind test is NEGATIVE, which argues against osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.' A negative grind test is still an answer — it supports the inflammatory picture, and reporting negatives with the same confidence as positives is what discriminating between two diagnoses looks like.

The grouped differential with a leading diagnosis, then investigations and referral (see dx). If the explanation used jargon he will say 'sorry — what does that mean?', and if never asked about his life he will say at the very end: 'Doctor — am I going to end up not being able to use them?' His hidden agenda, offered only if asked how he is managing at home: 'my wife does the jars now. And the buttons, if I'm honest.'

ask: 'Are your hands sore now — is anywhere especially painful?' / 'I can see ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints.' / 'Heberden's at the distal, Bouchard's at the proximal interphalangeal joints.' / 'There is wasting of the small muscles of both hands.' / 'The joints are swollen but not red.'

'I am palpating each joint for tenderness and for synovitis or effusion.' / 'A boggy, soft fullness rather than a hard bony node.' / 'I would repeat this identically on the other hand.' / 'Turn this key as if you were opening a lock.' / 'The patient has abnormalities in the practical functions of the hand.' / 'He holds the key within the palm rather than using a lateral grip.'

'The thumb grind test is negative, which argues against osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.' / 'My differentials, in groups, are...' / 'Less likely, because the distal joints are spared.' / 'I would refer urgently to rheumatology — outcomes depend on early disease-modifying treatment.' TWO WORDS EVERY TIME: 'I CAN SEE' — not 'I am looking for', not 'I would check for'.

THE OSTEOARTHRITIS SITTING — same stem, older patient, nodal rather than deviating deformity, and the thumb base is the giveaway: 'I can see HEBERDEN'S nodes at the distal interphalangeal joints of the index and middle fingers bilaterally, and BOUCHARD'S nodes at the proximal interphalangeal joints. There is squaring at the base of both thumbs. The metacarpophalangeal joints are SPARED. There is no ulnar deviation, no swan neck or boutonniere deformity, and no rheumatoid nodules.' On palpation: 'the nodes are HARD AND BONY rather than boggy, which favours osteoarthritis over synovitis.' And the grind test is POSITIVE bilaterally, supporting osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.

Deformity definitions to keep straight: swan neck = PIP hyper-extended; boutonniere = PIP flexed; Z thumb = MCP flexed with the IP hyper-extended. Distribution: OA takes DIP, PIP and first CMC and spares the MCPs; RA takes MCP, PIP and wrist and spares the DIPs. If the examiner offers to skip the second hand, ACCEPT and spend the time on function. Methotrexate is ONCE WEEKLY.
pefe: Role-player: Reg Callaghan, 60, retired shearer who still does fencing on the family farm an hour from town; eighteen months of pain in both hands, getting worse, worst first thing and taking A COUPLE OF HOURS to loosen up; paracetamol barely touches it; no allergies, no psoriasis or nail problems, no neck pain or night numbness. Stoic and understated — plays it down ('it's just wear and tear, isn't it?') and does not volunteer how much he has stopped doing. HIDDEN AGENDA: he has quietly stopped doing up his own shirt buttons and his wife opens the jars, and it embarrasses him — mentioned only if asked how he is managing at home, or at the very end. The partner also plays the EXAMINER and reads a findings card aloud as the candidate looks and feels, because they cannot grow deformities — and reads nothing the candidate has not gone looking for. How the objects are played: struggle visibly but keep trying, never refuse — key gripped in the palm and turned with the whole hand, coin managed slowly and clumsily on the second or third attempt, paperclip FAILED ('I can't get hold of that one'), bottle clamped with the whole palm and twisted with the arm. Grind test: 'no, that one's alright.'

How to run it: set a timer for eight minutes and call 'two minutes left' at six; put the four objects OUT of the direct line of sight; once during inspection interrupt with 'don't tell me what you're looking for — tell me what you see'; offer to skip the second hand only AFTER they have started it; and score honestly, because a tidy examination with no named findings is a fail.

The 18-point checklist: introduced, checked identity, explained, consented; exposed both arms on a pillow and washed hands; asked about pain before touching and stayed gentle; commented on general appearance; NAMED SPECIFIC FINDINGS rather than a generic list; used the words 'I can see'; named the deviation, the deformities and the wasting; looked at the nails, nail folds and for nodules; turned the hands over; temperature, capillary refill and pulses; palpated every joint group supporting and squeezing rather than prodding; stated they were feeling for tenderness AND synovitis; offered the second hand; active movement of thumb, fingers and wrist; tested grip; USED ALL FOUR OBJECTS, instructing rather than demonstrating; named the grips that were lost; performed the thumb grind test; and gave at least six differentials in named groups with a leading diagnosis.
fails: ★ A generic inspection naming no specific sign — 'no swelling, redness, rashes, bruises'
★ 'I am looking for' instead of 'I can see' — on a real patient with visible disease it is the sound of a candidate who cannot identify what is in front of them
Heberden's and Bouchard's the wrong way round (Heberden = DIP, Bouchard = PIP) — if unsure, describe the location instead
The four objects never used, or demonstrating how to hold the key instead of instructing, which destroys the test

Stopping the palpation at the first wince, so the distribution — the whole point — is never established; apologising and restarting when the examiner interrupts; a flat differential list with no groups and no leading diagnosis

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED, you are the resident, bell at 7 minutes. The whole station turns on ONE line: 'a FULL claw hand involving ALL FOUR FINGERS' — without those words the examiner cannot tell whether you have distinguished a lower-plexus lesion from an ulnar palsy. He fell from height, so the stability check comes before you touch him, and he will refuse every active movement: forcing passive movement on a painful un-imaged limb is an AUTOMATIC FAIL. Shape of the whole station: prove the limb is alive, prove the bones are intact, then prove which roots are out — out loud at every step.
stem: Emergency Department of a regional hospital. Max Trenowden, 30, right-hand dominant, brought in after falling about three metres from a tree while pruning it; he grabbed at a branch with his right hand as he fell. Pain and pins and needles in the right hand. Landed on his feet, no head strike, no loss of consciousness, no midline neck pain. HR 88, BP 128/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.8, GCS 15, BGL 5.4.
tasks: Perform a focused examination of the right upper limb, with a running commentary
Explain your findings and diagnosis to the patient in plain language
Answer the examiner's questions
time: STABILITY CHECK FIRST ('this gentleman has fallen from height, so may I confirm his observations are stable?') then WIPE with BOTH arms exposed to the shoulder and both hands on the pillow palms up · INSPECTION: the one line · 'a full claw hand of the right hand involving all four fingers, MCP joints hyper-extended and IP joints flexed, in index, middle, ring and little' · plus NO WASTING (which quietly excludes every chronic cause), no pallor or cyanosis, then the dorsum · PALPATION: PERFUSION FIRST (temperature at three levels including both shoulders and the base of the neck, capillary refill, radial pulses with the brachials and a listen over the supraclavicular fossa for a bruit), then bony tenderness DISTAL TO PROXIMAL and all the way up · phalanges, metacarpals, carpus, snuffbox, styloids, radius and ulna, elbow and epicondyles, then acromioclavicular joint, deltoid, THE WHOLE CLAVICLE, the supraclavicular fossa over the plexus, and the cervical spinous processes · MOVEMENT: he refuses everything, so ANNOUNCE THE OMISSION AND THE REASON · 'as this is a traumatic limb in which I have not excluded a fracture, I am deliberately omitting passive movement' · MOTOR BY MYOTOME, not nerve: demonstrate each movement C5 to T1 and name what cannot be demonstrated · SENSORY, one modality, five dermatomes: C5 lateral deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm below the elbow, and SILENCE IS THE POSITIVE FINDING · REFLEXES on the affected side only (biceps C5-6 present, triceps C7-8 ABSENT) · then the HORNER SCREEN, analgesia, the plain-English explanation and the summary.

back.dx: Traction injury to the LOWER TRUNK of the right brachial plexus, C8 and T1 (Klumpke) — a full claw involving all four fingers, C8 and T1 sensory loss, no demonstrable C8 or T1 power, and an ABSENT triceps jerk with a preserved biceps jerk, in a man whose arm was pulled up and out grabbing a branch as he fell. Negatives that matter: haemodynamically stable, limb warm and well perfused with equal radial pulses, no bony tenderness up to the clavicle, NO WASTING (so acute), NO HORNER SYNDROME, no midline neck tenderness. Why it is NOT an ulnar palsy: an ulnar lesion claws only the ring and little fingers because the lumbricals to index and middle are median-supplied — here all four claw, so every intrinsic is denervated, and every intrinsic is C8/T1; the sensory loss is also dermatomal rather than confined to the ulnar one and a half digits. Investigations: plain films of shoulder, clavicle, humerus, forearm and hand; chest X-ray for a first-rib fracture, apical pneumothorax and the hemidiaphragm level; C-spine imaging if the Canadian C-spine rule is not satisfied; CT angiogram for any pulse deficit; NCS and EMG at 3-4 weeks (not earlier — Wallerian degeneration takes 7-10 days and an early study is falsely reassuring); MRI plexus for a pseudomeningocele. Management: analgesia, broad arm sling, timed neurovascular chart, early referral to a brachial plexus service (RAH plastics), hand therapy for oedema control, passive range and an ANTI-CLAW SPLINT WITH THE MCPs BLOCKED IN FLEXION, never straight; amitriptyline for neuropathic pain; review at three months, surgical window 3-6 months with results falling away sharply beyond 9-12.
plan: 'Examiner, before I start — this gentleman has fallen from height, so may I confirm his observations are stable? Blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and saturations?' → stable → WIPE: '...I've been asked to examine your right arm and hand. I'll be looking at both hands, feeling them, and asking you to try some movements, comparing the injured side with the good side. I'll need both arms exposed to the shoulder. Is that alright? Please tell me straight away if anything hurts and I'll stop. Could you rest both hands on the pillow, palms up?'

INSPECTION — the line the station turns on: 'on general inspection Max is a well-looking young man, comfortable at rest, not in obvious pain or distress, with no protective posture. Inspecting the palmar surfaces: on the right I CAN SEE A FULL CLAW HAND INVOLVING ALL FOUR FINGERS — the metacarpophalangeal joints hyper-extended and the interphalangeal joints flexed, in the index, middle, ring and little fingers. The left hand is normal. There is no pallor and no cyanosis of the fingertips. Turning to the dorsal surfaces: no swelling, redness, bruising, lacerations or deformity other than the claw. NO MUSCLE WASTING — consistent with an acute injury. No scars, nails normal.'

PALPATION — perfusion first, then bone, HAND TO NECK: 'comparing temperature with the backs of my fingers at three levels — fingers, dorsum and wrist — symmetrical and warm, and I'm also comparing over both shoulders and the base of the neck. Capillary refill under two seconds and equal. Radial pulses present and of equal volume bilaterally; I would also feel the brachials and listen over the supraclavicular fossa for a bruit. Now palpating for tenderness, distal to proximal, watching his face: phalanges, metacarpals, carpus, snuffbox, both styloids, radius and ulna, elbow and epicondyles — all non-tender. I'm now examining the shoulder and root of the neck, BECAUSE THE PRESENTATION IS IN THE HAND BUT I SUSPECT THE LESION IS UP HERE: acromioclavicular joint, tip of the shoulder, deltoid, clavicle along its length, and the supraclavicular fossa over the plexus — all non-tender with no swelling or step. Cervical spinous processes non-tender in the midline.'

MOVEMENT and the automatic fail avoided: 'Max, can you bend and straighten your fingers? The wrist? The elbow? Can you lift the shoulder?' → refused, all painful → 'Examiner, my patient is unable to perform active movements of the fingers, thumb, wrist, elbow or shoulder because of pain. As this is a TRAUMATIC LIMB IN WHICH I HAVE NOT EXCLUDED A FRACTURE, I am deliberately omitting passive movement. I'd like to give him analgesia and reassess.' (Never 'let me move it for you then' — forcing passive movement on a painful un-imaged limb after a fall can displace a fracture.)

MOTOR BY MYOTOME, with the reason said first: 'because the claw involves all four fingers I suspect a lesion at the level of the NERVE ROOTS rather than a single peripheral nerve, so I'll examine motor and sensory function by myotome and dermatome rather than by nerve territory. My patient will not move, but I'll demonstrate each movement so you can see what I'm testing.' Then C5 elbows out to the side, C6 bend the elbow up, C7 push my hand away, C8 squeeze my two fingers both hands, T1 spread your fingers → 'C5, C6 and C7 cannot be assessed. He grips normally on the left but has no grip at all on the right — C8 power cannot be demonstrated. There is no finger abduction on the right — T1 cannot be demonstrated.' (Skipping this block because 'he can't move anyway' loses every motor mark; forty seconds buys five ticks. And do not run Froment's or Tinel's — nerve tests in a root problem.)

SENSORY — one modality, five points, and silence is the finding: 'this is cotton wool — I'll touch it on your breastbone first so you know what it feels like. Now close your eyes, and every time you feel me touch you, just say yes.' C5 lateral deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger — present and equal; C8 little finger and T1 medial forearm on the right — COMPLETE SILENCE. Do not wait for a 'no' that never comes: touch, pause one beat, announce it. 'Examiner, I have sensory loss in the C8 and T1 dermatomes of the right upper limb, with C5, C6 and C7 intact.'

REFLEXES on the affected side only, then the screen that changes management: 'there is no classical special test for this hand, so as the problem is neurological I'll extend the neurological examination and check the reflexes on the affected side. The biceps jerk — C5 and C6 — is present and normal. The TRICEPS jerk — C7 and C8 — is ABSENT, which fits a lesion involving C8. I'll skip the supinator jerk as it shares the roots of the biceps. To complete: I'm looking at his eyes for a ptosis or a constricted pupil — a HORNER'S SYNDROME — which would suggest the T1 root has been AVULSED rather than stretched. None present. Chest expansion is equal. And Max, before anything else, let's get on top of that pain.' (If you are behind at the 7-minute bell, sacrifice the reflexes, not the explanation — name them and move on.)

EXPLAIN in plain words, drawn in the air: nerves leave the spine in the neck and join into a bundle that runs into the arm, giving it movement and feeling; the bundle splits into three branches, and when he grabbed the branch and his body kept falling the arm was pulled further than it is meant to go and the LOWER branch has been stretched. Your reasons: all four fingers curled happens when the small muscles inside the hand stop working, and those are all supplied by that lower branch; and he could not feel the little finger or the inner forearm, which is exactly the skin those nerves supply. Plan: pain relief, sling, X-rays of arm and chest, referral to the Adelaide nerve team, and a nerve test in about a month. THEN BE STRAIGHT: 'most stretch injuries like this do recover, but it takes MONTHS, not weeks, and I can't promise you today how much comes back.' Safety-net: hand white, blue or cold, much worse pain, or a tight swollen forearm. His agenda, if concerns are never invited: 'I'm self-employed, doc. If I can't hold a strainer post I don't get paid. How long are we talking?'

May I confirm his observations are stable?' / 'On inspection I can see a full claw hand of the right hand involving all four fingers.' / 'There is no muscle wasting, consistent with an acute injury.' / 'Radial pulses are present and of equal volume bilaterally.' / 'I'm now examining the shoulder and the root of the neck, because the presentation is in the hand but I suspect the lesion is up here.'

'Active movements are limited by pain, so I am deliberately omitting passive movement in a traumatic limb in which I have not excluded a fracture.' / 'Because all four fingers are involved, I'll examine by myotome and dermatome rather than by nerve territory.' / 'He grips normally on the left but has no grip at all on the right — C8 cannot be demonstrated.' / 'I have sensory loss in the C8 and T1 dermatomes of the right upper limb.' / 'Biceps — C5, C6 — present. Triceps — C7 and C8 — absent.' / 'I'm checking for a ptosis and a constricted pupil — a Horner's syndrome — which would suggest the T1 root has been avulsed rather than stretched.'

Examiner questions: 'why is this not an ulnar nerve palsy?' → all four claw, so every intrinsic is denervated and every intrinsic is C8/T1, and the sensory loss is dermatomal rather than the ulnar one and a half digits. / 'What is the ULNAR PARADOX?' → the higher the ulnar lesion, the LESS the clawing, because a lesion at the elbow also denervates flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers so those fingers cannot flex at the IP joints. / 'Which muscles are affected?' → all the intrinsics (interossei, all four lumbricals, thenar and hypothenar) plus the long finger flexors, which are also C8. / 'What single sign would change your management today?' → a Horner's syndrome (the sympathetic supply to the eye leaves the cord with T1, so it means a PRE-GANGLIONIC avulsion, which will not recover spontaneously) — or any pulse deficit, which makes it a vascular emergency.

Variant 1 — HORNER'S PRESENT: 'I also note a ptosis and a constricted pupil on the right — a Horner's syndrome... this suggests a pre-ganglionic injury, a root AVULSION rather than a stretch. That carries a poor prognosis for spontaneous recovery and makes this an urgent referral. I'd want an MRI of the plexus looking for a pseudomeningocele.' To Max: 'one of the things I've found suggests the nerve may have been pulled right off where it leaves the spine, rather than just stretched.' / Variant 2 — WEAK OR ABSENT RADIAL PULSE: INTERRUPT YOUR OWN EXAMINATION — 'the right radial pulse is reduced compared with the left. Given the mechanism I'm concerned about a subclavian or axillary arterial injury. This becomes a vascular emergency — I'd auscultate for a bruit, arrange an urgent CT angiogram, and escalate to the vascular team and to MedSTAR now rather than complete the rest of my examination.' A pulse deficit outranks everything, and nobody has ever failed for interrupting an examination to declare a vascular emergency.

Variant 3 — ONLY THE 4th AND 5th CLAW: 'on inspection I can see a PARTIAL claw hand involving the ring and little fingers only. Because the index and middle lumbricals are median-supplied and are spared, this suggests an ULNAR NERVE PALSY rather than a lower plexus lesion. I'll therefore examine BY NERVE TERRITORY — Froment's sign, the card test, FDP to the ring and little fingers, sensation over the ulnar one and a half digits, and Tinel's at the cubital tunnel and Guyon's canal to localise the level.' / Variant 4 — HE AGREES TO MOVE: grade power 0-5 on the MRC scale comparing sides — C5 to C7 are 5/5 and equal, C8 and T1 are 0/5 on the right — then test the long flexors individually and check tone.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED. THE ONE THING: five isolated movement tests, each ending in a NAMED TENDON and a verdict — everything else is scaffolding. A normal FIST does not exclude a divided tendon, because an intact profundus pulls every finger in even when superficialis is cut. Count the five off on your own fingers as you go (wrist, fist, DIP, PIP, THUMB) — it is the most reliable way to stop the thumb being forgotten. Automatic fails: a generic range-of-movement sweep with no tendon isolated or named; thumb interphalangeal flexion never tested; removing the dressing or the foreign body; the bell going with no neurological examination performed.
stem: Emergency Department, regional South Australian hospital; you are the RMO. Jesse Hollows, 25, cut the VOLAR aspect of the left forearm just above the wrist on broken glass an hour ago. Primary survey complete, haemodynamically stable, analgesia given, and a BLOOD-SOAKED DRESSING covers the wound. No history or wound management required.

Version B (the scripted one): everything normal except LOSS OF FLEXION AT THE INTERPHALANGEAL JOINT OF THE THUMB — flexor pollicis longus. Version A is entirely normal; Version C is a hand of benediction with a numb index pulp (median nerve).
