time: WIPE with both arms uncovered to the elbow on a pillow, hand hygiene SAID, and an offer of more analgesia · GENERAL APPEARANCE then INSPECTION of both hands, both surfaces, with TWO key findings named first: NO PALLOR and a PRESERVED NORMAL FLEXED RESTING CASCADE of the fingers, symmetrical with the other side; the dressing is named ONCE and left alone ('the surgical team will look underneath in a controlled setting'), and any foreign body stays put because it may be tamponading a divided vessel · PALPATION, four steps: temperature (no cold clammy hand), capillary refill, radial pulse compared for VOLUME not rate, and tenderness over phalanges, metacarpals, wrist and snuffbox (he may have punched a wall or fallen through the glass · skipping this is how a metacarpal or distal radius fracture gets missed) · THEN THE SENTENCE BEFORE ANY MOVEMENT: 'the tendons crossing a volar wound are the FLEXORS, so I am going to test three flexor groups with five isolated movements, and I will name the tendon each one tests' · 1 wrist flexion (FCR and FCU), 2 the fist (superficialis AND profundus combined · A SCREENING TEST ONLY), 3 block the PIPs and flex the DIP (FDP), 4 hold three fingers flat and flex the free finger at the PIP (FDS), 5 hold the thumb base and flex the thumb IP (FPL) → IT WILL NOT GO · NEUROLOGICAL, NERVE-WISE not dermatomal ('a blade cuts nerves, not nerve roots'): median motor (thumb to the ceiling against resistance), ulnar motor (paper pinch, Froment's), radial motor (wrist extension), then one sensory modality at the index pulp, little finger pulp and snuffbox · then explain in three words: tendons, nerves, blood vessels.

back.dx: Division of FLEXOR POLLICIS LONGUS — loss of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, with wrist flexion, the fist, isolated DIP flexion (profundus) and isolated PIP flexion (superficialis) all intact, and median, ulnar and radial motor and sensory function normal. The hand is well perfused: normal colour and temperature, refill under two seconds, radial pulse of normal volume. Plan: analgesia, TETANUS review, plain X-ray for retained glass, and urgent referral to the hand surgical team for exploration and repair IN THEATRE — do not remove the foreign body or explore the wound in the department. To the patient, in three words: three things run through the front of the wrist — the NERVES which carry feeling and power, the BLOOD VESSELS which carry blood to the fingers, and the TENDONS, the cords that bend the wrist and fingers; the vessels are fine and the nerves are working, but the cord that bends the very tip of the thumb has probably been cut. Repairable, but by a surgeon in theatre, then months of hand therapy — and no promise of a perfect result. A NORMAL EXAMINATION DOES NOT EXCLUDE A PARTIAL LACERATION: a cord can be partly cut and still work, so formal exploration is still needed.
plan: WIPE, pillow, pain: '...I've been asked to examine your hand and wrist. I'll look at both hands, gently feel them, then ask you to copy some movements. Is that alright? I'll need both arms uncovered to the elbow, resting on this pillow. Are you in any pain — would you like more pain relief before we start?' (Hand washing is the step candidates forget once they are nervous — do it before you touch him and SAY so.)

Inspection with the TWO key findings first, and the dressing declined: 'may I look at both hands — and turn them over for me?' → 'do you want the bandage off?' → 'No — I'll leave that exactly where it is; the surgical team will look underneath in a controlled setting.' → 'Examiner, on inspection of both hands, front and back, my two key findings are NO PALLOR of the affected hand and a PRESERVED NORMAL FLEXED RESTING POSITION of the fingers, symmetrical with the other side. There is a blood-soaked dressing over the volar forearm, which I will not disturb. Otherwise no swelling, redness, bruising, deformity or scars.' If there is visible glass: 'I would not attempt to remove it here — it may be tamponading a divided vessel, and it should come out in theatre.'

PALPATION, four steps, done briskly and not skipped: 'temperature is normal and symmetrical, and I cannot feel a cold, clammy hand on the injured side. Capillary refill returns in under two seconds. The radial pulse is present with normal VOLUME and equal to the other side. And there is no tenderness over the phalanges, metacarpals, wrist or anatomical snuffbox.' (Commentating 'rate 90, regular' earns nothing — the answer they want is volume, compared with the other side.)

THE SENTENCE, then movements 1 and 2: 'Examiner, the tendons crossing a volar wound are the flexors, so I am going to test three flexor groups — the wrist flexors, the finger flexors and the thumb flexor — with five isolated movements, and I will name the tendon each one tests. Jesse, copy my movements. Bend your wrist forwards — wrist flexion is full, FLEXOR CARPI RADIALIS AND ULNARIS are intact. Now make a tight fist — that is the combined movement of superficialis and profundus, A SCREENING TEST ONLY. It does not exclude an isolated injury, so I'll separate them.'

Movements 3, 4 and THE FINDING: 'I'm holding your middle joints still — bend just the tips. Blocking the PIPs and testing distal interphalangeal flexion isolates FLEXOR DIGITORUM PROFUNDUS, which is intact. Now three fingers flat, the middle one free — bend that finger only: pure proximal interphalangeal flexion, isolating FLEXOR DIGITORUM SUPERFICIALIS, which is intact. Last one — I'm holding the base of your thumb still. Bend the tip of your thumb... and again for me...' → it will not go → 'Examiner, I am testing flexion at the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, which isolates FLEXOR POLLICIS LONGUS. The patient is unable to perform that movement, so I am concerned about an injury to that tendon.' (Never decide FOR the patient that a movement is too painful to attempt — attempt all five, and narrate any refusal.)

NERVES, nerve by nerve, with the reason: 'I am examining nerve-wise rather than by dermatome, because a laceration divides named peripheral nerves. Palm flat, point your thumb at the ceiling, don't let me push it down — strong, MEDIAN motor intact. Pinch this paper, don't let me pull it — the thumb stays straight, Froment's negative, ULNAR motor intact. Cock your wrist back and hold it — strong, RADIAL motor intact. Now close your eyes, tell me when you feel me and whether it's the same on both sides — sensation is intact and symmetrical over the index pulp (median), the little finger pulp (ulnar) and the snuffbox (radial).' (The radial takes fifteen seconds and completes the examination — skip it and expect 'where does the radial nerve cross to the dorsum?')

Explain in plain language, then summarise (see dx). His question: 'will I get the use of it back? I'm a chef — I need my hands.' → 'that's an important thing to tell me. This is repairable, and repaired tendons usually do well, but it takes surgery and then months of hand therapy, and I can't promise a perfect result until the surgeon has looked.' Then: operation yes, the wound needs formal exploration under anaesthetic; work — no number yet, and a ReturnToWorkSA claim today if it happened at work; driving — not today and not with a splint, so organise someone to collect him. NEVER 'it's only a small cut' — the size of the skin wound tells you nothing about what is divided beneath it.

Version A — EVERYTHING NORMAL: the difficulty is sounding certain without sounding dismissive, and not inventing a finding to fill the silence. 'Examiner, all five movements are intact — the wrist flexors, the deep and superficial finger flexors and flexor pollicis longus — and median, ulnar and radial motor and sensory function are normal. I have no clinical evidence of a complete flexor tendon or nerve division. I would add that a normal examination does not exclude a PARTIAL laceration, and I would still refer for formal wound exploration.' To the patient: 'everything I tested today was normal, which is genuinely good news. But it doesn't mean we can simply close this up — a cord can be partly cut and still work for now, so the team will look inside properly in theatre.'

Version C — MEDIAN NERVE: the abnormality appears ONLY on making a fist, so DESCRIBE it before you name it — 'on attempting to make a fist the second and third fingers remain extended while the fourth and fifth flex normally. This is the HAND OF BENEDICTION.' Then confirm: 'thumb abduction is weak against resistance, and sensation is reduced over the pulp of the index finger compared with the other hand. Froment's is negative and wrist extension is strong, so ulnar and radial function appear preserved. Taken together these point to a median nerve injury, and I cannot exclude an associated tendon injury clinically.' THE 2023 TRAP: candidates confused this with an ulnar CLAW, then found median sensory loss and unravelled — claw is a RESTING posture of the ring and little fingers; benediction appears only on making a fist and involves the index and middle.

back.dx: OCCULT SCAPHOID FRACTURE — a fall on an outstretched hand two hours ago with mild but definite tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox AND over the scaphoid tubercle and a POSITIVE axial compression test, on a background of a radiograph reported as normal. A normal film does not exclude it: the scaphoid commonly does not show for the first week or two, and its blood supply enters from ONE END ONLY, so a missed fracture can fail to unite — a far bigger problem than two weeks in a cast. Differentials given to the patient with reasons: distal radius fracture — no deformity and no tenderness there; tendon injury — all movements work; nerve injury — feeling and power normal; vascular injury — the hand is warm with a good pulse. MANAGEMENT, all four parts: analgesia; a THUMB SPICA CAST from below the elbow wrapping the thumb, holding it in the position you would hold a can, because the bone moves with the thumb; an MRI of the wrist if available (shows it straight away), and if not, keep the cast on and REPEAT THE X-RAY IN 10-14 DAYS; fracture clinic review either way. Safety-net: pain worse rather than better, pain not responding to analgesia, fingers numb or tingly, colour change, or inability to move them — which is the sentence that generates the compartment syndrome station three days later. Plus a work certificate and a ReturnToWorkSA claim if it happened at work.
plan: Name the film's limits FIRST: 'Examiner, before I start — the radiograph shows no visible fracture line, but in a patient with this mechanism A NORMAL FILM DOES NOT EXCLUDE A SCAPHOID FRACTURE, so my examination is directed at that.' Then WIPE with the pillow: '...I have been asked to examine your hand. I will be looking at your hands, feeling your hands, and asking you to do some movements, and then a couple of specific tests. I will be as gentle as I can — tell me if anything is sore. Could you rest both hands on this pillow for me? I will just wash my hands. Examiner, on general appearance my patient is uncomfortable but not distressed, with no protective posture and no sling.'

INSPECTION — three specific findings before the generic list: 'let me see the palms first. Now could you turn your hands over so I can see the backs? Examiner, inspecting the palmar and then the dorsal aspect of both hands: I cannot see any PALLOR, there are no lacerations and NO OPEN FRACTURES, and the KNUCKLE CONTOUR is preserved. In addition there is mild swelling over the radial side of the right wrist, but no bruising and no deformity.' (Each of the three changes what you do next; 'no swelling, no redness, no rashes' impresses nobody.)

PALPATION — where the diagnosis lives, one hand, zone by zone: 'temperature is normal and equal with no local rise. Capillary refill is under two seconds bilaterally. Radial pulses are present and equal with normal volume. I am now palpating the right hand only. Palpating the fingers and interphalangeal joints... the metacarpals and metacarpophalangeal joints... the wrist, supported from below. I am now palpating THE ANATOMICAL SNUFFBOX — any pain there?' → 'ooh, yes, a little' → 'and now THE SCAPHOID TUBERCLE, just here where I would take your pulse — and there?' → 'yeah, that's a bit sore too' → 'and finally the radial styloid and shaft, and the ulnar styloid and shaft. Examiner, there is MILD BUT DEFINITE tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and over the scaphoid tubercle, with no tenderness elsewhere including the styloids.' (She gives nothing unless the exact point is pressed — which is why the same case produces opposite recalls on the same day — and ANY tenderness at these two points is a positive.)

Movement and the nerve screen: 'copy my movements. Make a fist, and open. Now the thumb — out, in, across, out, and count your fingers with your thumb. Now the wrist — down, back, towards the thumb, towards the little finger. Examiner, active movements are present in all three groups with discomfort at the extremes of wrist movement. Since active movement is achievable I am not performing passive movement. Because this is a DISTAL injury my neurological screen is nerve-wise rather than dermatomes and myotomes: touch my finger with your thumb and hold it — median motor intact; grip this paper and don't let me take it — Froment's negative, ulnar motor intact; bend both wrists back and resist me — radial motor intact. Eyes closed, say yes when you feel the cotton — sensation intact at the index pulp, little fingertip and snuffbox.'

THE SPECIAL TEST, done correctly: 'Jenny, one last test. I am going to hold the base of your thumb and press gently along it — tell me if it hurts.' GRIP THE FIRST METACARPAL, not the thumb; support the wrist; compress in and out along the ray → 'yeah, that does hurt a bit' → 'Examiner, axial compression of the thumb ray reproduces her pain. That is a POSITIVE SCAPHOID COMPRESSION TEST.' (Grip the thumb phalanges instead and the MCP joint flexes, absorbs the force, and a genuinely positive case gives you a negative test.)

Diagnosis and differentials TO THE PATIENT: 'the X-ray does not show a break — but I am still concerned that you have one. There is a small bone in your wrist called the scaphoid, right here at the base of your thumb. It is well known for not showing up on an X-ray in the first week or two, even when it is broken, and everything I have found on examining you points to it.' Then each differential with its reason (see dx). She WILL push back once: 'but the X-ray was normal. Doesn't that mean it's just a sprain?' → 'I understand why it sounds like that, and I wish it did. But if we treat a broken scaphoid as a sprain, the bone can fail to heal, because its blood supply comes in from ONE END ONLY. That is a much bigger problem than two weeks in a cast, so we treat it as broken until we can prove it isn't.' Agreeing with her is the automatic fail this case exists to catch.

Elicit the agenda, then the four-part plan: 'before I go through the plan — what was worrying you most when you came in today?' → 'I'm a chef. I've got a wedding to cook for on Saturday, and I'm the only one who can do it. How long am I going to be in a cast?' → be honest: she will not be cooking on Saturday; if the scan is clear the cast can come off within a couple of weeks, and if it is broken it is longer; write the certificate so the employer understands what she CAN and cannot do rather than just 'unfit'; lodge with ReturnToWorkSA if it happened at work. Then analgesia, thumb spica cast NOW, MRI or repeat X-ray at 10-14 days, fracture clinic, and the safety-net (see dx).

Capillary refill under two seconds. Radial pulses present and equal with normal volume.'

'I am now palpating the anatomical snuffbox... and now the scaphoid tubercle.' / 'Since active movement is achievable I am not performing passive movement.' / 'Because this is a distal injury my neurological screen is nerve-wise rather than dermatomes and myotomes.' / 'Axial compression of the thumb ray reproduces her pain — a positive scaphoid compression test.'

To the patient: 'there is a small bone at the base of your thumb called the scaphoid. It is well known for not showing on an X-ray for the first week or two, even when broken.' / 'I am going to treat you as though it is broken until we can prove otherwise.' / 'Its blood supply comes in from one end only, so if a break is missed the bone can fail to heal.' / 'A cast from below your elbow, wrapped around the thumb — the position you would hold a can.' / 'An MRI if we can get one; otherwise repeat the X-ray in ten to fourteen days.' / 'Come straight back if the pain worsens, stops responding to painkillers, your fingers go numb or change colour, or you cannot move them.'

Variant B — THE X-RAY IS ABNORMAL (24M, obvious distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation): inspection changes to 'bruising over the dorsal distal forearm and a dorsal deformity — a DINNER-FORK appearance. No pallor, no open fracture, knuckle contour preserved.' Then the palpate-or-not decision, either answer of which passes as long as you SAY it: 'I am deliberately not palpating the distal radius and radial styloid — the fracture is confirmed radiologically, so palpation adds no diagnostic information and would cause unnecessary pain. I am still palpating the snuffbox and the scaphoid tubercle, because a visible radius fracture does not exclude a second injury.' / Variant C — FOUR MINUTES: 'given the four minutes I am prioritising the findings that change my management and will move quickly through the generic inspection.' Cut the generic sweep, the second press per finger, the unaffected side, finger movements and the elbow offer; KEEP the three specific inspection findings, temperature/refill/pulse in one pass, snuffbox and tubercle, wrist and thumb movement, sensation with commentary, and the axial compression test.

Variant D — THE PUNCH: 'loss of the normal knuckle contour over the fifth metacarpal head with local swelling — consistent with a metacarpal neck, or BOXER'S, fracture.' Then assess ROTATIONAL DEFORMITY — ask him to flex the fingers and check whether any finger crosses over its neighbour, because malrotation changes management from buddy strapping to surgical fixation and is the finding most often missed. Ask about the mechanism honestly: a punch to a face raises a FIGHT-BITE over the knuckle, a contaminated wound needing washout and antibiotics. / Variant E — THE WRONG JOINT: the stem says FOOSH but the pain is in the SHOULDER and the arm is held across the chest → 'although the mechanism is a fall on an outstretched hand, the pain is localised to the shoulder, so I will perform a shoulder examination. I would also screen the elbow and wrist briefly, because a fall of this kind transmits force along the whole limb and injuries at two levels are common.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Traill, 30, head chef at a pub in Kadina, right-handed, lives with her partner. Slipped on a wet kitchen floor AT WORK two hours ago and put the right hand out, landing on the palm with the wrist bent back; no head strike, nothing else injured. A dull ache on the thumb side about 5/10, swelled a little at first, nothing taken for it, can still move the hand though bending the wrist back hurts. Oral contraceptive only, no allergies, non-smoker, no medical history. Calm, practical, slightly impatient — treating it as an inconvenience UNTIL the doctor mentions a cast. HOW SHE PLAYS IT: tenderness ONLY in the anatomical snuffbox and over the scaphoid tubercle, given as 'ooh, yes, a little' — mild and understated, never a cry — and ONLY if the exact point is pressed; if the candidate announces the snuffbox but presses nearby, or grabs the whole hand, she says 'no, that's fine'. Movements all possible with pain at the extremes of wrist extension; power and sensation normal. AXIAL COMPRESSION: mild pain, but ONLY if the METACARPAL is held — if they grip the thumb itself, it does not hurt. THE X-RAY CHALLENGE, pushed once: 'but the X-ray was normal. Doesn't that mean it's just a sprain?' HIDDEN AGENDA: a 90-person wedding on Saturday that only she can cook — revealed to an open question about concerns or work, otherwise flatly at the close: 'so am I meant to just not work, then?'

Numbers: 4 palpation steps; capillary refill under 2 s; power 0-5; TWO must-press points — snuffbox and scaphoid tubercle; THREE specific inspection findings — pallor, open fracture, knuckle contour; 70-80% of scaphoid fractures are at the WAIST; re-X-ray at 10-14 days if MRI is unavailable VERIFY; 3 sensory safe points — index pulp, little fingertip, snuffbox. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; PATS beyond 100 km.

Scored checklist: introduced and confirmed the name; explained and consented; used the pillow; commented on general appearance, posture and sling; inspected palms AND backs; named pallor, open fracture and knuckle contour before the generic list; temperature, capillary refill and pulses both sides; palpated with ONE hand, zone by zone, with commentary; PRESSED AND NAMED the anatomical snuffbox; PRESSED AND NAMED the scaphoid tubercle; palpated the styloids; ACCEPTED MILD TENDERNESS AS A POSITIVE; asked about movement rather than presuming; justified skipping passive; said aloud they were testing nerves not roots; motor against resistance both sides with each nerve named; PERFORMED the axial compression test; GRIPPED THE METACARPAL not the thumb; did NOT reassure that nothing was broken; gave differentials in plain words with reasons; named the cast, the scan and the fallback; asked what was worrying her unprompted; safety-netted and offered a work certificate.
fails: ★ Reassuring her that nothing is broken because the X-ray is normal — the failure this station was built to catch
★ Not performing the axial compression test, or gripping the thumb phalanges instead of the first metacarpal so the force never reaches the scaphoid
Never pressing the snuffbox or the scaphoid tubercle — or announcing the snuffbox while pressing somewhere near it, which gets you nothing
Dismissing mild tenderness: any tenderness at those two points is a POSITIVE; and two-handed palpation, which makes localisation impossible
Discharging without immobilisation and without a plan to re-image; naming the investigation and stopping, with no cast now, no fallback if MRI is unavailable and no safety-net

70-80% of scaphoid fractures at the waist · blood supply enters from ONE end (risk of non-union and AVN) · thumb spica cast NOW · MRI, or repeat X-ray at 10-14 days VERIFY · fracture clinic · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, PATS beyond 100 km, ReturnToWorkSA

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION + PROCEDURE — regional ED, evening shift. FOUR tasks in eight minutes and one of them needs your hands: SLING IN YOUR HANDS BY 6:00 whatever is unfinished. The clavicle sits directly on the brachial plexus, the subclavian vessels and the lung apex, so the fracture is not the problem — its neighbours are, and naming all three is what Task 3 adds. Automatic fails: moving the shoulder passively; undressing him without asking; never applying the sling; never examining the neurovascular status; never listening to the chest.
stem: Emergency Department, regional South Australian hospital; you are the resident. Jake Mullins, 25, right-hand dominant, works in a shearing shed. Fell onto his outstretched right arm playing football this afternoon; pain in the right shoulder, no head strike, no loss of consciousness, no other injury. Alert, in obvious pain, sitting upright holding the right arm hard against his chest. HR 96, BP 132/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.8, GCS 15. Paracetamol 1 g and ibuprofen 400 mg given at triage. A radiograph in the room shows a fracture of the MIDDLE THIRD of the right clavicle with minimal displacement.
tasks: Explain the X-ray to the patient
Perform a focused physical examination of the right shoulder and upper limb, with a running commentary to your examiner
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain your immediate management — including applying the sling on the trolley — and your ongoing management
time: 0:00-0:45 introduce and OFFER ANALGESIA (never 'are you in pain?' to a man visibly in pain), then the film in THREE SENTENCES and forty seconds: fracture, site (middle third), displacement (minimal) · 0:45-1:15 consent and exposure: he will say 'you do it' · ASK before undoing the gown tapes and lower it only to the chest · 1:15-2:00 general appearance (pain, guarding, no sling, NO RESPIRATORY DISTRESS) and five chosen inspection findings, each mapping to a complication: shoulder sitting lower, bruising and erythema over the middle third, SKIN INTEGRITY with no laceration, open fracture or TENTING, and no pallor of either hand · 2:00-2:55 PALPATION: temperature over both clavicles and shoulders, both hands warm, capillary refill, radial pulses compared for VOLUME, then tenderness at the sternoclavicular joint, along the clavicle DELIBERATELY SKIPPING THE FRACTURED SEGMENT (confirmed radiologically), then AC joint, coracoid, acromion, humeral head and biceps tendon · 2:55-3:15 MOVEMENT: he refuses, so announce the omission of passive movement and the reason · 3:15-4:45 ROOTS not nerves, because you are looking for a brachial plexus injury: C5, C6 and C7 myotomes NAMED AS UNASSESSABLE because of pain, then C8 grip and T1 finger abduction, then dermatomes C5 badge, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 MEDIAL ELBOW (find it on the correct arm · it is folded across his chest) · 4:45-5:15 THE SPECIAL TEST: auscultate POSTERIORLY in six areas to exclude a pneumothorax, because his arms are across the front · 5:15-7:45 diagnosis (nerves, vessel, lung all checked and normal), SLING ON while you talk, RE-CHECK the limb afterwards, then immediate and ongoing management · 7:45-8:00 five red flags in one breath.

back.dx: Closed, minimally displaced fracture of the MIDDLE THIRD of the right clavicle, UNCOMPLICATED — the skin is intact with no tenting, there is no pallor, radial pulses are present and equal in volume with capillary refill under two seconds, C8 and T1 power is preserved with C5-C7 unassessable because of pain, sensation is intact C5-T1, and air entry is equal with no respiratory distress. That sentence — nerves, vessel and lung all checked and normal — is the entire point of Task 3. Immediate management: analgesia by the clock (paracetamol 1 g six-hourly to a maximum of 4 g/24 h, ibuprofen 400 mg eight-hourly with food unless contraindicated), ICE for the first couple of days, rest, and the arm propped on a PILLOW at night because a sling does nothing lying flat; broad arm sling with the elbow at a right angle, hand slightly higher than the elbow, fingertips visible and the knot padded to the SIDE of the neck. Ongoing: move fingers, wrist and elbow daily as soon as pain allows or he ends up with a stiff hand and shoulder on top of a healed fracture; physiotherapy once united; fracture clinic in 7-10 days; union about six weeks, contact sport about three months; work certificate and a ReturnToWorkSA claim if work-related; NO DRIVING in the sling. Talk to orthopaedics if: open, TENTED SKIN, neurovascular deficit, shortening 2 cm or more, 100% displaced with no cortical contact, floating shoulder, or an unstable lateral third.
plan: Analgesia first, then the film in three sentences: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. Is it Jake? I can see you're in a lot of pain — have you had anything for it?' → 'the nurse gave me some tablets' → 'Good. Let me show you the X-ray first, then I'll examine your shoulder. (turns the film towards him and points) THIS BONE HERE IS YOUR COLLARBONE, AND IT IS BROKEN — the medical name is a clavicle fracture. We divide the collarbone into three parts, and YOUR BREAK IS IN THE MIDDLE THIRD. And looking at the two broken ends, THEY'VE ONLY SHIFTED APART SLIGHTLY. That's the good version of this injury.' → 'so it's definitely broken? Does that mean surgery?' → 'it is definitely broken — and almost certainly no surgery. Let me examine you and then I'll explain the whole plan.' (Two minutes on the film is the commonest way to lose the sling.)

Consent and exposure in thirty seconds: 'I need to look at your shoulder and the top of your chest. Are you able to slip the gown down for me?' → he says 'yeah, okay' and does nothing, then 'you do it' → 'No problem at all. MAY I UNDO THE TAPES ON THE SHOULDER AND LOWER IT FOR YOU? I'll only bring it down to your chest. Stay just as you are — that's a good position. I'll clean my hands. Happy for me to start?' (Undressing him without asking, or giving up and examining through the gown, are both automatic fails.)

Five inspection findings, each mapping to a complication: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is a young man in pain and distress, sitting up, guarding the right arm in a protective posture, not wearing a sling, and importantly with NO RESPIRATORY DISTRESS. On inspection: the right shoulder sits LOWER than the left; there is bruising and erythema over the middle third of the right clavicle; SKIN INTEGRITY IS PRESERVED — no laceration, no open fracture and NO TENTING of the skin; and there is no pallor of either hand.'

Palpation, with the deliberate skip: 'Jake, I'm going to feel around your shoulder now. If it hurts, say so and I'll stop straight away. Examiner: back of my fingers over both clavicles and both shoulders — no local rise in temperature. Both hands warm, not cold and clammy. Capillary refill under two seconds bilaterally. Both radial pulses present and equal IN VOLUME. Now tenderness: sternoclavicular joint... along the clavicle... EXAMINER, I AM DELIBERATELY SKIPPING THE FRACTURED SEGMENT, WHICH IS ALREADY CONFIRMED RADIOLOGICALLY... acromioclavicular joint, coracoid, acromion, humeral head, biceps tendon — all non-tender.' (Version B, no film yet: palpate the whole clavicle, let him wince, say sorry, and report focal tenderness over the middle third, then request AP and 30-degree cephalic-tilt films.)

Movement, and the automatic fail avoided: 'can you lift the arm away from your side for me?' → 'no, too painful' → 'Examiner, my patient cannot perform active shoulder movement because of pain. As this is an ACUTE TRAUMATIC LIMB, I am deliberately not attempting passive movement.' → 'I won't make you. Can you bend the elbow at all? And can you wiggle your fingers for me?' (Never 'alright, let me move it for you then' — instant fail, and it can displace the fracture.)

ROOTS, not nerves, with every omission named: 'because I am looking for a BRACHIAL PLEXUS injury I am testing nerve roots, not individual nerves. C5 — skipping, he cannot abduct the shoulder because of pain. C6 — skipping, no elbow flexion. C7 — skipping, no elbow extension. Jake, squeeze my fingers as hard as you can... now spread your fingers and don't let me push them together. C8 and T1 power are preserved. I have DOCUMENTED that C5 to C7 could not be assessed because of pain, and I would reassess after analgesia.' Then dermatomes with ONE modality: 'this is cotton wool, it feels like this on your breastbone. Close your eyes, tell me when you feel it and whether it's the same on both sides. C5 over the deltoid badge area, C6 the thumb, C7 the middle finger, C8 the little finger, T1 the MEDIAL ELBOW, comparing both sides — sensation is intact and symmetrical C5 to T1.' (He never lets go of his shoulder, so find T1 on the correct medial elbow — candidates routinely test the wrong arm when it is folded across the chest.)

The special test, from behind: 'I'm going to listen to your breathing from behind. Stay just as you are, you don't need to move your arm. Examiner, THE CLAVICLE OVERLIES THE APEX OF THE LUNG, so my special test here is to exclude a PNEUMOTHORAX. His arms are crossed over the front of the chest so I will auscultate POSTERIORLY in six areas. For time I am omitting inspection, palpation, percussion and vocal resonance, and would perform them if I found any abnormality. Air entry is equal and normal bilaterally with no added sounds.' (Never picking up the stethoscope is an automatic fail; fighting to auscultate the front through his crossed arms loses forty seconds.)

Diagnosis — what the EXAMINATION added — then the sling while you talk: 'you have broken your collarbone, in the middle third, and the ends have only shifted a little. The reason I examined you so carefully is that THIS BONE SITS DIRECTLY ON TOP OF SOME IMPORTANT NERVES, A BIG BLOOD VESSEL AND THE TOP OF YOUR LUNG. I've checked all three and they are all normal — the feeling and circulation in your arm are fine and your lung sounds clear. So this is an uncomplicated break.' Then apply the sling, narrating: 'elbow bent at about a right angle... forearm across your chest... hand a touch higher than the elbow... the edge comes out to your little finger so I can still see your fingertips... and I'll tie the knot to the SIDE of your neck with padding, not on the bone at the back.' THEN RE-CHECK: 'let me just re-check your hand now the sling is on — pulse is good, the hand is warm, fingers move, feeling is normal' — a scoring line almost everyone misses.

Immediate then ongoing management, then the agenda and the red flags: analgesia BY THE CLOCK, ice for a couple of days, rest, and the arm propped on a pillow at night. Then: move fingers, wrist and elbow daily as soon as pain allows; physiotherapy once knitted; fracture clinic in 7-10 days; healed about six weeks, footy about three months → 'three months?! Shearing starts in three weeks — I don't get paid if I don't work.' → 'that's a real problem and I'm glad you raised it. You won't be shearing at three weeks. I'll write you a certificate now, the clinic will review the timing, and if this happened at work there's a ReturnToWorkSA claim we should start. You also can't drive while your arm is in the sling.' FIVE RED FLAGS IN ONE BREATH: short of breath (lung), pins and needles, numbness or weakness (nerve), a pale, blue or cold hand (vessel), pain the tablets won't touch (pain), or the skin over the break breaking down (skin).

ask: 'I can see you're in a lot of pain — have you had anything for it?' / 'This bone is your collarbone and it is broken. It's in the middle third, and the ends have shifted only slightly.' / 'May I undo the tapes on the shoulder and lower the gown for you?' / 'No respiratory distress on general appearance.' / 'The skin is intact — no laceration, no open fracture, no tenting.'

'Radial pulses present and equal in volume, capillary refill under two seconds.' / 'Examiner, I am deliberately skipping the fractured segment, which is confirmed on the film.' / 'I am deliberately not attempting passive movement in an acute traumatic limb.' / 'I'm testing roots, not nerves, because I'm looking for a brachial plexus injury.' / 'My special test here is to exclude a pneumothorax, so I'll auscultate posteriorly in six areas.'

'This bone sits on top of nerves, a blood vessel and the top of your lung — I've checked all three and they're normal.' / 'Let me re-check your hand now the sling is on.' / 'Move your fingers, wrist and elbow every day as soon as the pain lets you.' / 'Come straight back if you get short of breath, pins and needles, a pale or cold hand, uncontrolled pain, or the skin breaking down.' Do NOT say 'PRICE' or promise compression — there is nothing to compress in a clavicle fracture.

Variant C — THE SKIN IS TENTED: 'on inspection there is a tented, blanched area of skin over the fracture. This is an IMPENDING OPEN FRACTURE. I am not going to sling and discharge; I would give analgesia, keep him nil by mouth, mark the skin, and refer urgently to orthopaedics for consideration of fixation before the skin breaks down.' To Jake: 'the bone is pushing hard against the skin from underneath, so I need the orthopaedic surgeons to see you today rather than sending you home in a sling.' / Variant D — NUMB HAND OR ABSENT PULSE: 'the right hand is cool and pale, the radial pulse is reduced in volume compared with the left, and there is reduced sensation in the C8 and T1 dermatomes. This is a NEUROVASCULAR INJURY until proven otherwise. I am escalating to orthopaedics and vascular surgery now, keeping him nil by mouth, and I would request CT angiography. A sling and discharge would be inappropriate.'

Variant E — BREATHLESS WITH REDUCED AIR ENTRY: 'air entry is reduced on the right and his saturations are 92% on room air. This is a TRAUMATIC PNEUMOTHORAX until proven otherwise. Oxygen, sit him up, erect chest radiograph, senior and surgical review. If he became hypotensive with distended neck veins and a deviated trachea I would treat it as a TENSION pneumothorax and decompress immediately, without waiting for imaging.' / Variant F — PAEDIATRIC, explaining to a parent: 'children's bones bend and heal differently. He needs a sling for comfort for about two to three weeks, it should be knitted in three to four, and children REMODEL — even a bit of a bend straightens out as he grows. Surgery is almost never needed.'
pefe: Role-player: Jake Mullins, 25, shearing-shed hand from Kadina, right-handed, plays local footy; went up for a mark and landed on the outstretched right arm about two hours ago; no head knock, nothing else hurts, and he DROVE HIMSELF IN. Smokes about ten a day, six or seven beers on a Saturday, no medications, allergies or past fractures. Stoic — short answers, minimises the pain in words while never letting go of that shoulder, and gets slightly short if the doctor is slow or repeats a question. HOW HE PLAYS IT: sits upright with the left hand clamped on the right shoulder and the right arm folded across the chest, and DOES NOT LET GO at any point — not for sensory testing, not for the stethoscope; asked to take the gown down, says 'yeah, okay' and does nothing, then 'you do it — I can't move my arm', and allows the tapes to be opened once permission is asked; refuses ALL shoulder and elbow movement ('too sore') and says 'don't — that really hurts' if anyone tries to move it; wiggles the fingers a little; squeezes and spreads weakly ('that's all I've got'); sensation normal everywhere and 'same' on comparison. At about 6:00 he pushes once: 'am I going to need surgery?' HIDDEN AGENDA: shearing starts in three weeks and he is paid by the day, plus a quiet fear of an operation and a metal plate — released to any question about worries, otherwise when healing times are mentioned, and before the bell regardless.

Numbers: distribution — middle third 75-80%, lateral 15-20%, medial under 5%. Films: AP plus 30-degree cephalic tilt. Sling: broad arm, 1-3 weeks, for comfort only. Union about 6 weeks in an adult and 3-4 weeks in a child; contact sport about 3 months. Fracture clinic 7-10 days. Talk to orthopaedics if open, tented skin, neurovascular deficit, shortening 2 cm or more, 100% displaced with no cortical contact, floating shoulder, or an unstable lateral third. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g six-hourly (max 4 g/24 h), ibuprofen 400 mg eight-hourly with food. Roots: C5 badge, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 medial elbow. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33. CLOCK: sling in your hands by 6:00.

Marked out of 16: introduced and OFFERED analgesia without asking 'are you in pain?'; explained the film in plain English as fracture, middle third, minimal displacement, in about forty seconds; asked permission before lowering the gown and gained real exposure; said 'no respiratory distress' at general appearance; named the shoulder asymmetry, the bruise, and that the skin was intact with no tenting; checked capillary refill and BOTH radial pulses comparing volume; said out loud they were skipping the fracture site (or found focal tenderness in Version B); did not attempt passive movement and said why; tested myotomes and dermatomes C5-T1 naming what could not be assessed; auscultated the chest and NAMED pneumothorax as the reason; explained the diagnosis by saying nerves, vessel and lung were checked and normal; PHYSICALLY APPLIED THE SLING competently; RE-CHECKED the limb afterwards; gave fracture clinic 7-10 days with early finger and wrist movement and physiotherapy; gave five red flags; and picked up the work and income concern.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, prompt bell at six minutes. Gloves from the door and no basin, so do NOT announce hand washing. Three starred items, each a fail on its own: WATCH THE GAIT BEFORE NAMING ANYTHING; LOCATE the fibular head and then TAP it; and give at least four differentials WITH REASONS — which is where most candidates failed this station in 2023, having given a beautiful explanation and no list. The examination is NERVE-WISE, so report the movement that failed and end on the nerve, never 'that's L5'.
stem: General practice. A 35-year-old strawberry picker with difficulty walking and pins and needles in the lower limb. Sitting on the edge of the bed in shorts, comfortable and not in pain; a cotton wool ball is on the trolley. Some recalls word task 1 as 'perform a lower limb examination', and a pre-2017 version says 'lower limb NEUROLOGICAL examination'.
tasks: Perform the relevant physical examination with a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: 0:00-0:45 WIPE, both legs fully visible, and signpost the positions you will need; general appearance through BOTH LENSES · 'not in pain or distress, and from a neurological point of view I cannot see any fasciculations or tremor' · 0:45-1:35 GAIT before naming anything: a few steps → high-steppage on the right, then HEEL WALKING (cannot on the right = loss of dorsiflexion) and TOE WALKING (normal = plantarflexion intact) · this is the one AMC station where both are expected · 1:35-2:50 INSPECTION standing, naming the FIBULAR HEAD ('no swelling, redness or bruising over the lateral aspect of the knee at the fibular head'), then PALPATION seated, four steps: temperature at foot and fibular head, capillary refill, posterior tibial pulse, then quick tenderness through toes, metatarsals, anterior and lateral ankle joint line, anterior and lateral knee joint line, and SPECIFICALLY the fibular head 'knowing this is where the common peroneal nerve can be entrapped' · 2:50-4:20 KNEE MOVEMENTS ONLY (every ankle movement is about to be tested against resistance), then the four movements AGAINST RESISTANCE: dorsiflexion lost, eversion impaired, plantarflexion normal, inversion normal → THE SENTENCE THE BLOCK EXISTS FOR · 4:20-5:40 SENSATION with cotton wool, eyes closed, both sides: dorsum, first web space, soles · then THE TAP TEST, locating the fibular head first and tapping with FINGERS not a hammer, asking whether he feels anything · 5:40-6:00 offer the straight-leg raise and decline it for time · then diagnosis in four sentences and SIX differentials each with a reason.

back.dx: COMMON PERONEAL NERVE ENTRAPMENT AT THE FIBULAR HEAD — high-steppage gait, inability to heel-walk with normal toe-walking, loss of dorsiflexion and eversion against resistance with PRESERVED plantarflexion and INVERSION, sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the first web space with normal soles, and a POSITIVE tap sign over the fibular head, in a strawberry picker who squats for hours. The conclusion is a NERVE: 'loss of the motor function of the common peroneal nerve, with the motor function of the tibial nerve intact.' SIX differentials, each with its reason: L5 radiculopathy — inversion is normal and there is no back pain; lumbar canal stenosis — unlikely at 35 without leg pain on walking; a central cause (stroke, TIA, tumour) — everything points to one nerve rather than a brain pattern; multiple sclerosis — a single nerve and no previous episodes; peripheral neuropathy from B12 deficiency or diabetes — that affects both legs; and traumatic nerve injury — no history and nothing to see over the knee. THE DISCRIMINATOR: inversion is preserved in a common peroneal entrapment and WEAK in an L5 radiculopathy, because tibialis posterior is an L5 muscle supplied by the tibial nerve. Management: take the pressure off (kneeling stool, rotating tasks), an ankle-foot orthosis so he does not trip, physiotherapy, and nerve conduction studies with EMG at three to four weeks if it has not improved; most recover in weeks to a few months; review at four to six weeks; check HbA1c and B12.
plan: WIPE and the two-lens general appearance: '...I'll start by asking you to take a few steps for me, then I'll be looking at your legs, gently feeling them, asking you to do some movements, and checking the sensation. I'll need to see both legs fully. I'll tell you the position I need at each step — at one point standing, then sitting. Is that all right?' → 'do I need to take my shorts off?' → 'no, shorts are fine — I just need to see both legs from above the knee down.' Then: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is not in pain or distress, and FROM A NEUROLOGICAL POINT OF VIEW I cannot see any fasciculations or tremor.' (One extra clause tells the examiner you know which kind of station you are in. Do not announce hand washing — you are wearing the gloves the examiner handed you.)

GAIT FIRST, then heels and toes: 'could you get up and take a few steps for me? That's enough, thank you. Examiner, I can see a HIGH-STEPPAGE GAIT on the right — the patient lifts the right leg higher than the left and taps the foot down rather than making a heel strike.' Then: 'now could you take a few steps ON YOUR HEELS? And now ON YOUR TOES?' → 'Examiner, the patient is unable to walk on the right heel, so there is a LOSS OF DORSIFLEXION on the right. He walks on his toes normally, so plantarflexion is intact bilaterally.' (The stem says difficulty walking, not foot drop — announcing a foot drop before watching him walk skips the step that proves it; and 'no antalgic, ataxic, broad-based or shuffling gait' tells the examiner you do not know what you are looking for.)

Inspection with the fibular head named: 'just stand still for me a moment. Examiner, on inspection I'm looking for wasting and fasciculations — I can see neither. I'm also looking for signs of trauma, and specifically I cannot see any swelling, redness or bruising OVER THE LATERAL ASPECT OF THE KNEE AT THE FIBULAR HEAD. At the foot and ankle there is no swelling, redness, bruising or deformity.' (Not showing off — it demonstrates that you know a nerve entrapment at the knee causes symptoms in the foot, exactly as the cubital tunnel does for the hand.)

PALPATION, four steps and the route: 'have a seat for me. I'm going to feel your legs now — tell me if anything is uncomfortable. Examiner, no local rise of temperature at the foot or over the fibular head, capillary refill normal, and the posterior tibial pulse present and normal in volume bilaterally. Palpating quickly through the toes, metatarsals and the anterior and lateral ankle joint line — no tenderness. At the knee, anterior and lateral joint line — no tenderness. And SPECIFICALLY palpating the fibular head, knowing this is where the common peroneal nerve can be entrapped — no tenderness and no swelling.' (Vascular assessment costs fifteen seconds and belongs in any limb examination; skip the Achilles, it has nothing to do with dorsiflexion.)

KNEE movements only, then the four resisted movements: 'can you copy my movement and bend your knee? And straighten it. Knee flexion and extension are full and pain free.' Then 'pull your foot up towards you... now push up against my hand and don't let me push it down' → nothing → 'unable to dorsiflex the right ankle and cannot resist — loss of dorsiflexion.' 'Turn the foot outwards... push out against my hand' → weak → 'eversion is also impaired on the right.' 'Now push your foot down against my hand' → strong → 'plantarflexion is normal.' 'And turn the foot inwards, and hold it there while I pull it back' → strong → 'inversion is normal.' THEN THE SENTENCE: 'Examiner, I therefore have LOSS OF THE MOTOR FUNCTION OF THE COMMON PERONEAL NERVE, WITH THE MOTOR FUNCTION OF THE TIBIAL NERVE INTACT.' (Doing ankle movements at the movement step tests them twice and muddies the conclusion; 'copy my movement' alone demonstrates grade 3 at best — always resist.)

SENSATION, both sides, eyes closed: 'I'm going to check the feeling in your feet with some cotton wool. This is what it feels like [demonstrate on the forearm]. Now close your eyes and tell me each time you feel it, and whether it feels the same as the other side.' → silence on the right dorsum → 'Examiner, sensation is lost over the dorsum of the right foot — the common peroneal territory — and also in the first web space, the DEEP PERONEAL branch. Sensation over both soles is normal and symmetrical, so the tibial nerve is intact.'

THE TAP TEST, which the station turns on: 'I'm just going to feel around your knee again. Examiner, I've LOCATED the fibular head, and I'm going to tap over it, looking for reproduction of the pins and needles — a positive tap or Tinel's sign, which would confirm entrapment of the common peroneal nerve at this point.' Tap two or three times WITH YOUR FINGERS, then ASK: 'do you feel anything when I do that?' → 'pins and needles down my leg' → 'the tap test is positive, reproducing the patient's paraesthesia.' If nothing the first time, tap again and ask again — role-players often wait to be asked. Then: 'I would also like to perform a straight-leg raise to assess for lumbar nerve root irritation, but in the interests of time I'll move to my diagnosis and differentials.'

Diagnosis in FOUR sentences, then the six differentials (see dx): 'I think you have a common peroneal nerve entrapment. Entrapment means one of the nerves in your leg is under pressure. In your case it's under pressure just below the knee, on the outer side, at a bony bump we call the fibular head — and that's most likely because of all the squatting you do picking. When that nerve is squashed, the muscles that lift your foot go weak, and that's the foot drop — it's why walking is difficult. The same nerve carries feeling from the top of your foot, which is why it's numb and tingly there.' → 'will it get better? Can I keep working?' → most recover once the pressure comes off, weeks to a few months; change the squatting with a kneeling stool or rotating tasks; a brace to hold the foot up so he does not trip; physiotherapy; nerve tests if it has not improved.

ask: 'I'll need to see both legs fully, and I'll tell you the position I need at each step.' / 'Examiner, my patient is not in pain or distress, and I cannot see any fasciculations or tremor.' / 'Examiner, I can see a high-steppage gait on the right.' / 'Now could you take a few steps on your heels? And now on your toes?' / 'There is a loss of dorsiflexion on the right; plantarflexion is intact.'

'I cannot see any swelling, redness or bruising over the fibular head.' / 'I am palpating the fibular head, knowing this is where the common peroneal nerve can be entrapped.' / 'Copy my movement — now push against my hand.' / 'Examiner, I have loss of the motor function of the common peroneal nerve, with the tibial nerve intact.'

'Close your eyes and tell me each time you feel it, and whether it's the same as the other side.' / 'Sensation is lost over the dorsum and the first web space; both soles are normal.' / 'I've located the fibular head and I'm going to tap over it, looking for reproduction of the pins and needles.' / 'Examiner, the tap test is positive.' / 'I would also like to perform a straight-leg raise, but in the interests of time I'll move to my diagnosis and differentials.'

Examiner challenges: 'why didn't you do dermatomes and myotomes?' → 'the task asked for a RELEVANT lower limb examination rather than a neurological examination, and my leading diagnosis is a peripheral nerve entrapment. A nerve-wise assessment localises to a nerve, which is what I need to name a common peroneal entrapment; myotomes localise to a root, and testing L2 to S1 and L1 to S1 would not have fitted the time. I did test INVERSION specifically, which is how I separated the nerve from an L5 root lesion.' / 'How would you confirm it?' → 'nerve conduction studies with EMG at around three to four weeks — they confirm the lesion, localise it to the fibular head and separate it from a radiculopathy or a generalised neuropathy. I'd also check HbA1c and vitamin B12.' VARIANT 1 — the task says 'lower limb NEUROLOGICAL examination': run ITPRSC in full with myotomes L2-S1 and dermatomes L1-S1, then ADD the nerve-wise sweep and the tap test — two movements per nerve and one sensory area per nerve is enough, because the full myotome and dermatome examination is what eats the clock.

Variant 2 — HE DRAGS THE TOES instead of high-stepping: 'the patient is dragging the toes of the right foot along the floor rather than lifting the leg clear. The failure of dorsiflexion is the same; only the compensation is different. This is still a foot drop, and I'll confirm it by asking him to walk on his heels.' / Variant 3 — THE TAP GIVES NOTHING AT FIRST: tap, then ask; if silence, 'let me try once more... anything now, any tingling or shooting?' — do not conclude it is negative after one silent tap. / Variant 4 — INVERSION IS WEAK TOO, eversion preserved, back pain, tap negative: 'that pattern crosses two peripheral nerves and fits a single root, so my leading diagnosis is an L5 RADICULOPATHY rather than a common peroneal entrapment. I would like to perform a straight-leg raise, and I'd arrange an MRI of the lumbar spine if symptoms persist or progress.' / Variant 5 — UPPER MOTOR NEURONE SIGNS (sudden onset, increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar): 'these move me away from a peripheral entrapment entirely and towards a central cause. Given the sudden onset I would treat this as a STROKE until proven otherwise, arrange urgent brain imaging and activate the stroke pathway.' / Variant 6 — BILATERAL with numb hands and lost vibration and proprioception: a peripheral neuropathy — B12, diabetes or alcohol; check B12, FBC, HbA1c and thyroid function. ACUTE, after exertion or trauma, with a tense tender anterior compartment: 'pain out of proportion with a tense anterior compartment and severe pain on passive plantarflexion — ANTERIOR COMPARTMENT SYNDROME causing a deep peroneal palsy. Stop examining, remove any constricting dressing, limb at heart level, analgesia, urgent surgical referral for fasciotomy — I would not wait for the foot to become pulseless.' Bilateral foot drop with bladder or bowel change or saddle numbness is CAUDA EQUINA — emergency MRI and neurosurgical referral.
pefe: Role-player: James Whitlock, 35, picks strawberries on the Yorke Peninsula six days a week in season, squatting for hours down the rows. Three weeks ago he began catching the toes of the right foot and now lifts the leg high to walk; the top of the right foot is numb and tingly; gradual onset, NO pain, no back pain ever, no injury, falls or casts, no diabetes, no bladder or bowel change, no saddle numbness, ten cigarettes a day, no medications. Relaxed and cooperative, a bit puzzled rather than frightened. HIDDEN AGENDA: worried about losing the job as a seasonal worker with no sick leave — volunteered at the very end if concerns are never asked about: 'will I be able to keep picking? It's the only work I've got.' HOW HE PLAYS IT: walks lifting the right leg high with the foot slapping down; on the heels the right foot flops flat ('I can't do it on that side'); toes fine both sides; dorsiflexion right — NOTHING and no resistance; eversion right — almost no resistance; plantarflexion and inversion strong both sides; cotton wool on the right dorsum and first web space — SAYS NOTHING; everywhere else 'yes, I feel that'; when tapped just below the outer right knee — 'pins and needles shooting down my leg', but if they tap and say nothing, he WAITS to be asked.

Numbers and pairings: PED — Peroneal = Eversion + Dorsiflexion; tibial = plantarflexion + inversion. Peroneal sensory = dorsum of the foot plus the first web space; tibial sensory = sole. HEELS test dorsiflexion, TOES test plantarflexion. Site: the neck of the fibula, just below the knee laterally. ONE special test — the tap. Six-minute prompt bell; introduction 30-45 s maximum. Nerve conduction studies informative at 3-4 weeks VERIFY; review at 4-6 weeks. L2-S1 myotomes and L1-S1 dermatomes ONLY if the task says neurological examination.

Scored out of 23 with three starred items: watched the gait before naming anything; located the fibular head then tapped it; and gave at least four differentials with reasons. Also scored: introduced and consented, asked for full exposure of both legs, did NOT announce hand washing, general appearance covering pain AND fasciculation or tremor, named high-steppage gait and no other gait, heel walking, toe walking, looked for wasting and fasciculation, named the fibular head on inspection, temperature/capillary refill/distal pulse, palpated the fibular head and said why, knee movements only with no duplicated ankle range, dorsiflexion and eversion against resistance, plantarflexion and inversion tested and called normal, concluded with THE NERVE rather than a list of movements, cotton wool with eyes closed comparing sides, tested dorsum, first web space and sole, called the tap test positive out loud, named the diagnosis in plain words, and mentioned confirming with nerve conduction studies. 17 or more with all three stars = a pass.
fails: ★ Announcing a foot drop off the stem without watching him walk — the gait is what proves it

★ Finishing the neurological examination and stopping, with no tap test; or tapping where you think the fibular head is instead of palpating for it first, and using a tendon hammer rather than fingers
A polished ninety-second explanation with no differentials — where most candidates failed this station in 2023

Testing power by copying only, with no resistance; doing ankle movements twice (once as range, once as power) so weakness gets called a restricted range; skipping temperature, refill and pulse because 'it's a nerve case'

Running full dermatomes and myotomes when the task said RELEVANT examination; saying 'that's L5' in a nerve-wise examination; reciting a gait catalogue; getting the patient up and down for a straight-leg raise with a minute left

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — surgical ward, three hours post total thyroidectomy. THE ONE THING: reach TROUSSEAU'S SIGN with time to spare, and when the examiner asks what you are looking for, the scoring word is the FINDING — 'carpopedal spasm' with the posture described — not 'a positive Trousseau's', which is circular and scores nothing. The nerve examination will be entirely normal: that IS the result, so say what it excludes and move on rather than hunting. Four automatic fails: Trousseau's never performed; Chvostek's never performed; saying HYPERcalcaemia when you mean HYPOcalcaemia; and a diagnosis given with no differentials.
stem: Surgical ward; you are the RMO. Marion Petrakis, 42, underwent a TOTAL THYROIDECTOMY about three hours ago and has called you because of numbness and pins and needles in her hand. Alert, haemodynamically stable, observations normal, a dressing covers the neck wound. No full history required.
tasks: Perform a focused examination of the hand, with a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
time: WIPE with the hands on a pillow and THE FOUR-SECOND SCREEN THAT PROTECTS YOU: 'are you having any trouble with your breathing or your voice?' · it quietly screens the two post-thyroidectomy complications that cannot wait, neck haematoma and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury · GENERAL APPEARANCE plus ONE sentence on the neck: a clean flat dressing with no expanding swelling, speaking in full sentences with no stridor, and 'I will not disturb the dressing' · INSPECTION of both hands, both surfaces, NAMING thenar and hypothenar wasting (which is what actively excludes carpal and cubital tunnel) · PALPATION: temperature, capillary refill, radial pulse, and tenderness at the hand, the wrist AND THE ULNAR GROOVE at the elbow · MOVEMENT at fingers, wrist and elbow · NERVE-WISE motor and sensory: median (thumb to the ceiling against resistance), ulnar (paper pinch, Froment's), radial (wrist extension), then index pulp, little finger pulp and snuffbox comparing sides → THEN SAY WHAT NORMAL EXCLUDES: 'the neurological examination is entirely normal, which makes a compressive neuropathy unlikely and moves me towards a metabolic cause' · TROUSSEAU'S: warn her, inflate 20-30 mmHg above the pressure at which the radial pulse disappears, hold up to three minutes, and describe the posture as it appears · CHVOSTEK'S: tap over the facial nerve just anterior to the ear · then the diagnosis and THREE differentials in words she can use, the plan and the safety-net.

back.dx: HYPOCALCAEMIA from transient hypoparathyroidism after total thyroidectomy — paraesthesia in the hand with perioral tingling three hours post-operatively, an entirely normal hand neurological examination (which makes a compressive neuropathy unlikely), and POSITIVE Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Airway not compromised: clean flat dressing, no expanding swelling, no stridor, speaking in full sentences. Differentials, in plain words: carpal tunnel and cubital tunnel syndrome — power and feeling in every nerve were normal; cervical radiculopathy; hyperventilation from anxiety; hypomagnesaemia; and a positioning-related nerve stretch from how the arm lay during the operation. Plan: urgent CORRECTED CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM AND PHOSPHATE together, an ECG (looking for a long flat ST segment and a prolonged QT), calcium replacement guided by severity, and surgical and endocrine review. To her: four tiny glands behind the thyroid, each about the size of a grain of rice, keep the blood calcium steady; they are often bruised during the operation and go quiet for a while, and when calcium drops the nerves become irritable — common, expected and usually temporary. Safety-net: press the buzzer for worsening tingling, cramps or spasms, or ANY change in voice or breathing.
plan: WIPE with the airway screen built in: '...I understand you've got some pins and needles — I'd like to examine your hands. I'll look, gently feel, ask you to do some movements, check the feeling in your fingers, and finish with two quick tests — one with a blood pressure cuff, one where I tap gently on your cheek. Is that alright? Rest your hands on this pillow. ARE YOU HAVING ANY TROUBLE WITH YOUR BREATHING OR YOUR VOICE?' → 'breathing's fine, voice is a bit croaky but they warned me. It's my hand — and round my mouth, actually.' → 'around your mouth too — thank you, that's important. Let me examine you and then I'll explain what I think.' (Mild hoarseness on day zero is expected; stridor or worsening hoarseness is not.)

General appearance WITH the neck in one sentence: 'Examiner, on general appearance my patient is not in pain or distress, there is no protective posture, and she is alert and orientated. I can see a clean, flat neck dressing with no expanding swelling; she is speaking in full sentences with no stridor, so I have no concern about the airway. I WILL NOT DISTURB THE DRESSING.' (Removing it is an obvious fail; never mentioning the neck at all is subtler and, three hours post-thyroidectomy, worse clinically.)

Inspection and palpation: 'Marion, may I look at both hands, and turn them over? Examiner, on inspection of both hands, front and back, there is no THENAR or HYPOTHENAR wasting and no wasting of the small muscles, no fasciculation or tremor, and no swelling, redness, deformity or scars. On palpation: temperature is normal with no local rise, capillary refill is under two seconds, the radial pulse is present and of normal volume, and there is no tenderness over the hand, the wrist or THE ULNAR GROOVE at the elbow.' (Naming thenar and hypothenar shows you are actively excluding carpal and cubital tunnel — the two differentials the whole examination is built around.)

Movement then the nerve-wise examination: 'copy my movements. Make a fist and open... spread your fingers and close them... bend and straighten your wrist... and your elbow. Active movement is full and painless at the fingers, wrist and elbow. Now, palm flat, point your thumb at the ceiling; don't let me push it down — strong, MEDIAN motor intact. Pinch this paper and don't let me pull it — the thumb stays straight, Froment's is negative, ULNAR motor intact. Cock your wrist back — strong, RADIAL motor intact. Close your eyes and tell me when you feel me, and whether it's the same on both sides — sensation is intact and symmetrical over the index pulp, the little finger pulp and the snuffbox.' Then the interpretation: 'Examiner, THE NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION IS ENTIRELY NORMAL, WHICH MAKES A COMPRESSIVE NEUROPATHY UNLIKELY AND MOVES ME TOWARDS A METABOLIC CAUSE.' (Candidates who find nothing start hunting, repeat tests and run the clock down — a normal nerve examination IS the result. And do not run C5-T1: your differentials are compression at the wrist and elbow, so examine nerve-wise and say why.)

TROUSSEAU'S SIGN, warned and technically correct: 'Marion, I'm going to put a blood pressure cuff on your upper arm and pump it up. It will feel tight, and it may be uncomfortable for a couple of minutes — tell me if it's too much. Examiner, I am performing Trousseau's sign. I am inflating to TWENTY TO THIRTY MILLIMETRES OF MERCURY ABOVE THE PRESSURE AT WHICH THE RADIAL PULSE DISAPPEARS, and I will hold it for UP TO THREE MINUTES. I am looking for CARPOPEDAL SPASM.' → the examiner interrupts: 'what are you looking for?' → answer with the FINDING: 'carpopedal spasm — the wrist and knuckles flex, the fingers stay straight and held together, and the thumb is drawn across the palm.' → the hand adopts the posture → 'that's alright Marion, it will settle the moment I let the cuff down — and it actually tells me something useful. Examiner, this is a POSITIVE Trousseau's sign. Releasing the cuff now.'

CHVOSTEK'S SIGN: 'the last thing is that I'm going to tap gently on your cheek, just in front of your ear. It won't hurt. Examiner, I am performing Chvostek's sign, tapping over the FACIAL NERVE as it emerges anterior to the ear. I can see twitching of the facial muscles at the corner of the mouth — this is a POSITIVE Chvostek's sign.' Then her fear arrives: 'doctor, is this a stroke? My mum had a stroke at sixty.' → answer directly with the reason, then redirect: 'I don't think this is a stroke, and I can tell you why. A stroke usually affects one side of the body and often the face or speech, and everything I've tested in your nerves is normal. What I think is going on is different, and much more expected after this operation. May I explain?'

Diagnosis in plain words, then THREE differentials — do not skip them (see dx): the four grain-of-rice glands behind the thyroid, bruised at operation, calcium drops, nerves become irritable — which is the tingling in the hands and around the mouth; both tests point to a low calcium level; common, expected, usually temporary. Then the differentials she can follow: squeezed nerves at the wrist or elbow (power and feeling were normal), a trapped nerve in the neck, breathing quickly when anxious, and a nerve stretched by how the arm was positioned in theatre. → 'so what happens now? Do I need another operation?' → 'almost certainly not. I'll send a blood test now to check the calcium and a couple of related levels, do a quick heart tracing, and start you on calcium. We'll recheck it regularly. If the tingling gets worse, if you get cramps or spasms, or if your voice or breathing changes at all, press the buzzer straight away.'

I'm holding the cuff twenty to thirty above the pressure at which the pulse disappeared, for up to three minutes.'

In a patient who has just been anaesthetised I would consider positioning-related nerve injury as well as carpal tunnel syndrome — and I WOULD STILL SEND A CALCIUM, because the two can coexist.'
pefe: Role-player: Marion Petrakis, 42, teaches year three; whole thyroid removed this morning about three hours ago for a long-standing goitre; sitting up on the surgical ward. Pins and needles in the right hand starting about half an hour ago, AND tingling around the mouth — the mouth is mentioned only if asked an open question or about other symptoms, otherwise volunteered just before the diagnosis. No regular medications or allergies, otherwise well. Breathing completely fine; voice slightly croaky as warned, and nothing worsening. Polite and cooperative but FRIGHTENED — her mother had a stroke at sixty. HIDDEN AGENDA: she thinks she is having a stroke, and asks 'is this a stroke?' after the special tests, or at the very end regardless. HOW SHE PLAYS THE FINDINGS: everything normal until the two special tests — movements, thumb push-up, paper pinch (thumb straight) and wrist extension all full and strong, sensation felt everywhere and the same both sides. THE CUFF: 'ooh, that's tight', then after about thirty seconds — or immediately once the candidate says 'carpopedal spasm' — the hand goes into the posture and stays until the cuff comes down: wrist bent forwards, knuckles bent, fingers straight and pressed together, thumb tucked across the palm, with 'my hand's gone funny — I can't straighten it'. THE TAP: twitch the corner of the mouth two or three times. If they never do either test, do nothing and let them fail it.

Numbers: FOUR parathyroid glands; onset typically 24-72 hours but sometimes sooner; TWO special tests; cuff 20-30 mmHg above the pressure at which the pulse disappears, held up to THREE minutes; TROUSSEAU'S IS THE MORE SPECIFIC SIGN; tap anterior to the ear for Chvostek's; capillary refill under 2 s; 3 nerves and 3 sensory points — index pulp, little finger pulp, snuffbox; ECG shows a long flat ST segment giving a prolonged QT; send CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM AND PHOSPHATE TOGETHER.

17-point checklist: introduced, checked identity, explained, consented; positioned the hands, washed hands, asked about pain; asked about voice or breathing, or commented on the neck WITHOUT touching it; general appearance including level of consciousness; inspected both hands, both surfaces, NAMING thenar and hypothenar; temperature, capillary refill, pulse and tenderness INCLUDING the ulnar groove; active movement at fingers, wrist and elbow; motor testing of median, ulnar and radial; sensory at the three points comparing sides; STATED what the normal nerve examination excludes; PERFORMED Trousseau's with warning and correct technique; ANSWERED 'carpopedal spasm' when asked; described the posture before naming the sign; PERFORMED Chvostek's; named the diagnosis as low calcium and said HYPO not hyper; gave at least three differentials in plain language; addressed the stroke fear directly; and gave a plan and a safety-net about voice, breathing and spasms.

In the room: a role-player on a chair, a HALF-HEAD MANNEQUIN with a left ear on the bench, an otoscope (possibly unassembled) with a box of specula, tuning forks, and gloves.

Report your findings and state your most likely diagnosis
Give your differential diagnoses

back.dx: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA of the left ear — a red, inflamed, BULGING tympanic membrane with loss of the cone of light, no perforation and no attic debris, on a background of a recent head cold and three days of deep constant ache; no mastoid swelling or tenderness, no lymphadenopathy, facial nerve intact, whisper heard at both distances with Rinne AC>BC and a central Weber. THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST, recited: wax impaction; otitis externa; foreign body; otitis media with effusion; chronic suppurative otitis media; cholesteatoma; mastoiditis; tympanic membrane perforation; herpes zoster oticus; and referred otalgia from the teeth, the temporomandibular joint, the tonsil or the cervical spine — plus labyrinthitis and Meniere disease, where fullness can be described as pain. Why not cholesteatoma: it gives WHITE KERATIN DEBRIS IN THE ATTIC with chronic offensive discharge and a conductive loss; here the drum is diffusely red and bulging with no attic debris and the history is three days — but it stays on the list. Management: regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, review at 48-72 hours, antibiotics per guideline VERIFY. Safety-net: swelling behind the ear, facial weakness, or a bad headache with a stiff neck.
plan: Gloves, WIPE, and NAME THE EQUIPMENT: '...I'd like to examine that ear now. I'll look at both ears, then feel around the ear, then I'll use this — (hold up the otoscope) — it's called an otoscope and it lets me look inside. At the end I'll check your hearing. You can stay sitting exactly as you are, and you won't need to take anything off. EVERYTHING I DO, I'LL TELL YOU ABOUT FIRST. Is that all right?' → 'will it hurt?' → 'I'll be gentle, and NOTHING GOES DEEP INTO THE EAR. If anything is uncomfortable, tell me and I'll stop straight away.' If the otoscope is in pieces, assemble it out loud: 'the head lines up with the notch, press down against the spring, and turn.'

Inspection led by the COMPARISON sentence, then palpation warned: 'on general appearance James is comfortable, alert, not in pain at rest, and holds his head in a normal position. COMPARING BOTH EARS, they are symmetrical with no displaced earlobe. Looking at the left external ear: no rash, no redness, no swelling, no scars or deformity. BEHIND THE EAR, OVER THE MASTOID, there is no swelling, redness or engorgement. There is no discharge or bleeding from the canal.' Then: 'James, I've finished looking. I'm going to feel around the ear now — tell me straight away if anything is tender' — helix, lobule, tragus, then the mastoid, then movement of the pinna → 'no tenderness over the helix, lobule or tragus, no mastoid tenderness, and no tenderness on movement of the pinna.'

OTOSCOPY — the accuracy point: 'James, I'm going to look inside your ear now with the otoscope. IT WON'T GO INTO YOUR EAR — I only hold it at the opening. Examiner, I'll perform otoscopy on the mannequin. I'm using a PENCIL GRIP in my LEFT hand for the LEFT ear, with my free fingers resting on the cheek as a stable point. I'm pulling the pinna UP AND BACK to straighten the canal, and holding THE TIP AT THE ENTRANCE OF THE MEATUS. The canal is clear, with no discharge or foreign body. The tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging, with loss of the cone of light. There is no visible perforation and no attic debris.' (Advancing the speculum into the canal is described by examiners as the reason candidates fail this station outright — the TRACTION gives the view, the depth gives only pain. And ten seconds of silent peering is ten seconds the examiner cannot mark.)

Special tests, each move announced: 'James, I'm going to step behind you now and feel the glands in your neck with both hands. Tell me if anything is sore' — submental, submandibular, jugular, posterior cervical, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, then round to the front for supraclavicular → 'no cervical lymphadenopathy.' Then 'coming round to the front. Raise your eyebrows... screw your eyes shut, don't let me open them... puff out your cheeks... and show me your teeth. The facial nerve is intact and symmetrical.' (A candidate was asked mid-station what he thought he was doing, having walked behind a seated patient unannounced.)

WHISPER, from beside not in front: 'now I'll check your hearing. Please block your right ear with your finger, like this. I'm going to whisper a number close to your left ear — just repeat it back to me' [whisper 'ninety-nine'] 'good — and one more from further away' [arm's length, about a metre, whisper 'sixty-six'] → 'the whisper is heard at both distances on the left.' (Standing in front lets him lip-read and gives you a false pass.)

RINNE, with the THREE-PART instruction that unlocks the findings: 'James, this is a tuning fork. When I ring it, it sounds like this — [ring it at a distance] — and I need you to tell me when you can hear that ringing. THREE THINGS for me. ONE, I'll put it on the bone behind your ear — tell me WHEN YOU START HEARING IT. TWO, tell me the moment YOU STOP HEARING IT. THREE, I'll hold it in front of your ear, and all I need is YES OR NO — can you hear it again? Is that clear?' Then WEBER: 'one more with the same fork — I'll place it in the middle of your forehead, and all I need to know is which side you hear it louder: left, right, or the same.' → 'Examiner, AIR CONDUCTION IS BETTER THAN BONE CONDUCTION on the left, and the Weber is central.' (Ring it by pinching the tips, hold it distally, base FLAT on the mastoid — not the sternocleidomastoid — and do not repeat a test because the answer surprised you.)

The ordered presentation and ONE committed diagnosis (see dx), then the differential list RECITED without hesitation — sort it afterwards, out loud, only if asked. 'Why not cholesteatoma?' has a scripted answer. Then to James: 'the eardrum is inflamed — a middle ear infection. Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, and I'd like to see you in two or three days. Come back sooner if you get swelling behind the ear, weakness of the face, or a bad headache with a stiff neck.' (His hidden agenda, raised late if concerns are never invited: a fishing trip in four days — can he go, and can he get in the water?)
