'Pencil grip, left hand for the left ear, free fingers on the cheek as a stable point.' / 'Pulling the pinna up and back, and the tip stays at the entrance of the canal.' / 'The tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging, with loss of the cone of light.' / 'I'm going to step behind you now to feel the glands in your neck.'

'Tell me when you START hearing it... tell me when you STOP hearing it... then yes or no, can you hear it again?' / 'Which side do you hear it louder — left, right, or the same?' / 'Air conduction is better than bone conduction on the left; the Weber is central.' / 'The field is small and the appearances overlap, but the predominant colour is red, so on balance this is acute otitis media.' / 'I am unable to visualise the drum because of wax; I would soften and clear it and repeat otoscopy' — a finding and a plan, whereas inventing a drum you did not see is a claimed finding and a fail.

Variant 1 — THE TASK SAYS 'PERFORM A HEARING TEST' FIRST: open with the hearing tests in full (whisper, Rinne, Weber), then 'Examiner, I've completed the hearing tests. I'd now like to inspect and palpate the ear and perform otoscopy' — and expect 'skip inspection and palpation, go straight to otoscopy', which you take. Opening with inspection out of habit gets you stopped. / Variant 2 — THE ROLE-PLAYER WILL NOT GIVE FINDINGS ('hear what, sorry? I don't know what you want'): do NOT repeat the test — 'that's my fault, let me explain it again properly' and give all three parts, then test ONCE. He is briefed not to cooperate with an unclear instruction; nothing is wrong with the fork. / Variant 3 — DISCORDANT WEBER: 'the patient reports the sound lateralising to the right. I'll report that as found. MY DIAGNOSIS WAS MADE ON OTOSCOPY AND DOES NOT CHANGE, and my differentials are unaffected. May I move to those?' Candidates have repeated Weber four times and run out of clock before the only part they were still going to be marked on.

Variant 4 — HEARING LOSS STEM WITH WHITE ATTIC DEBRIS: 'the dominant appearance is a white, cheesy patch superiorly, in the attic — a CHOLESTEATOMA until proven otherwise. Bone conduction is better than air on the left and the Weber lateralises left, a conductive loss consistent with that. I'd want a CT of the temporal bones and an ENT opinion; the facial nerve is intact.' / Variant 5 — MASTOIDITIS: 'there is boggy redness behind the left ear with the auricle PUSHED FORWARD and mastoid tenderness. This is mastoiditis — admission, intravenous antibiotics and same-day ENT, with MedSTAR if he deteriorated.'

Three days ago a head cold; two days ago the left ear began a deep constant ache, worse lying down, about 6/10, with muffled sounds on that side; no discharge, bleeding, dizziness or measured fever; grommets as a small child; sometimes uses cotton buds (only if asked); paracetamol helped a little. Friendly and straightforward, mildly fed up, cooperative but NEVER volunteers. HOW HE PLAYS IT: no tenderness at helix, lobule, tragus or mastoid, and none on tugging the ear — 'it's deeper in that hurts'; OTOSCOPE INTO THE CANAL → 'ow! That really hurts', pulls away, and marks it; hand on the neck without warning → 'sorry, what are you doing back there?'; whisper repeated correctly at both distances, but if the candidate stands IN FRONT he repeats it and notes that he was allowed to lip-read; WITHHOLDS THE FORK FINDINGS until the instruction contains all three parts ('sorry — hear what? What do you want me to do?'); with a full instruction: 'yes, I hear it' ... five seconds ... 'it's stopped' ... 'yes, I can hear it again'; Weber 'about the same' (harder run: 'the right'). Hidden agenda raised at about seven minutes if concerns are never asked: a fishing trip on Saturday.

ACCURACY — correct hand and grip, pinna up and back, tip at the meatus, fork pinched and held distally and flat on the mastoid, Weber truly midline. COMMENTARY — a spoken conclusion after every block, and Rinne and Weber INTERPRETED out loud rather than reported raw. DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS — one committed diagnosis, and FEWER THAN SIX DIFFERENTIALS IS A FAIL. PATIENT INTERACTION — every movement announced including stepping behind him, pain acknowledged at the start, plain-language explanation and a specific safety-net in the last forty seconds.

TEMPERATURE 39.0 — nothing else is given. In the room: a seated role-player, a pen torch, wooden tongue depressors, an otoscope, a stethoscope, gloves.

back.dx: TWO diagnoses: ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA of the left ear AND EXUDATIVE TONSILLITIS, with reactive cervical lymphadenitis — the Eustachian tube opens into the back of the throat, which is how one led to the other. Differentials on TWO AXES. By condition: viral pharyngotonsillitis, group A streptococcal tonsillitis, glandular fever, acute otitis media, otitis externa, acute sinusitis and laryngitis — and the ones being ACTIVELY EXCLUDED: quinsy, epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, Lemierre syndrome, pneumonia and meningitis. By organism: Epstein-Barr virus, adenovirus, influenza, COVID-19 and rhinovirus; group A Streptococcus and Fusobacterium necrophorum; and with a sexual history, gonococcal or chlamydial pharyngitis. On Centor criteria he scores 3 or 4, but in Australian practice swabbing and antibiotics are reserved for those at higher risk of acute rheumatic fever. AVOID AMOXICILLIN until glandular fever is excluded, because it causes a widespread rash. Management: regular paracetamol or ibuprofen, cold fluids, review at 48-72 hours, phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days in adults when treatment is indicated VERIFY. Safety-net, symptom by symptom: drooling or inability to swallow saliva, a change in voice, noisy breathing, inability to open the mouth, or a bad headache with a stiff neck or a non-blanching rash.
plan: Observations by name, with the reason: 'Examiner, before I examine him, may I have his blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation? I have a temperature of 39 degrees, and IN A FEBRILE YOUNG ADULT WITH A SORE THROAT I WANT TO KNOW WHETHER HE IS SEPTIC OR HAS A THREATENED AIRWAY.' → 120/70, 84, 12, 98% → 'thank you — he is haemodynamically stable, not tachycardic, not tachypnoeic and not hypoxic.' Then WIPE naming the WHOLE route: 'I'll start by looking at you generally and checking your hands, then look in your ears, your nose and your throat, press over your sinuses, feel the glands in your neck, and then listen to your chest and your heart — so I'll need to get to your back at that point.'

General appearance SPOKEN — five sentences that exclude five emergencies: 'Bill is alert and orientated. He is NOT DROOLING and shows no evidence of DEHYDRATION — lips and tongue are moist. There is no RESPIRATORY DISTRESS: no tracheal tug, no accessory muscle use, no recession. There is no RASH on the exposed skin. I can hear no STRIDOR and no wheeze from where I stand, and his voice is hoarse but not muffled.' Then the hands: 'capillary refill under two seconds, skin turgor normal, radial pulse regular and of good volume, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.' (If interrupted with 'why are you looking for drooling?': 'because a patient who cannot swallow his own saliva has either a peritonsillar abscess or epiglottitis until proven otherwise, and that changes this from a GP problem to an airway problem.')

E and N: 'looking at both ears: symmetrical, no discharge, no redness or swelling behind the ear over the mastoid. Bill, I'll look inside now — this only goes to the opening of your ear, it doesn't go inside. Examiner: pencil grip, left hand for the left ear, free fingers braced on the cheek, pinna up and back, tip at the entrance of the canal. On the left the tympanic membrane is red, inflamed and bulging with loss of the cone of light. The right drum is normal.' Then 'Bill, I'm going to look up your nose. Can you tip your head back and look at the ceiling? I'll lift the tip of your nose gently with my thumb and use this torch. — Mild mucosal swelling with clear discharge on both sides, the inferior turbinates are not obstructing, no polyps, septum midline.'

T — and the habit that saves you: 'now your throat. I'll use this wooden spatula ON THE FRONT of your tongue — it may feel odd but it shouldn't hurt. Open wide and say aah. — Examiner: the oral mucosa is moist; both tonsils are enlarged, erythematous and covered in white exudate; THE SWELLING IS SYMMETRICAL; THERE IS NO PALATAL BULGE; THE UVULA IS MIDLINE; the posterior pharyngeal wall is injected but not bulging; and he opens his mouth fully, so there is no trismus.' (Describe symmetry and uvular position BEFORE you name anything — that single habit is what saves you when the photograph is a quinsy. And the blade goes on the ANTERIOR tongue: too far back and he retches.)

S and the neck: 'I'm going to press over your sinuses — tell me if any of it is tender. Over both eyebrows, the frontal sinuses... and over both cheekbones, the maxillary sinuses. No sinus tenderness. I'd offer transillumination for completeness.' Then 'Bill, I'm going to step behind you now and feel the glands in your neck with both hands' — submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior cervical, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital, then round to the front for supraclavicular → 'two enlarged, tender nodes in the left jugular chain; the rest are clear.' Then meningism WHILE SEATED: 'one more with your neck — can you put your chin on your chest? And turn side to side? — The neck is supple with no meningism.'

CHEST AND HEART — the commonest omission: 'Bill, I'd like to listen to your chest. Would you mind lifting your shirt at the back? — Chest expansion is symmetrical, and I'm listening front and back. Air entry is equal with vesicular breath sounds and no added sounds. And the heart, in the FOUR VALVE AREAS — aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, mitral. Heart sounds one and two are normal with no murmur. I LISTENED BECAUSE GROUP A STREPTOCOCCUS CAN BE FOLLOWED BY ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER. To complete the examination I'd like to lie him down and palpate for splenomegaly, as glandular fever is on my differential.' (Ask, adapt, listen through thin fabric if you must — and say that you have done so. 'You've got a shirt on so I'll skip the chest' is marked as abandoning the block.)

TASK 3, turned TOWARDS BILL and in his language: 'there are two things going on, and they're related. First, your tonsils — the two lumps at the back of your throat — are swollen and red with some white pus on them: a tonsil infection. Second, in your left ear the eardrum is red and bulging outwards, which means there's infected fluid trapped behind it — a middle ear infection. The tube that drains the middle ear opens into the back of your throat, which is how one led to the other. The glands in your neck are up and tender because your body is fighting the infection. Your chest is clear, your heart sounds normal and your neck isn't stiff, so there's nothing more serious going on today. Does that make sense? Anything you'd like me to go over?' → 'do I need antibiotics?' (his agenda — 'it worked last time, and I've got exams in ten days') → most sore throats like this are viral and settle without them; regular analgesia, cold fluids, review in two or three days; then the symptom-by-symptom safety-net. THEN task 4 to the examiner: the two-axis differential (see dx).

'I'll rest this on the front of your tongue — open wide and say aah.' / 'THE SWELLING IS SYMMETRICAL, THERE IS NO PALATAL BULGE, AND THE UVULA IS MIDLINE.' / 'I'm going to step behind you and feel the glands in your neck with both hands.' / 'Can you put your chin on your chest for me? — The neck is supple with no meningism.' / 'Would you mind lifting your shirt at the back so I can listen properly?'

'I listened for a murmur because group A streptococcus can be followed by acute rheumatic fever.' / 'To complete the examination I'd palpate the abdomen for splenomegaly, as glandular fever is on my differential.' / To Bill: 'there are two things going on, and they're related.' / 'Come back straight away if you start drooling, your voice changes, your breathing gets noisy, or you can't open your mouth.' / 'I'd avoid amoxicillin until glandular fever is excluded, because it causes a widespread rash.'

Variant 1 — THE QUINSY PHOTOGRAPH: describe first, then name — 'before I name this: the swelling is UNILATERAL, on the left, with a bulge in the soft palate above the tonsil, and THE UVULA IS PUSHED ACROSS TO THE RIGHT. That is not simple tonsillitis. Bill, can you open your mouth as wide as you can? Has your voice changed at all?' → trismus and a muffled voice → 'my diagnosis is a PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS — quinsy. He needs a same-day ENT opinion for needle aspiration or incision and drainage, with intravenous antibiotics, analgesia and a corticosteroid. From Wallaroo that means discussion with the on-call ENT registrar and transfer.' / Variant 2 — SINUS TENDERNESS GIVEN: 'then there are THREE diagnoses: acute otitis media, exudative tonsillitis, and acute sinusitis given the maxillary tenderness with nasal mucosal swelling and discharge. I'd ask how long the nasal symptoms have run and whether he improved and then worsened, since that distinguishes bacterial from viral.' Every abnormal site is a diagnosis — count them, then say the number out loud.

Variant 3 — SUSPECTED EPIGLOTTITIS (sitting forward, drooling, soft stridor): STOP THE EXAMINATION — 'he is drooling, sitting forward, with a muffled voice and audible stridor. I am concerned about EPIGLOTTITIS. I WILL NOT EXAMINE HIS THROAT WITH A SPATULA. I'd keep him upright and undisturbed, give oxygen, not attempt cannulation, and call for immediate senior airway help — in Wallaroo, a call to MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval while I stay with him.' Recognising that the safe examination is a LIMITED one is the answer. / Variant 4 — GLANDULAR FEVER: prominent POSTERIOR cervical nodes, petechiae at the junction of the hard and soft palate, two weeks of exhaustion → FBC and film, EBV serology, LFTs, and palpate for splenomegaly; avoid amoxicillin or ampicillin, and no contact sport or heavy lifting while the spleen is enlarged. / Variant 5 — 'WHAT ELSE WOULD YOU EXAMINE?': the abdomen for splenomegaly, the trunk for a rash, the palate for petechiae, and the tongue for the strawberry appearance of scarlet fever.
pefe: Role-player: Bill Nguyen, 20, second-year engineering student home for the holidays, works weekends at the pub; wearing a T-shirt with a light shirt over it. Three days of sore throat now 8/10 on swallowing, with a deep left ear ache worse since yesterday; hot and shivery, sleeping badly, eaten almost nothing for two days but still drinking. Voice HOARSE but not muffled, NOT drooling. Non-smoker, about ten standard drinks across a weekend, sexually active with one partner and condoms most of the time (only if asked directly), paracetamol helps a little, tonsillitis twice in two years that settled on its own, no allergies, no family history of rheumatic fever. Uncomfortable, flat, cooperative — answers what is asked and stops. HIDDEN AGENDA: he wants antibiotics because 'that's what fixed it last time' and he has exams in ten days — raised when the diagnosis is explained, and pressed once more if the answer is vague. THREE MOMENTS THE STATION IS DESIGNED TO TEST: otoscope in the canal ('ow — that hurts', pulls away); the blade too far back (retches, pulls back, hand up); a hand on the neck without warning ('whoa — what are you doing?'). If told 'you've got a shirt on so I'll skip the chest', he says nothing and marks it.

Numbers: observations to expect 120/70, HR 84, RR 12, SpO2 98% with T 39.0; station 8 minutes, OUT OF THE THROAT BY 4:30 and stethoscope in hand by 6:00; NINE cervical node chains; FOUR Centor criteria (fever above 38, exudate, tender anterior nodes, NO cough) VERIFY; phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days in adults when treatment is indicated VERIFY; review at 48-72 hours; NO NASAL SPECULUM since about 2017; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS National 131 450. The eight-to-eleven blocks: appearance, hands, E, N, T, S, neck nodes, neck stiffness, chest, heart, abdomen offered — most candidates get seven.

Scored out of 4 in each domain: CHOICE — how many blocks, did they ask for the observations, did they auscultate chest AND heart, did they offer the abdomen (seven or fewer blocks is a fail). TECHNIQUE — otoscope at the meatus, nasal tip lifted with a torch, blade on the anterior tongue, nine chains named aloud, neck stiffness screened. COMMENTARY — general appearance spoken with the two D's and two R's named, a conclusion after each block. DIAGNOSIS — both diagnoses stated, symmetry and uvula described before naming anything, differentials with the must-not-miss list named AS SUCH. COMMUNICATION — was task 3 delivered to the PATIENT, in his language, with understanding checked and a specific safety-net, or aimed at the examiner? Automatic fails: stopping at ear, nose and throat; one diagnosis when two are present; calling a unilateral swelling with a deviated uvula 'tonsillitis'; otoscope inserted into the canal; using a spatula in the airway-obstruction variant.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. The framework for the whole eye block: EIGHT steps — inspection, acuity, fields, colour, movements, accommodation, pupils, fundoscopy — NOMINATED OUT LOUD, because a step you were not allowed to do still had to be named. The clock is the enemy and it is the FRONT of the station where candidates waste it: four verbs is the whole explanation. Automatic fails: reading only the bottom line and calling it a visual acuity; holding the pen beside your own head during confrontation fields; reporting fields, pupils or fundi as normal without attempting them; omitting a step without ever nominating it; reassuring the patient before the pinhole result is known.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Snellen chart on the wall with a cross taped to the floor; pen torch, ophthalmoscope, pinhole and red-topped pin on the tray. Gary Whitmore, 50, storeman, with six months of gradually blurred vision. No pain, redness, discharge or headache. BP 128/78, HR 74, afebrile, BGL 5.6, no medications, no glasses. 8 minutes, aim 5:30 / 1:30 / 1:00.
tasks: Perform an eye examination with a running commentary
Explain your findings and most likely diagnosis to the patient
Give the examiner your differentials
time: 0:00-0:40 WIPE in FOUR VERBS ('looking at your eyes, reading letters off that chart, following my pen, and shining a light'), nothing hurts, no touching the eyeball, hands washed · then NAME THE EIGHT STEPS to the examiner · INSPECTION in THREE named groups: lids (swelling, redness, discharge, ptosis), globe (exophthalmos, enophthalmos, redness, subconjunctival haemorrhage), pupils and anterior chamber (round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon) · ACUITY, the step that carries the finding: on the cross, ONE EYE AT A TIME with the palm and no pressing, STARTING AT THE TOP LINE, at least two letters per line, then BINOCULAR · and the acuity is THE LAST LINE READ, not the first line failed · PINHOLE only on the reduced eye, with the reason said before you use it · FIELDS: bring a chair, sit FACING at the same level about an arm's length away, cover your own matching eye, pen EQUIDISTANT between you, 'look at my nose and don't follow the pen', four quadrants per eye and SWAP HANDS while covering the same eye · then COLOUR, MOVEMENTS (head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double), ACCOMMODATION, PUPILS (direct, consensual, swinging torch) and FUNDOSCOPY (right eye, right hand, dial at zero) run without pausing and taking every skip · then the explanation and GROUPED differentials.

back.dx: REFRACTIVE ERROR, most probably MYOPIA — a reduced monocular acuity FULLY CORRECTED BY PINHOLE, with normal inspection, fields, movements, pupils and fundi. The pinhole is the reasoning chain: if vision improves the problem is one of FOCUS; if it does not, the problem is the MEDIA, RETINA OR OPTIC NERVE. Differentials GROUPED, each with a reason for exclusion: in the eye — presbyopia, astigmatism, cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration; vascular and metabolic — diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vascular occlusion; neurological — optic neuritis, and a compressive lesion at the chiasm or behind it; inflammatory or infective — uveitis, keratitis; drug-related — hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, amiodarone, corticosteroids. Cataract and the retinal causes are less likely BECAUSE the pinhole fully corrected the acuity; the neurological causes are less likely BECAUSE fields, pupils and colour vision were normal. Plan: refer for formal refraction, and with a family history of eye disease ask the optometrist to check intraocular pressures and the optic nerve. Safety-net, same day: sudden worsening, eye pain, flashes or floaters, a curtain across the vision, or double vision. IF BOTH EYES ARE NORMAL: nothing about the technique changes — still do binocular acuity, still no pinhole — and the conclusion becomes 'the eye examination is normal; with persisting symptoms my differentials shift towards presbyopia, dry eye, early cataract, and a neurological cause with a normal fundus such as retrobulbar optic neuritis, and I would want formal refraction and a dilated fundus examination before reassuring him.'
plan: WIPE in four verbs and NAME THE EIGHT: '...I've been asked to examine your eyes today. That'll mean LOOKING at your eyes, asking you to READ letters off that chart, FOLLOWING my pen, and SHINING a light in your eyes. Nothing hurts and I won't touch the eyeball itself. I'll wash my hands. Happy for me to go ahead?' Then: 'Examiner, my eye examination has EIGHT parts: inspection, acuity, fields, colour vision, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy. I'll nominate each.' (Ninety seconds explaining all eight tests is how candidates lose the clock at the front of the station.)

INSPECTION in three named groups: 'general appearance: sitting comfortably, alert, not in pain or distress. On inspection — LIDS: no swelling, redness, discharge or ptosis. GLOBE: no exophthalmos, no enophthalmos, no redness, no subconjunctival haemorrhage. PUPILS AND ANTERIOR CHAMBER: both round, regular and symmetrical, with no hyphaema and no hypopyon.' ('Inspection is normal' as a single sentence scores nothing — the mark is in the three named groups. If asked what you look for in the anterior chamber: a HYPHAEMA, which is blood, or a HYPOPYON, which is pus.)

ACUITY: 'Gary, stand on the cross for me. Cover your left eye with your palm — don't press. START AT THE VERY TOP LINE and read across... and the next... and this one. Now swap: cover the right, same again from the top. Now both eyes together.' → 'Examiner, the right eye is 6/6, the left eye is 6/18, binocular 6/6.' THREE TRAPS: starting near the bottom; reporting the line he FAILED instead of the LAST LINE READ; and pinholing a normal eye, which shows you do not know what it is for.

THE PINHOLE, with the reason first: 'as the left is reduced I'd like to repeat it through a pinhole — because if the vision improves the problem is one of focus, and if it doesn't, the problem is further back in the eye. Cover the right, hold this over the left, and read from the top again.' → 'with the pinhole the left improves to 6/6.' Write the figures and READ THEM ALOUD as you hand them over: 'Left 6/18 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole. Right 6/6 uncorrected. Monocular figures only; binocular was 6/6.'

FIELDS — three ways to make the test meaningless, all visible from across the room: standing while he sits, sitting two metres away, or holding the pen beside your own head. 'I'll bring my chair across and sit facing you, about an arm's length away — sorry to be so close. Cover one eye. Now LOOK STRAIGHT AT MY NOSE and keep looking there, don't follow the pen. TELL ME THE MOMENT YOU SEE IT, THEN TELL ME IF IT DISAPPEARS.' Temporal upper and lower with one hand; then SWAP HANDS keeping the SAME eye covered for nasal upper and lower; then the other eye. → 'all four quadrants full in the right eye... and all four in the left. Fields are full to confrontation and comparable to my own.'

The remaining steps run without pausing, taking every skip: 'COLOUR VISION — I'd use an Ishihara chart, or failing that the red and green bands on the Snellen chart. MOVEMENTS — head still, follow my finger with your eyes only; tell me if you see double. Any double vision up? Down? Left? Right? — full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia. ACCOMMODATION — look at the far wall... now look at my pen. Convergence and constriction both present. PUPILS — direct and consensual on the right, direct and consensual on the left, and a swinging torch test: no relative afferent pupillary defect. FUNDOSCOPY — right eye, right hand, dial at zero. Gary, look past my ear at the wall behind me.' (A run of skips does not mean you have finished early — every step you were not allowed to do still had to be NAMED. And if a fundus photograph appears: DESCRIBE BEFORE YOU DIAGNOSE.)

Explain to Gary, then present: 'your right eye is normal. Your left eye can't see as far down the chart — but when I gave you that little card with the holes in it, your left eye read the whole chart. That tells me your eye itself is healthy, and the problem is simply that it isn't focusing light in the right place. That's called a refractive error — almost certainly short-sightedness. It's very common and completely correctable with glasses. I'd like an optometrist to measure it properly. Does that make sense so far?' → his hidden concern: 'so it's not something serious? My father went blind from something in his eyes' → 'that's an important thing to tell me... nothing I've found today points to anything serious — your side vision, your pupils and the back of your eyes were all normal. But a family history does matter, particularly for GLAUCOMA, so I'd like the optometrist to check your eye pressures and look at the nerve at the back when they do your glasses.' Then the same-day safety-net and the GROUPED differentials to the examiner (see dx).

'As that eye is reduced I'd like to repeat it through a pinhole.' / 'The pinhole improved it, so this is refractive rather than a media or retinal problem.' / 'Look straight at my nose and keep looking there — don't follow the pen.' / 'Tell me the moment you see it, and then tell me if it disappears.' / 'All four quadrants are full and comparable to my own.'

'Keep your head still and follow my finger — tell me if you ever see double.' / 'Direct and consensual present in both eyes, and no relative afferent pupillary defect.' / 'Right eye, right hand, dial at zero.' / 'To complete I'd check intraocular pressure and arrange a slit-lamp examination.' / 'Come back the same day for pain, flashes, floaters, a curtain, or double vision.'

Numbers behind the technique: 6/6 = 20/20 = normal, and 6/60 is the top line; at least TWO letters per line, starting at the top; the acuity is the LAST LINE READ; 6/18 means a normal eye reads it at 18 m and this eye at 6 m; the Snellen sits at 6 m (or 3 m) on the wall, handheld charts at about 1 m; fields are done sitting 1 m apart with the pen 50 cm from each face, four quadrants per eye and eight in total; three or four swings is enough for the swinging torch; the ophthalmoscope dial sits at 0 with the large round aperture; steps three to seven combined take about 90 seconds; WIPE is 40 seconds and no longer. All extraocular muscles are CN III except SO4 and LR6.

The differential discipline: GROUP them and attach ONE REASON to each exclusion — grouping is the difference between a candidate who memorised a list and one who examined a patient. And the scoring sheet's auto-fails are worth rehearsing as a checklist: bottom line only; pen beside your own head; reporting a step as normal without attempting it; omitting a step without nominating it; and reassuring before the pinhole result is known.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Whitmore, 50, storeman at a farm supplies depot in Kadina who drives a forklift. Distance vision blurring over about six months — road signs and the TV — with reading fine; no pain, redness, discharge, flashes, floaters, curtain, double vision, headaches or injury; never worn glasses; no diabetes and blood pressure fine two years ago; ten cigarettes a day for 25 years, four to six beers on a Friday. HIDDEN CONCERN: his father went blind in his sixties from what he was told was 'pressure in the eyes' — volunteered only if the candidate asks about family history, asks what is worrying him, or asks whether he has questions; otherwise raised at the very end as 'so it's not the thing my dad went blind from?' HOW HE PLAYS THE CHART: with the affected eye he reads down four lines and stops ('that next one's gone blurry'); with the other eye he reads the whole chart; through the pinhole he reads the whole chart. He does NOT read the bottom line unaided under any circumstances — and if asked to read the bottom line first, he says 'which one, the little ones?', reads it correctly, and lets the candidate mark themselves down.

Scored out of 20 across three domains. APPROACH AND COMMUNICATION: introduces, confirms identity, consents, washes hands; explains in four verbs rather than a lecture; instructs before each step; the commentary names FINDINGS, not movements; explains without jargon and checks understanding. TECHNIQUE: inspection in three named groups; acuity with the patient on the cross, one eye at a time, starting at the top, at least two letters per line, and binocular tested too; pinhole used because an eye was abnormal; fields done seated at the same level about a metre away, own opposite eye covered, pen equidistant, four quadrants each eye with hands swapped correctly; pupils in both eyes plus the swinging torch. COMPLETENESS AND REASONING: all eight steps nominated aloud; movements with the diplopia instruction; fundoscopy with the correct eye and hand; correct interpretation of the pinhole; differentials in groups with a reason for each exclusion.

Debrief prompts worth running on yourself: which line was the acuity, and why? How far away were you sitting, honestly? Where was the pen? Did you cover the correct eye after you swapped hands? Which of the eight did you forget to nominate? And what did the father's blindness turn out to matter for?

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice, and the task NOMINATES the acuity first. Four figures get written down and read aloud as you hand them over. The pinhole is a REASONING CHAIN, not a ritual: say the reason before you use it, use it only on the reduced eye, and follow where the result leads — if it does not improve, you are no longer looking at a refractive error. Automatic fails: testing both eyes together only; reading only the bottom line and calling it an acuity; finding a reduced acuity and never using the pinhole; ignoring a failed pinhole and diagnosing refractive error anyway; quoting a specific legal driving threshold as fact when unsure.

back.dx: REFRACTIVE ERROR, most likely MYOPIA — a right acuity of 6/12 FULLY CORRECTED BY PINHOLE, with normal inspection, near vision, fields, movements, pupils and fundi. Differentials, grouped with reasons: cataract and presbyopia first, then glaucoma, macular degeneration and retinopathy — each less likely because the pinhole fully corrected the acuity and the fields, pupils and fundi were normal. Plan: formal refraction by an optometrist, and address the occupational vision requirement honestly — there IS a legal vision standard for driving and a requirement for his forklift work, but a lens will correct him, so expect glasses to sort it out; do not quote a specific threshold as fact when unsure (the private driving standard is commonly quoted as binocular 6/12 VERIFY). Safety-net, same day: sudden worsening, eye pain, flashes or floaters, a curtain across the vision, or double vision. IF THE PINHOLE DOES NOT IMPROVE: 'that takes me away from a refractive error. I'd like to look at the RED REFLEX... it is dulled on the right. With full fields, normal colour vision and no relative afferent pupillary defect, my leading diagnosis is now a MEDIA OPACITY, most likely cataract, and I'd arrange slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressures rather than a refraction alone.' IF DISTANCE IS NORMAL BUT NEAR IS REDUCED: no pinhole is indicated; reduced near acuity with normal distance acuity at 50 is PRESBYOPIA — the lens stiffening with age, corrected by reading glasses.
plan: WIPE with the glasses question: '...I've been asked to check your vision and examine your eyes. I'll get you to read letters off that chart, follow my pen, and let me shine a light in your eyes — none of it hurts. BEFORE WE START, DO YOU WEAR GLASSES OR CONTACT LENSES AT ALL?' → 'never have' (or 'only some cheap readers from the chemist' — which hands you a presbyopia thread to follow). Then: 'Examiner, before the acuity I'll take thirty seconds on inspection' — lids, globe, pupils and anterior chamber, in three named groups. (The task says 'check the acuity', not 'do nothing else first'.)

DISTANCE ACUITY, monocular then binocular: 'stand on the cross for me. Cover your left eye with your palm — don't press, and DON'T PEEK THROUGH YOUR FINGERS. Start at the very top line and read across... and the next... and this one. Swap over — cover the right. Same again from the top. And now both eyes together.' → 'Examiner: right eye 6/12, left eye 6/6, binocular 6/6.' (Reporting 6/12 because that was the line he STRUGGLED on is the classic error — the acuity is the last line READ. Read the figure off the chart; do not estimate it.)

THE PINHOLE, reason first: 'as the right is reduced, I'd like to repeat that through a pinhole — BECAUSE IF THE VISION IMPROVES THE PROBLEM IS ONE OF FOCUS, AND IF IT DOESN'T, THE PROBLEM IS FURTHER BACK IN THE EYE. Cover the left, hold this over the right, and read from the top again.' → reads the whole chart → 'with the pinhole the right improves from 6/12 to 6/6. I'd also like to check near vision given his age.' (Pinholing the normal eye 'to be thorough' tells the examiner you are following a ritual rather than a reasoning chain — a 6/6 has nothing to improve.)

THE WRITTEN RECORD — four figures, written and read aloud as you hand it over: 'Right 6/12 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole. Left 6/6 uncorrected. Near vision normal both eyes. Monocular figures only; binocular was 6/6.' Expect the examiner probes: 'why the pinhole?' (give the REASON, not the name), 'what does that improvement tell you?' ('it is refractive'), 'what if it hadn't improved?' ('media, retina or optic nerve').

The rest, run without pausing and taking every skip: 'visual fields by confrontation — I'll bring my chair across... all four quadrants full in both eyes. Colour vision — Ishihara, or the red and green bands on the chart. Eye movements — head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double... full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia. Accommodation — convergence and constriction present. Pupils — direct and consensual in both eyes, and a swinging torch test with no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero.'

Explain in TWO SENTENCES AND A REASSURANCE — he drives a forklift, so no axial length and no focal points: 'the good news first: the back of your eyes, your side vision and your pupils are all normal. Your right eye couldn't read as far down the chart — but when you looked through that card with the tiny holes, it read the whole thing. That tells me your eye is healthy; it just isn't focusing the light in quite the right place. We call that a refractive error, and in your case almost certainly short-sightedness — close things stay clear, distant things blur. It's extremely common, it isn't a disease, and glasses correct it completely. I'd like an optometrist to measure it properly and make you a prescription. What questions do you have?' Then check understanding AND STOP TALKING.

The occupational concern, answered honestly: 'am I going to lose my forklift ticket over this?' → 'that's a fair thing to worry about, and I'm glad you raised it. There IS a legal vision standard for driving, and there will be a requirement for your forklift work too. But your vision came back to completely normal through the pinhole, which means a lens will correct it. So I'd expect a pair of glasses to sort this out entirely. The optometrist will measure it formally and we'll go through the paperwork for work together once you've got the prescription.' Then the same-day safety-net and the summary with grouped differentials (see dx).

'Your eye is healthy — it just isn't focusing the light in the right place.' / 'It isn't a disease, and glasses correct it completely.' / 'There is a legal vision standard for driving; the optometrist will measure it formally.' / 'Come back the same day for pain, flashes, floaters, a curtain, or double vision.' / 'To complete, I'd want formal refraction, a slit lamp and intraocular pressures.'

Numbers: 20/20 = 6/6; top line 6/60; two letters per line from the top; the acuity is the LAST LINE READ. Below 6/60 the sequence is: closer distance, then counting fingers, then hand movements, then perception of light, then none. Near print is read at 30 cm. Presbyopia from the forties. Myopia takes a CONCAVE / minus lens; hypermetropia a CONVEX / plus lens; astigmatism a cylindrical lens. Private driving standard commonly quoted as binocular 6/12 VERIFY — and quoting a specific threshold as fact when unsure is an automatic fail.

The two variants that change the diagnosis: PINHOLE FAILS → check the RED REFLEX, and a dulled reflex with full fields, normal colour vision and no RAPD makes CATARACT the leading diagnosis — to the patient, 'the lens inside your eye works like the lens in a camera, and yours has become a little cloudy. It's part of ageing rather than a disease, glasses won't clear it, but it is very treatable with a short operation that replaces the lens.' DISTANCE NORMAL, NEAR REDUCED → no pinhole indicated; reduced near acuity with normal distance acuity at 50 is PRESBYOPIA, the lens stiffening with age, corrected by reading glasses.
pefe: Role-player: Raymond Pascoe, 50, forklift driver at a grain terminal near Wallaroo for 22 years, with a car licence and a workplace forklift ticket. Several months of worsening distance vision — road signs, the footy scoreboard, the TV from the couch — with reading fine; no pain, redness, discharge, flashes, floaters, curtain, diplopia, headaches, glare or haloes; never worn glasses; no diabetes (checked yearly at work), no eye injury or surgery, no steroids; ex-smoker (quit eight years ago after 20 years), six or seven beers over a weekend; mother had cataract surgery in her seventies. Matter-of-fact, a bit blunt, mildly embarrassed about needing glasses at 50. HIDDEN AGENDA: worried about his forklift ticket and licence, and he has not told anyone at work his vision is going — raised only if asked about concerns, work or questions, otherwise at the very end. HOW HE PLAYS THE CHART: right eye reads down to the 6/12 line and stops; left eye reads the whole chart; through the pinhole over the right eye he reads the whole chart and sounds mildly surprised ('oh — that's better'). If asked to start at the BOTTOM line he says 'the little ones?', reads them WRONG, and lets the candidate draw their own conclusion. If the pinhole is never used he says nothing. If each eye is never tested separately, he happily reads the whole chart with both eyes open.

Scored out of 20. ACUITY TECHNIQUE (8): asks about glasses or contacts BEFORE testing; patient at the mark; each eye separately; starts at the top; at least two letters per line; reports the last line read correctly; tests binocular acuity too; offers near acuity. PINHOLE AND INTERPRETATION (4): uses it because an eye was reduced; states the reason BEFORE using it; does not pinhole the normal eye; correctly concludes refractive error from the improvement. COMPLETION AND COMMUNICATION (8): inspection in three named groups; all remaining steps nominated aloud; pupils in both eyes plus swinging torch; a legible written record with four figures and Right and Left in words; explains myopia without jargon and checks understanding; differentials grouped with a reason for each exclusion; addresses the driving and occupational concern honestly; and safety-nets pain, flashes, floaters, curtain and double vision.

Debrief prompts: which line was the acuity, and why that one? Why did you pinhole, and what would you have concluded if it hadn't helped? Did you test near vision? What were the four figures you wrote? And when did the forklift come up — who raised it?

★ Finding a reduced acuity and never using the pinhole; or ignoring a FAILED pinhole and diagnosing refractive error anyway
Reading only the bottom line and calling it an acuity; reporting the line he struggled on rather than the last line read
Quoting a specific legal driving threshold as fact when unsure

Skipping inspection because the task nominated acuity first; pinholing the normal eye 'to be thorough'; explaining axial length and focal points to a forklift driver instead of two sentences and a reassurance

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — hospital outpatient clinic. DECODE THE BLOOD TEST IN THE READING TIME: a high T4 and T3 with a TSH that has NOT been suppressed means the pituitary is not obeying feedback, so the pituitary is the lesion — and the pituitary sits under the optic chiasm. Walk in already expecting a field defect, and say your structure out loud so you do not drift to the neck: THE THYROID IS A CONSEQUENCE HERE, NOT THE LESION. The station turns on the field technique and on a THREE-PART diagnosis. Automatic fails: performing a thyroid examination instead of an eye examination; reporting the fields as normal; never naming the defect; giving only one of the three parts; saying 'brain tumour' and leaving it there; proposing antithyroid drugs as the treatment.

back.dx: CHIASMAL COMPRESSION by a TSH-SECRETING PITUITARY ADENOMA — a bitemporal hemianopia with 6/6 acuity, no exophthalmos, no ophthalmoplegia, no relative afferent pupillary defect and normal discs, in a man with thyrotoxic symptoms whose TSH is inappropriately non-suppressed against a high T4 and T3. THE THREE-PART DIAGNOSIS, all three said: (1) NAME THE FINDING in plain words — the outer half of vision is missing in both eyes, a bitemporal hemianopia; (2) LOCALISE IT — the nerves from each eye cross at one point behind the nose, the optic chiasm, and pressure there knocks out the outer half of vision in both eyes; (3) NAME THE CAUSE AND LINK IT — the commonest cause of pressure there is a growth in the pituitary sitting directly underneath, and that same gland controls the thyroid, so ONE growth explains the vision, the blood test and the shakes and sweats — delivered WITH the reassurance in the same breath: most are NOT cancer, they are benign and cause trouble by pressing, and they are treatable, usually through the nose. Differentials: craniopharyngioma, tuberculum sellae meningioma, carotid aneurysm and infiltrative causes; biochemically, assay interference and thyroid hormone resistance, NEITHER of which gives a field defect. Plan: MRI pituitary with contrast, formal perimetry, and a full anterior pituitary panel (TSH and free T4/T3, prolactin, 8 a.m. cortisol and ACTH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, testosterone or oestradiol), with urgent endocrine and neurosurgical referral and PATS for travel. Screen for apoplexy and the other pituitary effects: headaches, ring or shoe size, libido, thirst and polyuria. Same-day return for sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision, a drooping eyelid or a sudden drop in vision — and no driving until the field is formally assessed, because there is a legal standard.
plan: WIPE and NAME YOUR STRUCTURE: '...I've been asked to examine your eyes. I'll look at your eyes, get you to read some letters, follow my pen, and shine a light in your eyes. Partway through I'll bring a chair over and sit quite close — I'll explain why then. Nothing hurts.' Then: 'Examiner, the complaint is visual and the task is an eye examination, so THAT is my structure. I'll run the eight steps with particular attention to the VISUAL FIELDS, given the thyroid function result.' If asked why: 'because a non-suppressed TSH with a high T4 points at the pituitary, and the pituitary sits under the optic chiasm.' (Reaching for the neck is the drift this sentence prevents.)

Inspection with a purpose, and acuity: 'given the thyrotoxic features I am specifically looking for EXOPHTHALMOS, from above and from the side — there is none, and no lid retraction. Lids: no swelling, redness, discharge or ptosis. Globe: no redness. Pupils: round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon.' (Why: thyroid eye disease — its ABSENCE supports a central rather than a Graves cause, because proptosis is autoimmune, not an effect of the hormone.) Then 'cover your left eye, read from the top... and swap... and both together. Examiner, 6/6 right, 6/6 left, 6/6 binocular — so NO PINHOLE IS INDICATED.' (Do not let a normal acuity reassure you: chiasmal compression spares central acuity until late, so normal acuity is exactly what you expect.)

FIELDS — the instruction, given in full: 'I'm bringing my chair across and sitting facing you, about an arm's length away — sorry to be close, but the test only works at that distance. Cover one eye with your palm — I'll cover the matching one of mine. Look straight at my nose and keep looking at it; don't follow the pen. Tell me the moment you see it, then tell me if it disappears.'

AS THE DEFECT EMERGES — convert silence into words: [pen well inside your own field] 'Jim, CAN YOU SEE THE PEN YET?... And now?... Examiner, the pen is clearly within my own temporal field and the patient does not see it — the temporal upper quadrant of the right eye is ABSENT. Temporal lower — also absent. Nasal upper, nasal lower — both full. Repeating on the left... temporal upper and lower absent, nasal quadrants full. EXAMINER, THIS IS A BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA.' (Carrying on in silence when he does not answer is the trap — the absence of a reply IS the finding. And swapping the covered eye when you swap hands puts the nasal quadrants on the wrong eye.)

The remaining steps, each with its reason: colour vision offered; 'eye movements — head still, follow my finger, tell me if you see double. Up? Down? Left? Right? — full range, no nystagmus, no diplopia, and importantly NO OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, which would have suggested cavernous sinus involvement. Pupils — direct and consensual both eyes, and on the swinging torch no relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'M LOOKING SPECIFICALLY FOR OPTIC ATROPHY.'

THE THREE-PART DIAGNOSIS to Jim, all three parts: 'I found something definite. You're not seeing out to the side — the outer half of your vision is missing in the right eye, and in the left eye as well. That's called a bitemporal hemianopia.' → 'I've been clipping the door frames on site. Thought I was just tired.' → 'That fits exactly. Now — THAT PATTERN TELLS US WHERE THE PROBLEM IS. The nerves carrying vision from each eye cross over at one point inside your head, just behind your nose — the optic chiasm. Pressure on that one spot knocks out the outer half of vision in both eyes.' Then part three WITH the reassurance attached: 'the commonest cause of pressure there is a growth in a small gland sitting directly underneath — the pituitary... I know growth is a frightening word. Most of these are NOT cancer — they're benign and cause trouble by pressing. They're treatable, usually with an operation done through the nose.' Then the link: 'that same gland also controls your thyroid. Your blood test showed a high thyroid level with the control hormone that should have switched off — not switching off. So ONE growth explains your vision, your blood test, and the shakes and sweats.'

Screen the rest of the pituitary, then plan: 'any headaches? Any change in your ring or shoe size? Any problems with sex drive? Drinking or passing water much more than usual?' → daily headaches for two months, the rest negative. Then: MRI of the pituitary, formal perimetry, and blood tests for the other hormones that gland makes; urgent endocrine and neurosurgical referral to Adelaide with PATS for the travel; same-day return for a sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision, a drooping eyelid or a sudden drop in vision; and no driving until the field is formally assessed, because there is a legal standard for field of vision. Then the examiner summary with the differentials (see dx).

Numbers and rules: fields sitting 1 m apart, pen 50 cm from each face, four quadrants per eye and eight in total. THYROID FUNCTION — primary hyperthyroidism gives a LOW TSH; central hyperthyroidism gives a NORMAL OR HIGH TSH with a high T4. A chiasm compressed FROM BELOW takes the SUPERIOR TEMPORAL quadrants first. Pituitary panel: TSH and free T4/T3, prolactin, 8 a.m. cortisol and ACTH, IGF-1, LH, FSH, testosterone or oestradiol. Apoplexy: IV hydrocortisone plus neurosurgery — STEROID BEFORE THYROID HORMONE. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS National 131 450.

Variants: PROLACTINOMA (32-year-old woman with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea) — the same field defect, but the hormone is prolactin and the treatment differs: a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline is FIRST LINE and usually shrinks the tumour and restores the field without surgery VERIFY, with surgery reserved for failure, intolerance or acute visual compromise. / APOPLEXY — a sudden severe headache today with vomiting, new ophthalmoplegia and deteriorating vision in a patient with a pituitary mass: 'this changes the station. I would STOP examining, call for help, give intravenous hydrocortisone for likely adrenal insufficiency, obtain urgent imaging, and speak to neurosurgery immediately. In a rural site that is a MedSTAR retrieval call on 1300 13 12 33.' / HOMONYMOUS, NOT BITEMPORAL — the SAME half lost in both eyes: 'a left homonymous hemianopia localises to the right optic tract, radiation or occipital cortex, not the chiasm. My leading diagnosis is a right-sided stroke or space-occupying lesion, and I would image the BRAIN rather than the pituitary.'
pefe: Role-player: Jim Corradi, 40, self-employed builder on domestic sites around the Yorke Peninsula, driving a ute daily for work. Vision has felt 'narrow' for a few months — he keeps clipping door frames and nearly reversed into a stack of timber he did not see. Also shaky hands, sweating more, 4 kg of unintended weight loss, and HEADACHES most days for two months. Non-smoker, six or so beers a week, no medications, supplements or biotin, no relevant past or family history. NOT present if asked: galactorrhoea, ring or shoe size change, libido change, thirst or polyuria, double vision, eye pain. Practical and a bit impatient at first; when the word 'growth' is used he goes quiet and worried and asks 'is that a brain tumour?' HIDDEN CONCERN: his business depends on driving and being on site, and he is afraid of being told to stop working — 'can I still drive? I've got jobs booked in.'

HOW THE FIELDS ARE PLAYED, exactly: he sits still, covers whichever eye is asked and looks at the candidate's nose. TEMPORAL quadrants (pen coming in from his outer side), BOTH eyes: HE SAYS NOTHING. If asked 'can you see it?' he says 'no, nothing yet', and only once the pen reaches roughly the midline in front of his nose does he say 'yes, there it is now'. NASAL quadrants: 'yep, I can see it' as soon as it appears, and 'no, it hasn't disappeared' when asked. IF THE CANDIDATE NEVER ASKS whether he can see it and simply moves on, HE STAYS SILENT AND LETS THEM MISS IT — that is the failure this station is designed to expose. Acuity: he reads the whole chart with each eye.

Scored out of 20. FIELD TECHNIQUE (8): brings a chair and sits at the same level; about one metre away; covers their own opposite eye; holds the pen equidistant IN FRONT rather than beside their head; moves it slowly without waving; gives the full instruction including 'tell me if it disappears'; four quadrants in each eye, eight in total; swaps hands for the nasal field while covering the SAME eye. FINDING AND NAMING (4): ASKS when no reply comes; states each absent quadrant out loud as it is found; names the defect as a bitemporal hemianopia; comments on the absence of exophthalmos and its significance. DIAGNOSIS AND REASONING (8): runs the EYE examination not a thyroid examination; nominates all eight steps; part 1 names the finding in plain words; part 2 localises to the chiasm and explains why; part 3 names the pituitary; explicitly links the tumour to the thyroid result; reassures (mostly benign, treatable, through the nose) IN THE SAME BREATH; and screens for apoplexy and the other pituitary hormone effects.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice or outpatients. DO NOT DECIDE ANYTHING FROM THE STEM: the diabetes in Version A is a decoy and the age in Version B tells you nothing. THREE MOVEMENT CHECKS decide the diagnosis — both eyes open, then each eye alone — and they come first after inspection. Persists with one eye covered = MONOCULAR (the eye itself); resolves with either covered = BINOCULAR (alignment). Automatic fails: checking eye movements only once with no cover test; never asking the patient about double vision during the movements; naming a specific cranial nerve palsy from the direction of gaze; never examining the pupils; diagnosing from the stem's past history rather than the examination; sending a patient with new binocular diplopia away without addressing driving.

This is the important bit: TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY IF YOU SEE DOUBLE, and tell me WHERE YOU'RE LOOKING when it happens' · CHECK ONE, both eyes open, FULL big H out to the extremes; CHECK TWO, left eye covered with the patient's own palm, the SAME full H; CHECK THREE, right eye covered, the same again · then STATE THE CONCLUSION OUT LOUD (monocular or binocular) before going on · then acuity, fields, colour, accommodation, PUPILS (the triage question in a diplopia station) and fundoscopy looking specifically for papilloedema · then the fatigability and bulbar screen, the diagnosis, the driving advice and the safety-net.

back.dx: VERSION B — BINOCULAR DIPLOPIA, leading diagnosis OCULAR MYASTHENIA GRAVIS: diplopia present with both eyes open and resolving with EITHER eye covered, horizontal and worst on left gaze, with full movements, 6/6 acuity, full fields, equal briskly reactive pupils with no RAPD and normal discs — plus fatigability (worse in the evening) and evening ptosis. Binocular means each eye is normal alone, so this is a disorder of MOVEMENT AND ALIGNMENT. DO NOT NAME A SINGLE CRANIAL NERVE from the gaze: left gaze requires the left lateral rectus (VI) AND the right medial rectus (III). Differentials BY LEVEL — brain: tumour, multiple sclerosis, stroke, raised intracranial pressure; cranial nerves III, IV and VI: microvascular mononeuropathy, compressive lesion, aneurysm; neuromuscular junction: myasthenia gravis; muscle: thyroid eye disease, and traumatic entrapment if there were injury; plus giant cell arteritis in an older patient. Give the MONOCULAR list as well whichever version you have — cataract, astigmatism, refractive error, corneal irregularity or keratoconus, dislocated lens, dry eye — excluded here because the diplopia cleared with either eye covered. Plan: acetylcholine receptor antibodies, MRI brain and orbits, thyroid function, CT chest for thymoma if antibodies positive, neurology referral, AND ADVICE NOT TO DRIVE. Safety-net: trouble swallowing, slurred speech, breathlessness, limb weakness, sudden severe headache, or a large painful pupil.
plan: WIPE with the cover test flagged: '...I'll look at your eyes, get you to follow my pen, read a few letters, and I'll shine a light in your eyes. AT A FEW POINTS I'LL ASK YOU TO COVER ONE EYE — that's part of the test. Nothing hurts.' Then inspection with two named targets: 'Examiner, on inspection I'm looking particularly for STRABISMUS and PTOSIS. The corneal light reflexes are symmetrical, so no obvious squint, and no ptosis. Lids clear. No exophthalmos or enophthalmos, no redness. Pupils round, regular, symmetrical, no hyphaema or hypopyon.' (Why ptosis: third nerve palsy and myasthenia both cause it, and both cause diplopia.)

THE INSTRUCTION, given before anything moves: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only. This is the important bit: TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY IF YOU SEE DOUBLE AT ANY POINT, AND TELL ME WHERE YOU'RE LOOKING WHEN IT HAPPENS.' Then CHECK ONE, both eyes open, full big H out to the extremes: 'any double vision looking left? Up there? Down there? To the right? Up? Down?' → 'yes, two of everything — worst when I look off to my left' → 'with both eyes open the patient reports diplopia, and the range of movement is full.'

CHECKS TWO AND THREE, each with the SAME full H: 'now cover your left eye with your palm and we'll do exactly the same again. Any double vision here? Here?' → 'no, that's single now.' 'And now cover your right eye, same again.' → 'also single.' (Shrinking the H for checks two and three because time is running out is the trap — the finding may only appear at the extremes. And ask the patient to use their own palm rather than covering with your hand while holding the pen.)

STATE THE CONCLUSION OUT LOUD before moving on: 'Examiner: diplopia is present with both eyes open and RESOLVES WITH EITHER EYE COVERED. That is BINOCULAR diplopia — each eye is normal alone, so this is a disorder of ocular movement and alignment. The separation is horizontal and worst on left gaze. I'll record that as an observation, but I WOULD NOT LOCALISE IT TO A SINGLE CRANIAL NERVE on clinical grounds, because left gaze requires both the left lateral rectus and the right medial rectus.'

The remaining steps, taking the skips: 'acuity — 6/6 both, no pinhole needed. Fields by confrontation — full in all eight quadrants. Colour vision — Ishihara or the chart bands. Accommodation — convergence and constriction present. PUPILS — and these matter a great deal here: direct and consensual in both eyes, and on the swinging torch both pupils are equal, briskly reactive, and there is no relative afferent pupillary defect. No ptosis and a normal pupil makes a compressive third nerve lesion much less likely. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'm looking specifically for PAPILLOEDEMA.' (Skipping the pupils because the movements were the interesting bit is the auto-fail that matters most: in a diplopia station THE PUPIL IS THE TRIAGE QUESTION.)

The fatigability and bulbar screen, which turns the case: 'is the double vision worse at any particular time of day? Any trouble with chewing or swallowing? Any weakness in your arms or legs, or getting short of breath? Any droopy eyelid, especially in the evening? Headaches?' → 'definitely worse by the evening. And my husband says my left eyelid droops at night.'

Explain, then the driving conversation: 'with both eyes open you see double, but the moment you cover either eye it goes. That means each eye is working fine on its own — the problem is the two eyes not moving together, so your brain gets two pictures. The control of eye movement runs along a chain: the brain, the nerves to the eye muscles, the junction where nerve meets muscle, and the muscles. Yours being worse in the evening, with the eyelid droop your husband noticed, makes me think particularly about that junction — a condition called myasthenia gravis. It's treatable. But I don't want to guess, so we'll do a scan and blood tests to sort it out properly.' → 'is it a stroke?' → 'it can be, and that's one of the things we'll rule out — but nothing in your examination points that way today.' → 'can I still drive? I've got a 30-minute run to school.' → 'I'm sorry, but no — not until this is sorted out. Double vision isn't safe at the wheel and there's a legal standard as well. I'll write you a letter for work today.' Then the safety-net and the level-by-level differential (see dx).

VERSION A, MONOCULAR: 'with both eyes open, diplopia. With the LEFT eye covered — so the right eye working alone — THE DIPLOPIA PERSISTS. With the right eye covered, it resolves. That is monocular diplopia, and the affected eye is the RIGHT. I'd now concentrate on the light path of that eye: acuity WITH A PINHOLE, the red reflex, and a request for slit-lamp examination.' To Dennis: 'when you cover your right eye the doubling goes; when you cover the left it stays. So the problem is inside your right eye, not the two eyes working together. The commonest cause is clouding of the lens — a cataract... it could also be the shape of the front window of the eye, or a focusing problem. Cataracts are very treatable.' The diabetes in the stem is a DECOY — do not diagnose a microvascular palsy from the history.

THE PUPIL-INVOLVING THIRD NERVE PALSY — ptosis, a down-and-out eye, PAIN and a DILATED, poorly reactive pupil: 'this changes the station. A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated, poorly reactive pupil is a POSTERIOR COMMUNICATING ARTERY ANEURYSM until proven otherwise. I would stop, escalate immediately, arrange urgent CT or MR angiography, and speak to neurosurgery. From a rural site that is a MedSTAR call on 1300 13 12 33. I WOULD NOT ATTRIBUTE THIS TO DIABETES even if the patient is diabetic — the pupil involvement is what removes that option.'
pefe: Role-player: Anita Reddy, 40, primary school teacher in Kadina who drives 30 minutes each way. Three weeks of side-by-side double vision, worst looking to her left, much worse by the evening and often fine first thing; her husband has noticed her LEFT eyelid droops at night; generally tired; no trouble swallowing, chewing, speaking or breathing, no limb weakness, no headache, eye pain or injury; non-smoker, occasional wine, no medications, no diabetes or thyroid disease. Articulate and quietly anxious. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened it is a brain tumour or a stroke, and separately worried about the drive to work — neither raised unless asked. HOW SHE PLAYS THE DIPLOPIA, exactly: check 1 both eyes open — 'yes, two of everything', and if asked where it is worst, 'worst looking off to my left'; check 2 left eye covered — 'no, that's single'; check 3 right eye covered — 'also single'. IF THEY NEVER COVER AN EYE AT ALL she says nothing about it and lets them finish and fail — that is the point of the drill. IF THEY NEVER ASK ABOUT DOUBLE VISION during the movements she does not volunteer it, and only later, to an open question, says 'you didn't ask, but I was seeing double the whole way through that.' The fatigability and the ptosis come only if asked about the time of day, about ptosis, or through an open question.

Numbers and rules: THREE movement checks — both eyes, right alone, left alone. PERSISTS means monocular; RESOLVES means binocular. FOUR levels: brain, nerve III/IV/VI, junction, muscle. All extraocular muscles are CN III except SO4 and LR6. Left gaze = left lateral rectus (VI) plus right medial rectus (III), which is exactly why you cannot name one nerve. Ptosis plus a dilated pupil plus pain = aneurysm = same-day angiography. Myasthenia workup: acetylcholine receptor antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation, CT chest for thymoma. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; TIS National 131 450.

Scored out of 20. THE COVER TEST (7): instructs the patient to report diplopia BEFORE starting; big H taken to the extremes, not a small one; check 1 with both eyes open; check 2 with one eye covered; check 3 with the other covered; asks about diplopia in each direction ALL THREE TIMES; states the conclusion — monocular or binocular — out loud. REASONING (5): explains what binocular diplopia means mechanically; differentials by level brain to muscle; gives the monocular list as well; refuses to name a single cranial nerve from the gaze AND SAYS WHY; identifies fatigability as pointing to myasthenia. SAFETY AND COMMUNICATION (8): inspection for strabismus and ptosis; pupils in both eyes with the swinging torch; comments on the pupils being equal and reactive and why that matters; fundoscopy nominated for papilloedema; screens for bulbar and respiratory symptoms; explains without jargon and checks understanding; advises not to drive; and safety-nets swallowing, speech, breathing, limb weakness, sudden headache and a painful dilated pupil.
fails: ★ Checking eye movements only once — no cover test at all, so the station's single decisive manoeuvre never happens
★ Never asking the patient about double vision during the movements — she will not volunteer it
Naming a specific cranial nerve palsy from the direction of gaze; left gaze needs the left LR and the right MR
Never examining the pupils — in a diplopia station the pupil is the triage question, and ptosis with a dilated poorly reactive pupil and pain is an aneurysm, not an outpatient referral

Diagnosing from the stem's past history rather than the examination (the diabetes is a decoy); shrinking the H for checks two and three; sending a patient with new binocular diplopia away without addressing driving

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED. THIS IS A TRAUMA STATION WEARING AN EYE STATION'S CLOTHES: general appearance, inspection, PALPATION, then the eye examination WITH MOVEMENTS FIRST, then cranial nerves V and VII. stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia. Kyle Brennan, 30, brought in two hours after a motor vehicle accident (some recalls: punched in the face), complaining of double vision. Primary survey complete, vital signs stable, GCS 15, BP 128/74, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 98%, afebrile. Cotton wool, pen torch, ophthalmoscope, Snellen chart and a pen available. 8 minutes.

back.dx: LEFT ORBITAL FLOOR FRACTURE with inferior muscle tethering and infraorbital nerve injury — THE FLOOR TRIAD: tenderness at the inferior orbital rim, DIPLOPIA ON UPGAZE (tethering of the INFERIOR RECTUS AND INFERIOR OBLIQUE), and NUMBNESS IN THE V2 INFRAORBITAL TERRITORY. Relevant negatives: normal conscious level, no raccoon eyes, no Battle sign, no CSF leak, no hyphaema, no enophthalmos, 6/6 acuity, no RAPD, normal seventh nerve. Plan: CT FACIAL BONES AND ORBITS WITH FINE CORONAL CUTS (not plain films), analgesia, ice, head elevation, NO NOSE-BLOWING (it can force sinus air into the orbit), ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral, review at 7-14 days, and immediate escalation for bradycardia, vomiting or any fall in acuity. Surgery for persistent diplopia in primary or downgaze, enophthalmos greater than 2 mm, or a large defect VERIFY. To the patient, THREE REASONS: there is a bruise and tenderness exactly where that bone runs; looking up gives double vision because small muscles sitting on the floor of the socket get caught in the break; and the cheek is numb because a nerve runs along that same bone. Reassure specifically: vision is 6/6 in both eyes, the pupils work, the eyeball is not damaged, and the double vision is MECHANICAL and usually settles as swelling goes down over a week or two — with an operation available if it does not. Also: no driving while seeing double.
plan: WIPE with the warning, and ONE sentence on the primary survey: '...I've been asked to examine your face and your eyes. That means looking closely at your face, gently feeling around the bones of your face and head, getting you to follow my pen, and shining a light in your eyes. THE PRESSING MAY BE TENDER — tell me the moment anything hurts and I'll stop. I WON'T TOUCH THE EYEBALL.' Then: 'Examiner, I note the primary survey is complete and he is haemodynamically stable; I'M ASSUMING CERVICAL SPINE PRECAUTIONS REMAIN IN PLACE. On general appearance he is sitting comfortably, ALERT AND ORIENTATED with an intact conscious level, not in obvious distress, and there is no airway concern.' (Re-running the primary survey to look thorough is how you fail to finish.)

INSPECTION with the five named negatives: 'I can see a bruise below the left eye with some lower lid swelling. Specifically: NO RACCOON EYES; looking behind both ears, NO BATTLE SIGN; no clear discharge from the nose or ears to suggest a CSF LEAK. Looking from above and from the side, no exophthalmos and NO ENOPHTHALMOS. At the anterior chamber, NO HYPHAEMA. On the sclera, no subconjunctival haemorrhage. No ptosis, no laceration. The pupils are equal, round, regular and symmetrical — PUPIL SHAPE MATTERS AFTER FACIAL TRAUMA.' (A teardrop pupil means a ruptured globe: stop, shield the eye, call ophthalmology.)

PALPATION, five regions, uninjured side first, one side at a time: 'Kyle, I'm going to gently feel around the bones of your face. Tell me the moment it hurts. I'll start on the side that wasn't hurt. Examiner: SKULL — temporal, parietal, occipital and vertex — no tenderness, no step, no boggy swelling. Right orbital rim — no tenderness anywhere. Left orbital rim — superior no tenderness, LATERAL WALL no tenderness, INFERIOR RIM: definite tenderness, and I think a small step. Nasal bones — no tenderness, no deviation. Zygomatic arches — no tenderness. Mandible and the temporomandibular joints — no tenderness, and the bite feels normal. I'm deliberately NOT palpating the globe, in case it is ruptured.' (Two hands on both sides at once looks neat and wrecks the comparison; and forgetting the LATERAL WALL is exactly where Version 2 hides its only positive.)

EYE MOVEMENTS FIRST, given the complaint: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only. IMPORTANT: IF YOU SEE DOUBLE AT ANY POINT, TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY. Any double vision looking up?' → 'yeah — two of everything when I look up' → 'looking down? To the left? To the right?' → 'no, all fine' → 'Examiner, the range of movement is full and there is no nystagmus, but the patient reports DIPLOPIA ON UPWARD GAZE — consistent with tethering of the inferior rectus and inferior oblique in an ORBITAL FLOOR FRACTURE.' (Not asking about diplopia means the single best finding in the station never appears — he is briefed never to volunteer it.)

The rest of the eye examination, each with its reason: acuity each eye and binocular ('6/6 — an important negative'); fields and colour offered and skipped; 'PUPILS — direct and consensual in both eyes, and a swinging torch test: equal, briskly reactive, NO relative afferent pupillary defect, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST OPTIC NERVE COMPROMISE OR A RETROBULBAR HAEMORRHAGE. Fundoscopy — right eye, right hand, dial at zero; I'm looking for retinal detachment, commotio retinae or vitreous haemorrhage.' IF A FUNDUS PHOTOGRAPH APPEARS, describe and then park it: 'this shows arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, copper wiring, hard exudates and a cotton-wool spot — HYPERTENSIVE RETINOPATHY. That tells me he has had raised blood pressure for some time and needs it followed up, BUT IT DOES NOT CHANGE TODAY'S DIAGNOSIS, WHICH IS TRAUMATIC.'

CRANIAL NERVES V AND VII — the special test in facial trauma: 'fifth, MOTOR — clench your teeth; temporalis and masseter bulky and symmetrical. Fifth, SENSORY — cotton wool, demonstrated on the hand, eyes closed: FOREHEAD, yes both sides; CHEEK, yes right, nothing on the left — REDUCED SENSATION IN THE LEFT V2, INFRAORBITAL TERRITORY; JAW, yes both. SEVENTH — eyebrows up, eyes shut tight, cheeks blown out, show me your teeth: full and symmetrical.' (Testing sensation only on the injured side leaves nothing to compare it with.)

The diagnosis with THREE reasons, then the reassurance and the disposition: 'I think you've got a break in one of the bones around your eye — the floor of the socket, just under your left eye. An orbital floor fracture. THREE THINGS point to it. One, there's a bruise there and it's tender exactly where that bone runs. Two, when you look up you see double — small muscles sitting on the floor of the socket get caught in the break. Three, your cheek is numb, because a nerve runs along that same bone.' → 'am I going to lose the eye? Will the double vision stay?' → 'No — and I understand why you'd ask. Your vision itself is completely normal, 6/6 in both eyes, your pupils are working properly, and the eyeball hasn't been damaged. The double vision is a MECHANICAL problem from the muscles being caught, and in most people it settles as the swelling goes down over a week or two. If it doesn't, there's an operation that frees the muscle and repairs the floor.' Then: CT facial bones, analgesia and ice, referrals to eye and face surgeons, DON'T BLOW YOUR NOSE and DON'T DRIVE while seeing double, and return for worsening pain, a bulging eye, worsening vision, fever, or feeling faint or sick.

VERSION 2, LATERAL WALL (2019 onward) — three moments change: inspection, 'there is no bruise and no swelling'; palpation, 'the inferior orbital rim is not tender; there is tenderness over the LEFT LATERAL ORBITAL WALL'; movements, 'no diplopia in any direction — but the patient reports PAIN ON LOOKING TOWARDS THE INJURED SIDE. V and VII are both normal.' To the patient: 'a break in the bone on the outer side of your eye socket. Two things point to it: that's exactly where it's tender, and it hurts when you look towards that side. Reassuringly, you're not seeing double, your cheek sensation is normal, and your vision is fine — so I don't think a muscle is trapped or a nerve damaged. Next is a CT scan of the facial bones.'

THE TWO EMERGENCIES. RETROBULBAR HAEMORRHAGE — proptosis with a tense globe, severe pain, acuity 6/60 and an RAPD: 'this is orbital compartment syndrome and a SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY. I would stop examining, call for senior help, and proceed to LATERAL CANTHOTOMY AND CANTHOLYSIS immediately — this is a clinical diagnosis and I would NOT wait for a CT. In a rural site I'd do it here on telephone advice and call MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33.' RUPTURED GLOBE — a teardrop pupil or a soft eye: 'I would stop examining, NOT press on the eye, NOT measure intraocular pressure, and apply a RIGID SHIELD — never a pad. Nil by mouth, head up, analgesia and antiemetics, tetanus prophylaxis, intravenous antibiotics, and immediate ophthalmology.' And bradycardia with vomiting in a patient with entrapment is the OCULOCARDIAC REFLEX — escalate.
pefe: Role-player: Kyle Brennan, 30, self-employed fencing contractor who drives for work every day. Two hours ago his ute went off the road and he hit the LEFT side of his face on the door frame, seatbelt on, no loss of consciousness, no vomiting or fits, remembers everything. Face sore on the left, double vision looking UP, and the left cheek numb 'like after the dentist'. Smoker 15 a day, no alcohol before the crash, no medications, allergies or blood thinners, tetanus 'years ago, not sure'. Not present if asked: eye pain, flashes, floaters, curtain, fever, nausea, faintness, fluid from nose or ears, neck pain, headache. Sore and shaken but stoic. HIDDEN CONCERN: frightened he will lose the eye, and cannot afford time off work. HOW HE PLAYS THE FINDINGS, exactly: PALPATION — silent for the skull, the right orbital rim, the nose, the zygomatic arches, the mandible, AND the left superior rim and lateral wall; only the LEFT INFERIOR ORBITAL RIM gets 'ow — yeah, that's sore'. MOVEMENTS — he says NOTHING spontaneously; only if asked 'any double vision looking up?' does he say 'yeah, two of everything when I look up', and down/left/right are fine. IF THEY NEVER ASK, HE NEVER TELLS THEM — that is the failure this station exists to expose. COTTON WOOL — 'yes' for the forehead both sides, the right cheek and the jaw both sides; SILENCE over the left cheek. If they press on his eyeball: 'ow, don't push on my eye' — and it is an automatic fail.

Numbers: FIVE named inspection signs — raccoon eyes, Battle sign, hyphaema, enophthalmos, CSF leak. FIVE palpation regions — skull, orbital rims, nasal bones, zygomatic arch, mandible. THE FLOOR TRIAD — inferior rim tenderness, upgaze diplopia, V2 numbness. Muscles tethered: inferior rectus and inferior oblique. Nerve: infraorbital = V2. Imaging: CT facial bones and orbits with fine CORONAL cuts — plain films are an auto-fail as definitive imaging. Review 7-14 days. Operate for persistent diplopia in primary or downgaze, enophthalmos over 2 mm, or a large defect VERIFY. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS National 131 450, ReturnToWorkSA if work-related.

Scored out of 20. STRUCTURE AND INSPECTION (7): acknowledges the primary survey and C-spine; comments on conscious level; describes the bruise with the side; names raccoon eyes and Battle sign; names hyphaema at the anterior chamber; looks from above and the side for exophthalmos and enophthalmos; asks about or looks for CSF. PALPATION (5): warns and offers to stop; starts on the uninjured side; palpates one side at a time; covers all five regions INCLUDING the lateral wall; does not press on the globe. EYE EXAMINATION AND NERVES (8): does movements FIRST given the complaint; instructs the patient to report diplopia before starting; asks about diplopia in EACH direction including up; nominates the remaining eye tests; comments on acuity and pupils and why they matter here; tests V motor and V sensory in all three divisions BOTH sides; tests VII; and is not derailed by the fundus photograph.

★ Never asking about double vision, so the single best finding never appears; or PRESSING ON THE GLOBE, which would extrude intraocular contents if it were ruptured
'Inspection is normal apart from a bruise' — the marks are in the five named negatives
