NO bruise or swelling; the inferior rim is NOT tender but the LEFT LATERAL ORBITAL WALL is; NO diplopia, but pain on looking towards the injured side; V and VII normal

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, abdomen plus DRE on a mannequin. FLAG the back passage in ONE sentence at the start — front-loading the full sensitive-examination consent burns ninety seconds and you will still repeat it; saying nothing makes it an ambush. THE STATION'S FAIL IS STOPPING AT HAEMORRHOIDS: the word COLONOSCOPY must be spoken unconditionally, in the same breath as the diagnosis, never contingent on what you felt — and never offer a faecal occult blood test, because he is symptomatic and therefore on the DIAGNOSTIC pathway, not the screening one.
stem: VERSION A (the common recall): general practice. A 40-year-old with irregular bowel motions and rectal bleeding; a rectal examination mannequin is provided. 8 minutes. Patient in this script: John Whelan.

VERSION B (the old anaemia recall): a 45-year-old man with exertional chest pain radiating to the left arm and shoulder, palpitations, tiredness and bright red blood in the stools — iron deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss, unmasking stable angina. You are still asked for an abdomen and a rectum.
tasks: Talk to the patient and gain consent
Perform an abdominal and rectal examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
time: OPENING WIPE for the abdomen plus ONE flagging sentence about the back passage · GENERAL APPEARANCE, HANDS AND FACE with the anaemia signs made explicitly relevant (he is bleeding): pallor, bruising and petechiae, pale palmar creases, koilonychia, capillary refill and pulse volume, conjunctival pallor, sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes · and ASK FOR A POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE, which separates a candidate who is examining from one who is performing · THE ABDOMEN run without stopping: inspection (Cullen and Grey Turner named), cough, superficial then deep palpation of all nine regions, liver, spleen and kidneys, percussion for organomegaly and shifting dullness with the reason for NOT percussing rebound said aloud, bowel sounds · THE SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-40 seconds: steps, position (left side, knees up), exposure, privacy and a sheet, a STOP SIGNAL, and a CHAPERONE · then gloves ('I'll just get my gloves') · INSPECTION IN FOUR GROUPED BURSTS, then bearing down · THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION: pronate the forearm so the finger pad faces ANTERIORLY, sweep a full 360, ask about pain, say you are CHECKING the anal tone, offer the prostate in a man · WITHDRAW AND ACTUALLY LOOK AT THE GLOVE, naming blood, mucus AND melaena · then the diagnosis with COLONOSCOPY said unconditionally, the differential list and the safety-net.

back.dx: HAEMORRHOIDS as the most likely diagnosis — three soft, squishy, compressible lumps in the anal canal, a clean glove and a normal abdomen — BUT the station is about what you say next: a 40-year-old with rectal bleeding and a CHANGED BOWEL HABIT gets a COLONOSCOPY, said unconditionally, because you cannot see behind a haemorrhoid with your finger. Differentials in order: COLORECTAL CARCINOMA — the one that must be excluded and which the examination cannot exclude; haemorrhoids; anal fissure; inflammatory bowel disease; diverticular disease; polyps; anticoagulant or bleeding disorder; plus proctitis and a brisk upper GI bleed, which usually gives melaena but can present as fresh blood. Bloods today: FBC and iron studies. Never offer an iFOBT to a symptomatic patient — the NBCSP iFOBT is two-yearly, mailed 50-74 and requestable 45-49, for ASYMPTOMATIC people only VERIFY. Safety-net: heavy bleeding, feeling faint or dizzy, or severe abdominal pain means come straight back or go to ED rather than waiting for the appointment. VERSION B: two problems, one cause — chronic blood loss has caused iron deficiency anaemia, and the reduced oxygen delivery is what unmasks the exertional chest pain, so 'the chest pain is the alarm; the bleeding is the fire' — bloods, iron treatment and a colonoscopy.
plan: Opening WIPE plus ONE flagging sentence: '...for the first part I will be looking at your tummy, gently feeling it, gently tapping on it, and listening to your bowel sounds. I will need you lying flat with your tummy fully exposed. I will wash my hands before I forget. Are you happy for me to go ahead? THERE IS A SECOND PART WHERE I WILL NEED TO EXAMINE YOUR BACK PASSAGE — I will explain that part properly when we get there. Is that all right?'

General appearance, hands and face, with the anaemia made relevant, and the postural BP requested: 'on general appearance the patient is alert and orientated, comfortable at rest, not in pain and not cachectic. HE HAS BEEN BLEEDING, so I am specifically looking for pallor, and for bruising or petechiae. At the hands: pale palmar creases, koilonychia, capillary refill and pulse volume. At the face: conjunctival pallor, sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. MAY I HAVE A FULL SET OF OBSERVATIONS INCLUDING A POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE?' (Skipping the peripheries because 'it's a rectal case' throws away the diagnosis in Version B.)

The abdomen, run without stopping and with omissions NARRATED: 'the abdomen is not distended, moves symmetrically with respiration, no scars, no visible masses, no distended veins, no Cullen or Grey Turner sign. John, could you give me a cough? Any pain anywhere? — no pain on coughing. Superficial palpation of all nine regions, watching his face: no tenderness, no guarding, no rigidity. Deep palpation of all nine regions: no masses. Liver edge not palpable, spleen not palpable, kidneys not ballotable. THERE IS NO LOCALISED TENDERNESS, SO I AM NOT PERCUSSING FOR REBOUND; I will percuss for organomegaly and shifting dullness. Bowel sounds are present and normal in character.' (The task said perform an abdominal examination, not the relevant parts of one — a narrated omission is a clinical decision, a silent one is a missing mark.)

THE SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-40 seconds and no longer: 'now for the second part I need to examine your back passage. What I will do: first I will LOOK at the back passage, then INSERT ONE GLOVED, LUBRICATED FINGER to feel inside. It will feel uncomfortable and a little strange, but it should not be painful, AND I WILL STOP IMMEDIATELY IF YOU ASK ME TO. Position: lying on your LEFT SIDE, with your knees bent up towards your chest. Exposure: trousers and underwear off. I WILL STEP OUT AND GIVE YOU PRIVACY, and a sheet to cover yourself. Are you happy for me to go ahead? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE in the room with us?' Then: 'I'll just get my gloves' — now, not at the start — and say you would DOCUMENT the consent, the chaperone and the findings. If he pushes ('do you actually have to do that bit?'): 'I understand — nobody enjoys it. It is the only way for me to find where the bleeding is coming from, and it takes under a minute.'

INSPECTION IN FOUR GROUPED BURSTS, not one breathless list: 'one — no fissure, no haemorrhoids, no prolapse. Two — no skin tags and no external fistula openings. Three — no bleeding and no discharge. Four — no swelling, no redness and no abnormal mass.' Then: 'could you bear down for me as though you were opening your bowels? — on straining there is no prolapse and no faecal incontinence.'

THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION: 'John, I am going to insert my finger now. TAKE A BREATH IN FOR ME.' Small amount of lubricant; PRONATE THE FOREARM so the finger pad faces anteriorly; press on the posterior wall, then slide. '1. I am SWEEPING A FULL 360 DEGREES — anterior, right lateral, posterior, left lateral. Three soft, squishy, compressible lumps consistent with haemorrhoids; no hard or irregular mass, and the rectum is empty of hard stool. 2. John, any pain as I feel around? — no pain. 3. John, squeeze my finger for me. Examiner, I AM CHECKING the anal tone. 4. I would also palpate anteriorly for the prostate — size, consistency, surface and median sulcus.' (A supinated hand cannot sweep the circumference and the examiner can see it from your forearm. And never say 'anal tone is normal' — the mannequin cannot squeeze, so that is a finding you did not obtain.)

WITHDRAW AND LOOK AT THE GLOVE — the cheapest mark in the station and the most commonly dropped. Hold the finger up, give it a beat, actually look: 'Examiner, there is NO BLOOD, NO MUCUS AND NO MELAENA on my glove.' Then: 'all done, John. Please get dressed in your own time and I will talk you through what I found.'

THE EXPLANATION THAT PASSES THE STATION: 'the most likely cause of your bleeding is haemorrhoids — swollen, enlarged blood tubes in the back passage that bleed when you pass a motion. Very common, very treatable. BUT I WANT TO BE STRAIGHT WITH YOU. You are forty, you are bleeding, and your bowel habit has changed. I CANNOT SEE BEHIND A HAEMORRHOID WITH MY FINGER. So I am arranging a COLONOSCOPY — a camera test of the whole large bowel — to be certain we are not missing a growth or a cancer. Not because I think you have one, but because the only way to be sure is to look.' → 'cancer? You think I've got cancer?' → 'I do not think that is the most likely answer, and I am not trying to frighten you. But it is the one thing I am not willing to guess about. Most people who have this test are given the all-clear.' → 'my dad had bowel cancer, he was 61' → thank him, and say it makes you more certain you are doing the right thing and that you will ask about the rest of the family. Then the differential list, the FBC and iron studies, and the safety-net (see dx).

ask: 'There is a second part where I will examine your back passage — I will explain that properly when we get there.' / 'It should not be painful, and I will stop immediately if you ask me to.' / 'Lying on your left side, knees bent up towards your chest.' / 'I will step out and give you privacy, and a sheet to cover yourself.' / 'Would you like a chaperone in the room with us?' / 'I will just get my gloves — back in a moment.'

'One — no fissure, haemorrhoids or prolapse. Two — no tags or fistulae. Three — no bleeding or discharge. Four — no swelling, redness or mass.' / 'Take a breath in for me.' / 'I am pronating my forearm and sweeping a full 360 degrees.' / 'Examiner, I am checking the anal tone.' / 'There is no blood, no mucus and no melaena on my glove.'

'Haemorrhoids are swollen, enlarged blood tubes in the back passage.' / 'I cannot see behind a haemorrhoid with my finger.' / 'My most likely diagnosis is haemorrhoids; my primary concern is colorectal carcinoma.' / 'May I have a full set of observations including a postural blood pressure?'

VARIANT 1 — THE CANCER MANNEQUIN ('a hard, irregular, fixed mass at 5 cm, and fresh blood on your glove'): DO NOT SOFTEN IT — 'John, I would rather tell you straight than leave you guessing. I have felt a lump in the back passage, and there was blood on my glove. THAT LUMP IS NOT A HAEMORRHOID. It could be a growth, and I am concerned it could be a cancer. I cannot tell you for certain today. I am going to refer you urgently to the bowel surgeons for a camera test and a biopsy — a small sample — and take blood today. That will happen within a couple of weeks. I know that is a lot to hear. Is there someone you would like with you when we talk again?'

VARIANT 2 — VERSION B, ANAEMIA AND ANGINA (pale, pulse 104, postural drop 16 mmHg, fresh blood on the glove): 'two things are going on and they are connected. First, you have been losing blood from your back passage, so you have become anaemic — a low level of red cells and haemoglobin, the part of the blood that carries oxygen. Second, that is why your chest hurts when you walk: with less oxygen being delivered your heart works harder and faster, and complains. That is angina. THE CHEST PAIN IS THE ALARM; THE BLEEDING IS THE FIRE. So the question I care about is why you are bleeding — blood tests today, iron treatment, and a camera test of the bowel.' / VARIANT 3 — THE PAINFUL FISSURE (posterior midline tear with a sentinel tag, and he flinches): 'I can see a small tear — an anal fissure. Given how tender it is I WILL NOT FORCE a finger examination today. I would treat it and examine internally once you are comfortable.' Declining the DRE for a STATED reason is a pass behaviour, not an omission.
pefe: Role-player: John Whelan, 40, plumber, married with two children, ten cigarettes a day and about eight standard drinks a week, no medications or previous surgery. Three months of unpredictable bowels — some days loose, some constipated, going more often — and six weeks of BRIGHT RED blood, on the paper and in the bowl, not mixed in, and PAINLESS. A bit of slime sometimes, a few kilos of weight loss put down to work, always tired, often feels he has not fully emptied, and the motions are sometimes thinner. HIS FATHER HAD BOWEL CANCER AT 61 — not volunteered early, given only when asked about family history, or at seven minutes: 'doctor — my dad had bowel cancer. Is that what this is?' He came hoping for a cream. Flat and brusque at first, quietly reluctant about the back passage, and genuinely frightened and QUIET when cancer is mentioned. HE PUSHES ONCE on consent ('do you actually have to do that bit?') and agrees if the candidate explains why and offers to stop. IF THE CANDIDATE REASSURES TOO EASILY — 'it's just piles, nothing to worry about' — HE ACCEPTS IT CHEERFULLY AND SAYS 'great, so I don't need anything else?' That is the trap closing.

Numbers: station 8 min — abdomen 3 min, rectal wipe 40 s, rectal examination 1.5 min, diagnosis and differentials 1.75 min. Anal canal 3-4 cm; FOUR inspection groups; FOUR prostate characteristics; sweep 360 degrees. Sphincters: resting tone = INTERNAL; squeeze = EXTERNAL, S2-S4; anal wink = anocutaneous reflex, S2-S4. Haemorrhoid grades: I bleed only, II reduce spontaneously, III manual reduction, IV irreducible. NBCSP iFOBT two-yearly, mailed 50-74 and requestable 45-49, ASYMPTOMATIC ONLY VERIFY.

Scored out of 10: introduced and consented for the abdomen; FLAGGED the back passage in one sentence rather than front-loading or ambushing; ran a complete abdominal examination narrating any deliberate omission; full sensitive-examination consent covering steps, position, exposure, privacy, sheet, STOP SIGNAL and CHAPERONE; gloved at the right moment; inspection in FOUR grouped bursts; pronation with a full 360 sweep, pain checked, and said 'CHECKING' the anal tone; LOOKED at the glove and said so; SAID COLONOSCOPY UNCONDITIONALLY and named bowel cancer as the primary concern; and gave a plural differential list with a safety-net.
fails: ★ Stopping at haemorrhoids — the word COLONOSCOPY must be spoken unconditionally and in the same breath as the diagnosis, never made contingent on what you felt
★ Quiet self-editing of the abdominal examination — a narrated omission is a clinical decision, a silent one is a missing mark
Never looking at the glove; or a supinated hand with the finger straight in, so a full 360 sweep is physically impossible
Chaperone never offered and the stop signal never given; front-loading the whole sensitive consent at the start, or never flagging the back passage so it becomes an ambush

Saying 'anal tone is normal' when the mannequin cannot squeeze; offering a faecal occult blood test to a symptomatic patient; twelve inspection findings fired off in one breath instead of four grouped bursts

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, abdomen plus DRE on a mannequin after an episode of urinary retention. THE TRAP IS IN THE FIRST SENTENCE: the word CATHETER is bait, and there is no management step here — the tasks are examination, examination, explanation. Three things decide it: a complete abdominal examination with AUDIBLE SUPRAPUBIC EMPHASIS; a correctly consented DRE with the FINGER PAD ANTERIOR; and ALL FOUR PROSTATE CHARACTERISTICS spoken out loud. And the last mark is honesty: a DRE cannot exclude cancer.
stem: General practice. A man who had an episode of URINARY RETENTION three days ago, resolved with a catheter, presenting today for further examination. Age recalled as 46 or 76 — it changes nothing. Patient in this script: Gary Nolan, 76. 8 minutes. Some recalls ask you to explain to the examiner rather than the patient.
tasks: Perform an abdominal examination
Perform a rectal examination on the mannequin
Explain your findings and your diagnosis to the patient
time: OPENING WIPE plus the one-sentence flag about the back passage · and if pushed to re-catheterise, ONE sentence back: 'you were catheterised three days ago and that has settled, so my job now is to work out why it happened' · GENERAL APPEARANCE AND HANDS with each item made relevant in a clause (alert and orientated, BECAUSE neurological causes are on the differential; not in pain at rest, BECAUSE retention and prostatitis both hurt), and observations INCLUDING TEMPERATURE · THE ABDOMEN with three 'SPECIFICALLY' lines: no visible suprapubic masses, swellings or distension; no suprapubic TENDERNESS on superficial palpation; no suprapubic MASS on deep palpation · plus kidneys and renal angles · PERCUSSION from just above the symphysis working UPWARDS (distended = DULL and you cannot get below it; empty pelvis = RESONANT) and bowel sounds, with the faecal-impaction reason ready · SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT 30-45 seconds with stop signal and chaperone, then gloves · PERIANAL INSPECTION in four grouped bursts and bearing down, EVEN THOUGH none of it relates to retention · THE ANAL CANAL BEFORE THE GLAND: pronate, 360 sweep, pain checked, hard stool · THE FOUR CHARACTERISTICS in order every time · ANAL TONE and the ANAL WINK with the cauda equina reason ready · the glove looked at · then the explanation: gland, findings, name, and THE HONEST LIMIT.

back.dx: BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA — an enlarged gland (larger than a walnut, more than two finger-pads across) that is FIRM AND RUBBERY rather than hard, with a SMOOTH surface and no nodularity, a PRESERVED MEDIAN SULCUS and no tenderness, in a man with a poor stream, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, nocturia and incomplete emptying who went into retention. Explain it as: a walnut-shaped gland sitting just under the bladder with the urine pipe running THROUGH THE MIDDLE of it, so as it grows the flow gets squeezed. THEN THE HONEST LIMIT — a digital examination CANNOT rule out cancer: many tumours are impalpable and a smooth rubbery gland is compatible with an early carcinoma, so discuss PSA — deferred about SIX WEEKS after catheterisation, infection or retention, because all three push the number up (and finasteride halves it) VERIFY. Also today: urine test, bladder scan for post-void residual, renal function, and an alpha-blocker to relax the outlet (tamsulosin 400 micrograms daily; finasteride 5 mg daily with effect over 3-6 months VERIFY). Differentials for retention to keep visible: BPH, prostate carcinoma, prostatitis, urethral stricture, faecal impaction, DRUGS (he recently started a sedating antihistamine, and anticholinergics precipitate retention), and CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME. Safety-net: unable to pass urine at all, a painful swollen lower abdomen, fever and shakes, or numbness around the saddle area or leg weakness — straight back or to ED.
plan: WIPE, the flag, and the catheter question answered in ONE sentence: 'for the first part I will be looking at your tummy, feeling it, gently tapping on it, and I may listen to your bowel sounds at the end... there is a second part where I will need to examine your back passage — I will explain the steps when we get there.' → 'shouldn't you be putting that tube back in?' → 'Not today. You were catheterised three days ago and that has settled, so my job now is to examine you and work out why it happened in the first place.' If the examiner probes: 'I would never catheterise anyone without at least a brief history and an abdominal examination confirming a distended bladder — which is exactly the examination I am doing now.'

General appearance and hands, each made relevant in a clause: 'on general appearance Gary is ALERT AND ORIENTATED — relevant because neurological causes are on my differential list — and he is NOT IN PAIN AT REST, which matters because retention and prostatitis are both painful. At the hands I am looking for pale palmar creases. MAY I HAVE A FULL SET OF OBSERVATIONS, INCLUDING TEMPERATURE?' (In the prostatitis variant the answer is 38.8 and a pulse of 108.)

THE ABDOMEN with the suprapubic volume turned up — three 'specifically' lines: 'on inspection the abdomen is not distended, moves symmetrically, no scars or distended veins — AND SPECIFICALLY, IN THE SUPRAPUBIC AREA, no visible masses, swellings or distension. Gary, could you give me a cough? Any pain? — no pain. Superficial palpation of all nine regions: no tenderness, guarding or rigidity — AND SPECIFICALLY, NO SUPRAPUBIC TENDERNESS. Deep palpation of all nine: no masses — AND SPECIFICALLY, NO SUPRAPUBIC MASS. Kidneys not ballotable, no renal angle tenderness.' (What a suprapubic mass represents in retention is THE DISTENDED BLADDER — smooth, dull, tender, arising out of the pelvis and you cannot get below it. Bladder tumours are essentially never palpable abdominally.)

Percussion and auscultation, with both challenge answers ready: 'I will percuss from just above the symphysis pubis working UPWARDS. It is RESONANT — examiner, the bladder is not distended. Bowel sounds are present and normal in character.' → 'why not auscultatory percussion?' → 'stethoscope above the symphysis, direct percussion down the midline, a sudden increase in loudness at the upper border — but it only informs you when the bladder is ALREADY distended, which palpation has told me.' → 'why bowel sounds in a urinary case?' → 'faecal impaction is a genuine cause of retention, and the task asked for an abdominal examination, not part of one.' GET THE DIRECTION RIGHT: distended = DULL, empty pelvis = RESONANT.

SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION CONSENT, 30-45 seconds: steps (look, then one gloved lubricated finger to feel inside AND TO FEEL THE PROSTATE), 'uncomfortable but should not be painful, and I WILL STOP IMMEDIATELY IF YOU ASK', left side with knees to chest, trousers and underwear off, privacy and a sheet, 'are you happy for me to proceed? WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE with us? I will just get my gloves' — and document the consent, chaperone and findings. → 'is that the test for prostate cancer?' → 'it is part of assessing the prostate — it tells me the size, how it feels and whether the surface is smooth. It is not the whole answer on cancer; there is also a blood test we can talk about afterwards.'

Perianal inspection in four grouped bursts and bearing down — EVEN THOUGH none of it relates to retention, because skipping it tells the examiner you were pattern-matching the stem. Then THE ANAL CANAL BEFORE THE GLAND: 'take a breath in for me. Examiner, I am PRONATING MY FOREARM so the finger pad faces ANTERIORLY, and sweeping a full 360 degrees — anterior, right lateral, posterior, left lateral. No abnormal lumps, and the rectum is empty of hard stool. Gary, any pain as I feel around? — no pain.' (Supinated, the pad sits on the coccyx, and telling the examiner you are feeling the prostate while pointing at the sacrum is marked as an accuracy failure.)

THE FOUR CHARACTERISTICS — the scoring block, in this order every time and said aloud even when you can feel almost nothing: 'turning my finger anteriorly to the prostate. SIZE — larger than a walnut, spanning more than two finger-pads. CONSISTENCY — firm and rubbery, which is normal; not hard or stony. SURFACE — rubbing across the whole accessible surface, smooth, with no nodularity. MEDIAN SULCUS — the central groove is preserved. TENDERNESS — not tender.' Then: 'Gary, squeeze my finger for me. Examiner, I AM CHECKING the anal tone. May I have a cotton bud? I would like to check the ANAL WINK — if not I will stroke either side of the verge with my gloved finger: I am testing the anocutaneous reflex.' (Why bother: 'cauda equina syndrome causes painless retention with saddle anaesthesia and reduced anal tone, so tone and perianal sensation are how I screen for it. Resting tone is the internal sphincter; squeeze is the external, S2 to S4.') Withdraw, LOOK at the glove: 'no blood, no mucus and no melaena.'

THE EXPLANATION — gland first, then findings, then the name, then the LIMIT: 'today I was examining a gland called the prostate. It is a small walnut-shaped gland sitting just underneath the bladder, and the tube that carries urine out runs STRAIGHT THROUGH THE MIDDLE of it. I was checking four things. How big it is — yours is a little larger than we expect, common as men get older. How it feels — firm and rubbery, which is normal, not hard. The surface — smooth, no lumps. And a groove that normally runs down the middle — I could feel it clearly. Putting that together, I think you have BENIGN PROSTATIC HYPERPLASIA. Benign means not a cancer. The gland has grown, and because the pipe runs through it the flow gets squeezed — which is why you went into retention.' → 'so it's definitely not cancer then' → DO NOT AGREE: 'what I felt today is reassuring — nothing hard, no lumps, and the groove was normal. But I have to be straight with you: FEELING THE GLAND CANNOT RULE A CANCER OUT ON ITS OWN. So I would like to talk about a blood test called PSA. Because a catheter and the retention itself push that number up, the right time to check it is in about SIX WEEKS.' Then urine test, bladder scan for residual, renal function, an alpha-blocker, and the safety-net (see dx).

'I will stop immediately if you ask. Would you like a chaperone?' / 'I am pronating my forearm so the pad faces anteriorly.' / 'SIZE — CONSISTENCY — SURFACE — MEDIAN SULCUS — tenderness.' / 'Larger than a walnut, firm and rubbery, smooth with no nodularity, sulcus preserved.' / 'Examiner, I am checking the anal tone.'

'The prostate sits just under the bladder, and the pipe runs straight through the middle of it.' / 'Benign means not a cancer.' / 'Feeling the gland cannot rule a cancer out on its own.' / 'A catheter pushes the PSA up, so the right time to check it is in about six weeks.'

VARIANT 1 — THE CARCINOMA GLAND ('hard, craggy, nodular; you cannot feel the median sulcus'): to the examiner, 'the gland is enlarged, STONY HARD, with an irregular nodular surface and an OBLITERATED median sulcus — suspicious of prostate carcinoma.' To the patient, do not soften it: 'the gland felt harder and more irregular than I would expect, and the normal groove was not there. I cannot tell you today what that is, but it needs looking into urgently. I am referring you to a urologist and taking bloods including a PSA.'

VARIANT 2 — PAINLESS RETENTION WITH REDUCED TONE (younger man, back pain, numb when wiping, both legs heavy; 'anal tone is reduced'): THIS BECOMES AN EMERGENCY — 'I have painless retention with reduced anal tone. I would immediately test perianal sensation in the saddle distribution, lower limb power, reflexes and plantars. My primary concern is CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME, which requires an urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine and a same-day neurosurgical referral. This is time-critical and I would escalate before completing the examination.' / VARIANT 3 — 'EXPLAIN TO THE EXAMINER' rather than the patient: shorter and easier — 'the prostate is enlarged, of normal firm-rubbery consistency, with a smooth surface, no nodularity and a preserved median sulcus, and it is not tender. My diagnosis is benign prostatic hyperplasia. I WOULD NOT RELY ON THE DIGITAL EXAMINATION ALONE TO EXCLUDE CARCINOMA, and would discuss PSA testing in about six weeks.' Do not drop that last sentence just because you are talking to an examiner.
pefe: Role-player: Gary Nolan, 76, retired grain farmer, widowed and living alone, on amlodipine and a RECENTLY STARTED SEDATING ANTIHISTAMINE for hay fever (given only if asked directly — and it is the drug that precipitated the retention). Three days ago he could not pass urine at all, his lower abdomen swelled and became very painful, a catheter drained a great deal, the tube came out yesterday and he is passing urine again with a poor stream. Admits if asked: poor stream and terminal dribbling for a couple of years, hesitancy, up three or four times a night, never feels completely empty; NO burning, blood, fevers, back pain, saddle numbness, leg weakness or weight loss. HIS BROTHER HAD PROSTATE CANCER AT 70 — not volunteered early, given when asked about family or at seven minutes. Dry, understated, gruff; he minimises everything. HE OPENS WITH THE CATHETER QUESTION — 'shouldn't you be putting that tube back in?' — and if the candidate agrees to catheterise, that is the trap closing. He is mildly reluctant about the back passage and agrees if the steps are explained and a stop signal offered; if no chaperone is offered he does not help. WHEN THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN HE PUSHES ONCE: 'so it's definitely not cancer then.' If the candidate says yes, he accepts it happily — the second trap closing.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, pelvic model on the couch. THE CONSENT IS THE STATION: ANY missing consent or chaperone offer is a fail regardless of the total. Task one deserves 90 seconds and up to two minutes; the examination itself is only about two minutes of the eight. Say the words — SPECULUM, VAGINA, TWO FINGERS — because 'I'll just have a quick look down below' is not consent. And a normal examination changes NOTHING about the pathway: postmenopausal bleeding is abnormal until proven otherwise.
stem: General practice. Jenny Marsh, 54, with spotting and vaginal bleeding, otherwise well; no period for four years. She is seated; a pelvic model is on the couch. 8 minutes.

time: INTRODUCE AND SAY WHY, in her words and tied to her complaint ('I've been asked to examine your private parts today BECAUSE OF THE BLEEDING you've been having, so we can work out what is causing it') · EXPLAIN ALL THREE STEPS IN DETAIL: look; SPECULUM into the vagina to see the walls and the cervix; TWO FINGERS into the vagina with the other hand on the lower tummy to feel the womb and ovaries; 'it shouldn't be painful, but it will feel uncomfortable' · THEN THE SIX-PART CONSENT BLOCK: consent (1), privacy and a sheet with exposure explained, position (on your back, knees bent, knees fall out to the sides), STOP SIGNAL, CHAPERONE OFFERED, consent (2) · hand hygiene and gloves, general appearance · INSPECTION of vulva and perineum · SPECULUM: warn before insertion, blades vertical angled downward ~45 degrees, rotate 90, open and lock UNDER DIRECT VISION, keep one hand on it; describe the cervix AND THEN ASK ABOUT THE VAGINAL WALLS, because the model cannot show atrophy and the examiner only volunteers it if you say you are looking; warn before removal · BIMANUAL: cervical motion tenderness, then supinate and palpate suprapubically for uterine SIZE, BORDER and tenderness, then each adnexa · COVER HER, let her sit up · then the diagnosis, the grouped differentials and the plan.

back.dx: ATROPHIC VAGINITIS as the most likely cause of the spotting — thin, pale, dry vaginal walls after the menopause — BUT the station is what you say next: ANY BLEEDING AFTER THE MENOPAUSE IS ABNORMAL UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, and the thing you must exclude is ENDOMETRIAL CANCER (roughly 1 in 10 women with postmenopausal bleeding have it). Differentials in groups, in her words: cancer of the lining of the womb; thickening of the lining (hyperplasia); a polyp in the womb or on the cervix; cancer of the cervix; infection or inflammation of the cervix; the vaginal dryness itself; and bleeding that is not from the womb at all — bladder, back passage or skin. Fibroids are on the list but usually shrink after the menopause. Plan: TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND to measure the endometrium, bloods for anaemia, and SPECIALIST REFERRAL — urgent, not routine — with hysteroscopy and sampling if the lining is thickened (endometrial thickness over 4 mm triggers sampling VERIFY). Safety-net: heavy bleeding, faintness or dizziness, pain or fever means come back or go to ED. Postmenopausal means no period for 12 months.
plan: Introduce AND SAY WHY: 'Hello, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors here. Am I speaking with Jenny? Jenny, I've been asked to examine your private parts today BECAUSE OF THE BLEEDING you've been having, so we can work out what is causing it.' (Launching into the steps before saying why loses the mark — the examiner is listening for a reason, in her words, tied to her complaint.)

All three steps, in detail and unsoftened: 'there are three parts. First, I'll LOOK at your private parts. Second, I'll pass an instrument called a SPECULUM into the vagina so I can see the walls of the vagina and the cervix, which is the opening of the womb. Third, I'll place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while my other hand presses on your lower tummy, so that I can feel the womb and the ovaries between my hands. IT SHOULDN'T BE PAINFUL, BUT IT WILL FEEL UNCOMFORTABLE.'

The six-part consent block, in order: CONSENT 1 — 'is that all right with you — do I have your permission to go ahead?' PRIVACY — 'I'll give you privacy to undress from the waist down. There's a sheet to cover yourself with — tell me when you're ready. I will need to see the area fully.' POSITION — 'I'll ask you to lie on your back, bend your knees, and let your knees fall out to the sides.' STOP SIGNAL — 'if anything is uncomfortable, or you want me to stop, just say so and I'll stop straight away.' CHAPERONE — 'would you like me to arrange for a chaperone to be with us?' CONSENT 2 — 'and are you happy for me to begin now?' If she says YES to a chaperone, answer in one sentence and keep moving: 'I'll arrange one now, and we'll start as soon as they're with us.' If she declines, say you'll record the offer and the refusal.

Hands, gloves, general appearance, inspection: 'I'll clean my hands and put on gloves. On general appearance, Jenny is alert and comfortable at rest, she is not pale, and there is no cachexia.' Then 'Jenny, I'm going to uncover you and look now. On inspection of the vulva and perineum — the skin shows no rash, redness, ulceration or warts. There are no lumps or swellings and nothing visible descending. There is no bleeding or discharge.'

SPECULUM, warned both ways: 'Jenny, this is the speculum. I'm going to pass it now. It won't be painful but it will feel uncomfortable. Take a slow deep breath in for me. Examiner: inserting with the blades vertical, angled downward at about 45 degrees, rotating through 90 degrees, opening and locking UNDER DIRECT VISION, and holding it in place. Looking at the cervix — I can see the os; there is no abnormal growth, no polyp, and no bleeding or discharge from the os. LOOKING AT THE VAGINAL WALLS — are they normal, or is there anything you would like to tell me?' → 'the vaginal walls are thin, pale and dry' → 'thank you — thin, pale, dry vaginal walls, consistent with atrophic change.' Then 'that part's done, Jenny. I'm taking it out now — another deep breath.' (No sentence about the walls, no finding, no diagnosis.)

BIMANUAL: 'last part, Jenny. Two fingers into the vagina while I press on your lower tummy. Deep breath in. Examiner — checking for cervical motion tenderness. Jenny, any pain with that? No. Now SUPINATING MY FOREARM and palpating suprapubically: I'm assessing the SIZE of the uterus, its BORDER, and any TENDERNESS. Now the right adnexa — masses or tenderness? And the left adnexa?' If told the uterus is enlarged, ASK THE BORDER: 'and is the border regular or irregular?' — that single question turns a finding into reasoning. Then 'all done. Fingers coming out — deep breath. I'VE COVERED YOU UP. Take your time sitting up.'

Name it, then refuse to stop there: 'the examination was largely normal. The one thing I did find is that the lining of the vagina is thin and dry. That happens after the menopause when the oestrogen level falls, and it can cause spotting. We call it atrophic vaginitis, and it's easily treated.' → 'oh, that's a relief' → 'IT IS A COMMON CAUSE — BUT I DON'T WANT TO REASSURE YOU TOO QUICKLY. Any bleeding after the menopause has to be taken seriously, and the most important thing I have to rule out is a CANCER OF THE LINING OF THE WOMB. Most women with this turn out not to have a cancer, but we don't guess — we check.' → she becomes tearful: 'cancer? My sister had cancer.' → 'I can see that's frightening, and I'm sorry to bring it up. Let me tell you exactly what happens next, because there's a clear plan.'

The grouped differentials, the plan and the safety-net (see dx): ultrasound through the vagina to measure the lining, bloods for anaemia, specialist referral, and a camera and sample if the lining is thickened — soon rather than in a few months. Then: 'if the bleeding becomes heavy, if you feel faint or dizzy, or if you develop pain or a fever, come back or go to the emergency department.'

setting: PROCEDURE — general practice, cervical screening on a pelvic model with a full sampling pack laid out. What is really scored: whether you PREPARE BEFORE YOU START and say so, whether you NAME THE TRANSFORMATION ZONE, whether you choose the right sampler AND SAY WHY, and whether you can talk usefully for the LAST THREE MINUTES. Two traps sit on the tray: the lubricant, and the glass slide with its blue cover — Australia uses liquid-based cytology, and they are there to see whether you know it.

She is seated, a pelvic model is on the couch, and a complete sampling pack is laid out — broom, spatula, endocervical brush, a large swab, a glass slide and its blue cover, and a liquid-based cytology vial. 8 minutes.

Perform the cervical screening test on the model
Provide further advice to the patient
time: EXPLAIN THE PROCEDURE, NOT JUST THE EXAMINATION · she must know something is being TAKEN: two parts, look, then speculum, then 'a small soft brush to take a sample of cells from the surface of the cervix', a few seconds, 'you may feel a scrape, and a little spotting afterwards is normal' · SAY WHY: HPV, which causes almost all cervical cancers, and early cell changes long before they could become a cancer; vaccine question answered ('protects against the highest-risk types, but not every type') · the six-part consent block: consent (1), privacy and sheet, position and stop signal, CHAPERONE, consent (2) · PREPARE OUT LOUD: name the samplers available, CHECK THE EXPIRY DATE on the vial, OPEN THE VIAL BEFORE THE SPECULUM GOES IN because one hand is then committed, and decline lubricant in favour of warm water because gel interferes with the cytology · INSPECTION INCLUDING WARTS · SPECULUM with the 45/90 technique, one hand on it, describing vaginal walls AND cervix, then THE SENTENCE THAT CHOOSES YOUR SAMPLER: 'I can see the transformation zone, so I'll take the sample with the broom' · SAMPLE with the rotations COUNTED ALOUD, rinse vigorously, tap at the base, do not detach the head, cap and label · decline the bimanual (no indication) and TAKE THE SKIP · then THREE MINUTES of advice.

back.dx: ROUTINE CERVICAL SCREENING in an asymptomatic 22-year-old — and the marks are in the reasoning and the advice, not the findings. SAMPLER LOGIC: transformation zone VISIBLE (including an ectropion, where the zone has rolled outwards) = BROOM, five full clockwise rotations. Transformation zone NOT visible (atrophic cervix, or post-cone-biopsy where the junction sits higher in the canal) = SPATULA with one full turn on the surface PLUS ENDOCERVICAL BRUSH with a quarter turn in the canal, both rinsed into the same vial. Cervix obscured by discharge or blood = clear it with the large swab first, then sample, and add separate NAAT swabs if infection is suspected. RESULTS PATHWAY: HPV not detected = normal, repeat in 5 years. HPV 16 or 18 = straight to colposcopy. Other HPV type = reflex cytology — normal or low grade means repeat in 12 months to let the immune system clear it; higher grade means colposcopy. Colposcopy explained as 'very like today, but with a magnifying instrument, and they can take a tiny sample or treat on the spot'. Programme 25-74 with an exit test at 70-74, avoid intercourse 48 hours beforehand and aim for mid-cycle VERIFY — programme ages, intervals and self-collection eligibility change, so confirm before quoting.
plan: Explain THE PROCEDURE: 'you've come in for your cervical screening test today. Let me explain what that involves. There are two parts. First I'll LOOK at your private parts. Second I'll pass a SPECULUM into the vagina so that I can see the cervix — the opening of your womb. Once I can see it, I'll USE A SMALL SOFT BRUSH TO TAKE A SAMPLE OF CELLS from the surface of the cervix. That part takes only a few seconds. It shouldn't be painful, though you may feel a scrape, and a little spotting afterwards is completely normal.' Then WHY: 'we're looking for a virus called HPV, which causes almost all cancers of the cervix, and to pick up any early changes in the cells long before they could ever turn into a cancer. It's a screening test, so it's done when you're perfectly well.' → 'I've had the vaccine, do I still need it?' → 'the vaccine protects against the highest-risk types, but not every type, so screening still applies even if you've been vaccinated.'

The consent block: consent (1) 'do I have your permission to go ahead?'; privacy, sheet and exposure; position and stop signal; 'would you like me to arrange a chaperone to be with us?'; consent (2) 'and are you happy for me to begin now?' Record the offer if she declines.

PREPARE, OUT LOUD — the block most candidates skip: 'before I begin I'll prepare my equipment. I have a BROOM, a SPATULA and an ENDOCERVICAL BRUSH available, and a LARGE SWAB if I need to clear the cervix. I'M CHECKING THE EXPIRY DATE on the vial — it's in date. I'M OPENING THE VIAL NOW and putting it within reach, BECAUSE ONCE THE SPECULUM IS IN PLACE ONE HAND IS COMMITTED to holding it. I'd prefer WARM WATER rather than lubricant, because GEL CAN INTERFERE WITH THE CYTOLOGY.' (Do not touch the glass slide or the blue cover.)

Inspection WITH WARTS NAMED, then the speculum: 'on inspection — the skin shows no rash, redness or ulceration, and NO GENITAL WARTS. No lumps or swellings. No bleeding or discharge.' Then 'Jane, this is the speculum. I'm passing it now — slow deep breath in for me. Examiner: blades vertical, angled downward at about 45 degrees, rotating through 90 degrees, opening under direct vision and locking — and I'm keeping one hand on the speculum. Looking at the vaginal walls — normal. Looking at the cervix — no bleeding or discharge from the os, no abnormal growth or polyp. I CAN SEE THE TRANSFORMATION ZONE, SO I'LL TAKE THE SAMPLE WITH THE BROOM.' (The equipment mark is for the REASONING SAID ALOUD, not the object in your hand.)

TAKE THE SAMPLE AND COUNT: 'you may feel a slight scrape now. Examiner: passing the broom between the speculum handles, placing the LONG CENTRAL BRISTLES INTO THE OS and the SHORT BRISTLES FLAT ON THE ECTOCERVIX, and rotating CLOCKWISE — one, two, three, four, FIVE full rotations. Removing it, RINSING IT VIGOROUSLY in the vial and TAPPING IT against the base to release the cells. I'M NOT DETACHING THE HEAD. Capping the vial, and I'd LABEL IT with her name and date of birth before it leaves the room.' Then 'all done, Jane. Taking the speculum out now — another deep breath. I've covered you up.' → 'do you want to do a bimanual examination?' → 'No — there's no indication in an asymptomatic woman attending for screening. I'll move on.' TAKE THE SKIP and spend the time on task three.

THREE MINUTES OF ADVICE — the part candidates waste. IMMEDIATE: 'you may notice a little spotting for a day or so, which is normal. If you have heavy bleeding, pain or a fever, please come back.' WHAT THE TEST LOOKS FOR: 'the first thing they look for is HPV. It's a very common virus — most people who've ever been sexually active come into contact with it at some point, and in most people the immune system clears it without them ever knowing.' SAFE SEX, briefly: 'because it's passed on sexually, condoms reduce transmission though they don't eliminate it, and screening still matters even with one long-term partner.'

THE RESULTS PATHWAY, in full: 'if no virus is found, that's a normal result and I'd see you again in FIVE YEARS. If we find TYPE 16 OR 18 — the two highest-risk types — I'd send you straight to a specialist for a COLPOSCOPY. If we find a different type, the laboratory automatically looks at the cells: if they're normal or only mildly changed, we REPEAT IN 12 MONTHS to give your body a chance to clear the virus; if there are more marked changes, you'd go for colposcopy too.' Then colposcopy explained: 'very like today. A speculum again, but they use a magnifying instrument to look closely at the cervix, and if they see anything they can take a small sample or treat it on the spot. And remember, none of this means cancer — it means we're catching changes early, which is exactly what screening is for.' HER HIDDEN QUESTION, if given space: 'if they find the virus, does that mean my partner's cheated?' → HPV is extremely common, often carried for years without symptoms, and is NOT evidence of unfaithfulness.

Close with the practical points: 'the test is best done around the middle of your cycle, and it's better to avoid vaginal creams or intercourse for a couple of days beforehand — worth knowing for next time. Is there anything you'd like to ask?'

THE CO-TEST CASE — 36, postcoital bleeding, LSIL five years ago, and the task says 'pelvic examination' while the pack sits there unmentioned and the examiner says 'stick to your task': TAKE THE SAMPLE ANYWAY — 'cervical cancer is on my differential list, so I will take a sample from the cervix as part of assessing her bleeding. Examiner, I'd like this sent as a CO-TEST — HPV and cytology regardless of the HPV result, BECAUSE SHE IS SYMPTOMATIC.' If an ectropion is seen: 'that's common on the pill and can cause bleeding after sex. But the standard management of an ectropion is to make sure it isn't a cancer, so I'm still taking a co-test and I remain concerned until it's back.' If the examiner declares the bimanual normal: 'thank you — I'll accept that and move to my explanation' rather than arguing. If there is a VISIBLE IRREGULAR FRIABLE LESION: 'I'd still take a sample, but I would refer her directly for colposcopy and biopsy WITHOUT WAITING for the result.'

Other variants: ATROPHIC CERVIX, no transformation zone (57, screening) → 'a broom wouldn't reliably reach the canal. I'll use the spatula on the surface with one full turn, then the endocervical brush in the opening with a quarter turn, and rinse both into the same vial.' POST-CONE-BIOPSY → same, adding 'after treatment the junction sits higher in the canal, so I need the brush to reach it.' ECTROPION → 'the transformation zone has rolled outwards, so it IS visible. I'll use the broom.' CERVIX OBSCURED BY DISCHARGE OR BLOOD → clear it with the large swab first, then sample, and add NAAT swabs if infection is suspected. SHE DECLINES THE SPECULUM → 'that's completely your decision. There is another option: you can collect a swab YOURSELF, in private, and it's just as accurate at detecting the virus. It can't look at the cells, so if anything is found we'd need to see you again — but it's a much better option than not being screened at all.' BROKEN SPECULUM → ask for another, or proceed as far as safe and document the limitation.

A reminder letter brought her in; she has NO symptoms at all. Never had a screening test before, two sexual partners ever, HPV vaccine at school in Year 7, no pregnancies, periods regular and light. HIDDEN AGENDA: a friend told her it was 'agony' and she is genuinely nervous — and her real question, asked only if given space near the end, is 'IF THEY FIND THE VIRUS, DOES THAT MEAN MY PARTNER'S CHEATED?' Chatty and fidgety; if each step is explained before it happens she visibly relaxes and says 'that wasn't as bad as I expected'; if the doctor goes silent for more than about fifteen seconds she says 'is everything all right?' She stays seated and dressed, is quiet while they work on the model, takes a breath when told, says 'OW!' if the speculum goes in or out unwarned, and silently MARKS THEM DOWN if they touch the glass slide or reach for the lubricant.

Numbers: broom 5 full 360-degree clockwise rotations; spatula 1 full rotation; endocervical brush a quarter to half turn ONLY. Programme ages 25-74 with an exit test at 70-74. HPV not detected = 5 years. Non-16/18 HPV with normal or low-grade cytology = repeat at 12 months. Avoid intercourse for 48 hours beforehand; best around mid-cycle. High-risk types to name: 16 and 18; HPV has more than 100 types. Speculum 45 degrees downward, 90 degrees rotation. VERIFY programme ages, intervals, the exit-test window and self-collection eligibility — they change; if challenged and unsure: 'I'd follow the current National Cervical Screening Program guidelines; the principle is HPV first with reflex cytology, and direct colposcopy for 16 or 18.'

setting: PELVIC EXAMINATION + BREAKING BAD NEWS — emergency department, and THE ROLE-PLAYER IS ALREADY CRYING LOUDLY WHEN THE DOOR OPENS. TWO CRITICAL ERRORS, each of which fails the station whatever else you did: not saying 'THE OS IS OPEN', and not saying 'I WOULD REMOVE THE TISSUE NOW'. Then the news: a warning shot, ONE PLAIN SENTENCE, and 30-40 seconds of silence while she sobs — the statistics come AFTER the silence, never before, or they sound like brushing her off.

THE OS IS OPEN · clearly open, not just admitting a fingertip' · BIMANUAL with size, border, tenderness and both adnexae, then the interpretation ('no adnexal mass or tenderness makes an ectopic less likely; a uterus smaller than her dates is consistent with tissue already passed') · COVER HER, sit her up · then warning shot, one sentence, silence, 'it is not your fault', and only then the detail, the plan and the safety-net.

back.dx: INCOMPLETE MISCARRIAGE — an open cervical os with tissue visible at the os, fresh bleeding, and a uterus of six weeks in size against eight weeks by dates, with no adnexal mass or tenderness (making an ectopic less likely) and haemodynamic stability. Say it as ONE PLAIN SENTENCE FIRST — 'you are having a miscarriage' — not 'you're having an incomplete miscarriage', because she will hear one word and not the other. THE ACTION IS THE MARK: remove the tissue sitting in the canal with sponge forceps, because retained tissue causes continued bleeding and CERVICAL SHOCK — which is a VAGAL response with BRADYCARDIA, not tachycardia. Plan: remove the tissue, ultrasound to see what remains, CHECK HER BLOOD GROUP for anti-D (indications, dose and gestational thresholds VERIFY against Therapeutic Guidelines, SA Health Perinatal Practice Guidelines and RANZCOG), and bloods for anaemia; then the options for completing it — expectant, medical or a short procedure — discussed once she has had time. Miscarriage occurs in about 1 in 5 recognised pregnancies and most women go on to have a normal pregnancy. NOT HER FAULT: most early miscarriages happen because of a problem with how the pregnancy formed at the very beginning; nothing she lifted or did caused it. Safety-net: soaking a pad an hour, faintness, severe pain, fever or offensive discharge means be seen immediately — plus written information and support.
plan: ACKNOWLEDGE FIRST: 'Hello, I'm Dr -. Are you Jenny? I can see you're very upset, and I'm sorry. I'm here to help you. Would you like me to call your partner, or anyone else, to be with you?' → 'just tell me if I'm losing the baby' → 'I DON'T KNOW YET, AND I DON'T WANT TO GUESS. What I'd like to do is examine you, and then I'll tell you exactly what I've found. Would you like a moment first, or a sip of water?'

The explanation and consent, in full despite the distress: 'I need to examine your private parts, so we can find out what's happening. There are three parts. First I'll look. Then I'll pass a SPECULUM into the vagina so I can see the vaginal walls and the cervix, which is the opening of the womb. Then I'll place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while my other hand presses on your lower tummy. It shouldn't be painful but it will be uncomfortable. Do I have your permission?' Then privacy and sheet, position, stop signal, chaperone, and consent again. (Skipping consent 'because it's an emergency' is the trap — distress is a reason to explain more carefully, not less.)

Observations and inspection: 'Examiner, before I begin, may I have her pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature?' → 92, 112/70, 16, 36.8 → 'thank you — haemodynamically stable. On general appearance Jenny is alert, distressed but not confused, and she is not pale.' Then 'Jenny, I'm going to uncover you and look now. On inspection — skin shows no rash, redness or ulceration; no lumps or swellings; there is FRESH BLOOD AT THE INTROITUS.' (A young woman compensates until she does not — omitting observations in someone actively bleeding is a marked error.)

SPECULUM — BOTH CRITICAL SENTENCES LIVE HERE: 'Jenny, this is the speculum. I'm going to pass it now — slow deep breath in. Examiner, looking at the cervix. THERE IS TISSUE AT THE OS. I WOULD REMOVE THAT NOW WITH SPONGE FORCEPS, because tissue retained in the canal causes continued bleeding and can cause cervical shock. THE OS IS OPEN — clearly open, not just admitting a fingertip. Looking at the vaginal walls — normal.' Then 'that part's done. Taking it out now — another deep breath.' (Saying 'I can see tissue' and moving on gets nothing: the mark is for THE ACTION, not the observation.)

BIMANUAL and the interpretation: 'last part — two fingers into the vagina while I press on your lower tummy. Deep breath. Examiner: cervical motion tenderness — Jenny, any pain with that? No. Supinating my forearm and palpating suprapubically: uterine size, border, tenderness. Then each adnexa — masses and tenderness.' → uterus six weeks, regular, non-tender; adnexae normal → 'thank you — THE ABSENCE OF ADNEXAL TENDERNESS OR A MASS MAKES AN ECTOPIC PREGNANCY LESS LIKELY, and a uterus smaller than her dates is consistent with tissue already passed.' Then 'all finished, Jenny. Fingers coming out — deep breath. I'VE COVERED YOU UP. Come and sit with me when you're ready.'

THE WARNING SHOT, THEN ONE PLAIN SENTENCE: 'Jenny, would you like me to call your husband in before I tell you what I found?... I'M AFRAID I DON'T HAVE GOOD NEWS FOR YOU.' PAUSE. Let it land. 'YOU ARE HAVING A MISCARRIAGE.' She breaks down completely. THEN STOP TALKING — 30 to 40 seconds of silence, with only empathic lines: 'I'm so sorry. I wish I had better news for you today.' ... 'Take all the time you need.' ... 'This is not your fault. There is nothing you did that caused this.' (Continuing to talk over her is a marked fail, and so is leading with 'incomplete miscarriage' — she will hear one word and not the other.)

Her question, and only then the detail: 'was it because I was at work? I lifted a box on Tuesday.' → 'It was ABSOLUTELY NOT that. Most early miscarriages happen because of a problem with the way the pregnancy formed at the very beginning, and nothing anyone does causes it or prevents it.' → 'when I examined you, the opening of your womb was already open, and there was some pregnancy tissue sitting in it. That tells me the miscarriage has already started and that part of the tissue has come away. We call that an INCOMPLETE MISCARRIAGE. Over the next hours or days we'd expect the rest of it to come away.' Only NOW the statistics: 'miscarriage is common — about one in five pregnancies — and most women who have one go on to have a normal pregnancy afterwards.'

The plan and the safety-net: 'I'll remove the tissue that's sitting in the neck of the womb, which will help the bleeding settle. I'll arrange a scan to see whether anything is left inside. I'll check your blood group, because if you're a certain group you need an injection to protect future pregnancies. And I'll take some blood to make sure you're not anaemic. We'll talk through the options for completing this — waiting, medication, or a short procedure — once you've had time.' Then: 'if the bleeding becomes very heavy — soaking a pad an hour — or if you feel faint, get severe pain, or develop a fever or an offensive discharge, you need to be seen straight away. And there's support available; I'd like to give you some information before you go.'

THE EMERGENCIES: unilateral pain with adnexal tenderness → 'this raises an ECTOPIC pregnancy, which is my priority. I'd want IV access, a group and hold, a quantitative beta-hCG and an urgent transvaginal ultrasound, and I'd involve gynaecology now.' / Fever, offensive loss and a tender uterus → 'SEPTIC MISCARRIAGE — blood cultures and a high vaginal swab, empirical intravenous antibiotics, and gynaecology for urgent evacuation.' / Pulse 122, BP 80/50 with tissue in the canal → 'she is shocked. I'd REMOVE THE PRODUCTS FROM THE CANAL IMMEDIATELY, because that alone may correct a vagal bradycardia, and simultaneously resuscitate — two large-bore cannulas, fluids, cross-match, and call for help.' / 'Can you save it?' → 'I'm sorry — once the opening of the womb is open, the pregnancy can't be held in place, and there's no treatment that can change that. What we can do is look after you well from here.'

setting: PELVIC EXAMINATION — general practice, 45-year-old with intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding and a Mirena in situ. TWO THINGS ARE SCORED: 'I CANNOT SEE THE THREADS', and FIBROID VERSUS CANCER named in that order as the explanation for a bulky uterus. And never accept the word 'bulky' on its own — convert it into a NUMBER AND A BORDER, because bulky alone is not a finding you can reason from. Blaming the bleeding entirely on the device is the trap: the device explains irregular bleeding, it does not explain a ten-week uterus.

Perform a pelvic examination on the model
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

back.dx: TWO findings, TWO diagnoses. FIRST — a uterus of about ten weeks with an IRREGULAR BORDER in a woman with intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding: most likely a FIBROID, but ENDOMETRIAL CANCER cannot be separated from it by palpation, and that honesty is the mark — so a scan. SECOND — THE THREADS ARE NOT VISIBLE: the threads may simply have curled into the canal with the device in place, but the device may also have been expelled or displaced, so until the scan finds it you CANNOT promise she is protected — use condoms, and ask about unprotected sex in the last few days. Differentials, grouped and in her words: IN THE WOMB — fibroid, thickening of the lining, polyp, cancer of the lining; IN THE CERVIX — polyp, ectropion, cancer of the cervix (a normal screen a year ago is reassuring but does not exclude it when she is bleeding after sex); THE DEVICE ITSELF; INFECTION — chlamydia is a common and easily treated cause of postcoital bleeding; HORMONAL, including the approach to menopause and the thyroid; and rarely a BLEEDING DISORDER — plus check she is not pregnant. Plan: urine pregnancy test, swabs, a CO-TEST from the cervix (symptomatic, so cytology is reported whatever the HPV result), FBC and iron studies, then TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND to look at the womb, measure the lining and FIND THE DEVICE; hysteroscopy and sampling if indicated. Safety-net: heavy bleeding, faintness, pain or fever — come straight back.

And last I'll place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while my other hand presses on your lower tummy. It shouldn't hurt, but it will be uncomfortable. Do I have your permission to go ahead?' → 'will you check my coil while you're there?' → 'I WILL — I'll look for the threads while I'm there and I'll tell you what I find.' Then privacy and sheet, position, stop signal, chaperone, consent (2).

General appearance and inspection: 'Dana is alert and comfortable, not pale, and there is no cachexia. On inspection of the vulva — no rash, redness, ulceration or warts; no lumps, swellings or visible prolapse; no bleeding or discharge.'

SPECULUM, and the key sentence: 'Dana, this is the speculum. I'm going to pass it now. Take a slow deep breath in for me. Examiner: inserting with the blades vertical, angled downward at about 45 degrees, rotating and opening under direct vision, and holding it in place. Looking at the cervix — the os is closed, the surface is smooth, there is no polyp, no abnormal growth, and no bleeding or discharge from the os. I CANNOT SEE THE THREADS OF THE INTRAUTERINE DEVICE. Looking at the vaginal walls — normal.' Then warn before removal. (Reporting a normal cervix and moving on throws away the entire key point.)

BIMANUAL and the two questions: 'last part, Dana. Two fingers into the vagina while I press on your lower tummy. Deep breath in. Examiner — checking for cervical motion tenderness. Dana, any pain with that? Now supinating my forearm and palpating suprapubically: uterine size, border and tenderness.' → 'the uterus feels bulky' → 'THANK YOU — ROUGHLY WHAT SIZE IN WEEKS, AND IS THE BORDER REGULAR OR IRREGULAR?' → 'about ten weeks, irregular border, non-tender, adnexae normal.' Then 'that's everything, Dana. Fingers coming out — deep breath. I've covered you up; take your time sitting up.'

DIAGNOSIS ONE, in her words: 'two things came out of that examination. The first is that your womb feels larger than it should be for your age, and the surface felt uneven. You're bleeding between periods and after sex. Putting those together, there is most likely A LUMP GROWING IN THE WOMB. The commonest kind is benign — we call it a FIBROID, and it's very common. But there is a smaller chance that a lump like this is a CANCER OF THE LINING OF THE WOMB, and I want to be honest with you: I CANNOT TELL THOSE APART JUST BY FEELING. That is why I want a scan.' → 'cancer? I've got two kids at home' → 'I know that's a frightening word and I'm sorry to use it. I'm NOT telling you that you have cancer. I'm telling you it's on my list and it's the thing I'm going to rule out first, quickly, because that's the safest way to do this.'

DIAGNOSIS TWO, the threads: 'the second thing is that I couldn't see the threads of your Mirena. Sometimes the threads just curl up inside and the device is exactly where it should be. But it can also mean the device has come out without you noticing, or that it has moved out of position. UNTIL WE'VE FOUND IT ON THE SCAN, I CAN'T PROMISE YOU IT'S STILL PROTECTING YOU AGAINST PREGNANCY — so please use condoms in the meantime, and if you've had unprotected sex in the last few days let me know today.'

The grouped differentials and the plan (see dx), then the safety-net: 'if the bleeding becomes heavy, if you feel faint or dizzy, or if you get pain or a fever, come straight back or go to the emergency department. And use condoms until we know where the device is.' Her hidden agenda, if you leave a gap: 'I've been reading about cervical cancer online and I haven't slept for a week.'

VERSION 2, NO FINDINGS AT ALL → 'your examination today was completely normal. That's reassuring as far as it goes, but IT DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT I HAVE TO DO. You haven't had a period for four years and you're bleeding, and the first thing I must rule out is a cancer of the lining of the womb.' VERSION 3, TEN-WEEK UTERUS AFTER THE MENOPAUSE → ask the border, then 'your womb is larger than we expect after the menopause. Together with the bleeding, I'm concerned about a growth. Other variants: THREADS ARE VISIBLE → 'I can see the threads of your device, so it's in place' — then spend the recovered time on fibroid-versus-cancer and the differentials. ECTROPION SEEN → 'the red lining of the canal has rolled out around the opening — an ectropion. It's common and harmless and it can cause bleeding after sex. If it's in the right place we can leave it, and if it isn't, taking it out may need a different approach. The scan tells us which.' SHE IS ON TAMOXIFEN (62, one episode of spotting) → 'tamoxifen is a very effective breast cancer treatment, but it increases the risk of changes in the lining of the womb, so any bleeding needs looking into urgently, EVEN A SINGLE EPISODE.' ACTIVELY BLEEDING AND TACHYCARDIC → 'Examiner, before I go on, may I have her pulse, blood pressure and a haemoglobin? I'd like two large-bore cannulas, a group and hold and a full blood count.'

IF THEY BACKTRACK — 'no, no, it's nothing' — SHE LOOKS RELIEVED AND SAYS 'so I don't need the scan then?' That is the trap. She stays seated and dressed, is quiet at the model, takes a breath when told, says 'OW!' if the speculum goes in or out unwarned, and asks to be covered if left exposed.

back.dx: ONE CAUSE, THREE CONSEQUENCES — the pelvic floor muscles and supporting tissues are stretched and sometimes injured as the baby passes through: (1) STRESS INCONTINENCE — urine escaping when intra-abdominal pressure rises, coughing, sneezing, lifting the baby; (2) PROLAPSE — the vaginal wall or uterus sagging when the support is weakened, which explains the dragging lump even though the clinic examination did not reproduce it; and (3) DYSPAREUNIA from ATROPHIC VAGINAL WALLS — thin, pale, dry with loss of rugae, expected while breastfeeding because prolactin keeps oestrogen low, and it settles when feeding stops. The episiotomy has healed well. FIRST-LINE TREATMENT FOR BOTH THE LEAKING AND THE PROLAPSE IS THE SAME: supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a women's health physiotherapist, and it genuinely works; a vaginal moisturiser and lubricant for the dryness, with other options if that is not enough (topical vaginal oestrogen during lactation, pessary PBS availability and endometritis regimens all VERIFY). Keep it to one sentence of treatment and a referral — the task asked for findings. Ask how she is in herself and how feeding is going, and safety-net worsening leakage, pain, fever, or trouble controlling the bowels. National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66; PANDA 1300 726 306.
plan: WIPE with her three symptoms named back to her: 'you've come for your six-week check, and I can see you've had some discomfort during sex, some leaking of urine, and a feeling of a lump. I'd like to examine your private parts to look into all three of those. There are three parts: I'll look; then I'll pass a SPECULUM into the vagina to see the walls and the cervix; then I'll place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while my other hand presses on your lower tummy. It shouldn't be painful but it will be uncomfortable. Do I have your permission?' → 'will it hurt? It's been sore since the birth' → 'I'll be gentle, and I'll tell you before each step.' Then privacy and sheet, position, stop signal, chaperone, consent (2).

General appearance in TWO sentences: 'Julia is alert and comfortable at rest and is not pale. Feeling the pulse — regular, normal volume, no tachycardia.' Then inspection plus ADDED STEP 1: 'on inspection — the skin shows no rash, redness or ulceration; no lumps or swellings; no bleeding or discharge. I'M INSPECTING THE EPISIOTOMY WOUND to make sure it has healed well — looking for gaping, granulation tissue, discharge, or a scar that is tethered or tender.' → 'the model has no wound — assume it is well healed.'

ADDED STEP 2, the strain: 'Julia, could you BEAR DOWN for me as though you were straining? Just gently. Examiner, I'm looking for anything descending towards the introitus — the anterior wall, the cervix, or the posterior wall. I can see no prolapse.' (Saying 'I'd check for a prolapse' without ever asking her to strain does not assess it.) Then ADDED STEP 3: 'I'm placing a pad here. Could you give me a good strong cough? Examiner, I'M PERFORMING A COUGH STRESS TEST — looking for leakage at the moment of the cough, which would demonstrate stress incontinence. The pad is dry.' (Calling it a pad test is the language trap: a formal pad test is a weighed one-hour or twenty-four-hour investigation.)

SPECULUM, where the only positive finding lives: 'Julia, this is the speculum. I'm passing it now — slow deep breath in. Examiner: looking at the vaginal walls, SPECIFICALLY FOR ATROPHIC CHANGE — thin, pale, dry walls with loss of rugae. And the cervix — any bleeding or discharge from the os, any abnormal growth, polyp or ectropion.' → 'the vaginal walls are thin, pale and dry. The cervix is normal.' Then ADDED STEP 4: 'Julia, could you bear down for me again, please? Examiner, I'm SLOWLY WITHDRAWING THE SPECULUM WHILE SHE STRAINS, watching the anterior and posterior vaginal walls for descent. Ideally I'd use a Sims speculum in the left lateral position for this.' Then warn before removal. (Skip the walls and you lose the only positive finding — and the explanation for her dyspareunia.)

BIMANUAL and the optional extra: 'last part — two fingers into the vagina while I press on your lower tummy. Deep breath. Examiner: cervical motion tenderness — Julia, any pain? Then supinating my forearm: uterine size, border, tenderness. AT SIX WEEKS I'D EXPECT THE UTERUS TO HAVE RETURNED TO NORMAL SIZE. Then each adnexa.' Then: 'I'd also like to perform a digital rectal examination to assess ANAL SPHINCTER TONE, because she had an episiotomy and I want to exclude an unrecognised sphincter injury. Julia, do you ever have difficulty controlling wind, or have to rush to open your bowels?' → 'no, nothing like that' → 'that's everything, Julia. I've covered you up. Take your time sitting up.'

ONE CAUSE, then the three consequences in her words: 'everything you've described comes back to one thing. During a vaginal birth the muscles and supporting tissues at the base of your tummy get stretched, and sometimes injured, as the baby comes through. The first thing that causes is leaking urine when the pressure inside your tummy goes up — coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting the baby. That's STRESS INCONTINENCE, and it's very common after delivery. The second is the lump: when those muscles can't hold the organs in place as firmly, the wall of the vagina or the womb can sag downwards. That's a PROLAPSE. I didn't find one when I looked today -'

THE MOMENT THE STATION TURNS: 'so it's in my head?' → 'NOT AT ALL. I BELIEVE YOU. A prolapse can come and go with the time of day and with how much you've been on your feet, and a clinic examination doesn't always reproduce it. WHAT YOU'RE FEELING IS REAL, it has a name and it has a treatment.' Then the third: 'the discomfort during sex — when I looked, the lining of the vagina was thin and dry. That's expected while you're breastfeeding: the hormone that makes milk keeps your oestrogen low, and low oestrogen makes the tissue dry and easily irritated. It settles when you stop feeding. And the cut we made during the delivery has healed well.'

ONE SENTENCE OF TREATMENT, then stop: 'the first-line treatment for both the leaking and the prolapse is the same — PELVIC FLOOR MUSCLE TRAINING supervised by a women's health physiotherapist, and it genuinely works. For the dryness, a vaginal moisturiser and a lubricant will help, and there are other options we can discuss. I'll arrange the referral.' Then close: 'how are you in yourself, and how is feeding going? Come back sooner if the leaking gets worse, if you develop pain or a temperature, or if you have any trouble controlling your bowels.' (Five minutes of management is time you needed for the examination.)

CASE B — 28, BLEEDING ON DAY 10 with an episiotomy, lying on the bed, no model, and a fever in the observations: open with 'Examiner, before I begin, may I have her pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and temperature?', then 'I'd like to examine the abdomen, BECAUSE BY DAY TEN THE UTERUS SHOULD NO LONGER BE PALPABLE, so a palpable uterus would be abnormal.' Told 'you are feeling a mass', TWO follow-up questions decide it: 'is it tender? — and can I feel the lower border?' → 'I cannot feel the lower border, so the mass arises from the pelvis: it is the uterus, and at day ten it should not be palpable.' The pelvic examination becomes a REQUEST: inspection (bleeding? discharge? is the episiotomy intact or bleeding?), speculum (tears of the walls or cervix? is the os open? is there tissue in it?), bimanual (cervical motion tenderness? is the uterus enlarged and tender?). Then the explanation IN FOUR POINTS: 'I think you have an infection of the lining of the womb, called ENDOMETRITIS. Four reasons: you have a temperature; your womb is still large ten days after delivery when it should have shrunk out of reach; it was tender when I pressed; and the opening of the womb was still open with bleeding coming through.'

Other variants: POSITIVE COUGH STRESS TEST ('you can see the pad is wet') → 'thank you — that DEMONSTRATES stress incontinence', and in the explanation, 'I was able to show it when you coughed, which confirms what you've been describing.' / FAECAL URGENCY OR TROUBLE CONTROLLING WIND → 'that's important and I'm glad you've told me. It can mean the muscle ring around the back passage was injured during the birth and wasn't picked up at the time. I'd like to examine that, and refer you to a SPECIALIST PERINEAL CLINIC rather than just physiotherapy.' / TEARFUL AND NOT SLEEPING → 'before we finish — how are you in yourself? A lot of women find this time much harder than they expected, and it's something we take seriously and can help with.' / SHE INSISTS THE LUMP IS THERE despite a normal examination → believe her, and say why a clinic examination does not always reproduce it.
pefe: Role-player: Julia Bennett, 31, primary school teacher on maternity leave; first baby born six weeks ago by normal vaginal delivery with an episiotomy; fully breastfeeding, periods not returned, no medications or allergies, non-smoker, cervical screening two years ago normal. THREE THINGS she wants dealt with: burning, stinging pain at the ENTRANCE during sex since trying again two weeks ago (not deep); leaking urine when she sneezes, coughs or lifts the baby, several times a day, wearing a liner; and a dragging feeling and lump, worse at the end of the day and when coughing. NO bowel symptoms if asked. HIDDEN AGENDA: quietly convinced something has been 'permanently ruined' and that she will need surgery, and embarrassed about the leaking — she hasn't told her husband; asked only if given a gap: 'is it going to be like this forever? Will I need an operation?' Cheerful and practical on the surface, tired underneath. THE KEY MOMENT: when told there is no prolapse she interrupts with 'SO IT'S IN MY HEAD?' — a good doctor tells her it is real and comes and goes; a poor one lets it drop. She strains when asked, coughs when asked, and MARKS IT DOWN if never asked; says 'OW!' if the speculum goes in or out unwarned; asks to be covered if left exposed.

Numbers: the six-week check adds FOUR steps — episiotomy, strain, pad and cough, strain again. TWO strains: one on inspection, one on speculum withdrawal. Primary PPH is under 24 hours; SECONDARY PPH is 24 hours to 12 weeks. The uterus is impalpable abdominally by about day 10-14 and hard to feel beyond 2-3 days; the fundus descends roughly one finger-breadth a day. FOUR differentials for secondary PPH: infection, retained products, trauma, coagulopathy. A formal pad test is a weighed 1-hour or 24-hour test — NOT what you do at the bedside. National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66; PANDA 1300 726 306. Verify topical vaginal oestrogen in lactation, pessary PBS availability and the local endometritis regimen.

stem: General practice. Samantha Peel, 35, with heavy periods for three months, feeling tired and looking pale. She is seated. THERE IS NO PELVIC MODEL. A sphygmomanometer is on the trolley. 8 minutes.
