Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Request your investigations
time: EXPLAIN BOTH EXAMINATIONS AND CONSENT TO BOTH · the neck (because the thyroid is a common and treatable cause of heavy periods) AND the pelvic examination in full, including 'two fingers', because you are going to REQUEST the second · GENERAL APPEARANCE, HANDS (palmar pallor, palmar erythema, clubbing, pulse rate rhythm and volume, outstretched hands for tremor) and USE THE BLOOD PRESSURE MACHINE · FACE AND EYES: exophthalmos, lid retraction, eye movements for ophthalmoplegia and lid lag, then PULL DOWN THE LOWER LID for conjunctival pallor, and gums and tongue for hypertrophy, glossitis and angular stomatitis · THE THYROID: inspect front and side (cricoid-to-notch line), swallow, palpate from behind for size, LOWER BORDER, consistency, nodularity and tenderness, then nodes and trachea, and offer percussion and auscultation · taking every skip without arguing · THEN THE PIVOT: 'Examiner, I'd now like to perform a pelvic examination, WITH THE PATIENT'S CONSENT AND WITH A CHAPERONE PRESENT. Is there a model available, or would you like me to ask you for the findings?' · then ONE QUESTION AT A TIME through inspection, speculum and bimanual, ending with 'AND BEDSIDE TESTS, PLEASE · A URINE PREGNANCY TEST' · then the diagnosis, the anaemia, and the three-and-a-half investigations.

back.dx: A TEN-WEEK UTERUS with a regular border in a 35-year-old with menorrhagia — most likely a FIBROID (and her mother had them), but ENDOMETRIAL CANCER cannot be separated by palpation, so a scan; the thyroid is clinically normal, which matters because thyroid disease is a common and treatable cause of heavy periods; and the pregnancy test is negative, which had to be asked because AN ENLARGED UTERUS IN A 35-YEAR-OLD IS PREGNANCY UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Do not forget the SECOND diagnosis the stem handed you: losing this much blood monthly means IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA, which is why she is tired and breathless. Grouped differentials: growths in the lining — polyp or hyperplasia; problems in the cervix including cervical cancer; hormonal — thyroid, polycystic ovaries; infection; a BLEEDING DISORDER, especially if she has bled heavily since menarche (von Willebrand is commonest and often missed for years); and medications such as anticoagulants. INVESTIGATIONS — the three and a half: (1) TRANSVAGINAL ultrasound, better than transabdominal for the uterus and ovaries; (2) FBC and FERRITIN, because ferritin not serum iron measures stores; (3) serum beta-hCG to confirm the urine test; and (4) thyroid function. CA-125 IS THE RECALLED TRAP: 'no — it isn't a screening test, it's neither sensitive nor specific enough, and it would be more likely to mislead us than help.' Verify ferritin thresholds, endometrial cut-offs and PBS criteria before quoting.
plan: Explain BOTH examinations and consent to both: 'from your notes I can see you've been having heavy periods and feeling tired. I'd like to examine you to find the cause. There are TWO parts. First I'll look at and feel your neck, because the thyroid gland there can affect periods. Then I'll examine your private parts — I'll look, then pass a SPECULUM into the vagina to see the cervix, and then place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while my other hand presses on your lower tummy. Do I have your permission?' → 'my neck? What's that got to do with it?' → 'the thyroid gland sits at the front of your neck and controls how fast your body runs. If it isn't working properly it's a common and very treatable cause of heavy periods, so it's worth two minutes of checking.' Then privacy, position, stop signal, chaperone, consent (2).

General appearance, hands and the blood pressure: 'Samantha is alert and comfortable, dressed appropriately for the weather, not flushed or sweaty, no cachexia. Can I see your palms? And put your nails together for me. Examiner: no palmar pallor, no palmar erythema, no clubbing. Feeling the radial pulse for rate, rhythm and volume — EXAMINER, IS THERE A TIMER AVAILABLE?' → no → 'thank you, I'd count for fifteen seconds. Rhythm regular, volume normal, no tachycardia. Arms outstretched — no tremor. MAY I CHECK HER BLOOD PRESSURE?' (The machine is in the room deliberately.)

Face and eyes, both directions: 'look straight ahead for me, then follow my finger. And can you show me your gums with a big smile, and put your tongue out? Examiner: looking for exophthalmos and lid retraction, then eye movements for ophthalmoplegia and lid lag. Pulling down the lower lid — NO CONJUNCTIVAL PALLOR. No gum hypertrophy or bleeding, no glossitis or angular stomatitis.'

THE THYROID: 'inspecting the neck from the front — no visible swelling, redness or engorged veins. From the side — the line from the cricoid cartilage to the suprasternal notch is straight, with no bowing to suggest a goitre. Samantha, take a sip of water and swallow for me.' → 'skip the swallow' → 'thank you. Palpating from behind with the neck slightly flexed — assessing size, THE LOWER BORDER, consistency, nodularity and tenderness. Samantha, any pain? Then the cervical lymph node chains, and the position of the trachea. I'd also like to percuss for retrosternal extension and auscultate for a bruit.' → skips given → 'thank you — a clinically normal thyroid.' (If you cannot feel the lower border, the words are RETROSTERNAL EXTENSION. Never argue with a skip.)

THE PIVOT — the sentence that carries the station: 'Examiner, I'd now like to perform a pelvic examination, WITH THE PATIENT'S CONSENT AND WITH A CHAPERONE PRESENT. Is there a model available, or would you like me to ask you for the findings?' → 'ask me' → then ONE QUESTION AT A TIME, waiting for each answer: 'on inspection — is there any bleeding? ... Any discharge? ... Any rash or redness? ... Any lumps, swellings or prolapse?' (Firing all four as one sentence gets you stopped and told to slow down.)

Speculum and bimanual, by request: 'I'd like to proceed to a speculum examination. Looking at the vaginal walls — are they normal? And the cervix — is there any bleeding from the os, any discharge, any polyp or abnormal growth?' → normal → 'then a bimanual examination. Is there cervical motion tenderness? WHAT IS THE SIZE OF THE UTERUS, IS THE BORDER REGULAR, AND IS IT TENDER? And the adnexae — masses or tenderness?' → ten weeks, regular, non-tender, adnexae normal → THEN THE SENTENCE THAT PASSES THE STATION: 'AND BEDSIDE TESTS, PLEASE — A URINE PREGNANCY TEST.' → negative.

Explain, leading with the reassurance and then the honesty: 'first the good news — the pregnancy test is negative, so you're not pregnant. And your thyroid felt completely normal, which matters because an underactive or overactive thyroid is a common and treatable cause of heavy periods. What I did find is that your womb is bigger than I'd expect. With heavy periods as well, I'm thinking mainly about two things. The commonest is a benign growth in the womb, called a FIBROID. But I also have to consider a CANCER OF THE WOMB. I want to be honest with you: I CANNOT TELL THOSE TWO APART JUST BY FEELING, which is why I want a scan.' → 'cancer? At 35?' → 'fibroids are far more likely, especially with a family history, and cancer of the womb is uncommon at your age. But it isn't impossible, and the scan settles it.' Then the grouped list AND THE ANAEMIA: 'separately — losing this much blood every month, I'd expect your iron stores to be running low, and that's almost certainly why you've been tired.'

INVESTIGATIONS — four, said as four: 'one, an ultrasound — specifically a TRANSVAGINAL ultrasound, which gives a much better view of the womb and ovaries than scanning through the tummy. Two, blood for your full blood count and your FERRITIN, which is the best measure of your iron stores. Three, a blood pregnancy test to confirm the urine one. And four, your thyroid function.' → 'would you order a CA-125?' → 'NO. CA-125 isn't a screening test — it's neither sensitive nor specific enough, and it would be more likely to mislead us than help. The ultrasound is the right first test.' Then the safety-net: much heavier bleeding, faintness, dizziness or breathlessness means contact us straight away. Her hidden agenda, if you leave a gap: 'will I need my womb taken out? We wanted one more.'

CASE B — 54, hot flushes, nervousness, weight gain, LMP one year ago, family history of thyroid disease, and THE DIFFERENTIALS ARE ASKED FOR FIRST, before you touch her: 'the commonest cause at your age is the MENOPAUSE. I'd also think about an overactive thyroid, infections that cause months of sweats such as tuberculosis or HIV, cancers such as lymphoma, a rare adrenal tumour called a phaeochromocytoma, carcinoid syndrome, and medications such as some antidepressants.' The examination is normal APART FROM A TEN-WEEK UTERUS, and the closing is: 'the most likely cause of your flushes and irritability is the menopause, and your thyroid was normal today. But there's one thing I want to be open about: YOUR WOMB FELT LARGER THAN I'D EXPECT AFTER THE MENOPAUSE. It doesn't explain your symptoms, and I don't have an explanation for it — which is exactly why I'm not prepared to leave it. It may be a fibroid, but it can be a cancer of the womb, so I want a scan.'

Challenges: 'why did you ignore the weight gain?' → 'I didn't ignore it — I built my list around the flushing and the nervousness because those two share a differential list, and most of those differentials cause weight LOSS. The weight gain is the symptom that makes me want to image her.' / LIFELONG HEAVY PERIODS SINCE MENARCHE → 'if you've bled heavily since your very first period, I'd also want to check for an inherited bleeding disorder — VON WILLEBRAND DISEASE is the commonest and it is often missed for years.' / Menorrhagia is defined by IMPACT, not millilitres — flooding, clots, changing protection hourly, or restricting daily activity.

Exhausted, breathless on the stairs, occasionally dizzy standing. No thyroid symptoms, no neck swelling, no easy bruising, periods were normal until three months ago. HER MOTHER HAD FIBROIDS AND A HYSTERECTOMY AT 45 — given if asked about family history. Cervical screening two years ago normal. setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — general practice, manikin on the bed and the role-player in a chair across the room: talk to the man, examine the manikin, and narrate the turn between them. SIX WAYS TO FAIL IN ONE SENTENCE EACH: no chaperone offered; foreskin never retracted; cancer never named; only one testis examined; rough handling of the manikin; STI screen ordered without asking. And the safety sentence that must be said out loud: 'I CANNOT EXCLUDE A TESTICULAR CANCER ON EXAMINATION ALONE.'
stem: VERSION B (the lower pass rate): general practice. James Whitfield, 25, has come asking to be SCREENED FOR SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS. 8 minutes, no history asked for.

tasks: Perform a focused physical examination of the external genitalia and scrotum, with a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the further investigations you would arrange
time: THE ORDER OF MOVES AS A SINGLE STRING: consent, chaperone, privacy, stop signal, STAND, scrotum plus ELEVATE it, penis plus RETRACT the foreskin (and replace it), discharge with a squeeze of the tip, COUGH for a hernia, TEMPERATURE with the backs of the fingers both sides, testis one front-back-BORDER SWEEP, cord one, testis two front-back-border, cord two, CHARACTERISE, transilluminate, inguinal nodes, cremasteric BOTH sides, Prehn, cover-thank-wash, present, explain, differentials INCLUDING CANCER, ultrasound plus tumour markers plus STI SCREEN WITH ITS OWN CONSENT, safety-net · hold each testis between thumb in front and index and middle fingers behind, do NOT hold both at once, do NOT press hard, and do NOT try to stand the manikin up (it is heavy, it tips, and it has cost candidates three minutes) · if past 4:30 and still palpating, you will not finish.

back.dx: VERSION B — EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS, most likely secondary to a sexually transmitted infection, with an associated BALANITIS: warm left hemiscrotum, left testis about 25 mL against 15-20 on the right, a thick swollen epididymis in its normal position above and behind the testis, no nodularity, upper border palpable, transillumination NEGATIVE (solid, not fluid), cremasteric reflex present bilaterally, Prehn's sign POSITIVE, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, redness of the glans and inner foreskin. Differentials: TESTICULAR TUMOUR — which examination cannot exclude — mumps orchitis, scrotal abscess, hydrocele, epididymal cyst, varicocele, hernia, and torsion (against it: gradual onset over five days, cremasteric present, testis not high-riding or transverse, Prehn positive — but PREHN ALONE NEVER RULES OUT TORSION; if the story or position suggested it, theatre, not a scan). Investigations, three: scrotal ULTRASOUND; TUMOUR MARKERS — AFP, beta-hCG and LDH; and the FULL STI SCREEN WITH ITS OWN CONSENT — urine for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, bloods for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B and C. Treat today rather than waiting: antibiotics, analgesia, scrotal support, no sex until he and recent partners have completed treatment, contact tracing offered (can be anonymous), review 48-72 hours. VERSION A — a benign cystic lump of the cord: hydrocele of the cord, spermatocele or epididymal cyst — separate from the testis, upper border palpable, transilluminates — and you STILL want ultrasound and markers to exclude a tumour.
plan: The sensitive-examination opening, in full: 'I've been asked to examine you today. To explain what that involves — I'LL NEED TO EXAMINE YOUR PRIVATE PARTS. I'll look at your penis and your scrotum, feel each of your testicles gently, and at the end feel in your groin. Is that alright with you? I'll give you privacy to undress from the waist down and you can cover yourself with the sheet. WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT? If you feel uncomfortable at any point, or you want me to stop, just say so and I'll stop straight away. I'll wash my hands, and then we'll begin.' (If he declines a chaperone: 'that's fine, I'll document that I offered.')

Position and the three inspection boxes: 'James, COULD YOU STAND UP FOR ME, please, and expose the area. Examiner, on inspection of the scrotum — no redness, no swelling, no visible masses, no rashes, ulcers or sinuses. I'M LIFTING THE SCROTUM to see the under-surface — nothing there either. Moving to the penis — no rashes, ulcers or warts, meatus normal. I'M RETRACTING THE FORESKIN — examiner, there is redness of the glans and inner foreskin. I'll REPLACE the foreskin. James, could you SQUEEZE THE TIP OF THE PENIS for me — no discharge at the meatus. And could you give me a COUGH — no bulging mass in the scrotum or groin, so no clinical features of a hernia.' (Say 'stand' even if he does not move — the box is ticked by saying it. Never say 'asymmetry': the left normally hangs lower.)

PALPATION, both sides, before any conclusion: 'temperature first, with the backs of my fingers on each side — the left hemiscrotum is warmer than the right. Palpating the RIGHT testis, held between my thumb in front and index and middle fingers behind — front surface, back surface, AND SWEEPING THE THUMB AROUND THE BORDER. Normal size, smooth, no nodules. Steadying it, running up the right spermatic cord — normal. Now the left testis — front, back, border. And the left cord. James, tell me if this is uncomfortable at any point. EXAMINER, I HAVE NOW PALPATED BOTH TESTES AND BOTH CORDS. Let me characterise the abnormality on the left.' (Stopping the moment you find the big testis, skipping the border sweep, holding both testes at once, or pressing hard — candidates have failed on that alone.)

CHARACTERISE — where the marks are: 'the left testis is enlarged. Using the orchidometer it is about 25 millilitres, against 15 to 20 on the right. CONSISTENCY compared with the other side is the same — rubbery, not hard and stony. On the surface and around the border there is NO NODULARITY. I CAN FEEL THE UPPER BORDER, so this is a purely scrotal mass. There is a thick, swollen epididymis above and behind the testis, which is its normal anatomical position. I WANT TO BE CLEAR THAT I CANNOT EXCLUDE A TESTICULAR CANCER ON EXAMINATION ALONE.' → 'how would you quantify it with no orchidometer?' → 'I'd still commit to an estimate — around 25 millilitres — and quantify formally with an orchidometer if one were available.' (Never say 'there is no lump': THE TESTIS IS THE LUMP, and every characteristic still applies.)

The four special tests and closure: 'I'm shining a torch BESIDE the swelling — transillumination is negative, it stays dark, so this is solid rather than fluid. Palpating for inguinal lymph nodes — none. I'd add that THE TESTIS DRAINS TO THE PARA-AORTIC NODES, so normal inguinal nodes do not exclude a tumour. Cremasteric reflex — gentle stroke to the inner thigh, present on the right, AND present on the left. James, are you in any pain at the moment? I'm going to lift the scrotum gently. Is that any better?' → 'oh — yeah, that's better' → 'PREHN'S SIGN IS POSITIVE. Thank you James, you can cover up and get dressed; I'll wash my hands. To complete my assessment I would also examine the abdomen and the supraclavicular fossae.'

Present, then explain TO HIM: 'the left testicle is bigger than the right, and the tube behind it is swollen and tender. I think you have EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS — an infection and inflammation of the testicle and of that tube, which carries sperm away. There's some redness under the foreskin too, which fits the same picture.' Then the differentials in plain words, ending with the honesty: 'whenever I find a swollen testicle I keep TESTICULAR CANCER on my list until I've ruled it out. I don't think that's what this is — but I can't be certain just by feeling it, and it would be wrong of me to promise you otherwise.' (BOTH DIRECTIONS FAIL: leaving cancer out, and 'don't worry, it's definitely not cancer.')

His hidden agenda lands — 'my uncle had testicular cancer. He was thirty.' → 'thank you for telling me — that must make this a lot more frightening than it looks from the outside. That is exactly why I'm not going to guess.' Then the three investigations, WITH THE SECOND CONSENT: 'an ULTRASOUND of the scrotum. Blood tests called TUMOUR MARKERS — AFP, beta-hCG and LDH. And because you came in for a sexual health check and this infection is usually sexually transmitted, WITH YOUR CONSENT I'd like to do the full screen: a urine sample for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and bloods for HIV, syphilis and hepatitis. IS THAT ALRIGHT WITH YOU?' (Announcing the screen rather than asking loses a separately marked consent.)

Treatment and safety-net: 'I'll start you on antibiotics today rather than wait for results, with pain relief and a scrotal support. Please avoid sex until you and any recent partners have finished treatment, and I'll help you let them know — that can be done anonymously if you'd prefer. I'll see you again in two to three days. COME STRAIGHT BACK, or go to an emergency department, if the pain becomes suddenly severe, if you get a fever or feel unwell, or if the swelling is getting worse rather than better.' If asked who finds out about the HIV test: 'your results come to me and go in your record. Some infections are notified to the health department without your name attached, so they can be tracked. I'll always talk to you before anyone else is contacted' VERIFY notification rules.

VERSION A — THE CORD LUMP (60): 'in the left spermatic cord, ABOVE the testis, there is a lump of roughly one and a half centimetres. I CAN DIFFERENTIATE IT FROM THE TESTIS. I can feel its upper border. Smooth, no nodularity, rubbery, non-tender, and TRANSILLUMINATION IS POSITIVE — so it is fluid-filled.' To him: 'most likely this is a small collection of fluid alongside the cord that runs to your testicle. It could also be a cyst on the tube behind the testicle, or enlarged veins. I STILL WANT TO EXCLUDE A CANCER of the testicle, which is why I want a scan and blood tests.' / HARD, NODULAR TESTIS: 'the left testis is HARD AND STONY compared with the right, and I can feel a nodule on the lateral border. It does not transilluminate and I cannot separate it from the testis. THIS IS A TESTICULAR TUMOUR UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' To him: 'I've found something I'm not happy about, and I want to be straight with you... I'm arranging an urgent scan and blood tests today and I'll see you back with the results myself.'

HE REFUSES OR IS EMBARRASSED — 'do you really have to?' → 'I understand, and nothing happens without your say-so. The reason I'm asking is that a swelling in the scrotum can be a few different things, and some of them matter. Would it help if a chaperone were here, or if I explained each step as I go?' If he JOKES to cover it, acknowledge briefly and do not join in: 'it's an awkward one, I know. I'll be quick and I'll tell you what I'm doing as I go.' TORSION is the time-critical alternative: roughly a six-hour window, a CLINICAL diagnosis, straight to theatre — never wait for a scan.
pefe: Role-player: James Whitfield, 25, apprentice electrician in Kadina, sharing a house with two mates, seeing someone new for about six weeks; ten cigarettes a day, about ten standard drinks over a weekend, no medications or allergies. He booked saying he wanted a sexual health check — true — but has NOT led with the fact that for about FIVE DAYS the left side has ached (dull and dragging, not sharp) and looks bigger, with mild stinging on passing urine for a couple of days; no fever, no lump he can feel, no injury. Sexual history if asked: new female partner six weeks, condoms 'most of the time', previous relationship ended three months ago, no men, never tested before and embarrassed about it. HIDDEN AGENDA AND THE POINT OF THE STATION: HIS UNCLE HAD TESTICULAR CANCER AT THIRTY and he has thought about it every day for five days — it is the real reason he booked. If the doctor NAMES cancer, he goes quiet and then says it. If the doctor never names it and never asks what is worrying him, he says it flatly at about 6:30: 'doctor — my uncle had testicular cancer. Could this be that?' THEIR ANSWER TO THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST REVEALING THING IN THE STATION. IF THEY PROMISE HIM IT IS DEFINITELY NOT CANCER, HE LOOKS RELIEVED — AND MARKS THEM DOWN.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED. Three things are true of every sitting: THE PATIENT WILL REFUSE TO STAND OR WALK; the examiner will say 'normal' or 'skip' ten or more times and will sound impatient; and THE NYSTAGMUS FINDING IS ONLY GIVEN IF YOU ASK FOR IT BY NAME, often as a video on a device across the room. Say the framing sentence — inner ear, cerebellum, posterior circulation — before you touch him, ask for PAIN AND TEMPERATURE before cotton wool, and say NO HORNER SYNDROME three times. Explanation starts at 6:45 whatever is unfinished.
stem: Emergency Department, regional hospital. A 57-year-old man with GIDDINESS, NAUSEA and A BUZZING SOUND IN BOTH EARS; haemodynamically stable. Gloves at the bedside. 8 minutes, 2 minutes reading.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: GLOVES, WIPE, stability check and THE FRAMING SENTENCE ('because giddiness can arise from the inner ear, the cerebellum or the posterior circulation of the brain, I'm going to perform a cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, WITH A COMPLETE EAR EXAMINATION INSIDE CRANIAL NERVE EIGHT') · GENERAL APPEARANCE naming NO HORNER SYNDROME, then ATTEMPT gait and Romberg, be refused, and NARRATE THE OMISSION · CN I-VII: smell; optic (fundoscopy for papilloedema, pupils, acuity · and nothing else); III/IV/VI with the wide H and the words 'I AM SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR NYSTAGMUS'; V IN FOUR STEPS with PAIN ASKED FOR FIRST, then cotton wool, then masseter and temporalis, then JAW JERK AND CORNEAL REFLEX offered; VII · CN VIII IN FULL: inspect and palpate both ears including mastoid and pinna movement, offer otoscopy, then WHISPER (close, then arm's length), RINNE with a 512 Hz fork struck on your knee and the base on the mastoid, WEBER, then offer DIX-HALLPIKE · CN IX-XII, then RESTATE no Horner · LIMBS with PAIN AND TEMPERATURE REQUESTED BEFORE LIGHT TOUCH, then coordination · then diagnosis in lay words, ITEMISED reassurance, differentials BY SITE each with a reason, explicit exclusion of BPV, plan, driving and safety-net.

back.dx: ACUTE LABYRINTHITIS — giddiness, nausea and bilateral tinnitus after a head cold, with a horizontal nystagmus (fast phase left) and an otherwise entirely normal cranial nerve, limb and cerebellar examination. Explain it as: deep in the ear is a small organ that does two jobs — it hears, and it tells the brain which way up you are; it is inflamed, usually after a virus, so it sends the wrong balance signals. THE REASSURANCE MUST BE ITEMISED, naming each serious thing you looked for and the finding that argues against it. DIFFERENTIALS BY SITE, each with a reason: EAR — vestibular neuritis (but tinnitus puts the cochlea in it), Meniere disease (this is a single episode, not recurrent 20-minute-to-12-hour attacks with aural fullness), acoustic neuroma (usually gradual and unilateral); BRAIN — posterior circulation stroke, particularly lateral medullary/PICA (excluded by intact facial pain, normal corneal reflex and jaw jerk, no Horner and normal crossed pain and temperature), cerebellar or cerebellopontine angle tumour (normal fundoscopy, no cerebellar signs), multiple sclerosis; plus DRUGS — aminoglycosides, frusemide, high-dose aspirin — and B12 deficiency. NOT BPV: he has tinnitus and sustained nausea, and neither belongs to benign positional vertigo. Plan: antiemetic for a day or two only, because longer slows recovery; fluids and rest; formal audiometry; vestibular rehabilitation; NO DRIVING while symptomatic (he drives trucks — do not improvise a return-to-work date, and mention the duty to notify the licensing authority if he remains unfit); safety-net for a bad headache, weakness or numbness, slurred speech, double vision or a sudden drop in hearing. Imaging if any central feature appears: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, not plain CT, which is normal in most posterior fossa infarcts in the first hours.
plan: Gloves, WIPE, stability, and THE FRAMING SENTENCE: '...I've washed my hands and I've put gloves on. I'd like to examine you to work out what's causing the giddiness. I'll check some nerves in your face — your eyes, your facial movements and the feeling in your face — then look at your ears and test your hearing, and finally check the power, reflexes and sensation in your arms and legs. Is that alright? Are you in any pain at the moment? Examiner, may I confirm the observations are stable and the blood glucose is normal? And — BECAUSE GIDDINESS CAN ARISE FROM THE INNER EAR, THE CEREBELLUM OR THE POSTERIOR CIRCULATION OF THE BRAIN — I'm going to perform a cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, with a complete ear examination inside cranial nerve eight.'

General appearance, then ATTEMPT AND NARRATE: 'alert and orientated, looks unwell and is keeping very still. No abnormal limb postures, no facial asymmetry, and I CANNOT SEE A HORNER SYNDROME — there is no ptosis and no miosis. James, would you be able to stand up and walk a few steps for me?' → refused → 'that's fine. Could you at least stand still with your feet together, so I can check your balance?' → refused → 'Examiner, THE PATIENT IS UNABLE TO STAND OR WALK, so I am unable to assess his gait or perform Romberg's test, and I cannot obtain a lying and standing blood pressure. I'll note that and move on.' (Two opposite errors: not asking at all because the recalls told you he refuses — THE ASK IS THE MARK — and asking, being refused, then moving on silently, which the examiner records as an omission rather than an obstacle.)

CN I-VI, with the biggest trap in the station: smell; then 'for the optic nerve I'd like fundoscopy, looking particularly for PAPILLOEDEMA; then the pupils for size, symmetry and direct and consensual reaction — and again NO HORNER SYNDROME; then visual acuity.' (Nothing else — candidates who offer fields, colour vision and accommodation run out of time before the hearing tests, where the marks live.) Then the wide H: 'eye movements are full in all directions with no diplopia, AND I AM SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR NYSTAGMUS.' → you are walked to a laptop → COMMIT: 'I can see a HORIZONTAL nystagmus with the FAST PHASE TO THE LEFT. There is no vertical or rotatory component.' ('There's something there' scores nothing.)

CN V IN FOUR STEPS, pain first: 'I don't appear to have a neurological pin — MAY I HAVE THE PAIN SENSATION over the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions?' → normal → then cotton wool on forehead, cheek and jaw, left against right; then 'clench your teeth' with masseter and temporalis palpated and the jaw opening without deviation; then 'I would also like to test THE JAW JERK AND THE CORNEAL REFLEX.' Then VII: eyebrows, eyes shut, cheeks blown out, teeth — full and symmetrical. (Pain and temperature travel with the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the lateral medulla; light touch does not.)

CN VIII — THE COMPLETE EAR EXAMINATION: inspect and compare both ears (pinna, mastoid, discharge or blood), palpate helix, tragus and lobule, press over the mastoid, MOVE THE PINNA, then offer otoscopy. Then WHISPER: 'block your other ear with your finger. I'm going to whisper a number close to this ear — just repeat it back.' Ninety-nine close, sixty-six at arm's length, both ears. Then RINNE: 'I'm using a 512 HERTZ tuning fork... I'm going to put the bottom of it on the bone behind your ear — tell me the moment you stop hearing it. Then I'll hold it in front of your ear and you tell me whether you can hear it again.' Then WEBER on the forehead: 'louder on the left, louder on the right, or the same?' Then STATE THE RULE, THEN THE CONCLUSION — and offer DIX-HALLPIKE: 'head turned 45 degrees, dropped rapidly to supine with the head extended below the horizontal, watching the eyes for nystagmus for thirty to forty-five seconds.' (Omitting the whisper leaves you unable to interpret your own Rinne: air better than bone means either a normal ear OR a sensorineural loss. Findings are ROTATED within the same day — recite what the patient told you, not what you revised.)

CN IX-XII and the restatement: uvula central and palate rising, cough, 'say ahhh', gag offered but not performed, shoulder shrug, head turn against resistance both sides, tongue out with no deviation, wasting or fasciculation. Then: 'that completes the cranial nerves. TO RESTATE: THERE IS NO HORNER SYNDROME — no ptosis, no miosis and no reported loss of sweating on either side.'

THE LIMBS, with the sentence that saves the PICA variant: 'inspection, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination, upper then lower. FOR SENSATION I'D LIKE TO START WITH PAIN — I don't have a neurological pin, so may I have the pain sensation? And I don't have hot and cold tubes — MAY I HAVE THE TEMPERATURE SENSATION?' → normal all four limbs → 'thank you — that argues strongly against a lateral medullary infarct.' Then light touch, vibration and joint position, then finger-nose, rapid alternating movements and heel-shin: 'no past-pointing, no intention tremor, no dysdiadochokinesis, no cerebellar signs.' (In a lateral medullary infarct light touch, vibration and joint position are ALL normal — the only abnormality is crossed pain and temperature. Never ask, and that patient examines as normal.)

Diagnosis, itemised reassurance, differentials and safety-net (see dx). 'So it's not a stroke? My brother-in-law's stroke started with dizziness' → validate, then name each thing you checked. THE THIRTY-SECOND RESCUE if you are badly behind at six minutes: 'Examiner, in the interest of time I'll assume the remaining limb findings are normal — may I explain my diagnosis?' A complete examination with no explanation FAILS; a slightly abbreviated examination with a reasoned explanation PASSES.

ask: 'Because giddiness can come from the inner ear, the cerebellum or the posterior circulation of the brain, I'm going to do a cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, with a complete ear examination inside cranial nerve eight.' / 'I cannot see a Horner syndrome — there is no ptosis and no miosis.' / 'The patient is unable to stand or walk, so I cannot assess gait, Romberg or a lying and standing blood pressure — I'll note that and move on.'

'Eye movements are full in all directions, there is no diplopia, and I am specifically looking for nystagmus.' / 'I can see a horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase to the left; there is no vertical or rotatory component.' / 'I don't appear to have a neurological pin — may I have the pain sensation over the three trigeminal divisions?' / 'I would also like to test the jaw jerk and the corneal reflex.'

'Please block your other ear with your finger. I'll whisper a number close to this ear — just repeat it back.' / 'I'm using a 512 hertz tuning fork.' / 'Air conduction better than bone conduction means either a normal ear or a sensorineural loss — which is why I performed the whisper test.' / 'For sensation I'd like to start with pain, then temperature, then light touch, vibration and joint position.' / 'I do not think this is benign positional vertigo, because he has tinnitus and sustained nausea, and neither belongs to BPV.'

VARIANT B — THE PICA / LATERAL MEDULLARY VERSION. Examiner: 'pain sensation is absent over the left side of the face. The left corneal reflex is absent and the jaw jerk is absent. Light touch is normal.' → SAY IT IMMEDIATELY: 'that is a significant finding. Loss of pain sensation on the left face with an absent corneal reflex localises to the SPINAL TRIGEMINAL NUCLEUS IN THE LEFT LATERAL MEDULLA. I'd now like to look particularly carefully for HORNER SYNDROME on the left, and for PAIN AND TEMPERATURE LOSS ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE BODY.' → left ptosis and miosis, right-sided pain and temperature loss with normal vibration and joint position → 'this is a CROSSED SENSORY DEFICIT — that is a left lateral medullary or WALLENBERG syndrome, from occlusion of the left PICA or vertebral artery. Immediate management: stroke call, urgent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging rather than plain CT, SWALLOW SCREEN BEFORE ANYTHING BY MOUTH because dysphagia is prominent, blood glucose, ECG for atrial fibrillation, and admission to a stroke unit. From a rural site I would activate MedSTAR retrieval on 1300 13 12 33. I'd also ask about recent neck trauma or manipulation, because vertebral artery dissection is the commonest cause in a younger patient.'

VARIANT C — CONDUCTIVE LOSS (whisper fails on the left, Rinne bone better than air on the left, Weber lateralises left): interpret it cleanly and do not panic — 'both findings indicate a CONDUCTIVE hearing loss in the left ear. Given the drum is reported normal and there was no mastoid tenderness, I'd want otoscopy and formal audiometry.' If challenged that labyrinthitis is an inner ear condition: 'I accept it classically produces a sensorineural pattern... either way the hearing finding here is SUPPORTIVE rather than diagnostic — my diagnosis rests on the symptom cluster with an otherwise normal neurological examination. If you'd prefer, I'm happy to call it an acute vestibular syndrome with auditory involvement and confirm the type of loss with audiometry.' / VARIANT D — VERTIGO AND TINNITUS WITH NO NAUSEA: 'the absence of nausea makes an acute inflammatory labyrinthitis less likely, because nausea is near-universal in an acute vestibular syndrome. I would put ACOUSTIC NEUROMA higher — unilateral tinnitus, sensorineural loss and unsteadiness rather than violent spinning — and the diagnostic test is MRI of the internal auditory meati with gadolinium.'
pefe: Role-player: James Whitfield, 57, LONG-HAUL TRUCK DRIVER, married, lives two hours from the city; 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years, four to six beers on a Friday; perindopril and atorvastatin with patchy compliance; A HEAD COLD ABOUT TEN DAYS AGO. Woke yesterday morning with the room spinning, has vomited four times, is pale and clammy and holds very still because any head movement makes it worse, and has a constant high-pitched buzzing in BOTH ears. Short answers, volunteers nothing. HE REFUSES TO STAND OR WALK, twice, politely — 'I can't. I'm too unwell' — and does not explain unless asked why. HIDDEN AGENDA: his brother-in-law had a stroke last year that began with dizziness, and he is frightened this is the same; raised only if asked about his concerns, or at about 6:30 regardless: 'doctor — is this a stroke?' SECOND HIDDEN AGENDA: he drives trucks for a living, mentioned only if asked what he does or if driving is raised. He becomes visibly relieved if the reassurance is ITEMISED, and stays anxious at a bare 'nothing serious'.

How the partner plays the EXAMINER: impatient, interrupting with 'normal' before the candidate finishes the sentence at least five times, not smiling. GIVE THE NYSTAGMUS ONLY IF THE WORD IS SAID — then beckon them to a laptop or describe a horizontal nystagmus with the fast phase left; if the word is never said, GIVE NOTHING. Everything else: observations and BSL stable and normal; fundoscopy normal; pupils normal, skip; acuity normal, don't do it; fields and colour vision 'not needed, move on'; facial pain normal both sides; jaw jerk and corneal reflex both normal; no otoscope, assume the drums are normal; Dix-Hallpike 'too unwell, take it as normal'; limb inspection, tone, power and reflexes normal in rapid fire; limb pain and temperature normal in all four limbs; light touch, vibration, joint position and coordination normal. End probes: 'why not benign positional vertigo?' — 'what is the one diagnosis you must not miss?' — 'what imaging?' — 'would you let him drive?'

Numbers: 512 Hz tuning fork; whisper close then one arm's length; DIX-HALLPIKE head 45 degrees, extended 20-30 degrees below horizontal, watch 30-45 seconds, and a positive test shows latency, torsional nystagmus, under a minute, and fatigues; Meniere attacks 20 minutes to 12 hours; prochlorperazine 5-10 mg oral 8-hourly or 12.5 mg IM, metoclopramide 10 mg, VESTIBULAR SEDATIVES FOR A MAXIMUM OF ABOUT 3 DAYS; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; station 8 minutes with the explanation starting at 6:45. Pass mark 13/20, with starred items: saying nystagmus unprompted and describing it, asking for facial pain sensation, offering jaw jerk and corneal reflex, stating no Horner syndrome, asking for limb pain and temperature before light touch, and explicitly excluding BPV and central causes.
fails: ★ Never saying the word NYSTAGMUS — the finding is only given if you ask for it by name, and it is the only abnormality in the station

★ Reaching for cotton wool first and never asking for PAIN AND TEMPERATURE — in a lateral medullary infarct everything else is normal, so that patient examines as normal and you confidently give the wrong diagnosis
Not attempting gait and Romberg because the recalls say he refuses — the ask is the mark; or being refused and moving on silently, so it is recorded as an omission rather than an obstacle

Omitting the whisper test, which leaves you unable to interpret your own Rinne; giving instructions while the fork is ringing, or striking it on a table or metal rail; reciting the findings you revised rather than the ones the patient gave you

Turning the optic nerve into an ophthalmology station and running out of time before the hearing tests; blanket reassurance instead of ITEMISED reassurance; a differential list with no reasons; forgetting the safety-net and the driving advice in a man who drives trucks

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional SA general practice. TWO PHASES, PLANNED BEFORE YOU ENTER: chair, gait, standing inspection — then COUCH for everything else, because Buerger's cannot be done in a chair and attempting it there is remembered. THE HARD RULE: special tests begin at 4:20 whatever is unfinished. PRESENT PULSES ARE NOT REASSURANCE — mild disease has palpable pulses — and the examiner will be silent until you ask for the ABI, which is the only objective abnormality in the station and is marked on what you DO with it.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Mr Ronald Whitmore, 68, with pain in BOTH legs coming on after about 200 metres and settling when he stops, worse over six months; 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years. BP 148/86 — HR 78 — RR 16 — SpO2 97% RA — T 36.7 — BGL 5.4. 8 minutes.
VERSION B is word-for-word identical except he is 52 with twelve years of type 2 diabetes, and there is COTTON WOOL AND A NEUROTIP on the trolley.
tasks: Perform the relevant physical examination, with a running commentary
Ask the examiner for any bedside investigation you would like
Explain your most likely diagnosis to the patient in plain language
Give your differential diagnoses to the examiner
time: WIPE and exposure IN UNDER 40 SECONDS · he is in shorts and will not undress further, so ask ONCE and say 'ideally I'd expose to the groin · I'll work with what we have' · DECLARE THE STRUCTURE: 'the history is pain on walking relieved by rest, so I'm treating this as claudication. I'll look for the two big causes, VASCULAR AND NEUROGENIC, and finish with my special tests' · GENERAL APPEARANCE, then WALK HIM and INTERPRET THE GAIT OUT LOUD (relief by standing still points vascular, not neurogenic) · INSPECTION IN TWO NAMED LISTS while he stands: ARTERIAL (pallor, hyperpigmentation as a venous marker, shiny atrophic skin, hair loss, ulcers, gangrene) and NEUROPATHIC (clawed toes, bunion, varus/valgus, rocker-bottom Charcot foot, ulceration over the metatarsal heads, wasting) · ONTO THE COUCH: PALPATION IN FOUR NAMED STEPS · temperature at FOUR levels looking for a DROP distally, capillary refill at both great toes, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis, then brief tenderness · MOVEMENT kept deliberately brief WITH THE ANNOUNCEMENT that saves the station · THE THREE B's: BUERGER'S (raise, wait for pallor, name the angle, then hang for reactive hyperaemia), then the femoral BRUIT at ONE site, then the ankle-BRACHIAL index · INTERPRET THE ABI UNPROMPTED · then plain-language explanation, one-sentence answers to his fears, and four GROUPED differentials.

back.dx: BILATERAL PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE — intermittent claudication: a fixed, reproducible 200-metre distance worsening over six months in a 45-pack-year smoker, relieved by STANDING STILL, with hair loss over the shins, otherwise normal legs, PRESENT distal pulses, negative Buerger's, no femoral bruit, and an ABI of 0.7 on the left and 0.9 on the right — mild-to-moderate disease, worse on the left, entirely consistent with palpable pulses. DIFFERENTIALS IN FOUR GROUPS, each with a discriminator: VASCULAR — PAD (most likely), chronic venous insufficiency, acute limb ischaemia (no sudden onset, no pallor, pulselessness or paralysis); NEUROGENIC — lumbar canal stenosis and radiculopathy, less likely because the distance is fixed and reproducible and he is relieved by standing still rather than sitting or leaning forward; JOINT AND SOFT TISSUE — osteoarthritis, inflammatory or gouty arthritis, tendinopathy, bursitis, chondromalacia, all less likely with no tenderness, no swelling and full pain-free movement; OTHER — diabetic peripheral neuropathy in a diabetic, and cauda equina never to be missed in anyone with bilateral leg symptoms, bladder or bowel change or saddle anaesthesia. Management: SMOKING CESSATION as the single most powerful intervention (Quitline 13 7848), SUPERVISED EXERCISE — walking through the discomfort, 30-45 minutes at least three times a week for at least twelve weeks — an antiplatelet (aspirin 100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg) and a statin (atorvastatin 40-80 mg nocte), foot care and podiatry, with arterial duplex to confirm. Safety-net: pain at rest or at night, a sore that will not heal, or a toe changing colour means urgent review.
plan: WIPE, exposure in under 40 seconds, and the structure declared: '...I've been asked to examine your legs today. I'll look at them, then feel them, then ask you to move them, and at the end I'll do a few special tests. It shouldn't be painful, but please tell me if anything hurts. To examine properly I need your legs uncovered from the groin down — is that alright?' → 'I've got shorts on, that's as far as I go' → 'that's absolutely fine. IDEALLY I'D EXPOSE TO THE GROIN; I'll work with what we have.' Then: 'Examiner, the history is pain on walking relieved by rest, so I'm treating this as CLAUDICATION. I'll perform a lower limb examination looking for the two big causes — VASCULAR AND NEUROGENIC — and I'll finish with my special tests.' (You will get silence or a nod. SILENCE IS NOT DISAPPROVAL — candidates who read it as 'I'm doing this wrong' change structure mid-station.)

General appearance and THE GAIT, interpreted out loud: 'alert and comfortable at rest, not in pain, no protective posture and no walking aids. Ron, could you stand and walk a few steps towards the door and back for me? Stop if the pain comes on.' → he walks normally → 'thank you — he bears weight fully on both legs and there is no antalgic gait over this short distance. THAT FITS HIS HISTORY: the pain only appears after a couple of hundred metres, and it settles when he STANDS STILL, which points to a VASCULAR rather than a NEUROGENIC cause.' (Picking that clue up out loud is worth a mark.)

INSPECTION IN TWO NAMED LISTS, while he is standing: 'looking for ARTERIAL DISEASE — no pallor of the feet; no hyperpigmentation, which would suggest venous rather than arterial disease; the skin is not shiny or atrophic; there is some HAIR LOSS over the lower shins; no ulcers on the dorsum, and I'll check the soles when he lies down; no gangrene. Looking for NEUROPATHY — no clawing of the toes, no bunion, no varus or valgus deformity, no rocker-bottom Charcot foot, no ulceration over the metatarsal heads, no wasting. Generally no swelling, redness, rash, bruising or scars, and the legs are symmetrical.' (If the legs are hairy, say 'hair distribution is preserved' — a legitimate negative, and examiners notice honesty.)

ONTO THE COUCH, then PALPATION SAID AS FOUR STEPS: 'temperature — backs of my fingers at FOUR LEVELS, mid-thigh, knee, shin, ankle, comparing sides; I'm looking for A DROP DISTALLY, a cold clammy foot. Warm and symmetrical. Capillary refill at both big toes — under two seconds. Pulses — posterior tibial behind each medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis on the mid-dorsum LATERAL TO THE EXTENSOR HALLUCIS LONGUS TENDON. Tenderness — brief sweep of ankles and knees, non-tender, calves soft.' → 'as you can feel on the patient' → 'thank you — both distal pulses present and symmetrical. I'LL NOTE THAT PRESENT PULSES DO NOT EXCLUDE MILD ARTERIAL DISEASE — I'll need the ankle-brachial index.' (Concluding 'vascular causes are unlikely' here has already failed the station.)

Movement, and THE ANNOUNCEMENT that saves the station: 'point your feet up towards you and then down. Any pain? Now bend and straighten each knee. And bring each knee up towards your chest. Active movements at the ankles, knees and hips are full and pain-free. EXAMINER, IN THE INTEREST OF TIME I'VE KEPT MY JOINT PALPATION AND RANGE OF MOVEMENT BRIEF, BECAUSE THE STEM DESCRIBES CLAUDICATION RATHER THAN JOINT PAIN. I'd now like to move to the special tests that will make the diagnosis.' (The full hip-knee-ankle joint survey is what eats Buerger's.)

THE THREE B's: 'BUERGER'S — I'm passively raising the leg and holding it, waiting for the foot to become pale; the angle at which that happens is the BUERGER'S ANGLE, and below 20 degrees would indicate severe ischaemia. No pallor at 90 degrees. Now hanging the leg over the edge of the couch, looking for REACTIVE HYPERAEMIA — a dusky red flush. None. Buerger's is negative. Given this is bilateral, and for time, I've demonstrated on the left; the findings would apply to both. Now a femoral BRUIT — diaphragm at the mid-inguinal point, each side in turn. No bruit audible.' (Auscultate one bruit site, not four. You will be told nothing — do not wait, do not repeat the request.)

THE BEDSIDE TEST AND ITS INTERPRETATION: 'Examiner, I'd like to measure the ANKLE-BRACHIAL INDEX in both legs — the higher ankle Doppler pressure divided by the higher brachial pressure.' → 'left 0.7, right 0.9' → INTERPRET IMMEDIATELY AND UNPROMPTED: 'thank you. A NORMAL ANKLE-BRACHIAL INDEX IS 0.91 TO 1.30. A value of 0.7 on the left and 0.9 on the right places him in the MILD-TO-MODERATE range and confirms peripheral arterial disease, worse on the left. That is entirely consistent with palpable pulses.' (Quoting 'normal is 0.9 to 1.0' invites the follow-up about a diabetic with an ABI of 1.4.)

Explain in plain language, sitting at eye level: 'the blood is carried to your leg muscles through pipes called arteries. Over many years, smoking has furred up and NARROWED those pipes. When you sit still your muscles get enough blood. When you walk, they need much more — and the narrowed pipes can't deliver it, so the muscle cramps. That's why the pain comes on after a couple of hundred metres and goes away when you stop. The name is PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE. The most powerful thing in the world for it is STOPPING SMOKING — I can help you with that. Walking regularly, even through the discomfort, actually opens up smaller vessels and lengthens the distance you can manage. And I'd start a blood-thinning tablet and a cholesterol tablet to protect your heart and brain as well as your legs.' Then ONE-SENTENCE answers, not a counselling consultation: 'will I lose my leg?' → 'at this stage no — your circulation is only mildly reduced and your feet look healthy. The risk rises if the smoking continues, which is exactly why I want to act now.' 'Should I rest it?' → 'the opposite — supervised walking is the single most effective treatment.' 'I've failed at quitting' → 'most people need several attempts; that's normal. Patches, tablets, and Quitline on 13 7848.'

The four grouped differentials in 40 seconds (see dx), then the safety-net: 'come back straight away if the pain starts at rest or at night, or if a sore won't heal or a toe changes colour — that means the circulation has worsened and you need to be seen urgently.' Summarise for the examiner with the ABI and the plan: arterial duplex, smoking cessation, supervised exercise, antiplatelet and statin.

VERSION B — THE DIABETIC MIXED CASE: at about 6:10, after interpreting the ABI, 'because this patient has diabetes I'd also like a brief SENSORY examination of the lower limbs. This is cotton wool — I'll touch it on your forehead so you know what it feels like. Now close your eyes and say yes every time you feel it.' → yes at groin (L1), mid-thigh (L2) and anterior knee (L3); SILENCE at the medial malleolus (L4), dorsum (L5) and lateral foot and sole (S1) → say it immediately: 'there is sensory loss at L4, L5 and S1 bilaterally, so I'd like to FIND THE SENSORY LEVEL' → work up from the toe until 'yes' → 'I've found a sensory level in the lower shin.' Then the TWO-DIAGNOSIS explanation: 'two things have been going on in your legs, and they have the same two causes — your smoking and your sugar levels. The pipes have narrowed, which is why they cramp when you walk. And the high sugars have damaged the nerves in your feet, so the feeling has been dulled — which matters because you can injure your foot and not feel it.' Daily foot checks, proper shoes, never barefoot, podiatry and a high-risk foot service. TRAPS: choosing BOTH the cotton wool and the neurotip (there is time for one — pick one and do it properly), and finding the sensory loss but still giving only one diagnosis.

THE OLD SEVERE-DISEASE FORMAT, if the examiner starts giving findings: 'the distal pulses are absent' → 'thank you — absent distal pulses significantly raise my suspicion of PAD. I'll take that as absent and move to my special tests rather than checking further pulses.' 'There is a femoral bruit' → 'turbulent flow through a stenosed vessel, supporting proximal aorto-iliac or femoral disease.' 'Buerger's is positive' → 'pallor on elevation with reactive hyperaemia on dependency indicates significant arterial insufficiency.' 'The ABI is 0.35' → 'that is under 0.40, which is SEVERE disease. Together with rest pain, this is CRITICAL LIMB-THREATENING ISCHAEMIA and needs same-day vascular surgical assessment, not an outpatient referral.' Patient adds 'it wakes me at night and I hang my leg out of bed' → that is ISCHAEMIC REST PAIN, and he needs to be seen today. Rural disposition: vascular surgery is in Adelaide — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval in critical or acute limb ischaemia; PATS for routine travel; Country Health Connect for community nursing; ACCHS and Closing the Gap co-payment for the aspirin and statin; TIS 131 450 for an interpreter.
pefe: Role-player: Ron Whitmore, 68, retired grain handler in Wallaroo, widowed, lives alone, drives; 25 a day since 23, two failed patch attempts lasting three weeks each; six or seven beers on a Friday; perindopril 5 mg most days; no diabetes, heart disease or stroke. HIS LEGS ARE NORMAL TO LOOK AT AND TO TOUCH — whatever is tested, there is nothing to find. He starts flat and slightly dismissive (his daughter nagged him into coming) but cooperates fully and moves without being told twice. HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS FATHER HAD A LEG AMPUTATED IN HIS SEVENTIES and he is frightened of the same — never told a doctor, given only if asked about concerns, otherwise volunteered the moment the diagnosis is said: 'am I going to lose the leg? My father had his off.' Then he goes quiet and waits. HE ALSO PLAYS THE EXAMINER, silent throughout with exactly two lines: at the foot pulses, 'as you can feel on the patient' (= present); and ONLY when asked for the ankle-brachial index, 'left 0.7, right 0.9'. Anything else — bruits, Buerger's, Doppler — 'whatever you find on the patient.' If asked for a proximal pulse after the distal ones: 'take the distal pulses as present. Please move on.' TWO PUSH POINTS: when told to expose, 'I've got shorts on, that's as far as I go' — see whether they waste time; and after the walk, if they do not comment, 'was that alright?' — see whether they interpret the gait.

History he gives if asked: both calves, tight like a cramp; about 200 metres, 'you could set your watch by it'; used to be a kilometre; relieved by STANDING STILL for a minute or two, NOT by sitting or bending forward; much worse uphill; no rest or night pain; no ulcers; no numbness or pins and needles (Version B: 'my feet feel a bit dead sometimes'); no back, bladder or bowel symptoms.

Numbers: ABI over 1.30 non-compressible, 0.91-1.30 normal, 0.41-0.90 mild-moderate, 0.40 or less severe — in this station left 0.7, right 0.9. Buerger's angle normal to 90 degrees; pallor under 20 degrees is severe. Capillary refill under 2 seconds; temperature at FOUR levels. Posterior tibial 2 cm below and behind the medial malleolus. Claudication distance 200 m, fixed, worsening over 6 months. Exercise therapy 30-45 minutes at least three times a week for at least twelve weeks. Aspirin 100 mg daily or clopidogrel 75 mg daily; atorvastatin 40-80 mg nocte. Dermatomes L1 groin, L2 mid-thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot. Quitline 13 7848, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. CLOCK: SPECIAL TESTS BEGIN AT 4:20.

Under 2 seconds at both great toes
PRESENT and symmetrical — which does NOT exclude mild disease
NEGATIVE — no pallor at 90 degrees, no reactive hyperaemia
LEFT 0.7 · RIGHT 0.9 — mild-to-moderate disease, worse on the left
Loss at L4, L5 and S1 bilaterally with a level in the LOWER SHIN

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional ED, red colouring on the left shin. ASK FOR THE VITAL SIGNS BEFORE YOU CROSS THE ROOM, and the marks are the WORDS 'FEBRILE BUT NOT SEPTIC', not the figures. THIS IS A MIXED CASE BY DESIGN: cellulitis PLUS the second diagnosis the stem planted — diabetes in Version A, an absent dorsalis pedis in Version B — so a single-diagnosis explanation is a half-answer however fluent. Automatic fails: never palpating the rash itself; never asking for the lymph nodes; finishing with one diagnosis and the cotton wool untouched.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia. Mr Daniel Rowe, 45, with a painful left leg THREE DAYS AFTER SCRATCHING IT WHILE GARDENING; history of TYPE 2 DIABETES. Red colouring applied to the left shin between knee and ankle; on the trolley a stethoscope, COTTON WOOL and a NEUROTIP. 8 minutes.
VERSION B (2023) is identical except there is no diabetes — and when you palpate the dorsalis pedis the examiner volunteers 'ABSENT'. That version is cellulitis plus peripheral arterial disease.
tasks: Perform the relevant physical examination, with a running commentary
Ask the examiner for any observations or bedside tests you require
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Give your differentials to the examiner
time: VITAL SIGNS FIRST, with the reason ('cellulitis can progress to sepsis, and the temperature will also support the diagnosis'), then INTERPRET THEM UNPROMPTED · WIPE and declare the structure: focused on the rash, screening for a NECROTISING infection, and checking the joints and lymph nodes · GENERAL APPEARANCE aimed at sepsis (alert, not drowsy or confused, no rigors, no dehydration) and gait · INSPECT THE RASH IN FIVE PARTS: SITE (with dimensions and laterality), COLOUR (and that you would confirm it BLANCHES), PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY (flat and over a centimetre = a PATCH), SECONDARY MORPHOLOGY (no bullae, erosions, discharge, scratch marks or punctum), BORDERS (poorly defined, favouring cellulitis over erysipelas) · PALPATION IN FOUR STEPS AIMED AT THE RASH: local rise in temperature compared with the same level on the other leg, capillary refill, BOTH pulses (never deleted 'because it's only cellulitis' · that is where the 2023 station hid its second diagnosis), then PRESS THE RASH GENTLY · MOVEMENT of the joints either side only, to exclude septic arthritis · SPECIAL TEST ONE, THE INGUINAL NODES, asked EARLY at about 4:40 so a refusal costs nothing · SPECIAL TEST TWO, chosen by THE STEM not by you · then bedside tests, a TWO-DIAGNOSIS explanation and three grouped differentials.

back.dx: CELLULITIS of the left lower leg PLUS the planted second diagnosis. VERSION A — DIABETIC SENSORY NEUROPATHY: febrile at 38.5 but not septic; a tender, warm, poorly demarcated erythematous patch about 12 x 8 cm; no features of necrotising infection; present distal pulses; full pain-free adjacent joint movement; a reactive left inguinal node; and sensory loss at L4, L5 and S1 with a level in the lower shin — which is WHY it happened: he did not feel the scratch. VERSION B — PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE: absent dorsalis pedis, positive Buerger's, femoral bruit — 'that combination matters because the reduced blood supply will slow healing, so as well as antibiotics I'd want an ankle-brachial index and a vascular surgical opinion — AND I WOULD NOT APPLY COMPRESSION TO THIS LEG.' DIFFERENTIALS IN THREE GROUPS: INFECTIVE — cellulitis (most likely), erysipelas (border poorly defined rather than sharply demarcated), abscess (no fluctuance), septic arthritis (full pain-free movement), and NECROTISING FASCIITIS, actively screened for and excluded — no pain out of proportion, no crepitus, no bullae, no dusky skin, sensation intact; VASCULAR — DVT (less likely with demarcated erythema and fever), venous eczema and lipodermatosclerosis (this is unilateral, acute and painful rather than chronic and itchy), and PAD; OTHER — gout or pseudogout, ruptured Baker's cyst, contact dermatitis, insect bite, trauma or haematoma — plus diabetic neuropathy, osteomyelitis and Charcot neuroarthropathy in a diabetic. Plan: bloods and glucose, FLUCLOXACILLIN 500 mg orally six-hourly for five days (cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity; 2 g IV six-hourly if severe VERIFY), MARK THE BORDER and note the time, elevate, review at 48 hours, podiatry and high-risk foot clinic.
plan: OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU CROSS THE ROOM: 'Examiner, before I examine him, may I have the vital signs — temperature, blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation? CELLULITIS CAN PROGRESS TO SEPSIS, and the temperature will also support the diagnosis.' → 38.5, 110/70, 88, 16, 98% → INTERPRET UNPROMPTED: 'thank you. HE IS FEBRILE, which supports an infective cause, BUT HE IS HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE WITH NO FEATURES OF SEPSIS at this point. I'll keep monitoring him.'

WIPE and structure: '...I've been asked to examine your leg. I'll look at it, feel it, ask you to move it, and do a couple of extra tests at the end. I KNOW IT'S SORE — tell me the moment anything hurts and I'll stop. I need both legs uncovered from the groin down. Examiner, I'll perform a lower limb examination focused on the rash, looking for features of cellulitis, SCREENING FOR A NECROTISING INFECTION, and checking the joints and lymph nodes.' Then general appearance aimed at sepsis: 'alert and orientated, NOT DROWSY OR CONFUSED, which is reassuring against sepsis; in some discomfort but not distressed; no rigors and no clinical dehydration — lips and tongue are moist. Danny, could you walk a few steps? — he bears weight, with a mildly antalgic gait on the left.'

THE RASH IN FIVE PARTS, in order: 'SITE — a lesion on the anterior aspect of the left lower leg, between knee and ankle, roughly 12 by 8 centimetres, unilateral. COLOUR — erythematous, dark red, and I would want to confirm IT BLANCHES. PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY — flat and larger than a centimetre, so it is A PATCH. SECONDARY MORPHOLOGY — no blisters or bullae, no erosions or ulceration, no discharge or pus, no scratch marks, so it is painful rather than itchy, and no punctum to suggest a bite, although there may be a small break in the skin as the entry point. BORDERS — poorly defined, merging into normal skin, FAVOURING CELLULITIS OVER ERYSIPELAS, with surrounding swelling. The right leg is normal.' → 'it came up overnight and it's spreading' → 'thank you — a rash that has spread over three days fits cellulitis; a rash spreading over HOURS would worry me about a much more serious infection.' ('I can see a red rash' describes a colour, not a lesion. If you say one extra word, make it PATCH.)

PALPATION IN FOUR STEPS, AIMED AT THE RASH: 'temperature — backs of my fingers ON THE RASH, compared with the same level on the right leg; I'm looking for a LOCAL RISE, and the affected area is clearly warmer. Capillary refill at both big toes — under two seconds. Pulses — posterior tibial behind each medial malleolus; dorsalis pedis lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. Tenderness — Danny, I'm going to press VERY GENTLY on the red area; tell me if it hurts.' → he winces → 'thank you, I'll be gentle. Tender to light palpation, consistent with infection. And the joints above and below — the knee and ankle are non-tender.' (Two failures live here: palpating ASIS, iliac crest, joint lines and popliteal fossa and NEVER PRESSING THE RASH; and deleting the pulses 'because it's only cellulitis', which is exactly where the 2023 station hid its second diagnosis.)

Movement of the adjacent joints ONLY, thirty seconds: 'because this is an infective process I want to check the joints closest to it for spread. Bend and straighten your left knee — any pain? And point your foot up and down, and turn it in and out. Active movements at the left knee and ankle are full and pain-free with no joint swelling or effusion, SO I HAVE NO EVIDENCE OF SEPTIC ARTHRITIS.' (Rash on the shin means knee and ankle; rash on the thigh means hip and knee. All six joints on both legs is the error.)

SPECIAL TEST ONE — THE INGUINAL NODES, the single most common omission: 'Examiner, given I am thinking about a soft-tissue infection, I would like to examine the inguinal lymph nodes on the affected side. Danny, I need to press just at the top of your leg, in the groin — is that alright?' → 'a single tender mobile node on the left' → CHARACTERISE IT: 'a tender, mobile node is REACTIVE, consistent with infection — hard, fixed or matted would make me think of malignancy.' (Ask early; even a refusal earns the mark.)

SPECIAL TEST TWO — THE STEM DECIDES. Version A, diabetes: 'because this patient has diabetes I'd like a brief sensory examination. This is cotton wool — I'll touch it on your forehead so you know the feeling. Now close your eyes and say yes each time you feel it.' → yes at groin, mid-thigh and knee; SILENCE at medial malleolus, dorsum and sole → 'sensory loss at L4, L5 and S1 bilaterally' → then walk proximally from the toe until 'yes' → 'I've found a SENSORY LEVEL IN THE LOWER SHIN.' Version B, absent pulse: 'thank you — I'll take that as an absent dorsalis pedis. Rather than working proximally through the popliteal and femoral pulses, I'd like to add BUERGER'S TEST and listen for a FEMORAL BRUIT.' (And do not get so excited by the absent pulse that you abandon the cellulitis — you still owe the nodes, the joints and the infective diagnosis.) Bedside tests: 'a capillary blood glucose and ketones; I'd look between the toes for TINEA as a portal of entry; and in practice I would MARK THE BORDER of the erythema and note the time — though I won't mark the patient here.'

THE TWO-DIAGNOSIS EXPLANATION, sitting at eye level: 'two things, and they're linked. First, when you scratched your leg, bacteria got in under the skin and you've developed an infection in the deeper layers — that's the redness, heat, swelling and pain, and why you have a temperature. It's called CELLULITIS and it responds well to antibiotics. Second — and this is WHY it happened — your diabetes has damaged the feeling nerves in your feet and legs. When I tested you just now you couldn't feel the cotton wool below your shin. That means you can injure yourself and not notice, so small things become big things.' Then: antibiotic tablets, elevate the leg, mark the redness, review in two days, podiatrist and high-risk foot clinic, daily foot checks, proper shoes, never barefoot even in the garden. Safety-net: 'come back sooner if the redness spreads past the line, if you get fevers or shivers, if you feel unwell, or IF THE PAIN BECOMES MUCH WORSE THAN THE LEG LOOKS.' One-sentence answers: 'will I lose the leg?' → 'no — this is an infection we can treat with tablets. What protects the leg long term is looking after the nerve damage.' 'Do I need admission?' → 'not at the moment — you're stable and it's localised.' 'I never felt the scratch' → 'that's exactly the nerve damage I mentioned, and it's the most important thing we found today.'

The three grouped differentials in 40 seconds (see dx), then the summary with the plan. IF THE OBSERVATIONS CHANGE MID-STATION — BP 88/50, pulse 126, RR 28, confused, dusky patches and a blister, pain far worse than it looks — ABANDON THE ROUTINE EXAMINATION: 'Examiner, I'm going to stop my examination. This patient is now SEPTIC and I am concerned about a NECROTISING SOFT-TISSUE INFECTION — pain out of proportion, dusky skin and a bulla, with haemodynamic instability. I'd call for help, two large-bore cannulas, blood cultures, lactate and a venous gas, a fluid bolus, high-flow oxygen, and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics WITHIN THE HOUR. Most importantly this is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY — I'd speak to the surgical registrar immediately about urgent debridement rather than waiting for imaging, and contact MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval advice IN PARALLEL, not afterwards.'
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run, Version A
ask: 'Examiner, may I have the vital signs before I examine him?' / 'He is febrile, but haemodynamically stable with no features of sepsis.' / 'I know it's sore — tell me the moment anything hurts and I'll stop.' / 'It is flat and larger than a centimetre, so it is a patch.' / 'I'd want to confirm that it blanches.'

'No blisters, no erosion or ulceration, no discharge, no scratch marks, no punctum.' / 'The border is poorly defined and merges into normal skin, favouring cellulitis over erysipelas.' / 'I'm looking for a local rise in temperature over the rash.' / 'Tender to light palpation, consistent with infection.' / 'Because this is an infective process I'll check the joints closest to it for spread.'

'Given I am thinking about a soft-tissue infection, I'd like to examine the inguinal lymph nodes.' / 'Tender and mobile is reactive; hard, fixed or matted would make me think of malignancy.' / 'No pain out of proportion, no crepitus, no bullae, no dusky skin, sensation intact — no features of a necrotising infection.' / 'Bacteria got in under the skin and you've developed an infection in the deeper layers.' / 'Come back if it spreads past the line, if you get fevers, or if the pain becomes much worse than the leg looks.'

VERSION B — THE 2023 CASE, no diabetes and a pulse goes missing: 'the dorsalis pedis is absent' → 'thank you — I'll take that as absent. Rather than working proximally through more pulses, I'd like to add Buerger's test and listen for a femoral bruit.' 'Take this as an absent pulse, please move on' → 'of course — thank you', and MOVE; do not ask again. Buerger's positive → 'pallor on elevation with reactive hyperaemia on dependency indicates significant arterial insufficiency.' Femoral bruit → 'turbulent flow through a stenosed vessel, supporting proximal arterial disease.' Closing: 'my diagnosis is cellulitis of the left lower leg ON A BACKGROUND OF PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE. That combination matters because the reduced blood supply will slow healing, so as well as antibiotics I'd want an ankle-brachial index and a vascular surgical opinion — and I WOULD NOT APPLY COMPRESSION to this leg.'

Two more traps worth rehearsing: producing a pen and DRAWING on a role-player to mark the border — describe it, do not do it, because the ink cues the next candidate; and finishing the lymph nodes and the sensory examination on a patient who has just become septic. WHEN THE OBSERVATIONS CHANGE, THE STATION HAS CHANGED — say so out loud and switch to resuscitation, because that recognition is the whole mark.
pefe: Role-player: Danny Rowe, 45, fencing contractor in Moonta, married with two teenagers; type 2 diabetes nine years on metformin taken 'most days', last HbA1c 'about nine, they said', never seen a podiatrist; ex-smoker six years, four beers most nights, no allergies, tetanus 'years ago, no idea'. Scratched the shin on wire while gardening three days ago, DID NOT CLEAN IT AND DID NOT FEEL IT HAPPEN — noticed blood on his sock. Hot and cold since yesterday. Matter-of-fact and a bit impatient — he has a job on and thinks this is a fuss. Says 'it's pretty tender' early, and WINCES AND PULLS BACK when the rash is pressed. HIDDEN AGENDA: his uncle lost a toe to diabetes and he is quietly frightened of the same — given if asked about his concerns, otherwise volunteered the moment they explain: 'I never even felt the scratch. Am I going to lose the leg?' HE ALSO PLAYS THE EXAMINER: observations only if asked (T 38.5, BP 110/70, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 98%) — IF THEY NEVER ASK, SAY NOTHING ALL STATION; foot pulses 'as you can feel on the patient'; inguinal nodes 'go ahead — there is a single tender, mobile node in the left groin'; anything else 'whatever you find on the patient'; and at six minutes, if they are still examining, 'please move to your diagnosis'. THE SENSORY PATTERN: yes at groin, mid-thigh and anterior knee; NOTHING at the medial malleolus, dorsum, and sole or lateral foot; then working up from the toe, nothing until a few centimetres above the ankle — 'yes, I feel that one'. DO NOT HELP — if they never pick up the cotton wool, let the station end without it.

Numbers: vitals T 38.5, BP 110/70, HR 88, RR 16, SpO2 98%. MORPHOLOGY — macule flat under 1 cm, PATCH flat over 1 cm, papule raised under 1 cm, plaque raised over 1 cm. Lesion roughly 12 x 8 cm, anterior left shin, unilateral. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Flucloxacillin 500 mg orally six-hourly for 5 days; 2 g IV six-hourly in severe disease VERIFY; cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity. Review at 48 hours; mark the border and note the time. Dermatomes L1 groin, L2 mid-thigh, L3 anterior knee, L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum, S1 lateral foot and sole. ABI 0.91-1.30 normal, 0.41-0.90 mild-moderate, 0.40 or less severe. Antibiotics within 1 hour in sepsis. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. CLOCK: lymph nodes at 4:40, second special test at 5:10.

Scored out of 10: asked for the vital signs BEFORE examining and called him febrile but not septic; introduced, consented, gloved and warned it might hurt; described the rash with primary AND secondary morphology and the border; screened OUT LOUD for necrotising fasciitis; checked temperature ON THE RASH looking for a local rise; did all four palpation steps INCLUDING pulses; PRESSED THE RASH gently and responded to the wince; examined the joints either side and excluded septic arthritis; ASKED FOR THE INGUINAL LYMPH NODES; and used the cotton wool, found the level, and gave TWO diagnoses with safety-netting.
fails: ★ Never palpating the rash itself — candidates work through ASIS, iliac crest, joint lines and popliteal fossa and never once press the red area
★ Never asking for the inguinal lymph nodes — the single most common omission in this station
Finishing with a single diagnosis and the cotton wool untouched, when the station is built as a mixed case
Deleting the pulses 'because it's only cellulitis' — exactly where the 2023 version hides its second diagnosis; or chasing more pulses after being told to move on

Taking the observation numbers without saying 'febrile but not septic'; describing a colour rather than a lesion; examining all six joints on both legs; drawing on the role-player to mark the border; and continuing the routine examination after the observations turn septic
