time: WIPE TO JENNY, not to the manikin · she is the one who consents · THE RASH IN FOUR FEATURES, ninety seconds, holding the photograph so she can see it: WHAT KIND (purpuric · a small amount of bleeding under the skin), SYMMETRY (both legs, both buttocks), SITE (legs and bottom, nothing on tummy, chest or back), and NON-BLANCHING (the colour doesn't fade when pressed) · if she raises MENINGITIS, answer IMMEDIATELY with the evidence: no neck stiffness, alert and interacting, normal observations, and children with meningococcal infection get very unwell very quickly · CONSENT FOR THE EXAMINATION, then general appearance NAMING EACH SIGN because it is a manikin, with the blood pressure flagged as the marker of RENAL involvement · THE ARTHRITIS BLOCK AT 3:20: the ANKLE as the joint most typically involved, inspection for swelling and redness, palpation for tenderness and PERI-ARTICULAR swelling, range of movement, then the other joints named · NODE SURVEY with every chain named aloud · THE ABDOMEN IN FIVE NAMED STEPS, going beyond the spleen because THE GUT IS ONE OF THE FOUR INFLAMED ORGANS: inspection, superficial palpation of nine regions, DEEP palpation for masses AND SPECIFICALLY INTUSSUSCEPTION, organs, bowel sounds · OFFER the inguinal nodes AND THE SCROTUM, because scrotal involvement occurs and torsion must be excluded · STOP EXAMINING AT 7:10 and turn to Jenny.

back.dx: HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA (IgA vasculitis) — ONE PROCESS IN FOUR ORGANS, which is how you explain it: the small blood vessels become inflamed, usually set off by an infection (the cold a fortnight ago), and inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak a little blood (the rash), in the KIDNEYS give blood in the urine, in the BOWEL cause the colicky tummy pains, and in the JOINTS cause the puffy tender ankles. So it is NOT a bleeding disorder and NOT meningitis. THE PLATELET COUNT IS WHY: purpura with a LOW platelet count is a different disease, and normal platelets with normal clotting are what allow you to call this a vasculitis rather than ITP, leukaemia or DIC. Diagnostic criterion: PALPABLE PURPURA without thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy is mandatory, plus at least one of diffuse abdominal pain, arthritis or arthralgia, renal involvement, or biopsy showing IgA deposition VERIFY. Management is the FOLLOW-UP: most children settle in four to six weeks and recover completely, but urine and blood pressure are checked regularly for SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS VERIFY, plus bloods today to confirm it is not a bleeding problem. Admit for severe abdominal pain, vomiting or GI bleeding, hypertension, renal impairment, inability to walk, scrotal involvement, or a family too far from care to return easily. Home safety-net: severe or constant tummy pain, repeated vomiting or blood in the stool; much less urine, or urine like cola or blood; puffiness of the face or ankles; scrotal pain or swelling; not drinking, drowsiness or a new fever; a rash spreading to the trunk or new bruising elsewhere.
plan: WIPE TO JENNY: '...are you Jenny, Liam's mum? And this must be Liam. I can see you're worried about this rash. I'd like to go through it with you and then examine him. Before I start — I'll wash my hands.' → 'doctor, is it meningitis? I read about the glass test' → ANSWER NOW, WITH EVIDENCE: 'that's exactly the right thing to think about with this kind of rash, and I'm glad you asked. The good news is that Liam has NO NECK STIFFNESS, he's ALERT AND INTERACTING, and all his observations — temperature, heart rate and blood pressure — are NORMAL. Children with meningococcal infection are usually very unwell very quickly, and Liam isn't. So I don't think that's what this is — but I'll tell you what I do think once I've examined him.' (Addressing the manikin instead of Jenny, or deferring the meningitis question, both cost marks.)

THE RASH — FOUR FEATURES IN NINETY SECONDS, photograph turned towards her: 'FIRST, what kind of rash it is. These little red-purple spots are what we call a PURPURIC rash — in plain terms, there's a small amount of BLEEDING UNDER THE SKIN. It's not a simple red rash like a heat rash. SECOND, it's on BOTH SIDES — the same on both legs and both buttocks, a symmetrical rash, and that pattern is a clue. THIRD, WHERE IT IS — his legs and his bottom, and none on his tummy, chest or back. That distribution is quite characteristic. And FOURTH, the important one — WHEN I PRESS ON THIS RASH, THE COLOUR DOESN'T FADE. We call that NON-BLANCHING, and it tells us the colour is blood in the skin.' → 'bleeding under his skin? Is that dangerous?' → 'it sounds alarming, and I understand that. It's a small amount, and there are several possible reasons — I'd like to examine Liam now and then explain what I think is going on.' (Primary morphology, borders and secondary change score NOTHING here; and every sentence past ninety seconds is stolen from the abdomen.)

Consent from Jenny, then general appearance with EVERY SIGN NAMED: 'Examiner, I appreciate this is a manikin, so I'll NAME EACH SIGN I'm looking for as I go. On general appearance I'm assessing his LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS — alert or drowsy; looking for PALLOR; and for CACHEXIA. I note the blood pressure is given and normal — IN THIS CONDITION I WOULD OTHERWISE MEASURE IT MYSELF, BECAUSE HYPERTENSION INDICATES RENAL INVOLVEMENT. Taking the hands — nails for clubbing, palms for pale palmar creases, and the pulse for tachycardia.' (Putting a stethoscope or hands on plastic and reporting a result you were not given is an automatic fail.)

THE ARTHRITIS BLOCK — here, not at the end: 'Examiner, I'd now like to examine for ARTHRITIS, which is one of the features of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Taking the ANKLE, WHICH IS THE JOINT MOST TYPICALLY INVOLVED — on inspection, no swelling and no redness. On palpation I'm feeling for TENDERNESS and for PERI-ARTICULAR SWELLING. I'd like to take the joint through its range of movement. And I would examine the other joints in the same way — knees, wrists, elbows and hips.' → 'there is mild puffiness and tenderness around both ankles' → 'thank you — that's consistent with the joint involvement we see in this condition.' (It is the only HSP-specific item on the mark sheet and the first casualty when the station runs long. Do NOT describe deformity — that belongs to chronic arthritis and it sounds like recitation.)

THE NODE SURVEY, every chain named even though the plastic is unconvincing: arms for purpura and scratch marks; epitrochlear both sides with the corresponding thumb; axillae with the five groups named and the positions shown; mouth for gum hypertrophy and bleeding, glossitis, angular cheilitis, tonsils and Waldeyer's ring and PALATAL AND BUCCAL PETECHIAE, plus THE THROAT for redness or exudate given the infection two weeks ago; eyes for pallor and jaundice; the neck FROM THE FRONT since the manikin cannot sit, all eight chains, saying that normally you would stand behind; and pressing the clavicles and sternum for bone tenderness. (The mark is for NAMING the chains, not for the tactile quality of the plastic.)

THE ABDOMEN IN FIVE NAMED STEPS — and it goes beyond the spleen: 'on INSPECTION — whether it moves symmetrically with respiration, and any visible masses or distension. SUPERFICIAL PALPATION across all nine regions — tenderness, guarding, rigidity. DEEP PALPATION across all nine regions — masses, AND SPECIFICALLY A MASS THAT WOULD SUGGEST INTUSSUSCEPTION. ORGANS — the liver edge from the right iliac fossa; then the spleen, bimanually. I'd like to percuss with Castell's method. And BOWEL SOUNDS.' → 'soft, mildly tender centrally, no guarding, no masses, no organomegaly, bowel sounds present' → 'thank you — CENTRAL TENDERNESS WITHOUT GUARDING OR A MASS FITS THE ABDOMINAL INVOLVEMENT OF THIS CONDITION RATHER THAN A SURGICAL ABDOMEN.' (Examining the abdomen as though this were the CLL station — spleen only — misses the organ that puts a child in theatre.)

WHAT YOU OFFER RATHER THAN DO: 'to complete the survey I'd palpate the inguinal nodes along the inguinal ligament. AND IN A BOY WITH THIS CONDITION I'D WANT TO EXAMINE THE SCROTUM, BECAUSE SCROTAL INVOLVEMENT OCCURS IN HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA AND MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM TESTICULAR TORSION.' → 'that's fine, don't do it — the scrotum is normal.' (Eight seconds, and it is where the torsion mark lives.)

STOP EXAMINING AND TURN TO JENNY: 'I think Liam has a condition called HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA — it's a mouthful, and doctors also call it IgA vasculitis. It's the commonest condition of its type in children. What happens is that the SMALL BLOOD VESSELS BECOME INFLAMED — the tiny tubes that carry blood around the body — usually set off by an infection, which fits with the cold he had a fortnight ago. AND ONE THING EXPLAINS EVERYTHING YOU'VE NOTICED: inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak a little blood — that's the rash. Inflamed vessels in the KIDNEYS are why the urine test showed blood. Inflamed vessels in the BOWEL are causing his tummy pains. And it can affect the JOINTS, which is why I checked his ankles. So it ISN'T a bleeding disorder, and it ISN'T meningitis. In most children it settles by itself over a few weeks.' → 'will his kidneys be alright?' → 'most children recover completely. Because the kidneys can be involved, WE'LL CHECK HIS URINE AND BLOOD PRESSURE REGULARLY — FOR THE NEXT SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS — and that's how we make sure nothing is missed. I'll also send some blood tests today to confirm this isn't a bleeding problem.' (Blanket reassurance with no follow-up plan is a missed management point — THE RENAL FOLLOW-UP IS THE MANAGEMENT.)

ask: 'These spots are a purpuric rash — a small amount of bleeding under the skin.' / 'It's the same on both legs and both buttocks — a symmetrical rash.' / 'It's on his legs and bottom, and nothing on his tummy, chest or back.' / 'When I press on it, the colour doesn't fade — that's a non-blanching rash.' / 'He has no neck stiffness, he's alert, and his observations are normal — so I don't think this is meningitis.'

'Examiner, I appreciate this is a manikin — I'll name each sign I'm looking for.' / 'I'd like to examine for arthritis — taking the ankle, the joint most typically involved.' / 'Inspection for swelling and redness; palpation for tenderness and peri-articular swelling.' / 'Deep palpation for masses, specifically anything suggesting intussusception.' / 'I'd want to examine the scrotum — scrotal involvement occurs, and torsion must be excluded.'

'The small blood vessels become inflamed — usually set off by an infection.' / 'We check his urine and blood pressure for the next six to twelve months.' FOUR SENTENCES THAT LOSE MARKS: 'the primary morphology is purpuric with well-demarcated borders' (noise, to a mother); 'his chest is clear and his pulse is 96' said with a stethoscope on plastic (automatic fail); 'he'll be completely fine' without the follow-up plan; and 'let me first exclude meningitis before I answer' — SHE ASKED NOW. Examiner extras: the platelet count matters because purpura with a LOW platelet count is a different disease; admission for severe pain, vomiting or GI bleeding, hypertension, renal impairment, inability to walk, scrotal involvement, or distance from care; the rash spares the trunk because the distribution follows gravity and hydrostatic pressure in dependent skin, which is why a non-ambulant infant gets it on the back and face instead.

VARIANT A — AN ABDOMINAL MASS ('tenderness in the right side of the abdomen, and you can feel a mass') → NAME IT AND CHANGE GEAR: 'a palpable mass with colicky abdominal pain in a child with HSP makes me concerned about INTUSSUSCEPTION. I'd stop examining, keep him nil by mouth, obtain intravenous access, give analgesia, and arrange an URGENT ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND and surgical review. In this condition the intussusception is typically ILEO-ILEAL, so ultrasound is the diagnostic test rather than an air enema.' And to Jenny: 'I've found something on Liam's tummy that I want a surgeon and a scan to look at straight away... I'm going to ask him not to eat or drink for now.' (Receiving that finding, saying 'thank you' and continuing unchanged means the station has told you the child is sick and you did not hear it.)

VARIANT B — SCROTAL PAIN reported mid-examination → 'scrotal pain and swelling in a boy with this condition CAN be part of the vasculitis — BUT I CANNOT ASSUME THAT. Testicular torsion must be excluded, so I'd request urgent surgical review and a Doppler ultrasound. Torsion is time-critical, so I would not wait for it to settle.' / VARIANT C — THE MOTHER'S REAL FEAR IS LEUKAEMIA ('my niece had leukaemia. She had bruises like this') → REASSURE WITH EVIDENCE, NOT TONE: 'that's part of what I was checking for when I examined him. In leukaemia we'd usually expect enlarged glands, an enlarged spleen, tenderness over the bones and often bleeding gums — and Liam has none of those. He's also not pale and not unwell. The blood test I'll send today will confirm it, and I'll make sure you get the result.' / VARIANT D — THE FEBRILE, UNWELL CHILD (drowsy, poorly perfused, non-blanching rash) → THE STATION STOPS BEING AN EXAMINATION: 'my immediate concern is MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS. I would call for senior help, give high-flow oxygen, obtain intravenous or intraosseous access, take blood cultures if it does not delay treatment, and give EMPIRICAL INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS IMMEDIATELY, with a fluid bolus. I would not continue a routine examination.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 33, teacher's aide in a South Australian country town; Liam is 5, her youngest, and she has a daughter of 9; she drove forty minutes tonight while her husband stayed home. THE RASH appeared two days ago on his shins and is now up to his thighs and bottom, not itchy and not sore. THE COLD about two weeks ago — runny nose, sore throat, mild fever for three days, better on its own. TUMMY PAIN in waves that makes him curl up for a few minutes, started yesterday, no blood in his poo, vomited once this morning. JOINTS — 'he's been limping a bit', and his ankles look puffy to her. Urine — she hasn't noticed anything odd. No fever now, eating a bit less, drinking normally. Well child, immunisations up to date, no medications or allergies. HER NIECE HAD LEUKAEMIA AT SIX and is well now. TWO FEARS: MENINGITIS, raised in her first or second sentence ('is it meningitis? I read about the glass test'), and LEUKAEMIA, held back and raised only if asked about other worries or as the doctor wraps up. Anxious but articulate; not tearful unless the doctor is cold or dismissive, in which case she goes quiet and volunteers nothing; VISIBLY RELAXES when the meningitis question is answered properly. IF THE DOCTOR TALKS TO THE MANIKIN INSTEAD OF HER: 'sorry — are you talking to me?' If they use jargon: 'sorry — I don't understand what that means.'

Numbers: 4 rash features, 4 organs, 5 abdominal steps, 8 cervical chains, 5 axillary groups. Onset 1-3 weeks post-infection; peak age 3-10 years. PLATELETS NORMAL is the fact that excludes ITP, and clotting is normal. Ankles and knees are the typical joints. Intussusception here is ILEO-ILEAL, so ULTRASOUND is the test. Renal follow-up 6-12 months VERIFY; most settle in 4-6 weeks, with recurrence — usually milder — in a substantial minority, most often within the first few months VERIFY. CLOCK: rash 1:30, joints 3:20, stop examining 7:10.

Pass mark 17 of 24, and ALL of: ARTHRITIS EXAMINED, NON-BLANCHING NAMED, NO INVENTED FINDINGS, and A FOLLOW-UP PLAN GIVEN. Also scored: named the rash type, symmetry and site; plain English throughout; finished the rash inside 1:30; answered the meningitis question when asked; consent taken from HER, not the manikin; named every target before touching; inspection and palpation of the joint; all node groups named both sides; abdomen covering tenderness, guarding, masses, organs and bowel sounds; offered inguinal nodes and scrotum; named the condition; gave ONE mechanism — inflamed blood vessels — and linked skin, kidney, gut and joints to it; linked it to the infection two weeks ago; did not over-reassure; talked to her throughout, checked understanding and invited questions.
fails: ★ Claiming a finding you were not given — a stethoscope on plastic followed by 'his chest is clear and his pulse is 96' is an automatic fail
★ Leaving the joints until after the abdomen, so the only HSP-specific item on the mark sheet is the casualty when time runs out
Deferring the meningitis question until the end — she asked now, so answer now, with the evidence rather than the tone
Addressing the manikin instead of the mother, who is the person who consents; jargon in the rash explanation — primary morphology, borders and secondary change score nothing here

Running past ninety seconds on the rash, every extra sentence stolen from the abdomen; examining the abdomen as though it were the CLL station, spleen only; not offering the scrotum because you expect to be stopped; blanket reassurance with no renal follow-up plan, when the follow-up IS the management

Red-purple, flat and over a centimetre — a PATCH; SYMMETRICAL on both legs and buttocks; nothing on the trunk, chest or back; NON-BLANCHING
MILD PUFFINESS AND TENDERNESS around BOTH ankles — the only HSP-specific examination finding
Soft with MILD CENTRAL TENDERNESS; NO guarding, NO mass, no organomegaly; bowel sounds present

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — GP antenatal check. A PREGNANT WOMAN IS IN THE CHAIR AND A MANNEQUIN IS ON THE COUCH: consent HER, palpate IT — if you start on her abdomen she will let you once and then say 'wasn't there a model you were meant to use?'. THE THREE-WAY TRIANGLE: before each step turn your head to her and say what is coming; while your hands work, speak to the examiner. TWO ACCURACY POINTS SEPARATE CANDIDATES — VISIBLY TURNING TO FACE THE FEET FOR GRIP FOUR, and ACTUALLY COUNTING THE FETAL HEART RATE, which half of candidates forget. Palpation and commentary finished by 5:30.
stem: VERSION A: GP registrar. Jenny Marsh, 31, G3 P2, 37+2 WEEKS by an 8-week dating scan, routine antenatal visit, no symptoms and normal movements; two previous normal vaginal births. T 36.8. BLOOD PRESSURE AND URINALYSIS ARE NOT RECORDED — a BP machine is in the room. 8 minutes.
VERSION B: 29-year-old primigravida at 40+4 weeks, all normal — and the tasks add diagnosis, causes, implications and MANAGEMENT: the post-dates case.
tasks: Perform an obstetric abdominal examination (Leopold's manoeuvres)
Explain your findings to the patient
Version B only: explain your diagnosis, its causes and implications, and your management
time: ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS FIRST and NOTICE THE MISSING BP · offering to measure it screens for pre-eclampsia without being prompted · WIPE with a rapport line, then the full explanation: look, feel to work out how the baby is lying, and LISTEN TO THE HEARTBEAT at the end; exposure from mid-chest to just above the pubic bone, chaperone offered, and HEAD SUPPORTED WITH A 15-30 DEGREE LEFT LATERAL TILT · PERIPHERIES CAPPED AT 30 SECONDS (the one worth naming is PERIORBITAL OEDEMA, because it points to pre-eclampsia) and accept redirection instantly · INSPECTION: distended consistent with term, longitudinally ovoid, scars, linea nigra, striae · SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT: locate BOTH landmarks out loud, zero at the symphysis, measure in the midline, and if the number looks impossible RE-MEASURE BEFORE YOU SPEAK · THE FOUR GRIPS with running commentary, grips 1-3 facing her head and GRIP 4 FACING THE FEET, reporting findings and concluding only at the end · THE FETAL HEART: ask for the Doppler or stethoscope AND A TIMER, count fifteen seconds, and PALPATE HER RADIAL PULSE AT THE SAME TIME · cover her, offer to complete with a urine dipstick, weight, growth chart and GBS swab, then explain in plain words: SIZE, then POSITION, then HEARTBEAT.

back.dx: VERSION A — a normal late third-trimester examination: SFH 36 cm, appropriate for 37 weeks (gestation in weeks plus or minus 2-3 cm); LONGITUDINAL lie with the back on the LEFT; CEPHALIC presentation; head THREE-FIFTHS palpable, so engaging but not yet engaged; FHR 144, within 110-160; BP normal. Explain it as size, then position, then heartbeat, in plain words, then safety-net: reduced movements, bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain, or a bad headache with blurred vision. IF NOTHING IS PALPABLE, DO NOT CLAIM IT IS FINE — name what you did assess, name what you could not determine, and say a bedside ultrasound will resolve it. VERSION B — PROLONGED PREGNANCY at 40+4: causes are usually none, with inaccurate dates the commonest explanation (hers are certain), plus nulliparity, family history, previous post-dates, a male fetus, older age, obesity, and rarely a fetal hormonal cause. Implications — FOR HER: longer harder labour, more instrumental delivery and caesarean, more tearing and postpartum haemorrhage; FOR THE BABY: continued growth and macrosomia with shoulder dystocia, reducing liquor with cord compression, meconium aspiration, and rising risk beyond 41 weeks. Management in three parts: CHECK THE BABY (CTG plus ultrasound for liquor and growth); CHECK THE CERVIX with a speculum and A BISHOP SCORE — omitting it is how this station fails; and GET THINGS MOVING — offer a membrane sweep now, and INDUCTION FROM 41 WEEKS, ripening with gel or a balloon if the Bishop score is 6 or less, then ARM and oxytocin. IT IS HER DECISION: if she declines, twice-weekly CTG and liquor volume, and delivery by 42 weeks. TRANSVERSE LIE: scan for placental position and liquor, offer ECV from 37 weeks, caesarean around 39 weeks if it fails or is declined — and if her waters break or contractions start, COME IN IMMEDIATELY BY AMBULANCE because of the cord prolapse risk.
plan: OBSERVATIONS FIRST, then the missing BP noticed: 'Examiner, before I start, may I have Jenny's observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature? I notice the blood pressure hasn't been recorded — may I measure it?' Then hand hygiene and gloves, and the WIPE with a rapport line: '...can I confirm your full name and date of birth? How has the pregnancy been going so far — have you been enjoying it?' (The chit-chat is RAPPORT, NOT HISTORY — if she opens a symptom door, acknowledge, park it and come back: 'thank you for telling me — I'll come back to that properly once I've examined you.')

The explanation, exposure, chaperone and POSITION: 'today I've been asked to examine your tummy. I'll LOOK at your tummy first, then gently FEEL it to work out how the baby is lying, and at the end I'll LISTEN TO YOUR BABY'S HEARTBEAT with a stethoscope or a handheld Doppler. It shouldn't hurt at all, but if anything is uncomfortable please tell me straight away and I'll stop. I'll need to uncover your tummy from about the middle of your chest down to just above your pubic bone, and I'll keep you covered everywhere else. WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT? I'd also like you lying back with your head supported and TILTED SLIGHTLY TO YOUR LEFT, which keeps the blood flowing well to the baby.' Then move to HER RIGHT SIDE — and to the mannequin.

PERIPHERIES IN 30 SECONDS, and accept the cut instantly: 'alert, comfortable at rest, not pale, not jaundiced. May I look at your hands? No palmar pallor, no swelling of the fingers, radial pulse regular at about 84. Blood pressure 118 over 76, normal. On the face there is NO PERIORBITAL OEDEMA, no chloasma, no conjunctival pallor and no scleral jaundice.' → 'skip the peripheral signs' → 'thank you, examiner — I'll move straight to the abdomen.' Then inspection: 'the abdomen is distended consistent with a term pregnancy, LONGITUDINALLY OVOID, no visible fetal movements, no surgical scars, no linea nigra and no striae gravidarum.' (Ninety seconds on peripheries and the grips get rushed; arguing with the redirection is worse.)

SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT, landmarks located out loud: 'Jenny, I'm going to start feeling your tummy now. I'll be gentle — tell me if anything is uncomfortable. Examiner, I'm using the ULNAR BORDER of my hand from just below the xiphisternum to locate the top of the uterus... I have the fundus. I'm now identifying the UPPER BORDER OF THE SYMPHYSIS PUBIS... I have it. ZERO AT THE SYMPHYSIS, measuring in the midline, crossing the umbilicus, up to the highest point of the fundus. The symphysio-fundal height is 36 centimetres, APPROPRIATE FOR 37 WEEKS — I accept gestation in weeks plus or minus 2 to 3 centimetres. I'd plot this on her customised growth chart.' (If the number looks impossible, RE-MEASURE BEFORE YOU COMMENT: 'that's not what I expected — I'll re-check my landmarks.' One candidate read the inches side and reported 11 cm at 37 weeks. Re-checking is a mark, not a weakness.)

THE FOUR GRIPS, findings reported and conclusions saved for the end. GRIP 1, FUNDAL, facing her head: 'cupping both hands over the fundus, I'm checking which part of the baby occupies the fundus. A broad, softer, irregular pole that moves with the trunk — consistent with the BREECH.' GRIP 2, LATERAL: 'stabilising with my left hand and palpating with the palm of my right, then swapping. I'm assessing the LIE and the POSITION OF THE BACK. On the left, firm, flat, continuous resistance — the fetal back. On the right, small, irregular, mobile parts — the limbs. The lie is LONGITUDINAL.' GRIP 3, PELVIC: 'using the thumb and fingers of one hand suprapubically, checking the PRESENTING PART. A hard, round, smooth mass — the presentation is CEPHALIC.' (Both hands rubbing at once on the lateral grip is wrong — one hand stabilises. And do not announce a diagnosis at grip two.)

GRIP 4 — THE ACCURACY POINT: 'I'm NOW TURNING TO FACE JENNY'S FEET to assess engagement. Placing both hands on the lower abdomen and sliding them down towards the pelvic brim, I can feel about THREE-FIFTHS of the head above the brim, so the head is beginning to engage but is not yet engaged.' TURN YOUR BODY AND LET IT BE SEEN — doing grip four facing her head is the single accuracy point that separates candidates. IF YOU FEEL NOTHING AT ALL, do not press harder and do not invent: 'Examiner, I'm unable to define a fetal pole at the fundus. I'll continue — on the lateral grip I'm assessing the lie, on the pelvic grip the presenting part, and facing the feet, the degree of descent. I would confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.'

THE FETAL HEART — the step half of candidates forget: 'Jenny, last part — I'd like to listen to your baby's heartbeat. Examiner, DO I HAVE A HANDHELD DOPPLER, OR WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO USE MY STETHOSCOPE? I'm placing the diaphragm OVER THE FETAL BACK, below the umbilicus on the left. MAY I HAVE A TIMER? Counting for fifteen seconds... that is 36, giving a fetal heart rate of 144 beats per minute, within the normal range of 110 to 160. I'M PALPATING JENNY'S RADIAL PULSE AT THE SAME TIME to confirm this is the baby's heart rate and not hers.' (NEVER GUESS THE NUMBER — every candidate that day gets the same recording and the examiner already knows it. If you lose count: 'I lost count — may I have another fifteen seconds?' That costs nothing; inventing a plausible number costs the accuracy domain.)

Cover her, help her sit up, complete, then EXPLAIN IN PLAIN WORDS — size, position, heartbeat: 'your womb measured 36 centimetres and at 37 weeks we'd expect between 34 and 40, so your baby is growing exactly as we'd expect. Your baby is lying UP AND DOWN rather than across, with his HEAD DOWN at the bottom and his bottom at the top — the ideal position for a normal birth. His back is along your left side. His head has just started to settle down into your pelvis, which is exactly what we like to see at this stage. And his heartbeat is 144, right in the normal range. Your blood pressure is normal too.' Then questions, and the safety-net: reduced movements, bleeding, fluid loss, tummy pain, or a bad headache with blurred vision. Her hidden agenda if you leave a gap: 'my sister said I look small for 37 weeks — is the baby big enough?' → 'that's exactly what I was measuring... if it were ever more than about three centimetres off, we'd simply arrange a scan.'
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run, Version A: consent and peripheries by 2:00, fundal height by 3:00, four grips by 5:00, fetal heart by 5:30
ask: 'Examiner, may I have the observations before I begin?' / 'I notice the blood pressure hasn't been recorded — may I measure it?' / 'How has the pregnancy been going so far — have you been enjoying it?' / 'I'll look at your tummy, gently feel it, and then listen to your baby's heartbeat.' / 'I'll uncover you from mid-chest to just above the pubic bone and keep you covered otherwise.'

'I'm using the ulnar border of my hand to locate the fundus.' / 'Zero at the symphysis, measuring in the midline across the umbilicus.' / 'I'm checking which part of the baby occupies the fundus.' / 'I'm assessing the lie and the position of the back.' / 'I'm checking the presenting part.' / 'I'm now facing the feet to assess the degree of descent in fifths.'

'Examiner, do I have a Doppler, or shall I use my stethoscope? May I have a timer?' / 'Your baby is lying up and down with his head down — the ideal position for a normal birth.' / 'I couldn't determine the position by feel today; the simplest way to be certain is a scan.' / 'Please come straight back if the baby moves less, you bleed, your waters break, or you feel unwell.'

VERSION B — THE POST-DATES CASE, four blocks: DIAGNOSIS ('the good news first: your baby is head-down, growing well, and the heartbeat is normal. My concern is how far along you are... once a pregnancy goes past 41 weeks we call it a PROLONGED PREGNANCY, and beyond that the risks slowly start to rise'); CAUSES (usually none, dates checked first because inaccurate dates are the commonest explanation, then first baby, family history, previous post-dates, a boy, older age, extra weight — 'none of these are anything you have done'); IMPLICATIONS (for her: longer labour, instruments or caesarean, tearing, heavier bleeding; for him: continued growth and a difficult shoulder delivery, reducing fluid pressing on the cord, meconium, and rising risk past 41 weeks); MANAGEMENT (CTG and ultrasound; SPECULUM AND A BISHOP SCORE; a membrane sweep now; induction from 41 weeks, ripening first if the Bishop score is 6 or less, then ARM and oxytocin — AND IT IS HER DECISION, with twice-weekly CTG and liquor if she waits, and delivery by 42 weeks). This station fails on OMISSION OF THE BISHOP SCORE and on STEAMROLLING THE INDUCTION.

VARIANTS: THE EMPTY MANNEQUIN — 'don't tell me what you're looking for, tell me what you feel' → 'Examiner, I'm not able to define a fetal pole here. I'll continue through the remaining grips and tell you anything I do feel, and I'd confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.' DO NOT PRESS HARDER AND DO NOT INVENT — candidates have passed feeling absolutely nothing. / TRANSVERSE LIE — 'the abdomen appears BROADER TRANSVERSELY than it is long. On the fundal grip I can't define a pole. On the lateral grip a hard, round, ballottable mass in the right flank — most likely the head... no presenting part at the brim. My conclusion is a TRANSVERSE LIE at 37 weeks.' To her: scan first, then ECV offered at about 37 weeks in hospital with monitoring, caesarean if it fails or she declines — and IF YOUR WATERS BREAK OR CONTRACTIONS START, COME IN IMMEDIATELY BY AMBULANCE, because the cord can come down first. / SHE DECLINES INDUCTION — never pressure, never simply agree and walk away: acknowledge the pain concern, give the reason the risks rise, then 'if that's your choice we'll support it and watch closely — twice a week for a CTG and a scan of the fluid, and I'd recommend we plan the birth by 42 weeks whatever happens.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Marsh, 31, primary school teacher on maternity leave, living with her partner Dave and children of 5 and 3, both born vaginally at term. Third pregnancy, 37+2 by an 8-week dating scan; routine care, all screening normal, no gestational diabetes or hypertension, blood group O positive; never smoked, no alcohol, pregnancy multivitamin taken reliably; mother had high blood pressure in her last pregnancy. Warm, chatty, a little tired, mildly anxious underneath — she wants to be told the baby is all right and a normal birth is still on the cards. HIDDEN AGENDA: her sister told her she 'looks small for 37 weeks' and she has been quietly worried since; not volunteered — given if asked about worries, or raised near the very end. HOW SHE PLAYS IT: SAY 'OW' LOUDLY if the doctor presses hard, digs fingertips in, or palpates roughly, then look at them and wait — THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING SHE DOES. If they go silent at the mannequin for more than about 30 seconds: 'is everything all right?' If they never explain what they are about to do: 'what are you doing now?' IF THEY START PALPATING HER ABDOMEN, allow it once, then: 'sorry — wasn't there a model you were meant to use?' Warm with a doctor who talks to her; quieter and more anxious with one who ignores her. When the heartbeat is heard: 'is that fast? It sounds fast.'

Numbers: FIVE steps — four grips plus the fetal heart. Grips 1-3 face the head; GRIP 4 FACES THE FEET. SFH = gestation in weeks plus or minus 2-3 cm, 34-40 cm at 37 weeks, plotted from 24 weeks. Engagement 5/5 free to 2/5 or less = engaged, to 0/5. FHR 110-160, counted for 15 seconds and multiplied by four. Tilt 15-30 degrees left lateral. GBS swab at 35-37 weeks. ECV offered from 37 weeks, caesarean around 39 weeks if it fails. PROLONGED PREGNANCY 41+0, POST-TERM 42+0. Induction offered from 41+0, delivery by 42 weeks. BISHOP SCORE 6 or less means ripen first; 7 or more means ARM plus oxytocin. If she declines: twice-weekly CTG and liquor volume.

Score out of 10, one point each: asked for observations before starting; introduced, confirmed identity, took consent, offered a chaperone; explained each step before doing it; stood on the RIGHT and worked on the MANNEQUIN, not on her; located the landmarks before measuring the fundal height; did all four grips in order with commentary; TURNED TO FACE THE FEET for the fourth grip; LISTENED TO AND COUNTED the fetal heart rate; stayed gentle throughout and responded properly to 'ow'; explained findings in plain words, asked for questions, and safety-netted.
fails: ★ Doing grip four facing her head instead of visibly turning to face the feet — the single accuracy point that separates candidates
★ Never listening to or counting the fetal heart rate — half of candidates forget it — or inventing a plausible number when the examiner already knows the recording
Palpating the woman's abdomen instead of the mannequin, or going silent at the mannequin for two minutes
Ninety seconds on peripheries so the grips are rushed, or arguing when the examiner cuts you short; pressing harder when you feel nothing, and pressing hard enough to earn an 'ow'

Announcing a diagnosis at grip two instead of reporting findings and concluding at the end; saying 'everything is completely fine' when you determined nothing; in Version B, omitting the Bishop score or steamrolling the induction

setting: MIXED STATION — hospital antenatal clinic, and THE WHOLE THING IS A RACE. You pass by ticking off key points COMPLETELY AND QUICKLY, not by doing any one system beautifully. Splits: HISTORY DONE BY 3:30, EXAMINATION DONE BY 7:00, DIAGNOSIS BY 7:45. Warn her you are running a list, then run ELEVEN QUESTIONS IN UNDER TWO MINUTES — and never forget the three fetal questions. THREE THINGS NEVER TO SAY: 'try not to worry', 'it's probably nothing', 'we'll see you next week'.
stem: Hospital antenatal clinic; you are the resident. Sarah Whitfield, 28, G1 P0, 30 WEEKS by early dating scan, routine visit, NO presenting complaint recorded. BP 158/98, REPEATED FOUR HOURS LATER 162/102. URINE DIPSTICK PROTEIN 3+, no blood, nitrites or leucocytes. PR 88, RR 18, T 36.9, SpO2 98%. 8 minutes.
Recall variants: Version B has a HEADACHE for two days in the stem; Version C has swelling of the legs and face — in both you explore that complaint first, then run the red-flag list.

She feels COMPLETELY WELL. Two positives only, and only if asked: PUFFY ANKLES in the evenings, and 3 KG WEIGHT GAIN IN A FORTNIGHT. Risk factors: first pregnancy, and her mother had hypertension in pregnancy. Examination: pitting oedema to mid-shin, brisk ankle jerk, no sustained clonus, SFH 30 cm, FHR 148.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient (about 3 minutes)
Perform the relevant physical examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
time: SIGNPOST THE WHOLE PLAN IN ONE SENTENCE, then an OPEN question · do not open with reassurance and do not open with alarm · THE RED-FLAG BLOCK, warned then run fast: headache not settling with paracetamol, visual change, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea or vomiting, chest pain, breathlessness or cough, dizziness or confusion, swelling of legs hands or face, SUDDEN RAPID WEIGHT GAIN, reduced urine output, jaundice or easy bruising, blackouts or fits · THEN THE THREE FETAL QUESTIONS: movements, bleeding or fluid loss, tightenings or pain · RISK FACTORS in one minute, and NULLIPARITY AND FAMILY HISTORY ARE BOTH POSITIVE HERE, so if you never ask you never get to say 'she has two risk factors' · EXAMINATION, twelve steps out loud: general and hands, MEASURE THE BP YOURSELF, eyes, FUNDOSCOPY ASKED FOR BY NAME looking for papilloedema and hypertensive retinopathy, heart, CHEST FROM BEHIND for bibasal crackles of pulmonary oedema, abdomen for RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT AND UTERINE tenderness, SFH, Leopold's, fetal heart rate, LEGS asking three things at once (oedema, does it pit, to what level), ANKLE JERK AND CLONUS, and the dipstick · then NAME IT, SAY IT IS SERIOUS, SAY WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, AND STOP.

back.dx: PRE-ECLAMPSIA with SEVERE-RANGE HYPERTENSION at 30 weeks — new hypertension after 20 weeks (158/98 then 162/102, both in the severe range at or above 160/110) with 3+ proteinuria, plus pitting oedema, rapid weight gain and brisk reflexes, in a nulliparous woman with a family history. Explain it as: it happens in the second half of pregnancy, the blood pressure rises and the kidneys leak protein, and it can affect several other organs and the baby's growth and blood supply — and 'I KNOW YOU FEEL COMPLETELY WELL, AND THAT IS VERY COMMON WITH THIS CONDITION, but I want to be honest with you: it is serious, for you and for the baby, and it can change quickly.' PLAN: admit today; bloods including FBC, LFTs, U&E and coagulation; urine PROTEIN:CREATININE RATIO (30 mg/mmol or more); CTG; LABETALOL 100-200 mg orally two to three times daily targeting about 130-150 over 80-100; BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM twice, 24 hours apart, because she is under 34 weeks; consider MAGNESIUM SULFATE 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour, continued 24 hours after delivery or the last fit; and call the obstetric registrar now. THE ONLY CURE IS DELIVERY, so the team weighs up timing. Platelets under 100 is a severe feature. Next pregnancy: aspirin 100-150 mg nightly from 12 weeks to about 36 weeks. SUSTAINED CLONUS (more than five beats) indicates CNS irritability and IMPENDING ECLAMPSIA — that makes it severe regardless of the blood pressure, and it means magnesium now.
plan: SIGNPOST, then open: '...I've been asked to see you because your blood pressure has come back higher than we'd like today and there's some protein in your urine. I'd like to ask you some questions first, then examine you, and then explain what I think is going on. Is that all right? To start with — how has the pregnancy been going so far?' → 'fine, really — I feel completely normal. Is something wrong?' → NEITHER REASSURE NOR ALARM: 'it might be something we need to act on — let me ask a few questions and examine you, and then I'll be able to tell you properly.'

THE RED-FLAG BLOCK — where the marks are — warned and then run fast: 'I'm going to ask about some specific symptoms — most of them will be a no, but I need to check each one. Any HEADACHES, particularly ones that don't settle with paracetamol? Any changes in your VISION — blurring, double vision, flashing lights or spots? Any pain up under your ribs on the RIGHT, or in the pit of your stomach? Any NAUSEA OR VOMITING? Any CHEST PAIN? Have you become SHORT OF BREATH, or noticed a new cough? Any DIZZINESS, or felt muddled or unusually drowsy? Any SWELLING of your legs, hands or face? And have you noticed any SUDDEN RAPID WEIGHT GAIN? Are you passing LESS URINE than usual? Any YELLOWING of your skin or eyes, or BRUISING more easily? Any BLACKOUTS OR FITS?' → the two positives come only if asked: puffy ankles in the evenings, and three kilos in a fortnight → ACKNOWLEDGE AND MARK IT: 'thank you — that's important and it changes how urgently we need to act', then CONTINUE THE LIST.

THE THREE FETAL QUESTIONS — never skip them: 'and how is the baby — are you feeling him move as much as usual? Any bleeding from below, or any fluid loss? Any tightenings, contractions or tummy pain?' Then RISK FACTORS in one minute, prioritising the two that are positive: 'have you ever had high blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease? IS THIS YOUR FIRST PREGNANCY? Single baby or twins? DOES HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE IN PREGNANCY RUN IN YOUR FAMILY? Any autoimmune conditions such as lupus? Was it conceived through IVF? Were your early bloods and scans normal, and did you have the sweet-drink diabetes test? And do you smoke, take any medications, or have any allergies?' (Two risk-factor questions are worth more than eight background ones. If the clock beats you: 'in the interest of time I'll move on to examining you — I'd also want to review her booking bloods, growth scans and blood pressure record.')

CONSENT AND EXPOSURE, then steps 1-5: 'I'll look at your eyes with a small torch, listen to your heart and chest, feel your tummy and check on the baby, then look at your legs and test your reflexes. I'll need your tummy uncovered and your legs from the knee down. Would you like a chaperone?' Then: 'alert and orientated, comfortable at rest, NO PURPURIC RASH, PETECHIAE OR BRUISING. Hands — no pallor of the palmar creases, no swelling of the fingers. MAY I CHECK YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE MYSELF? 162 over 102, CONFIRMING THE SEVERE RANGE. Look up — no conjunctival pallor. Look down — no scleral jaundice. NO PERIORBITAL OEDEMA. EXAMINER, MAY I HAVE THE OPHTHALMOSCOPE? I'd like to perform FUNDOSCOPY, LOOKING FOR PAPILLOEDEMA AND HYPERTENSIVE RETINOPATHY.' → 'you cannot obtain a view' → 'thank you — I'd want a formal assessment, AND I WOULDN'T DELAY TREATMENT FOR IT.'

HEART, CHEST, ABDOMEN AND FETUS: 'heart sounds are dual, no murmurs. Could you sit forward for me? I'm auscultating the LUNG BASES FROM BEHIND, SPECIFICALLY LISTENING FOR BIBASAL CRACKLES THAT WOULD SUGGEST PULMONARY OEDEMA — the chest is clear. I'm going to feel your tummy gently now — specifically checking RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT TENDERNESS — none — and UTERINE TENDERNESS, WHICH WOULD CONCERN ME ABOUT PLACENTAL ABRUPTION — the uterus is soft and non-tender. Symphysio-fundal height 30 centimetres, appropriate for 30 weeks. On Leopold's the lie is longitudinal, the presentation cephalic. May I have a stethoscope or Doppler and a timer for the fetal heart rate? 148, normal.'

LEGS, REFLEXES, URINE — three things asked at once: 'Examiner, IS THERE ANY OEDEMA — AND IF SO, DOES IT PIT, AND TO WHAT LEVEL DOES IT EXTEND?' → pitting to the mid-shin → 'Sarah, I'm going to test your reflexes — just let your leg go floppy. The ANKLE JERK IS BRISK. Now I'm testing for CLONUS — a quick stretch of the ankle — there are no sustained beats of clonus. The urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. That completes my examination — let me cover you up.' (The examiner gives findings only in response to a PRECISE question: 'is there oedema?' gets you less than the three-part version.)

NAME IT, SAY IT IS SERIOUS, SAY WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, THEN STOP: 'Sarah, from your blood pressure and the protein in your urine, I believe you have a condition called PRE-ECLAMPSIA. It happens in the second half of pregnancy — the blood pressure rises and the kidneys start to leak protein into the urine, and it can affect several other parts of the body too... I KNOW YOU FEEL COMPLETELY WELL, AND THAT IS VERY COMMON WITH THIS CONDITION — but I want to be honest with you: IT IS SERIOUS, FOR YOU AND FOR THE BABY, AND IT CAN CHANGE QUICKLY. So what I'd like to do is ADMIT YOU TO HOSPITAL TODAY. Blood tests, a monitor for the baby, a tablet to bring your blood pressure down, and the obstetric team to see you. Because you're 30 weeks they may also give an injection that helps the baby's lungs mature. THE ONLY THING THAT FULLY CURES PRE-ECLAMPSIA IS DELIVERING THE BABY, so the team will be weighing up the best timing — but nothing is happening this minute. What questions do you have?' (Under-selling — 'a bit of high blood pressure, we'll keep an eye on it' — misses the severity mark; over-selling with fits and stillbirth loses the communication mark.)

HER PUSHBACK, and the summary: 'admitted? Today? I've got work tomorrow — can't I just come back tomorrow? I feel fine' → 'I understand, and I'm sorry to disrupt your day. But THIS IS ONE OF THE CONDITIONS WHERE FEELING WELL DOESN'T TELL US HOW YOU'RE DOING — it can change over hours. I'd be doing you a disservice if I sent you home. Is there someone we can call to bring some things in for you?' If she asks about the baby: 'today his heartbeat is normal and his growth measures right for your dates, which is reassuring... I can't promise you an outcome, but I can promise you'll both be watched extremely closely.' Then to the examiner: pre-eclampsia with severe-range hypertension at 30 weeks — admit, bloods, urine protein:creatinine ratio, CTG, labetalol, betamethasone, consider magnesium sulfate, and call the obstetric registrar now.
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute splits: history 3:30, examination 7:00, diagnosis 7:45
ask: 'I'd like to ask some questions, then examine you, then explain what I think is going on.' / 'I'm going to ask about some specific symptoms — most will be a no, but I need to check each one.' / 'Any headaches that don't settle with paracetamol?' / 'Any blurring of vision, double vision, or flashing lights?' / 'Any pain up under your ribs on the right, or in the pit of your stomach?' / 'Have you noticed any sudden rapid weight gain?'

'Is the baby moving as much as usual? Any bleeding or fluid loss?' / 'Examiner, may I have the ophthalmoscope? I'm looking for papilloedema and hypertensive retinopathy.' / 'I'm listening at the bases specifically for bibasal crackles suggesting pulmonary oedema.' / 'I'm checking right upper quadrant tenderness, and uterine tenderness which would concern me about abruption.' / 'Examiner, is there oedema — does it pit, and to what level does it extend?' / 'The ankle jerk is brisk — I'm now testing for clonus.'

'I know you feel completely well, and that's very common with this condition.' / 'It is serious, for you and for the baby, and it can change quickly.' / 'I'd like to admit you today so we can look after you and the baby closely.' / 'Feeling well doesn't tell us how you're doing — it can change over hours.' THREE THINGS NEVER TO SAY: 'try not to worry', 'it's probably nothing', 'we'll see you next week' — and if you do say one, the role-player brightens and asks 'oh good, so I can go home then?' to see whether you correct yourself.

VARIANT 1 — HEADACHE IN THE STEM: explore for 30-40 seconds, then get back on the list — 'how bad is it out of ten? Worse at any time of day? Anything make it better or worse? And has anything come with it — any change in your vision, any nausea?' → a headache unresponsive to paracetamol PLUS FLASHING SPOTS puts her in SEVERE pre-eclampsia with neurological features: say so in your summary and make MAGNESIUM SULFATE part of the plan. / VARIANT 2 — SUSTAINED CLONUS ('the reflexes are brisk and there are more than five sustained beats') → 'thank you — THAT IS A SIGNIFICANT FINDING. Sustained clonus indicates central nervous system irritability and marks IMPENDING ECLAMPSIA. This makes her SEVERE pre-eclampsia regardless of the blood pressure. I'd escalate immediately: call the obstetric registrar now, move her to a monitored area, LOAD MAGNESIUM SULFATE 4 grams IV over 20 minutes then 1 gram per hour, control the blood pressure, give betamethasone as she is under 34 weeks, and prepare for delivery once she is stable.' If she says 'you're scaring me': 'I don't want to frighten you, but I do want to be straight with you... you're in the safest place you could be.'

VARIANT 3 — SHE REFUSES ADMISSION: respect autonomy WITHOUT simply letting her walk out — 'I can hear how disruptive this is, and I'm sorry. Can I explain why I'm being firm about it? Pre-eclampsia is one of the few conditions where how you feel doesn't tell us how you're doing. It can change over hours, and the two things I worry about — FITS, and THE BABY'S BLOOD SUPPLY — can happen without warning.' → 'and if I still say no?' → 'then it remains your decision, and I won't force you. But I'd ask you to let me do the blood tests and the baby's monitoring before you go, and to come straight back — day or night — if you get a headache, any change in your vision, pain under your ribs, swelling that comes on quickly, or if the baby moves less. I'd also like to arrange review tomorrow morning and, with your permission, speak to your partner. WOULD YOU BE WILLING TO TALK IT THROUGH WITH THE OBSTETRIC CONSULTANT BEFORE YOU DECIDE?' The marks are autonomy, specific safety-netting, a compromise, and escalation to a senior.
pefe: Role-player: Sarah Whitfield, 28, primary school teacher still working, living with her partner Tom; first pregnancy, 30 weeks, single baby conceived naturally. SHE FEELS COMPLETELY WELL and was not expecting anything to be wrong — the midwife took her blood pressure twice and asked her to wait. NO serious symptoms. TWO THINGS ONLY, AND ONLY IF ASKED: puffy ankles in the evenings, and about 3 kg gained in two weeks which she assumed was the baby. No hypertension, diabetes or kidney disease; MOTHER HAD HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE WHEN PREGNANT with her younger brother; pregnancy multivitamin only, no allergies, never smoked; booking bloods, dating and 20-week scans and the 26-week glucose test all normal. Cheerful and cooperative at the start, increasingly worried as the questions go on; if told she needs admission she becomes UPSET AND RESISTANT — she has work tomorrow and nothing packed. HIDDEN AGENDA: frightened of a caesarean and of the baby being born early, not said unless the doctor asks about worries or invites questions, otherwise raised at the very end: 'does this mean he'll have to be born early?' She answers 'no' briskly to the red-flag questions and volunteers NOTHING. If told 'try not to worry' or 'it's probably nothing', she looks relieved and says 'oh good, so I can go home then?' If examined roughly or without warning: 'what are you doing?' Tearful only if told the baby may need to be born early.

Numbers: hypertension = systolic 140 or more, or diastolic 90 or more, NEW AFTER 20 WEEKS; SEVERE RANGE 160/110 or more; treatment target about 130-150 over 80-100. Dipstick screens, PCR 30 mg/mmol or more confirms. LABETALOL 100-200 mg orally two to three times daily. MAGNESIUM SULFATE 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour, continued 24 hours after delivery or the last fit. BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM twice, 24 hours apart, if under 34 weeks. Aspirin 100-150 mg nightly from 12 weeks to about 36 weeks in the next pregnancy. PLATELETS UNDER 100 is a severe feature. FHR 110-160. SFH weeks plus or minus 2-3 cm. SPLITS: history 3:30, examination 7:00, diagnosis 7:45.

Score out of 10, one point each: introduced, confirmed identity, signposted the plan; asked an OPEN question before the list; covered ALL the red flags — headache, vision, epigastric pain, nausea, chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, swelling and weight, urine output, jaundice or bruising; asked about FETAL MOVEMENTS, bleeding, fluid loss and contractions; asked risk factors INCLUDING first pregnancy and family history; consented and exposed appropriately; ASKED FOR THE OPHTHALMOSCOPE BY NAME; examined heart and chest, and abdomen for right upper quadrant AND uterine tenderness; checked fetal wellbeing and tested the ankle jerk AND clonus; and NAMED PRE-ECLAMPSIA, said it was serious, arranged admission, and invited questions.
fails: ★ Opening with reassurance ('it's probably nothing') or with alarm before you have any information — and 'try not to worry' or 'we'll see you next week' at any point
★ Missing the two positives because you never asked about swelling or sudden weight gain — she volunteers nothing
Forgetting the three fetal questions — movements, bleeding or fluid loss, contractions
Chasing a positive down a rabbit hole: thirty to forty seconds on the headache, then back to the list, because THE LIST is what is scored

Asking eight background questions and never asking the two risk factors that are positive here, so you never get to say 'she has two risk factors'; asking 'is there oedema?' instead of oedema-pitting-level; skipping clonus because time ran out; and under-selling or over-selling the diagnosis instead of naming it, saying it is serious, saying what happens next, and stopping

setting: POSTNATAL WARD ROUND — day 1 after a caesarean. THIS IS A REFERENCE RUN-SHEET RATHER THAN A SCRIPTED STATION, so use it for a postnatal review station, a ward-round handover, or a written note. THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: THE COMMONEST DAY-1 MISS IS ANCHORING ON THE WOUND. Fundal tone, the pad, the calves and the FIRST VOID AFTER IDC REMOVAL are where the pathology actually is — and HEADACHE WITH VISUAL SYMPTOMS ON DAY 1 IS PRE-ECLAMPSIA UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, not a spinal headache.

BEFORE YOU WALK IN, READ THE CHART: the op note (indication, elective versus emergency and category, incision, uterine closure, estimated blood loss, complications); the ANAESTHETIC chart (spinal, epidural or GA, intrathecal morphine, last top-up, block height); the DRUG chart (is VTE prophylaxis charted? Is analgesia regular or PRN only?); bloods (group and screen, ANTI-D STATUS, rubella and varicella immunity, pre- and post-op Hb); the BABY'S chart (weight, Apgars, vitamin K, hepatitis B, newborn exam); and the observation and MEOWS trend with fluid balance and urine output.

time: WHAT TO ASK, in blocks: PAIN AND RECOVERY · how she feels, did she sleep, pain score AT REST AND ON MOVEMENT, wound pain versus uterine cramping (afterpains, worse with feeding), nausea, ITCH from intrathecal morphine, tolerating diet and fluids · BLEEDING, BLADDER, BOWELS · lochia by pads and how soaked, clots, odour; IDC in or out and when, VOIDED SINCE REMOVAL, volume, stream, dysuria, incomplete emptying; flatus, bowel motion, distension suggesting ileus · MOBILITY · out of bed, walking, dizzy on standing, RESIDUAL LEG WEAKNESS OR NUMBNESS · ASK DIRECTLY AND DO NOT ASSUME: VTE (calf pain or swelling, chest pain, breathlessness); SEPSIS (fever, rigors, wound discharge, offensive lochia, urinary symptoms); HEADACHE · postural after neuraxial block versus headache with visual disturbance or epigastric pain, because LATE PRE-ECLAMPSIA CAN PRESENT UP TO SIX WEEKS POSTPARTUM · FEEDING AND BABY · latch, nipple pain, milk coming in, feed frequency; wet nappies, meconium, jaundice, sleepy or poor feeder; vitamin K, hepatitis B, newborn exam, hearing screen, and the NEWBORN SCREEN DUE DAY 2-3 · PSYCHOSOCIAL · mood, tearfulness, coping, support at home, other children, transport home.

back.dx: WHAT TO CHECK, system by system: OBS — temperature, heart rate, BP, respiratory rate, saturations, MEOWS trend, urine output, fluid balance. GENERAL — pallor, hydration, comfort, sitting up or lying flat. CHEST AND LEGS — air entry and respiratory rate (atelectasis after GA), calf tenderness or swelling, TEDs on, residual motor or sensory block. ABDOMEN — soft versus distended, bowel sounds, tenderness BEYOND the wound. FUNDUS — firm and contracted, at or just below the umbilicus by day 1; BOGGY OR TENDER MEANS ATONY OR ENDOMETRITIS. WOUND — dressing intact, ooze, haematoma, erythema, drain output. PAD — lochia rubra, volume, clots, smell. BREASTS — engorgement, cracked nipples, erythema or mastitis. LINES — IDC and IVC, and remove whatever is no longer needed. INVESTIGATIONS: FBE on day 1 if EBL over 500-1000 mL, symptomatic or clinically pale; group and hold; add CRP, MSU and blood cultures ONLY if febrile or unwell, because DAY-1 CRP IS UNHELPFULLY RAISED BY SURGERY ALONE. THE PLAN, eleven items: (1) regular paracetamol 1 g QID plus an NSAID unless contraindicated, with oxycodone PRN — all breastfeeding-compatible, and AVOID CODEINE because of the ultra-rapid metaboliser risk to the neonate; (2) IDC out at 12-24 hours once the block has worn off, documenting first void and volume, with a post-void residual if retention is suspected; (3) VTE prophylaxis — enoxaparin per local risk assessment, TEDs, early mobilisation, hydration, continued on discharge if risk factors persist; (4) free diet with aperients written up; (5) wound dressing down at 24 hours; (6) ANTI-D 625 IU IM WITHIN 72 HOURS if she is Rh negative and the baby Rh positive; (7) MMR before discharge if rubella non-immune, avoiding pregnancy 28 days, and dTpa if not given antenatally; (8) iron if anaemic; (9) lactation consultant for any feeding difficulty; (10) CONTRACEPTION BEFORE DISCHARGE — implant or POP immediately, IUD at 6 weeks (or immediate post-placental if inserted at the caesarean), COC from 6 weeks if breastfeeding; (11) discharge day 2-4 with a wound check day 5-7, GP six-week check, child health nurse, pelvic floor advice, no heavy lifting for about six weeks, and driving once she can brake hard without hesitation and is off sedating analgesia — flagging VBAC versus elective repeat caesarean for next time.
plan: CHART

Read before you walk in: op note, anaesthetic chart, drug chart (VTE prophylaxis charted? analgesia regular or PRN?), bloods including ANTI-D STATUS and rubella immunity, the baby's chart, and the obs and MEOWS trend with fluid balance.
ASK

Pain at rest AND on movement; wound pain versus afterpains; nausea and ITCH; lochia by pads with clots and odour; IDC status and THE FIRST VOID; flatus and bowel motion; mobility and residual block; and then ASK DIRECTLY for VTE, sepsis and the headache distinction — postural after a block, versus visual disturbance or epigastric pain, which is PRE-ECLAMPSIA UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.
ASK

Feeding and baby: latch, nipple pain, milk coming in, feed frequency; wet nappies, meconium, jaundice, sleepiness; vitamin K, hepatitis B, newborn exam, hearing screen, and the newborn screen due day 2-3. Then MOOD, coping, support at home, other children, transport home, smoking and alcohol, and a safe sleeping plan.
EXAMINE

Obs and MEOWS; general appearance; chest and CALVES with TEDs and residual block; abdomen soft or distended with tenderness BEYOND the wound; FUNDUS firm and 1 cm below the umbilicus; wound dressing; THE PAD; breasts; and the lines — remove what is not needed.
INVESTIGATE
FBE if EBL over 500-1000 mL, symptomatic or pale; group and hold. CRP, MSU and cultures only if febrile or unwell — day-1 CRP is raised by the surgery itself.
PLAN

The eleven items (see dx): analgesia without codeine, IDC out with a documented void, VTE prophylaxis, diet and aperients, wound dressing, anti-D within 72 hours, MMR and dTpa gaps, iron, lactation support, CONTRACEPTION BEFORE DISCHARGE, and discharge planning with the wound check, six-week GP review and driving advice.
SAFETY-NET

Say these out loud before she leaves: heavy bleeding or large clots; fever or rigors; offensive discharge; wound redness, discharge or breakdown; calf pain or swelling; chest pain or breathlessness; severe headache or visual disturbance; and LOW MOOD OR THOUGHTS OF HARMING HERSELF OR THE BABY.
ISBAR

Presenting her in thirty seconds: I — 'it's [name], [role], on the postnatal ward.' S — 'day 1 post [emergency Cat 2 / elective] caesarean for [indication]. She's well and stable.' B — 'spinal, lower segment transverse, EBL __ mL, uncomplicated. Baby feeding well.' A — 'obs normal, MEOWS 0. Fundus firm, lochia normal, wound clean, calves soft, VOIDED AFTER IDC REMOVAL. Pain controlled. Hb __.' R — 'plan is analgesia, VTE prophylaxis, aperients, MMR, contraception counselling, discharge day 3. Happy for you to review the wound — anything you'd like added?'

THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE, worth rehearsing on its own: the commonest day-1 miss is ANCHORING ON THE WOUND. Fundal tone, the pad, the calves and the first void after IDC removal are where the pathology actually is — and headache with visual symptoms on day 1 is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise, not a spinal headache.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — postnatal ward, MANNEQUIN AND EXAMINER ONLY, so you introduce yourself to the EXAMINER. FIVE STARRED ITEMS, ANY ONE MISSED IS A FAIL: the RED REFLEX through the ophthalmoscope in both eyes; the PHRASE 'dysmorphic features' with three or four named; HIPS — creases first, then Barlow, then Ortolani, both named; BOTH TESTES palpated with 'undescended testis' said aloud; and a MORO demonstrated and described as symmetrical. Plus commentary maintained throughout — SILENCE IS THE COMMONEST REASON CANDIDATES FAIL. And because the stem says INSTRUMENTS: fontanelle not bulging, clavicles intact, Moro symmetrical.
stem: Postnatal ward. A neonatal mannequin supine on the cot; the examiner is the only other person in the room. A NEWBORN BOY, SIX HOURS OLD, delivered vaginally WITH INSTRUMENTS. His mother has already consented and is not present. 8 minutes.

Background held by the examiner: forceps for a prolonged second stage at 39+4, birth weight 3.4 kg, head circumference 35 cm, Apgars 8 and 9; fed once, passed urine, no meconium yet. HIDDEN FINDING: A FIRM SWELLING OVER THE RIGHT PARIETAL BONE THAT DOES NOT CROSS THE SUTURE LINES — released only when you palpate the skull AND say what you are looking for.

back.dx: A NORMAL SIX-HOUR-OLD TERM MALE — or, in the scripted run, normal APART FROM A CEPHALOHAEMATOMA. THE SCALP TRIAD AND THE SUTURE RULE: CAPUT SUCCEDANEUM is oedema above the periosteum, present at birth, soft, pits, CROSSES suture lines, resolves in 24-48 hours; CEPHALOHAEMATOMA is subperiosteal blood, appears hours after birth, firm then fluctuant, LIMITED BY the suture lines, resolves over two weeks to three months; SUBGALEAL HAEMORRHAGE CROSSES the sutures, is boggy, SHIFTS WITH HEAD POSITION, can hold a large proportion of the blood volume and CAN KILL — volume resuscitation, cross-match, coagulation screen, serial head circumference, neonatal unit. Manage a cephalohaematoma CONSERVATIVELY — no imaging, NEVER aspirate or incise — monitor bilirubin because resorbing blood causes jaundice, check haemoglobin if large, confirm vitamin K, and safety-net for worsening jaundice, poor feeding, unusual sleepiness or an enlarging swelling. OTHER ANSWERS TO HAVE READY: absent or white red reflex means CONGENITAL CATARACT or RETINOBLASTOMA — same-day ophthalmology, cataract needs early surgery to prevent amblyopia and retinoblastoma is life-threatening. A positive Ortolani is DEVELOPMENTAL DYSPLASIA — hip ultrasound at about six weeks and paediatric orthopaedics — and BREECH, FEMALE SEX, FIRST-BORN, FAMILY HISTORY AND OLIGOHYDRAMNIOS ALL WARRANT IMAGING EVEN WITH A NORMAL EXAMINATION. An undescended testis is re-examined at six weeks and three months, referred by three to six months, orchidopexy by twelve. Bilateral impalpable testes WITH hypospadias raise a difference of sex development — urgent paediatric endocrine and surgical review, DO NOT confirm sex assignment, check for a salt-losing crisis, and NO CIRCUMCISION because the foreskin is needed for repair. Screening before discharge: bloodspot at 48-72 hours, hearing screen, pulse oximetry with pre- and post-ductal saturations, vitamin K and hepatitis B, measurements plotted in the state child health record, six-week check.
plan: WIPE TO THE EXAMINER, because he is the only person in the room: 'good morning, I'm Dr -, one of the doctors on the postnatal ward. I'm washing my hands and putting on gloves. Before I begin I'd like to confirm baby's identity against his wristband, and confirm that his mother has consented. COULD I ALSO HAVE HIS OBSERVATIONS, WEIGHT AND HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE, AND CONFIRM WHETHER HE HAS FED, PASSED URINE AND PASSED MECONIUM? I'll examine him head to toe on a warmed surface, keeping him covered between regions.' (The stem gives consent, so candidates skip the opening and dive at the doll — say it anyway, it costs eight seconds and it is scored. No meconium yet is fine: expected within 24-48 hours.)

APPEARANCE, THEN AUSCULTATE BEFORE HE CRIES: 'he is pink — no jaundice, cyanosis or pallor. He is lying with his arms and legs FLEXED AND HELD THERE, which tells me his tone is normal — this is not a floppy baby. There is NO RESPIRATORY DISTRESS: no grunting, no nasal flaring, no tracheal tug, no intercostal or subcostal recession. Before he starts crying I'll auscultate first. The neonatal chest is smaller than my diaphragm, so TWO POSITIONS COVER ALL FOUR VALVE AREAS — upper chest, lower chest. Rate regular, normal first and second heart sounds, no murmur. Now the lungs, two levels, comparing side with side — air entry equal, no added sounds.' (Respiratory distress is an INSPECTION finding of the chest — say it while looking, not while listening. And a soft systolic murmur at six hours is often a closing duct: if well with normal pulses and pre- and post-ductal saturations, re-examine before discharge; if it persists, echocardiogram.)

THE SKULL — what this stem was written for: 'given that instruments were used, I'm paying particular attention to the head. Inspecting and palpating the skull, I'm looking for a CEPHALOHAEMATOMA, WHICH WOULD BE LIMITED BY THE SUTURE LINES, and for a SUBGALEAL SWELLING, WHICH WOULD CROSS THEM and feel boggy and shift with head position.' → 'there is a firm swelling over the right parietal bone' → ASK BEFORE YOU NAME IT: 'DOES THE SWELLING CROSS THE SUTURE LINE, OR DOES IT STOP AT IT?' → 'it stops at the suture' → 'then this is a cephalohaematoma — subperiosteal blood following the instrumental delivery.' Then: 'skull shape otherwise normal, no plagiocephaly or moulding ridge. The ANTERIOR FONTANELLE IS SOFT AND FLAT — NOT BULGING, which is reassuring after an instrumental delivery — posterior fontanelle palpable, sutures neither overriding nor widely separated.' (That single anatomical question is the mark, and the strongest moment in the station.)

EYES, MOUTH, EARS, DYSMORPHISM: 'eyes normally spaced and symmetrical, no strabismus, no subconjunctival haemorrhage. COULD I HAVE THE OPHTHALMOSCOPE? HOLDING IT A SHORT DISTANCE AWAY AND LOOKING THROUGH IT, I'm checking each eye and then comparing the two for a symmetrical RED REFLEX. An absent or white reflex would mean a congenital cataract or a retinoblastoma.' Then rooting, sucking with a gloved little finger while running it along the hard and soft palate for a cleft, plus bifid uvula and tongue tie; ears for deformity, low set, preauricular pits or tags, and the hearing screen. Then STAND BACK: 'looking at the face as a whole, I'M SCREENING FOR DYSMORPHIC FEATURES — no upslanting palpebral fissures, no epicanthic folds, no flat nasal bridge, no low-set ears, no short neck, no micrognathia. THE FACE IS NOT DYSMORPHIC.' (Doing fundoscopy up close instead of the distance red reflex loses the technique mark; and doing the individual features without ever saying the PHRASE misses the box the examiner is ticking.)

NECK, LIMBS, PULSES, ABDOMEN, STUMP: 'in the neck I'm feeling for a MIDLINE lump suggesting a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST and a LATERAL lump suggesting a BRANCHIAL CYST — no lumps. Given the instrumental delivery I'm also palpating BOTH CLAVICLES for a fracture — no step, no crepitus. Arms move symmetrically and are held flexed — no Erb's palsy. Digits fully formed, no polydactyly or syndactyly. Brachial and radial pulses present and equal, and I'll compare them with the FEMORAL PULSES, because RADIO-FEMORAL DELAY AND WEAK FEMORAL PULSES ARE THE SIGNS OF COARCTATION. Abdomen soft, not distended. BECAUSE HE IS ONLY SIX HOURS OLD I want to examine the UMBILICAL STUMP — clean and dry, three vessels, no redness or discharge to suggest omphalitis. No hernias. Liver edge one to two centimetres below the costal margin is normal at this age; no splenomegaly, no masses.' (Radio-RADIAL delay is a subclavian lesion; say the femoral version. And the stump is remembered, not seen — the doll has no cord, and it is a deliberate discriminator against the six-week version.)

THE HIPS — the step you will not pass without: 'now the most important part of the neonatal examination. The nappy is off. FIRST, INSPECTION, BEFORE ANY MANOEUVRE: the skin creases of the thighs and buttocks are symmetrical, and I'd compare limb length, which is difficult on this model. BARLOW first — I flex both hips and knees to ninety degrees, thumb on the inner thigh and fingers over the greater trochanter, adducting slightly while pushing posteriorly, one side then the other. I AM TRYING TO DISLOCATE A HIP THAT IS CURRENTLY IN JOINT. No clunk. Now ORTOLANI — holding both thighs, abducting both hips together like opening a book, lifting anteriorly. I AM TRYING TO RELOCATE A HIP THAT IS ALREADY DISLOCATED, feeling for a clunk as the femoral head slides back into the acetabulum. No clunk, abduction full and symmetrical.' (Skipping inspection is the single commonest fail; performing both manoeuvres without naming them or their purpose loses the mark; and arriving here with forty seconds left loses the station.)

GENITALIA, ANUS, LOWER LIMBS: 'genitalia are normal male. PALPATING GENTLY FROM THE INGUINAL CANAL DOWN INTO THE SCROTUM on each side — I'm checking that BOTH TESTES ARE DESCENDED, because an UNDESCENDED TESTIS is one of the key findings of this examination. No hydrocele, no inguinal hernia. The urethral meatus is at the tip — no hypospadias, no epispadias. The anus is patent and normally positioned — no imperforate anus — and I'd confirm meconium has been passed. Legs move symmetrically, no talipes.' (Inspecting from a metre away and calling them normal fails — you must be SEEN to palpate, and the words must be said. The mannequin is a boy for exactly this reason.)

MORO, SPINE, TONE, THEN THE FORTY-SECOND SUMMARY: 'the MORO — I support the head and shoulders in one hand, lift slightly and allow a SMALL CONTROLLED DROP — the sensation of falling, never an actual drop. A normal Moro is SYMMETRICAL abduction and extension of the arms with opening of the hands, then adduction back in; asymmetry would suggest a brachial plexus injury or a fractured clavicle. Turning him over: no midline swelling, defect or hairy patch to suggest spina bifida, no sacral dimple or naevus. VENTRAL SUSPENSION — prone along my forearm, he holds his head roughly in the plane of his body and keeps his limbs flexed against gravity, so tone is normal; a HYPOTONIC baby would drape over my hand. I'll dress him, settle him and wash my hands.' Then the summary as a rehearsed block, ending with the plan: plot measurements in the child health record, confirm vitamin K and hepatitis B, bloodspot at 48-72 hours, hearing screen, six-week check. (Floppy is HYPOtonia; hypertonia is the stiff, extended, fisted baby with scissoring legs. And reserve the last forty seconds — a structured summary is worth more than one extra reflex.)

THE THREE SENTENCE SHAPES THAT CARRY THE STATION: 'I am looking for [named condition] — I do not find it'; 'the model doesn't allow this; on a baby I would [do X], looking for [named condition]'; and 'for time I will state rather than perform the following, and I'm happy to demonstrate any of them.'

EXAMINER QUESTIONS: caput versus cephalohaematoma (above versus below the periosteum, crosses versus limited by sutures, 24-48 hours versus 2 weeks to 3 months); WHICH WORRIES YOU MOST — neither: the SUBGALEAL, which crosses the sutures, is boggy, shifts with head position, can hold a large proportion of the blood volume, and needs volume resuscitation, cross-match, coagulation screen, serial head circumference and neonatal unit care; managing the cephalohaematoma conservatively with bilirubin monitoring and NEVER aspirating; the five key points; why auscultate first; what screening before discharge; and the rural retrieval answer — stabilise locally, call the neonatal consultant early, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, RFDS for remote fixed-wing, keep the parents with the baby, and involve an Aboriginal Liaison Officer or the Aboriginal Family Birthing Program if the family identifies.

VERSION B — THE SIX-WEEK CHECK WITH THE MOTHER AT THE BEDSIDE: everything changes except your hands. You obtain consent yourself, explain in lay terms, and candidates historically failed by translating every single step and never reaching the hips. THE OPENING CONTRACT THAT BUYS THE STATION: 'I'll work through him fairly quietly so I can hear his heart properly, and then I'll SIT DOWN AT THE END and tell you everything I've found. Please stop me at any point.' — NEVER promise a running explanation. THREE MID-EXAMINATION REASSURANCES ONLY: after the chest ('his heart and breathing sound completely normal'), after the eyes ('a healthy red glow at the back of the eye'), after the hips ('some babies are born with a hip that isn't sitting properly in its socket, and it's much easier to treat when picked up early'). Two items drop out — the umbilical stump, and cephalohaematoma — and two gain weight: head circumference plotted, and feeding and weight gain. Keep SIXTY SECONDS for a lay-terms closing summary, invite questions, and safety-net poor feeding, unusual sleepiness or floppiness, fever, or simply being worried. Her likely questions: the soft spot ('a normal gap that lets his brain grow, usually closes between twelve and eighteen months, safe to touch and wash'), why you keep checking the hips, and 'he was pulled out with forceps — has that damaged him?'
pefe: Partner brief: THEY PLAY THE EXAMINER, NOT A PATIENT — sit with a rolled towel or soft toy as the doll, hold a stopwatch, and SUPPLY FINDINGS ONLY WHEN THE CANDIDATE EXAMINES FOR THEM AND SAYS WHAT THEY ARE LOOKING FOR. If they touch something silently, say nothing. That asymmetry is the whole point. Be FLAT AND UNHELPFUL by default — do not nod encouragingly, do not finish their sentences, do not rescue them from silence. PUSH ONCE ON THE SKULL: give the swelling, then WAIT; if they name it without asking about the suture, ask 'how do you know it isn't a subgaleal haemorrhage?' PUSH ONCE ON THE HIPS: 'if this baby had been breech and your examination were entirely normal, would you do anything else?' — the highest-yield question you can ask. VOLUNTEER THE MISSED ITEM LATE: if they never mention the umbilical stump, wait until the summary and then ask 'he is six hours old — was there anything else on the abdomen?' Call the bell at exactly eight minutes, mid-sentence if necessary. AND START A TALLY EVERY TIME THEY GO QUIET FOR MORE THAN FIVE SECONDS — report the count at the end, because silence is the commonest reason candidates fail this station.

SCORING — ANY STARRED ITEM MISSED IS A FAIL: red reflex with the ophthalmoscope in both eyes; the phrase 'dysmorphic features' plus three or four named; hip INSPECTION then Barlow then Ortolani, all named; scrotum palpated and 'undescended testis' said aloud; Moro performed and described as symmetrical; and commentary maintained with fewer than three silences. Also marked: introduced self, gloves, identity, consent, observations; auscultated before disturbing the baby; named all three scalp swellings and the suture rule; ASKED whether the swelling crossed the suture; linked fontanelle, clavicles and Moro symmetry to the instruments; mentioned the umbilical stump; femoral pulses and coarctation; anus and spine; ventral suspension; kept the baby warm, covered and handled gently with hands washed; and delivered a structured summary with a plan before the bell.
