Examiner, there is TENDERNESS ACROSS THE LEFT ANTERIOR CHEST WALL IN A SEATBELT DISTRIBUTION, with no crepitus and no palpable step. On auscultation, air entry is equal and vesicular bilaterally with no added sounds. EXAMINER, MAY I HAVE THE RESPIRATORY RATE COUNTED OVER ONE FULL MINUTE, AND THE OXYGEN SATURATION?' → 18 and 98% → 'breathing is adequate, though THE CHEST WALL TENDERNESS WILL NEED A CHEST X-RAY AND ADEQUATE ANALGESIA TO PREVENT HYPOVENTILATION.' (Percussion, tactile fremitus and vocal resonance belong to a full respiratory examination and the secondary survey — if asked, say exactly that.)

C — AND WHERE BLOOD HIDES: 'assessing circulation. The RADIAL PULSE is present, regular and of GOOD VOLUME. I would also confirm a CENTRAL pulse. Capillary refill is under two seconds, and his peripheries are warm and well perfused with no pallor. EXAMINER, MAY I HAVE A BLOOD PRESSURE AND A PULSE RATE? I can see no external bleeding. I WOULD LOOK FOR CONCEALED BLEEDING IN FIVE PLACES — THE CHEST, THE ABDOMEN, THE PELVIS, THE LONG BONES AND ON THE FLOOR. I would site TWO LARGE-BORE CANNULAE and send bloods including a group and hold. Circulation is stable. Moving to disability.' → 'why is his blood pressure high?' → 'in a 25-year-old with a GCS of 15, I would attribute that to PAIN AND ANXIETY with catecholamine release rather than to a rising intracranial pressure. A CUSHING RESPONSE IS HYPERTENSION WITH BRADYCARDIA AND AN IRREGULAR RESPIRATORY PATTERN, and his pulse and respiratory rate are normal. I would treat his pain and recheck it.'

D — DISABILITY, including the two things candidates drop: 'John, squeeze my fingers for me. Examiner: his eyes are open spontaneously, that is 4; he is talking and orientated, that is 5; he obeys commands, that is 6 — A GCS OF 15 OUT OF 15. Pupils are equal at 3 millimetres, reactive directly and consensually, with an intact swinging light test. He moves all four limbs on command. I WOULD LIKE A BEDSIDE BLOOD GLUCOSE. John, ARE YOU IN ANY PAIN? Where is it, and out of ten? I WOULD GIVE HIM TITRATED INTRAVENOUS ANALGESIA NOW.' (Forgetting the glucose misses that a crash may have been CAUSED by hypoglycaemia; and no analgesia despite a stated pain score is an automatic fail.) If the torch is too close: 'not too close, please' — apologise and continue.

E — EXPOSURE, named and not argued: 'I would fully expose the patient to complete my assessment, KEEPING HIM WARM with a blanket and warmed fluids and PRESERVING HIS DIGNITY.' → 'no — please don't' → ONE SENTENCE: 'that is fine, John. Examiner, I will note that I WOULD expose him fully in a real resuscitation.' Then, if he asks about the driver: 'I do not have that information yet, and I PROMISE I WILL FIND OUT FOR YOU as soon as I can. Right now my whole job is you — is that all right?'

THE CERVICAL SPINE — DISCUSS, DO NOT DO: 'Examiner, I would now like to assess the cervical spine and decide whether it can be CLEARED CLINICALLY or whether he needs imaging. I would apply THE NEXUS CRITERIA: no midline cervical tenderness on palpation of the spinous processes, no focal neurological deficit, a normal level of alertness, no evidence of intoxication and no painful distracting injury. If all five were satisfied I would ask him to move his neck actively through a full pain-free range. HE HAS TOLD ME HIS NECK IS SORE, SO ON THE INFORMATION I HAVE HIS SPINE IS NOT CLEARABLE AND THE COLLAR STAYS ON PENDING IMAGING. I AM NOT GOING TO REMOVE THE COLLAR MYSELF.' → 'what imaging?' → 'CT cervical spine.'

THE HANDOVER, LETTER BY LETTER, then the plan: 'in summary, a haemodynamically stable trauma patient with a normal primary survey apart from chest wall tenderness in a seatbelt distribution and midline neck pain. I would like a CHEST AND PELVIC X-RAY AND AN eFAST as adjuncts, ANALGESIA, a CT CERVICAL SPINE, and then a SECONDARY SURVEY INCLUDING A LOG ROLL.' → 'why not do a secondary survey?' → 'the task was a primary survey, and I would not begin a head-to-toe assessment until the primary survey is complete and the adjuncts are under way. If there is time I am happy to outline it: head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, limbs, log roll and back, then the perineum.'

pefe: Role-player: John Delaney, 25, diesel mechanic, front-seat passenger when his mate's ute left the road on the way back from Kadina and hit a tree two hours ago; seatbelt on, airbag deployed, no loss of consciousness, remembers everything. Lie on the trolley in a gown and a hard collar, FULLY ALERT, co-operative and a bit frightened, answering normally in short sentences. FINDINGS: MIDLINE NECK SORENESS about six out of ten — say so if asked about pain, AND THIS IS THE FINDING THAT STOPS THE COLLAR COMING OFF; chest tender across the left side where the belt sat, about five out of ten, with 'ah, there' and a wince when palpated; mouth opens fully with mild jaw ache; everything else normal.

HOW TO PLAY IT: SAY 'HI DOCTOR' AS SOON AS THEY REACH YOU, BEFORE THEY START — and watch whether they use it. If they shine the torch close to your face: 'can you not shine that right in my eye' — they should apologise and continue. If they try to expose you: 'NO — PLEASE DON'T', and the examiner voice says 'that is fine' — they should accept it in ONE sentence, not argue. IF THEY TRY TO TAKE THE COLLAR OFF OR ASK YOU TO TURN YOUR HEAD, DO NOT MOVE — examiner voice: 'no' — AND MARK IT AS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL. At around minute five, ask 'WHAT ABOUT THE DRIVER?' and note whether they acknowledge it and return to the task. IF THEY NEVER ASK ABOUT PAIN, SAY NOTHING AND MARK IT DOWN. If they start palpating the abdomen or doing a full chest examination: 'your task is the primary survey.' If the summary is unstructured: 'can you structure that for me?'

Scored out of 20: introduced and gained assent; danger, response, send for help; excluded catastrophic haemorrhage; airway voice and stridor; airway face and mouth with a torch; airway neck, emphysema, trachea, COLLAR KEPT ON; breathing inspection, palpation and auscultation both sides; asked for respiratory rate and saturations; circulation pulse rate, rhythm and volume; capillary refill and perfusion; asked for blood pressure; NAMED THE FIVE SITES OF CONCEALED BLEEDING; GCS in three components; pupils and gross limb movement; ASKED FOR A BLOOD GLUCOSE; PAIN SCORE AND OFFERED ANALGESIA; named exposure and warming; and a handover structured letter by letter.

THE MANNEQUIN GIVES YOU NOTHING: every observation you would have made must be SPOKEN, or it did not happen. SIX AUTOMATIC FAILS: a bare total with no components; a score of 8 with NO MENTION OF THE AIRWAY; THREE SEPARATE PAINFUL STIMULI; nail-bed pressure used to score the motor component; saying 'the motor scale is different in children'; and any mention of a GCS of zero.
stem: Emergency department, regional hospital; you are the HMO. THOMAS, 8 YEARS OLD, brought in by ambulance after being FOUND UNRESPONSIVE AT HOME. His mother is on her way and NO HISTORY IS AVAILABLE. Primary survey complete, on oxygen by mask, cervical spine immobilised AND CLEARED RADIOLOGICALLY. Full-body ALS mannequin; the examiner reads out the responses when you apply each stimulus. A GCS chart and pen on the trolley. 8 minutes.
tasks: Assess this child's level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale, explaining each step to the examiner
State his score with its components
Answer the examiner's questions
time: ENTRY, HAND HYGIENE, CONTEXT · and ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS INCLUDING THE BLOOD GLUCOSE, which is four extra words and the one reversible cause you can exclude at the bedside · GENERAL APPEARANCE BEFORE YOU TOUCH HIM, with NAMED NEGATIVES: no decorticate flexion, no decerebrate extension, not pale or cyanosed, no Cheyne-Stokes or Kussmaul pattern, no external injury, no scalp swelling, AND NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES · THE VERBAL SCREEN, four sentences with four pauses, then SAY WHAT IT WAS FOR · ONE PAINFUL STIMULUS, WARNED AND CENTRAL, a trapezius squeeze sustained up to ten seconds, which gives you all three components at once · THE ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION WORTH ASKING: did the arm cross the midline towards the stimulus, or move away from it · SCORE ALOUD COMPONENT BY COMPONENT WITH THE BEHAVIOUR JUSTIFYING EACH, and say WHICH SCALE YOU USED AND WHY · THEN THE AIRWAY SENTENCE IMMEDIATELY, the completion offers, the repeat at fifteen minutes, and THE SAFEGUARDING SENTENCE · then the six viva questions.

back.dx: E2 V2 M4 = 8 OUT OF 15, IN THE SEVERE RANGE — eyes did not open to voice but opened to pain (E2); an incomprehensible sound with no recognisable word (V2); the limb PULLED AWAY WITHOUT CROSSING THE MIDLINE, so WITHDRAWING rather than localising (M4). AND SAY WHICH SCALE: 'at eight years I have used the standard adult scale, SINCE THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR.' THE AIRWAY SENTENCE MUST FOLLOW THE TOTAL: a GCS of 8 or less means he is unlikely to protect his own airway, so arrange airway protection NOW with anaesthetics and intensive care in parallel. THE SIX VIVA ANSWERS. (1) WHICH COMPONENT DIFFERS IN A CHILD: THE VERBAL RESPONSE, BELOW FOUR YEARS — under four, 5 is alert and babbling or words normal for age, 4 is fewer words than usual or a spontaneous irritable cry, 3 is crying only to pain, 2 is moaning to pain, 1 is none; the EYE column is identical at every age, and the motor column changes only at the top, where 6 becomes spontaneous purposeful movement and 5 becomes withdrawal to touch. (2) LOWEST SCORE: THREE, one per component, NO ZERO AT ANY AGE — a deceased patient still scores 3. (3) INTUBATED AND SEDATED: V1 WITH A T ANNOTATION — and say explicitly that sedation and paralysis invalidate the eye and motor components too, so the post-intubation score cannot be compared with the pre-intubation one, which is why documenting the score BEFORE intubation matters. (4) WHY NOT NAIL-BED PRESSURE: it is PERIPHERAL, producing a SPINAL REFLEX withdrawal rather than a brain-mediated response, so it cannot score the motor component — trapezius is central, reproducible and does not bruise; a sternal rub bruises and makes localisation harder to demonstrate; supraorbital pressure risks eye injury. (5) ASYMMETRY: score the BEST response on the BETTER side, so M5 — but REPORT THE ASYMMETRY SEPARATELY, because a difference between sides suggests a lateralised intracranial lesion and matters more than the total. (6) WHAT WOULD MAKE YOU DISTRUST THE SCORE: sedation or paralysis, intubation, PERIORBITAL SWELLING preventing eye opening (E1 with a C annotation), hypoglycaemia or hypothermia, a pre-existing developmental or speech disorder, and a language barrier — recording the limitation beside the score rather than presenting the number as clean.
plan: ENTRY AND THE GLUCOSE: 'Hello, my name is Doctor -, one of the doctors here in the emergency department. THOMAS, I AM GOING TO CHECK YOU OVER NOW. I WILL BE GENTLE AND I WILL TELL YOU BEFORE I DO ANYTHING.' [Sanitise hands.] 'Examiner, I note the primary survey is complete and the cervical spine has been immobilised and cleared. BEFORE I BEGIN, MAY I HAVE HIS OBSERVATIONS, INCLUDING HIS BLOOD GLUCOSE?' → 5.1 → 'thank you — the glucose is normal, SO I HAVE EXCLUDED HYPOGLYCAEMIA AT THE BEDSIDE.'

GENERAL APPEARANCE, BEFORE YOU TOUCH HIM, with named negatives: 'on general appearance he is lying still with NO ABNORMAL POSTURING — no decorticate flexion and no decerebrate extension. He is not pale and not cyanosed. His breathing is regular, with no CHEYNE-STOKES or KUSSMAUL pattern. I can see no obvious external injury, no scalp swelling and NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES.' → 'why do you mention bruising?' → 'BECAUSE IN A CHILD WITH AN UNEXPLAINED REDUCED CONSCIOUS STATE I HAVE TO CONSIDER NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY.' (On a mannequin, the named negatives are the only thing you can be marked for at this step.)

THE VERBAL SCREEN — four sentences, four pauses, then say what it was for: 'Thomas, can you hear me?' ... 'Thomas, open your eyes.' ... 'What is your name?' ... [fingers placed into his palm] 'Can you squeeze my fingers?' → no response → 'THOSE FOUR QUESTIONS SCREEN EYE OPENING TO VOICE, THE VERBAL RESPONSE AND MOTOR OBEDIENCE TO COMMAND, WITHOUT HURTING HIM. As there is no response to any of them, I now need a painful stimulus.' (Going straight to the sternum is both unkind and lower-scoring — the verbal screen is free and covers three components.)

ONE PAINFUL STIMULUS, WARNED AND CENTRAL: 'Examiner, I am going to apply A SINGLE CENTRAL PAINFUL STIMULUS. Thomas, I am going to squeeze your shoulder now, and it may be uncomfortable.' [Trapezius squeeze, firm, SUSTAINED UP TO TEN SECONDS.] → 'he opens his eyes; he makes a groaning sound with no recognisable words; his right arm pulls away from your hand but does not come across his body towards it.' (THREE SEPARATE STIMULI, ONE PER COMPONENT, IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL — one sustained stimulus gives you all three at once, and using three tells the examiner you do not understand the test.)

THE ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION WORTH ASKING: 'thank you. CAN I JUST CONFIRM WHETHER THE ARM CROSSED THE MIDLINE TOWARDS THE STIMULUS, OR MOVED AWAY FROM IT? THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN LOCALISING AND WITHDRAWING.' → 'it moved away; it did not cross the midline.' (Asking it once, precisely, shows you know the discriminator BEFORE you use it. Repeatedly asking the examiner to interpret findings for you is a different behaviour and scores badly.)

SCORE ALOUD, COMPONENT BY COMPONENT: 'on EYE OPENING, he did not open his eyes to voice but opened them to the painful stimulus, so that is E2. On BEST VERBAL RESPONSE, he made an incomprehensible sound with no recognisable word, so that is V2. On BEST MOTOR RESPONSE, he pulled the limb away from the stimulus without bringing it across the midline towards it, so he is WITHDRAWING RATHER THAN LOCALISING — M4. That gives a total GCS of 8 OUT OF 15, WHICH IS IN THE SEVERE RANGE. AT EIGHT YEARS I HAVE USED THE STANDARD ADULT SCALE, SINCE THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR.' (A bare 'his GCS is 8' is an automatic fail — on a mannequin the commentary is the ONLY evidence you performed the assessment.)

THE AIRWAY SENTENCE IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE TOTAL, then the completion offers: 'A GCS OF 8 OR LESS MEANS HE IS UNLIKELY TO BE ABLE TO PROTECT HIS OWN AIRWAY, SO I WOULD ARRANGE AIRWAY PROTECTION NOW and involve anaesthetics and intensive care in parallel. To complete my neurological assessment I would examine his PUPILS for size, symmetry and the direct light reflex; perform FUNDOSCOPY looking for papilloedema and RETINAL HAEMORRHAGES; assess TONE, REFLEXES AND PLANTARS ON BOTH SIDES LOOKING FOR ASYMMETRY; look for signs of a BASE-OF-SKULL FRACTURE; assess for NECK STIFFNESS, since the cervical spine is cleared; and REPEAT THE SCORE IN FIFTEEN MINUTES, BECAUSE THE TREND MATTERS MORE THAN ANY SINGLE READING.' Then the parallel management if pushed: high-flow oxygen, IV access, bloods including a gas, electrolytes, liver and renal function, FBC and a TOXICOLOGY SCREEN, urgent CT head, empirical meningitis cover if febrile, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval.

THE SAFEGUARDING SENTENCE, said once and neutrally — not saying it at all is the more common error: 'I would also want a careful, NON-JUDGEMENTAL history from his mother about how he was found and what happened beforehand, BECAUSE IN A CHILD WITH AN UNEXPLAINED REDUCED CONSCIOUS STATE I HAVE TO ACTIVELY CONSIDER ACCIDENTAL INGESTION AND NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY.' IF THE MOTHER ARRIVES: 'hello, I am Doctor -, one of the doctors looking after Thomas. I am very glad you are here. Thomas is unconscious and we do not yet know why, so we are checking him thoroughly and getting the team ready to help him breathe safely. I am not going to guess at a cause until we have looked properly. CAN I ASK YOU TWO QUICK QUESTIONS THAT WILL HELP HIM RIGHT NOW — HOW WAS HE FOUND, AND IS THERE ANY MEDICINE IN THE HOUSE HE COULD HAVE REACHED?' (Two targeted questions from a parent are worth more than anything else in the room; reassuring her he will be fine, or making her wait, is the trap.)

THE SIX VIVA QUESTIONS (see dx), answered precisely. AND IF THE EXAMINER DISAGREES WITH YOUR SCORE — 'I would have called that M5' — neither argue nor collapse: 'THAT MAY WELL BE RIGHT, AND I WOULD BE HAPPY TO BE CORRECTED. My reasoning was that the arm moved away from the stimulus rather than crossing the midline towards it, which is the discriminator I use between withdrawal and localisation. IF IT DID CROSS THE MIDLINE THEN IT IS M5 AND THE TOTAL BECOMES 9.' State the discriminator, accept the correction, and RECOMPUTE THE TOTAL OUT LOUD.

THERE IS NO ZERO. This is a peri-arrest situation: confirm he has a pulse and is breathing, call a resuscitation team immediately, and secure the airway.'

THE DETERIORATING CHILD, fifteen minutes later — no eye opening, no sound, BOTH ELBOWS FLEX ONTO THE CHEST, pulse 48, BP 132/80 → 'E1, V1, M3 — ABNORMAL FLEXION, WHICH IS DECORTICATE POSTURING — a total of 5. THAT IS A FALL OF THREE POINTS, which is a significant deterioration in its own right. THE BRADYCARDIA WITH HYPERTENSION IS A CUSHING RESPONSE and indicates raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation. I would call for immediate senior help, secure the airway, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, NURSE HIM HEAD-UP AT THIRTY DEGREES, arrange an urgent CT head and speak to neurosurgery, AND I WOULD NOT PERFORM A LUMBAR PUNCTURE.'
pefe: Partner brief: THERE IS NO PATIENT ROLE — the patient is a mannequin (a pillow, a rolled towel, or a housemate lying still with eyes shut and instructed not to react). YOU ARE THE EXAMINER: stand beside the candidate, say nothing unless asked, and READ OUT THE FINDINGS ONLY WHEN THE CORRECT STIMULUS IS APPLIED, then ask the six questions. The correct answer is E2 V2 M4 = 8. Observations on request: HR 72, BP 108/64, RR 12, SpO2 97% on oxygen, T 36.4 — AND THE GLUCOSE 5.1 ONLY IF THEY ASK, never volunteered. On general appearance: 'that is all correct', then 'WHY DO YOU MENTION BRUISING?' To the verbal screen: 'there is no response to any of those.' To ONE warned central stimulus: 'he opens his eyes; he makes a groaning sound with no recognisable words; his right arm pulls away from your hand.' To a second or third stimulus: repeat the same findings AND MARK IT DOWN. To nail-bed or earlobe pressure: 'the arm pulls away', then ask question 4 early. Pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm; fundi normal; tone, reflexes and plantars normal and symmetrical; no neck stiffness.

THE THREE MOMENTS THAT DECIDE THE STATION: do they WARN THE CHILD before the painful stimulus? Do they GIVE THE COMPONENTS, or just the total — a bare '8' is a fail, and DO NOT PROMPT THEM, wait and let the silence sit. And do they SAY THE AIRWAY SENTENCE — a score of 8 without any mention of airway protection is the second automatic fail. Timing prompts: at 4 minutes, if they have not scored, 'please give me your score'; at 5 minutes start the six questions regardless of where they are; and throughout, if they ask you to interpret a finding more than once, say 'YOU TELL ME'.

Numbers: E 1-4, V 1-5, M 1-6, total 3-15, NO ZERO. This station E2 V2 M4 = 8. THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR YEARS VERIFY. Verbal under 4: 5 alert or babbling normally, 4 fewer words than usual or irritable cry, 3 cries only to pain, 2 moans to pain, 1 none. Motor under 4: 6 spontaneous purposeful movement, 5 withdraws to touch; rows 4 to 1 unchanged. THE EYE COLUMN IS UNCHANGED AT EVERY AGE. M5 LOCALISES — crosses the midline, above the clavicle, reaches you; M4 WITHDRAWS — away, never reaches you. Severity mild 13-15, moderate 9-12, severe 8 or less VERIFY. A fall of 2 or more triggers senior review and re-imaging. One central stimulus, warned, up to 10 seconds. Best response, better side, then report asymmetry separately. Intubated V1 T; eyes swollen shut E1 C. Weight (age + 4) x 2 = 24 kg at eight. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, WCH paediatric retrieval, Poisons Information 13 11 26 VERIFY.

Lying still; NO decorticate or decerebrate posturing; not pale or cyanosed; breathing regular with no Cheyne-Stokes or Kussmaul; no external injury, no scalp swelling, NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES
NO response to any of the four questions
HE OPENS HIS EYES (E2) · A GROANING SOUND WITH NO RECOGNISABLE WORDS (V2) · THE RIGHT ARM PULLS AWAY WITHOUT CROSSING THE MIDLINE (M4)
E2 V2 M4 = 8 — the SEVERE range
Pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm; fundi normal with no papilloedema or retinal haemorrhages; tone, reflexes and plantars normal and symmetrical; no neck stiffness

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED, RESUSCITATION MANNEQUIN, and THE FATHER IS THE ONLY PERSON IN THE ROOM WHO CAN TALK. ONE WARM SENTENCE TO HIM INSIDE THE FIRST FIFTEEN SECONDS, then narrate the sequence out loud. FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: never naming a diagnosis; never speaking to the father at all; CALLING THE CHILD STABLE BECAUSE THE SATURATIONS ARE 98% ON OXYGEN; and PROMISING HIM THE CHILD WILL BE FINE. The three words that must be said: STRIDOR, WHEEZE, ANAPHYLAXIS.
stem: Emergency department. A 2-YEAR-OLD BOY brought in by his father with SWOLLEN LIPS AND DIFFICULTY BREATHING; background of ATOPY (eczema and hay fever), a flu-like illness two weeks ago, and TODAY HE ATE PEANUTS AT A BIRTHDAY PARTY. Symptoms over the last 60 minutes. Full-body resuscitation mannequin, supine, OXYGEN MASK IN PLACE; the father is at the bedside and frightened. PAEDIATRIC CUFFS IN THREE SIZES, an aneroid sphygmomanometer, stethoscope, pulse oximeter and thermometer on the trolley. 8 minutes.
tasks: Measure the vital signs and explain the steps of measuring them
Perform an anterior chest examination
Give your diagnosis
time: HAND HYGIENE, THEN THE FATHER: 'I can see you are very worried, and I would be too... he is in safe hands', and permission in one sentence, because for a two-year-old CONSENT COMES FROM THE PARENT · THEN DRSABCD, EACH NUMBER INTERPRETED AGAINST THE CHILD'S AGE: general appearance and AIRWAY FIRST, looking for foreign body, vomitus and LIP AND TONGUE SWELLING · BREATHING: look, listen and feel, RESPIRATORY RATE OVER A FULL SIXTY SECONDS, and SATURATIONS BOTH WITH AND WITHOUT THE MASK · CIRCULATION: BRACHIAL pulse in a two-year-old, rate over sixty seconds with rhythm and volume, capillary refill centrally and peripherally · THE CUFF, justified by the 40% RULE and chosen from the labels rather than measured with a tape · BLOOD PRESSURE IN TWO STEPS, palpatory THEN auscultatory, naming K1 AND K5 · TEMPERATURE, which is one of the five AND does diagnostic work here · THEN THE ANTERIOR CHEST: inspect (naming the specific signs of distress and the skin), palpate expansion and trachea, percuss, auscultate side against side in three zones and the axillae · AND CONNECT THE TWO SOUNDS · then the diagnosis to the examiner and ONE PLAIN SENTENCE to the father.

back.dx: ANAPHYLAXIS, most likely to PEANUT, WITH AIRWAY INVOLVEMENT — a two-year-old with a background of atopy who developed swollen lips and difficulty breathing within an hour of eating peanut; tachypnoeic at 44, tachycardic at 168, normotensive at 88/54, afebrile at 36.9, and OXYGEN DEPENDENT at 98% on the mask and 91% off it; with STRIDOR indicating UPPER airway obstruction and WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE indicating BRONCHOSPASM, plus lip swelling and urticaria. Differentials, all less likely given the acute onset after a known allergen, the lip swelling and THE ABSENCE OF FEVER: croup, epiglottitis, an inhaled foreign body, and acute asthma. MANAGEMENT even though not asked: INTRAMUSCULAR ADRENALINE IMMEDIATELY — 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 into the OUTER MID-THIGH, about 0.12 mL for an estimated 12 kg — KEPT LYING FLAT, oxygen continued, and senior paediatric and anaesthetic help called; repeat at five minutes; 20 mL/kg saline if hypotensive; observe at least four hours after the last dose. AND THE INTERPRETATIONS THAT CARRY THE MARKS: RR 44 is well above the normal 20-30 for a two-year-old; HR 168 is above the normal 90-140, and A SLOW HEART RATE WOULD WORRY YOU FAR MORE, because BRADYCARDIA IN A DISTRESSED CHILD IS A PRE-ARREST SIGN; 88 systolic is normal, with the threshold roughly 70 PLUS TWICE HIS AGE, about 74 — and HYPOTENSION IN ANAPHYLAXIS IS A VERY LATE SIGN, SO A NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE IS NOT REASSURING; and the absence of fever is what makes croup and epiglottitis less likely.
plan: HANDS, THEN THE FATHER — one warm sentence inside fifteen seconds: [sanitise hands] 'Hello, my name is Doctor -, I am one of the doctors here. Are you Jack's dad? I CAN SEE YOU ARE VERY WORRIED, AND I WOULD BE TOO. I am going to check him over now, find out what is going on, and give him the best treatment we have. HE IS IN SAFE HANDS. I will talk you through everything as I go. Is it all right with me to examine him?' (If he interrupts again mid-examination: 'THAT IS A REALLY IMPORTANT QUESTION AND I PROMISE I WILL ANSWER IT FULLY IN JUST A MINUTE. Right now the fastest way I can help Jack is to finish checking him over. STAY RIGHT WHERE HE CAN SEE YOU.' Acknowledge, promise, keep going — and NEVER say 'he will be fine'.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND AIRWAY FIRST: 'Examiner, on general appearance I am assessing whether Jack is ALERT AND RESPONSIVE — looking at me, reaching for his father, crying or resisting — and I am LISTENING FROM THE END OF THE BED for audible noisy breathing, stridor or wheeze. Moving to airway: I would look in the mouth for a foreign body or vomitus, and SPECIFICALLY FOR SWELLING OF THE LIPS AND TONGUE. May I have those findings?' → 'the airway is patent; the child has stridor; the lips are swollen' → SAY WHAT IT MEANS IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you — STRIDOR MEANS OBSTRUCTION OF THE UPPER AIRWAY, and in this context that is a serious sign that changes my urgency.' (Being handed the word stridor and not interpreting it is exactly what the examiner is testing.)

BREATHING — and ask for BOTH saturations: 'assessing breathing. I would LOOK for chest movement, and LISTEN AND FEEL for air at the mouth and nose. I would COUNT THE RESPIRATORY RATE OVER A FULL 60 SECONDS and measure the oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter on the finger or toe. Examiner, MAY I HAVE HIS RESPIRATORY RATE, AND HIS SATURATIONS BOTH WITH AND WITHOUT THE MASK?' → 44, and 98% with, 91% without → INTERPRET BOTH: 'a respiratory rate of 44 is well above the normal 20 to 30 for a two-year-old — he is TACHYPNOEIC. And HE IS ONLY MAINTAINING HIS SATURATIONS ON OXYGEN, so he is OXYGEN DEPENDENT and the mask stays on.' (Asking only for saturations on the mask, reporting 98% and calling the child stable is an automatic fail.)

CIRCULATION — pulse first, and the bradycardia line: 'assessing circulation. HE IS BREATHING AND HAS A PULSE, SO I AM NOT STARTING COMPRESSIONS. In a two-year-old I would use the BRACHIAL pulse, count the rate over 60 seconds and comment on rhythm and volume, and check capillary refill centrally and peripherally.' → HR 168, refill 2 s → '168 is above the normal 90 to 140 for his age — he is tachycardic, which fits distress and early shock. I WOULD BE FAR MORE WORRIED BY A SLOW HEART RATE IN A CHILD THIS UNWELL, BECAUSE BRADYCARDIA IN A DISTRESSED CHILD IS A PRE-ARREST SIGN.'

THE CUFF AND THE BLOOD PRESSURE IN TWO STEPS: 'before I take a blood pressure I want the correct cuff size. THE BLADDER WIDTH SHOULD BE ABOUT 40% OF THE MID-ARM CIRCUMFERENCE, and the length should encircle 80 to 100% of the arm. The paediatric cuffs are labelled, and IF TWO SIZES WOULD FIT, GUIDANCE IS TO TAKE THE LARGER. For a two-year-old I will take the small child cuff.' → 'what happens if the cuff is too small?' → 'IT OVER-READS the blood pressure; too large UNDER-READS.' Then: 'I would measure it in two steps. FIRST, PALPATORY: I palpate the brachial pulse, inflate until it disappears, then deflate slowly — the pressure at which the pulse returns is my estimated systolic. THAT STEP PREVENTS ME BEING CAUGHT BY AN AUSCULTATORY GAP. SECOND, AUSCULTATORY: stethoscope over the brachial artery below the cuff, inflate 20 to 30 mmHg above the palpated systolic, deflate slowly. THE FIRST KOROTKOFF SOUND IS SYSTOLIC; THE DISAPPEARANCE OF SOUND, THE FIFTH, IS DIASTOLIC.' → 88/54 → 'normal for his age — the threshold I would worry about is roughly 70 plus twice his age, about 74 — BUT HYPOTENSION IN ANAPHYLAXIS IS A VERY LATE SIGN, SO A NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE IS NOT REASSURING.' (Measuring the mannequin's arm with a tape, or spending two minutes comparing cuffs, wastes the station: name the rule, read the label, choose.)

TEMPERATURE AND THE SUMMARY OF THE VITALS: 'finally I would take his temperature, ideally axillary or tympanic in a child of this age.' → 36.9 → 'so to summarise the vital signs: he is TACHYPNOEIC at 44, TACHYCARDIC at 168, NORMOTENSIVE at 88 over 54, AFEBRILE at 36.9, and OXYGEN DEPENDENT with saturations of 98% on the mask and 91% off. THE ABSENCE OF FEVER IS IMPORTANT — IT MAKES CROUP AND EPIGLOTTITIS LESS LIKELY.' (Forgetting the temperature is an automatic fail — it is one of the five, and here it also does diagnostic work.)

THE ANTERIOR CHEST, in order and with the specific signs named: '[to father] I am going to lift his top so I can see his chest. [To examiner] Inspecting the anterior chest. I am looking at chest movement in the upper and lower zones for symmetry, and for signs of respiratory distress: TRACHEAL TUG, INTERCOSTAL RECESSION, SUBCOSTAL RECESSION, PARADOXICAL ABDOMINAL MOVEMENT, ACCESSORY MUSCLE USE, NASAL FLARING, HEAD BOBBING AND GRUNTING. I am also looking at the skin for URTICARIA, flushing or swelling. Palpating for chest expansion, hands on the lateral chest with my thumbs toward the xiphisternum, comparing sides. Two fingers into the suprasternal notch — checking the trachea is central. Percussing both sides at the same level, comparing left with right down to the bases. Auscultating the same points, side against side, in the upper, mid and lower zones and out into the axillae — I would use a PAEDIATRIC DIAPHRAGM if available. I would also assess vocal resonance, ALTHOUGH A TWO-YEAR-OLD WILL NOT SAY NINETY-NINE ON REQUEST, so I would listen while he cries or talks.' (If tempted to roll the mannequin: 'THE TASK IS THE ANTERIOR CHEST, SO I AM NOT EXAMINING THE BACK.')

CONNECT THE TWO SOUNDS, THEN NAME IT: 'so he has STRIDOR, WHICH IS INSPIRATORY AND COMES FROM THE UPPER AIRWAY, and WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE, WHICH COMES FROM THE LOWER AIRWAY. HE HAS OBSTRUCTION AT BOTH LEVELS.' Then the full diagnosis to the examiner with the differentials and the management sentence (see dx), and finally ONE PLAIN SENTENCE TO THE FATHER: 'Jack is having a SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION, almost certainly to the peanuts. It is making his airways swell and tighten. WE HAVE A MEDICINE CALLED ADRENALINE THAT WORKS VERY QUICKLY, AND I AM GOING TO GIVE IT NOW.' (Describing the findings without ever saying the word ANAPHYLAXIS fails task 3; and a three-minute explanation of IgE and mast cells to a frightened father is the opposite error.)
back.planNote: the source's eight-minute run
ask: 'I can see you are very worried, and I would be too. He is in safe hands.' / 'That is an important question and I will answer it fully in one minute — let me finish checking him first.' / 'Stridor means obstruction of the upper airway.' / 'Look, listen and feel — and I would count the respiratory rate over a full sixty seconds.'

'May I have his saturations both with and without the mask?' / 'He is only maintaining his saturations on oxygen — he is oxygen dependent.' / 'Bradycardia in a distressed child is a pre-arrest sign, not reassurance.' / 'The bladder width should be about 40% of the mid-arm circumference; if two would fit, take the larger.' / 'Too small over-reads; too large under-reads.' / 'First Korotkoff sound is systolic; disappearance, the fifth, is diastolic.'

'Stridor is upper airway and inspiratory; wheeze is lower airway and expiratory. He has obstruction at both levels.' / 'My diagnosis is anaphylaxis, most likely to peanut, with airway involvement.' / 'The task is the anterior chest, so I am not examining the back.' / To the father: 'Jack is having a severe allergic reaction... we have a medicine called adrenaline that works very quickly, and I am going to give it now.'

VARIANTS: HYPOTENSION AND COLLAPSE (BP 62/30, floppy and drowsy) → 'that systolic is well below the threshold for his age, roughly 70 plus twice his age, about 74. With drowsiness this is ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK. He needs intramuscular adrenaline immediately, TO BE KEPT LYING FLAT WITH HIS LEGS RAISED — NEVER STOOD UP — high-flow oxygen, intravenous or intraosseous access and a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, with the adrenaline repeated at five minutes and an infusion considered if he does not respond.' / IT IS CROUP (T 38.6, barking cough, hoarse voice, no lip swelling or rash, three days of coryza) → 'the barking cough, hoarse voice, fever and gradual onset over days fit CROUP — laryngotracheobronchitis — and the absence of an allergen, lip swelling and urticaria argues against anaphylaxis. Keep him CALM ON HIS FATHER'S LAP, avoid upsetting him, and give ORAL DEXAMETHASONE, with nebulised adrenaline if the stridor is severe or at rest.' VERIFY / IT IS EPIGLOTTITIS (T 39.2, drooling, sitting forward, muffled voice, not fully immunised) → 'this is EPIGLOTTITIS until proven otherwise. I WOULD NOT EXAMINE HIS THROAT, WOULD NOT LIE HIM DOWN AND WOULD NOT DISTRESS HIM. Leave him on his father's lap, oxygen if tolerated, and call immediately for senior ANAESTHETIC AND ENT help for a definitive airway IN THEATRE, with intravenous antibiotics once the airway is secure.'

MORE: THE FOREIGN BODY (wheeze only over the right chest, no rash or lip swelling, violent coughing while eating) → 'unilateral wheeze after a choking episode makes an INHALED FOREIGN BODY the leading diagnosis. HE IS CURRENTLY ABLE TO BREATHE, SO I WOULD NOT PERFORM BLIND FINGER SWEEPS OR BACK BLOWS — keep him calm, give oxygen, and arrange urgent ENT or paediatric surgical review for bronchoscopy.' / 'WHY NOT ANTIHISTAMINE FIRST?' → 'because antihistamines DO NOT TREAT AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION OR HYPOTENSION, and delay in giving adrenaline is one of the recognised contributors to FATAL anaphylaxis. Adrenaline is first line and there is NO ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION. Antihistamines have a role for the skin symptoms afterwards, and I would avoid promethazine in a child this young.' / THE EXAMINER RUSHES YOU ('assume all the vital signs are normal') → 'thank you. FOR COMPLETENESS, the observations I would have wanted are the respiratory rate over sixty seconds, saturations on and off oxygen, heart rate, rhythm and volume, capillary refill, blood pressure with an appropriately sized cuff, and temperature. Moving to the chest.' / THE FATHER BREAKS DOWN ('is he going to die?') → 'he is very unwell, AND I AM NOT GOING TO PRETEND OTHERWISE. But this is something we treat every week and we have the medicine for it right here. I am giving it now. STAY WHERE HE CAN SEE YOU AND HOLD HIS HAND — THAT HELPS HIM.'
pefe: Partner brief — THEY PLAY BOTH THE FATHER AND THE EXAMINER. Sam Whitlock, 34, father of Jack, 2: an hour ago Jack was at a cousin's birthday party and ate something with peanuts — a satay skewer or a slice of cake. Within about twenty minutes his lips went puffy and he started making a noise breathing in, and Sam drove him straight here. Jack has ECZEMA AND HAY FEVER, had a bad cold two weeks ago, HAS NEVER HAD A REACTION LIKE THIS BEFORE and has never been told he is allergic to anything; THERE IS NO EPIPEN AT HOME. No regular medicines except a steroid cream, immunisations up to date, no choking, no vomiting or diarrhoea, and the father's SISTER HAS A NUT ALLERGY. HE IS FRIGHTENED: start standing, leaning over the trolley, IN THE DOCTOR'S WAY — not aggressive, just scared and asking questions. IF THE DOCTOR ACKNOWLEDGES THE FEAR SPECIFICALLY IN THEIR FIRST FEW SENTENCES, sit down, calm noticeably, and interrupt only twice more. IF THEY WALK STRAIGHT PAST TO THE MANNEQUIN, INTERRUPT EVERY THIRTY SECONDS — 'what are you doing?', 'is he getting worse?', 'why is nobody doing anything?' — until they address you. If they say 'he will be fine', accept it BUT MARK IT DOWN, because nobody can promise that. At about six minutes ask once: 'IS HE GOING TO DIE?' At the end: 'WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG WITH HIM?' — and they must answer in PLAIN ENGLISH, not 'anaphylaxis with airway involvement'.

EXAMINER FINDINGS, GIVEN ONLY WHEN ASKED: mouth — 'no foreign body, no vomitus, the airway is patent'; general appearance and audible sounds — 'the child has STRIDOR'; lips and tongue — 'the lips are swollen, the tongue is not'; respiratory rate 44; saturations '98% with the mask' — AND GIVE THE 91% ONLY IF THEY ASK ABOUT OFF OXYGEN; pulse 'present, 168, regular, good volume'; capillary refill 2 seconds; BLOOD PRESSURE 88/54 — BUT ONLY AFTER THEY HAVE DESCRIBED BOTH THE PALPATORY AND AUSCULTATORY STEPS; temperature 36.9; inspection — 'tracheal tug and intercostal recession, urticarial rash over the trunk'; expansion symmetrical, trachea central, resonant and equal; auscultation — 'widespread expiratory wheeze in all zones'; the back — 'the task is the anterior chest'; blood gas, chest X-ray or tryptase — 'not available. What is your diagnosis?' IF THEY NEVER ASK FOR OBSERVATIONS, SAY NOTHING AT ALL AND MARK IT DOWN. Prompts: at 4 minutes 'please move on to the chest examination'; at 6:30 'what is your diagnosis?'; if they name anaphylaxis, 'what would you give, and by what route?'; if they choose a cuff, 'what happens if the cuff is too small?'

Numbers: cuff bladder width about 40% of mid-arm circumference, length 80-100%, TAKE THE LARGER of two. BP palpatory THEN auscultatory, inflating 20-30 mmHg above the palpated systolic; K1 systolic, K5 diastolic (K4 muffling in young children). NORMAL AT 2 YEARS VERIFY: HR 90-140, RR 20-30, systolic 85-100, SpO2 95% or more on air, T 36.5-37.5. HYPOTENSION FOR AGE is roughly systolic under 70 + (2 x age), about 74 mmHg. WEIGHT (age + 4) x 2 = 12 kg. ADRENALINE 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM, OUTER MID-THIGH, max 0.5 mg, repeat every 5 minutes — about 0.12 mL here. Autoinjector 150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 mcg over 20 kg. Saline 20 mL/kg bolus if hypotensive. OBSERVE AT LEAST FOUR HOURS after the last dose. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450, WCH for paediatric retrieval. Scored out of 10, one point each, with the automatic fails listed on the front of this card.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional GP, and THE STEM FORBIDS A CRANIAL NERVE EXAMINATION IN CAPITALS. THE STATION IS ONE SENTENCE: you will find the tender temporal artery early, AND FINDING THE SIGN AND STOPPING IS THE SINGLE COMMONEST FAIL — say out loud that you are completing a systematic examination before you commit. Six automatic fails: doing cranial nerves after the stem forbade it; stopping when you find the tenderness; OMITTING FUNDOSCOPY; OMITTING THE SHOULDER GIRDLE; reassuring her it is the jaw joint; and DELAYING STEROID FOR THE BIOPSY OR THE ESR.
stem: Regional general practice, Copper Coast. Mary Whitfield, 68, with HEADACHES rated 7/10, WORSE ON CHEWING, and feeling tired. BP 138/82 — pulse 84 — TEMPERATURE 37.4 — RR 16 — SpO2 98% — BGL 6.1. On the trolley: one handle with the OTOSCOPE AND OPHTHALMOSCOPE HEADS SUPPLIED SEPARATELY, gloves, tongue depressor, torch, Snellen chart. 8 minutes; STOP EXAMINING AT 6:20.
VERSION B: James Corby, 35, nasal congestion and headache worse leaning forward — acute sinusitis.
tasks: Perform a focused physical examination with a running commentary
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
time: ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS FIRST, then WIPE · AND WARN HER ABOUT TENDERNESS BEFORE YOU TOUCH HER, because she is briefed to wince · GENERAL APPEARANCE naming CACHEXIA AND PTOSIS, the two systemic and neurological items you can still have without cranial nerves · INSPECTION of scalp and face, every negative a differential excluded aloud · SYSTEMATIC PALPATION starting at the OCCIPUT and working forward, so the tender temple is found in sequence rather than jabbed at · THEN THE SENTENCE: 'that is highly suggestive, BUT I AM GOING TO COMPLETE A SYSTEMATIC EXAMINATION BEFORE I COMMIT' · periorbital margins, zygoma, mandible, SINUSES, parotid and salivary glands, and the GLOBES OFFERED BUT NOT PRESSED · THE TWO KEY POINTS: FUNDOSCOPY for a swollen pale chalky white disc, and THE SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLES for polymyalgia, which overlaps in about one in five · EARS with the otoscope ASSEMBLED, nose, mouth, throat and nine node groups, each site NAMED · THE TMJ examined SEPARATELY with one finger · neck and shoulders · then diagnosis in lay words WITH THE EYE RISK NAMED, and differentials in lay words.

back.dx: GIANT CELL ARTERITIS (TEMPORAL ARTERITIS) — a 68-year-old with six weeks of right-sided headache, JAW CLAUDICATION (pain worse on chewing), scalp tenderness, weight loss and fatigue, with a THICKENED, TENDER, NON-PULSATILE right superficial temporal artery and overlying erythema, a low-grade temperature, and SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLE STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER suggesting overlapping polymyalgia rheumatica. TO THE PATIENT IN LAY WORDS: a blood vessel running up the side of your head has become inflamed and swollen; chewing hurts because those muscles need extra blood and the narrowed vessel cannot deliver it; your immune system has started attacking your own blood vessels. THEN THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS: THE SAME VESSELS SUPPLY THE EYE, AND UNTREATED IT CAN CAUSE PERMANENT LOSS OF VISION — which is why treatment starts TODAY, BEFORE THE TESTS COME BACK. Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily VERIFY; IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for three days if there is visual loss VERIFY; ESR and CRP; temporal artery biopsy with an adequate segment WITHIN ONE TO TWO WEEKS, which stays useful after steroids have started VERIFY — and WAITING IS THE ONE THING THAT COSTS PEOPLE THEIR SIGHT. DIFFERENTIALS IN LAY WORDS: the jaw joint itself (her joint was not sore), a tooth or gum infection, a sinus infection, a salivary gland problem which can hurt with eating, an ear infection spreading to the bone behind the ear, and the commoner headaches — migraine and neck-related headache — 'none of them fit as well, AND NONE OF THEM CAN TAKE YOUR SIGHT'. Safety-net: any change in vision — blurring, a shadow, double vision — straight to an emergency department. IMPORTANT PHRASING: report the girdle as LIMITED BY PAIN AND STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER; polymyalgia does not cause true weakness, and reporting 'proximal weakness' describes a myositis instead. And a NORMAL FUNDUS DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, WIPE, AND THE WARNING: 'Examiner, may I have this patient's vital signs before I begin?' Then: '...I have been asked to examine your head and face today. I will look at your head, feel over different parts of it, look in your ears, eyes and mouth, and finish with some special tests. PARTS OF IT MAY BE TENDER, SO PLEASE TELL ME THE MOMENT ANYTHING HURTS AND I WILL STOP. Is that all right? I will just clean my hands and put on gloves.' (She is briefed to wince — a candidate who never warned her looks careless when she does.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND INSPECTION, both spoken: 'on general appearance my patient is sitting comfortably, alert and orientated with a normal level of consciousness, and not in obvious pain or distress. THERE IS NO CACHEXIA, NO PTOSIS, no facial asymmetry, no tremor and no abnormal limb posture.' Then: 'on inspection of the scalp and face, ON THE RIGHT I CAN SEE A PROMINENT, THICKENED, TORTUOUS, CORD-LIKE TEMPORAL ARTERY WITH OVERLYING REDNESS. No temporalis wasting. No vesicular rash. No periorbital swelling, no proptosis, no red eye. No raccoon eyes or Battle sign. No parotid swelling.' (Cachexia and ptosis are the two the examiner is listening for, because they are the systemic and neurological items you can still have without cranial nerves. And inspecting in silence throws away every excluded differential.)

SYSTEMATIC PALPATION — START AT THE BACK: 'Mary, I am going to feel gently through your hair now. Tell me if anything is sore. Starting at the back of the head... over the top... and forward to the forehead.' → she pulls away: 'ooh, that's very tender' → 'I'M SORRY, I'LL BE GENTLER. Examiner, there is MARKED TENDERNESS OVER THE RIGHT TEMPORAL REGION. THE RIGHT SUPERFICIAL TEMPORAL ARTERY IS THICKENED, TENDER AND NON-PULSATILE; THE LEFT IS NORMAL AND PULSATILE. THAT IS HIGHLY SUGGESTIVE, BUT I AM GOING TO COMPLETE A SYSTEMATIC EXAMINATION BEFORE I COMMIT. Periorbital margins, zygomatic arch, along the mandible — all non-tender.' (SAY THE COMPLETION SENTENCE OUT LOUD so the examiner records the decision — finding the sign and stopping is the single commonest fail in this station.)

SINUSES, GLANDS, GLOBES: 'pressing up under the brow ridges for the FRONTAL sinuses — any pain? And up under the cheekbones for the MAXILLARY sinuses? No sinus tenderness. Now over both cheeks for the PAROTID glands, and I would like to perform BIMANUAL PALPATION OF ALL THE SALIVARY GLANDS. Examiner, I would also like to MENTION gently assessing the globes for a hard, stony eye suggesting ACUTE GLAUCOMA — I WILL NOT PERFORM IT.' (Offer it; never press on the eyes.)

THE TWO KEY POINTS — both are automatic fails if omitted: 'Examiner, two things specific to my working diagnosis. FIRST, FUNDOSCOPY, LOOKING FOR A SWOLLEN, PALE, CHALKY WHITE DISC and for papilloedema.' → normal → 'thank you — NOTING THAT A NORMAL FUNDUS DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS. SECOND, THE SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLES, BECAUSE POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA OVERLAPS IN ABOUT ONE IN FIVE. Mary, lift both arms out to the side and hold them against my hands — and now stand up from the chair without using your arms.' → 'they've been stiff, especially first thing' → REPORT IT CORRECTLY: 'Examiner, SHOULDER GIRDLE MOVEMENT IS LIMITED BY PAIN AND STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER.' (Reporting 'proximal weakness' is wrong — polymyalgia does not cause true weakness, and if power really were reduced you would be describing a myositis.)

EAR, NOSE, MOUTH, THROAT, NODES — each site named, because each clears a differential: 'Examiner, I would like to examine the ears — MAY I ASSEMBLE THE OTOSCOPE?' [swap the heads] 'canals clear, drums intact, no bulging. Pressing behind the ears over the MASTOIDS — non-tender, no swelling. I would like to look inside the nose: septum central, no polyps, no discharge. Mary, open wide for me — I am looking for DENTAL CARIES OR AN ABSCESS, and for any ulcers or lesions in the mouth or throat. No caries, NO TENDER TOOTH ON PERCUSSION, no ulcers, no exudate. I will step behind you now for the neck glands: submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital and supraclavicular. No lymphadenopathy.' (Asking to do 'an ENT examination' as one lump loses the marks that live in the individual sites.)

THE TMJ, EXAMINED SEPARATELY WITH ONE FINGER, then neck and completion: 'a finger just in front of each ear — any pain? Now open and close slowly, and pretend to chew.' → 'no, that bit's not sore — the sore part is higher up' → 'joints non-tender, no crepitus or clicking, no deviation, OPENING ADMITS THREE FINGERS.' Then: 'down the spinous processes and paraspinal muscles — no tenderness. Show me your neck movements — full and pain-free. Now the shoulders themselves, actively and then passively. To complete I would CHECK THE BLOOD PRESSURE IN BOTH ARMS, PALPATE ALL PULSES AND LISTEN FOR BRUITS, take a focused history for VISUAL SYMPTOMS AND JAW CLAUDICATION, and perform a full neurological examination if permitted.' (Pressing with a flat hand over the temple and the joint together and then calling the joint tender is the trap — one finger, named landmark.)

DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS IN LAY WORDS (see dx), with THE EYE RISK NAMED and treatment started today. She pushes once: 'shouldn't you wait and see what the tests say?' → 'it's a fair question, but no. WAITING IS THE ONE THING THAT COSTS PEOPLE THEIR SIGHT, and the biopsy stays useful for a week or two after we start.' Then the differentials in her words and the safety-net. HER HIDDEN AGENDA: 'last Tuesday everything went dark in my right eye for a couple of minutes' — IF SHE SAYS THIS, STOP EVERYTHING: 'thank you for telling me — THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING YOU HAVE SAID TODAY... Examiner, this is AMAUROSIS FUGAX in the context of suspected giant cell arteritis. I would treat this as a SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY: intravenous methylprednisolone in the order of 500 to 1000 mg daily for three days, urgent ESR and CRP, and a SAME-DAY discussion with the on-call ophthalmology registrar. I will finish examining her, but I AM NOT WAITING FOR RESULTS BEFORE TREATING.' VERIFY (Filing it away and carrying on palpating converts a pass into a fail.)

'That is highly suggestive, but I will complete a systematic examination before I commit.' / 'I would like to MENTION assessing the globes rather than perform it.' / 'Fundoscopy, looking for a swollen, pale, chalky white disc.' / 'A normal fundus does not exclude the diagnosis.' / 'Girdle movement limited by pain and stiffness, WITH PRESERVED POWER.' / 'May I assemble the otoscope?'

'There is a blood vessel that runs up the side of your head, and it has become inflamed.' / 'The same vessels supply the eye.' / 'I want to start treatment today, before the tests come back.' / 'If your vision changes in any way, go straight to an emergency department.'

VERSION B — SINUSITIS AT 35: out go the temporal artery key points, arteritis-framed fundoscopy and the shoulder girdle; IN come a fuller nose examination, throat, teeth, and the cervical and supraclavicular nodes — and TEMPERATURE BECOMES A LIVE FINDING rather than a formality. The finding: 'tenderness over both maxillary sinuses, the turbinates are oedematous and there is purulent postnasal discharge... I would like to MENTION sinus transillumination, THOUGH I WOULD NOT RELY ON IT.' To the patient: 'the air spaces in your cheekbones and forehead are inflamed — that is why leaning forward makes it worse, the pressure builds. MOST OF THESE ARE VIRAL and settle in a week or so with saline rinses, a steroid nasal spray and simple painkillers; ANTIBIOTICS USUALLY DO NOT HELP. But I want you back straight away if the skin around your eye becomes swollen or red, if your eye starts to bulge or you see double, or if you become drowsy or very unwell.' VERIFY

VARIANT — THE DECOY JOINT: she says 'it's sore right here, IN FRONT of my ear — and it clicks when I open wide' → 'the tenderness is ON THE JOINT ITSELF, immediately in front of the tragus, with palpable crepitus and clicking on opening. THE TEMPORAL REGION ABOVE IT AND THE TEMPORAL ARTERY ARE NORMAL AND PULSATILE. That moves me AWAY from giant cell arteritis and towards TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DYSFUNCTION. I would still send ESR and CRP given her age, and I would tell her exactly what visual symptoms would bring her straight back.' (Diagnosing arteritis anyway because of the age and the chewing is exactly what the variant tests — whether you examine or pattern-match.) / THE EXAMINER SHUTS YOU DOWN — 'stick to your task, doctor' → 'THANK YOU, EXAMINER', then move straight on: no justification, no second attempt, no visible irritation.
pefe: Role-player: Mary Whitfield, 68, retired schoolteacher in Kadina, still driving and doing the church flowers; polite, understated, slightly apologetic, not wanting to make a fuss. Six weeks of right-sided headache most of the day at 7/10, barely touched by paracetamol; JAW ACHES AFTER A FEW MOUTHFULS so she leaves the crusts and cuts up meat; THREE KILOGRAMS LOST without trying; SCALP SORE WHEN BRUSHING HER HAIR; shoulders and hips stiff for an hour every morning; feels drained and a bit warm at night. Perindopril and knee osteoarthritis, non-smoker, two wines on a Friday. HIDDEN AGENDA: LAST TUESDAY HER RIGHT EYE WENT COMPLETELY DARK FOR ABOUT TWO MINUTES and came back — she has told nobody, having decided it was the heat. She volunteers it ONLY if the doctor asks about her eyes or vision, looks into her eyes with the ophthalmoscope, or asks whether anything else is worrying her — AND IF NOTHING IS ASKED BY SEVEN MINUTES she says it anyway, quietly: 'doctor — is it silly to mention my eye went dark for a minute last week?'

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: THE WINCE — when the right temple is palpated, pull the head away and say 'ooh, that's very tender', AND ONLY FOR THE TEMPLE; nothing else hurts. THE JOINT — if the doctor presses in front of the ear, say clearly 'NO, THAT BIT ISN'T SORE — THE SORE PART IS HIGHER UP.' THE GIRDLE — lift the arms slowly and wince, BUT DO NOT GIVE WAY: she is STIFF, NOT WEAK. PUSH ONCE when steroids are mentioned: 'shouldn't you wait and see what the tests say?' Become emotional ONLY if the word blindness is used bluntly without warning — then go quiet: 'I look after my husband. I have to be able to drive.' If the doctor never speaks to her and only narrates to the examiner, SAY NOTHING AND LET THEM LOSE THE MARKS.

Numbers: 8-minute station, STOP EXAMINING AT 6:20. GCA essentially only over 50. Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily VERIFY; IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for three days if visual loss VERIFY; BIOPSY WITHIN 1-2 WEEKS with an adequate segment VERIFY. PMR overlap about ONE IN FIVE. Acuity is 6/6, NEVER 20/20. Mouth opening THREE FINGERS. Sinusitis antibiotics only if severe or beyond 7-10 days VERIFY. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. Scored out of 14: observations first; full WIPE with consent, hand hygiene and gloves; WARNED ABOUT TENDERNESS; general appearance and inspection out loud; SYSTEMATIC skull palpation rather than a jab at the temple; commented on the artery pulse BOTH SIDES; KEPT EXAMINING AFTER FINDING THE TENDERNESS; sinuses, parotid and salivary glands; FUNDOSCOPY; SHOULDER GIRDLE; ears, mastoids, nose, mouth, throat, cervical nodes; TMJ examined SEPARATELY from the temple; diagnosis in words she understood WITH THE EYE RISK NAMED; and at least four differentials in lay language.
fails: ★ Stopping the examination when you find the tenderness — the single commonest fail, and the completion sentence must be said out loud
★ Omitting fundoscopy, or omitting the shoulder girdle — both are automatic fails
Performing a cranial nerve examination when the stem forbade it in capitals
Delaying steroid for the biopsy or the ESR; or reassuring her it is the jaw joint

Never warning her about tenderness before touching a patient briefed to wince; pressing on the globes instead of offering; reporting 'proximal weakness' rather than stiffness with preserved power; asking for 'an ENT examination' as one lump; and filing away the two minutes of darkness in her right eye and carrying on palpating

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional GP, cranial nerves. 'RELEVANT' DOES NOT MEAN PICK A FEW: with eight minutes you FINISH ALL TWELVE — it means you may drop colour vision, accommodation and the gag reflex OUT LOUD, and that you do NOT palpate the head, ears, sinuses or jaw joint. THE FIELDS ARE THE STATION, AND A BITEMPORAL DEFECT IS INVISIBLE WITH BOTH EYES OPEN — cover one of his eyes and the opposite one of yours, every time. START TALKING AT 7:10. And do not send him home to drive.

back.dx: BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA FROM A PITUITARY MACROADENOMA COMPRESSING THE OPTIC CHIASM — upper and lower temporal fields impaired in BOTH eyes with nasal fields full, normal acuity, no RAPD and normal fundi, in a 46-year-old with four months of morning headaches plus fatigue, reduced libido and weight change. LOCALISE IT, DO NOT JUST SAY 'A BRAIN TUMOUR': the nerves from the two eyes cross at a junction sitting just above a small gland at the base of the brain, the PITUITARY, and the pattern lost tells you something is pressing on that junction FROM BELOW. Reassure honestly: these are almost always non-cancerous, they are treatable, and some shrink on tablets alone — but promise nothing before a scan. Plan: URGENT MRI BRAIN AND PITUITARY WITH CONTRAST, a full anterior pituitary panel, and referral to neurosurgery and endocrinology. DIFFERENTIALS in lay words: other things pressing in the same place; a problem further back in the brain (which THE PATTERN ARGUES AGAINST, because bitemporal means the chiasm and homonymous means behind it); raised pressure inside the head (which the normal eye examination argues against); and migraine, which comes and goes rather than staying. THEN THE TWO THINGS BEFORE HE LEAVES: NO DRIVING until his vision is formally tested, WITH THE DUTY TO NOTIFY THE LICENSING AUTHORITY ON HIM, because with this pattern he cannot see what is coming from either side; and an emergency safety-net — sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision or drowsiness means call an ambulance, do not wait for the scan. LOCALISING RULES: BITEMPORAL = CHIASM = PITUITARY; HOMONYMOUS = BEHIND THE CHIASM, OPPOSITE SIDE; superior quadrants = temporal radiation (Meyer loop); inferior quadrants = parietal radiation. Uvula deviates AWAY, tongue deviates TOWARDS. Head turned left tests the RIGHT sternocleidomastoid.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, WIPE, AND A PLAIN EXPLANATION: 'Examiner, may I have this patient's vital signs?' Then: '...I have been asked to examine the nerves that supply your face and head. MOSTLY THAT MEANS YOUR EYES: I will ask you to read some letters, shine a light in them, and look into the back of them. Then I will check the feeling on your face, ask you for some facial movements, and check your hearing. NOTHING WILL HURT. Happy to go ahead?' (Listing twelve nerves to the patient burns forty seconds and communicates nothing.) Then appearance and nerve I: 'sitting, alert and orientated, no ptosis, no facial asymmetry, no abnormal head posture, no obvious squint. Tim, any change in your sense of smell? CRANIAL NERVE ONE IS INTACT BY HISTORY.'

ACUITY IN NINETY SECONDS: 'Tim, stand on the cross for me, glasses on if you wear them for distance. Cover your left eye with your palm and read down from the top as far as you can. Good. Now swap and cover the right. Examiner: VISUAL ACUITY IS 6/6 IN THE RIGHT EYE AND 6/6 IN THE LEFT. AS ACUITY IS NORMAL THERE IS NOTHING FOR A PINHOLE TO IMPROVE.' (Saying 20/20 is the correction to make now — Australian charts are metric.)

THE FIELDS — the station, and the technique that makes it work: 'sit facing me, about an arm's length away. COVER YOUR RIGHT EYE AND I WILL COVER MY LEFT. Keep looking straight at my nose. TELL ME THE MOMENT YOU SEE THE PEN TIP APPEAR.' Four diagonals, each ending at the centre, then swap. THEN REPORT IT EXACTLY LIKE THIS: 'RIGHT EYE: UPPER AND LOWER TEMPORAL FIELDS ARE IMPAIRED, NASAL FIELDS FULL. LEFT EYE: UPPER AND LOWER TEMPORAL FIELDS ARE IMPAIRED, NASAL FIELDS FULL. EXAMINER, MY PATIENT HAS A BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA. I will finish with DOUBLE SIMULTANEOUS STIMULATION for visual inattention — none.' (Testing with both eyes open makes a bitemporal defect INVISIBLE, and the role-player is briefed to say 'now' immediately every time and let you find nothing.)

PUPILS AND FUNDI IN UNDER A MINUTE: 'pupils are equal, round and about four millimetres. Light into the right: DIRECT response present — AND CONSENSUAL on the left. Light into the left: direct present — and consensual on the right. SWINGING LIGHT TEST: NO RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT. Examiner, I am performing FUNDOSCOPY, looking for PAPILLOEDEMA AND DISC PALLOR. In the interests of time I will not formally test colour vision or accommodation, though I will ask: Tim, does the red top of this pen look the same brightness to both eyes?' (Direct only, with no consensual and no swinging light, misses the test that separates a chiasmal lesion from an optic nerve lesion. And omitting fundoscopy in a headache station is an automatic fail.)

III, IV, VI — and name the movement, not the nystagmus: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only — TELL ME IF YOU SEE DOUBLE.' Wide H, pausing at the extremes. 'Examiner: eye movements are full and conjugate, THERE IS NO OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, no diplopia, no nystagmus, no ptosis, and no pupil-involving third nerve palsy.' Then V IN FOUR STEPS: 'clench your teeth — masseter and temporalis bulk and tone normal and symmetrical. Open your jaw against my hand — no deviation. THIS IS COTTON WOOL; IT FEELS LIKE THIS ON YOUR CHEST. NOW CLOSE YOUR EYES and say yes each time you feel it' — forehead, cheek, jaw, left against right — 'ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions symmetrical. Examiner, I WOULD ALSO LIKE TO TEST THE JAW JERK AND CORNEAL REFLEX.' (Offer the corneal reflex; never perform it. And test sensation with his eyes CLOSED, after a demonstration.)

VII AND VIII, with the masking that makes the whisper mean something: 'copy what I do: raise your eyebrows; screw your eyes tight shut and don't let me open them; puff out your cheeks; show me your teeth. Facial movements full and symmetrical, UPPER AND LOWER FACE. Now your hearing.' [Stand behind, RUB THE TRAGUS OF THE OTHER EAR, breathe out fully, whisper.] 'Repeat what I said. Normal to whispered voice in both ears; AS THERE IS NO HEARING LOSS I WILL NOT PROCEED TO RINNE AND WEBER.'

IX TO XII TOGETHER, under a minute: 'open wide and say aah — now a cough. PALATE RISES SYMMETRICALLY, UVULA CENTRAL, COUGH NOT BOVINE; I would OFFER the gag reflex but not perform it. Shrug and stop me pushing down — trapezius five out of five. Turn your head left, stop me — and right. Tongue resting on the floor of your mouth: no wasting, NO FASCICULATION. Stick it out: no deviation. Examiner, that completes twelve nerves. To complete I would examine the limbs, arrange FORMAL AUTOMATED PERIMETRY, and take a focused history.'

START TALKING — the defect, the localisation, then the reassurance: 'Tim, I've found something and I want to explain it clearly. YOU'VE LOST THE OUTER HALF OF THE VISION IN EACH EYE. You may not have noticed, because your brain fills the gap in.' → 'actually — I nearly clipped a cyclist a fortnight ago. He came out of nowhere on my left' → 'thank you for telling me — that fits exactly, and it matters. THE NERVES FROM YOUR TWO EYES CROSS AT A JUNCTION SITTING JUST ABOVE A SMALL GLAND AT THE BASE OF THE BRAIN, THE PITUITARY. The pattern you've lost tells me something is pressing on that junction FROM BELOW, and the commonest cause is a growth on the pituitary gland. I know that word is frightening. THESE ARE ALMOST ALWAYS NON-CANCEROUS, THEY ARE TREATABLE, AND SOME SHRINK ON TABLETS ALONE.' → 'so it's a tumour. Is it going to kill me?' → 'most of these are benign and very treatable. But I CAN'T PROMISE YOU ANYTHING BEFORE A SCAN, so I'm arranging an urgent MRI and blood tests today, and referring you to the brain surgeons and the hormone specialists in Adelaide.' Then the differentials in lay words, and THE TWO THINGS BEFORE HE LEAVES: 'PLEASE DON'T DRIVE UNTIL YOUR VISION IS FORMALLY TESTED; with this pattern you can't see what's coming from either side, and YOU HAVE TO NOTIFY THE LICENSING AUTHORITY. Is there someone who can drive you home? And if you get a sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision or feel drowsy, CALL AN AMBULANCE — don't wait for the scan.'

'Upper and lower temporal fields impaired; nasal fields full.' / 'That is a bitemporal hemianopia, which localises to the optic chiasm.' / 'Swinging light test — no relative afferent pupillary defect.' / 'Performing fundoscopy, looking for papilloedema and disc pallor.' / 'Eye movements are full and conjugate; there is no ophthalmoplegia.'

'This is cotton wool; it feels like this on your chest. Now close your eyes.' / 'I would also like to test the jaw jerk and the corneal reflex.' / 'Hearing is normal to whispered voice, so I will not proceed to Rinne and Weber.' / 'Something is pressing on that junction from below — a growth on the pituitary gland.' / 'PLEASE DON'T DRIVE UNTIL YOUR VISION HAS BEEN FORMALLY TESTED.'

VERSION A — RIGHT HOMONYMOUS HEMIANOPIA: 'RIGHT EYE: temporal field impaired, nasal field full. LEFT EYE: NASAL field impaired, temporal field full. Examiner, THE RIGHT HALF OF THE VISUAL FIELD IS LOST IN BOTH EYES — a right homonymous hemianopia. That localises BEHIND THE CHIASM ON THE LEFT SIDE: tract, radiation or occipital cortex.' And if the onset was SUDDEN: 'a sudden homonymous defect is A STROKE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I would activate the stroke pathway, arrange urgent non-contrast CT and CT angiography, check the blood glucose, and discuss with the on-call stroke service BEFORE HE LEAVES THE BUILDING.' VERIFY (Calling a homonymous defect a pituitary problem is the trap — only the chiasm gives bitemporal.) / A QUADRANTANOPIA: 'the defect is confined to the UPPER quadrants on the right in both eyes. Superior quadrants are carried in the TEMPORAL radiation, MEYER LOOP, so the lesion is in the left temporal lobe. If it were the LOWER quadrants I would be localising to the left PARIETAL radiation.'

MORE VARIANTS: PAPILLOEDEMA ('the discs are swollen with blurred margins bilaterally') → CHANGE GEAR: 'bilateral disc swelling means RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE. That converts this from an outpatient problem into a SAME-DAY one: urgent imaging today INCLUDING VENOUS IMAGING to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, discuss with neurosurgery before he leaves, and warn him that headache worse lying flat or on coughing, vomiting, or drowsiness means an emergency department immediately.' / PITUITARY APOPLEXY (thunderclap headache an hour ago, vomiting twice, pale) → 'a thunderclap headache with vomiting, ophthalmoplegia and a visual field defect in a patient with a probable pituitary lesion is PITUITARY APOPLEXY. This is an emergency: INTRAVENOUS HYDROCORTISONE, resuscitate, urgent imaging, urgent bloods including electrolytes and a CORTISOL, and speak to neurosurgery and endocrinology now — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval.' VERIFY / HE REFUSES TO STOP DRIVING ('I can't not drive, it's my whole job') → neither back down nor threaten: 'you couldn't see a cyclist on your left a fortnight ago, and next time it might not be a near miss. THE LAW PUTS THE DUTY TO NOTIFY ON YOU, and I have to tell you clearly that you are not currently safe to drive AND TO RECORD THAT I HAVE TOLD YOU. The good news is this is often reversible — if the pressure comes off the nerves, fields can recover and licences can be reinstated. In the meantime, who can drive you?' VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: Tim Halloran, 46, farm machinery sales rep in Kadina driving about 60,000 km a year; married with two teenagers; practical, a bit blunt, mildly impatient with work to get back to. Four months of dull headaches across the front and behind the eyes, WORSE FIRST THING IN THE MORNING, about 4/10 but constant. HIS VISION: he cannot describe it well — things 'come out of nowhere' at the sides, he has clipped the door frame twice and knocked a mug off the bench. If asked: FLAT AND TIRED for months, LIBIDO DROPPED OFF (put down to work), SHIRTS FEEL LOOSER, and he gets up once or twice at night to pass urine. No medications, non-smoker, four or five beers a week. HIDDEN AGENDA: A FORTNIGHT AGO HE NEARLY HIT A CYCLIST on the Copper Coast Highway who 'came out of nowhere on my left' — he has told nobody including his wife, because he is FRIGHTENED OF LOSING HIS LICENCE AND THEREFORE HIS JOB. He volunteers it only if told he has lost part of his vision, asked about driving, or asked whether anything else is worrying him — otherwise at the very end: 'doctor — would this explain nearly hitting a cyclist a couple of weeks ago?'

HOW HE PLAYS IT — THE FIELDS ARE THE WHOLE PERFORMANCE: when the doctor brings a pen in FROM THE OUTER SIDE of whichever eye is uncovered, DO NOT SAY 'NOW' UNTIL THE PEN IS ALMOST DIRECTLY IN FRONT; when it comes in FROM THE NOSE SIDE, say 'now' straight away. BOTH EYES, exactly the same. IF THE DOCTOR TESTS WITH BOTH EYES OPEN, SAY 'NOW' IMMEDIATELY EVERY TIME — AND LET THEM FIND NOTHING. Acuity: read the whole chart with each eye. Everything else is normal — do exactly what is asked and give no other findings. PUSH ONCE when the word tumour is used: 'so it's a tumour. Is it going to kill me?' PUSH AGAIN ON DRIVING: 'I can't not drive — it's my whole job', giving way only if the doctor is honest and offers a way forward. If the doctor never speaks to him and narrates only to the examiner, stay silent and let the marks go.

Numbers: 8-minute station, TALK FROM 7:10. Acuity 90 s, fields 60 s, pupils 30 s, fundi 15 s. 6/6, NEVER 20/20. Two letters per line to move down. FOUR QUADRANTS PER EYE, target midway. BITEMPORAL = CHIASM = PITUITARY; HOMONYMOUS = BEHIND THE CHIASM, OPPOSITE SIDE. Uvula deviates AWAY, tongue deviates TOWARDS. Head turned LEFT tests the RIGHT sternocleidomastoid. Tuning fork 512 Hz. MRI brain and pituitary WITH CONTRAST, urgent. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. Scored out of 14, with the starred items: fields tested WITH ONE EYE COVERED and four quadrants each; the defect reported BY EYE AND QUADRANT and named bitemporal; FUNDOSCOPY requested; the lesion LOCALISED to chiasm and pituitary rather than called 'a brain tumour'; and DRIVING addressed with emergency safety-netting.
fails: ★ Testing the fields with both eyes open — a bitemporal defect is invisible that way, and the role-player will let you find nothing
★ Sending him home to drive, or backing down when he pushes on his licence
Running out of time inside the eye and never reaching nerves IX to XII, or sacrificing tasks 2 and 3 for them
Describing the defect in the wrong eye or the wrong quadrant; saying 'a brain tumour' without localising it to the chiasm and the pituitary

back.dx: THE FRAMEWORK THAT CARRIES EVERY MEDICATION CHART STATION. FIVE BOXES BEFORE ANY DRUG: (1) ID FRONT — URN, family name, given names, address only if given, DOB, sex ticked, and THE PATIENT'S NAME PRINTED in 'first prescriber to print patient name' — writing your own name there is a fail, because the label is checked against the wristband; (2) ID BACK — turn the chart over IMMEDIATELY, same identifiers on the PRN page, patient's name printed again, with the year optional unless charting a PRN — MORE THAN HALF THE ROOM NEVER TURNS THE CHART OVER; (3) ALLERGIES AND ADR — a real entry (peanuts / anaphylaxis / 2002) or NIL KNOWN if the stem is silent, or UNKNOWN if the history could not be obtained — always initialled, signed, printed and dated, because A SILENT STEM MEANS TICK A BOX AND SIGN IT; (4) MEDICINES TAKEN PRIOR TO PRESENTATION — filled if the stem lists home medicines, left empty if not, and NEVER filled with today's inpatient orders; (5) VTE PROPHYLAXIS — completed on EVERY chart, ticked 'prophylaxis not required' with signature and date when nothing is needed. THEN THE ORDER: year, dated columns, and inside the box the date, generic name, route, ONE dose, frequency written IN FULL (never OD, never Q24H), indication, prescriber signature, printed name and contact, administration times in the grid — and, IF A DURATION WAS SPECIFIED, EVERY REMAINING COLUMN CROSSED OUT so the nurse knows it stops. HERE: ceftriaxone IV 1 g daily for pneumonia, 0800 on days 1-5, days 6-8 blocked. Any single dose in range passes — 1 g daily, 2 g daily, 1 g BD, 500 mg BD — but '1-2 g' is not a prescription. 'CAP' is accepted as the indication; 'pneumonia' is safer.
plan: DECIDE

Before you open the book: 'the stem says FOR FIVE DAYS. That is a REGULAR medicine with a FIXED DURATION — page 3, right-hand inside page.' Named indications carry their own doses; EVERYTHING ELSE TAKES THE GENERAL DOSE — so 'pneumonia isn't in the list, so I'll pick meningitis' is wrong. And never write the range: '1-2 g' is not a prescription and the nurse will ring you.
BOX 1

ID FRONT: URN as given, family name CITIZEN, given names JAMES, address only if given, DOB, sex ticked. FIRST PRESCRIBER TO PRINT PATIENT NAME: JAMES CITIZEN — THE PATIENT, NOT YOU. (Writing your own name there is a fail on its own.)
BOX 2

ID BACK — TURN THE CHART OVER NOW, immediately after box 1 and before the allergy box: same identifiers on the PRN page, patient's name printed again. The year on the PRN page is optional — fill it if you are charting a PRN. (More than half the room never turns the chart over.)
BOX 3

ALLERGIES AND ADR: medicine or other — PEANUTS; reaction, type and date — ANAPHYLAXIS 2002; initials; then SIGN, PRINT YOUR NAME AND DATE IT. If the stem gives no allergy, tick NIL KNOWN and sign; if the history could not be obtained — unconscious, no ID — tick UNKNOWN. A SILENT STEM MEANS TICK A BOX AND SIGN IT.
BOX 4

MEDICINES TAKEN PRIOR TO PRESENTATION: nothing here, because the stem lists no home medicines — leave it empty, and DO NOT put today's inpatient orders in it. (The opposite error is skipping this box when the stem DOES list home medicines.)
BOX 5

VTE PROPHYLAXIS: tick PROPHYLAXIS NOT REQUIRED, signature, date. Guidance is that this box is completed on EVERY chart even when nothing is needed — and the worse error is a THERAPEUTIC anticoagulant written into it.
THE BOOK

Back index, C, ceftriaxone, bold page number, FINGER IN THE INDEX. The page lists a general dose and specific doses for meningitis, cellulitis, meningococcal disease and influenza-type infection. PNEUMONIA IS NOT LISTED, SO THE GENERAL ADULT DOSE APPLIES: 1-2 g daily in one or two doses. 'I'll use 1 g daily.' Close the book.
THE ORDER

YEAR 2026 top-left. DATED COLUMNS across the top — exam date then the following days, seven or eight columns. Then the first regular box on the right-hand page: DATE 3/11/26 — MEDICINE ceftriaxone — ROUTE IV — DOSE 1 g — FREQUENCY daily (written in full, NEVER OD) — INDICATION pneumonia — PHARMACY left empty — SIGNATURE, PRINTED NAME, CONTACT — ADMINISTRATION TIMES 0800 in the first column and repeated across days 1 to 5 — THEN DAYS 6, 7 AND 8 CROSSED OUT, a cross through each box or the whole remaining area blocked. COUNT 1-2-3-4-5 ALOUD IN YOUR HEAD, THEN CROSS OUT: the critical error of this case is a specified duration with the later columns left open.
RE-CHECK

Say it in your head before you leave: 'ID front — done. ID BACK — done. Allergy — SIGNED. Prior — nil. VTE — ticked and signed. Year — yes. Dates — yes. Times — five of them. BLOCK-OUT — yes.' Only now leave. (Walking out at four minutes without re-checking is marked.)

Passing dose choices: 1 g daily, 2 g daily, 1 g BD, or 500 mg BD — any single dose inside the AMH general range. 'Daily' written in full, never OD or Q24H. Indication written — 'CAP' is accepted but 'pneumonia' is safer. Five days counted from today, with everything after day 5 blocked. The examiner may treat an unblocked specified duration as a CRITICAL ERROR. Write SUBCUT, not SC. Write 60 mg, NOT '1 mg/kg' — the calculation is yours to do. And the VTE box on page 2 is STILL ticked 'prophylaxis not required', because this is treatment, not prophylaxis. ASPIRIN: the AMH acute-conditions line is 150-300 mg initially with long term 100-150 mg daily, and NSTEMI is an acute coronary syndrome, so take the ACUTE line — 150 mg PO daily, indication NSTEMI, 0800 in EVERY column, OPEN-ENDED because aspirin continues and nothing is blocked. If challenged that Therapeutic Guidelines uses 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily: 'I USED THE AMH SUPPLIED IN THE STATION; A 300 MG LOADING DOSE WOULD FOLLOW LOCAL ACS PROTOCOL.' Frequency is written in full — 'daily', never OD, which nurses have read as QID; and BD rather than 'q12h' or '12/24', because BD is the regular-page convention. VARIANTS: WEIGHT 80 kg AND eGFR 25 — 80 mg per dose, but SEVERE RENAL IMPAIRMENT reduces enoxaparin to ONCE DAILY (1 mg/kg daily) below a CrCl of 30, so READ THE RENAL LINE ON THE PAGE AND CHART WHAT IT SAYS. 'CHART VTE PROPHYLAXIS' POST-OPERATIVELY — now it IS the VTE box: risk assessed yes, enoxaparin subcut 40 mg daily, indication VTE prophylaxis, signed with a prescribing plan, plus the mechanical prophylaxis line for stockings. 'CHART WARFARIN FOR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION' — warfarin has its OWN box on page 2: select brand, route PO, TARGET INR 2-3, indication AF, sign, then enter the day-one dose with your initials and 1600 as the time, with INR results and later doses entered day by day.

'The word THERAPEUTIC is the whole case. The VTE box on page 2 is labelled PROPHYLAXIS: it is for prophylactic enoxaparin or stockings. TREATMENT DOSES — DVT, PE, ACS — ARE REGULAR MEDICINES. PAGE 3.' (Enoxaparin written into the VTE prophylaxis lines because 'it's enoxaparin' is the fail this station exists for — the examiner reads the box label, and the dose is wrong for that box anyway.)
BOXES

The same five as every chart station: ID FRONT with the patient's name printed AND THE WEIGHT 60 kg recorded; FLIP IMMEDIATELY for the ID box on the BACK; ALLERGY — tick NIL KNOWN, initials, sign, print, date; MEDICINES PRIOR TO PRESENTATION left empty because none are listed; VTE BOX — tick PROPHYLAXIS NOT REQUIRED, sign, date, thinking 'treatment dose, not prophylaxis'.
THE BOOK

Back index, A, aspirin, bold page: ACUTE CONDITIONS 150-300 mg initially, once daily may be required; long term 100-150 mg daily. NSTEMI is an acute coronary syndrome, so the ACUTE line — and 150 mg sits in both ranges, so take it. Finger back in the index, E, enoxaparin, bold page, scroll past the many indications to UNSTABLE ANGINA / NSTEMI: 1 mg/kg subcut every 12 hours for 2-8 days. 60 kg gives 60 mg. Twelve-hourly is BD. Pick a number of days inside 2-8 — eight is taught, five or seven are fine.
ASPIRIN

Year 2026, dates across the top, then the first regular box: DATE — MEDICINE aspirin — ROUTE PO — DOSE 150 mg — FREQUENCY daily (NEVER OD) — INDICATION NSTEMI — sign, print, contact — TIMES 0800 IN EVERY COLUMN, ongoing, NOTHING BLOCKED, because aspirin continues. (A candidate asked in class whether OD was acceptable — it is not; nurses have read it as QID.)
ENOXAPARIN

The second regular box: DATE — MEDICINE enoxaparin — ROUTE SUBCUT (not SC) — DOSE 60 mg (the calculated number, NOT '1 mg/kg') — FREQUENCY BD (twelve-hourly means the same, but BD is the regular-page convention, and 'q12h' is marked amber) — INDICATION NSTEMI — sign, print, contact — TIMES 0800 IN THE TOP SQUARE AND 2000 TWO SQUARES BELOW IT, in each of eight columns, WITH A GAP so the nurse's initials do not overlap — THEN CROSS OUT THE REMAINING COLUMNS.
VTE BOX

Page 2 STILL reads: prophylaxis not required, signed, dated. This is a TREATMENT dose, and it belongs on page 3. Saying that to yourself as you tick the box is what stops the pen drifting to the wrong page.
RE-CHECK
'Enoxaparin on PAGE 3, not page 2 — yes. BLOCKED AFTER 8 — yes. SUBCUT — yes. Aspirin DAILY, not OD — yes. WEIGHT — yes. ID BACK — yes.' Only then leave.
