back.dx: THE DISCRIMINATING SENTENCE, said out loud in every version: NOT 'there is protein, so this is chronic kidney disease', BUT 'PUTTING THE PROTEIN AT THREE PLUS TOGETHER WITH A 50-YEAR-OLD MAN WHO HAS OEDEMA TO THE KNEES AND HYPERTENSION AND NO PAST HISTORY, MY MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS IS NEPHROTIC SYNDROME.' That sentence is what tells the examiner you performed a CLINICAL ASSESSMENT rather than a laboratory test — and it is the only thing that changes between the four versions. VARIANT C — NEPHROTIC SYNDROME within the broader picture of chronic kidney disease, which you would then STAGE. Differentials in TWO GROUPS: for the PROTEINURIA — primary glomerular disease (membranous, FSGS), diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, glomerulonephritis, myeloma light chains, and the benign causes (orthostatic, exercise-induced, fever, infection); for the OEDEMA — heart failure, chronic liver disease, protein-losing enteropathy or malnutrition, hypothyroidism, venous insufficiency or DVT, and medication, particularly a calcium channel blocker. Investigations: first morning urine ACR, UEC with eGFR, urine microscopy for DYSMORPHIC RED CELLS AND CASTS, serum albumin and lipids, glucose and HbA1c, FBE, calcium, phosphate and PTH, renal tract ultrasound — adding an immunology screen and SERUM FREE LIGHT CHAINS WITH ELECTROPHORESIS if nephrotic or unexplained — nephrology referral, and RENAL BIOPSY AS THE DEFINITIVE INVESTIGATION. VARIANT A — a PULMONARY-RENAL SYNDROME, leading diagnosis ANTI-GBM (GOODPASTURE) DISEASE, differentials the other pulmonary-renal causes (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, lupus nephritis), then the respiratory causes of haemoptysis alone and the renal causes of haematuria alone — and remember a positive blood pad can mean HAEMOGLOBINURIA OR MYOGLOBINURIA. TIME-CRITICAL: anti-GBM antibody, ANCA, ANA and complement, urgent renal function, chest X-ray, urine microscopy, and speak to the renal team TODAY about transfer, biopsy, corticosteroid, cyclophosphamide and plasma exchange. VARIANT B — GLYCOSURIA: confirm with fasting glucose and HbA1c, BUT ASK EXACTLY WHICH MEDICINES HE TAKES, because an SGLT2 INHIBITOR PRODUCES GLYCOSURIA WITH A NORMAL BLOOD GLUCOSE — then familial renal glycosuria and Fanconi syndrome — and if diabetes is confirmed, assess him whole: ACR and eGFR, lipids, absolute cardiovascular risk with an ECG, feet with pulses, monofilament and tuning fork, and retinal screening. VARIANT D — ACUTE NEPHRITIC SYNDROME from an acute glomerulonephritis: post-infectious, IgA nephropathy, vasculitis or lupus — ask about a sore throat or skin infection in the preceding two to three weeks, and send ASOT and anti-DNase B, complement C3 and C4, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, hepatitis and HIV serology with same-day nephrology discussion.
plan: SET UP OUT LOUD: 'before I start I'll set myself up. I'm performing hand hygiene and putting on gloves. I'm laying out a few tissues here on the bench. I can see there is a timer, and I'll place it beside the tissues SO I CAN START IT THE MOMENT THE STRIP GOES DOWN. I'm opening the container of reagent strips, taking out ONE strip, AND CLOSING THE BOTTLE AGAIN — the strips are moisture-sensitive and I don't want to spoil the rest of them. Before I handle the sample: I would normally CHECK THE LABEL ON THE SPECIMEN against the patient's name, date of birth and identification number. May I confirm this is the correct patient's sample?' → 'yes' or 'there is no label; assume it is correct' → 'THANK YOU' and MOVE ON. (Arguing the point after the examiner has answered is a mark lost, not a mark gained.)

INSPECTION, including the smell: 'on inspection, the specimen is a pale, whitish-grey fluid and it is CLOUDY rather than clear. It is not frankly blood-stained, NOT DARK LIKE COLA, and NOT TEA-COLOURED. I'm removing the lid. There is NO FOUL OR OFFENSIVE SMELL to suggest infection, and NO SWEET OR KETOTIC SMELL. I'll replace the lid loosely and put it where it won't be knocked over.' (If challenged 'do you really smell urine samples in practice?': 'not deliberately — smell is an incidental observation rather than a manoeuvre, and I wouldn't inhale over a clinical specimen. I commented on it because an offensive or sweet smell is a genuine clinical finding and I didn't want to leave it unsaid.')

THE DIP — two technique points the examiner leans in for: 'I'm dipping the strip now. I'M BENDING IT AGAINST THE INNER WALL OF THE CONTAINER SO THAT EVERY PAD IS SUBMERGED — if the strip stays straight the upper pads sit above the fluid line and READ FALSELY NEGATIVE. One dip, about one second. Now A HORIZONTAL TAP against the rim to take off the excess. I TAP SIDEWAYS RATHER THAN DOWNWARDS, because a vertical tap runs the reagents from one pad onto the next and contaminates the colours. Strip down on the tissue, pads facing up — AND I'M STARTING THE TIMER NOW. Lid back on the specimen and out of the way.'

THE WAITING, USED — not silence: 'while the pads develop I'm writing the ten analytes down the page so that I report them in order and don't miss one: GLUCOSE, BILIRUBIN, KETONES, SPECIFIC GRAVITY, BLOOD, pH, PROTEIN, UROBILINOGEN, NITRITE, LEUCOCYTES. Each has its own reading time printed on the bottle — thirty, thirty, forty, forty-five, then sixty seconds for the next five, and TWO MINUTES FOR LEUCOCYTES.' THEN RE-READ THE STEM SILENTLY and decide your answer BEFORE you read the abnormal pad, so the reading CONFIRMS a hypothesis rather than replacing one.

READ AND REPORT PAD BY PAD, holding the strip beside the guide on the bottle and NAMING THE NEGATIVES: glucose negative — bilirubin negative — ketones negative — SPECIFIC GRAVITY 1.010, 'a mid-range, adequately concentrated sample, SO I CAN RELY ON THE OTHER PADS' — blood negative — pH six — PROTEIN 'strongly positive, THREE PLUS; it sits between the three and four plus blocks, so I would report it as AT LEAST three plus' — urobilinogen within the normal range — nitrite negative — leucocytes negative. Then: 'I'm wrapping the used strip in the tissue and disposing of it in the bin, removing my gloves and performing hand hygiene.' (Reporting only the abnormal pad and saying 'everything else was normal' loses marks; REPORTING A PAD YOU NEVER READ IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL — if you missed one, SAY SO.)

THE SUMMARY, THEN THE STEM-LINKED DIAGNOSIS: 'to summarise my findings: a cloudy, pale urine with no abnormal smell, and on dipstick a SINGLE abnormality — protein at three plus, with a specific gravity of 1.010 and a pH of six. Glucose, bilirubin, ketones, blood, urobilinogen, nitrite and leucocytes were all negative.' Then THE SENTENCE: 'PUTTING THAT TOGETHER WITH THE HISTORY IN THE STEM — a 50-year-old man with oedema extending to the knees and a high blood pressure, with no past medical history — MY MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS IS NEPHROTIC SYNDROME: heavy protein loss in the urine, a low serum albumin, and oedema as a consequence. That sits within the broader picture of chronic kidney disease, WHICH I WOULD THEN STAGE FORMALLY.'

DIFFERENTIALS IN GROUPS, then investigations in TIERS ending with the definitive test (see dx). And if the examiner pushes back — 'I think the answer here is chronic kidney disease, not nephrotic syndrome' → 'I agree this sits within chronic kidney disease, and I'd want to confirm that with an eGFR and an ACR and stage it. I NAMED NEPHROTIC SYNDROME FIRST BECAUSE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE IS A STAGING FRAMEWORK RATHER THAN A DIAGNOSIS — it tells me how bad the kidney function is, but not WHY this man's legs are swollen. The combination of heavy proteinuria and oedema is the syndrome I want to act on today.'
CHALLENGES

'The pad is for nitrates, isn't it?' → 'NITRATE is what comes in through the diet. Gram-negative uropathogens with nitrate reductase convert it to NITRITE, and the Griess reaction on the pad detects the nitrite.' / 'So a negative nitrite means no infection?' → 'no — nitrite is SPECIFIC BUT NOT SENSITIVE. It is negative when the urine has not been in the bladder long enough, roughly four hours, and when the organism does not reduce nitrate — ENTEROCOCCUS, STAPHYLOCOCCUS SAPROPHYTICUS AND PSEUDOMONAS. In a symptomatic patient I would treat and send a culture regardless.' / 'A negative protein pad excludes myeloma?' → 'NO. The pad measures ALBUMIN and is close to blind to immunoglobulin light chains — I'd ask for serum free light chains and serum and urine electrophoresis.' / 'How would you tell acute from chronic?' → repeat eGFR for the trajectory, previous results, KIDNEY SIZE AND ECHOTEXTURE on ultrasound (small echogenic kidneys mean chronic), and the markers of established disease: normocytic anaemia, low calcium, high phosphate, raised PTH. / 'Isn't this simply an acute kidney injury?' → 'AKI is DEFINED by a change in creatinine or urine output over a stated time — a rise of 26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours, or 1.5 times baseline within seven days, or under 0.5 mL/kg/hour for six hours VERIFY. What the two-day history describes is an ACUTE NEPHRITIC PRESENTATION, and I'd expect an AKI to accompany it.' / 'Goodpasture is a vasculitis?' → grouped with the small-vessel vasculitides, but the mechanism is an AUTOANTIBODY against the ALPHA-3 CHAIN OF TYPE IV COLLAGEN, shared by alveolar and glomerular basement membrane — which is why exactly those two organs bleed. / 'Wegener's?' → 'GRANULOMATOSIS WITH POLYANGIITIS — the eponym was retired in 2011.'

'Specific gravity 1.010 — a mid-range, adequately concentrated sample, so I can rely on the other pads.' / 'At least three plus.' / 'Putting that together with the history in the stem...' / 'Chronic kidney disease is a staging framework rather than a diagnosis.'

THE FOUR STEMS AND THEIR CLOSING SENTENCES: VARIANT A — 'a young woman with chronic cough, breathlessness and haemoptysis, and haematuria at the same time. THAT COMBINATION IS A PULMONARY-RENAL SYNDROME, and my leading diagnosis is ANTI-GLOMERULAR BASEMENT MEMBRANE DISEASE... this is TIME-CRITICAL: untreated, anti-GBM disease can destroy renal function within days.' / VARIANT B — 'my most likely diagnosis is GLYCOSURIA. The commonest cause is diabetes, so I would confirm with a fasting glucose and HbA1c. BUT THE STEM TELLS ME HIS BLOOD SUGAR IS NORMAL AND HE IS ALREADY ON TREATMENT, so I would want to know EXACTLY WHICH MEDICINES HE TAKES: AN SGLT2 INHIBITOR PRODUCES GLYCOSURIA WITH A NORMAL BLOOD GLUCOSE, and in that case the pad is the drug working rather than a new diagnosis.' / VARIANT D — 'a two-day history of sudden bilateral swelling, nocturia and NEW hypertension: my leading diagnosis is an ACUTE NEPHRITIC SYNDROME due to an acute glomerulonephritis — post-infectious, IgA nephropathy, a vasculitis, or lupus nephritis.'

THE VARIANT B ROLE-PLAYER, when present, DOES NOT TALK — he TAPS ONE FOOT REPEATEDLY AND RUBS HIS EYES, and gives the answer only if asked: 'there's one for the blood pressure. And the doctor added another one last year — something for my heart and kidneys, she said. I'd have to check the box.' THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE VARIANT. If asked about his feet: 'a bit numb and tingly at night.' About his eyes: 'my vision's been a bit blurry when I read.' About thirst: 'I drink a lot of water and get up once or twice at night.'

PARTNER PRACTICE: set a bench with a cup of water and a splash of milk, a strip bottle, a phone timer, tissues, paper and a bin; your partner reads one of the four stems, starts eight minutes, hands over the result card AT THE MOMENT YOU READ THE PAD, then asks three challenges one at a time. Run the same variant twice — once slowly and correctly, once deliberately rushed — so you can feel the difference in how the reading goes. (LACTOSE-FREE MILK gives a positive glucose pad as well as protein, because the lactose has already been split into glucose and galactose.)
pefe: RESULT CARDS — read out when the candidate reads each pad. VARIANT A: glucose negative, bilirubin negative, ketones negative, SG 1.020, BLOOD 4+, pH 6, PROTEIN 1+, urobilinogen normal, nitrite negative, leucocytes negative; appearance CLOUDY, FAINTLY PINK; AND A SECOND CONTAINER OF PINK SPUTUM ON THE BENCH. VARIANT B: GLUCOSE 4+, everything else negative, SG 1.015, pH 6; appearance clear, pale. VARIANT C: PROTEIN 3+, everything else negative, SG 1.010, pH 6; appearance cloudy, pale. VARIANT D: PROTEIN 3+, BLOOD 1+, SG 1.020, pH 6.5, rest negative; appearance cloudy, pale. IF THE CANDIDATE ASKS FOR SOMETHING NOT PROVIDED — serum albumin, creatinine, a blood glucose, a chest X-ray — answer 'that is not available in this station — TELL ME WHAT YOU WOULD EXPECT AND WHY', and DO NOT INVENT NUMBERS: asking for them is correct behaviour and should be credited.

MARKING CHECKLIST: hand hygiene and gloves before touching anything; tissues laid out and timer placed ready; bottle opened, ONE strip removed, BOTTLE CLOSED; identification stated ONCE then dropped when answered; colour and clarity out loud; smell out loud; STRIP BENT SO ALL PADS SUBMERGED with one dip of about a second; HORIZONTAL tap, not vertical; strip on tissue and TIMER STARTED IN THE SAME MOVEMENT; WAITING TIME USED — list written, stem re-read, no silence; each pad read at or near its printed time; ALL TEN PADS NAMED INCLUDING THE NEGATIVES; strip and tissue disposed of, gloves off, hand hygiene; ABNORMAL PAD CORRECTLY IDENTIFIED AND GRADED; DIAGNOSIS EXPLICITLY LINKED TO THE STEM IN ONE SENTENCE; differentials as a GROUPED list; the not-to-miss diagnosis named for that variant; investigations in TIERS with the definitive test named; URGENCY stated where the variant demands it (A and D); and finished inside eight minutes without rushing the procedure.

AUTOMATIC FAILS: reporting a pad you never read — reciting ten results after one glance; misreading the abnormal pad, calling 4+ protein 'trace' or the blood pad negative in Variant A; a diagnosis with NO LINK TO THE STEM — naming diabetes in Variant C or chronic kidney disease in Variant D; MISSING THE SECOND CONTAINER in Variant A; and reading a contaminated strip after a vertical tap and reporting the results confidently. MARKS LOST BUT NOT FAILS: no gloves or disposal; bottle left open; no timer started; silence through the two-minute wait; reporting only the abnormal pad; pressing the identification question after it has been answered; one differential where a grouped list was asked for; and finishing in three minutes and standing there.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — GP or ED. ONE-LINE STRATEGY: PROVE THERE IS A LOSS, PROVE IT IS SENSORINEURAL, THEN EXAMINE THE NEIGHBOURS OF THE EIGHTH NERVE — THE FIFTH AND THE SEVENTH — AND THE CEREBELLUM BEHIND THEM. WHISPER DECIDES WHETHER; RINNE AND WEBER DECIDE WHICH. Two structural fails: going straight to the tuning fork, because Rinne with air better than bone is BOTH the normal result AND the sensorineural result; and finishing at the tuning fork, when the whole point is a mass in the cerebellopontine angle. AND NOBODY TELLS YOU HOW FAST THE LOSS CAME ON — YOU HAVE TO ASK.
stem: General practice or emergency department. A 27-YEAR-OLD WOMAN with HEARING LOSS IN THE LEFT EAR and A BUZZING NOISE in the same ear. NO NAUSEA AND NO VOMITING. HER TYMPANIC MEMBRANES HAVE BEEN INSPECTED AND ARE NORMAL. Gloves, an otoscope and a 512 Hz TUNING FORK are available. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination — the examiner will provide findings you cannot elicit yourself
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
time: WIPE, a pain check, AND THE QUESTION THE STEM LEFT OUT · 'did the hearing loss come on SUDDENLY, over a few hours or overnight, or has it CREPT UP over weeks or months?' · then THE FRAMING SENTENCE naming external, middle, cochlear and retrocochlear · GENERAL APPEARANCE including CAFE-AU-LAIT PATCHES AND CUTANEOUS NEUROFIBROMAS · INSPECT both pinnae and mastoids, PALPATE including MOVING THE PINNA, then OFFER OTOSCOPY, GOOD EAR FIRST, naming the five things you would look for · THE THREE HEARING TESTS IN SEQUENCE: WHISPER close then at arm's length, good ear first, to prove there IS a loss; then RINNE with a 512 Hz fork struck on your knee; then WEBER on the forehead · AND STATE THE RULE BEFORE THE CONCLUSION · THE NEIGHBOURS: CN V with cotton wool and THE CORNEAL REFLEX OFFERED BY NAME as the earliest additional sign of a CPA tumour; CN VII with taste and hyperacusis asked about; eye movements WITH NYSTAGMUS NAMED, and Dix-Hallpike offered · CEREBELLUM, GAIT, ROMBERG AND JOINT POSITION SENSE, because she can walk and there is no excuse to omit them · fundoscopy offered · THEN THE DIAGNOSIS in lay words with THE THREE QUALIFIERS, a pause for her reaction, ITEMISED reassurance, differentials BY SITE, and the investigation NAMED IN FULL.

back.dx: ACOUSTIC NEUROMA (VESTIBULAR SCHWANNOMA) — a gradual unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus, a normal drum, and no other cranial nerve or cerebellar signs. THE INTERPRETATION THAT CARRIES THE STATION: the whisper proves there IS a loss; Rinne air better than bone bilaterally with WEBER LATERALISING TO THE BETTER-HEARING EAR gives the rule — WEBER LATERALISES AWAY FROM A SENSORINEURAL LOSS AND TOWARD A CONDUCTIVE ONE — so in an ear already shown to be deaf, this is a LEFT SENSORINEURAL loss, and with a normal drum the lesion is COCHLEAR OR RETROCOCHLEAR. DIFFERENTIALS BY SITE: RETROCOCHLEAR — acoustic neuroma, another CPA lesion such as meningioma which cannot be separated clinically, and multiple sclerosis in a 27-year-old; COCHLEAR — idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss (excluded on the gradual onset, but AN EMERGENCY if she had woken with it), Meniere disease (against: no fluctuation, no aural fullness, no recurrent vertigo), and ototoxic or noise-induced loss (usually bilateral and symmetrical); LABYRINTHINE — acute labyrinthitis, against which NO NAUSEA, NO VOMITING AND NO NYSTAGMUS is a positive argument, not a throwaway; CONDUCTIVE causes excluded by the normal drum and the test pattern. INVESTIGATION NAMED IN FULL: PURE-TONE AND SPEECH AUDIOMETRY, and MRI OF THE INTERNAL AUDITORY MEATI WITH GADOLINIUM — a plain CT can miss a small tumour inside the canal. TO HER: a small, SLOW-GROWING, NON-CANCEROUS swelling on the nerve between the inner ear and the brain, which ISN'T A CANCER AND DOESN'T SPREAD — but because of where it sits, we need to find out whether it's there and how big it is. Then ITEMISED reassurance: the feeling in her face, the reflex in her eye, her facial movements, balance, coordination and the back of her eyes were ALL NORMAL, and those are the things that change when one gets large. Treatment options if asked: OBSERVATION with serial MRI for small tumours, STEREOTACTIC RADIOSURGERY for small-to-medium, and MICROSURGICAL EXCISION for larger — with hearing preservation NOT GUARANTEED and FACIAL NERVE FUNCTION THE MAIN RISK. Safety-net: sudden worsening of hearing, facial numbness or weakness, double vision, headache with vomiting, or unsteadiness.
plan: WIPE, PAIN, AND THE QUESTION THAT CHANGES THE DIAGNOSIS: '...I'd like to examine you to work out what's causing it. I'll look at both your ears and inside them, then test your hearing with a whisper and a tuning fork, and then check the nerves in your face and your balance and coordination. Do you have any pain in or around the ear? BEFORE I START — CAN I JUST CHECK: DID THE HEARING LOSS COME ON SUDDENLY, OVER A FEW HOURS OR OVERNIGHT, OR HAS IT CREPT UP GRADUALLY OVER WEEKS OR MONTHS?' → 'gradually, over about four months.' Then THE FRAMING SENTENCE: 'Examiner, because one-sided hearing loss with tinnitus can arise anywhere from the external ear through the middle ear and cochlea to the eighth nerve and the cerebellopontine angle, I'll perform a complete ear examination with hearing tests, and then examine the fifth, seventh and eighth cranial nerves and the cerebellum.' (SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL LOSS — HOURS TO THREE DAYS — IS AN OTOLOGICAL EMERGENCY because corticosteroids only work if started early; a candidate who never asks has guessed correctly rather than reasoned correctly.)

THE EXTERNAL EAR: 'on general appearance she is alert, comfortable and not distressed. No facial asymmetry at rest, no hearing aid, no post-auricular scar, and NO CAFE-AU-LAIT PATCHES OR CUTANEOUS NEUROFIBROMAS. Comparing both sides, then the left: the pinna is normally formed — helix, antihelix, tragus, antitragus, concha and lobule — with no rash, redness, swelling or deformity. Behind the ear, the mastoid is not swollen or erythematous. At the canal, no discharge and no blood.' Then palpation: 'helix... tragus... lobule... pressing over the mastoid... AND NOW MOVING THE EAR ITSELF. No tenderness on palpation and NO TENDERNESS ON MOVEMENT OF THE PINNA, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST AN EXTERNAL EAR INFECTION. I'd also palpate for pre-auricular and post-auricular nodes.'

OTOSCOPY OFFERED ANYWAY, GOOD EAR FIRST: 'Examiner, I NOTE THE DRUMS ARE REPORTED NORMAL, BUT I'D STILL LIKE TO PERFORM OTOSCOPY ON BOTH EARS, STARTING WITH THE NORMAL RIGHT EAR, pulling the pinna up and back, looking for WAX, A MIDDLE EAR EFFUSION, PERFORATION, A RETRACTION POCKET OR CHOLESTEATOMA, and identifying the CONE OF LIGHT AND THE HANDLE OF THE MALLEUS.' (Skipping it because the stem gave you the answer tests whether you EXAMINE or whether you READ — and the sentence is the mark, not the instrument. Good ear first gives her a reference sensation, is more comfortable, and avoids carrying wax into a healthy ear — say why.)

THE THREE HEARING TESTS IN SEQUENCE — WHISPER FIRST: 'please block your left ear with your finger — I'LL START WITH THE GOOD SIDE. I'm going to whisper a number close to your right ear; just repeat it back.' Ninety-nine close, sixty-six at arm's length, then the same on the left → she cannot repeat it even close in → 'Examiner, the whisper test is normal on the right, but on the left she cannot repeat the number even at close range. THERE IS A GENUINE HEARING LOSS IN THE LEFT EAR. I'LL NOW DETERMINE WHETHER IT IS CONDUCTIVE OR SENSORINEURAL.' (GOING STRAIGHT TO THE TUNING FORK IS THE ONE THAT FAILS MOST CANDIDATES: Rinne with air better than bone is the NORMAL result AND the SENSORINEURAL result, because both routes are attenuated equally — only the whisper or audiometry establishes that there IS a loss.)

RINNE AND WEBER, then the rule before the conclusion: 'I'm using a 512 HERTZ tuning fork. Sarah, it makes a sound like this. I'll place the BASE on the bone behind your ear — tell me the moment you STOP hearing it. Then I'll hold it in front of your ear and you tell me whether you can hear it again.' Strike on your knee, right ear first. Then: 'now I'll ring it once more and place it IN THE MIDDLE OF YOUR FOREHEAD. Do you hear it louder on the left, louder on the right, or the same?' → 'Examiner: whisper reduced on the left; Rinne air conduction better than bone conduction bilaterally; Weber lateralises to the right, the better-hearing ear. WEBER LATERALISES AWAY FROM A SENSORINEURAL LOSS AND TOWARD A CONDUCTIVE ONE, so in an ear I have already shown to be deaf, THIS IS A LEFT SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS. With a normal drum, the lesion is COCHLEAR OR RETROCOCHLEAR.' (Technique the examiner leans in for: strike on your knee or palm, NOT a table or rail; give the instruction BEFORE the fork is ringing; base ON the mastoid; tines IN LINE with the canal.)

THE NEIGHBOURS OF THE EIGHTH NERVE: 'Examiner, BECAUSE THE EIGHTH NERVE SHARES THE CEREBELLOPONTINE ANGLE WITH THE FIFTH AND THE SEVENTH, I'd like to examine both, and the cerebellum behind them.' CN V — cotton wool demonstrated on the neck, eyes closed, V1, V2, V3 left against right; pain and temperature requested; masseter and temporalis; AND 'I WOULD PARTICULARLY LIKE TO TEST THE CORNEAL REFLEX ON THE LEFT, BECAUSE A DIMINISHED CORNEAL REFLEX IS OFTEN THE EARLIEST ADDITIONAL SIGN OF A CEREBELLOPONTINE ANGLE TUMOUR.' CN VII — eyebrows, eyes shut, cheeks, teeth, upper AND lower face — plus 'have you noticed any change in TASTE at the front of your tongue, or that ordinary sounds seem UNCOMFORTABLY LOUD on that side?' Then eye movements: 'full range, no diplopia, AND I AM SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR NYSTAGMUS' → none → USE THE NEGATIVE: 'THE ABSENCE OF NYSTAGMUS, WITH NO NAUSEA AND NO VOMITING, ARGUES AGAINST AN ACUTE VESTIBULAR SYNDROME SUCH AS LABYRINTHITIS.' And offer Dix-Hallpike.

BALANCE, CEREBELLUM AND THE FUNDUS — she can walk, so there is no excuse: finger-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin — 'no past-pointing, no intention tremor, no dysdiadochokinesis'; then GAIT to the door and back with heel-to-toe; then ROMBERG with you standing beside her; then JOINT POSITION SENSE at the big toe. 'Examiner, I'd complete by OFFERING FUNDOSCOPY, LOOKING FOR PAPILLOEDEMA, SINCE A LARGE CEREBELLOPONTINE ANGLE TUMOUR CAN OBSTRUCT CEREBROSPINAL FLUID FLOW; and I'd screen the remaining cranial nerves.' (Romberg tests PROPRIOCEPTION, not the cerebellum: swaying only AFTER the eyes close means dorsal column or vestibular loss, while unsteadiness BEFORE they close is cerebellar. A normal finding you have actively looked for is worth a mark; one you never tested is worth nothing.)

THE DIAGNOSIS, WITH THE THREE QUALIFIERS AND A PAUSE: 'the tests show that the hearing loss is in your left ear, and that it's coming from the inner ear or the hearing nerve rather than from a blockage — your eardrum is completely normal. The commonest reason for that pattern in someone your age is A SMALL, SLOW-GROWING, NON-CANCEROUS SWELLING on the nerve that runs between the inner ear and the brain. It's called an acoustic neuroma. IT ISN'T A CANCER AND IT DOESN'T SPREAD — but because of where it sits, we do need to find out whether it's there and how big it is.' → 'a growth? On my brain?' → PAUSE, VALIDATE, CORRECT GENTLY, THEN ITEMISE: 'it's not on the brain itself — it's on the nerve just outside it... and I want to tell you WHAT I DIDN'T FIND TODAY: the feeling in your face, the reflex in your eye, your facial movements, your balance, your coordination and the back of your eyes were all completely normal. THOSE ARE THE THINGS THAT CHANGE WHEN ONE OF THESE GETS LARGE.' Then the differentials BY SITE to the examiner, THE INVESTIGATION NAMED IN FULL, and the safety-net. (Using the word tumour without the three qualifiers and without pausing is one error; 'just a little growth, nothing to worry about' is the worse one.)

ask: 'Did the hearing loss come on suddenly, over a few hours or overnight, or has it crept up gradually over weeks or months?' / 'Because one-sided hearing loss with tinnitus can arise anywhere from the external ear through the middle ear and cochlea to the eighth nerve and cerebellopontine angle...' / 'I note the drums are reported normal, but I'd still like otoscopy on both ears, starting with the normal side.' / 'No tenderness on movement of the pinna, which argues against an external ear infection.'

'Please block your other ear with your finger. I'll whisper a number close to this ear — just repeat it back.' / 'There is a genuine hearing loss in the left ear. I'll now determine whether it is conductive or sensorineural.' / 'I'm using a 512 hertz tuning fork.' / 'Weber lateralises AWAY from a sensorineural loss and TOWARD a conductive one.' / 'This is a left sensorineural hearing loss; with a normal drum, the lesion is cochlear or retrocochlear.'

'Because the eighth nerve shares the cerebellopontine angle with the fifth and seventh, I'd like to examine both — and I would particularly like the corneal reflex, which is often the earliest additional sign.' / 'The absence of nystagmus, with no nausea and no vomiting, argues against an acute vestibular syndrome such as labyrinthitis.' / 'It's a small, slow-growing, non-cancerous swelling on the nerve between the inner ear and the brain.' / 'Pure-tone and speech audiometry, and an MRI of the INTERNAL AUDITORY MEATI WITH GADOLINIUM — a plain CT can miss a small tumour inside the canal.'

VARIANT B — SUDDEN LOSS, and only the answer to your onset question changes: 'I woke up two days ago and the hearing had just gone' → CHANGE GEAR OUT LOUD: 'a sensorineural hearing loss developing over HOURS TO THREE DAYS is an IDIOPATHIC SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS until proven otherwise, and it is an OTOLOGICAL EMERGENCY. I would speak to ENT TODAY rather than referring routinely, because the benefit of corticosteroids falls away with delay: urgent audiometry to confirm and quantify, high-dose oral corticosteroid after discussion with ENT — and I'd check the current regimen against Therapeutic Guidelines rather than quote a dose from memory — and STILL request MRI of the internal auditory meati with gadolinium, because a proportion of sudden losses are the presentation of a vestibular schwannoma.' / VARIANT C — A CONDUCTIVE PATTERN (bone better than air on the left, Weber to the left): 'both findings indicate a CONDUCTIVE loss on the left... that moves my thinking toward the external and middle ear. I'd re-examine for wax, effusion, perforation, retraction pocket or cholesteatoma, and consider OTOSCLEROSIS, which classically presents in a young adult with progressive conductive loss and tinnitus and may have a family history. I'd confirm with TYMPANOMETRY and pure-tone audiometry.' If challenged that the drum was normal: 'A NORMAL-LOOKING DRUM DOES NOT EXCLUDE A CONDUCTIVE LOSS — otosclerosis, ossicular discontinuity and an early effusion can all give a normal drum. That is exactly why I'd add tympanometry, and why I performed the tuning fork tests rather than relying on the reported otoscopy.'

VARIANT D — VERTIGO AND TINNITUS WITHOUT NAUSEA: 'that makes an acute inflammatory labyrinthitis unlikely, because nausea is NEAR-UNIVERSAL in an acute vestibular syndrome. In that setting I'd put an acoustic neuroma at the top: it typically produces unilateral tinnitus, progressive sensorineural loss and MILD UNSTEADINESS RATHER THAN VIOLENT SPINNING, because the tumour grows slowly enough for the brain to compensate.' / VARIANT E — A LARGE TUMOUR (reduced facial sensation, ABSENT corneal reflex, past-pointing, broad-based gait): 'those findings indicate a LARGE left cerebellopontine angle lesion compressing the fifth nerve AND the cerebellum, not just the eighth. That raises the urgency substantially: urgent MRI brain and internal auditory meati with gadolinium, check the fundi for papilloedema, ask about morning headache and vomiting, and refer to NEUROSURGERY as well as ENT.' AND IF BILATERAL: 'bilateral vestibular schwannomas are effectively diagnostic of NEUROFIBROMATOSIS TYPE 2 — examine the skin for cafe-au-lait patches and neurofibromas, ask about family history and cataracts in youth, image both meati AND the whole neuraxis, and refer for genetic counselling, since it is autosomal dominant.' THE THIRTY-SECOND RESCUE if behind at six minutes: 'Examiner, in the interest of time I'll assume the cerebellar examination and fundoscopy are normal — may I explain my diagnosis?'
pefe: Role-player: Sarah Nguyen, 27, primary school teacher in a regional town, ENGAGED AND GETTING MARRIED IN SIX MONTHS; non-smoker, no medications, no past illness, no head injury, no family history of deafness, no noise exposure. Over about FOUR MONTHS the hearing in her LEFT ear has become progressively muffled — she keeps swapping the phone to the right ear and struggles in a noisy staff room — with a CONSTANT HIGH-PITCHED BUZZING worse at night that stops her sleeping. She feels occasionally 'a bit off-balance' but has NEVER had spinning vertigo and has NEVER been nauseated or vomited. SHE IS WELL: sits comfortably, answers clearly, cooperates with everything, walks normally. ONLY SAY THE ONSET WAS GRADUAL IF THE CANDIDATE ASKS — IF THEY NEVER ASK, DO NOT OFFER IT. HIDDEN AGENDA: she has read online that ringing in one ear can mean a brain tumour and is frightened — raised only if asked about concerns, or as 'A GROWTH? ON MY BRAIN?' when the diagnosis is first said. SECOND HIDDEN AGENDA: the wedding in six months, mentioned only if asked about work, plans or worries. SHE BECOMES VISIBLY CALMER IF THE REASSURANCE IS ITEMISED, and STAYS ANXIOUS at a bare 'nothing to worry about' or if the word tumour is used without the qualifiers.

How she plays the findings: whisper on the RIGHT — repeats both numbers correctly; whisper on the LEFT — 'sorry, I can't hear anything at all on that side', EVEN CLOSE IN; Rinne behind the left ear — 'it's gone now'; in front of the left ear — 'yes, I can hear it, but very faintly'; right ear — 'gone... yes, I can hear it clearly in front'; WEBER — 'LOUDER ON THE RIGHT'. Cotton wool on the face — 'yes... yes... yes' equally both sides. Facial movements full and symmetrical. No taste change, no hyperacusis. Finger-nose, heel-shin and walking all accurate. Romberg — stands steady, no sway. EXAMINER'S FINDINGS, GIVEN ONLY WHEN ASKED: otoscopy — 'both tympanic membranes are normal, move on'; facial pain and temperature — normal all three divisions; CORNEAL REFLEX — 'present and equal both sides', AND IF NEVER REQUESTED, GIVE NOTHING AND MARK IT AS MISSED; nystagmus BY NAME — 'no nystagmus'; Dix-Hallpike — 'not required'; fundoscopy — normal; remaining cranial nerves and limb examination — normal. Probe questions at the end: why not labyrinthitis; what exactly would you request; why not a CT; treatment options; what if she had woken deaf two days ago; what if it were both ears.

Scored out of 20, pass 13, with the starred items: ASKED ABOUT SPEED OF ONSET (2); WHISPER PERFORMED BEFORE THE TUNING FORK (2); STATED THE LOSS IS SENSORINEURAL AND RETROCOCHLEAR (2); EXAMINED CN V AND CN VII AND OFFERED THE CORNEAL REFLEX BY NAME (2); MRI INTERNAL AUDITORY MEATI WITH GADOLINIUM PLUS AUDIOMETRY NAMED IN FULL (1). Also: WIPE, consent, pain check and exposure; the framing sentence naming external, middle, cochlear and retrocochlear; inspected and palpated both ears and moved the pinna; offered otoscopy and named what to look for; examined the GOOD EAR FIRST; Rinne and Weber with 512 Hz named and correct instructions; asked for nystagmus by name AND USED THE NEGATIVE IN THE REASONING; cerebellar screen, gait, Romberg and joint position sense; diagnosis with reasoning plus differentials by site; and a lay explanation with calibrated reassurance and a safety-net. NUMBERS: 512 Hz fork; whisper close then one arm's length; Dix-Hallpike head 45 degrees, extended 20-30, watched 30-45 s; SUDDEN SNHL = onset over hours to 3 days with a steroid window measured in WEEKS NOT MONTHS; Meniere attacks 20 min to 12 h; CPA order VIII, V, cerebellum, VII, IX/X; BILATERAL SCHWANNOMAS = NF2; hearing tests done by 3:45 and explanation from 6:00.
fails: ★ Going straight to the tuning fork — Rinne with air better than bone is BOTH the normal and the sensorineural result, so only the whisper establishes that there IS a loss
★ Finishing at the tuning fork — a flawless ear examination with no cranial nerve examination misses the point, which is a mass in the cerebellopontine angle
Never asking whether the onset was sudden or gradual, when sudden sensorineural loss is an otological emergency and the steroid window is measured in weeks
Never offering the corneal reflex by name; running all twelve cranial nerves in full and never reaching the cerebellum or the explanation

Reporting without interpreting — 'Rinne is AC greater than BC and Weber goes to the right' is a data point, not an answer; skipping otoscopy because the stem gave the answer; examining the affected ear first; skipping Romberg and joint position sense because 'she isn't dizzy'; asking for 'a scan' or 'a CT head' rather than MRI of the internal auditory meati with gadolinium; and the word tumour without its three qualifiers

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — cranial nerves, and HE ASKS 'IS IT A STROKE?' IN HIS FIRST OR SECOND LINE. Do not answer it yet and do not dismiss it: acknowledge, defer, and PROMISE A STRAIGHT ANSWER. THE STATION IS BUILT ON ONE WORD — FOREHEAD. Structure it by the nerve's course: brainstem, cerebellopontine angle, EAR, skull base, PAROTID — and if you find no cause, the diagnosis becomes BELL'S PALSY, A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION. Automatic fails: never testing or commenting on the forehead; diagnosing Bell's in the forehead-SPARED variant; reassuring about stroke without examining; AND GIVING NO EYE PROTECTION ADVICE.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Dale Kirkbride, 46, WOKE THIS MORNING WITH THE LEFT SIDE OF HIS FACE NOT WORKING. HE IS FRIGHTENED HE IS HAVING A STROKE — HIS BROTHER HAD ONE AT 52. A photograph of the face at rest is provided, and the examiner may hand you further photographs for each movement you test. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a relevant physical examination with a running commentary, to identify or exclude a cause for his facial weakness
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
time: NAME HIS FEAR, THEN DEFER IT · 'I'm going to examine you carefully and then tell you exactly what I think, INCLUDING WHETHER I'M WORRIED ABOUT A STROKE' · THEN STATE THE STRUCTURE BY THE NERVE'S COURSE · GENERAL APPEARANCE (alert, fluent speech, no limb weakness, RED WATERY EYE) and INSPECTION AT REST, SAYING THE WORD FOREHEAD · THE FIVE MOVEMENTS, DEMONSTRATED YOURSELF AND TESTED AGAINST RESISTANCE: forehead, eyes (NOT forced open, looking for BELL'S PHENOMENON), cheeks, teeth, lips and platysma · THEN THE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE STATION: forehead involvement makes this LOWER MOTOR NEURONE, so a cortical stroke is very unlikely · TWO QUESTIONS WORTH ADDING: TASTE and HYPERACUSIS, which localise the lesion inside the canal · THE EAR (pinna and canal for VESICLES, otoscopy for CHOLESTEATOMA, then whisper, Rinne and Weber because an acoustic neuroma affects VII and VIII together) · THE PAROTID (swelling, displaced lobe, palpation, bimanual intraoral offered) · THE TRIGEMINAL, because V, VII and VIII leave the brainstem together · completion: fundoscopy, trauma signs, full cranial nerve and limb examination TO EXCLUDE A STROKE · then ANSWER THE FEAR FIRST WITH THE REASON, name it, give the differentials in plain words, and EYE PROTECTION BEFORE PROGNOSIS.

back.dx: BELL'S PALSY — an idiopathic LOWER MOTOR NEURONE facial nerve palsy, and A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION. THE DISCRIMINATOR: the upper face has BILATERAL CORTICAL INNERVATION, so a unilateral cortical lesion SPARES the forehead — here the forehead IS involved, which places the lesion in the nerve itself, after it leaves the brain. Say it to him in those words: 'your forehead gets its nerve supply from BOTH sides of the brain, so when someone has a stroke on one side, the forehead usually still works and only the lower half of the face droops. In your case the forehead IS affected.' DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS, matching the nerve's course: a stroke or problem in the brain; a GROWTH ON THE NERVE near the hearing nerve (acoustic neuroma); problems in the EAR — cholesteatoma, or a SHINGLES INFECTION giving blisters around the ear (Ramsay Hunt); a GROWTH IN THE SALIVA GLAND; and INJURY, such as after a skull fracture. MANAGEMENT, EYE FIRST: PREDNISOLONE, best started within 72 hours VERIFY — and then THE PART THAT CAUSES LASTING HARM IF MISSED: the lid does not close, so EXPOSURE KERATOPATHY is the real complication. LUBRICATING DROPS THROUGH THE DAY, OINTMENT AT BEDTIME, TAPE THE EYE SHUT BEFORE SLEEP, and sunglasses outside. PROGNOSIS WITHOUT OVER-PROMISING: most people recover and most recover fully, usually improving in TWO TO THREE WEEKS and settling over THREE TO SIX MONTHS VERIFY — 'I can't promise you it'll be perfect, but the odds are good.' NO RECOVERY BY THREE MONTHS means image and refer. SAFETY-NET: eye painful, red or vision changing; a rash or blisters around the ear; weakness anywhere else; or the OTHER side of the face starting to go. IMAGING is not needed in a typical unilateral LMN palsy with an otherwise normal examination — image if the forehead is SPARED, if it is BILATERAL, RECURRENT or SLOWLY PROGRESSIVE, or if there is NO RECOVERY BY THREE MONTHS.
plan: NAME THE FEAR, DEFER THE ANSWER, THEN STATE THE STRUCTURE: 'hello Dale, I'm Dr -. I CAN SEE YOU'RE WORRIED. I'm going to examine you carefully and then tell you exactly what I think, INCLUDING WHETHER I'M WORRIED ABOUT A STROKE. Is that alright?' → 'my brother had a stroke at 52. Is that what this is?' → 'THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT I'M GOING TO CHECK. Let me examine you properly first, and then I'll give you a straight answer.' Then to the examiner: 'because the facial nerve travels FROM THE BRAINSTEM, THROUGH THE CEREBELLOPONTINE ANGLE, THROUGH THE EAR, OUT OF THE SKULL AND THEN THROUGH THE PAROTID GLAND, I will examine each of those areas in turn to look for a cause. If I find none, the diagnosis becomes BELL'S PALSY, A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION.' (Answering 'is it a stroke?' before you have examined him is unsupported either way.)

APPEARANCE AND INSPECTION — and say the word: 'on general appearance he is alert and orientated, speech is fluent with no dysarthria and no obvious limb weakness. There is a RED, WATERY LEFT EYE, which is common in facial palsy because the lid does not close overnight and the cornea dries. Inspecting the face at rest: asymmetry affecting the left. MOST IMPORTANTLY THERE IS LOSS OF THE WRINKLES ACROSS THE LEFT FOREHEAD — THE FOREHEAD IS INVOLVED. There is also drooping of the left eyebrow and eyelid, loss of the left nasolabial fold and drooping of the left corner of the mouth. No facial swelling and no parotid mass. I am inspecting the left pinna and ear canal for VESICLES OR A RASH.' (Describing the droop and the nasolabial fold and never saying FOREHEAD misses the one word the station is built on.)

THE FIVE MOVEMENTS, DEMONSTRATED AND RESISTED: 'Dale, COPY WHAT I DO AND HOLD IT AGAINST ME. Raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead — now stop me pushing them down. Screw your eyes tightly shut and don't let me open them — I'M NOT GOING TO FORCE THEM OPEN, I'm looking for BELL'S PHENOMENON. Puff out your cheeks and hold the air in. Show me your teeth in a big smile. Purse your lips as if to whistle, and tense the muscles in your neck.' (Testing the smile alone, or testing movement WITHOUT RESISTANCE, is the common failure — these are POWER tests, and the forehead is the branch that matters most.)

THE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE STATION, then the two localising questions: 'there is weakness of ALL BRANCHES of the left facial nerve, INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD, with a POSITIVE BELL'S PHENOMENON. FOREHEAD INVOLVEMENT MAKES THIS A LOWER MOTOR NEURONE PALSY, NOT UPPER MOTOR NEURONE, SO A CORTICAL STROKE IS VERY UNLIKELY.' Then: 'Dale, have you noticed any CHANGE IN YOUR SENSE OF TASTE? And does any sound seem UNCOMFORTABLY LOUD in that ear?' → 'my coffee tasted odd this morning... and the telly seemed really loud on that side' → 'thank you — that fits with the nerve being affected INSIDE THE EAR CANAL, before it gives off its branches to the tongue and to a small muscle in the ear.' (Taste is the CHORDA TYMPANI, anterior two-thirds; hyperacusis is the NERVE TO STAPEDIUS.)

THE EAR, THE PAROTID, AND THE TRIGEMINAL: 'now the ear, because the seventh and eighth nerves travel together. On inspection of the pinna and canal I'm looking for VESICLES OR A RASH SUGGESTING RAMSAY HUNT SYNDROME, and I'd look at the palate and tongue too. On otoscopy I'm looking for vesicles, otitis media, and most importantly WHITE CHEESY DEBRIS OR AN ATTIC RETRACTION SUGGESTING CHOLESTEATOMA. I would then test the hearing with a whisper test, then RINNE AND WEBER, BECAUSE AN ACOUSTIC NEUROMA CAN AFFECT BOTH THE SEVENTH AND THE EIGHTH NERVE. The nerve then passes through the PAROTID GLAND — there is no swelling or visible mass and THE EAR LOBE IS NOT DISPLACED. I'm palpating the gland, and I would offer a BIMANUAL INTRAORAL PALPATION. And because V, VII and VIII leave the brainstem together at the cerebellopontine angle, I'm checking the TRIGEMINAL — cotton wool demonstrated first, eyes closed, V1, V2 and V3 left against right, then masseter and temporalis on clenching.' (When told to skip something, NAME THE STEP AND WHAT YOU WOULD LOOK FOR, THEN MOVE — being stopped is not the same as omitting.)

COMPLETION: 'to complete, I would perform FUNDOSCOPY for papilloedema; look for TRAUMA SIGNS, specifically RACCOON EYES AND BATTLE'S SIGN, and any clear discharge from the nose or ears suggesting a BASAL SKULL FRACTURE; and perform a FULL CRANIAL NERVE EXAMINATION WITH AN UPPER AND LOWER LIMB NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION TO EXCLUDE A STROKE.'

ANSWER THE FEAR FIRST, WITH THE REASON: 'Dale, THE GOOD NEWS FIRST: I DON'T THINK THIS IS A STROKE. The reason I can say that is YOUR FOREHEAD. It gets its nerve supply from BOTH sides of the brain, so when someone has a stroke on one side, the forehead usually still works and only the lower half of the face droops. In your case the forehead IS affected, which tells me the problem is IN THE NERVE ITSELF, after it leaves the brain. I've also checked your arms, legs, speech and the other nerves in your face, and they're all normal.' Then name it: 'it's called BELL'S PALSY... we think a viral infection is often behind it, but honestly, WE DON'T ALWAYS FIND A REASON. That's why it's diagnosed by RULING OTHER THINGS OUT — which is exactly what I've just been doing.' Then the differentials in plain words (see dx).

THE PLAN, EYE FIRST, THEN PROGNOSIS AND SAFETY-NET: 'two things. I'll start you on a short course of STEROID TABLETS, which works best if we start early — so, today. AND THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE: YOUR EYE. That eyelid isn't closing properly, so the surface of your eye can dry out and get damaged. THAT'S THE PART OF THIS THAT CAN CAUSE LASTING HARM. So: LUBRICATING DROPS THROUGH THE DAY, OINTMENT AT BEDTIME, AND TAPE THE EYE SHUT BEFORE YOU SLEEP. Sunglasses outside.' Then: 'most people recover, and most recover fully. It usually starts improving in two to three weeks and can take a few months to settle completely. I CAN'T PROMISE YOU IT'LL BE PERFECT, BUT THE ODDS ARE GOOD. Come back sooner if your eye becomes painful or red or your vision changes, if you get a rash or blisters around your ear, if you get weakness anywhere else, or if the OTHER side of your face starts to go. I'll see you in a week.' (Promising full recovery is a claim you cannot support; FORGETTING THE EYE IS THE OMISSION THAT CAUSES REAL HARM AND FAILS THE STATION.)

ask: 'I'll examine you carefully and then tell you exactly what I think, including whether I'm worried about a stroke.' / 'The facial nerve runs from the brainstem, through the ear, through the parotid, to the face — I'll examine each in turn.' / 'There is loss of the wrinkles across the left forehead.' / 'THE FOREHEAD IS INVOLVED.' / 'Copy what I do, and hold it against me.' / 'I'm not going to force the lids open — I'm looking for Bell's phenomenon.'

'Forehead involvement makes this a lower motor neurone palsy.' / 'Any change in your taste? Does any sound seem uncomfortably loud?' / 'I'm looking for vesicles on the pinna and in the canal.' / 'On otoscopy, white cheesy debris would suggest cholesteatoma.' / 'I'm palpating the parotid for a mass.' / 'I would complete a full cranial nerve and limb examination to exclude a stroke.'

'The good news first: I don't think this is a stroke.' / 'Your forehead gets its nerve supply from BOTH sides of the brain.' / 'Drops through the day, ointment at night, and tape the eye shut before you sleep.' EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'how do you know this isn't a stroke?' → the forehead is involved, the upper face has bilateral cortical innervation, and the limb and cranial nerve examination is normal. 'Would you scan him?' → not in a typical unilateral LMN palsy with an otherwise normal examination; image if the forehead were SPARED, if it were BILATERAL, RECURRENT or SLOWLY PROGRESSIVE, or if there were NO RECOVERY BY THREE MONTHS. 'The single most important part of your management?' → EYE PROTECTION, because exposure keratopathy is the complication that causes permanent harm.

VARIANT — THE FOREHEAD IS SPARED: 'Examiner, THE FOREHEAD IS SPARED — he can wrinkle it normally on both sides. That makes this an UPPER MOTOR NEURONE lesion and I am treating it as a STROKE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I would stop here, establish the TIME OF ONSET, check a BLOOD GLUCOSE, perform a full limb, speech and cranial nerve examination, and activate the stroke pathway with urgent imaging — and in this rural setting I would call MedSTAR on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval.' / VARIANT — BILATERAL WEAKNESS: 'the weakness is BILATERAL. That takes this out of Bell's palsy altogether. I would examine the limbs for ASCENDING WEAKNESS AND AREFLEXIA and ask about a recent diarrhoeal or respiratory illness, because GUILLAIN-BARRE SYNDROME is the diagnosis I must not miss. I would also consider Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV and infiltrative causes. This needs URGENT ADMISSION with monitoring of VITAL CAPACITY — NOT oxygen saturation, which falls late.'

VARIANT — RAMSAY HUNT, vesicles on the pinna and in the external canal with severe ear pain: 'with a facial nerve palsy and severe ear pain, this is RAMSAY HUNT SYNDROME — herpes zoster of the facial nerve. That changes my management: I would ADD AN ANTIVIRAL to the corticosteroid, start both as early as possible, ASSESS HEARING AND BALANCE because the eighth nerve is often involved, and refer to ENT. THE PALSY IS USUALLY MORE SEVERE AND THE RECOVERY LESS COMPLETE than in Bell's palsy.' Numbers: FIVE branches — temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical. FIVE movements — forehead, eyes, cheeks, teeth, lips and platysma. Bell's phenomenon: eyeball UP AND OUT with sclera visible. Taste = anterior two-thirds via chorda tympani; hyperacusis = nerve to stapedius. Prednisolone within 72 hours VERIFY. House-Brackmann 1 to 6. Improvement 2-3 weeks, recovery 3-6 months VERIFY.
pefe: Role-player: Dale Kirkbride, 46, drives a header and does contract harvesting on the Yorke Peninsula, married with two teenagers, NOT A WORRIER AS A RULE. He WOKE THIS MORNING with the left side of his face not working — his mouth wouldn't hold coffee, his left eye wouldn't shut properly and it has been WATERING AND STINGING all morning. It came on OVERNIGHT and was fine when he went to bed. HIS FEAR, STATED EARLY: 'my brother had a stroke at 52. Is that what this is?' DETAILS ONLY IF ASKED: a dull ache behind the left ear yesterday; his coffee tasted odd this morning; the television seemed too loud on that side. NO rash or blisters, no ear discharge, no hearing loss, no dizziness, no head injury, no limb weakness or numbness, speech fine, no lumps in front of the ear, no medications or allergies, non-smoker. Frightened underneath a calm exterior — short answers, jaw set. WHEN THE DOCTOR SAYS IT IS NOT A STROKE, EXHALE VISIBLY AND RELAX. Then ask the two things that actually matter: 'WILL MY FACE GO BACK TO NORMAL?' and 'CAN I STILL WORK?'

ON EXAMINATION, KEEP THE WHOLE LEFT SIDE COMPLETELY STILL: wrinkle your forehead — THE LEFT FOREHEAD DOES NOT MOVE AT ALL; close your eyes tightly — THE LEFT EYE WILL NOT CLOSE, LEAVE A GAP; puff out your cheeks — LET AIR ESCAPE FROM THE LEFT; show me your teeth — THE SMILE PULLS TO THE RIGHT and the left corner stays down; purse your lips — CANNOT DO IT ON THE LEFT. Cotton wool feels the same on both sides; clenching is normal and equal. THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: moving the left forehead; VOLUNTEERING THE TASTE AND THE LOUD TELEVISION, which should WAIT TO BE ASKED because they are the details that show the candidate understands where the lesion is; and staying tense after the reassurance, when visibly relaxing rewards the explanation and tells them it landed.

Scored out of 20: washed hands, introduced, consented; ACKNOWLEDGED THE STROKE FEAR WITHOUT ANSWERING IT PREMATURELY; stated a structure based on the nerve's course; commented on the red watery eye; COMMENTED ON THE FOREHEAD ON INSPECTION; described the ptosis, nasolabial fold and mouth corner; looked at the pinna and canal for vesicles; TESTED ALL FIVE MOVEMENTS AGAINST RESISTANCE; tested Bell's phenomenon WITHOUT FORCING THE LIDS; SAID LOWER MOTOR NEURONE AND EXPLAINED WHY; asked about TASTE AND HYPERACUSIS; offered otoscopy and named CHOLESTEATOMA; offered a hearing test WITH A REASON; palpated the parotid; tested the trigeminal, sensory and motor; offered fundoscopy and looked for trauma signs; offered a limb and cranial nerve examination; ANSWERED THE STROKE QUESTION; and GAVE EYE PROTECTION ADVICE.
fails: ★ Never testing or commenting on the FOREHEAD — it is the one word the station is built on
★ Diagnosing Bell's palsy in the forehead-SPARED variant, which is an upper motor neurone lesion and a stroke until proven otherwise
Giving no eye protection advice — the omission that causes real harm
Reassuring him it is not a stroke without examining, or offering the limb and cranial nerve examination; and answering 'is it a stroke?' either way before you have examined him

Testing the smile alone, or testing movement without resistance; falling silent when told to skip a step, instead of naming what you would have looked for; promising full recovery; and examining only the affected side in the bilateral variant

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — head and neck, WITH THE SITE OF THE LUMP MARKED ON THE ROLE-PLAYER'S FACE. TASK ONE IS TO ASK THE EXAMINER FOR THE FEATURES, IN A STRUCTURED ORDER — and consistency, border and fixation are the three that separate benign from malignant. THE SINISTER TRIAD IS PAINLESS, RECENT GROWTH, FACIAL PALSY. THE SPECIAL TEST IS THE FACIAL NERVE, and the station is earned by linking the palsy to the mass out loud. Automatic fails: never testing the facial nerve; testing only the smile and calling it an examination; telling him the lump is almost certainly harmless; stating flatly that he has cancer; and arranging no referral.

back.dx: MALIGNANT PAROTID TUMOUR WITH FACIAL NERVE PALSY — a five-year painless swelling that has grown over three months, firm to hard with an irregular border and poor mobility, DISPLACING THE EAR LOBE, with WEAKNESS OF ALL BRANCHES OF THE IPSILATERAL FACIAL NERVE INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD. THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE STATION: 'forehead involvement makes this a LOWER MOTOR NEURONE lesion, and WITH AN IPSILATERAL PAROTID MASS THAT IS MALIGNANT INFILTRATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' THE SINISTER TRIAD: PAINLESS, RECENT GROWTH, FACIAL PALSY. TO HIM, HONEST WITHOUT OVER-CLAIMING: 'when a lump that's been there for years starts to grow, and the nerve running through it stops working properly, THAT MAKES ME CONCERNED THIS COULD BE A CANCER. I can't be certain today — that needs a scan and a sample. BUT I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND I'M NOT WORRIED.' DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS: a non-cancerous growth of the gland, which can sit there for years; an inflamed or infected gland, unlikely with no pain and no fever; a gland of the immune system inside the parotid (lymphoma); and A SKIN CANCER THAT HAS SPREAD INTO IT, which is why you examine the scalp and ears. MANAGEMENT: SCAN, SAMPLE, SURGERY — ultrasound of the gland, then ULTRASOUND-GUIDED FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION OR CORE BIOPSY by the specialist service, then parotidectomy with radiotherapy if indicated VERIFY — referred URGENTLY, TODAY. NEVER an incisional biopsy in primary care: it risks TUMOUR SEEDING and compromises the definitive operation. AND A NORMAL FACIAL NERVE DOES NOT EXCLUDE CANCER — palsy is HIGHLY SPECIFIC BUT INSENSITIVE, and most parotid cancers present with an intact nerve, so image and refer anyway. Surgical risks to name if asked: FACIAL NERVE INJURY, numbness of the ear lobe from the greater auricular nerve, FREY SYNDROME, salivary fistula, haematoma and infection — leaving detailed consent to the surgeon. Support: PATS for travel from a country town, Cancer Council SA 13 11 20. Safety-net: rapid growth, skin breakdown over the lump, or the face getting weaker.
plan: TEMPERATURE FIRST, WITH THE REASON: 'Examiner, before I begin, MAY I HAVE THE TEMPERATURE? SIALADENITIS AND PAROTITIS ARE ON MY DIFFERENTIAL LIST, so that is the vital sign that matters here.' → 36.8. Then THE STRUCTURED REQUEST: 'could you please tell me the features of the swelling: its SITE AND SIZE, its SHAPE AND SURFACE, its CONSISTENCY, its BORDER, whether it is TENDER, whether it is MOBILE OR FIXED to the skin or the underlying tissue, and whether it is FLUCTUANT OR PULSATILE?' (Asking in a random order, or asking only for size and tenderness, misses what is being marked — a SYSTEM — and consistency, border and fixation are the three that separate benign from malignant.)

IF GIVEN A SHORT HISTORY, one question per turn — and the one that sets up the station: 'how long has the lump been there? Has it changed recently? Is it painful at all? DOES IT SWELL OR HURT WHEN YOU EAT? Have you had any fevers? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY WEAKNESS OR CHANGE IN THE MOVEMENT OF YOUR FACE? Any trouble opening your mouth or swallowing? Any lumps elsewhere, weight loss or night sweats? HAVE YOU EVER HAD A SKIN CANCER ON YOUR SCALP, EAR OR FACE?' → five years, bigger over three months, no pain, no change with eating, no fevers, HIS WIFE SAYS HIS SMILE LOOKS CROOKED, no trismus, no other lumps, and SKIN CANCERS CUT OFF HIS FOREARMS YEARS AGO.

INSPECTION: 'there is a swelling in the LEFT PAROTID REGION, in front of and below the ear, LIFTING AND DISPLACING THE LEFT EAR LOBE OUTWARDS. The overlying skin shows no redness, ulceration, tethering or scars. Looking at the FACE AT REST, I am comparing both sides for asymmetry, ptosis, loss of the nasolabial fold and drooping of the corner of the mouth, and inspecting the ear and canal for vesicles.'

THE MOUTH: 'Gordon, could you open your mouth as wide as you can? There is NO LIMITATION OF JAW OPENING. The SOFT PALATE IS SYMMETRICAL with no pharyngeal asymmetry or medial bulging. I am looking at the opening of STENSEN'S DUCT, OPPOSITE THE UPPER SECOND MOLAR, for bulging, redness, a stone or purulent discharge — it appears normal.'

PALPATION AND NODES: 'TEMPERATURE with the backs of my fingers ON BOTH CHEEKS — no local rise. Gordon, I'm going to feel the lump; tell me if it's tender. It is about 3 by 4 centimetres, FIRM TO HARD, NON-TENDER, with an IRREGULAR BORDER and a NODULAR SURFACE, and it is POORLY MOBILE in both planes with no fixation to the skin. Not fluctuant, not pulsatile.' Then from behind: 'PRE-AURICULAR, POST-AURICULAR, OCCIPITAL, SUBMENTAL, SUBMANDIBULAR, ANTERIOR AND POSTERIOR CERVICAL CHAINS AND THE SUPRACLAVICULAR FOSSA — no lymphadenopathy.'

THE SPECIAL TEST: 'MY SPECIAL TEST IS THE FACIAL NERVE. Gordon, COPY WHAT I DO AND HOLD AGAINST ME: raise your eyebrows and wrinkle your forehead; screw your eyes shut and don't let me open them; puff out your cheeks; show me your teeth; purse your lips and tense your neck.' → weakness of all branches including the forehead → THE SENTENCE: 'there is weakness of ALL BRANCHES of the left facial nerve, INCLUDING THE FOREHEAD. Forehead involvement makes this a LOWER MOTOR NEURONE lesion, and WITH AN IPSILATERAL PAROTID MASS THAT IS MALIGNANT INFILTRATION UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' Then completion: 'I would MASSAGE THE GLAND ALONG THE DUCT, perform a BIMANUAL INTRAORAL PALPATION, examine the other salivary glands, and EXAMINE THE SKIN OF THE SCALP, EARS AND FACE FOR A PRIMARY SKIN CANCER.' (Testing the smile only, or finding the weakness and never saying what it means, are both common and both cost the station.)

WARNING SHOT, THEN THE HONEST ANSWER: 'Gordon, I've found something I need to be straight with you about. Is now a good time? The lump is in your PAROTID GLAND — the big saliva gland in front of your ear. The important part is that the LEFT SIDE OF YOUR FACE ISN'T MOVING NORMALLY, and THE NERVE THAT CONTROLS YOUR FACIAL MUSCLES RUNS STRAIGHT THROUGH THAT GLAND.' → 'is it cancer?' → 'when a lump that's been there for years starts to grow, and the nerve running through it stops working properly, THAT MAKES ME CONCERNED THIS COULD BE A CANCER. I can't be certain today — that needs a scan and a sample. But I'm not going to pretend I'm not worried.' (Answering 'is it cancer?' with either 'yes it is' or 'no, I'm sure it's fine' fails: the first is not supportable on examination alone, the second is dishonest and unsafe.)

DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS, THEN SCAN, SAMPLE, SURGERY (see dx), then support and safety-net: 'there's a scheme called PATS that helps with travel and accommodation to get to Adelaide, and CANCER COUNCIL SOUTH AUSTRALIA ON 13 11 20 can help with information and support. I'll see you again this week. COME BACK SOONER IF THE LUMP GROWS QUICKLY, IF THE SKIN OVER IT BREAKS DOWN, OR IF YOUR FACE GETS WEAKER. What questions do you have?'

'Firm to hard, non-tender, irregular border, poorly mobile.' / 'MY SPECIAL TEST IS THE FACIAL NERVE.' / 'Copy what I do and hold it against me.' / 'Forehead involvement makes this a lower motor neurone lesion.' / 'WITH AN IPSILATERAL PAROTID MASS, THAT IS MALIGNANT UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.' / 'I would also examine the scalp and ears for a skin cancer.' / 'Scan, then sample, then surgery.'

EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'does a normal facial nerve exclude cancer?' → 'NO. Palsy is HIGHLY SPECIFIC for malignancy BUT INSENSITIVE — most parotid cancers present with an intact nerve. I would still image and refer.' / 'Why not just biopsy it in your rooms?' → 'an open or incisional biopsy of a parotid mass risks TUMOUR SEEDING and compromises the definitive operation. The sampling method is ULTRASOUND-GUIDED FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION OR A CORE BIOPSY, done by the specialist service.' / 'What are the risks of the operation?' → 'facial nerve injury, numbness of the ear lobe from the greater auricular nerve, FREY SYNDROME, salivary fistula, haematoma and infection — I would leave the detailed consent to the surgeon.'

VARIANTS: THE NERVE IS NORMAL → 'the facial nerve is intact in all five branches, WHICH IS REASSURING BUT DOES NOT EXCLUDE MALIGNANCY, because most parotid cancers present with a normal nerve. The HARD CONSISTENCY, IRREGULAR BORDER AND RECENT GROWTH remain sinister, so MY MANAGEMENT IS UNCHANGED: ultrasound, guided sampling and urgent referral.' / THE INFECTIVE VARIANT — temperature 38.4, tender hot diffusely swollen gland, PUS AT THE DUCT ON MASSAGE → 'this is ACUTE BACTERIAL SIALADENITIS. I would send a swab of the pus, start antibiotics, rehydrate him, and use SIALAGOGUES AND GLAND MASSAGE, image if I suspected an abscess, and review within 24 to 48 hours.' / THE STONE VARIANT — PAIN AND SWELLING THAT COME ON WHEN HE EATS and settle afterwards → 'characteristic of a SALIVARY DUCT STONE. I would look at the duct orifice and perform a BIMANUAL PALPATION along the duct for a palpable stone, arrange an ultrasound, and refer for consideration of SIALENDOSCOPY or surgical removal.' VERIFY

THE URGENT REFERRAL TO DICTATE BEFORE HE LEAVES: a five-year history of a painless left parotid swelling that has increased over three months; a 3 by 4 cm firm-to-hard non-tender mass with an irregular border and reduced mobility, DISPLACING THE EAR LOBE; and CRITICALLY a complete left lower motor neurone facial nerve palsy INVOLVING THE FOREHEAD. No fever, no local temperature rise, no skin ulceration or tethering, no trismus, symmetrical palate and pharynx, normal duct orifice with no pus, and no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Past history: multiple previously excised cutaneous malignancies. Ultrasound requested locally; urgent assessment sought with a view to guided sampling and definitive management; the patient is aware of the concern about malignancy; and he will need PATS support for travel.
pefe: Role-player: Gordon Whitely, 55, shearing contractor on the Yorke Peninsula, married thirty years, PRACTICAL, DRY, NOT A COMPLAINER, and he has not seen a doctor in four years. His wife made the appointment. The lump has been there ABOUT FIVE YEARS and he always ignored it BECAUSE IT HAS NEVER HURT — but over the last THREE MONTHS it has clearly got bigger. HIDDEN AGENDA, NOT SAID FIRST: his wife has been telling him HIS SMILE HAS GONE CROOKED and that he DRIBBLES TEA from the left side of his mouth — he thinks she is fussing. ONLY MENTION IT IF THE DOCTOR ASKS ABOUT HIS FACE, OR ASKS WHAT HIS WIFE HAS NOTICED. Background: ex-smoker, gave up at 40 after about 20 a day; four or five beers on a Friday; SEVERAL SKIN CANCERS CUT OFF HIS FOREARMS AND ONE OFF HIS EAR, said if asked; no fevers, no weight loss, no night sweats, no other lumps; HIS FATHER DIED OF THROAT CANCER AT 61 AND IT WAS A BAD DEATH. He is frightened but will not say so unless asked about concerns or until cancer is named — then quietly: 'IS IT CANCER?' and 'HOW LONG HAVE I GOT BEFORE I KNOW?' Understated, dry humour early, quieter once the doctor becomes serious — and if the doctor is honest: 'THANKS FOR BEING STRAIGHT WITH ME.'

ON EXAMINATION: open the mouth fully with no difficulty; THE LEFT FOREHEAD DOES NOT MOVE; the left eye does not close fully; air escapes from the left on puffing; THE SMILE PULLS TO THE RIGHT and the left corner does not move. THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: VOLUNTEERING THE CROOKED SMILE — wait to be asked, because it is the question that carries the station; MOVING THE LEFT SIDE OF THE FACE — keep the forehead, eye, cheek and mouth still; and BECOMING TEARFUL — Gordon is understated, and going quiet is more useful to the candidate than crying, because it tests whether they notice.

Scored out of 20: washed hands, introduced, consented; ASKED FOR THE TEMPERATURE BEFORE EXAMINING; asked for the lump features IN A STRUCTURED ORDER INCLUDING CONSISTENCY, BORDER AND FIXATION; commented on the DISPLACED EAR LOBE and the skin; looked at the face at rest; asked him to OPEN HIS MOUTH and commented on jaw opening, soft palate AND STENSEN'S DUCT; compared TEMPERATURE OVER BOTH CHEEKS; palpated the lump and reported the FULL FEATURE SET; examined the cervical node chains in order; TESTED ALL FIVE FACIAL MOVEMENTS and the FOREHEAD SPECIFICALLY; SAID LOWER MOTOR NEURONE AND EXPLAINED WHY; LINKED THE PALSY TO MALIGNANCY; offered bimanual palpation and the SCALP AND EAR EXAMINATION; explained SCAN, SAMPLE, SURGERY without a tutorial; and WAS HONEST ABOUT CANCER WITHOUT OVER-CLAIMING.
fails: ★ Never testing the facial nerve at all, or testing only the smile and calling it a facial nerve examination
★ Telling him the lump is almost certainly harmless — or stating flatly that he has cancer, on examination alone
Finding the weakness and never saying what it means: forehead involvement plus an ipsilateral parotid mass is malignant infiltration until proven otherwise
Arranging no referral or follow-up; suggesting an incisional biopsy in your rooms, which risks tumour seeding

Asking for the lump features in a random order, or asking only size and tenderness; never asking about facial movement in the history; and forgetting the scalp and ear examination for a primary skin cancer

setting: HISTORY THEN EXAMINATION — rural GP, a photograph of a red linear rash, A THERMOMETER AND A TIMER ON THE DESK. YOU ARE PROMPTED AT THREE MINUTES, so ask ONE QUESTION PER TURN: bundle four into a breath and the role-player answers only the last, and you lose THE DIRECTION OF SPREAD, WHICH IS THE DIAGNOSIS. Two palpation failures live in this station: palpating landmarks and NEVER ONCE PRESSING THE RASH, and going to the axilla while SKIPPING THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE — the node the forearm actually drains to, and the special test the examiner is waiting for.
stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Alex Brennan, 32, with A RASH ON HIS RIGHT FOREARM. A photograph shows a RED LINEAR RASH; a thermometer and a timer are on the desk; VITAL SIGNS AVAILABLE FROM THE EXAMINER ON REQUEST. 8 minutes, PROMPTED AT THREE MINUTES.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient — you will be prompted at three minutes
Perform a relevant physical examination, giving a running commentary
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

back.dx: LYMPHANGITIS OF THE RIGHT FOREARM — a well-defined LINEAR erythematous patch running PROXIMALLY from a portal of entry at the wrist, warm and tender, with a REACTIVE EPITROCHLEAR NODE and no systemic upset. TO HIM IN ONE SENTENCE: 'under the skin there are small drainage channels called LYMPHATIC VESSELS. Bacteria have got in through a small break in the skin — most likely from the gardening — and THEY'RE TRAVELLING ALONG ONE OF THOSE CHANNELS, which is why it looks like A LINE RATHER THAN A PATCH.' THEN ANSWER THE FEAR DIRECTLY: 'IT'S NOT BLOOD POISONING, and it's very treatable with tablets. But it CAN turn into a more serious infection if it's left, which is exactly why I want to see you again in two days AND WHY I'VE DRAWN THAT LINE ON YOUR ARM.' DIFFERENTIALS IN PLAIN WORDS — and keep them to this consultation: CELLULITIS, the same sort of infection but spread over an AREA instead of a line; INFLAMMATION OF A VEIN, which usually gives a FIRM TENDER CORD you can feel, and there isn't one; A PLANT REACTION, which would be ITCHY AND BLISTERY rather than sore; AN INSECT BITE; and A CLOT IN THE DEEP VEINS OF THE ARM, which usually swells THE WHOLE arm. (Listing meningococcaemia, HSP, ITP, lymphoma and viral exanthems belongs in a lecture on rashes, not here — it frightens the patient for no clinical gain.) HOW LYMPHANGITIS DIFFERS FROM CELLULITIS: SHAPE. Cellulitis spreads LATERALLY with a POORLY DEFINED margin; lymphangitis travels IN A CHANNEL and gives a WELL-DEFINED LINE running toward the draining node. WHY THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE: it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE FOR THE FOREARM, a reactive node there SUPPORTS a lymphatic infection, and involvement of the node itself is LYMPHADENITIS. MANAGEMENT: flucloxacillin 500 mg orally six-hourly for five days, or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly VERIFY; TETANUS if over five years VERIFY; DRAW A LINE AT THE TOP OF THE REDNESS WITH TODAY'S DATE; review at 24-48 hours; and come straight back IF THE REDNESS PASSES THAT LINE, if fevers or shakes develop, IF THE PAIN GETS MUCH WORSE THAN IT LOOKS, or if the elbow becomes painful to move.
plan: STABILITY FIRST, BUT NOT THE FULL VITALS: 'Examiner, IS MY PATIENT STABLE ENOUGH FOR ME TO PROCEED WITH THE HISTORY?' → 'yes, please proceed.' (Asking for the full set of vital signs here is the trap: you have been asked to take a history, the examiner will LET you start examining, and your structure collapses into examine, history, examine again.) Then WIPE and AN OPEN QUESTION FOLLOWED BY SILENCE: 'Alex, CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THIS RASH?'

ONE QUESTION PER TURN, IN THIS ORDER: 'when exactly did it start?' — 'WHERE ON THE ARM DID IT START?' — 'IS IT SPREADING, AND IN WHICH DIRECTION?' — 'has this ever happened before?' — 'IS IT ITCHY, OR IS IT PAINFUL?' — 'does it feel warm to touch?' — 'is there any oozing or discharge?' → Monday, near the wrist, MOVING UP TOWARD THE ELBOW, never before, SORE NOT ITCHY, warm, no discharge. (Bundling four questions into one breath means the role-player answers ONLY THE LAST, and you lose the direction of spread — which IS the diagnosis.)

THE PORTAL OF ENTRY — and then narrow it: 'WHAT WERE YOU DOING IN THE COUPLE OF DAYS BEFORE IT STARTED?' → 'I was out in the garden on Sunday, cutting the roses back.' → 'DID YOU NOTICE ANY CUTS, SCRATCHES OR THORN PRICKS? Any insect or spider bites? Were you wearing gloves? Any recent injections, drips or blood tests in that arm?' → a scratch on the wrist he barely noticed, no gloves, no cannula. (ACCEPTING 'I WAS GARDENING' AND MOVING ON IS THE TRAP: gardening is the CONTEXT, the SCRATCH is the FINDING. And gardening also opens contact dermatitis and, if it were nodular and slow, sporotrichosis — so the same answer serves three differentials.)

SYSTEMIC SCREEN, FEVER FIRST: 'HAVE YOU HAD ANY FEVERS, CHILLS OR SHIVERING EPISODES? Do you feel generally unwell in yourself? Any swelling of the whole arm, or heaviness? Have you been doing any repetitive overhead work with that arm? Any history of eczema, hay fever or asthma, in you or your family? Any new soaps, creams, lotions or sunscreens? Any injury to the arm? What do you do for work?' (IF THE PROMPT IS COMING, ASK FEVER FIRST AND DROP THE ATOPY QUESTIONS — fever changes management, atopy does not.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND THE VITALS, NOW: 'Examiner, the patient is alert and orientated, comfortable at rest, WITH NO RIGORS. AS THIS IS AN INFECTIVE RASH I WOULD LIKE THE FULL VITAL SIGNS.' → a thermometer and a timer are handed over → USE THEM AND READ THE NUMBERS ALOUD: 'pulse 82, regular, normal volume. Temperature 37.2. HE IS AFEBRILE AND HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE.'

INSPECTION IN FIVE PARTS, PLUS THE ENTRY POINT: 'SITE — flexor aspect of the right forearm, wrist to antecubital fossa, about 15 by 2 centimetres, UNILATERAL. COLOUR — erythematous. PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY — flat and larger than a centimetre, so A PATCH, IN A LINEAR DISTRIBUTION running proximally. SECONDARY MORPHOLOGY — no vesicles, no scratch marks, no erosions, no discharge, no scale, AND NO VISIBLE VENOUS CORD. BORDERS — WELL DEFINED. There is no swelling of the whole limb. I AM ALSO LOOKING FOR AN ENTRY POINT — a bite, scratch, thorn prick or injection mark — and I can see a small linear abrasion at the wrist.'

PALPATION — and PRESS THE RASH: 'TEMPERATURE with the backs of my fingers, ON THE RASH AND COMPARED WITH THE OTHER FOREARM — there is a local rise. CAPILLARY REFILL under two seconds. RADIAL PULSE present. Alex, I'M GOING TO PRESS GENTLY ALONG THE LINE — tell me if it hurts.' → he winces → 'thank you, I'll be gentle. TENDER TO LIGHT PALPATION, consistent with infection. The lesion is NOT ELEVATED and the surface is SMOOTH. I am pressing to CHECK FOR BLANCHING — I WOULD EXPECT THIS TO BLANCH; THE APPLIED COLOURING LIMITS MY INTERPRETATION, so I am not relying on it.' (Asserting a NON-BLANCHING rash and then treating it as lymphangitis is an automatic fail — handle blanching honestly.)

THE ELBOW, THEN THE SPECIAL TEST: 'THE RASH CROSSES THE ELBOW, SO I WANT TO EXCLUDE JOINT INVOLVEMENT. The joint line is not tender and there is no effusion. Alex, bend and straighten your elbow, and turn your palm up and down.' → full pain-free movement → 'no evidence of septic arthritis. MY SPECIAL TEST IS THE REGIONAL NODES ON THE AFFECTED SIDE: THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE, ABOUT THREE CENTIMETRES ABOVE THE MEDIAL EPICONDYLE, then the axilla — apical, central, anterior, posterior and lateral chains.' → a single tender mobile epitrochlear node, axilla clear → 'A TENDER, MOBILE NODE IS REACTIVE and consistent with infection — a hard, fixed or matted node would make me think about malignancy. To complete, I would MEASURE BOTH FOREARMS AT THE SAME LEVEL for a size difference, given upper limb DVT is on my list.'

NAME IT, ANSWER THE FEAR, GIVE THE DIFFERENTIALS, DRAW THE LINE (see dx). → 'is that blood poisoning? That's what my mate reckoned.' → 'IT ISN'T, and it's very treatable with antibiotic tablets. But it can become a more serious infection if it's left, which is why I want to see you again in two days.' Then: 'I'll start you on antibiotics, and I'VE DRAWN A LINE AT THE TOP OF THE REDNESS WITH TODAY'S DATE. COME STRAIGHT BACK IF THE REDNESS PASSES THAT LINE, if you get fevers or shakes, IF THE PAIN GETS MUCH WORSE THAN IT LOOKS, or if your elbow becomes painful to move.'
