'The rash crosses the elbow, so I want to exclude joint involvement.' / 'My special test is the epitrochlear node, then the axilla, affected side only.' / 'I've drawn a line at the top of the redness with today's date on it.' EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'did the rash blanch?' → 'it did not blanch on my testing, BUT THE RASH HAS BEEN APPLIED TO THE SKIN, so I do not think that finding is interpretable. Clinically, lymphangitis blanches, and nothing else in the examination suggests a purpuric process.' / 'Why the epitrochlear node?' → 'it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE FOR THE FOREARM. A reactive node there supports a lymphatic infection, and involvement of the node itself is LYMPHADENITIS.' / 'How do you tell this from cellulitis?' → 'SHAPE. Cellulitis spreads laterally and gives an AREA with a poorly defined margin. Lymphangitis travels in a channel and gives a WELL-DEFINED LINE running toward the draining node.'

VERSION B — FEBRILE AND TACHYCARDIC: INTERRUPT YOURSELF. 'Examiner, I want to STOP AND FLAG that the temperature is 38.6 and the pulse is 108. I AM TREATING THIS AS SEPSIS FROM A SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE SOURCE. I would like large-bore intravenous access, BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, FBE, CRP, UEC, glucose and lactate, intravenous fluids, and INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS NOW. I would then complete my examination.' (Continuing a calm examination in the febrile, tachycardic variant without recognising sepsis is an automatic fail.)

THE PAIN-OUT-OF-PROPORTION MOMENT — ask, then escalate: 'Alex, IS THE PAIN MUCH WORSE THAN THE RASH LOOKS? Does the skin feel NUMB anywhere over it? And how fast has it changed — over days, or over HOURS?' → if yes, yes, hours → 'Examiner, PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION, ALTERED SENSATION OVER THE RASH AND SPREAD OVER HOURS make me concerned about NECROTISING FASCIITIS. THIS IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS AND A SURGICAL EMERGENCY — I would resuscitate, give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and CALL THE SURGICAL REGISTRAR IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN ARRANGE IMAGING.' / THE NODULAR VARIANT, when the line is made of LUMPS and has evolved over WEEKS: 'the lesions are NODULES ARRANGED IN A LINE rather than a continuous streak. That pattern is NODULAR OR SPOROTRICHOID LYMPHANGITIS. I would ask specifically about ROSE THORNS AND SPHAGNUM MOSS, which points to SPOROTHRIX, and about FISH TANKS OR FISH HANDLING, which points to MYCOBACTERIUM MARINUM. It needs a BIOPSY WITH TISSUE CULTURE, and I would TELL THE LABORATORY WHAT I SUSPECT so the cultures are held long enough.'
pefe: Role-player: Alex Brennan, 32, works at the Wallaroo grain terminal, lives with his partner and a four-year-old, plays footy on Saturdays and almost never sees a doctor. Two days ago he noticed a red mark near his right wrist; it is now a RED LINE RUNNING HALFWAY UP THE FOREARM, SORE NOT ITCHY, hot, with nothing coming out of it. WHAT HE DID: on Sunday he spent the afternoon CUTTING BACK THE ROSES WITHOUT GLOVES and got scratched a few times, thinking nothing of it — ONLY VOLUNTEER THIS IF ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING. No medications or allergies, non-smoker, six to eight beers a week; no eczema, hay fever or asthma in him or the family; no cannulas, injections or blood tests; no overhead work; no new soaps or creams; last tetanus probably at school. HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS MATE AT WORK TOLD HIM THIS WAS 'BLOOD POISONING' and that people lose arms from it — he is more worried than he is letting on. Raise it WHEN THE DOCTOR NAMES THE DIAGNOSIS, or in the last minute if they never ask about concerns, AND NOT IN THE FIRST THREE MINUTES. Practical, cheerful, slightly embarrassed to be here, not distressed.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CUE: IF THE DOCTOR PRESSES ON THE RASH, WINCE AND SAY IT IS TENDER — and IF THEY NEVER PRESS THE RASH, DO NOT PROMPT THEM. Move the elbow freely when asked: 'that's fine, no pain.' THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: VOLUNTEERING THE GARDENING — wait to be asked, because it is the single most discriminating question in the history; ANSWERING A BUNDLED QUESTION FULLY — if four questions arrive at once, ANSWER ONLY THE LAST, which is what a real patient does; and FORGETTING TO WINCE, when tenderness is a physical sign the candidate has to elicit and report.

Scored out of 20: washed hands, introduced, consented; ASKED THE EXAMINER ABOUT STABILITY FIRST; used an open question and let him answer; ASKED WHERE IT STARTED AND ESTABLISHED THE DIRECTION; asked itchy versus painful; ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING BEFOREHAND; asked about scratches, thorns or bites; asked about cannulas or injections; ASKED ABOUT FEVER AND CHILLS; asked for the FULL VITAL SIGNS AND USED THE EQUIPMENT; described site, colour, primary and secondary morphology and borders; COMPARED TEMPERATURE WITH THE OTHER ARM; PRESSED THE RASH FOR TENDERNESS; commented on elevation and surface; HANDLED BLANCHING WITHOUT ASSERTING NON-BLANCHING; EXAMINED THE ELBOW by palpation and movement; EXAMINED THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE AND THE AXILLA; gave a shaped differential with reasons in plain words; and gave a safety net with named reasons to return. Numbers: capillary refill under 2 s; PATCH flat and 1 cm or more, MACULE flat and under 1 cm, PLAQUE raised and 1 cm or more, PAPULE raised and under 1 cm; VESICLE under 5 mm, BULLA 5 mm or more; epitrochlear node about 3 cm above the medial epicondyle; 5 axillary chains; flucloxacillin 500 mg PO six-hourly for 5 days or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly VERIFY; review 24-48 h; tetanus if over 5 years VERIFY; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.

back.dx: ACUTE VIRAL GASTROENTERITIS WITH CLINICAL DEHYDRATION of about 5% in an 18-month-old — vomiting first then watery diarrhoea, TWO CHILDREN AT DAYCARE WITH THE SAME THING and a partner unwell midweek, alert but flat and clinging, drinking only sips, and WET NAPPIES DOWN FROM THREE OR FOUR A DAY TO ONE. GRADE IT OUT LOUD: 11.4 to 10.8 kg is 600 g, about 5.3% of body weight, and it is all fluid. THE EXCLUSIONS, NAMED IN PLAIN WORDS RATHER THAN LISTED: green vomit would mean a BLOCKAGE needing surgery — it isn't; screaming in episodes going pale would mean the bowel TELESCOPING — he isn't; ears, throat and chest are clear so nothing else is driving it; THE URINE IS CLEAR, which matters because a urine infection in a toddler looks exactly like this; sugar and ketones are normal so it is not DIABETES; and there is no rash, so this is not MENINGOCOCCAL. MANAGEMENT: antibiotics do not help and make the diarrhoea worse. ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION — Hydralyte or Gastrolyte — as ABOUT A TEASPOON EVERY FIVE MINUTES by syringe, because a whole cup comes straight back; four hours then RE-WEIGH. NO juice, cordial, sports drinks or lemonade — too sugary and they worsen the diarrhoea; water alone is not ideal because he is losing salts; keep milk going and let him eat as soon as he wants. IF HE CANNOT MANAGE BY MOUTH THE NEXT STEP IS A NASOGASTRIC TUBE, NOT A DRIP — it works better than a drip for this — and intravenous fluid is for the child who becomes really unwell. SAFETY-NET WITH SIX SPECIFIC TRIGGERS: floppy or hard to wake; FEWER THAN THREE WET NAPPIES IN A DAY; nothing kept down over six hours; VOMIT TURNS GREEN; blood in the vomit or the nappy; a rash that does not fade under a glass — plus 'or you are simply worried, because you know him better than I do'. In writing, review in 24 hours regardless, and PATS covers travel for country families.
plan: OPEN AND LET HER TALK: '...you must be Danielle, and this must be Riley. Hello, mate. I can see he's had a rough couple of days. I'd like to ask you some questions, then examine him, then we'll make a plan together. TELL ME, IN YOUR OWN WORDS, WHAT'S BEEN HAPPENING.' THEN DO NOT INTERRUPT FOR THIRTY SECONDS — onset, sequence, behaviour change and her own worry are all in that first answer.

THE VOMITING, quantified and coloured: 'how many times in the last twenty-four hours? What does it look like — is it milk, is it food, OR IS ANY OF IT GREEN? Any blood? Does it just come up, or does it SHOOT RIGHT OUT?' (If the answer is 'a funny colour', DISAMBIGUATE: 'GREEN LIKE GRASS OR SPINACH, OR YELLOW LIKE CURDLED MILK?' Green is malrotation until excluded and it ends the outpatient conversation.)

THE DIARRHOEA, and the one question that separates the diagnoses: 'how many times a day, and how loose? Any blood or mucus, anything like JELLY? DOES HE GO PALE AND PULL HIS KNEES UP IN EPISODES?' (That question separates gastroenteritis from INTUSSUSCEPTION at exactly this age, and there is a mark for it.)

EXCLUDE THE OTHER CAUSES: fever measured; ANY RASH, and does it fade under a glass; ears, cough, hard breathing; offensive urine; DRINKING AND WEEING FAR MORE THAN USUAL over the last week; access to medicines or chemicals → 'he did tug his ear a bit yesterday' → DO NOT DISCARD IT: 'that's worth knowing, I'll make sure I look in his ears' — parenteral diarrhoea from otitis media is genuine, and the ear-pulling is deliberate misdirection.

THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS, flagged as important: 'now some questions about how well Riley is in himself — THESE MATTER MOST TO ME. Is he ALERT AND ACTIVE AND PLAYFUL as usual, or drowsy? IS HE DRINKING as he normally would, and what about eating? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES would he normally have, and how many today? Any other change in his bowel motions?' (Asking only about EATING loses the mark — it is attached to DRINKING. And 'not many wet nappies' must be QUANTIFIED, because the numbers are what let you grade the dehydration.)

TARGETED BINDSMA ONLY — immunisations including ROTAVIRUS, SICK CONTACTS at home and daycare, medicines and allergies, one line on growth and development. Then CONCERNS: 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?' → tearful: 'my sister's little boy ended up in hospital on a drip for three days. I keep thinking I've left it too long' → NAME IT AND HOLD IT: 'it sounds like watching that was really frightening. YOU HAVE NOT LEFT IT TOO LONG — he is alert and still taking fluid, and those are the two things that matter most.' Then SUMMARISE BACK before examining.

REQUEST THE EXAMINATION — the marks are in the hydration assessment and the deliberate search for another source: weight undressed; full observations with CENTRAL capillary refill; HYDRATION SIGNS — eyes, membranes, tears, turgor, fontanelle; full abdomen and HERNIAL ORIFICES; EARS, THROAT AND CHEST; full skin inspection; BEDSIDE GLUCOSE AND KETONES; CLEAN-CATCH URINE. Then GRADE IT ALOUD: 'that is CLINICAL DEHYDRATION, NOT SHOCK... with a 600 gram loss I'd put him at about FIVE PER CENT.'

EXPLAIN, WITH THE EXCLUSIONS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'the good news first: I think this is a tummy bug — gastroenteritis — almost certainly the virus going round his daycare... I did think about some other things, and I want you to know I've checked for them' — green vomit, telescoping bowel, ears and chest, the urine, sugar and ketones, the rash. (Listing differentials as NAMES loses the mark. And do not say 'he'll be fine': say what you are watching and what would change your mind.)

MANAGEMENT AND SIX TRIGGERS: antibiotics declined WITH A REASON, then the TECHNIQUE — 'tiny amounts, very often: about a teaspoon every five minutes, by syringe. If you give him a whole cup he'll bring it straight back' — four hours then re-weigh; the explicit NOT-list; nasogastric before intravenous; the six return triggers IN WRITING; review in 24 hours; PATS so cost never stops her coming in. ('Come back if he gets worse' is scored as ABSENT safety-netting.)

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED — do not offer the EAR-PULLING, the DAYCARE OUTBREAK or the NAPPY NUMBERS unless a question opens the door. IF THE DOCTOR ASKS ONLY ABOUT EATING, ANSWER ONLY ABOUT EATING AND SAY NOTHING ABOUT DRINKING. To an open question, give a good 20-30 second answer then stop. PUSH ONCE at about four minutes: 'DOES HE NEED ANTIBIOTICS?' — accept a clear explanation, press once more if it is vague. Become emotional only when asked about concerns, or volunteer it by minute six: 'can I just tell you what I'm scared of?' If the doctor uses jargon, say 'sorry — what does that mean?' once, which is a deliberate test. IF THE DOCTOR SAYS 'COME BACK IF HE GETS WORSE' WITHOUT SPECIFICS, ASK 'WORSE HOW? WHAT AM I LOOKING FOR?'

back.dx: SEPSIS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE in an 18-month-old — fever 39.4 with tachycardia at 168 (the limit is about 150 between one and four years), tachypnoea, CAPILLARY REFILL OF THREE SECONDS, drowsy and floppy with poor eye contact and a WEAK HIGH-PITCHED CRY, not drinking, and only TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE LAST NIGHT. THE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE STATION: 'I am very concerned that Noah has SEPSIS — a serious infection that has spread into his blood and is affecting his whole body. The reasons are his high fever, that he is drowsy and floppy, his heart is racing, his circulation is slow, and he isn't drinking or passing much urine. THE SLIGHTLY RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN HOW UNWELL HE IS. This needs the hospital, now.' THE PLAN IN FOUR PARTS, NAMING ACTIONS RATHER THAN A REFERRAL: (1) MY NURSE IS CALLING AN AMBULANCE NOW — ring the emergency department so they are ready, and if he needs Adelaide THE RETRIEVAL TEAM COMES TO HIM; (2) the work-up: blood count, INFECTION MARKERS AND A BLOOD CULTURE, a urine sample, possibly a chest X-ray, and ONCE HE IS STABLE possibly a lumbar puncture; (3) ANTIBIOTICS INTO A VEIN WITHIN THE HOUR — AND IF THE AMBULANCE IS DELAYED, THE FIRST DOSE HERE AS AN INJECTION — plus intravenous fluids because he is dry and cannot drink, and paracetamol for comfort; (4) continuous monitoring by the paediatric team. Then honestly: 'he is seriously unwell, but WE'VE CAUGHT IT AND WE'RE STARTING TREATMENT NOW, which is what matters most.' Ask him to ring the mother to meet them there, and stay with the child until the ambulance arrives. IF THE CARD SHOWS PURPURIC SPOTS: meningococcal disease until proven otherwise — CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg INTRAMUSCULARLY RIGHT NOW, BEFORE the ambulance, notify SA Health today, and household contacts need clearance antibiotics. THE FEBRILE CONVULSION AT 14 MONTHS IS A DECOY: there are no seizure features today — say so out loud and STAY ON SEPSIS.
plan: VITALS FIRST, AND INTERPRET THEM: 'could I have Noah's observations? ... 39.4, heart rate 168, breathing 38, oxygen 96, capillary refill 3 seconds. HIS HEART RATE AND CIRCULATION ARE ABNORMAL FOR AN 18-MONTH-OLD, so I'll be quick and thorough.' Then the open question: 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'fever and vomiting for two days and now he's floppy and won't look at me. I THINK IT'S GASTRO. CAN YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' TIMING OF ALL THREE, SEPARATELY: 'when did the fever, the vomiting and the floppiness EACH start — and is it getting worse?' Then 'have you measured the temperature? Paracetamol — did it help?' Then THE VOMIT: 'any green? Any blood? Is he keeping anything down?'

CLARIFY 'UNRESPONSIVE' — three options, then the seizure questions: 'when you say unresponsive — is he SLEEPY AND HARD TO WAKE, FLOPPY AND NOT RESPONDING, or has he been FITTING?' → 'sleepy and floppy, wakes when I pick him up, cries and shuts his eyes.' Then 'sudden or gradual?' and 'any JERKING? EYES ROLLING UP? WET OR SOILED himself?'

THE FEVER SPINE, hunting the source: ears, runny nose, DROOLING, CHANGE IN THE CRY OR VOICE, neck lumps → 'his cry has gone WEAK AND SQUEAKY'. RASH: 'any spots that don't fade under a glass?' Chest: cough, noisy or fast breathing, recession → 'no cough, but he's breathing fast'. Contacts and travel. GI: diarrhoea, blood, drawing the legs up. URINARY: crying on weeing, smelly urine. MENINGISM WITHOUT THE JARGON: 'does he DISLIKE BEING PICKED UP? Does he turn away from the light? Is his neck stiff?' → 'HE CRIES WHEN I PICK HIM UP.'

WELL-BABY WITH NUMBERS, then the rest: 'is he drinking? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES IN THE LAST TWELVE HOURS? Bowels? Alert or drowsy?' → 'two, and he won't drink.' Then joints and limping, then KAWASAKI features — red eyes, cracked lips, swollen hands or feet. Then targeted BINDSMA: term birth, IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE, growth, medicines and allergies, PREVIOUS FITS, who is at home → 'he had a fit with a fever at 14 months' → NAME IT AND MOVE ON: 'that was a febrile convulsion; there are NO seizure features today, so this is different.'

READ THE CARD BACK IN ONE LINE: 'so he is DROWSY, whimpers on handling, hot and dry with a capillary refill of three seconds; the only source is a MILDLY RED THROAT; no rash, no neck stiffness, chest and abdomen clear.'

THE DIAGNOSIS SENTENCE, said plainly to the father (see dx) — fever, drowsiness, racing heart, slow circulation, not drinking or weeing, AND THE RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN IT. → 'sepsis? He's only got a cold. CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM ANTIBIOTICS HERE?' → 'the antibiotics he needs go INTO A VEIN, with fluids and monitoring, and that needs the hospital team.'

THE FOUR-PART PLAN IN ORDER (see dx), then CONSENT AND CLOSE: 'is that okay with you? Could you ring his mum and ask her to meet you there? I'LL STAY WITH NOAH UNTIL THE AMBULANCE ARRIVES. Do you have any questions?' → 'is he going to die?' → 'he is seriously unwell, but we've caught it and we're starting treatment now, which is what matters most.' (Opening with 'I'll refer him to a paediatrician' is the trap — NAME THE ACTIONS; the referral is how they happen.)

back.dx: POORLY CONTROLLED ASTHMA in a 9-year-old ON RELIEVER ALONE, with adherence unverified and inhaler technique NEVER CHECKED. NAME IT AND GIVE THE FOUR REASONS: he coughs at night ALMOST EVERY NIGHT; he cannot exercise normally and HAS GIVEN UP FOOTBALL; he has daytime symptoms on MOST DAYS, well over two a week; and he needs his reliever on MOST DAYS, again well over two. WELL-CONTROLLED ASTHMA MEANS NO NIGHT SYMPTOMS, NO LIMITATION ON EXERCISE, AND SYMPTOMS AND RELIEVER USE ON NO MORE THAN TWO DAYS A WEEK — he fails all four. MANAGEMENT, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. FIRST, ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE: 'if the medicine isn't reaching his lungs, ADDING A SECOND ONE WON'T HELP EITHER' — watch him use it now WITH A SPACER, which he does not own: shake it, ONE PUFF into the spacer, FOUR TO SIX NORMAL BREATHS, then repeat for the second puff, ONE PUFF AT A TIME AND NEVER TWO TOGETHER. SECOND, STEP UP, explaining the two kinds of puffer: a RELIEVER opens the airways when symptoms come and is used as needed; a PREVENTER is taken every day whether he feels well or not and stops the airways becoming narrowed in the first place. Add a LOW-DOSE INHALED CORTICOSTEROID twice daily — AND HE KEEPS THE VENTOLIN. Then walk the rest of the ladder so the examiner hears the sequence: next is MONTELUKAST 5 mg at night on top; after that a COMBINATION INHALER containing a preventer and a long-acting reliever. NON-DRUG MEASURES: the smoking, addressed with a realistic fallback ('if that's not realistic right now, SMOKING ENTIRELY OUTSIDE would still make a real difference'); the carpet and dust mite; the cat out of the bedroom; and GET HIM BACK TO FOOTBALL, because 'NOT BEING ABLE TO PLAY IS A SIGN THE ASTHMA ISN'T CONTROLLED, NOT A REASON TO STOP'. Then a WRITTEN ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, review in FOUR TO SIX WEEKS with technique rechecked at every visit, step down only after THREE MONTHS STABLE, and two sets of red flags — chronic (night symptoms return, sport affected, reliever more than a couple of days a week) and acute (sudden worsening, real difficulty breathing, CANNOT SPEAK IN FULL SENTENCES, or the reliever stops lasting).
plan: VITALS FIRST, THEN OPEN: 'before I begin, could I have Liam's vital signs — RESPIRATORY RATE AND OXYGEN SATURATION PARTICULARLY, plus heart rate and temperature.' Then: 'what's been happening? And is there anything in particular that's worrying you today?' → 'he's had asthma for years, but THE PUFFER DOESN'T SEEM TO BE DOING ANYTHING ANY MORE. I'm worried we need something stronger.'

THE COUGH — TWO MINUTES, NOT A FULL DIFFERENTIAL: 'is it dry, or is he bringing anything up? Any wheeze? IS IT WORSE AT NIGHT? IS IT WORSE WHEN HE'S RUNNING AROUND OR PLAYING SPORT? And how is it affecting him — at school, at home, with his friends?' → dry, wheezy, WORST AT NIGHT, and HE HAS STOPPED GOING TO FOOTY TRAINING. (Running croup, pertussis, post-nasal drip and reflux here is the trap — this is a KNOWN-CONDITION station.)

THE FOUR KNOWN-ASTHMA QUESTIONS: 'when was he diagnosed? WHAT TREATMENT IS HE ON at the moment? AND IS HE TAKING IT AS PRESCRIBED? HAS ANYONE EVER WATCHED HIM USE HIS INHALER AND CHECKED HIS TECHNIQUE? Is he having regular reviews, with a GP or a specialist? Has he ever been admitted to hospital, the emergency department, or INTENSIVE CARE because of his asthma?' → 'just the blue one, Ventolin' ... 'HONESTLY? I'M NOT SURE. I give it to him but I don't stand over him' ... 'NO. NEVER.' → ACKNOWLEDGE IT WITHOUT BLAMING: 'thank you for being straight with me — that's genuinely useful AND IT CHANGES WHAT I'D DO NEXT.' (Asking what treatment he is on and STOPPING THERE loses the mark: it lives in adherence and technique, and her uncertainty is the planted finding.)

THE FOUR CONTROL QUESTIONS — the stated pass/fail item: 'now four questions I ask everyone with asthma, to work out how well controlled it is. ONE, any symptoms at night? TWO, any limitation with exercise? THREE, HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK does he cough or wheeze during the day? FOUR, HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK does he need his Ventolin?' She answers vaguely first — 'a fair bit', 'quite often' — SO PUSH FOR NUMBERS: 'five or six days' and 'nearly every day'. (Questions three and four have a THRESHOLD; the other two do not, and any night symptoms or exercise limitation counts.)

TRIGGERS AND THE LAST TWO DIFFERENTIALS: 'does anyone smoke at home? Pets, carpet, a recent move? Does he have eczema or hay fever, and is there asthma or allergy in the family?' → HIS DAD SMOKES IN THE KITCHEN WITH THE WINDOW OPEN, they moved six months ago to a fully carpeted house, and there is an indoor cat. Then, quickly: 'HAS HE EVER HAD AN EPISODE OF CHOKING? Has he had a lot of chest infections, and any concerns about his growth or development?' (Those two questions are what stop you being the candidate who never considered an inhaled foreign body or cystic fibrosis.)

EXPLAIN THE CONDITION — and the condition is NOT 'asthma': 'you already know Liam has asthma... BUT THE IMPORTANT THING I WANT TO TELL YOU TODAY IS THAT HIS ASTHMA IS CURRENTLY POORLY CONTROLLED. And I want to tell you exactly why I say that' — then the four reasons, then the definition of good control. 'Any one of those would tell me his asthma isn't well controlled. HE HAS ALL FOUR.' → 'I thought the puffer was supposed to fix it' → 'the puffer he's on is a RELIEVER — it opens the airways when symptoms come, but it doesn't stop them coming. That's the gap we need to close.'

ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE BEFORE ANY PRESCRIPTION: 'two things have to happen, AND THE ORDER MATTERS. The first is making sure he is actually getting the medicine he already has... IF THE MEDICINE ISN'T REACHING HIS LUNGS, ADDING A SECOND ONE WON'T HELP EITHER. So I'd like to watch him use it right now, WITH A SPACER' — then the concrete steps, and supply one today. (Reaching for the prescription pad first is the clinical error the station is built around. And offering to check technique WITHOUT KNOWING THE STEPS is worse than not offering.)

STEP UP, WALK THE LADDER, THEN THE REST: reliever versus preventer explained in plain words, ADD A DAILY PREVENTER while KEEPING THE VENTOLIN, then name montelukast and then the combination inhaler so she can see there is a sequence. Then the smoking with a realistic fallback, carpet and cat, BACK TO FOOTBALL, a WRITTEN ACTION PLAN, review at FOUR TO SIX WEEKS with technique rechecked, step down only after three months stable, and both sets of red flags. (Finishing on the drug is the common failure — the action plan, review interval, smoking conversation and red flags are all separately marked, so PROTECT THE LAST NINETY SECONDS.)

VARIANT D — THE STEROID-AVERSE PARENT: 'I'd much rather talk that through than talk you out of it. Can I tell you what I know, and then we decide together?' The inhaled dose is small and goes STRAIGHT INTO THE AIRWAYS, quite different from steroid tablets; AT LOW DOSES THE EFFECT ON GROWTH IS SMALL — the honest position, not 'no effect' — and it must be weighed against what UNCONTROLLED asthma does: broken sleep, missed school, giving up sport, emergency visits. Rinsing the mouth deals with most local side effects. THEN OFFER THE GENUINE ALTERNATIVE: montelukast, not a steroid, generally a bit less effective, with its own mood and sleep caveat — 'both are reasonable places to start. WHICH WOULD YOU RATHER TRY, and I'll review him in four to six weeks either way?' VERIFY current wording on inhaled corticosteroids and growth before quoting figures.
pefe: Role-player: Sarah Doyle, 37, works part-time at a childcare centre in Mount Gambier; husband Mark works at the timber mill; Liam is 9 with a 13-year-old sister. Diagnosed at about four, ON SALBUTAMOL ALONE, NO SPACER — he puffs it straight into his mouth — NO preventer, repeats collected from the pharmacy without seeing a doctor, ONE emergency department visit last year for a nebuliser, never intensive care. Eczema as a baby, father has hay fever, otherwise healthy and growing normally, NO choking episodes, no recurrent chest infections. Home: moved six months ago to a fully carpeted house, one indoor cat, and MARK SMOKES IN THE KITCHEN WITH THE WINDOW OPEN. Tired and mildly frustrated, convinced the medication has stopped working and here to ask for SOMETHING STRONGER — not hostile, and she softens once someone finally explains what is happening.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT — the withheld findings: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. If asked what treatment he is on, say 'just the blue one, Ventolin' — AND ONLY IF ASKED WHETHER HE IS TAKING IT does she admit 'honestly? I'm not sure. I give it to him but I don't stand over him.' The SPACER only comes up if technique is asked about. The SMOKING only if asked — and if the doctor lectures, become slightly defensive: 'he's trying to cut down.' ON THE CONTROL QUESTIONS, GIVE VAGUE ANSWERS FIRST — 'sometimes', 'a fair bit' — AND ONLY GIVE NUMBERS IF THE DOCTOR ASKS SPECIFICALLY HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK. Push once at about minute six: 'IS THAT A STEROID? I'm not sure about a child being on steroids.' If the doctor finishes early, ask 'how long before it works?' and 'will he be on it forever?' If jargon is used — corticosteroid, exacerbation, adherence, bronchodilator — say 'sorry, what does that mean?' once.

Numbers: CONTROL THRESHOLD is MORE THAN 2 DAYS A WEEK of daytime symptoms or reliever use; ANY night symptoms or exercise limitation counts. Good control means all four favourable; poor means three or four adverse; TREAT PARTIAL THE SAME AS POOR. STEPS AT 6-11 YEARS: reliever as needed, then add LOW-DOSE INHALED CORTICOSTEROID twice daily, then add MONTELUKAST, then an ICS/LABA COMBINATION. back.dx: PULLED ELBOW — RADIAL HEAD SUBLUXATION — in a 2-year-old after a classic traction mechanism, with the arm held pronated and slightly flexed, NO tenderness anywhere from clavicle to wrist, distress ONLY on attempted supination, and normal distal neurovascular status. TO THE MOTHER IN LAY WORDS: 'the good news is I don't think anything is broken. One of the forearm bones, the radius, has a ROUNDED HEAD held in the elbow by a BAND called a ligament. A sudden pull on the hand stretches that band and THE HEAD SLIPS PARTLY OUT FROM UNDER IT. A SMALL SLIP — NOT A TRUE DISLOCATION, NOT A FRACTURE — and it only hurts when the elbow moves, which is why he keeps it so still.' NEVER SAY 'DISLOCATED' ON ITS OWN. ANSWER THE GUILT DIRECTLY: 'thousands of children a year get this — a quirk of the joint at his age, not something you did wrong.' THE MANOEUVRE, DESCRIBED WORD FOR WORD: he sits ON HIS MOTHER'S LAP FACING YOU; support the right elbow in your LEFT hand with YOUR THUMB OVER THE RADIAL HEAD — outside the elbow, just below the crease; your right hand on his wrist, ELBOW AT NINETY DEGREES; then FIRMLY HYPERPRONATE the forearm — palm down and beyond — in ONE SMOOTH MOVEMENT, FEELING FOR A CLICK UNDER YOUR THUMB. If that fails, the second option is SUPINATE FULLY THEN FLEX THE ELBOW COMPLETELY, hand to shoulder. Then LET GO, STEP BACK AND OFFER A TOY ABOVE HEAD HEIGHT. Success is normal use within FIVE TO THIRTY MINUTES. THE RULES SAID OUT LOUD BEFORE THE FINDINGS ARRIVE: TWO FAILED ATTEMPTS, or ANY change on examination, means an X-RAY; an injury over twelve hours old can take a day or two to recover; NO SLING once he is using it. PREVENTION: lift under the arms, NOT by the hands, and no swinging — RECURRENCE IS ABOUT ONE IN FOUR while he is small. SAFETY-NET: back tomorrow, or to hospital, if he is not using it normally, if it swells, or if the hand goes pale or cold. VERSION B: 'tenderness and swelling — I AM CONCERNED ABOUT A FRACTURE AND WILL NOT ATTEMPT REDUCTION.' Paracetamol 15 mg/kg (about 180 mg at 12 kg) and a sling, ELBOW AP AND LATERAL today looking for a SUPRACONDYLAR FRACTURE, a POSTERIOR FAT PAD and the ANTERIOR HUMERAL LINE, pulse and hand rechecked before he leaves; normal film, consider reduction; fracture, orthopaedic registrar and PATS if transfer is needed.
plan: OPEN AT THE CHILD'S LEVEL, AND DISARM THE GUILT EARLY: 'hello, I'm Dr -, one of the GPs here. Sarah? And this is Oliver — hi mate.' THE INCIDENT AND THE ARM: 'when was it? Was there a POP OR CLICK? DID HE FALL, or bump his head?' → a little click, no fall. Then: 'since then, is he using it AT ALL, or not at all? And is there anything else worrying you?' → 'IS IT BROKEN? DOES HE NEED AN X-RAY?' → NOT A FLAT NO: 'if the examination is as I expect we usually don't need one — I'll explain why. ASK FOR THE EXAMINATION, NAMING THE PARTS — you get exactly what you ask for: 'Examiner, could I have general appearance and observations, then the right upper limb: INSPECTION for swelling, bruising or deformity; PALPATION FROM THE CLAVICLE through humerus, elbow and RADIAL HEAD, forearm and wrist; posture and tolerated movement; and DISTAL NEUROVASCULAR STATUS — RADIAL PULSE, capillary refill, hand colour and finger movement.' (Asking for 'an elbow examination' means the clavicle and the pulse never appear.)

CONSENT AND WARN OF THE CRY: 'I can put it back right now — it takes a few seconds. I hold his elbow and turn his forearm in one quick movement. HE'LL PROBABLY CRY FOR A MOMENT, then within minutes to half an hour he should be using the arm normally. Painkillers usually aren't needed — THE MOVEMENT TAKES THE PAIN AWAY — but I can give paracetamol first if you'd prefer. Happy for me to go ahead?' → 'yes — can I hold him?' → 'please, on your lap, facing me.'

DEMONSTRATE THE MANOEUVRE, NARRATED TO THE EXAMINER (see dx) — thumb over the radial head, elbow at ninety, ONE SMOOTH HYPERPRONATION feeling for the click, then the supination-and-full-flexion alternative, then LET GO, STEP BACK AND OFFER A TOY ABOVE HEAD HEIGHT. → 'you feel a click; after a few minutes the child reaches for a toy with the right hand.' → [to Oliver] 'all done, mate. THE KNEE PAIN IS ACTUALLY COMING FROM THE HIP; IN CHILDREN HIP PROBLEMS OFTEN SHOW UP AS KNEE PAIN.' THREE REASONS: he can still stand and walk even though he is limping; he had a cold two weeks ago; and on examination THE HIP WAS THE ONLY SORE THING, with a positive log roll. FIVE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON: SEPTIC ARTHRITIS OR OSTEOMYELITIS — no fever, well in himself, joint not hot or swollen, BUT IT IS THE ONE THAT CANNOT WAIT; PERTHES DISEASE — less likely because he still weight-bears and this followed a cold, BUT ONLY AN X-RAY EXCLUDES IT, so if it has not settled in two weeks we do one; BLOOD OR BONE CANCER — nothing points there today; FRACTURE OR INJURY; and CHILDHOOD ARTHRITIS. PLAN: rest, paracetamol 15 mg/kg or ibuprofen 10 mg/kg with food, no sport this week, REVIEW IN TWO DAYS, X-ray at two weeks if unresolved, and THE THREE-ITEM RETURN LIST — FEVER, CANNOT WEIGHT-BEAR AT ALL, or the leg becomes HOT, RED OR SWOLLEN. Growing pains do not cause a limp — say so if she raises it. VERSION B — PERTHES DISEASE. EXPLAIN THE X-RAY NORMAL SIDE FIRST: 'white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air. This long bone is the thigh bone; at the top it has a rounded head that sits in the hip bone like A BALL IN A CUP. Look at the normal side first: the head is ROUND, like a ball. Now the other side: THE HEAD IS FLAT, IT HAS LOST ITS CURVE, and it doesn't match the other side.' Then: 'the head of the thigh bone is damaged because ITS BLOOD SUPPLY WAS CUT OFF FOR A TIME; we don't know why it happens, AND IT'S NOTHING YOU DID.' Never say sclerosis, epiphysis or avascular necrosis to a parent, and NEVER POINT AT THE ABNORMAL HIP FIRST. Then the same differential list, then referral to the children's orthopaedic service, no running or jumping, and pain relief.

How can I help you both today?' → limping since Saturday, now says his knee hurts → 'I can hear how worried you are, and A LIMP IN A CHILD IS SOMETHING I TAKE SERIOUSLY, so I'm going to ask quite a few questions, SOME ABOUT SERIOUS THINGS I ASK EVERY PARENT.' Then the two separate questions: 'CAN HE PUT ANY WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL? IS HE STILL WALKING?' (Accepting 'limping' without asking about weight-bearing is the trap — the examiner is listening for both.)

THE LIMP AND THEN THE PAIN: constant or on and off, getting worse, morning versus evening, rest versus activity, anything that helps. Then: 'is he in any pain? WHERE EXACTLY — show me on your own leg. ANYWHERE ELSE? WHAT ABOUT THE HIP? The ankle? Out of ten? Dull ache or sharp? Does it travel anywhere? AND DOES IT WAKE HIM AT NIGHT?' → 'just his knee. He only says his knee.' (Do NOT argue that it is really the hip — note it and examine the hip. And do not skip night pain because the child looks well: it is the malignancy question.)

THE THREE RED-FLAG BOXES, IN ORDER: MSK first — swelling, redness, rash, stiffness. INFECTION — 'any fever or chills? Is the joint hot, red or swollen? Has he been unwell in himself?' MALIGNANCY — 'any weight loss? Lumps or bumps? Unusually tired or pale? Bruising easily?' → she goes slightly sharp: 'WHY, WHAT ARE YOU THINKING?' → 'these are questions I ask EVERY child with leg pain, to be sure I'm not missing something rare. NOTHING YOU'VE TOLD ME POINTS THAT WAY.' FRACTURE AND NAI — 'any falls, injuries or knocks? Does he play sport? HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME? And childcare — any problems or bullying?' → 'I'm not sure, he might have fallen at childcare, nobody said anything.' (That is NOT an admission and NOT a red flag on its own — it tests whether you ask the social questions calmly and without accusation.)

THE VIRAL QUESTION AND THE REST — number seven, but it must be reached: 'any recent flu-like illness, a cold, or a virus?' → 'yes, a cold about two weeks ago.' Then other joints and family arthritis (her mother's hand osteoarthritis is a distractor), rashes, tummy pain, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, waterworks, pregnancy and birth, THE SIX-WEEK CHECK, and the well-child wrap-up.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, IN A FIXED ORDER, TEMPERATURE FIRST: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, any rash? CAN HE BEAR WEIGHT, and if so I'd like to observe his gait. Vital signs: TEMPERATURE FIRST, then heart rate and blood pressure. May I see his growth chart? Then LOWER LIMB — HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE, comparing both sides: inspection for swelling, redness, deformity or abnormal posture; palpation for local warmth and tenderness; active and passive movement for pain and restricted range; TRUE LEG LENGTH measured and compared; SPECIAL TEST, THE LOG ROLL; and an abdominal examination, with a urine dipstick if there is time.' (Asking for 'a knee examination' gets you a normal knee and nothing else.)

DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS: 'Jack's knee is actually fine; THE SORENESS IS COMING FROM HIS HIP, and in children hip problems very often show up as knee pain. I think he MOST LIKELY has transient synovitis, sometimes called an irritable hip...' then the three reasons. → 'is it serious?' → 'usually not; it settles on its own in one to two weeks. BUT LET ME TELL YOU WHAT ELSE I CONSIDERED, BECAUSE SOME OF THOSE MATTER.'
FIVE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON (see dx), leading with septic arthritis as the one that cannot wait and naming the honest limit on Perthes — only an X-ray excludes it.

Then ask what worried her → 'I thought it might be growing pains, or that he'd broken something' — and her hidden fear, a colleague's child with leukaemia → 'GROWING PAINS DON'T CAUSE A LIMP, so I wouldn't put it down to that.' pefe: Role-player (Version A): Emma Harper, 34, part-time bookkeeper; partner Dan is a plumber; daughter Mia is 2. Jack is 5, at childcare three days a week, plays Saturday soccer; no medicines, no allergies, fully immunised, normal pregnancy and birth, SIX-WEEK CHECK DONE. Her own mother has osteoarthritis of the hands — A DISTRACTOR, mentioned only if family history of arthritis is asked. HIDDEN AGENDA: she is frightened it is 'SOMETHING IN THE BONE' because a work colleague's child had leukaemia, and she half-wonders whether he fell at childcare and nobody told her. Worried but composed; she becomes slightly sharp — 'WHY, WHAT ARE YOU THINKING?' — when asked about weight loss and lumps, and softens if the doctor explains why they ask. She volunteers the leukaemia fear ONLY if asked what worries her, or in the last minute if never asked.

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: SAY 'KNEE' EVERY TIME, and only concede the hip if asked directly — and even then, 'he only ever says his knee'. NEVER VOLUNTEER THE COLD TWO WEEKS AGO; answer it only if asked about viral illness. 'I'M NOT SURE IF HE FELL AT CHILDCARE' is the answer to any injury question — DO NOT ELABORATE. If the doctor says 'definitely synovitis' or 'just a virus', ask 'BUT HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING IN THE BONE?' If they never give a safety-net, ask 'AND WHAT IF HE GETS WORSE TONIGHT?' in the final thirty seconds. IF THEY EXAMINE ONLY THE KNEE, DO NOT CORRECT THEM — the examiner reports normal knee findings and nothing else.

Mark them on: asked weight-bearing AND walking as separate questions; asked about the hip when she said knee; asked fever and chills, and REQUESTED TEMPERATURE FIRST in the examination; asked night pain, weight loss, lumps and bruising; asked home and childcare; asked recent viral illness; requested HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE plus leg length, log roll and abdomen; said 'MOST LIKELY' transient synovitis with reasons; NAMED AND EXCLUDED SEPTIC ARTHRITIS; named Perthes with the X-ray limit; gave at least three further differentials; gave the THREE-ITEM RETURN LIST and a review time; asked what worried her and addressed the leukaemia fear directly; and finished with a summary inside eight minutes.

back.dx: A SEIZURE CAUSED BY A HEAD INJURY — a MILD HEAD INJURY WITH RISK FACTORS. NAME IT IN PLAIN WORDS: 'a seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain, and a knock to the head can set that off. The jerking of all four limbs, the eyes rolling and the drowsiness afterwards are what tell me it was a seizure.' THEN CATEGORISE IT, AND THIS IS THE SENTENCE THE STATION IS BUILT ON: 'we grade head injuries by HOW AWAKE AND ALERT a child is. Liam is FULLY ALERT, so this is a MILD head injury. But because he was KNOCKED OUT and then HAD A FIT, we count those as RISK FACTORS — things that make us more careful — so we call it A MILD HEAD INJURY WITH RISK FACTORS.' Calling it moderate because of the seizure is an automatic fail. THEN SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED: normal sugar, no fever, no medications, no previous seizures, normal examination — 'so I'm not finding any sign of bleeding inside the head or a neck injury RIGHT NOW.' AND WHEN SHE ASKS 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?': 'I CAN'T PROMISE THAT YET — THAT'S EXACTLY WHY WE WATCH HIM.' It is not epilepsy; it was a one-off fit triggered by the knock, though a small number of children have another fit in the first week. VERIFY MANAGEMENT: (1) OBSERVE AT LEAST FOUR HOURS with regular neurological observations — conscious level, pupils, strength — half-hourly for two hours then hourly; (2) IMAGING WITH THREE NAMED TRIGGERS, because a CT is radiation to a growing brain and most mild injuries do not need one — SCAN IF HE BECOMES DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE, VOMITS REPEATEDLY, OR HIS HEADACHE WORSENS — and discuss him with the paediatric NEUROSURGEON so the decision is made together; (3) paracetamol 15 mg/kg for the headache, an antiemetic if needed, and the NECK PROTECTED until fully examined; (4) HOME ONLY IF HE STAYS WELL, with a WRITTEN SHEET OF WARNING SIGNS — repeated vomiting, worsening headache, hard to wake, confusion, another fit, weakness, or fluid from the nose or ears — A RESPONSIBLE ADULT OVERNIGHT, GP review in two to three days, and NO CONTACT SPORT UNTIL SYMPTOM-FREE AND CLEARED. 'Should I keep him awake tonight?' — no: let him sleep, check every few hours, and make sure he ROUSES NORMALLY. VERIFY
plan: STABILITY, GLUCOSE, THEN OPEN: 'may I confirm the primary survey is complete, and have his vitals, GCS and a BEDSIDE GLUCOSE?' → 5.6. Then: 'hello Lily, I'm Dr -. LIAM IS IN SAFE HANDS. Can you tell me what happened?' → 'he was tackled and went down head-first. He just lay there, and then he started shaking all over. I THOUGHT HE WAS DYING.' → ADDRESS IT AND EXPLAIN THE QUESTIONS: 'that sounds absolutely terrifying, and YOU DID THE RIGHT THING calling the ambulance. I'm going to ask a lot of questions — they help me work out HOW SERIOUS this is, and that decides what we do next.'

THE INCIDENT: 'when did this happen? Was it a DIRECT BLOW to the head, or a FALL ONTO HIS HEAD OR NECK? How hard, roughly — was he running at full pace? Any other injuries or pain anywhere else? ANY NECK PAIN?'

THE RED-FLAG BOX — twelve questions, and the two durations kept separate: 'when he hit his head, did he LOSE CONSCIOUSNESS COMPLETELY, or was he awake and aware? HOW LONG? And SEPARATELY, the shaking — were his arms and legs jerking? ALL FOUR LIMBS, or one side? Eyes rolling up? Tongue bite? Frothing? Did he wet himself? HOW LONG DID THE SHAKING LAST? Any vomiting since? Was he CONFUSED OR DROWSY when he woke — BETTER NOW OR WORSE? Any problems with vision, weakness, numbness, speech or walking? DOES HE REMEMBER what happened? Is he complaining of headache — IS IT GETTING WORSE? Any FLUID OR BLOOD FROM HIS NOSE OR EARS?' (Hearing 'seizure' and stopping is the trap: the marks are in the other ten.)

THE CAUSES OF THE SEIZURE — the half candidates drop: 'what was he doing just before? Did he complain of anything — feeling sick or dizzy — BEFORE the tackle? HAD HE MISSED ANY MEALS? Any fever or rash in the last few days? Is he on any medications, or could he have taken anything?' → guiltily: 'HE SKIPPED BREAKFAST — we were running late. DOES THAT MATTER?' → 'it can, because a low sugar can cause a fit — THAT'S WHY I CHECKED IT, AND IT'S NORMAL.' (Missed breakfast is planted: it is not the cause, but the examiner marks whether you asked AND whether you checked the glucose.)

BACKGROUND: 'any blood thinners, or does he bruise or bleed easily? Any seizures before? Any concerns about his development? HOW ARE THINGS AT HOME — who lives there, any stress? How's school, any bullying? Any family history, especially of seizures? Immunisations up to date?' (Nothing about non-accidental injury is planted here — you still ask about home.)

READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRET IT, THEN ADD: 'GCS 15, normal neurology, no neck tenderness, normal glucose. THAT PLACES LIAM IN THE MILD CATEGORY, and it excludes a current deficit and hypoglycaemia. I'd like to ADD: pupils and fundoscopy, a look at the scalp for a BOGGY SWELLING, BEHIND THE EARS and AROUND THE EYES for bruising, and a check of the EARDRUMS FOR BLOOD.' (Treating the card as the end of the examination is the trap — base-of-skull signs are the classic omission.)

NAME IT, CATEGORISE IT, SAY WHAT YOU EXCLUDED (see dx) → 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?' → 'I can't promise it isn't yet — and that's exactly why he's staying with us. But everything I can see is reassuring.'

THE PLAN, AND NEVER A BARE YES OR NO ON THE CT: four hours of observation with regular neurological checks; the THREE named scan triggers with the reason a CT is not automatic; the neurosurgeon informed; paracetamol and neck protection; then home only if he stays well, WITH THE WRITTEN WARNING SHEET, a responsible adult overnight, GP in two to three days, and no contact sport until cleared. → 'SHOULDN'T YOU JUST DO A SCAN?' → answer with the radiation reason and the three triggers. Then summarise and invite questions.

VERSION B — A 4-YEAR-OLD, 'FELL OFF THE COUCH', with a boggy scalp swelling and BRUISES OF DIFFERENT AGES: 'can I ask exactly what time that was, and who was with him?' I'm also arranging a CT scan of his head now, and he'll be admitted under the paediatric team.' SHE WATCHED THE TACKLE FROM THE SIDELINE: he went down head-first with another boy on top, LAY STILL FOR ABOUT A MINUTE, then ALL FOUR LIMBS JERKED AND HIS EYES ROLLED BACK FOR ABOUT A MINUTE. setting: HISTORY, EXPLANATION AND MANAGEMENT — GP clinic. THE CUE IS NON-VERBAL: the mother cradles a doll with THREE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK, and NOBODY WILL POINT THEM OUT. If you do not look at the doll you will not find the case. Notice them, say nothing, and use them at the right moment. THE SECOND-COMMONEST REASON CANDIDATES FAIL IS FORGETTING THE ACUTE INJURY: a bruised, crying infant needs an INTRACRANIAL INJURY EXCLUDED TODAY, not deferred to child protection. Excluding the medical causes of crying is a SEPARATELY SCORED TASK — skipping it fails you even if you name the abuse.

back.dx: SUSPECTED NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY in a 4-month-old presenting with excessive crying — facial bruising in an infant who is not yet rolling, a history of REPEATED DROPS by a partner who is NOT the biological father, arguing at home, increasing alcohol use, financial stress and a flat, exhausted mother. THE ORDER IS: ACUTE INJURY, THEN NOTIFY, THEN ED, THEN DOCUMENT. FIRST NAME WHAT YOU EXCLUDED, ALOUD AND TO HER: 'I was looking for causes of the crying — an infection like an ear or urine infection, a problem in the tummy such as reflux or a blockage — AND I HAVEN'T FOUND ANYTHING TO SUGGEST THOSE TODAY.' THEN RAISE IT WITHOUT THE WORD ABUSE FIRST: 'what I am concerned about is HIS SAFETY. You've told me about the falls, you've told me how hard things have been, and I CAN SEE BRUISES ON HIS CHEEK. Bruises like that in a baby who isn't yet rolling over are unusual, and I have to take them seriously. I'm worried about the possibility of a NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY — an injury that wasn't caused by an accident.' THEN THE RESCUE LINE, WORD FOR WORD: 'JENNY, I WOULD NEVER ACCUSE YOU OR YOUR PARTNER OF DOING SUCH A THING. I can see how overwhelming things have been for you. MY JOB IS SIMPLY TO MAKE SURE YOUR SON IS SAFE, and to make the safest decisions in his best interest. That is all this is.' THEN THE NOTIFICATION: 'I am LEGALLY REQUIRED to let the child protection service know. EVERY DOCTOR HAS TO DO THIS — it isn't a choice I'm making about you, and it isn't a punishment.' ANSWER 'WILL THEY TAKE MY BABY AWAY?' BEFORE SHE ASKS IT: no — what they do is A FULL ASSESSMENT; they talk with you, see him, speak with your family and look at what supports you need, and MOST OF THE TIME CHILDREN STAY WITH THEIR FAMILY with services in place. Do not guarantee an outcome: 'I can't promise you what they'll decide, but removal is NOT what a notification automatically means.' THEN THE PART CANDIDATES FORGET: 'because he has bruising to his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about AN INJURY OR BLEEDING INSIDE HIS HEAD. THAT HAS TO BE CHECKED TODAY, so I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department NOW' — ring ahead. THEN SUPPORT HER: normalise the frustration, give the SAFE-PLACE-AND-WALK-AWAY advice — put him down somewhere safe like his cot, leave the room, ring someone — offer the Parent Helpline and child health nurse, review her own mood, and screen for family violence. FINALLY DOCUMENT in her words and record where the bruises are. CARL 13 14 78, mandatory notifier, and the threshold is SUSPICION ON REASONABLE GROUNDS — YOU NOTIFY, YOU DO NOT INVESTIGATE.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, THEN AN OPENING THAT NAMES HER EXHAUSTION: 'could I have his observations, please?' Then: 'hello Jenny, I'm Dr -. You must be Jenny, and this must be the little man. I CAN SEE HE'S BEEN GIVING YOU A HARD TIME. Crying that goes on for hours is EXHAUSTING and it can be really OVERWHELMING. Is it alright if I ask a few questions so I can work out why he's crying, and then we'll make a plan together?' NOTE THE BRUISES AND SAY NOTHING YET.

THE CRYING, INCLUDING HER: 'when did it start? Constant or in episodes? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse? What have you been doing to settle him — AND HOW ARE YOU COPING WITH IT?' → three weeks, evenings worst, hours at a time, nothing works, 'I'M EXHAUSTED, HONESTLY.'

THE MEDICAL DIFFERENTIALS — A SEPARATELY SCORED TASK, so do not skip it even though you have seen the bruises. INFECTION: fever, cough or runny nose, ear pulling, crying with nappy changes or offensive urine, rash, feeding, unusual sleepiness. GI AND SURGICAL: 'any vomiting — ANY GREEN IN IT? Does he arch his back with feeds? Any blood or REDCURRANT-JELLY stool? Constipated? ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN OR SCROTUM? ANY HAIR WRAPPED ROUND A FINGER OR TOE? Any red, watery eye?' Then feeding, wet nappies and weight gain.

OPEN THE ACCIDENTAL DOOR AND DETAIL IT: 'has he had any falls, knocks or head injuries lately?' → 'my partner dropped him the other day while he was changing his nappy.' → 'THAT MUST HAVE BEEN FRIGHTENING. Tell me exactly what happened — how far did he fall, what did he land on, did he cry straight away, was he floppy, did he vomit or go drowsy afterwards?' → change table onto floorboards, screamed, seemed alright, SHE WASN'T IN THE ROOM.

THE PIVOT — one question, asked flatly: 'HAS ANYTHING LIKE THAT HAPPENED BEFORE?' → 'a couple of times, I think. He's dropped him three or four times now', delivered casually. DO NOT REACT VISIBLY. Keep your voice level and keep going.

THE HOUSEHOLD, ASKED NEUTRALLY: 'can I ask who lives at home with you? ... AND IS HE YOUR SON'S BIOLOGICAL FATHER? ... How are things between you two at the moment, and how is he coping with the crying?' → not the father, they separated before the birth, HE HAS BEEN ASKING ABOUT THAT, there is arguing, and he gets frustrated with the noise.

THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION AND THE SAFETY SCREEN: 'Jenny, looking after a baby who cries for hours is really hard, and SOME PARENTS GET SO FRUSTRATED THAT THEY SHAKE OR SMACK THE BABY. Has that ever happened with you or your partner?' → a firm denial, and YOU STILL GET THE MARK FOR ASKING IT SAFELY. Then: 'how are things financially? HOW HAS YOUR OWN MOOD BEEN? Does anyone at home use alcohol or other drugs? Who supports you? And DO YOU EVER FEEL UNSAFE AT HOME?' → money tight, flat and crying a lot, he drinks more than he used to, and 'no, I'm fine' said quickly.

NAME WHAT YOU EXCLUDED, THEN RAISE THE CONCERN, THEN THE RESCUE LINE (see dx) → she pulls the doll closer and looks away: 'ARE YOU SAYING I DID THIS?' → SLOW DOWN, LOWER YOUR VOICE, AND DO NOT RETREAT FROM THE CONCERN. (Saying 'your son has child abuse', leading with the word abuse, arguing back when she becomes defensive, or DROPPING THE CONCERN ALTOGETHER WHEN SHE CRIES are the four ways this goes wrong.)

NOTIFICATION, AND ANSWER THE REMOVAL QUESTION BEFORE SHE ASKS IT (see dx), then THE ACUTE INJURY: 'there's something JUST AS IMPORTANT. Because he has bruising to his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about the possibility of an injury or BLEEDING INSIDE HIS HEAD. That has to be checked TODAY, so I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department NOW. They'll examine him, and they may do a scan. The child protection team can talk with you there too.' → 'today? Right now?' → 'yes, straight from here. I'LL RING AHEAD so they're expecting you.'

SUPPORT HER, SAFETY-NET, DOCUMENT, SUMMARISE: 'and I HAVEN'T FORGOTTEN YOU. What you're doing is exhausting, and it's normal to feel frustrated — THAT'S NOT A FAILING. If it ever gets to the point where you feel you can't cope, PUT HIM DOWN SOMEWHERE SAFE LIKE HIS COT, WALK OUT OF THE ROOM, AND RING SOMEONE.' Parent Helpline and child health nurse, review of her own mood, family-violence support. Then: 'I'll write down what you've told me in his notes, IN YOUR WORDS, and record where the bruises are.' Then the four-part summary and questions.

PROPS: HOLD A DOLL THROUGHOUT, cradled as a baby, WITH THREE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK — DO NOT POINT THEM OUT, but hold it so they are visible. The baby is formula fed three-hourly, posits after feeds, no fever, vomiting, blood in stool, groin lump or rash; nappies fine; weighed once at the child health nurse a while ago and was fine; immunisations probably due. CRYING for three weeks, worst in the evenings, sometimes hours, nothing settles him. THE INJURY STORY: her partner dropped him from the change table onto floorboards a few days ago — he screamed, seemed fine after, AND SHE WASN'T IN THE ROOM. IF ASKED WHETHER IT HAS HAPPENED BEFORE, SAY YES — THREE OR FOUR TIMES — AND SAY IT CASUALLY, AS IF IT'S CLUMSINESS.

HOUSEHOLD: she lives with her partner, who is NOT the baby's biological father — she separated from the father before the birth, and her partner HAS RECENTLY BEEN ASKING WHETHER THE BABY IS HIS. There is arguing; he drinks more than he used to; he gets very frustrated with the crying. She is flat, tearful and exhausted, and says she feels safe at home — BUT ANSWERS THAT ONE QUICKLY AND MOVES ON. HIDDEN AGENDA: she is frightened of losing the baby, and will not raise it until the doctor mentions child protection.

HOW TO PLAY IT: volunteer the drop ONLY when asked about falls or injuries; volunteer the REPETITION only when asked whether it has happened before; volunteer the BIOLOGICAL-FATHER fact only when asked directly. THE MOMENT THE DOCTOR SAYS 'CHILD PROTECTION', BECOME DEFENSIVE — hide the doll behind your arm, stop making eye contact, answer in short sentences: 'we'd never do that, we're not those kind of people.' RECOVER ONLY if they use non-accusatory, safety-focused language. IF THE DOCTOR ACCUSES, INTERROGATES, OR ASKS 'DID YOUR PARTNER HIT HIM?', SHUT DOWN COMPLETELY and answer in one word. If the doctor does not answer it first, ask 'WILL THEY TAKE MY BABY AWAY?' — that is the marked moment. IF THE DOCTOR NEVER MENTIONS THE HEAD INJURY OR THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT, ASK AT THE END: 'SO WE JUST GO HOME?' If the doctor never asks how you are, DO NOT VOLUNTEER IT.

back.dx: CONJUGATED HYPERBILIRUBINAEMIA — 60 of 200, nearly a third — with BILIARY ATRESIA at the top of the list. EXPLAIN THE RESULT IN PLAIN WORDS FIRST: 'bilirubin is the yellow pigment made when old red blood cells break down; the liver processes it and sends it out in the bile into the bowel. Harry's total is 200, and 60 of that is the PROCESSED type. When the processed type builds up, IT MEANS IT CAN'T DRAIN OUT OF THE LIVER PROPERLY. The pale poos and the dark wee tell me exactly the same thing.' THEN NAME IT WITH THREE REASONS: biliary atresia, A BLOCKAGE OF THE TUBES THAT CARRY BILE FROM THE LIVER TO THE BOWEL — because of the PALE STOOLS AND DARK URINE, because HE ISN'T GAINING WEIGHT, and because of the HIGH PROCESSED FRACTION. Alternatives at that level: hepatitis, or a CHOLEDOCHAL CYST. THE FULL DIFFERENTIAL IN ORDER, CONJUGATED FIRST: infection in the liver or bloodstream, a blocked-duct cyst, GALACTOSAEMIA; then the unconjugated causes — HYPOTHYROIDISM, blood-group INCOMPATIBILITY, BRUISING from birth, and INADEQUATE INTAKE; and LAST, physiological and breast-milk jaundice, which are harmless and common BUT DO NOT CAUSE PALE STOOLS OR THIS BLOOD PATTERN. MANAGEMENT IN TWO PARTS: TREAT THE BILIRUBIN — plotted on a chart for his age, PHOTOTHERAPY if above the line, exchange transfusion in rare severe cases; and TREAT THE CAUSE — liver and CLOTTING bloods, ULTRASOUND of the liver and bile ducts, a bile-flow scan, and sometimes a LIVER BIOPSY. IF IT IS BILIARY ATRESIA, THE KASAI PROCEDURE connects the bowel directly to the liver so bile can drain, AND IT WORKS BEST BEFORE ABOUT SIXTY DAYS OF AGE — which is why you ring the children's hospital NOW and send them TODAY. SAY 'KEEP BREASTFEEDING — THERE IS NOTHING WRONG WITH YOUR MILK', and 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS'. SAFETY-NET: drowsy, feeding poorly, fever, or THE YELLOW REACHING PALMS AND SOLES. Referral without urgency — 'see the paediatrician next month' — is the fail.
plan: OBSERVATIONS FIRST, BECAUSE SEPSIS IS ON EVERY JAUNDICE LIST: 'may I have Harry's observations — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, and is he alert?' → 36.8, 140, 40, alert. Then: 'Priya, tell me what's been worrying you.' → 'he went yellow on about day three and it's getting worse... I'm SCARED IT'S HIS LIVER.' → 'YOU'VE DONE THE RIGHT THING. A yellow baby is something we look into carefully. Let me ask some questions and then explain the blood test.'

THE JAUNDICE AND THEN THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE STATION: 'when did you first notice it — WAS IT THERE ON THE FIRST DAY? Which parts are yellow — face, chest, tummy, arms, legs, PALMS? Constant, or coming and going? Getting worse?' Then: 'HAVE YOU NOTICED HIS WEE BEING DARK, OR HIS POOS PALE, WHITE OR CHALKY?' → 'yes — the wee's a dark yellow-brown, and the poos went pale, like putty, over the last three or four days.' → SAY IT BACK: 'THAT'S THE MOST IMPORTANT THING YOU'VE TOLD ME — it tells me the bile isn't getting through.'

PREGNANCY: 'any infections or fevers during the pregnancy? DID YOU HAVE THE GROUP B STREP SWAB — and antibiotics in labour? High blood sugar or blood pressure? Medicines, alcohol, drugs? Were your antenatal blood tests and scans normal — DO YOU KNOW YOUR BLOOD GROUP, AND WHETHER YOU HAD ANTIBODIES?' → all clear, GBS negative, A positive with no antibodies.

DELIVERY AND AFTER: 'term or early — how many weeks? Vaginal or caesarean? Long labour, FORCEPS OR VACUUM? ANY BRUISING OR A LUMP ON HIS HEAD? Did he need resuscitation? WAS THE HEEL-PRICK TEST DONE AND NORMAL? Vitamin K given?' → 39 weeks, normal delivery, no instruments, no bruising, cried straight away, heel-prick normal on day three, vitamin K given.

FEEDING IN SIX QUESTIONS, NOT ONE LINE: 'breast or formula? How many feeds in 24 hours? How long on each side? Any problems — pain, attachment, cracked nipples? DO YOU FEEL YOU HAVE ENOUGH MILK — is he satisfied? What was his birth weight, AND WHAT IS HE NOW — is he on his growth chart?' → breastfed eight times a day, fifteen minutes each side, no problems, satisfied — BUT 3.4 kg AT BIRTH AND 3.1 kg YESTERDAY, and the nurse said he should be climbing by now.

SEPSIS, WELL-BABY, THYROID AND FAMILY: 'any fever, or feeling hot or cold? Any rash? Is he alert and active, or drowsy and hard to wake? Fewer wet nappies? Any DRY SKIN, HOARSE CRY, CONSTIPATION? Thyroid problems in the family? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY JAUNDICED AS A BABY FOR WEEKS, or with a blood disorder like G6PD DEFICIENCY OR SPHEROCYTOSIS?' → no to all.

READ THE RESULT ALOUD IN PLAIN WORDS, THEN NAME IT WITH THREE REASONS (see dx) → 'IS IT MY FAULT? Did I do something in pregnancy?' → 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS.' Then the full differential list, conjugated first, with physiological and breast-milk jaundice explicitly at the bottom AND WHY.

MANAGEMENT — TREAT THE BILIRUBIN, TREAT THE CAUSE, REFER TODAY (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → the Kasai, and THE SIXTY-DAY WINDOW, which is why you are ringing the hospital now. Then 'PLEASE KEEP BREASTFEEDING — there is nothing wrong with your milk', the safety-net, travel support, written information, and a four-line summary.

Offering crutches, or 'rest and review', is the fail — and the mother will accept it happily.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. ETHAN, 12, brought in by his mother SHARON with LIMPING AND KNEE PAIN FOR TWO WEEKS, which started while he was playing BASKETBALL. Afebrile, NO TRAUMA RECALLED. He is a keen basketballer.
The examiner will give you physical examination findings ON REQUEST, and TWO X-RAYS — KNEE AND HIP. 8 minutes. The mother mentions 'the hip is a bit sore too' ONLY IF ASKED.

Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings

back.dx: SLIPPED CAPITAL FEMORAL EPIPHYSIS — a slipped hip growth plate — in a 12-year-old boy with a BMI of 30 who has grown and gained weight this year, with two weeks of knee AND hip pain, no injury, an out-toed antalgic gait, LOSS OF INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION AND FLEXION WITH OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION ON FLEXION, a leg 1.5 cm short, and a normal knee film. EXPLAIN THE FILMS KNEE FIRST: 'bone is white, soft tissue grey, air black. This is the knee — IT'S COMPLETELY NORMAL, so the knee isn't the problem. This is his hip. The hip is a BALL-AND-SOCKET joint. ON THE RIGHT, the round head of the thigh bone sits NEATLY ON TOP of its growth plate. ON THE LEFT, THE HEAD HAS SLIPPED OFF THE GROWTH PLATE — it's sitting lower and further back.' Never mention Klein's line or say 'epiphysis' to the mother without translating it. THEN NAME IT AND REMOVE THE BLAME: 'in growing boys, particularly around Ethan's size and during the growth spurt, THE GROWTH PLATE IS WEAKER and the head can slip off it. IT'S NOT BROKEN, AND BASKETBALL DIDN'T CAUSE IT — it just showed up during the game.' THEN THE TWO BULLET POINTS, IN THIS ORDER: (1) FROM NOW ETHAN MUST NOT WALK ON THAT LEG AT ALL — A WHEELCHAIR, NOT CRUTCHES — AND NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK until the surgeon has seen him; (2) PHONE THE CHILDREN'S ORTHOPAEDIC TEAM NOW, because this needs an operation soon to PIN THE HEAD OF THE BONE IN PLACE. THE REASON FOR THE RUSH: 'EVERY STEP RISKS THE HEAD SLIPPING FURTHER AND DAMAGING ITS BLOOD SUPPLY, which can permanently damage the joint — that's why it's a wheelchair and an ambulance rather than the car.' THE OTHER HIP: slips are bilateral in about one in five, and the second is often silent, so the surgeon may pin both. AFTERCARE: about six weeks on crutches, physiotherapy, NO BASKETBALL UNTIL THE SURGEON CLEARS HIM — never promise a return date — X-rays until the growth plates close, and weight management later, once he has recovered. UNSTABLE SLIP — cannot weight-bear at all: the risk to the blood supply is much higher (AVN up to about 50%), so he stays exactly where he is, ambulance and orthopaedic registrar now, nil by mouth, MedSTAR Kids if there is any delay. THE ATYPICAL PATIENT — younger, shorter, or bilateral: screen for an underlying cause with THYROID FUNCTION, RENAL FUNCTION AND A GROWTH-HORMONE ASSESSMENT alongside the orthopaedic management.
plan: WIPE AND OPEN WITH ETHAN, NOT ABOUT HIM: 'Sharon, and you must be Ethan. I'll just clean my hands. Ethan, I hear the knee's been sore and you've been limping — TELL ME WHAT'S BEEN GOING ON.' → it started at basketball two weeks ago, no fall. → 'two weeks of limping when you love basketball — that's frustrating, and I can see it's worrying you both. I'll ask some questions, examine you, and WE'LL LOOK AT THE X-RAYS TOGETHER.'

REFUSE THE KNEE ANCHOR: 'was there a SPECIFIC MOMENT — a twist, a landing, a fall — or did it just start hurting?' → no fall. 'WHERE EXACTLY is the pain — can you point? IS IT IN THE KNEE ONLY, OR THE THIGH, THE GROIN OR THE HIP AS WELL?' → 'mostly the knee. BUT THE HIP'S SORE TOO, NOW YOU ASK.' → SAY THE PIVOT ALOUD: 'THAT'S IMPORTANT — KNEE PAIN WITH HIP PAIN AT YOUR AGE MAKES ME THINK ABOUT THE HIP JOINT ITSELF.' (Hearing it and not saying so loses the mark — the examiner needs to hear you pivot.)

THE REST OF THE LIMP: constant or with activity, getting worse, CAN HE WEIGHT-BEAR AND WALK, has there been a time he COULDN'T AT ALL, HAS THE FOOT TURNED OUT OR THE LEG LOOKED SHORTER, swelling, redness, clicking or locking, AND ANY EARLIER EPISODES → the foot points out, and there was A SORE HIP A COUPLE OF MONTHS AGO THAT WENT AWAY (given only if asked).

DIFFERENTIAL SCREEN: fever, feeling unwell, recent cold or gastro; injuries or falls AND WHO WAS THERE, home and school; NIGHT PAIN THAT WAKES HIM, weight loss, tiredness, bruising, lumps; other joints, morning stiffness, rashes, eye problems; tummy pain or vomiting; and, to Ethan, ANY PAIN OR SWELLING IN THE TESTICLES.

BINDS, GROWTH AND WEIGHT: birth and immunisations; 'tell me about his diet and weight — HAS HE PUT ON WEIGHT RECENTLY? HAS HE HAD HIS GROWTH SPURT? Is he growing like his classmates?'; past problems, medications, allergies, THYROID OR KIDNEY PROBLEMS; family hip problems as a child; and how much basketball.

SUMMARISE AND TRANSITION: 'so: two weeks of left knee AND hip pain with a worsening limp, no injury, in a boy who has GROWN AND GAINED WEIGHT this year; no fever, night pain or other joints. KNEE PAIN WITH HIP PAIN AT THIS AGE MAKES ME THINK ABOUT THE HIP JOINT ITSELF. I'd like to examine him.'

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, EVERY ITEM NAMED: 'general appearance — well, in pain, any rash? HIS HEIGHT, WEIGHT AND BMI, PLEASE. Temperature and vital signs. Can he stand and walk — is the gait ANTALGIC, is the foot OUT-TOED, Trendelenburg? Inspection of both legs. Palpation — warmth, tenderness, THE TIBIAL TUBEROSITY, the knee joint lines. Movement — BOTH HIPS, active and passive, specifically INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION AND FLEXION, AND WHETHER FLEXION FORCES THE HIP INTO EXTERNAL ROTATION; knee range and stability. TRUE LEG LENGTH. LOG ROLL. The abdomen, AND INSPECTION AND PALPATION OF THE SCROTUM.' Then PRESENT IT BACK before asking for the films. (Forgetting BMI, or asking only about the knee — the examiner gives nothing you did not name.)
EXPLAIN THE FILMS, KNEE FIRST, THEN THE HIP WITH THE NORMAL SIDE FIRST (see dx) → 'SLIPPED? HOW DOES A BONE SLIP? IS IT BROKEN? IS THAT FROM BASKETBALL?' → name it, and remove the blame.

THE TWO BULLET POINTS, IN ORDER, THEN THE REASON FOR THE RUSH (see dx) → 'AN OPERATION? TODAY? CAN'T HE JUST REST IT? CAN WE DRIVE HIM DOWN OURSELVES?' → 'every step on it risks the head slipping further and damaging its blood supply... so he'll go BY AMBULANCE, with the orthopaedic team expecting him.' (Offering crutches, or 'rest and review', is the fail — AND SHARON WILL ACCEPT IT HAPPILY. And never offer PATS or the family car for an acute slip.)

THE OTHER HIP, AFTERCARE, EXPECTATIONS: the screw across the growth plate; pinning the other side because it happens bilaterally in about one in five; six weeks of crutches, physiotherapy, X-rays until the growth plates close; weight worked on later; and NO BASKETBALL UNTIL THE SURGEON CLEARS HIM — never a return date. Then analgesia now, written information, and questions. → 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?' asked at about 6:30 if you never asked what she was hoping for.

'HIS HEIGHT, WEIGHT AND BMI, PLEASE.' / 'Internal rotation, abduction and flexion of BOTH hips — and does flexion force the hip into external rotation?' / 'True leg length, log roll, the abdomen and the scrotum.' / 'The knee X-ray is COMPLETELY NORMAL, so the knee isn't the problem.' / 'On the normal side the round head sits on top of the growth plate; on this side IT HAS SLIPPED OFF.'

'Two things straight away: NO WEIGHT ON THAT LEG — A WHEELCHAIR, NOT CRUTCHES — and NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK. And I'm phoning the orthopaedic team NOW.' / 'Every step risks the blood supply to the head of the bone.' / 'A screw holds the head where it is; they may pin the other hip too — it happens on both sides in about one in five.' / 'No basketball until the surgeon clears him.'

VARIANT — OSGOOD-SCHLATTER (one finding changed: tender swollen tibial tuberosity, hips normal, BMI 19, both films normal): 'with normal hips and normal films, this is OSGOOD-SCHLATTER DISEASE — the tendon from the kneecap pulls on the growing bump of bone below the knee, which gets inflamed with jumping. IT SETTLES AS HE FINISHES GROWING. Cut back the jumping sports for a few weeks, ice after activity, paracetamol or ibuprofen, and thigh stretches — HE CAN KEEP PLAYING AS PAIN ALLOWS. Come back if the pain becomes constant, wakes him at night, the hip becomes sore, or he can't put weight on it.' / VARIANT — UNSTABLE SLIP, cannot weight-bear at all: 'that makes this an UNSTABLE slip — the risk to the blood supply is MUCH higher. He stays exactly where he is; ambulance and orthopaedic registrar now, nothing to eat or drink, and MedSTAR Kids if there's any delay.'

VARIANT — 'WHAT ABOUT THE OTHER HIP?': 'slips are bilateral in about one in five, AND THE SECOND SLIP IS OFTEN SILENT, so I'd ask the surgeon about PROPHYLACTIC PINNING of the right hip — particularly if there's an endocrine cause or if follow-up from the country is difficult. If it isn't pinned, we watch it with X-rays and a low threshold for review.' / VARIANT — THE ATYPICAL PATIENT, 9 years old, short, both hips: 'he's younger and shorter than the typical patient and both hips are affected, so I'd SCREEN FOR AN UNDERLYING CAUSE — thyroid function, renal function, and a growth-hormone assessment through paediatric endocrinology — alongside the orthopaedic management.' / 'CAN HE JUST TAKE ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES AND REST?': 'I understand why that sounds reasonable, BUT REST DOESN'T PUT THE HEAD BACK OR STOP IT SLIPPING FURTHER — only pinning does, and DELAY IS WHAT DAMAGES THE JOINT.'
pefe: Role-player: Sharon, 44, works at the Kadina supermarket; partner Mick is a farm contractor; Ethan, 12, is the youngest of three. No family history of hip problems; Mick had a knee reconstruction from football. Ethan: normal birth, immunised, no medical problems, medicines or allergies; ALWAYS 'A BIG BOY', and he HAS PUT ON A LOT OF WEIGHT AND GROWN FAST IN THE LAST YEAR; basketball three times a week, FINALS IN THREE WEEKS. Two weeks ago his LEFT KNEE started aching during a game — NO FALL, NO TWIST — limping since and worse, and yesterday he could barely walk on it.

WHAT TO WITHHOLD: LEAD WITH THE KNEE AND BASKETBALL. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE HIP, THE OUT-TOEING OR THE EARLIER EPISODE UNLESS ASKED DIRECTLY. The hip is sore too — only if asked about hip, groin or thigh. The foot points outward — only if asked about the foot or leg. A SORE HIP TWO MONTHS AGO THAT WENT AWAY — only if asked about previous episodes. No fever, no night pain, no weight loss, no other joints, no rash, no injuries; home and school fine; Ethan says no testicular pain, embarrassed. Ethan answers symptom questions in short sentences; Sharon fills in the background.

REGISTER: practical, slightly impatient; SHOCKED AND THEN TEARFUL WHEN 'OPERATION' IS SAID, recovering if the doctor explains why and what happens next. HIDDEN AGENDA: she wants him fit for the finals and is hoping for 'rest and physio' — ASK 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?' at about 6:30 if the doctor never asks what she is hoping for. IF THE DOCTOR OFFERS CRUTCHES OR 'REST AND REVIEW', ACCEPT HAPPILY — THAT IS THE FAIL. If the doctor says wheelchair and ambulance, PUSH BACK ONCE: 'can't we just drive him?' If they say Klein's line or 'epiphysis' without explaining, LOOK BLANK: 'what does that mean?'
fails: ★ Offering crutches, or 'rest and review' — and the mother will accept it happily, because that is the trap
★ Accepting the basketball anchor and asking knee-only questions, so the hip is never asked about
Hearing 'the hip's sore too' and not saying aloud that this changes the picture
Reading the normal knee film and calling it a strain; or talking about Klein's line and 'epiphysis' to the mother

Forgetting BMI, or not asking for both hips, internal rotation, obligatory external rotation on flexion, leg length and the scrotum by name; promising a return date for basketball; and offering the family car or PATS for an acute slip
numbers: SCFE: 10-16 years, boys, obese, during the growth spurt · BMI 30 on the card · LOST: internal rotation, abduction, flexion, WITH OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION ON FLEXION · leg 1.5-2 cm short with out-toeing · AP plus FROG-LEG LATERAL, and Klein's line should cut the head

BILATERAL IN ABOUT 20-25%, and the second slip is often silent · UNSTABLE (cannot walk) means AVN risk up to about 50% · about 6 weeks on crutches after pinning VERIFY · management order: WHEELCHAIR AND NIL BY MOUTH, then orthopaedics by phone and an ambulance, then pinning, the other hip, aftercare · MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND EXPLANATION — general practice. ONE STRUCTURE, FIVE RECALLS, AND THE STEM WILL NOT TELL YOU WHICH ONE YOU ARE IN: tension-type, brain tumour, benign intracranial hypertension, migraine, or a viral upper respiratory infection. TWO AUTOMATIC FAILS: not asking THE EIGHT RED FLAGS OUT LOUD, and not requesting FUNDOSCOPY BY NAME. Then COMMIT TO ONE DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS and ANSWER THE TUMOUR QUESTION THE PARENT RAISED, using her own negatives back to her. Do NOT reassure before the red flags — acknowledge, promise to return to it, and move on.
stem: VERSION A (master): general practice, Wallaroo. EMILY, 9, brought by her mother KAREN, with HEADACHES FOR SIX MONTHS. NO vitals on the card; growth chart available on request; the mother answers for Emily. History FOUR MINUTES ONLY, then examination findings from the examiner, then diagnosis, differentials and management. 8 minutes.

THE OTHER FOUR RECALLS: (B) 9 years, months of headache WITH WEIGHT LOSS, BLURRED VISION AND MORNING VOMITING. (C) 16 years, brought by her father, ON DOXYCYCLINE FOR ACNE, with blurred vision and buzzing, overweight, BP high, FUNDI NOT ON THE CARD. (D) 9 years, EPISODIC right-sided throbbing with nausea and flashing lights, mother has migraine. (E) 6 years, a few days of dull headache all over WITH FEVER AND A SORE THROAT.

Alert. BP 150/90, PULSE 54, RR normal, afebrile. Cranial nerves and limbs normal. PAPILLOEDEMA. ENT normal, neck supple. WEIGHT DOWN A CENTILE
HYPERTENSION WITH BRADYCARDIA IS A CUSHING RESPONSE — raised intracranial pressure, and the fundus says the same thing
