back.dx: VERSION A — TENSION-TYPE HEADACHE. 'It's a stress-related headache — we think it comes from tightening of the muscles around the head and neck.' FOUR REASONS: REAL STRESS AT SCHOOL WITH THE BULLYING; THE HEADACHES ONLY HAPPEN ON SCHOOL DAYS; SHE STILL PLAYS AND EATS THROUGH THEM; and the examination is COMPLETELY NORMAL. THEN ANSWER THE TUMOUR QUESTION WITH HER OWN NEGATIVES: 'I know your neighbour's diagnosis frightened you. I DON'T THINK THIS IS A BRAIN TUMOUR: no night headaches, no morning vomiting, no weight loss, no weakness or numbness, no vision problems, and THE BACK OF HER EYES AND HER NERVES ARE NORMAL.' Then at least four more differentials WITH REASONS — migraine (no nausea, no photophobia, no aura, no family history), infection of ears, throat, sinuses or teeth (no fever, all normal), and eye strain (vision fine). MANAGEMENT: 'A SCAN WOULDN'T HELP HER and isn't needed with a normal examination — AND I'LL TELL YOU WHAT WOULD CHANGE THAT.' The treatment IS the bullying: with permission, write to the SCHOOL'S WELLBEING LEADER; child psychologist or school counsellor; regular sleep, meals, water, less screen time; PARACETAMOL ONLY OCCASIONALLY, BECAUSE DAILY USE CAUSES HEADACHES ITSELF; a headache diary; review in two weeks; and return for night or morning headache, vomiting, vision change, weakness or drowsiness. VERSION B — A BRAIN TUMOUR: 'in Emily's case, I AM CONCERNED ABOUT THE POSSIBILITY OF A GROWTH IN THE BRAIN.' [PAUSE.] Reasons: weight loss, vision problems, MORNING VOMITING, and on examination HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE WITH A SLOW PULSE, which happens when the pressure around the brain is raised, plus SWELLING AT THE BACK OF THE EYES. 'I CAN'T TELL YOU TODAY WHAT IT IS OR HOW SERIOUS — ONLY A SCAN CAN. What I can promise is that this happens FAST': urgent MRI — better than CT and NO RADIATION — urgent neurosurgical and paediatric referral, and because the pulse and blood pressure show the pressure is already high, PHONE THE ON-CALL PAEDIATRICIAN NOW and transfer today. PATS covers travel; call 000 for drowsiness, repeated vomiting or a fit. VERSION C — BENIGN INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION, most likely TRIGGERED BY THE DOXYCYCLINE: STOP IT TODAY, urgent MRI FIRST because a growth must still be excluded, URGENT OPHTHALMOLOGY because untreated pressure on the optic nerve can damage sight, and paediatric neurology, who may do a lumbar puncture to measure the pressure ONCE THE SCAN IS CLEAR. VERSION D — MIGRAINE, and stress is the TRIGGER, NOT A SECOND DIAGNOSIS: ibuprofen 10 mg/kg at the first sign, water, a dark quiet room, a trigger diary, and a paediatrician about preventers if they become frequent. VERSION E — VIRAL URTI: redness WITHOUT PUS and a temperature of 38.3, so antibiotics will not shorten it but can cause diarrhoea and rashes; paracetamol 15 mg/kg four to six hourly, fluids, home from school, review at 48 hours, and return immediately for NECK STIFFNESS, A RASH THAT DOES NOT FADE UNDER A GLASS, drowsiness, floppiness, stopping drinking, or a climbing fever. E-HARD: ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV NOW, MedSTAR, AND DO NOT DELAY FOR A LUMBAR PUNCTURE.
plan: VITALS, OPEN QUESTION, AND ACKNOWLEDGE WITHOUT REASSURING: 'Examiner, before I start, could I have Emily's blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' Then: 'Karen, tell me about Emily's headaches from the beginning.' → six months, Panadol doesn't help, 'OUR NEIGHBOUR WAS JUST DIAGNOSED WITH A BRAIN TUMOUR AND I'M TERRIFIED IT'S THAT.' → 'I can hear how frightening that is, especially with what happened next door. I'M GOING TO ASK A LOT OF QUESTIONS, INCLUDING SOME SPECIFICALLY ABOUT THE SERIOUS CAUSES, AND THEN I'LL TELL YOU EXACTLY WHAT I THINK.' (Saying 'I'm sure it's nothing' before the red flags is the trap — she will come back with 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?')

SICORA AND IMPACT: where, one side or both, out of ten, THROBBING OR DULL AND PRESSING, on and off or constant, GETTING WORSE, does it spread, what helps or worsens it, WORSE WHEN SHE RUNS AROUND, and how it affects her at home and at school. → right side mostly, five or six, mixed quality, not worsening, nothing helps, SHE CAN STILL PLAY, and she has MISSED NEARLY A DAY A WEEK OF SCHOOL. (Deciding migraine or tension from 'right-sided' and 'throbbing' is the trap — the recall deliberately mixes site and quality.)
THE WEEKEND QUESTION: 'does she get the headaches ON WEEKENDS AND IN THE HOLIDAYS TOO?' → [pause] 'no. NOW THAT YOU SAY IT — IT'S ONLY EVER SCHOOL DAYS.'

THE EIGHT RED FLAGS, IN WORDS, EVEN THOUGH SHE HAS SAID SIX MONTHS AND NOTHING SERIOUS: 'does it WAKE HER AT NIGHT? Headache or VOMITING FIRST THING IN THE MORNING? Worse when she COUGHS, SNEEZES OR STRAINS? Any BLURRED OR DOUBLE VISION? WEAKNESS in an arm or leg? NUMBNESS or pins and needles? Any change in her SCHOOL WORK, SPEECH OR WALKING? Any HEAD INJURY, even months ago? Losing weight, off her food, unusually tired, any lumps?' THEN MEDICATIONS BY NAME: 'is she on any regular medicines — anything for SKIN OR ACNE, VITAMIN A TREATMENTS, THE PILL, STEROIDS?'

THE MIGRAINE FIVE: 'when she has it — does she feel SICK OR VOMIT? Is she LIGHT AND NOISE SENSITIVE? Does she see SPARKLING OR FLASHING LIGHTS before it, or hear buzzing? Does ANYONE IN THE FAMILY get migraines? Does it come on with certain FOODS, MISSED MEALS, POOR SLEEP OR STRESS?'

HOME AND SCHOOL — AND GO DEEP ONCE BULLYING APPEARS: 'how are things at home? How does she get on with you and her brother? And school — any bullying that you know of? How is her school performance?' → [quieter] 'there's a group of girls. It started about six months ago — leaving her out, saying things. She cries about it. I'VE TOLD THE TEACHER, BUT NOTHING'S REALLY CHANGED.' → DO NOT MOVE ON: 'has it affected her mood, her sleep, her wanting to go to school? HAS SHE EVER SAID ANYTHING ABOUT HURTING HERSELF?' Then the quick sweep: fever, sore throat, earache, toothache, stiff neck, rash, neck lumps, SQUINTING AT THE BOARD, well-child questions, growth, development, immunisations, allergies.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, BY SYSTEM, WITH FUNDOSCOPY NAMED: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydration, rash, limb posture, PTOSIS. Vital signs. Neurological examination: CRANIAL NERVES AND SPECIFICALLY FUNDOSCOPY; upper and lower limbs for power, sensation and reflexes. ENT: tympanic membranes, nose, throat for redness, swelling or exudate, SINUS TENDERNESS, teeth. NECK: STIFFNESS, pain on movement, lymph nodes. AND THE GROWTH CHART.' (Not saying 'fundoscopy' in Versions B and C is an automatic fail — and in C it is deliberately left off the card.)
ONE DIAGNOSIS, WITH REASONS, THEN THE TUMOUR ANSWERED WITH NEGATIVES, THEN FOUR MORE DIFFERENTIALS (see dx). → 'so it's the bullying? ARE YOU SURE SHE DOESN'T NEED A SCAN?'

MANAGEMENT — AND FOR VERSION A THE TREATMENT IS THE BULLYING (see dx): the school wellbeing leader, psychology, sleep and meals, ANALGESIC CAUTION because daily paracetamol causes headaches itself, a diary, review in two weeks, and the red-flag safety-net. Then invite questions. (If the tumour question was never answered explicitly, she asks it at the end: 'SO YOU DON'T THINK IT'S A TUMOUR?')

E-HARD: 'a febrile child with headache, NECK STIFFNESS, A NON-BLANCHING RASH AND DROWSINESS is MENINGITIS until proven otherwise. pefe: Role-player (Version A): Karen, 38, dental receptionist in Wallaroo; married to Dave, a grain-truck driver; son Liam is 6. HOME IS SETTLED — no separation, no deaths, no moves. Emily is 9, bright and sensitive, in Year 4. THE HEADACHES: six months, right side mostly but sometimes both, five or six out of ten, sometimes throbbing and sometimes a squeezing pressure, ON AND OFF, NOT WORSENING, no spread, nothing helps, SHE CAN STILL PLAY. Never at night, never in the morning, no vomiting, not worse on coughing. No vision problems, weakness, numbness or injuries. Eating well, weight fine, no lumps, not tired. NO medications and no creams. No nausea, no light or noise sensitivity, no flashing lights, no family migraine. NEVER ON WEEKENDS OR HOLIDAYS — BUT YOU HAVE NOT NOTICED THIS UNTIL ASKED.

HIDDEN AGENDA: your neighbour, 44, was diagnosed with a brain tumour two months ago and you are convinced Emily has one — MENTION THE NEIGHBOUR IN YOUR OPENING, and if the doctor never comes back to it, ASK 'SO YOU DON'T THINK IT'S A TUMOUR?' at the end. THE REAL STORY: a group of girls has been excluding and taunting Emily since the start of the year; her marks have slipped, she dreads Mondays, she cries about it. You told the teacher once and nothing changed, AND YOU FEEL GUILTY THAT YOU DIDN'T PUSH HARDER. VOLUNTEER THIS ONLY WHEN ASKED ABOUT SCHOOL — if asked about home first, say home is fine. REGISTER: anxious and talkative, quick to relief; TALK FAST FOR THE FIRST THIRTY SECONDS; GO QUIET AND TEARFUL ON THE BULLYING; brighten quickly once reassured WITH REASONS. IF THE DOCTOR REASSURES BEFORE ASKING THE RED FLAGS, SAY ONCE: 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?'

Score them on: asked vitals before starting; acknowledged the fear WITHOUT reassuring early; ASKED ALL EIGHT RED FLAGS; asked impact AND the weekend question; asked medications; asked the migraine five; WENT DEEP ON SCHOOL once bullying appeared, including mood and self-harm; requested the examination by system AND SAID 'FUNDOSCOPY'; gave ONE diagnosis — tension-type, NOT 'psychogenic' — with reasons; EXPLICITLY ANSWERED THE TUMOUR QUESTION WITH NEGATIVES; named at least four specific differentials; and gave school liaison, psychology, analgesic caution, review and a red-flag safety-net. Numbers: 8 red flags — Cushing BP 150/90 with HR 50-54 — the migraine five — URTI 38.3 — paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4-6 hourly, maximum 4 doses — ibuprofen 10 mg/kg 8 hourly — ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg, maximum 2 g — medication-overuse headache at 15 or more days a month — review 2 weeks in A and D, 48 hours in E — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450.

Reassuring before the red flags are asked, which earns 'but how can you be sure?'
Giving two diagnoses — 'migraine and tension' — or labelling benign intracranial hypertension without imaging first

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND EXPLANATION — regional ED. ONE STRUCTURE, AND ONE QUESTION DECIDES WHICH STATION YOU ARE IN: 'WHAT WAS HE DOING IN THE SECONDS JUST BEFORE — DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM?' A jammed finger and a scream make it a BREATH-HOLDING SPELL; nothing at all makes it a BRUE. Work it BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER — that is how you tell it from a seizure. THREE AUTOMATIC FAILS: calling Version B a BRUE because the trigger was never asked; giving a diagnosis with NO differentials excluded; and reassuring that 'it was nothing' before the screen and the examination.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia. OLIVER, 7 MONTHS, brought in by his mother MARY after an EPISODE OF UNRESPONSIVENESS about thirty minutes ago. HE LOOKS WELL NOW. Vitals on request. History 4 minutes with a prompt, examination findings 2 minutes, then diagnosis and differentials 2 minutes.

VERSION A — BRUE: no fever, no seizure features, NO TRIGGER, no head injury, normal social history; he 'went floppy and blank for a few seconds, then came back to normal'. VERSION B — BREATH-HOLDING SPELL: getting into the car, HIS MOTHER JAMMED HIS FINGER IN THE DOOR, he cried, went pale, stopped breathing and went floppy for a few seconds, then suddenly back to normal and NOT drowsy.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother (4 minutes — you will be prompted)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings (2 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the mother (2 minutes)
time: ASK FOR OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU SIT DOWN · no vitals means no primary survey · then acknowledge how terrifying it was AND that he is well NOW, and SIGNPOST THE STRUCTURE: 'I'm going to ask a lot of small questions about the seconds BEFORE, DURING and AFTER, because that is how we work out what it was' · DURING: when, how long, first time; THE THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS · jerking, eyes rolling up, wet or soiled; then COLOUR, BREATHING, TONE and CHOKING · BEFORE, AND THIS IS THE QUESTION: what was he doing in the seconds just before, AND DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM · A BUMP, A FRIGHT, A JAMMED FINGER · then missed feeds, fever, rash or illness, falls or head bumps, and anything he could have got into · AFTER: SUDDEN OR GRADUAL, and WAS HE DROWSY · EXCLUSION SCREEN: cough, snuffles, vomiting, diarrhoea, sick contacts, immunisations; GREEN VOMIT, BLOOD IN THE STOOL, DRAWING THE LEGS UP, LUMPS IN THE TUMMY OR GROIN; home, who was present, stress, childcare; FAMILY SUDDEN DEATH, FAINTING WITH EXERCISE, DEAFNESS, SEIZURES; and the well-baby and birth questions · THEN THE EXAMINATION BY SYSTEM, INCLUDING BRUISING BEHIND THE EARS, FUNDOSCOPY, TONE AND REFLEXES, AND A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · then the diagnosis WITH THE EXCLUSIONS NAMED, what to do if it recurs, and the follow-up.

Alert, smiling, WELL HYDRATED, NO RASH, AND NO BRUISING ANYWHERE INCLUDING BEHIND THE EARS
FONTANELLE SOFT — FUNDI NORMAL — pupils equal and reactive — TONE AND REFLEXES NORMAL, movement symmetrical
Clear — normal work of breathing, air entry equal, no added sounds
Heart sounds normal, NO MURMUR, FEMORAL PULSES PRESENT

back.dx: VERSION B — A BREATH-HOLDING SPELL. 'When a young child gets a SUDDEN PAIN OR FRIGHT, they cry hard, and AT THE END OF THE CRY THE BREATH CATCHES — they stop breathing for a few seconds, go pale or blue, and go limp. IT LOOKS DREADFUL, BUT IT IS A REFLEX. It is not dangerous, IT DOES NOT DAMAGE THE BRAIN, and children grow out of it by school age.' THEN NAME THE EXCLUSIONS, WHICH IS A SEPARATE MARK: not a seizure — no jerking, alert straight afterwards; not a serious infection — no fever, well; not a bowel problem, not a head injury, not a heart rhythm problem, not low sugar; and the examination is completely normal. VERSION A — A BRIEF RESOLVED UNEXPLAINED EVENT, AND TRANSLATE THE WORDS: 'BRIEF — it lasted seconds. RESOLVED — he came back to normal on his own. UNEXPLAINED — after asking about seizures, infection, bowel problems, injury, heart problems and low sugar, and examining him, WE HAVE FOUND NO CAUSE. It is a diagnosis we reach ONLY AFTER RULING OUT THE SERIOUS THINGS, and he is in the LOWEST-RISK GROUP.' MANAGEMENT. BREATH-HOLDING: check a FULL BLOOD COUNT AND IRON, because LOW IRON MAKES SPELLS MORE LIKELY AND IS EASY TO FIX; and if any spell is ever WITHOUT A TRIGGER, LASTS OVER A MINUTE, OR HAPPENS WITH EXERCISE, do an ECG. IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN: 'LAY HIM FLAT ON HIS SIDE, STAY CALM, DON'T SHAKE HIM, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH — IT STOPS ITSELF.' Come back or call 000 if he does not recover within a minute, if there is fever or drowsiness, or if there is any jerking. LOWER-RISK BRUE: observation on a monitor for a couple of hours if she would like, TEACH INFANT CPR, review tomorrow — NO TESTS ARE NEEDED TODAY, AND HOME MONITORS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED. GP review in 48 hours and written information. AND ADDRESS THE GUILT IN ONE SENTENCE WHEN IT APPEARS, THEN KEEP GOING: 'that was an accident, and what happened next is A KNOWN REFLEX IN SOME CHILDREN, NOT AN INJURY TO HIS BRAIN — I'll explain it properly in a moment.' Do not stop the screen to comfort her at length.
plan: OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU SIT: 'could I have Oliver's observations first, please?' → all normal, alert. → 'ALL NORMAL AND HE LOOKS WELL — THAT'S REASSURING. Mary, I'm Dr -. THIS MUST HAVE BEEN TERRIFYING. Tell me what happened.' → 'he went floppy and wasn't breathing, his lips went blue. I THOUGHT HE WAS DEAD.' → 'I'm so sorry. He's well right now, which is the most important thing. I'm going to ask a lot of small questions about the seconds BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER, because that is how we work out what it was.'

DURING — timing and the three seizure questions: 'when did it happen, and how long did it last? First time? While he was floppy, WAS THERE ANY JERKING of his arms or legs? DID HIS EYES ROLL UP? DID HE WET OR SOIL HIMSELF?' → half an hour ago, about twenty seconds, never before, no jerking, no eye rolling, nappy dry.

DURING — colour, breathing, tone, choking: 'did he go PALE OR BLUE? Did his BREATHING STOP or change? FLOPPY OR STIFF? Any choking, gagging or coughing — anything he could have swallowed?' → Version B: white first, then bluish round the mouth, not breathing at all, FLOPPY LIKE A DOLL, no choking.

BEFORE — THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE STATION: 'what was he doing in the seconds just before? DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM JUST BEFORE — A BUMP, A FRIGHT, A JAMMED FINGER?' → [tearful] 'I SHUT HIS FINGERS IN THE CAR DOOR. He screamed, and then it happened. IT'S MY FAULT.' → ONE SENTENCE OF COMFORT, THEN CONTINUE THE SCREEN: 'that was an accident, Mary, and what happened next is a known reflex in some children, NOT AN INJURY TO HIS BRAIN. I'll explain it properly in a moment. A few more questions first.' Then: missed feeds, fever, rash or illness this week, falls or bumps to the head, anything he could have got into.

AFTER: 'did he come back SUDDENLY OR GRADUALLY? Was he DROWSY afterwards, or straight back to himself?' → suddenly, smiling before she got him out of the seat, NOT DROWSY. (That answer is what separates this from a seizure with a postictal phase.)

THE EXCLUSION SCREEN, FAST: infection — cough, snuffles, vomiting, diarrhoea, sick contacts at home, immunisations. GI — GREEN VOMIT, BLOOD IN THE POO, DRAWING HIS LEGS UP, LUMPS IN THE TUMMY OR GROIN. SOCIAL — 'how are things at home? Who lives with you? WHO WAS WITH HIM? Any stress? Childcare?' CARDIAC AND FAMILY — 'HAS ANYONE IN THE FAMILY DIED SUDDENLY OR YOUNG, FAINTED WITH EXERCISE, OR BEEN DEAF FROM CHILDHOOD? Any seizures in the family?' Then well-baby and birth: alert and active, feeding, wet nappies, term, growth and development, medicines and allergies.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, BY SYSTEM: 'general appearance — alert, interactive? Hydration? Any rash, AND ANY BRUISING ANYWHERE, INCLUDING BEHIND THE EARS? Vitals including temperature. Growth chart. FONTANELLE, FUNDOSCOPY, PUPILS, TONE IN ALL FOUR LIMBS, symmetrical movement, REFLEXES. Chest — work of breathing, air entry, added sounds. HEART SOUNDS, MURMUR, FEMORAL PULSES. Abdomen — distension, mass, HERNIAL ORIFICES. And A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE.'

THE DIAGNOSIS, WITH THE EXCLUSIONS NAMED (see dx) → 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK ANYTHING?' if you named the spell without the exclusion list, or 'WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?' if you said BRUE without translating the words.

PLAN AND SAFETY-NET: blood count and iron, the ECG triggers, and 'IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN: LAY HIM ON HIS SIDE, STAY CALM, DON'T SHAKE HIM, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH — IT STOPS BY ITSELF.' Then the 000 criteria, GP review in two days, and the fact sheet. → 'I really thought I'd hurt him.' → 'YOU DIDN'T. YOU DID EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN.'

Numbers: BRUE is under 12 months and under 1 minute — LOWER-RISK requires over 60 days old and 32 weeks or more gestation — breath-holding spells run from 6 months to 5 years — review at 24-48 hours — call 000 if over a minute, fever, drowsiness or jerking.
pefe: Role-player: Mary, 29, part-time bookkeeper; first child Oliver, 7 months; partner Dave, a plumber. Term normal birth, breastfed then formula, immunisations up to date, SITTING WITH SUPPORT, a happy baby. VERSION B: this morning, getting into the car, SHE SHUT HIS FINGERS IN THE DOOR. He screamed, went WHITE THEN BLUE ROUND THE MOUTH, stopped breathing, went limp 'LIKE A DOLL' for about twenty seconds, then SUDDENLY SMILED. NOT DROWSY. Snuffle last week, gone; nobody sick at home; NO family history of sudden death, seizures or deafness; no medicines in reach, no falls; home is stable. VERSION A is identical EXCEPT there was no door — he was in his bouncer, nothing happened, and she is NOT SURE ABOUT THE COLOUR.

REGISTER: frightened and fast-talking at first; IF THE DOCTOR ASKS THE TRIGGER QUESTION, GO TEARFUL AND SAY 'IT'S MY FAULT.' HIDDEN AGENDA: she is afraid it is EPILEPSY and that SHE CAUSED BRAIN DAMAGE — volunteer 'IS IT EPILEPSY? DID I HURT HIS BRAIN?' late, if never asked about concerns. IF THE DOCTOR STARTS WITHOUT ASKING FOR OBSERVATIONS, answer normally and MARK IT MISSING. IF THEY SAY 'BREATH-HOLDING SPELL' WITHOUT THE EXCLUSION LIST, ASK 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK ANYTHING?' IF THEY SAY 'BRUE' WITHOUT EXPLAINING THE WORDS, ASK 'WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?' IF THEY SAY 'IT'S NOTHING' BEFORE EXAMINING, ASK 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW THAT?'

Score out of 18, 13 to pass: asked for observations first; empathy plus early reassurance about NOW; timing, duration, first episode; THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS; colour, breathing, tone, choking; ASKED WHAT HAPPENED IMMEDIATELY BEFORE AND ABOUT A PAINFUL TRIGGER; missed feeds, fever or rash, head injury; SUDDEN VERSUS GRADUAL AND DROWSINESS; infection screen; GI screen; social history for non-accidental injury; FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN DEATH OR SEIZURES; well-baby and birth; examination requested by system INCLUDING BRUISING, FUNDI, TONE AND REFLEXES, AND GLUCOSE; correct diagnosis for the version; NAMED THE EXCLUDED SERIOUS DIFFERENTIALS; what to do if it recurs and when to call 000; and follow-up with blood count and ferritin or 24-hour review, plus written information.

Vitals on request: afebrile at 37.4 — HR 150 — RR 34 — BP 85/50 — STABLE, alert, crying intermittently. History 4 minutes, then examination findings GIVEN ONLY FOR WHAT YOU SPECIFICALLY ASK, then diagnosis, differentials and management. 8 minutes.

Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings

back.dx: INCARCERATED (IRREDUCIBLE) INGUINAL HERNIA in a 9-month-old — intermittent screaming in bouts, two vomits, and an IRREDUCIBLE, TENDER GROIN SWELLING extending toward the scrotum, with the testis palpable separately and no transillumination. TO THE FATHER: 'a hernia is A POUCH THAT BULGES OUT THROUGH A WEAK SPOT IN THE TUMMY WALL — in his case in the groin. A LOOP OF BOWEL HAS SLIPPED INTO THAT POUCH AND GOT STUCK, which is why he's in pain and vomiting. I'm confident because the lump CAN'T BE PUSHED BACK and IS PAINFUL TO TOUCH.' THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST HAS SIX OR SEVEN ITEMS AND 'INTUSSUSCEPTION, GASTRO, COLIC' SCORES TWO: intussusception, TESTICULAR TORSION, reflux disease, his brother's gastroenteritis, a urinary or ear infection or serious infection, food allergy, a head injury, and simple colic — each named and then excluded on the examination. MANAGEMENT, AND THE FIRST SENTENCE CARRIES THE MARK: 'HE NEEDS TO GO TO HOSPITAL NOW, BY AMBULANCE — THIS NEEDS AN OPERATION.' Then: the surgeons will give pain relief and sedation and TRY TO EASE THE BOWEL BACK; if it will not go, they OPERATE TODAY to free the bowel and close the pouch. NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK from now, A DRIP FOR FLUIDS, and analgesia. Ring the retrieval service and the children's surgeon NOW. AND ADDRESS THE GUILT UNASKED: 'THIS ISN'T SOMETHING YOU MISSED — IT'S HIDDEN UNDER A NAPPY.' DO NOT ATTEMPT REDUCTION YOURSELF IN THE ROOM, and if the father says he tried, ask him not to try again. If the bell goes after 'I'd give him paracetamol and some fluids', the task is failed — SURGERY FIRST, ALWAYS. STRANGULATION: red or dusky skin, a tense lump, a distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds and green vomit — 'this is a STRANGULATED hernia with obstruction: nil by mouth, NASOGASTRIC TUBE, intravenous fluid bolus, analgesia, and IMMEDIATE RETRIEVAL FOR EMERGENCY SURGERY.' TORSION: a sudden swollen, tender, HIGH-RIDING testis with no cough impulse — 'a twisted testicle until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency WITHIN HOURS, AND I WON'T DELAY FOR AN ULTRASOUND.' A REDUCIBLE HERNIA IN A WELL BABY: it still needs repair, referred today for surgery in the next few weeks, with return criteria if it will not go back, goes red, or he screams and vomits.
plan: VITALS, OPEN QUESTION, AND DO NOT ADOPT THE GASTRO THEORY: 'Examiner, the vital signs please.' Then: 'hello John, I'm Dr -. Tell me what's been happening with him.' → 'he's been screaming on and off since last night, he's thrown up twice, AND HIS BROTHER'S GOT A TUMMY BUG SO I FIGURED IT'S THAT — BUT HE'S NEVER SCREAMED LIKE THIS.' → 'it's frightening to watch. Let's work out what's going on together — I'll ask you some specific questions.' ('I figured it's that' is the bait: acknowledge it and keep all four buckets open.)

THE VOMIT, THEN THE SCREAMING: onset, how many, pattern, worsening, COLOUR, blood, volume, FORCEFUL, smell, better or worse with anything, position, relation to feeds. Then: 'when did the screaming start? HOW OFTEN? HOW LONG DOES EACH BOUT LAST? IS HE SETTLED IN BETWEEN? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME, OR HAS HE HAD CRYING SPELLS LIKE THIS FOR MONTHS?' → every fifteen to twenty minutes, a couple of minutes each, grizzly in between, NEVER LIKE THIS BEFORE. (That last question is what removes colic — not asking it leaves colic live and unexcludable.)

THE GI BUCKET AND THE GROIN QUESTION: 'when did he last open his bowels? Passing wind? Diarrhoea? ANY BLOOD IN THE NAPPY? Is his tummy bloated?' Then: 'ANY LUMP OR SWELLING IN THE GROIN OR HIS SCROTUM?' → 'no, I haven't seen anything — HE'S IN NAPPIES ALL DAY.' → MOVE ON CALMLY; the examination will find it. Then THE INTUSSUSCEPTION TRIO: 'does he GO PALE when he screams? Does he DRAW HIS KNEES UP? ANY RED JELLY-LIKE POO? Any cold recently? Any vaccinations in the last few weeks?' → he goes RED not white, he pulls his legs up, no jelly stool, a cold two weeks ago. Then the GORD block: vomiting only after feeds, refusing feeds, arching, WEIGHT GAIN, sleep.

THE INFECTION LADDER AND THE REST: fever and whether it was measured, anything given; travel; runny nose, cough, DROOLING; pulling at his ears; crying with nappy changes and offensive urine; rash. Then well-baby — alert or drowsy, drinking, wet nappies; falls or knocks to the head; how things are at home; new foods and a rash around the mouth; immunisations.

THE EXAMINATION, HEADLINED — AND THE INGUINAL REGION ASKED FOR BY NAME: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? Dehydration? Rash? Could I see his GROWTH CHART? ENT: throat and drums? Chest: air entry, added sounds? Abdomen: distension or visible mass on inspection; mass, tenderness or rigidity on palpation; bowel sounds? I'D NOW LIKE TO EXAMINE THE INGUINAL REGION AND THE SCROTUM — IS THERE ANY LUMP OR SWELLING?' → the photograph is handed over.

CHARACTERISE IT BEFORE YOU NAME IT: 'there is a groin swelling extending toward the scrotum. IS IT REDUCIBLE — can I push it back in? IS IT TENDER? Is there ANY REDNESS OR DISCOLORATION of the skin over it? CAN I FEEL THE TESTIS SEPARATELY? DOES IT TRANSILLUMINATE? Is there a cough impulse?' Then a urine dipstick and the fontanelle. (Do NOT attempt reduction yourself in the room, and do NOT say 'strangulated' with no skin change or toxicity — say INCARCERATED, AT RISK OF STRANGULATION.)
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS, THEN SIX OR SEVEN GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS (see dx) → 'STUCK? IS THAT DANGEROUS?' / 'CAN'T YOU JUST PUSH IT BACK?' / 'IS IT BECAUSE I DIDN'T NOTICE?'

MANAGEMENT IN TEN TO THIRTY SECONDS, SURGERY FIRST (see dx), then the guilt addressed unasked and the walk to the treatment room. → 'WILL HE BE OKAY?' → 'CAUGHT NOW, THIS IS VERY TREATABLE — that's why we're moving fast. Let's go through to the treatment room.'

pefe: Role-player: John, 34, fly-in fly-out mine worker home in Wallaroo. His son is 9 months, BORN AT 34 WEEKS, bottle-fed with some solids; his 3-year-old brother HAS HAD GASTRO FOR TWO DAYS. Since about 10 last night the baby has SCREAMED IN BOUTS EVERY 15-20 MINUTES, a couple of minutes each, grizzly and off his food in between; HE PULLS HIS LEGS UP AND GOES RED, NOT PALE. HE HAS NEVER DONE THIS BEFORE. He vomited twice this morning: milky, a bit yellow, small, NOT forceful, not related to feeds. Bowels yesterday afternoon, wind yes, no diarrhoea, no blood, not bloated. Cold two weeks ago, no recent vaccines. Warm but not measured. Alert but miserable, drinking less, a few fewer wet nappies. No falls; home chaotic with two sick kids but fine. Immunised, nurse happy with weight.

THE CRUCIAL BIT: YOU HAVE NOT NOTICED A GROIN LUMP — 'he's in nappies and I haven't looked.' IF THE DOCTOR ASKS A SECOND TIME, OR ASKS YOU TO LOOK NOW: 'now you mention it, THERE'S A BUMP ON THE LEFT.' REGISTER: worried, guilty and a bit defensive — KEEP STEERING BACK TO THE GASTRO ONCE: 'it's the same as his brother, right?' Become upset if told 'surgery' without explanation, and settle once the plan is clear. ASK 'CAN'T YOU JUST PUSH IT BACK?' after the diagnosis. HIDDEN AGENDA: you are afraid you missed something because you have been away on shift — volunteer it at the diagnosis if never asked what worries you: 'DID I MISS SOMETHING BEING AWAY?'

Score them on: vitals; open question and concern; vomit colour; screaming explored INCLUDING first-time; four bowel questions plus bloating; GROIN LUMP ASKED; the intussusception trio — pale, red jelly stool, recent viral illness or vaccine; the GORD block including growth; the infection ladder; well-baby; falls and home; food allergy; immunisations; examination headlined including the growth chart; THE INGUINAL REGION ASKED BY NAME; REDUCIBLE AND TENDER ASKED BEFORE NAMING IT; 'incarcerated inguinal hernia' with reasons; SIX TO SEVEN SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS; management OPENING with hospital, ambulance and surgery; nil by mouth, fluids, analgesia and retrieval named; NO ATTEMPT TO REDUCE IN THE ROOM; and the father's guilt addressed.

setting: HISTORY, A HANDED EXAMINATION CARD, AND EXPLANATION — paediatric outpatients or GP. TWO THINGS FAIL THIS STATION: ASSESSING ONLY THE DOMAIN NAMED IN THE STEM, and SAYING 'GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY' WITHOUT A STRUCTURED LIST OF CAUSES AFTER IT. GDD IS A DESCRIPTION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS — two or more domains behind, and it does not tell you why. THE MOTHER ANSWERS ONLY WHAT IS ASKED: if you never ask about hands, speech or social, she says nothing about them, and you cannot call it global. You CANNOT ask for extra findings — the card is the examination, so INTERPRET IT ALOUD, including WHAT IS MISSING.
stem: Paediatric outpatients or general practice, regional South Australia. RUBY, 9 MONTHS, brought in by her mother, who is worried that SHE CANNOT SIT WITHOUT SUPPORT.
History, then THE EXAMINATION FINDINGS ARE HANDED TO YOU ON A CARD — YOU CANNOT ASK FOR ANYTHING EXTRA — then diagnosis and differentials to the mother.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother
Read the physical examination findings on the card
Give your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the mother
time: OPEN, AND ANNOUNCE THE STRUCTURE: 'I'm going to ask about ALL the areas of her development, NOT JUST THE SITTING, then her birth and her health, and then I'll tell you what I think' · GROSS MOTOR, WORKING BACKWARDS DOWN THE LADDER, because every backward step is a scored question: can she sit WITH support, does her HEAD FLOP when you pick her up, can she roll, does she push up on her tummy, does she take weight on her legs · AND SAY THE LEVEL OUT LOUD: 'head control is a skill we expect at around four months, so that tells me how far behind she is' · THEN THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS, WHICH IS WHERE THE CASE IS WON: FINE MOTOR AND VISION (transfers hand to hand, reaches, HANDS OPEN OR FISTED, one hand more than the other, follows with her eyes); COMMUNICATION AND HEARING (TWO-PART BABBLE, turns to voice, NEWBORN HEARING SCREEN, waves); SOCIAL (shares enjoyment, knows you from a stranger, peekaboo) · RED FLAGS: HAS SHE LOST ANY SKILL, fits, HEAD GROWING ALONG ITS LINE · BIRTH HISTORY IN THREE ZONES: pregnancy, delivery INCLUDING RESUSCITATION, and postnatal INCLUDING THE HEEL-PRICK · CAUSES BY SYSTEM: brain infection, injury, seizures; THYROID · constipation, dry skin, HOARSE CRY; nerve and muscle · FLOPPY OR STIFF, weak cry, feeding or choking; genes and senses · family history, CONSANGUINITY, hearing and vision · WELL-BABY, AND HOW THE MOTHER IS COPING · THEN READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRET IT · then NAME AND DEFINE GDD, give SIX GROUPS OF CAUSES WITH AN EXAMPLE EACH, and refer WITH THERAPY STARTED NOW.
findings: ALERT, NO DYSMORPHIC FEATURES — TRUNCAL HYPOTONIA WITH HEAD LAG ON PULL-TO-SIT — REFLEXES NOT STATED — HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE ON THE 10TH CENTILE — weight and length appropriate — NO ORGANOMEGALY
The card IS the examination — so the marks are in INTERPRETING IT ALOUD
Fits a child who cannot sit or hold her head
10th centile is WITHIN THE NORMAL RANGE — what matters is THE TRAJECTORY, so ask for the previous measurements
Makes a recognisable syndrome LESS LIKELY but DOES NOT EXCLUDE ONE
THE REFLEXES — absent reflexes with a tongue fasciculation would move SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY to the top of the list. Say so

Then it is an UPPER MOTOR NEURON pattern — ask for reflexes, clonus, scissoring and early hand preference; cerebral palsy is commonest. It is STILL global developmental delay, because tone does not give you a cause
Alert and socially responsive, MARKED HYPOTONIA, REFLEXES ABSENT, TONGUE FASCICULATION, BELL-SHAPED CHEST, PARADOXICAL BREATHING, WEAK CRY
Increased tone, BRISK REFLEXES, ANKLE CLONUS, SCISSORING, RIGHT HAND PREFERENCE — born at 32 weeks, resuscitated and cooled

back.dx: GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY — significant delay in TWO OR MORE DOMAINS — CAUSE NOT YET KNOWN. DEFINE IT RATHER THAN ANNOUNCE IT: 'what we've found is called GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY. That means TWO OR MORE AREAS of her development are behind where we'd expect at nine months. For Ruby it's her MOVEMENT — she isn't sitting and she isn't holding her head — and her HAND SKILLS, because she isn't passing a toy between her hands, which most babies do by about seven months. HER UNDERSTANDING, HER HEARING AND HER SOCIAL SIDE ARE DOING WELL, which is genuinely good news.' THEN BE STRAIGHT: 'GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY DESCRIBES WHAT WE'RE SEEING, IT DOESN'T TELL US WHY, and today I can't tell you which cause applies to Ruby. What I can do is tell you the groups we look at.' THE SIX GROUPS, EACH WITH A NAMED EXAMPLE — THE HIGHEST-SCORING THIRTY SECONDS OF THE STATION: GENETIC, of which Down syndrome is the best known; HORMONE AND METABOLIC, where AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID IS THE IMPORTANT ONE BECAUSE IT IS TREATABLE; CONDITIONS AFFECTING THE BRAIN, mainly cerebral palsy; INJURY TO THE BRAIN from a difficult birth, an infection or a head injury — and nothing in her history suggests that; NERVE AND MUSCLE conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy or a muscle disease; and HEARING OR VISION PROBLEMS, WHICH CAN LOOK EXACTLY LIKE THIS — the hearing screen was normal but both get checked formally. THE HONEST ANSWER TO 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?': 'I can't promise you that, AND I'D BE DOING YOU NO FAVOURS IF I PRETENDED OTHERWISE. What I can say is that WE'VE FOUND IT EARLY, that SOME OF THESE CAUSES ARE TREATABLE, and that THE THERAPY HELPS WHATEVER THE CAUSE TURNS OUT TO BE.' PLAN: formal HEARING AND VISION testing; bloods including THYROID FUNCTION, CREATINE KINASE and a CHROMOSOMAL MICROARRAY WITH FRAGILE X; MRI brain if the specialist thinks it is needed; referral to a developmental paediatrician; AND PHYSIOTHERAPY STARTED NOW — 'WE DON'T WAIT FOR A DIAGNOSIS TO START HELPING HER.' Safety-net: loss of any skill, a fit, or stopping feeding. Then: 'IS THERE ANYONE YOU'D LIKE WITH YOU AT THE NEXT APPOINTMENT?'
plan: OPEN AND ANNOUNCE THE STRUCTURE: 'you must be Ruby's mum — and hello Ruby. Tell me what's been worrying you.' → 'she's nine months and she still can't sit up. EVERYONE ELSE'S BABY WAS SITTING AGES AGO... I keep thinking I'm being silly.' → 'YOU'RE NOT BEING SILLY AT ALL — YOU KNOW HER BEST, and I'm glad you came. I'm going to ask about ALL the areas of her development, not just the sitting, then about her birth and her health, and then I'll tell you what I think.' (Diving straight into the sitting is the trap — announcing the structure buys her patience and shows the examiner where you are going.)

GROSS MOTOR, BACKWARDS DOWN THE LADDER: 'can she sit WITH support — with a cushion or your hands?' → 'no. NOT EVEN WITH SUPPORT.' 'When you pick her up, does she hold her head up, OR DOES IT FLOP?' → 'it flops.' 'Can she roll over? On her tummy, does she lift her head and shoulders? Does she take weight on her legs if you stand her up?' → rolls onto her side, doesn't push up, legs buckle. THEN SAY THE LEVEL: 'HEAD CONTROL IS A SKILL WE EXPECT AT AROUND FOUR MONTHS — that tells me how far behind she is.' (Accepting 'she can't sit' and moving on throws away every scored backward step.)

THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS — WHERE THE CASE IS WON. FINE MOTOR AND VISION: 'can she hold a toy AND PASS IT FROM ONE HAND TO THE OTHER? Does she reach? ARE HER HANDS OPEN, OR CLENCHED IN FISTS? DOES SHE USE ONE HAND MORE THAN THE OTHER? Does she follow you with her eyes?' → grabs but does not transfer, HANDS OFTEN FISTED, eyes fine. COMMUNICATION AND HEARING: 'is she babbling WITH TWO PARTS — ba-ba, ma-ma? Does she turn to your voice or startle at a loud noise? DID SHE PASS THE NEWBORN HEARING SCREEN? Does she wave?' → ma-ma-ma all day, turns, screen fine. SOCIAL: 'does she SHARE HER EXCITEMENT with you — smiling, laughing? Does she know you from a stranger? Does she like peekaboo?' → a happy baby who belly-laughs at her brother. (Never leaving the presenting domain is THE fail: two affected domains is what makes it GLOBAL, and if you do not ask, you cannot say it.)

RED FLAGS: 'HAS SHE LOST ANY SKILL SHE USED TO HAVE? Any fits or funny turns? IS HER HEAD GROWING ALONG ITS LINE ON THE CHART?' → never gone backwards, no fits, head always on the smaller side but the nurse was not worried.

BIRTH HISTORY IN THREE ZONES — a scored block, and where cerebral palsy is supported or excluded: PREGNANCY — illness, blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid, infections, medicines, alcohol, smoking, drugs, scans and growth. DELIVERY — term, mode, LONG LABOUR, FORCEPS OR VACUUM, birth weight, DID SHE BREATHE STRAIGHT AWAY OR NEED HELP. POSTNATAL — special care, JAUNDICE NEEDING TREATMENT, feeding problems, fits, infections, AND THE HEEL-PRICK TEST.

CAUSES BY SYSTEM, THEN THE MOTHER: BRAIN — meningitis, head injury, seizures. THYROID — constipated, dry skin, HOARSE OR UNUSUAL CRY. NERVE AND MUSCLE — 'DOES SHE FEEL FLOPPY WHEN YOU PICK HER UP, OR STIFF?' plus weak cry, feeding, coughing or choking → 'SHE IS FLOPPY — LIKE A RAG DOLL WHEN I LIFT HER' (only if asked). GENES AND SENSES — family history of a developmental or genetic condition, ARE YOU AND HER FATHER RELATED BY BLOOD, and any concerns about hearing or sight. Then well-baby, immunisations, AND 'HOW ARE YOU GOING — WHO'S AT HOME TO HELP?' (Forgetting the mother costs nothing to ask and is scored — and she is about to be told her baby has a developmental delay.)

READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRET IT, INCLUDING WHAT IS MISSING (see findings and dx) — low tone fitting the history, the head circumference trajectory, the absence of dysmorphism, and THE REFLEXES AS THE FINDING YOU MOST WANT AND DO NOT HAVE. (Reading the card silently throws away marks worth as much as the history.)

NAME IT, DEFINE IT, THEN THE SIX GROUPS (see dx) → 'SO WHAT'S CAUSING IT?' → 'I'm going to be straight with you...' → 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?' → the honest answer, then the plan: hearing and vision, thyroid, CK and genetic testing, MRI if the specialist wants it, developmental paediatrician, AND PHYSIOTHERAPY STARTED NOW. Then the safety-net and 'is there anyone you'd like with you at the next appointment?'

VERSION D — REGRESSION: 'she used to wave and say ma-ma and she's stopped doing both.' → 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME THAT — IT'S THE MOST IMPORTANT THING YOU'VE SAID. LOSING SKILLS A CHILD ALREADY HAD IS NEVER NORMAL AT ANY AGE, and it changes what I do. It raises conditions affecting the body's chemistry or the brain over time, and it needs URGENT specialist assessment rather than a routine appointment.' MILESTONES: 9 MONTHS — sits unsupported, transfers hand to hand, two-part babble, shares enjoyment. 12 MONTHS — pulls to stand and cruises, immature pincer, one to two words, takes turns. 18 MONTHS — walks well, neat pincer and scribbles, six or more words, plays with others. RED FLAGS: no social smile by 8 weeks, FISTING AFTER 3-4 MONTHS, no head control by 4 months, NOT SITTING BY 9 MONTHS, HAND PREFERENCE BEFORE 12-18 MONTHS, not walking by 18 months, and LOSS OF SKILLS AT ANY AGE.
pefe: Role-player: Kate, 29, at home with Ruby and her 3-year-old brother; Ruby's father works away on a fortnightly roster. RUBY, 9 MONTHS: cannot sit without support AND, IF ASKED, NOT EVEN WITH SUPPORT; her head flops when picked up; she rolls onto her side sometimes, does NOT push up on her arms, and her legs buckle if stood up. HANDS: she grabs a toy but DOES NOT PASS IT HAND TO HAND, and HER HANDS ARE OFTEN IN FISTS — SAY THIS ONLY IF ASKED. She follows with her eyes and uses both hands equally. TALKING AND HEARING FINE: ma-ma-ma all day, turns to your voice, passed the newborn screen. SOCIALLY LOVELY: smiles, belly-laughs at her brother, knows you from a stranger. NO loss of skills, NO fits; head 'always on the smaller side' but the nurse was not worried. BIRTH: 39 weeks, normal delivery, 3.2 kg, cried straight away, no special care, no jaundice treatment, normal heel-prick, uncomplicated pregnancy. HEALTH: no meningitis, head injury or seizures; not constipated, normal skin and cry; feeding, nappies and immunisations fine; no family history, parents not related.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED, in one or two sentences, AND MAKE THE DOCTOR WORK FOR THE DETAIL. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE FISTING OR THE 'RAG DOLL' LINE — the one word you offer if asked how she feels to hold is 'FLOPPY — LIKE A RAG DOLL.' IF THE DOCTOR ONLY ASKS ABOUT SITTING AND NEVER ABOUT HANDS, SPEECH OR SOCIAL, SAY NOTHING ABOUT THEM — THAT IS THE TRAP. REGISTER: apologetic and self-doubting at first ('I'm probably being silly'); open up if taken seriously; become QUIETLY FRUSTRATED if only asked about sitting; GET UPSET if told 'she'll grow out of it' — 'THAT'S WHAT EVERYONE KEEPS TELLING ME.' HIDDEN AGENDA: she has been told twice that she is worrying over nothing and is frightened of being dismissed again. PUSH ONCE: 'what's causing it?' and once more: 'WILL SHE BE NORMAL? WILL SHE WALK?' If they never ask how she is coping, do not raise it.

Score them on: introduced and gained permission; SAID THEY WOULD ASSESS ALL AREAS; sitting with support; head control; rolling, prone push-up and weight bearing; FINE MOTOR — TRANSFERRING A TOY (auto-fail if missed); fisting or one-sidedness; babble, response to voice and the hearing screen; SOCIAL INTERACTION AND SHARED ENJOYMENT; LOSS OF SKILLS; seizures; head growth; pregnancy history; delivery history INCLUDING RESUSCITATION; postnatal history INCLUDING THE HEEL-PRICK; screened brain, thyroid, muscle, genetic and sensory causes; family history and CONSANGUINITY; ASKED HOW THE MOTHER IS COPING; READ THE CARD ALOUD AND INTERPRETED IT INCLUDING THE MISSING REFLEXES; SAID GLOBAL DEVELOPMENTAL DELAY AND DEFINED IT; GAVE A STRUCTURED DIFFERENTIAL LIST BY GROUP (auto-fail if missed); avoided promising she would be normal or grow out of it; arranged hearing and vision testing; and REFERRED AND STARTED THERAPY WITHOUT WAITING FOR A DIAGNOSIS.
fails: ★ Assessing only the domain named in the stem — two affected domains is what makes it GLOBAL, and the mother volunteers nothing
★ Saying 'global developmental delay' without a structured list of causes after it
Reading the examination card silently instead of interpreting it aloud, including the missing reflexes
Telling her the child will grow out of it, or promising she will be normal

back.dx: A MILD ALLERGIC REACTION TO FOOD — most likely the peanut butter, WITH THE NEW SUNSCREEN ALSO ON THE LIST because it went on exactly where the rash is. SAY ONE LABEL AND PROVE IT WITH THE NEGATIVES: 'I want to tell you WHY I'M CONFIDENT IT'S THE MILD KIND. I WAS DELIBERATELY LOOKING FOR THE SIGNS OF A SEVERE REACTION: swelling of the tongue, tightness in the throat, a change in his voice, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, dizziness or drowsiness. HE HAS NONE OF THEM. His oxygen level is normal, his blood pressure and heart rate are NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD, and his chest is clear. The rash itself is HIVES — itchy and dramatic-looking, but it settles.' WHEN HE ASKS 'ARE YOU SURE?', DO NOT HEDGE INTO ANAPHYLAXIS — ANSWER WITH THE PLAN: 'I'm confident on what I can see now, AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHY I WANT TO KEEP HIM HERE AND WATCH HIM rather than send him home.' MANAGEMENT IN FOUR PARTS: (1) an ANTIHISTAMINE — cetirizine — for the hives and the itch; (2) OBSERVE HIM HERE FOR A FEW HOURS with observations, because a reaction can occasionally come back; (3) NAMED WARNING SIGNS HANDED TO THE FATHER IN PLAIN WORDS — tongue swelling, voice change, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, or going floppy or dizzy — tell us immediately; (4) NO PEANUT BUTTER AND NO MORE OF THAT SUNSCREEN until we know more. BEFORE HOME: an ALLERGY ACTION PLAN — not an anaphylaxis action plan — referral to the ALLERGY CLINIC for skin-prick or blood testing, WHICH IS WORTH DOING BECAUSE CAKE AND BISCUITS CAN CONTAIN EGG, MILK, WHEAT AND NUT ALL AT ONCE, and GP review. THE PEN, REFUSED WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY, NEVER A FLAT NO: 'not from today, and let me explain why rather than just say no. ADRENALINE PENS ARE FOR CHILDREN WHO HAVE HAD A SEVERE REACTION, OR WHO THE ALLERGY SPECIALIST DECIDES ARE AT HIGH RISK. Ryan has had a mild one. IF I GAVE A PEN TO EVERY CHILD WITH A MILD REACTION, ALMOST EVERY FAMILY WOULD HAVE ONE AND IT WOULD STOP MEANING ANYTHING. What I'm doing instead is referring him to the allergy clinic, and if they find he needs one, THEY will prescribe it — that decision belongs with them, not with a single visit here.' AND THE HONEST CLOSE: 'I CAN'T PROMISE IT WILL NEVER HAPPEN AGAIN, BUT I CAN TELL YOU EXACTLY WHAT TO DO IF IT DOES.'
plan: WIPE, ACKNOWLEDGE, SIGNPOST — before any questions: 'I'm Dr -, one of the emergency doctors. Are you Ryan's dad? I CAN SEE THE RASH AND I CAN SEE YOU'RE WORRIED — YOU DID THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM STRAIGHT IN. I'm going to ask some questions, then examine him, then tell you what I think.' → he interrupts once, early: 'IS IT SERIOUS?' → answer it properly by promising an answer in a couple of minutes; answering with a diagnosis before examining gets 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW ALREADY?'

THE RASH, WITH THE INTERVAL PINNED IN MINUTES: 'when did he have breakfast, AND HOW LONG AFTER THAT DID THE RASH COME UP? Is it spreading? WHEREABOUTS ON HIS FACE — AROUND THE EYES, OR THE LIPS? Is it raised or flat? Itchy or painful?' → fifteen to twenty minutes later, cheeks then chest, raised and bumpy, very itchy. ('On his face' is NOT an answer — accepting it means you never establish that THE LIPS ARE SPARED.)

THE SIX RED FLAGS, SIGNPOSTED AS A BLOCK — the scored block, and the examiner is counting: 'I'm going to run through a short list of specific things I need to check for. JUST YES OR NO. Any swelling of his LIPS OR TONGUE? Any DROOLING, or trouble swallowing his saliva? Any NOISY BREATHING — a wheeze, or a harsh sound breathing in? Any DIFFICULTY BREATHING or shortness of breath? Has his VOICE OR CRY CHANGED — gone hoarse? Any NAUSEA OR VOMITING? Has he been DIZZY, FLOPPY OR DROWSY, or passed out?' → all negative. (Asking three of six and moving on is the fail; asking them as a named block is what makes it audible as a SYSTEM rather than luck. And if you ask 'any other symptoms?' as one vague question, the father answers 'no'.)

THE TRIGGER HUNT — and say out loud that you are not assuming the food: 'what exactly did he eat? WAS THAT THE FIRST TIME HE'S HAD IT? Any new medicine recently, EVEN ONE DOSE? Any chance of an insect bite or sting? ANYTHING NEW ON HIS SKIN — SOAP, BODY WASH, CREAM, SUNSCREEN? Has this ever happened before?' → toast with peanut butter, FIRST TIME, no medicines, no stings — 'OH — I DID PUT A NEW SUNSCREEN ON HIM THIS MORNING, ON HIS FACE AND HIS CHEST.' → 'that's useful, thank you — IT WENT ON EXACTLY WHERE THE RASH IS, SO IT GOES ON MY LIST TOO.'

ATOPY AND FAMILY — a distractor to note, not to escalate on: family food allergy or anaphylaxis; asthma, eczema or hay fever in him or the family; normally well, medicines, immunisations, behaving normally. → bronchiolitis as a baby, mother has hay fever, sister has asthma. → note that it SLIGHTLY RAISES HIS BACKGROUND RISK, and DO NOT let it change your severity label.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, IN ORDER: 'general appearance and level of consciousness — alert or drowsy? ANY AUDIBLE STRIDOR OR WHEEZE? FULL VITAL SIGNS PLEASE, INCLUDING OXYGEN SATURATION. Is there a rash, and IS IT RAISED WITH WELL-DEFINED MARGINS? Any swelling of the lips or tongue? Any hoarseness? Respiratory examination — air entry equal, added sounds? Heart sounds and murmurs? Abdomen — any tenderness?' Then INTERPRET: 'thank you — AND THOSE OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.' (Announcing shock because the blood pressure is not 120/80 is a named fail.)

ONE LABEL, PROVED WITH NAMED NEGATIVES (see dx) → 'SO IT'S NOT THE SERIOUS KIND? But it looks so bad — are you sure? MY FRIEND'S SON HAD SOMETHING LIKE THIS AND HE STOPPED BREATHING.' → answer with the plan, not with a hedge.

THE FOUR-PART MANAGEMENT, THE PEN REFUSED WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY, AND THE ALLERGY ACTION PLAN (see dx) → 'SHOULD HE HAVE ONE OF THOSE EPIPENS? A boy at his school carries one.' → the scripted refusal. Then the specific red flags handed to him in plain words, the observation period, the clinic referral and GP review, and 'how does that sound?'

VARIANT — THE BEE STING: ask where he was stung, IS THE STING STILL IN THE SKIN, has he been stung before and what happened, and HAS HE VOMITED OR HAD TUMMY PAIN SINCE. 'I can see the sting is still there. I'm going to FLICK IT OUT SIDEWAYS RATHER THAN SQUEEZE IT, because squeezing pushes more venom in.' THE CATCH: FOR INSECT VENOM, PERSISTENT ABDOMINAL PAIN OR VOMITING COUNTS AS ANAPHYLAXIS — WHICH IT DOES NOT FOR FOOD. Repeated vomiting with cramping pain after a sting IS adrenaline, even with no airway sign; and confirmed sting anaphylaxis earns referral for VENOM IMMUNOTHERAPY, which is genuinely disease-modifying. / VARIANT — THE WHEEZING ASTHMATIC: THE LABEL FLIPS, AND SAY IT FAST: 'Ryan is wheezing after eating something new. I CANNOT SAFELY SEPARATE AN ASTHMA ATTACK FROM A SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION HERE, SO I AM TREATING IT AS THE SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION. Adrenaline first, intramuscular, outer thigh — then salbutamol, then oxygen.' If challenged: 'because DELAY TO ADRENALINE is the recognised contributor to death in food anaphylaxis, and adrenaline treats bronchospasm as well. If I'm wrong, I've given adrenaline to a child having an asthma attack, WHICH IS SAFE. If I withhold it and I'm wrong, HE CAN DIE.'

VARIANT — 'IT HAPPENED BEFORE', volunteered late: 'thank you — THAT CHANGES WHAT I DO NEXT, THOUGH NOT WHAT I DO TODAY. Today is still a mild reaction and today's treatment is the same. BUT A SECOND REACTION TO THE SAME FOOD MAKES THE ALLERGY FAR MORE CERTAIN, and it moves him up the list for the allergy clinic. I'll mark the referral URGENT and ask them specifically to do A RISK ASSESSMENT FOR AN ADRENALINE PEN.' (This version punishes candidates who stopped taking a history the moment they had a diagnosis.) / THE DETERIORATION VERSION: 'THIS HAS CHANGED — I'M STOPPING AND TREATING THIS AS A SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION NOW.' Lay him flat, IM ADRENALINE 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 into the OUTER MID-THIGH, call for help, high-flow oxygen, repeat at five minutes, IV access, 20 mL/kg if hypotensive, OBSERVE AT LEAST FOUR HOURS AFTER THE LAST DOSE. IN THIS VERSION, AND ONLY THIS VERSION, YOU SAY THE WORD.
pefe: Role-player: James, 38, diesel mechanic, father of Ryan, 5; his wife is at work and does not know yet. He drove Ryan straight to ED twenty minutes after the rash appeared. REGISTER: FRIGHTENED BUT CONTROLLED — not hostile, does not cry. HE INTERRUPTS ONCE, EARLY, WITH 'IS IT SERIOUS?' — if the doctor promises an answer in a couple of minutes, he settles; IF THEY GIVE A DIAGNOSIS BEFORE EXAMINING, HE PRESSES: 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW ALREADY?' HIDDEN AGENDA: a boy at Ryan's school carries an EpiPen and he wants one — DO NOT RAISE IT until the diagnosis has been explained; if the doctor never invites questions, ASK AT ABOUT SEVEN MINUTES: 'SHOULDN'T HE HAVE ONE OF THOSE EPIPENS?'

THE ANSWERS: breakfast about half an hour ago, rash fifteen to twenty minutes later, started on the cheeks and now on the chest, RAISED AND BUMPY, VERY ITCHY; LIPS NORMAL; no drooling, no noisy breathing, no shortness of breath, VOICE THE SAME, no vomiting, COMPLETELY WITH IT — he has been running around the waiting room. TOAST WITH PEANUT BUTTER, AND IF ASKED, THE FIRST TIME HE HAS HAD IT. No medicines, no stings. THE NEW SUNSCREEN ON HIS FACE AND CHEST THIS MORNING IS VOLUNTEERED ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT CREAMS OR ANYTHING NEW ON THE SKIN. Never happened before. No family food allergy; mother has hay fever, sister has asthma, Ryan had bronchiolitis as a baby; otherwise well, no medicines, immunisations up to date, behaving normally.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. DO NOT OFFER the sunscreen, the first-time peanut butter, or the family history unprompted. IF THE DOCTOR ASKS 'ANY OTHER SYMPTOMS?' AS ONE VAGUE QUESTION, ANSWER 'NO' — MAKE THEM ASK THE SIX RED FLAGS INDIVIDUALLY. If they ask about the rash as 'on his face?', answer 'yes, his face' AND WAIT — only if they ask WHERE on the face do you say cheeks, not lips. IF THEY SAY THE WORD ANAPHYLAXIS TO YOU, LOOK ALARMED: 'IS THAT THE ONE THAT KILLS PEOPLE?' If they promise he will be completely fine, ask 'CAN YOU GUARANTEE THAT?' Close by asking 'SO WHAT DO I DO IF IT HAPPENS AGAIN?' Mark out of 10: introduction and fear acknowledged in fifteen seconds; interval established; asked WHERE on the face; ALL SIX RED FLAGS; medicines, stings and skin products with the SUNSCREEN FOUND; ASKED FOR OXYGEN SATURATION; said the observations were normal FOR AGE; ONE severity label justified with named negatives; THE PEN REFUSED WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY; specific red flags given and the ALLERGY ACTION PLAN named.
fails: ★ Saying the word ANAPHYLAXIS as part of the diagnosis, or hedging between two labels — 'it's an allergic reaction, though it might be anaphylaxis' is the single commonest fail
★ Giving, or offering to prescribe, adrenaline to a stable child with skin-only signs — and handing over a pen to stop the father worrying
Discharging him from the cubicle with no observation period, or promising he will be completely fine
Asking three of the six red flags and moving on, or asking 'any other symptoms?' as one vague question, which the father answers 'no'

Accepting 'on his face' and never establishing that the lips were spared; deciding it was the food before asking about the sunscreen; forgetting to ask for saturations; and announcing shock because the blood pressure was not 120/80

Fluid bolus 20 mL/kg normal saline if hypotensive · cetirizine 5 mg daily for 2-5 years, or loratadine 5 mg VERIFY · weight (age + 4) x 2, so a 5-year-old is about 18 kg · TWO PENS AND TWO PLANS, home and school · ABOUT 1 IN 5 ANAPHYLAXIS PRESENTATIONS HAS NO SKIN SIGN · FOR INSECT VENOM, vomiting or abdominal pain COUNTS as anaphylaxis; for food it does not · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

back.dx: A POSSIBILITY OF AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER — never a flat diagnosis. DEFINE IT IN LAY WORDS: 'a DEVELOPMENTAL CONDITION that affects HOW A PERSON PROCESSES INFORMATION, BEHAVES AND SEES THE WORLD. It shows up as DIFFICULTY WITH SOCIAL INTERACTION, DIFFICULTY WITH COMMUNICATION, AND REPETITIVE BEHAVIOURS — AND IT IS A SPECTRUM, so it looks different in every child.' THE REASONS, DRAWN FROM THEIR OWN WORDS: he avoids eye contact and cuddles and prefers to be alone — THE SOCIAL PART; his speech is limited to what he can say and he repeats words — COMMUNICATION; he plays only with the curtain and is very distressed by change — REPETITIVE BEHAVIOURS; AND IT IS HAPPENING BOTH AT SCHOOL AND AT HOME. THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON: ADHD — he is NOT hyperactive or impulsive and CAN concentrate on things he likes; OPPOSITIONAL DEFIANT DISORDER — his outbursts come WITH CHANGE, not with defiance; SLEEP APNOEA — he does not snore; HEARING OR VISION PROBLEMS, WHICH CAN CAUSE EXACTLY THIS, and although the school checks were normal you want A FORMAL HEARING TEST; head injury, seizures and thyroid problems — nothing in the history; and LOW MOOD, ANXIETY OR STRESS AT SCHOOL OR HOME — he is frustrated rather than sad, and home is settled. WHAT HAPPENS NEXT: 'NOBODY SHOULD USE THE WORD AUTISM UNTIL A PROPER ASSESSMENT HAS BEEN DONE — that means a CHILDREN'S SPECIALIST AND A TEAM INCLUDING A PSYCHOLOGIST AND A SPEECH PATHOLOGIST, who will see him MORE THAN ONCE AND IN MORE THAN ONE SETTING, and gather information from his school.' Arrange the referral AND A HEARING TEST TODAY, connect them with SPEECH THERAPY, SCHOOL LEARNING SUPPORT AND A PARENT SUPPORT SERVICE, and review in a few weeks. AND 'IS IT OUR FAULT?' GETS ONE SENTENCE, NOT A LECTURE ON CAUSES: 'NO — IT IS NOT CAUSED BY ANYTHING YOU HAVE DONE.' VERSION B — A POSSIBILITY OF ADHD: 'a condition of brain development that affects a child's ability to CONCENTRATE, TO SIT STILL, AND TO STOP AND THINK BEFORE ACTING.' Reasons: it happens at school AND at home, he cannot wait his turn or finish tasks, he acts without thinking, AND IT OFTEN RUNS IN FAMILIES. Excluded: autism — he makes friends, talks well and has no rituals; ODD — he is restless rather than defiant; sleep apnoea — no snoring; hearing, vision, seizures, head injury and stress — nothing found. Diagnosis needs A PAEDIATRICIAN WITH RATING SCALES FROM BOTH THE PARENTS AND THE TEACHER; treatment is behavioural strategies and school support, and MEDICATION IS A SPECIALIST DECISION AFTER DIAGNOSIS.

AND WE'VE BEEN WORRIED ABOUT HIS SPEECH for a while.' → 'SO THERE ARE TWO THINGS: what happened at school, AND HIS SPEECH. I understand how worrying that call from the school must have been. Is it all right if I ask some questions to understand him properly? We'll make a plan together.' (Choosing one complaint and forgetting the other is the first trap.)

THE EVENT AND SCHOOL: 'can you describe exactly what happened? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME, or have there been other episodes? Overall, how are things at school? ANY BULLYING OR STRESS at school that you know of? Any drop in his school performance?' → he slapped a boy who took his seat, a couple of smaller incidents before, behind in reading and writing, no known bullying.

HOME AND FAMILY — TWO SETTINGS, WHICH IS WHAT THE DIAGNOSIS RESTS ON: 'ANY SIMILAR BEHAVIOUR AT HOME? How are things at home generally? HOW IS HIS RELATIONSHIP WITH YOU BOTH, AND WITH HIS SISTER? Is there anyone in the family with similar behaviour or problems — siblings, parents, OR YOURSELVES AS CHILDREN?' → yes at home too, close family, not close to his sister, nobody in the family. (Accepting 'fine at home' and moving on is the trap — ASK THE RELATIONSHIP QUESTION REGARDLESS, because it is where abuse and stress surface.)

SPEECH: 'tell me about your concern with his speech. Can he talk in FULL SENTENCES? Does he use REPETITIVE WORDS, or repeat things back? Does he UNDERSTAND INSTRUCTIONS? HAS HE EVER LOST WORDS HE USED TO HAVE?' → he can talk but cannot tell you what he wants, repeats the same words and phrases, understands if kept simple, never gone backwards.

THE ASD BLOCK, PREFACED SO IT DOESN'T SOUND ODD — 'some of my next questions may sound unrelated; THEY HELP ME RULE THINGS OUT': 'does he KEEP EYE CONTACT? Does he show emotion and empathy — DOES HE LIKE CUDDLES AND HUGS? Is he interested in MAKING FRIENDS? Is he OBSESSED WITH ANY OBJECT OR TOY? Does he INSIST ON ROUTINES? Does he GET UPSET BY ANY CHANGE in his routine or surroundings?' → looks past you, hates cuddles, prefers his own company, THE CURTAIN FOR HOURS, screams if furniture is moved.

THE ADHD BLOCK IN THREE COMPONENTS — ASK IT ANYWAY: 'is he VERY ENERGETIC AND DIFFICULT TO SLOW DOWN? CAN HE WAIT IN A LINE OR WAIT HIS TURN? Any trouble concentrating — DOES HE FINISH HIS HOMEWORK? Does he REMEMBER INSTRUCTIONS? DOES HE ACT WITHOUT THINKING?' → no, he sits for hours; finishes homework if he likes it; not impulsive. THEN ODD: 'any ANGER OUTBURSTS or temper tantrums? Does he REFUSE TO FOLLOW INSTRUCTIONS?' → he does not accept no, but it is that he CANNOT COPE, not defiance. (Skipping ADHD because the answers already say autism is the named trap — the component questions ARE the marks.)

DEVELOPMENT, SENSES, SLEEP, ORGANIC, MOOD AND BINDS: development and growth; VISION AND HEARING; 'how is his sleep — ANY SNORING OR GASPING?'; head injury; STARING SPELLS OR SEIZURES; mood — sad or worried; pregnancy and delivery; immunisations; other medical problems, medicines and allergies. → slow to talk, school screens normal, sleeps well WITHOUT SNORING, no injuries or seizures, FRUSTRATED RATHER THAN SAD, normal pregnancy and term birth. back.dx: A SCALD BURN IN A 3-YEAR-OLD, and the station is a DISPOSITION decision. SAY IT FIRST: 'THE MOST IMPORTANT THING I NEED TO TELL YOU IS THAT CHARLIE DOES NEED TO COME INTO HOSPITAL, AND I'LL EXPLAIN WHY. The burn covers about twelve percent of his body. IN SMALL CHILDREN, ONCE A BURN GOES PAST ABOUT TEN PERCENT, THEY LOSE FLUID AND BODY HEAT MUCH FASTER THAN AN ADULT WOULD, and they can get dehydrated and their salts can go out of balance. That needs a drip and careful monitoring, which we can't do at home.' THEN THE PLAN: stronger analgesia FIRST; clean the burn and apply A NON-ADHERENT DRESSING — 'ordinary gauze sticks to a burn and hurts coming off'; PHOTOGRAPH IT WITH PERMISSION so it can be compared as it heals; a drip with fluids and A STRICT FLUID BALANCE, which may mean a urinary catheter; bloods; KEEP HIM WARM, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN YOU'D THINK; and discuss with the burns team. She can stay with him. THE SCARRING ANSWER, HONEST RATHER THAN REASSURING: 'burns at this depth usually heal in about two weeks without much scarring, BUT THE DEEPER PATCHES CAN SCAR, and we won't know exactly how deep it is for a day or two, BECAUSE BURNS DECLARE THEMSELVES. That's one of the reasons we watch it closely.' Telling her he definitely will not scar is a named fail. THE GUILT ANSWER: 'NO. THIS IS THE SINGLE COMMONEST WAY A THREE-YEAR-OLD GETS BURNT, and it happens in careful households every day. When he's better I'll give you a couple of practical things — hot drinks and bowls right back from the edge, kettle cords tucked away — BUT THAT'S FOR LATER, NOT NOW.' Lecturing her on kitchen safety while she is crying makes the role-player go quiet and stop cooperating. VERSION A, 8%: THE DISPOSITION SENTENCE FLIPS — 'THE GOOD NEWS FIRST: CHARLIE DOESN'T NEED TO STAY IN HOSPITAL', because it is 8%, not on the face or genitals, breathing normal, nothing else going on — then dressing, regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, push fluids, photographs, keep him warm, REVIEW IN 24 TO 48 HOURS, and red flags: FEVER, DROWSINESS, NOT DRINKING, INCREASING PAIN, OR A SMELL FROM THE DRESSING. VERSION D, 20% WITH THE FACE: SAY THE AIRWAY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — burns around the mouth and nose, SINGED NASAL HAIRS, soot, hoarseness or noisy breathing, ANAESTHETIC TEAM EARLY BECAUSE SWELLING CAN CLOSE AN AIRWAY OVER HOURS — and examine the eyes, because eye involvement is managed completely differently. Then admit for BOTH size and site, fluids, catheter, bloods, warmth, photographs, burns unit and early retrieval.

THE BURN, AND INTERROGATE THE FIRST AID: 'when did it happen? HOW did it happen — TELL ME EXACTLY WHAT HE WAS DOING. What did he burn himself with — hot water, soup, a hot surface, electricity, a chemical? Where on his body? WHAT DID YOU DO STRAIGHT AFTERWARDS — did you run it under water, AND FOR HOW LONG? Did you put anything on it? Did you take his clothes off?' → she says she ran it under the tap; ONLY IF YOU ASK HOW LONG does she say TWO OR THREE MINUTES. (Accepting 'I ran it under water' without asking how long is the named trap.)

CORRECT IT KINDLY AND ACT ON IT: 'THAT WAS EXACTLY THE RIGHT INSTINCT. The recommendation is TWENTY MINUTES of cool running water, and BECAUSE IT'S ONLY BEEN AN HOUR WE CAN STILL DO SOME OF THAT HERE — it's still worth it UP TO THREE HOURS AFTER A BURN.' Then: 'nothing else went on it? No ice, no cream?' → 'I nearly put butter on it — my mum said to — but I didn't.' → 'good, and that's worth knowing for next time: BUTTER AND ICE BOTH MAKE BURNS WORSE.' (That is an ACTION, not a history question.)

THE FIVE RED FLAGS, SIGNPOSTED AS A BLOCK: 'I'm going to ask a few specific things THAT CHANGE HOW I TREAT THIS. Are there any BLISTERS? IS THERE ANY OTHER BURN OR INJURY ANYWHERE ON HIM, EVEN AN OLD ONE? Is there any burn to his FACE, HIS EYES, OR HIS PRIVATE PARTS? Any burn AROUND HIS MOUTH? Have you noticed any NOISY BREATHING, or any change in his VOICE OR HIS CRY?' ('Any other injuries' is the one candidates drop — it is BOTH a trauma question AND a safeguarding question, and the only question in the station that opens both doors at once.)

Pulling something hot down is one of the commonest accidents there is at this age, AND YOU BROUGHT HIM STRAIGHT IN, which is the important part.' (Asking it apologetically, or not at all because she seemed nice, is the fail — and asking it when NOTHING in the case demands it is exactly what earns the mark.)

pefe: Role-player: Kate, 29, mother of Charlie, 3, and a daughter of 6; husband at work and texted; she drove Charlie in herself. WHAT HAPPENED: she made soup and put the bowl on the table to cool, TURNED TO THE SINK FOR A FEW SECONDS, and he reached up and pulled the bowl over himself — down his front and his right arm. She got his top off and held him under the cold tap FOR TWO OR THREE MINUTES, NOT TWENTY, then put a wet tea towel on it and drove in. She gave Panadol. HER MOTHER TOLD HER TO PUT BUTTER ON IT AND SHE DID NOT. Charlie is well, no medicines or allergies, immunisations up to date, never in hospital; home is her, her husband and the two children, her mother ten minutes away, no stresses, no alcohol or drug issues, AND SHE WAS THE ONE SUPERVISING HIM.

REGISTER: guilty and tearful but coherent; she apologises twice. HER DOMINANT FEAR IS BEING BLAMED, and she is quietly frightened someone will report her. HIDDEN AGENDA: she wants to be told it was not her fault — she asks 'IS THIS MY FAULT?' after the plan is explained, or at seven minutes if never given the chance. HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED — DO NOT VOLUNTEER THAT THE COOLING WAS ONLY TWO OR THREE MINUTES; if they ask 'did you run it under water?' and stop there, just say 'yes' AND WAIT. IF THEY ASK THE HOME QUESTIONS WITHOUT NORMALISING THEM FIRST, BECOME DEFENSIVE: 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ME THAT? AM I IN TROUBLE?' If they normalise it, answer openly and relax. IF THEY SAY HE WILL DEFINITELY NOT SCAR, LOOK RELIEVED AND MARK THEM DOWN. IF THEY NEVER SAY WHETHER HE IS BEING ADMITTED, ASK 'SO IS HE STAYING IN?' AND MARK THEM DOWN. If they lecture about kitchen safety while she is crying, GO QUIET AND STOP COOPERATING.

VERSION C role-player: Darren, 34, Charlie's UNCLE, who brought him because his sister 'WASN'T UP TO IT — SHE'D BEEN DRINKING'. She lives with a boyfriend who is not Charlie's father. He does not know exactly how it happened; not hostile, just uncomfortable; VOLUNTEER THE DRINKING ONLY IF ASKED WHY THE MOTHER DIDN'T COME. The chart says 10%. MARK OUT OF 10: introduction and analgesia early; full mechanism — when, how, what with, where; FIRST AID AND FOR HOW LONG; corrected it kindly with the 20 minutes and 3 hours rule; ALL FIVE RED FLAGS; tetanus; HOME SCREEN NORMALISED FIRST; card read with depth and size separately; DISPOSITION STATED FIRST AND JUSTIFIED WITH THE PERCENTAGE; and the scarring and guilt questions answered honestly. AUTOMATIC FAIL: never saying whether he is being admitted; ADMITTING THE 8% VERSION OR DISCHARGING THE 12%; missing the airway in the facial version; not reporting in the uncle version; or telling her he will definitely not scar.

back.dx: A BUTTON BATTERY IN THE OESOPHAGUS in a 15-month-old — a halo on the film, drooling and feed refusal, with the earliest possible ingestion about ninety minutes ago. EXPLAIN THE FILM LANDMARKS FIRST: 'there are THREE COLOURS on an X-ray: WHITE is bone, GREY is soft tissue like muscle and organs, and BLACK is air. Down the middle is his spine, these curved lines are his ribs, and these two dark areas are his lungs full of air, which look normal. HIS WINDPIPE IS HERE AND IT IS OPEN.' Only then the object: 'this bright white circle is a metal object. IT IS SITTING IN HIS FOOD PIPE, THE OESOPHAGUS... IT IS NOT IN HIS WINDPIPE. AROUND THE EDGE I CAN SEE A SECOND RING, A HALO. THAT IS THE SIGN OF A BUTTON BATTERY.' Never say 'radio-opaque' to a parent. MANAGEMENT: NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK FROM NOW, because it must come out under a short anaesthetic; call the paediatric GASTROENTEROLOGIST AND SURGEON NOW; removal is by ENDOSCOPY — 'a thin flexible tube with a camera passed through the mouth, down the food pipe, to grab the object and lift it out. NO CUT, and he usually goes home the same day or the next'; AND THE URGENCY TIED TO THE OBJECT: 'A BATTERY IN THE FOOD PIPE CAN BURN THE WALL WITHIN TWO HOURS AND CAN MAKE A HOLE IN IT. That is why I asked you about batteries so carefully.' Transfer to the children's hospital, and FOR A BATTERY THAT IS BY THE EMERGENCY RETRIEVAL TEAM. Monitor and a drip while waiting, and BECAUSE HE IS OVER TWELVE MONTHS, 10 mL OF HONEY EVERY TEN MINUTES UP TO SIX DOSES, WHICH COATS THE BATTERY AND SLOWS THE BURN — within twelve hours of ingestion. VERIFY She travels with him. RED FLAGS for the nurses: vomiting ESPECIALLY WITH BLOOD, tummy pain, fever, trouble breathing, or BLACK STOOL. THE GUILT: 'THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT — TODDLERS PUT EVERYTHING IN THEIR MOUTHS, AND YOU ACTED QUICKLY.' Then prevention for later: batteries, magnets and coins up high, and a lock on the grandparents' cabinet. VERSION A — A SMOOTH DISC WITH NO DOUBLE EDGE, most likely a coin: it is STUCK IN THE LOWER FOOD PIPE AND HE CANNOT FEED, SO IT COMES OUT BY ENDOSCOPY TODAY — 'if he were comfortable and swallowing we could watch for up to a day, BUT HE ISN'T.' VERSION C — A BATTERY MISSING FROM A TOY AND THE MOTHER UNSURE: 'BECAUSE A BATTERY IS MISSING AND WE CAN'T BE SURE, I TREAT HIM AS IF HE SWALLOWED IT. We X-ray from neck to bottom to find it, and if it is anywhere in him we plan removal urgently.'
plan: OPEN, SAY HE IS STABLE, SIGNPOST THE THREE TASKS: 'hello Jane, I'm Dr -. THIS MUST HAVE BEEN A FRIGHTENING MORNING. The nurses have checked Mohammed's breathing and oxygen AND HE IS STABLE RIGHT NOW. I'd like to ask some questions to work out what he swallowed, then look at his X-ray with you, then explain what happens next. Tell me what happened.' (She arrives standing and holding him — she sits once reassured.)

THE INCIDENT, AND THE EARLIEST TIME SAID ALOUD: 'when did you first notice the drooling? Can you guess WHEN he might have swallowed it? DID ANYONE SEE HIM PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH? DID IT START WITH A SUDDEN COUGH OR CHOKE?' → found him half an hour before arrival, alone for about an hour, nobody saw it, his brother said he coughed once. → SAY IT: 'SO UP TO AN HOUR AND A HALF AGO.' (The time you need is the EARLIEST POSSIBLE INGESTION, not the time of arrival — a battery clock runs from ingestion.)

THE OBJECT — THE PASS MARK: 'you mentioned a coin or an ornament. Can you describe the ornament? What is it made of? IS THERE ANY CHANCE IT WAS A SMALL ROUND BATTERY, THE FLAT BUTTON BATTERIES THAT GO IN TOYS, REMOTES AND HEARING AIDS? COULD IT HAVE BEEN A MAGNET, OR MORE THAN ONE MAGNET? Roughly what size? Was anything sharp? IS ANYTHING MISSING AT THE HOUSE — a battery from a toy, coins from a jar?' → 'NOW THAT YOU SAY IT, THE CABINET HE WAS NEAR HAS DAD'S COINS AND THE SPARE BATTERIES FOR THE REMOTES.' → 'are those the small flat round button batteries?' → 'yes. IS THAT BAD?' → 'IT CHANGES HOW QUICKLY WE ACT, and I'll explain in a moment.'

SYMPTOMS AND THE HIGH-RISK CHILD: alert or sleepier; vomiting; TAKING HIS FEEDS; tummy pain; BLOOD in vomit or nappy; breathing difficulty, noisy breathing or wheeze; coughing since; EVER HAD A PROBLEM WITH HIS FOOD PIPE OR BOWEL, ANYTHING FROM BIRTH, OR AN OPERATION ON HIS TUMMY; swallowed anything before; conditions, medicines, allergies, immunisations; who is at home and how things are going. → alert but crying, REFUSED HIS BOTTLE AND GAGGED, no vomiting, breathing slightly faster with no noise. (Do NOT turn the social question into a child-protection interview — ingestion is rarely non-accidental.)

THE X-RAY — LANDMARKS BEFORE ABNORMALITY (see dx): three colours, spine, ribs, lungs normal, WINDPIPE OPEN, then the bright circle IN THE FOOD PIPE, NOT THE WINDPIPE. → 'IS IT THE COIN? CAN YOU TELL IF IT'S A BATTERY? IS IT IN HIS LUNGS?'

NAME THE HALO AND COMMIT: 'AROUND THE EDGE I CAN SEE A SECOND RING, A HALO. THAT IS THE SIGN OF A BUTTON BATTERY. I am now certain enough to treat this as a battery, WHICH MEANS WE ACT IMMEDIATELY.' → 'OH NO. WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?' → 'it means WE MOVE FAST, and it means YOU WERE RIGHT TO BRING HIM IN.'

MANAGEMENT (see dx): nil by mouth; the gastroenterologist and surgeon called NOW; endoscopy explained in plain words with no cut; THE TWO-HOUR BURN as the reason for the urgency; transfer by retrieval; monitor and drip; and HONEY, because he is over twelve months. → 'WILL HE BE IN PAIN? CAN I GO WITH HIM?'

RED FLAGS, GUILT, PREVENTION, SUMMARY: 'watch for vomiting, ESPECIALLY WITH BLOOD, tummy pain, fever, trouble breathing OR BLACK POO — tell the nurses straight away.' Then: 'THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT: toddlers put everything in their mouths, and you acted quickly. Once he is home, batteries, magnets and coins go up high and out of reach, AND THE GRANDPARENTS' CABINET GETS A LOCK.' Then summarise and ask 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST RIGHT NOW?' → 'just that he'll be okay' → 'CAUGHT THIS EARLY, WITH THE BATTERY OUT WITHIN HOURS, MOST CHILDREN DO VERY WELL.'

pefe: Role-player: Jane, 31, part-time bookkeeper, two boys aged 4 and 15 months, visiting her parents in the country for the weekend. Mohammed is FULLY IMMUNISED, no allergies, no medical conditions, NO OPERATIONS. SHE ARRIVES STANDING, HOLDING HIM, CLOSE TO TEARS, BLAMING HERSELF — she SITS AND SETTLES once the doctor acknowledges her fear and says he is stable. SHE GETS TEARFUL AGAIN WHEN THE WORD BATTERY IS SAID, and recovers if the doctor is calm and specific. UNDERLYING WORRY: that it is IN HIS LUNGS, and that this is her fault.

HIDDEN AGENDA (VERSION B): THE CABINET HE WAS NEAR HOLDS HER FATHER'S COIN JAR AND SPARE BUTTON BATTERIES. SHE DOES NOT SAY THIS UNLESS THE DOCTOR ASKS SPECIFICALLY ABOUT BATTERIES OR WHAT WAS IN REACH. IF NEVER ASKED BY 3:30, SHE SAYS AT THE X-RAY: 'COULD IT BE ONE OF DAD'S BATTERIES?' — AND IF THE DOCTOR STILL DOES NOT REACT, THAT IS A FAIL. She asks 'IS IT IN HIS LUNGS?' at the X-ray if the doctor has not said 'not the windpipe'; 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' after the word endoscopy; 'CAN I GO WITH HIM?' after transfer is mentioned; and says 'IT'S MY FAULT' near the end.

Mark them on: reassured her and signposted the three tasks; asked WHEN SHE LAST SAW HIM WELL and how long he was alone; ASKED BATTERY BY NAME AND MAGNET BY NAME — THE PASS MARK; asked size, shape and anything missing at home; GI symptoms — vomiting, feeds, pain — and respiratory — noisy breathing, cough, wheeze — and alert versus drowsy; asked about food-pipe or bowel conditions and previous operations; X-RAY WITH THREE COLOURS AND LANDMARKS BEFORE THE ABNORMALITY, 'food pipe, not windpipe', AND NAMED THE HALO; nil by mouth, specialists named, endoscopy explained without jargon, URGENCY TIED TO THE BATTERY; transfer and retrieval with her travelling too; red flags, 'it is not your fault', asked what worries her most, and summarised.
