back.dx: DEVELOPMENTAL DYSPLASIA OF THE LEFT HIP. READ THE FINDINGS ALOUD AND TRANSLATE THEM: 'the left leg is 2 CENTIMETRES SHORTER, the THIGH CREASES ARE ASYMMETRIC and LEFT HIP ABDUCTION IS RESTRICTED, in an afebrile child with no warmth or tenderness. On the X-ray THE RIGHT HIP IS NORMAL; on the left THE BALL SITS HIGH AND OUTSIDE A SHALLOW SOCKET, and THE SMOOTH CURVE WE CALL SHENTON'S LINE IS BROKEN.' THEN EXPLAIN IT, NORMAL SIDE FIRST, IN PLAIN WORDS: 'THE HIP IS A BALL-AND-SOCKET JOINT — the round top of the thigh bone sits in a cup in the pelvis. IN JAYDEN'S LEFT HIP THE CUP DIDN'T FORM DEEPLY ENOUGH, SO THE BALL HAS SLIPPED UP AND OUT OF IT. That's why his LEFT LEG IS SHORTER, why THE SKIN FOLDS ON HIS THIGHS DON'T MATCH, and why THAT HIP DOESN'T OPEN OUT AS FAR — AND IT'S WHY HE LIMPS.' THE REASONS AND THE BLAME REMOVED: 'BEING BREECH, BEING A FIRST BABY AND HAVING A FAMILY HISTORY ALL MAKE IT MORE LIKELY — NONE OF THAT IS ANYTHING YOU DID. IT'S CALLED DEVELOPMENTAL BECAUSE THE HIP CAN LOOK NORMAL EARLY ON AND SLIP OUT LATER AS THE BABY GROWS, SO IT CAN BE MISSED AT SIX WEEKS EVEN BY A CAREFUL EXAMINER. What matters is that WE'VE FOUND IT NOW, WHILE TREATMENT IS STILL STRAIGHTFORWARD.' WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, WITH HONEST EXPECTATIONS: X-ray today, PHONE THE CHILDREN'S ORTHOPAEDIC TEAM so he is seen quickly, and PATS for travel. 'AT HIS AGE THE USUAL TREATMENT IS TO PUT THE BALL BACK INTO THE SOCKET UNDER A SHORT ANAESTHETIC AND HOLD IT THERE WITH A PLASTER CAST FOR A FEW MONTHS; SOMETIMES AN OPERATION IS NEEDED' — NEVER 'he'll grow out of it' AND NEVER 'the brace will fix it', because A 15-MONTH-OLD IS PAST THE BRACE WINDOW. SAFETY-NET: 'if he gets A FEVER, STOPS WALKING ON THE LEG, OR THE HIP BECOMES HOT OR SWOLLEN, bring him straight in — THAT WOULD BE SOMETHING DIFFERENT AND URGENT.' Then offer to write it down for his father. VARIANTS: BILATERAL DDH in a waddling girl — 'BECAUSE BOTH HIPS CAN BE AFFECTED, SYMMETRICAL CREASES DON'T REASSURE ME': ask whether abduction is restricted on BOTH sides, whether there is a WADDLING GAIT WITH A PRONOUNCED LOWER-BACK CURVE, and X-ray both hips — 'both sockets are shallow, so both balls sit out of place, WHICH IS WHY SHE ROCKS FROM SIDE TO SIDE RATHER THAN LIMPING ON ONE LEG.' THE EXAMINER PUSHES ON THE X-RAY: 'a horizontal line through the growth cartilage of the pelvis and a vertical line from the edge of the socket — A NORMAL HEAD SITS IN THE LOWER-INNER QUADRANT; HERE IT'S UPPER-OUTER. And SHENTON'S LINE, the curve from the femoral neck to the pubic bone, IS BROKEN ON THE LEFT. I'M NOT MEASURING ANGLES — THAT'S FOR ORTHOPAEDICS.' FEBRILE AND REFUSING TO WEIGHT-BEAR — THE CASE FLIPS: 'A FEBRILE TODDLER WHO WON'T BEAR WEIGHT HAS A SEPTIC HIP UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE' — temperature, the position he holds the hip in, warmth and tenderness, SAME-DAY BLOODS AND ULTRASOUND, phone the orthopaedic registrar, and MedSTAR Kids if he is unwell. AND WHEN SHE SAYS HER MOTHER TOLD HER NOT TO FUSS: 'I understand — AND A FAMILY HISTORY OF HIP PROBLEMS ACTUALLY MAKES IT MORE LIKELY, NOT LESS. This is one where WAITING MAKES THE TREATMENT BIGGER.'
plan: WIPE, OPEN, ACKNOWLEDGE — AND DO NOT AGREE WITH GRANDMA: 'that does sound worrying, especially when he's only just started walking. I'll ask you a number of questions, INCLUDING ABOUT HIS BIRTH AND DEVELOPMENT, and then we'll work out what's going on.' (Reassuring before the history is the first trap — and if you do, she pushes back: 'SO WHY IS THE LEG SHORTER?')

EXPLORE THE LIMP: 'can he stand and put weight on both legs? WHICH LEG DOES HE FAVOUR? When did he first pull to stand, and when were his first steps? HAS THE LIMP BEEN THERE SINCE THOSE VERY FIRST STEPS, OR DID IT START LATER? Is it getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse?' → left, FROM THE VERY FIRST STEPS, unchanged. (Asking 'where does it hurt?' or 'is the pain sharp or dull?' of a 15-month-old is what the examiner listens for — THE TIMING QUESTION REPLACES PAIN.)

WHAT SHE SEES, AND THE SEPTIC-HIP SCREEN: 'any swelling or redness around his hips, knees or ankles? ANY DEFORMITY — A FOOT TURNING IN, A LEG THAT LOOKS SHORTER? DOES HE SEEM IN PAIN — CRYING WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY OR MOVE THE LEG? ANY FEVER? HAS THERE EVER BEEN A TIME HE WOULDN'T PUT WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL? Has he been unwell recently?' → the left leg does look shorter when she changes him.

THE BIRTH HISTORY — SIGNPOSTED, EARLY AND DEEP, AND THIS IS THE AUTO-FAIL BLOCK: 'because this has been there since his first steps, I NEED TO GO BACK TO WHEN HE WAS BORN. How was the pregnancy? Any medications, alcohol or drugs? The delivery — was it long, forceps or vacuum, WAS HE BREECH? WAS HE YOUR FIRST? Born at term? Any special care? WAS HE SWADDLED TIGHTLY? DID HE HAVE HIS SIX-WEEK CHECK — WAS ANYTHING SAID ABOUT HIS HIPS, AND DID HE EVER HAVE A HIP ULTRASOUND? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH HIP PROBLEMS AS A CHILD?' → BREECH, caesarean, first baby, swaddled, six-week check normal, NO SCAN, AND HER SISTER WORE A BRACE. (Hearing 'breech' and not chaining to the ultrasound, the six-week check and the family history is the fail — and hearing 'normal six-week check' and dropping DDH is the other one, because A NORMAL EARLY CHECK DOES NOT EXCLUDE A DEVELOPMENTAL DISLOCATION.)

THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS IN THIRTY SECONDS: 'walking is one part of his development — a few quick questions on the rest. Can he pick up small things like A SULTANA WITH HIS THUMB AND FINGER? Does he babble, any words? Does he notice strangers, play peekaboo, roll a ball back? AS A BABY WAS HE FLOPPY OR STIFF? WHEN DID HE SIT?'

TRAUMA, NAI, GROWTH AND BINDS — fifteen seconds that are marked even though the mother seems lovely: 'any falls or injuries to the legs — DID ANYONE SEE THEM HAPPEN? Any bruises you couldn't explain? How are things at home? WHO LOOKS AFTER HIM — does he go to childcare? Any stress at home lately? Is he growing and gaining weight as expected? Any pallor, or waking at night crying? Immunisations, other problems, medicines, allergies?'

SUMMARISE AND TRANSITION: 'so: A PAINLESS LIMP ON THE LEFT SINCE HIS FIRST STEPS A MONTH AGO, in a well boy who was BREECH AND FIRST-BORN, with a normal six-week check BUT NO HIP SCAN, other development on track, no injury or fever. I'd like to examine him now.'

THE CARD AND THE X-RAY — READ THEM ALOUD AND TRANSLATE (see dx). IN THE FACE-TO-FACE VERSION, REQUEST BY NAME: general appearance, temperature and growth chart; WATCH HIM STAND AND WALK — weight-bearing, and is the gait A LIMP, A WADDLE OR OUT-TOEING; inspection of both legs INCLUDING WHETHER THE THIGH AND GLUTEAL CREASES ARE SYMMETRICAL; palpation for warmth or tenderness; movement, SPECIFICALLY HIP ABDUCTION WITH HIPS AND KNEES FLEXED; TRUE LEG LENGTH, ASIS TO MEDIAL MALLEOLUS; BARLOW AND ORTOLANI, NOTING THEY ARE UNRELIABLE AFTER THREE MONTHS; tone and reflexes; and the spine for a dimple or hair tuft. (A generic 'lower limb examination' request gets 'normal' and loses creases, length and abduction — THE THREE MARKED FINDINGS.)

NAME IT, BALL AND SOCKET, NORMAL SIDE FIRST, THEN THE REASONS AND THE BLAME REMOVED (see dx) → 'IS THAT BECAUSE HE WAS BREECH? DID I DO SOMETHING WRONG?' and 'WHY DIDN'T THEY PICK IT UP AT THE CHECK?' (Become tearful at the words 'developmental dysplasia' if no plain-language explanation follows within fifteen seconds.)

THE PLAN, THE HONEST EXPECTATIONS AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → it depends on what the specialist finds: cast, sometimes an operation — NOT A BRACE. Then offer to write it down for his father.

VARIANT — BILATERAL DDH, a waddling girl where 'both sides look the same': 'BECAUSE BOTH HIPS CAN BE AFFECTED, SYMMETRICAL CREASES DON'T REASSURE ME. I'd like to know whether ABDUCTION IS RESTRICTED ON BOTH SIDES, whether she has A WADDLING GAIT WITH A PRONOUNCED LOWER-BACK CURVE, and I'd X-RAY BOTH HIPS.' Explaining it: 'both hip sockets are shallow, so both balls sit out of place — THAT'S WHY SHE ROCKS FROM SIDE TO SIDE RATHER THAN LIMPING ON ONE LEG.' / THE EXAMINER PUSHES ON THE X-RAY — 'what lines are you using?': 'a horizontal line through the growth cartilage of the pelvis and a vertical line from the edge of the socket — A NORMAL HEAD SITS IN THE LOWER-INNER QUADRANT; HERE IT'S UPPER-OUTER. And SHENTON'S LINE is broken on the left. I'M NOT MEASURING ANGLES — THAT'S FOR ORTHOPAEDICS.'

VARIANT — FEBRILE AND REFUSING TO WEIGHT-BEAR, WHERE THE CASE FLIPS: 'THIS CHANGES EVERYTHING: A FEBRILE TODDLER WHO WON'T BEAR WEIGHT HAS A SEPTIC HIP UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I need a temperature, THE POSITION HE HOLDS THE HIP IN, warmth and tenderness, and I'd send him for SAME-DAY BLOODS AND AN ULTRASOUND — I'd phone the orthopaedic registrar and, from here, MedSTAR Kids if he's unwell.' / VARIANT — 'MY MUM SAYS DON'T FUSS, HIS DAD WALKED LIKE THAT': 'I understand — AND A FAMILY HISTORY OF HIP PROBLEMS ACTUALLY MAKES IT MORE LIKELY, NOT LESS. This is one where WAITING MAKES THE TREATMENT BIGGER, so I'd like him seen soon. Can I explain what I found?'
pefe: Role-player: Kelly, 27, part-time hairdresser who stopped work when Jayden was born; partner Dean drives trucks and is away a lot; money is tight. JAYDEN: FIRST CHILD, BREECH, ELECTIVE CAESAREAN AT 39 WEEKS, 3.4 kg, home day 3, SWADDLED, breastfed then formula, immunisations up to date, no illnesses except a cold two months ago. Sat 7 months, crawled 9, stood 12-13 months, FIRST STEPS 4-5 WEEKS AGO — AND HE LIMPED ON THE LEFT FROM THE FIRST STEP. NO pain, NO fever, NEVER REFUSED TO WALK. HIS LEFT LEG LOOKS SHORTER WHEN SHE CHANGES HIM — volunteer only if asked about deformity or leg length. SIX-WEEK CHECK 'NORMAL', NO HIP ULTRASOUND. HER SISTER WORE A HIP BRACE AS A BABY — volunteer only when family history is asked. No falls, no bruises. HER MOTHER AND DEAN BOTH SAY 'DON'T FUSS'.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. IF THE DOCTOR ASKS 'ANY PROBLEMS WITH THE BIRTH?', SAY 'NO, IT WAS A CAESAREAN' — DO NOT VOLUNTEER BREECH UNLESS THEY ASK ABOUT BREECH OR WHY THE CAESAREAN. IF PAIN QUESTIONS ARE ASKED, LOOK PUZZLED: 'HE CAN'T TELL ME, HE'S ONE.' IF THE DOCTOR REASSURES EARLY — 'probably nothing' — PUSH: 'SO WHY IS THE LEG SHORTER?' BECOME TEARFUL AT 'DEVELOPMENTAL DYSPLASIA' IF NO PLAIN-LANGUAGE EXPLANATION FOLLOWS WITHIN FIFTEEN SECONDS. HIDDEN AGENDA: you fear he will need surgery AND THAT YOU CAUSED IT BY SWADDLING OR BY THE BREECH BIRTH — raise it late as 'DID I DO SOMETHING WRONG?' unless the doctor asks what worries you most; if never asked, at 6:30 say 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION? WAS IT THE SWADDLING?' REGISTER: anxious, slightly defensive — 'I'M NOT OVERREACTING' — and visibly relaxing when the doctor explains without blame.

Score them on: WIPE and concern acknowledged; 'SINCE FIRST STEPS?' ASKED; NO PAIN QUESTIONS; fever and refusal to weight-bear; BIRTH HISTORY EARLY AND SIGNPOSTED, WITH BREECH CHAINED TO ULTRASOUND, THE SIX-WEEK CHECK AND FAMILY HISTORY; swaddling; FINE MOTOR PLUS SPEECH PLUS SOCIAL PLUS TONE; trauma and NAI including home and carers; growth; EXAMINATION — CREASES, TRUE LENGTH, ABDUCTION, Barlow and Ortolani WITH THE AGE CAVEAT, tone and reflexes, spine; FINDINGS READ ALOUD; BALL-AND-SOCKET EXPLANATION WITH THE NORMAL SIDE FIRST; three reasons; BLAME REMOVED; orthopaedics plus X-ray plus PATS; SAFETY-NET — fever, refusal, hot hip; and the concern elicited.
fails: ★ Hearing 'breech' and not chaining immediately to the hip ultrasound, the six-week check and the family history
★ Hearing 'normal six-week check' and dropping DDH — a normal early check does not exclude a developmental dislocation
Asking a 15-month-old's mother where it hurts or whether the pain is sharp or dull, instead of asking whether the limp has been there since his first steps
Promising a brace, or saying he'll grow out of it — a 15-month-old is past the brace window, and the honest answer is cast or operation depending on what the specialist finds

Agreeing with grandma and reassuring before the history; a generic 'lower limb examination' request, which returns 'normal' and loses creases, length and abduction; and skipping the home and childcare questions because the mother seems lovely

back.dx: AN UNDISPLACED SPIRAL FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL TIBIA — A TODDLER'S FRACTURE. NAME THE FILM PRECISELY TO THE EXAMINER: 'a FINE SPIRAL LUCENCY IN THE DISTAL THIRD OF THE TIBIAL SHAFT, UNDISPLACED, FIBULA INTACT.' Do not explain the film to the mother — it is not a task — and NEVER SAY 'NORMAL'. TO THE MOTHER, IN PLAIN WORDS: 'Noah has A BROKEN BONE: A FINE SPIRAL CRACK IN THE LOWER PART OF HIS SHIN BONE, THE TIBIA. THE BONE HASN'T MOVED OUT OF PLACE. We call it A TODDLER'S FRACTURE because it happens in children his age WHO ARE NEW WALKERS, FROM A TWIST OF THE LEG, OFTEN ON A SLIDE OR WHEN A FOOT GETS CAUGHT, AND VERY OFTEN NOBODY SEES IT. SO PLEASE DON'T FEEL YOU MISSED SOMETHING.' THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH EXCLUDED WITH ITS REASON — the task says DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS, so this half is not optional: 'AN INFECTION IN THE BONE OR JOINT — he has NO FEVER, he's WELL, HIS HIP MOVES FREELY, so that doesn't fit. A BLOOD PROBLEM LIKE LEUKAEMIA — GOOD COLOUR, NO BRUISING, NO NIGHT PAIN, so no. AN IRRITABLE HIP AFTER A COLD — NO RECENT COLD, and the hip is fine. JOINT INFLAMMATION — NO RASH OR SWOLLEN JOINTS. And, AS I ASK EVERY FAMILY, NOTHING ABOUT HOW THIS HAPPENED WORRIES ME.' WHEN SHE ASKS 'DID HIS SISTER PUSH HIM?': 'nothing suggests that; A TWIST ON THE SLIDE IS ENOUGH. HIS SISTER DIDN'T DO ANYTHING WRONG EITHER.' MANAGEMENT IS NOT A TASK — ONE SENTENCE IF ASKED: 'pain relief and A PLASTER FROM ABOVE THE KNEE for some weeks, with the bone doctors reviewing him. CHILDREN'S BONES HEAL FAST AND COMPLETELY; HE WILL WALK NORMALLY AGAIN.' Then summarise and close with 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST?' → 'just that I didn't see it' → 'THAT'S THE USUAL STORY WITH THIS FRACTURE. YOU BROUGHT HIM IN WITHIN A DAY, WHICH IS EXACTLY RIGHT.' VERSION B — THE FILM IS REPORTED NORMAL: 'THE X-RAY DOESN'T SHOW A BREAK, BUT A WELL CHILD WHO IS TENDER OVER THE SHIN BONE AND WON'T BEAR WEIGHT HAS A TODDLER'S FRACTURE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE; THE CRACK IS OFTEN INVISIBLE FOR THE FIRST WEEK OR TWO. WE TREAT IT AS A FRACTURE WITH A PLASTER AND REPEAT THE X-RAY IN TEN TO FOURTEEN DAYS, WHEN THE HEALING BONE SHOWS.' VERSION C — FEBRILE WITH A HIP HELD STILL, AND THE STATION STOPS: 'Emma, I'M GOING TO STOP HERE. A FEVER WITH A HIP HE WON'T LET ANYONE MOVE IS AN INFECTION IN THE JOINT UNTIL WE PROVE OTHERWISE, AND THAT CAN DAMAGE THE JOINT WITHIN HOURS. He needs BLOOD TESTS, AN ULTRASOUND OF THE HIP AND THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY; I'M ARRANGING THAT NOW' — and name the KOCHER criteria. THE PALE CHILD: 'PALE, TIRED AND NOW LEG PAIN IS A COMBINATION I NEVER LEAVE: we do A BLOOD COUNT TODAY, BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.' BRUISES OF DIFFERENT AGES ON THE BACK: 'bruises on the back AT DIFFERENT AGES in a three-year-old are unusual. I'll ask the children's team to see him TODAY and do A FULL CHECK OF HIS BONES; I'M REQUIRED TO SPEAK WITH THE CHILD PROTECTION SERVICE, AND I'LL KEEP YOU INFORMED.'
plan: VITALS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE: 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs INCLUDING TEMPERATURE?' → 36.9, HR 110. Then: 'Emma, tell me what's been happening with his leg.' → 'since yesterday afternoon HE WON'T WALK. NOBODY SAW HIM FALL, and now I'm worried something's really wrong.' → 'THAT'S FRIGHTENING WHEN THERE'S NO OBVIOUS REASON, AND IT'S EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING TO BRING HIM IN.'

DEFINE THE LIMP: 'when you say he won't walk — CAN HE PUT ANY WEIGHT ON IT AT ALL, OR DOES HE WALK WITH A LIMP? When did it start, and was it sudden? Is it getting better or worse? Worse in the morning or the evening? Anything that helps?' → NO WEIGHT AT ALL, sudden at about 3 pm, same or a bit worse, happy sitting. (NON-WEIGHT-BEARING IS A KOCHER CRITERION — register it. And do NOT suggest a mechanism yet.)

THE PAIN AND THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SWEEP: 'WHERE IS THE PAIN — HIP, THIGH, KNEE, SHIN, ANKLE OR FOOT? CAN HE POINT? Constant or does it come and go? Does it go anywhere? DOES IT WAKE HIM AT NIGHT? How bad? Any swelling, redness, warmth, bruising or change in the shape of the leg? ANY OTHER JOINTS SORE OR SWOLLEN?' → lower shin, sometimes the ankle, slept okay, nothing visible. (KNEE PAIN IS HIP PAIN UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, so at least ask where — and NIGHT PAIN WOULD MOVE MALIGNANCY UP THE LIST.)

THE DIFFERENTIALS IN ORDER — THE PASS MARK. INFECTION: 'any fever? Is he unwell, off his food? ANY RECENT COLD, EAR INFECTION OR SKIN INFECTION?' BLOOD PROBLEMS: 'has he been PALE, TIRED, BRUISING EASILY, LOSING WEIGHT, SWEATING AT NIGHT?' ONLY THEN INJURY, AND OPEN FIRST: 'WHAT WAS HE DOING YESTERDAY? Any fall, twist, jump, trampoline, SLIDE, FOOT CAUGHT IN A COT OR A FENCE? WHO WAS WITH HIM? Any injuries or broken bones before?' IRRITABLE HIP: 'any cold or tummy bug in the last couple of weeks?' JOINT INFLAMMATION: 'any rash, red eyes, swollen joints, STIFF IN THE MORNINGS?' (Asking trauma first because the stem smells of fracture is exactly what this station tests.)

THE NAI BLOCK, FRAMED AS ROUTINE BEFORE SHE CAN TAKE IT PERSONALLY: 'and AS I ASK EVERY FAMILY: WHO WAS LOOKING AFTER HIM YESTERDAY? Who lives at home? Any brothers or sisters? Any stresses at the moment? Does he go to childcare?' → 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ABOUT HOME?' → 'BECAUSE WHEN A CHILD HAS AN INJURY THAT NO ONE SAW, I ASK EVERY FAMILY THE SAME QUESTIONS. IT PROTECTS HIM, AND IT'S ROUTINE.' Then: walking on time, growth and development, birth and WERE HIS HIPS CHECKED, immunisations, medicines, allergies, AND ANY HIP OR BONE PROBLEMS IN THE FAMILY.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE EVERY TIME: 'general appearance — well or unwell, alert, colour, growth chart? WILL HE STAND OR WEIGHT-BEAR? With BOTH LEGS EXPOSED: any swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, rash, OR BRUISES ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY? FEEL: the hip, the knee, the ankle, THEN BONE BY BONE ALONG THE TIBIA, AND THE SOLE OF THE FOOT; any warmth? MOVE: hip range of movement AND A LOG ROLL TEST; knee; ankle? Leg lengths equal? Spine and abdomen? LYMPH NODES, PALLOR, BRUISING?' (A candidate who palpates the tibia only has not run the limping examination — and SAY 'LOG ROLL' BY NAME.)
THE FILM, NAMED PRECISELY TO THE EXAMINER (see dx) — trace the distal tibia and say SPIRAL, UNDISPLACED, DISTAL TIBIA, FIBULA INTACT.
THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS, WITH THE BLAME REMOVED (see dx) → 'DID HIS SISTER PUSH HIM?' → nothing suggests that, and a twist on the slide is enough.

THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH EXCLUDED WITH ITS REASON (see dx) — infection, leukaemia, irritable hip, joint inflammation, and 'nothing about how this happened worries me'. Then ONE SENTENCE OF MANAGEMENT IF ASKED, a summary, and 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST?'

pefe: Role-player: Emma, 29, works part-time at the supermarket; partner Dan is a farmhand; daughter Ruby is 5. NOAH, 3: walked at 13 months, normal birth, HIPS CHECKED, fully immunised, no medicines, no allergies, well, eating normally. YESTERDAY AFTERNOON he was playing in the backyard with Ruby, RUNNING AND USING THE SLIDE, while she hung washing. AROUND 3 PM HE SAT DOWN CRYING AND HAS REFUSED TO STAND SINCE. NO ONE SAW A FALL. HE POINTS TO THE LOWER SHIN. He slept normally. No fever, not pale, no bruising or weight loss, no recent colds, no rash or stiff joints, no previous fractures, no family bone problems.

REGISTER: anxious and A LITTLE GUILTY — 'I DIDN'T SEE IT' — BRIEFLY DEFENSIVE WHEN ASKED ABOUT HOME — 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ABOUT HOME?' — and settling if told it is routine; relieved at the end. HIDDEN AGENDA: SHE IS AFRAID RUBY PUSHED HIM AND THAT SHE WILL BE BLAMED FOR NOT WATCHING. ONLY ASK 'DID HIS SISTER PUSH HIM?' AFTER THE DIAGNOSIS. IF THE DOCTOR NEVER ASKS WHO WAS THERE OR ABOUT HOME, DO NOT VOLUNTEER IT. If pushed on stresses, add 'DAN'S BEEN WORKING LONG HOURS WITH HARVEST.' Close by asking 'WILL HE NEED A CAST? WILL HE WALK AGAIN?'

Mark them against: ASKED FOR VITALS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE and acknowledged the fear; DEFINED THE LIMP — no weight-bearing, onset, pattern; full pain history INCLUDING SITE AND NIGHT PAIN; swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, other joints; INFECTION AND MALIGNANCY ASKED BEFORE TRAUMA — the pass mark; AN OPEN QUESTION ABOUT YESTERDAY BEFORE SUGGESTING A MECHANISM, AND WHO WAS THERE; recent viral illness, rash, eyes, morning stiffness; HOME, SIBLINGS, STRESS AND CHILDCARE, FRAMED AS ROUTINE; walking age, growth, birth and hip check, immunisations, family history; EXAMINATION — general, weight-bearing, look, HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE, TIBIA BONE BY BONE, SOLE, LOG ROLL, LEG LENGTH; NAMED THE FILM — SPIRAL, UNDISPLACED, DISTAL TIBIA, FIBULA INTACT, AND DID NOT SAY NORMAL; and explained in plain words, SAID NO ONE IS BLAMED, LISTED THE DIFFERENTIALS EXCLUDED WITH REASONS, summarised, and asked what worries her most.
fails: ★ Asking trauma first because the stem smells of fracture — infection and malignancy come before injury, and that order is the pass mark
★ Skipping the non-accidental injury block, or asking it without framing it as routine — she never volunteers who was there
Saying the film is 'normal', or failing to name it as spiral, undisplaced, distal tibia with the fibula intact
Giving the diagnosis and skipping the differentials, when the task explicitly says diagnosis AND differentials

Palpating the tibia only instead of hip, knee and ankle with the log roll named; not registering non-weight-bearing as a Kocher criterion; suggesting a mechanism before asking an open question about yesterday; and spending the station on management, which is not a task

setting: HISTORY, X-RAY EXPLANATION AND DIAGNOSIS — regional ED. THE MORE QUESTIONS YOU ASK ABOUT THE INJURY, THE HAPPIER THE EXAMINER — A ONE-LINE FALL IS NOT A HISTORY. HEAD INJURY OUTRANKS THE WRIST: ask it BEFORE the pain questions, not as an afterthought. stem: Emergency department, regional hospital. OLIVER, 4 YEARS, brought by his father JAMES. HE HAD A FALL LAST NIGHT, WITNESSED BY THE FATHER, and is complaining of PAIN IN HIS LEFT WRIST AND FOREARM. HE HAS A HISTORY OF A LEFT ARM FRACTURE FOUR MONTHS AGO, WITNESSED BY THE MOTHER. Observations normal. AN X-RAY OF THE FOREARM HAS BEEN TAKEN.

History about 5 minutes, then THE EXAMINER HANDS YOU THE X-RAY AND YOU EXPLAIN IT TO THE FATHER; in the older online format, also EXPLAIN THE PHYSICAL EXAMINATION YOU WOULD PERFORM; then explain the diagnosis. MANAGEMENT IS NOT ASKED. 8 minutes.

'IT LOOKED FINE' — the father will quote that back, so the line is 'IT'S EASY TO MISS'
Chasing his sister, TRIPPED ON THE RUG, HAND OUT FLAT, PALM DOWN, WRIST BENT BACK, from standing onto FLOORBOARDS, WITNESSED, about 7 pm — iced, slept, and this morning he would not use it
NO head strike, NO loss of consciousness, NO vomiting — and no other injuries, bruises or limp
Pain just above the wrist ON THE THUMB SIDE, moderate, A LITTLE SWOLLEN WITH NO ODD SHAPE, will not bend the wrist BUT MOVES THE FINGERS, COLOUR NORMAL AND WARM, NO pins and needles
FELL OFF THE SLIDE AT THE PARK, WITNESSED BY HIS MOTHER, forearm, cast for a few weeks
Father, mother, Oliver and TWO SISTERS — 'WE'RE A HAPPY FAMILY' — kindy three days a week, grandparents babysit, NO stresses (and if pushed once more, 'money's a bit tight, like everyone')
HIS BROTHER HAS BRITTLE BONES AND HAS BROKEN HEAPS — given ONLY if you ask about family bone problems, and it is his hidden worry
The story CHANGES BETWEEN TELLINGS — first off the couch, later tripped in the yard — IT HAPPENED TWO DAYS AGO, THE MOTHER IS AWAY AND UNCONTACTABLE, and he says 'HE BRUISES EASILY'

back.dx: A BUCKLE (TORUS) FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL RADIUS. EXPLAIN THE FILM WITH THE NORMAL LANDMARKS FIRST, POINTING ON BOTH VIEWS: 'this is an X-ray of Oliver's forearm FROM THE FRONT AND THE SIDE. WHITE IS BONE, GREY IS SOFT TISSUE, BLACK WOULD BE AIR, AND THERE'S NONE HERE. The hand, finger and wrist bones ALL LOOK NORMAL. These are the two forearm bones: THE ULNA on the little-finger side, WHICH IS FINE, and THE RADIUS on the thumb side. Just above the wrist on the radius you can see A SMALL BULGE, A BUMP IN THE EDGE OF THE BONE, HERE ON BOTH PICTURES. THAT'S THE INJURY.' When he says the nurse thought it looked normal: 'IT'S EASY TO MISS.' NEVER SAY 'NORMAL' AND NEVER SAY 'STRESS FRACTURE'. THEN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'this is called A BUCKLE FRACTURE. When he landed on his outstretched hand, THE SOFT BONE JUST ABOVE THE WRIST WAS SQUASHED AND BUCKLED OUTWARDS, LIKE A DENT IN A CAN, RATHER THAN SNAPPING. It's THE MILDEST AND ONE OF THE COMMONEST FRACTURES IN CHILDREN, because THEIR BONES ARE SOFTER THAN OURS. IT HASN'T MOVED AND IT DOESN'T NEED TO BE PUT BACK INTO PLACE. IT HEALS IN ABOUT THREE WEEKS.' THEN ANSWER THE TWO THINGS HE IS ACTUALLY ASKING: 'NOTHING YOU'VE TOLD ME SUGGESTS WEAK BONES OR ANYTHING YOU DID WRONG: TWO WITNESSED FALLS IN AN ACTIVE FOUR-YEAR-OLD, NORMAL GROWTH, NO BONE PAIN. TWO BREAKS IN FOUR MONTHS WITH A GOOD STORY EACH TIME IS NOT UNUSUAL.' MANAGEMENT IS NOT A TASK — one sentence if he asks: 'pain relief, and A SPLINT OR A HALF-PLASTER ON THE BACK OF THE ARM FOR ABOUT THREE WEEKS, with a GP check-up. HE WON'T NEED ANOTHER X-RAY unless something changes — and come back sooner if his fingers go PALE OR NUMB or the pain gets worse in the splint.' Then summarise and CLOSE WITH A CONCERN CHECK: 'is there anything worrying you?' THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED TO THE FATHER, IN LAYMAN'S TERMS AND UNDER TWO MINUTES — do NOT list radial, median and ulnar nerves to a parent: 'I'll LOOK at both hands and forearms for swelling, bruising, cuts and any difference in shape. I'll GENTLY FEEL them: compare the warmth, CHECK THE PULSE AT THE WRIST, PRESS THE NAILS TO CHECK THE BLOOD FLOW, and press along each bone to find where it's sore. I'll ask him to MOVE his fingers, wrist and elbow. Then I'll CHECK THE NERVES with a piece of cotton wool and a few hand shapes. I'll wash my hands first.' VERSION C — THE STORY CHANGES: 'James, I NEED TO BE HONEST. THE STORY HAS CHANGED A LITTLE BETWEEN TELLINGS, and IT'S BEEN TWO DAYS, and THIS IS HIS SECOND FRACTURE IN FOUR MONTHS. FOR EVERY CHILD IN THAT SITUATION I'M OBLIGED TO LOOK FURTHER. I'M NOT ACCUSING YOU. The children's doctors will see him TODAY and may do EXTRA X-RAYS AND BLOOD TESTS TO CHECK HIS BONES, and I'LL BE SPEAKING WITH THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM, WHICH IS MY LEGAL DUTY. I'll keep you informed.' 'HE BRUISES EASILY': 'WHERE, AND HOW OFTEN? Any NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, or FAMILY BLEEDING PROBLEMS? I'll examine his skin all over and CHECK A BLOOD COUNT.' A DEFORMITY ON THE FILM — AN ANGULATED GREENSTICK RATHER THAN A BUCKLE: 'THIS ONE HAS BENT AND CRACKED ON ONE SIDE; IT NEEDS TO BE STRAIGHTENED UNDER SEDATION AND PUT IN A PLASTER BY THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY.'
plan: OPEN, REASSURE, SIGNPOST: 'I can see you're worried about Oliver's arm. HIS OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL AND HE'S HAD SOME PAIN RELIEF. I'd like to hear exactly what happened, then LOOK AT THE X-RAY WITH YOU. Tell me what happened.' (The father starts standing and anxious, and sits once reassured.)

THE INJURY IN DETAIL — and the lecture's own phrase is THE MORE QUESTIONS YOU ASK ABOUT THE INJURY, THE HAPPIER THE EXAMINER: 'can you take me through it STEP BY STEP? What was he doing, HOW DID HE FALL, AND HOW DID HE LAND? WAS HIS HAND OUT FLAT, AND WAS THE WRIST BENT BACK? HOW HIGH WAS HE, AND ONTO WHAT SURFACE? YOU SAW IT YOURSELF? WHAT TIME WAS IT, AND WHAT DID YOU DO THEN?' (A one-line fall is not a history — and TIMING MATTERS, because a story that fits, promptly presented, IS the first NAI screen.)

HEAD AND OTHER INJURIES — BEFORE THE PAIN QUESTIONS, BECAUSE HEAD INJURY OUTRANKS THE WRIST: 'DID HE HIT HIS HEAD? DID HE LOSE CONSCIOUSNESS AT ALL, EVEN BRIEFLY? HAS HE VOMITED SINCE? ANY OTHER INJURIES — swelling, redness, BRUISES ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY? IS HE LIMPING, or complaining of pain anywhere else?'

THE PAIN AND ALL THREE SYSTEMS — BONES, BLOOD SUPPLY, NERVES: 'where exactly is the pain — the wrist or further up? How bad is it, and IS HE USING THE HAND AT ALL? Does it go anywhere else? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY DIFFERENCE IN SHAPE COMPARED WITH THE OTHER ARM? Any pain or difficulty moving the arm, the wrist, the fingers? ANY CHANGE IN COLOUR OF THE HAND — PALE, BLUE, BLOTCHY? IS IT COLD? ANY PINS AND NEEDLES, or not using his fingers?' (A selective SOCRATES — site, severity, radiation only — is the trap, and DEFORMITY MEANS DISPLACEMENT AND A DIFFERENT FILM.)
THE PREVIOUS FRACTURE, EXPLORED: 'the notes say he broke the same arm four months ago. CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THAT? WHAT HAPPENED, WHO SAW IT, WHERE WAS THE BREAK AND WHAT TREATMENT DID HE HAVE?'

HOME AND BONE, FRAMED AS ROUTINE — AND 'HAPPY FAMILY' IS SCRIPTED TO SEE WHETHER YOU STOP: 'tell me about home: who lives with you? Any siblings? ANY RECENT STRESSES OR PROBLEMS AT HOME — WORK, MONEY, RELATIONSHIPS? DOES HE GO TO CHILDCARE OR KINDY — ANY CONCERNS THERE? WHO ELSE LOOKS AFTER HIM?' → 'WE'RE A HAPPY FAMILY, DOCTOR. Why all the questions?' → 'WHEN A CHILD HAS HAD TWO BREAKS IN A FEW MONTHS I ASK EVERY FAMILY THESE QUESTIONS; SOMETIMES THE REASON IS IN THE BONES, AND IT PROTECTS HIM.' Then: 'any concerns about his growth or weight? HAS HE EVER COMPLAINED OF BONE PAIN, OR DOES ANYONE IN THE FAMILY BREAK BONES EASILY?' → 'MY BROTHER HAS BRITTLE BONES, HE'S BROKEN HEAPS. DOES THAT MATTER?' (Given only if you ask — and it is his hidden worry.)
THE X-RAY — NORMAL LANDMARKS FIRST, THEN POINT ON BOTH VIEWS (see dx) → 'I THOUGHT THE X-RAY WAS NORMAL, THE NURSE SAID IT LOOKED FINE' → 'IT'S EASY TO MISS.'
THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED IN LAYMAN'S TERMS, UNDER TWO MINUTES (see dx) — look, gently feel, move, check the nerves, hands washed first.

THE DIAGNOSIS — A DENT IN A CAN, SOFTER BONES, HASN'T MOVED, HEALS IN THREE WEEKS — THEN ANSWER THE WEAK-BONES AND THE FAULT QUESTIONS (see dx), one sentence of management if asked, a summary, and a concern check.

I'll keep you informed.' NAME THE CONCERN, DO NOT CONFRONT, AND FOLLOW THE MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY.

'HE BRUISES EASILY': 'WHERE, AND HOW OFTEN? Any NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, or FAMILY BLEEDING PROBLEMS? I'll examine his skin all over and CHECK A BLOOD COUNT.' / A DEFORMITY ON THE FILM — AN ANGULATED GREENSTICK: 'THIS ONE HAS BENT AND CRACKED ON ONE SIDE; IT NEEDS TO BE STRAIGHTENED UNDER SEDATION AND PUT IN A PLASTER BY THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY.' / IF MANAGEMENT IS ASKED: 'pain relief, a REMOVABLE SPLINT OR A HALF-PLASTER on the back of the arm for about THREE WEEKS, GP review, NO REPEAT X-RAY. Back sooner for pain, swelling, or PALE OR NUMB FINGERS.' Numbers: HEALS 3 WEEKS — splint or backslab 3 weeks — SPORT AT 6 WEEKS — NO REPEAT FILM — capillary refill under 2 seconds — paracetamol 15 mg/kg, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg — SKELETAL SURVEY IF UNDER 2 — CARL 13 14 78. VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: James, 36, diesel mechanic; wife Sarah is a teacher; OLIVER HAS TWO SISTERS, 7 AND 2. Oliver is fit, TALL, fully immunised, no medicines, no allergies, kindy three days a week, GRANDPARENTS BABYSIT. FOUR MONTHS AGO he fell off a slide at the park WITH SARAH and had a forearm cast for a few weeks. LAST NIGHT AT 7 PM you saw him TRIP ON THE RUG CHASING HIS SISTER and land PALM-DOWN, WRIST BENT BACK, ONTO FLOORBOARDS; you iced it, he slept, and this morning he would not use the hand.

REGISTER: STANDING AND ANXIOUS AT THE START, SITTING WHEN REASSURED. MILDLY DEFENSIVE WHEN ASKED ABOUT HOME — 'WHY ALL THE QUESTIONS?' — and settling if the doctor explains it is routine for every family. GUILTY NEAR THE END: 'IS IT OUR FAULT?' HIDDEN AGENDA: YOU ARE WORRIED THE TWO FRACTURES MEAN HIS BONES ARE WEAK, BECAUSE YOUR BROTHER HAS 'BRITTLE BONES' — BUT YOU ONLY MENTION THE BROTHER IF ASKED ABOUT FAMILY BONE PROBLEMS, AND IF NEVER ASKED BY 5:00 YOU ASK 'IS HIS BONE WEAK?' AT THE X-RAY. At the film, say 'THE NURSE THOUGHT IT LOOKED NORMAL.' If pushed once more on stresses, add 'money's a bit tight, like everyone.' VERSION C: first say he fell off the couch, LATER SAY HE TRIPPED IN THE YARD; it happened TWO DAYS AGO; Sarah is away and uncontactable; BECOME QUIET AND DEFENSIVE RATHER THAN ANGRY.

Mark them against: reassured you and signposted the plan; MECHANISM IN DETAIL — how he fell, landing, wrist position, height, surface, witnessed, time, delay; HEAD INJURY, LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS, VOMITING; other injuries, bruises, limping; site, severity, radiation, DEFORMITY, movement, COLOUR, PINS AND NEEDLES; THE PREVIOUS FRACTURE EXPLORED IN DETAIL; home, who lives there, siblings, stresses, CHILDCARE, OTHER CARERS, framed as routine; GROWTH AND BONE PAIN, AND ASKED ABOUT FAMILY BONE PROBLEMS — FINDING THE BROTHER; the X-ray with THREE COLOURS, NORMAL STRUCTURES FIRST, THEN THE BULGE ON BOTH VIEWS, NAMED A BUCKLE FRACTURE, AND NEVER CALLED NORMAL OR A STRESS FRACTURE; explained a buckle in plain words and that it heals in three weeks; the examination explained in layman's terms in under two minutes; and a summary with a concern check.
fails: ★ A one-line fall instead of a step-by-step mechanism — the more questions about the injury, the happier the examiner
★ Asking about the head injury as an afterthought, or not at all — it outranks the wrist and comes before the pain questions
Stopping at 'we're a happy family' instead of continuing through childcare, other carers, growth and bone pain
Calling the film normal, or calling it a stress fracture — and the father will quote the nurse's 'it looked fine' back at you

A selective SOCRATES with no deformity, colour or pins-and-needles questions; never asking about family bone problems, so the brother with brittle bones is never found; listing radial, median and ulnar nerves to a parent; and spending the station on management, which is not a task

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND MANAGEMENT — regional GP, AND THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN TO YOU. DO NOT SPEND FOUR MINUTES RE-DERIVING IT. TWO BLOCKS ARE THE PASS MARK: THE IMMUNE STATE, WHICH DECIDES THE ANTIVIRAL, AND THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN — BRAIN, EYE, CHEST, SKIN. SAY THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION AND ITS REASON IN ONE SENTENCE: 'we could give aciclovir' WITHOUT A DECISION HAS NOT ANSWERED THE TASK. The mother wants a prescription in the first thirty seconds — acknowledge, promise pain relief, and KEEP THE HISTORY MOVING. And COUNT THE WEES: two today is the measurable red flag you hand back to her.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. LIAM, 5 YEARS, brought by his mother MARY. He has presented with LESIONS IN THE MOUTH AND HAS BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS. A PHOTOGRAPH OF THE MOUTH IS PROVIDED.

Take A FURTHER RELEVANT HISTORY from the mother (about 4 minutes), ASK THE EXAMINER FOR THE RELEVANT PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDINGS, then EXPLAIN YOUR MANAGEMENT. 8 minutes. VERSION B: the same child but ON MAINTENANCE PREDNISOLONE for nephrotic syndrome, or with TYPE 1 DIABETES, or post-chemotherapy. VERSION C: a VESICLE ON THE THUMB if you ask about rash elsewhere.

time: ASK FOR THE VITALS BEFORE YOU START, acknowledge her exhaustion, AND PROMISE PAIN RELIEF · THE LESIONS: when first noticed, FIRST TIME, getting worse, WHERE EXACTLY · gums, tongue, lips, the skin around the mouth, WERE THERE BLISTERS FIRST, any pus or discharge, painful or itchy · GENERAL FEATURES AND SOURCE: fever and whether anything helped, tired or flat, ANY RASH ANYWHERE ELSE · ON HIS HANDS OR FINGERS, lumps in the neck, and ANYONE AT HOME OR SCHOOL WITH COLD SORES · THEN THE IMMUNE BLOCK, WHICH IS THE PASS MARK, PREFACED SO IT MAKES SENSE: 'some questions about his general health, BECAUSE THEY CHANGE HOW I TREAT THIS' · any long-term medical conditions, DOES HE GET INFECTIONS MORE OFTEN OR TAKE LONGER TO GET OVER THEM, ANY REGULAR MEDICINES PARTICULARLY STEROIDS LIKE PREDNISOLONE OR ANYTHING FOR HIS IMMUNE SYSTEM, growth and weight, AND ANY DIABETES, KIDNEY OR BLOOD PROBLEMS · THEN THE COMPLICATIONS BY NAME: BRAIN · headache, drowsy or hard to wake, vomiting, blurred vision, unusual behaviour, FITS; EYE · RED EYE, SPOTS ON THE EYELIDS, discharge, PHOTOPHOBIA; CHEST · cough or fast breathing; SKIN · ECZEMA AND WHETHER IT IS FLARING · THEN HYDRATION: DROOLING, HOW MUCH IS HE DRINKING COMPARED WITH NORMAL, HOW MANY WEES TODAY, bowels, alert and playing or flat · then BINDSMA and home · then the examination in order, and management with THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION STATED.

As in the photograph — and when the examiner says 'AS YOU CAN SEE', NAME WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR ANYWAY — discharge, extent, tonsils — then move on
SEVERAL TENDER ENLARGED NODES BOTH SIDES
THREE DAYS, first time, gums, inside the lips, a few on the tongue and CRUSTY BITS ON THE LIP — LITTLE BLISTERS ON THE LIP FIRST, then they popped — no pus, PAINFUL
NO conditions, no recurrent infections, NO MEDICINES, growing fine — which is exactly why he does NOT get an antiviral
ON PREDNISOLONE FOR NEPHROTIC SYNDROME, or TYPE 1 DIABETES, or FINISHED CHEMOTHERAPY LAST YEAR — given only if you ask about conditions or medicines
If she mentions a puffer, ASK WHETHER IT IS A STEROID PREVENTER AND WHETHER HE HAS HAD ORAL STEROID COURSES — INHALED STEROIDS ALONE DO NOT MAKE HIM IMMUNOCOMPROMISED
ALL NEGATIVE — tired but wakes easily, no vomiting or fits, EYES FINE, no cough, NO ECZEMA
DROOLING — DRINKING ABOUT HALF OF NORMAL, IN SMALL SIPS OF JUICE — AND TWO WEES TODAY. She is frightened about this and volunteers it at 3:30 if you have not asked
A VESICLE ON THE THUMB — a herpetic whitlow, from sucking it — found only if you ask about rash on the hands or fingers

back.dx: HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS in an IMMUNOCOMPETENT child with MILD DEHYDRATION — supportive care, NO ANTIVIRALS, AND THE REASON SAID ALOUD. EXPLAIN IT: 'Liam has HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS: A VIRAL INFECTION, THE HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS, in his mouth, on his gums and tongue and around his lips. It's VERY COMMON IN YOUNG CHILDREN, THIS FIRST EPISODE IS ALWAYS THE WORST, and it RUNS ITS COURSE OVER ABOUT ONE TO TWO WEEKS. ANTIBIOTICS DON'T WORK ON VIRUSES. THE TREATMENT IS PAIN RELIEF SO THAT HE CAN DRINK.' THE PAIN LADDER, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT: PARACETAMOL every four to six hours, NO MORE THAN FOUR TIMES A DAY; IBUPROFEN with food; and A NUMBING GEL, LIGNOCAINE, DABBED ON THE SORES WITH A COTTON BUD ABOUT TEN MINUTES BEFORE HE DRINKS OR EATS. THEN FLUIDS: SMALL SIPS OFTEN, cool drinks, ICY POLES, oral rehydration like Hydralyte, WATER OR MILK RATHER THAN JUICE, WHICH STINGS. THEN THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE WITH ITS REASON: 'there IS an antiviral, BUT BECAUSE LIAM HAS NO CONDITION AND NO MEDICINE THAT WEAKENS HIS IMMUNE SYSTEM, HE DOESN'T NEED IT; HIS OWN IMMUNE SYSTEM WILL CLEAR THIS, and the tablets make little difference in a healthy child. IF HE WERE ON STEROIDS OR HAD DIABETES, I'D GIVE IT.' THEN EXCLUSION AND HYGIENE: HOME FROM SCHOOL UNTIL THE SORES HAVE DRIED, wash hands, NO SHARING CUPS, AND NO KISSING THE BABY. REVIEW IN A DAY OR TWO. THE RED FLAGS, INCLUDING A MEASURABLE URINE-BASED ONE: 'come straight back or go to the emergency department if he becomes DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE, complains of HEADACHE, VOMITS, HAS A FIT, gets A RED OR SORE EYE OR BLISTERS ON THE EYELID, or if he STOPS DRINKING OR HAS NO WEE FOR EIGHT HOURS. COUNT THE WEES: FEWER THAN THREE A DAY, or none for eight hours, or too drowsy to drink — BRING HIM STRAIGHT IN AND WE'LL GIVE FLUIDS THROUGH A TUBE OR A DRIP.' Then summarise and ask what worries her most. VERSION B — PREDNISOLONE OR ANOTHER IMMUNOCOMPROMISING CONDITION: 'BECAUSE LIAM IS ON PREDNISOLONE HIS IMMUNE SYSTEM IS WEAKER, SO THIS INFECTION CAN SPREAD FURTHER AND LAST LONGER. I'm going to START AN ANTIVIRAL, ACICLOVIR, FIVE TIMES A DAY FOR A WEEK, and I'll SPEAK TO THE CHILDREN'S TEAM TODAY. IF HE CAN'T KEEP FLUIDS DOWN HE NEEDS TO COME IN.' VERSION C — THE WHITLOW: 'THE BLISTER ON HIS THUMB IS THE SAME VIRUS, SPREAD FROM HIS MOUTH WHEN HE SUCKS IT. It's painful BUT IT HEALS BY ITSELF; WE DON'T CUT IT. Keep it covered and wash hands, SO IT DOESN'T SPREAD TO HIS EYES.' THE RED EYE: 'a red, sore eye with this infection CAN BE THE VIRUS ON THE SURFACE OF THE EYE. That needs AN EYE SPECIALIST TODAY, with A DYE TEST AND ANTIVIRAL DROPS. PLEASE DON'T USE ANY LEFTOVER EYE DROPS AT HOME.' DROWSY AND VOMITING: 'drowsiness and vomiting with this infection CAN MEAN THE VIRUS HAS REACHED THE BRAIN. I'M STOPPING HERE and arranging the emergency department now; he'll need A DRIP AND AN ANTIVIRAL THROUGH THE VEIN.'
plan: VITALS, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE AND PROMISE: 'Examiner, may I have Liam's vital signs?' → 38.4, HR 118. Then: 'I've read that Liam has a herpes infection in his mouth AND I CAN SEE HOW SORE IT IS. I'd like to ask how he's been, examine him, and then go through the plan.' → 'he's screaming when he eats, he's not sleeping, and now he won't drink either. CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' → 'THAT SOUNDS MISERABLE FOR BOTH OF YOU, AND YES, THERE'S A LOT WE CAN DO FOR HIS PAIN. Let me ask a few things first.' (She wants a prescription now — acknowledge, promise, and keep moving. And do NOT spend the four minutes re-deriving a diagnosis you were given.)

THE LESIONS: 'when did you first notice the sores? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME? Getting worse? WHERE EXACTLY — gums, tongue, lips, the skin around the mouth? WERE THERE BLISTERS FIRST? Any pus or discharge? Painful, or itchy?'

GENERAL FEATURES AND SOURCE: 'any fever or chills? Did you give anything, and did it help? Is he tired or flat? ANY RASH ANYWHERE ELSE, ON HIS HANDS OR FINGERS? Any lumps in his neck? Anyone at home or at school with cold sores or something similar?' (A NEGATIVE CONTACT HISTORY IS NORMAL — most sources shed without symptoms — so do NOT chase the source at the cost of the immune block.)

THE IMMUNE BLOCK — THE PASS MARK: 'now some questions about his general health, BECAUSE THEY CHANGE HOW I TREAT THIS. Does he have ANY LONG-TERM MEDICAL CONDITIONS? Does he GET INFECTIONS MORE OFTEN THAN OTHER CHILDREN, OR TAKE A LONG TIME TO GET OVER THEM? IS HE ON ANY REGULAR MEDICINES, PARTICULARLY STEROIDS LIKE PREDNISOLONE, OR ANYTHING FOR HIS IMMUNE SYSTEM? Any concerns about his growth or weight? ANY DIABETES, KIDNEY OR BLOOD PROBLEMS?'

THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN, BY SYSTEM AND BY NAME: 'HIS BRAIN: any headache? Is he DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE? Vomiting? Blurred vision or unusual behaviour? ANY FITS? HIS EYES: any RED EYE? SPOTS ON THE EYELIDS? Discharge? DOES LIGHT BOTHER HIM? HIS CHEST: any cough or fast breathing? HIS SKIN: DOES HE HAVE ECZEMA, AND IS IT FLARING?'

HYDRATION, WITH NUMBERS: 'is he DROOLING? HOW MUCH IS HE DRINKING COMPARED TO NORMAL? HOW MANY WEES TODAY? Bowels? Alert and playing, or flat?' → drooling, half of normal in small sips of juice, TWO WEES TODAY. (JUICE STINGS — swap to water, milk, oral rehydration or icy poles. And TWO WEES IN A DAY IS YOUR MEASURABLE MARKER TO HAND BACK TO HER AS A RED FLAG.) Then birth and development, immunisations, allergies, home and school.

THE EXAMINATION, IN ORDER: 'general appearance — is he alert, and how does he look? HYDRATION — mucous membranes, tears, skin turgor, CAPILLARY REFILL? Growth chart? MOUTH — site of the ulcers, any blisters, any discharge, tonsils? CERVICAL LYMPH NODES? EYES — conjunctival redness, LID VESICLES, discharge, visual acuity, fundi? NEUROLOGICAL — conscious level, NECK STIFFNESS, cranial nerves, limbs, gait? CHEST — air entry, added sounds? SKIN AND HANDS — ANY VESICLES OR ECZEMA?' (Do not lead with a urine dipstick or blood sugar; if you mention ketones, do it last.)

MANAGEMENT: the virus explained, ANTIBIOTICS DON'T WORK, the pain ladder with LIGNOCAINE GEL TEN MINUTES BEFORE DRINKS, and fluids in small sips WITHOUT JUICE (see dx) → 'SO NOTHING TO MAKE IT GO AWAY?'

THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE WITH ITS REASON, THEN EXCLUSION, REVIEW AND THE RED FLAGS (see dx) → 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S GETTING DEHYDRATED?' → COUNT THE WEES. Then summarise and ask what worries her most. ('We could give aciclovir' with no decision has not answered the task.)

pefe: Role-player: Mary, 34, WORKS IN THE LOCAL PHARMACY, so she knows Panadol and WANTS 'SOMETHING STRONGER'. Liam is her only child, in reception. Normal birth, fully immunised, no allergies, NO MEDICAL CONDITIONS, NO MEDICINES (VERSION B: ON PREDNISOLONE FOR NEPHROTIC SYNDROME — SAY IT ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT MEDICINES OR CONDITIONS). Her husband works away on a mine roster and SHE HAS HAD THREE NIGHTS WITHOUT SLEEP. THE STORY: three days of sores on the gums, inside the lips, a few on the tongue and crusty bits on the lip, WITH LITTLE BLISTERS FIRST; no pus; painful enough that he screams; FEVER UP TO 39 with Panadol helping for a few hours; flat but played a bit this morning; no other rash; NECK LUMPY BOTH SIDES; no known cold-sore contacts.

REGISTER: FRAYED AND A LITTLE SHARP AT THE START — 'CAN'T YOU JUST GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' — softening when the doctor promises to deal with the pain, and TEARFUL ONCE when asked what worries her most. HIDDEN AGENDA: SHE IS FRIGHTENED HE IS DEHYDRATED BECAUSE HE HAS ONLY DONE TWO WEES TODAY, BUT SHE DOES NOT SAY THE NUMBER UNLESS ASKED ABOUT WEES OR DRINKING — AND IF NOT ASKED BY 3:30 SHE VOLUNTEERS 'HE'S HARDLY WEED TODAY'. UNDERLYING BELIEF: that ANTIBIOTICS would fix it faster — push once, then accept a clear explanation. Ask 'ISN'T THERE A TABLET TO KILL IT?' after the antibiotic answer, and 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S DEHYDRATED?' if no urine-based red flag has been given.

Mark them against: ASKED THE EXAMINER FOR VITALS and acknowledged your exhaustion; characterised the lesions — site, blisters, discharge, pain; fever, tiredness, RASH ELSEWHERE, neck lumps, contacts; THE IMMUNE STATE — conditions, recurrent infections, MEDICINES OR STEROIDS, which is the pass mark; COMPLICATIONS BY NAME — BRAIN, EYE, CHEST, SKIN; drooling, drinking, WEES, bowels, alertness, and BINDSMA; examination in order — general and hydration, mouth, nodes, eyes, neurology, chest, skin; explained A VIRUS, NO ANTIBIOTICS, FIRST EPISODE WORST, 1-2 WEEKS; paracetamol, ibuprofen, LIGNOCAINE GEL BEFORE DRINKS, cool fluids, small sips, ORS, NO JUICE; STATED THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION WITH THE REASON; exclusion until dry, hygiene and a review time; and RED FLAGS INCLUDING A URINE-BASED ONE, a summary, and asking what worries you most.
fails: ★ Saying 'we could give aciclovir' without making a decision — the antiviral decision and its reason belong in one sentence
★ Skipping the immune block, which is the pass mark and the only thing that changes the treatment
Never screening the complications by name — brain, eye, chest, skin
Spending the four minutes re-deriving a diagnosis you were handed in the stem

Chasing the cold-sore contact at the cost of the immune block, when a negative contact history is normal; letting her keep offering juice, which stings; giving no measurable dehydration marker when two wees a day is sitting there; and treating an inhaled steroid preventer as immunocompromise without asking about oral courses

Take a history from the mother, RECEIVE THE EXAMINATION FINDINGS ON A CARD, then explain the diagnosis and management. 8 minutes. VARIANT: THE CARD SHOWS BLISTERS AND INNER-THIGH BRUISING.

back.dx: VULVOVAGINITIS — NON-SPECIFIC VULVAL ERYTHEMA — IN A WELL, HAPPY 4-YEAR-OLD, WITH NO FEATURE OF ABUSE ON HISTORY OR EXAMINATION. EXPLAIN IT: 'Jenny, I COMPLETELY UNDERSTAND WHY YOU WERE WORRIED. Having gone through everything with you and examined Mia, I believe the likely cause is A CONDITION CALLED VULVOVAGINITIS — AN INFLAMMATION OF THE SKIN OF THE PRIVATE PARTS. It's VERY COMMON IN YOUNG GIRLS, because THE SKIN THERE IS THIN AND SENSITIVE AND GETS IRRITATED EASILY by moisture, urine, soaps and bubble bath.' THEN GIVE THE REASONING BEFORE SHE ASKS FOR IT — this is a required item: 'LET ME TELL YOU WHY I DON'T THINK THIS IS ABUSE. THE SKIN IS SIMPLY RED — THERE IS NO BRUISING, NO TEARS, NO DISCHARGE, NO BLISTERS OR SORES, AND THOSE ARE THE THINGS I SPECIFICALLY LOOK FOR. SHE'S HAPPY, SLEEPING WELL AND KEEN TO SEE HER DAD. And THE PATTERN FITS THE DAILY BUBBLE BATH AND THE LEGGINGS. I did consider other skin irritations and infections, AND I FOUND NOTHING ELSE.' THE MANAGEMENT, AND IN MILD CASES NO TESTS ARE NEEDED: keep the area CLEAN AND DRY; WIPE FRONT TO BACK; wash with WATER OR A SOAP-FREE CLEANSER; STOP THE BUBBLE BATH AND ANY SCENTED WIPES; ABOUT HALF A CUP OF WHITE VINEGAR IN A SHALLOW BATH FOR TEN MINUTES; LOOSE COTTON UNDERWEAR, NO LEGGINGS FOR NOW, AND NOTHING AT NIGHT; a mild moisturiser and A ZINC BARRIER CREAM to the red skin; and if she is itchy or it is not settling, A THIN LAYER OF ONE-PERCENT HYDROCORTISONE TWICE A DAY FOR ABOUT A WEEK. SORT OUT THE CONSTIPATION. REVIEW IN ONE TO TWO WEEKS. SAFETY-NET: 'if anything changes — BRUISING, DISCHARGE, BLEEDING, OR A CHANGE IN HOW SHE'S BEHAVING — I want to see her straight away.' AND WHEN SHE SAYS 'HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?' — RE-EXPLAIN ONCE, THEN OFFER THE PATHWAY, NEVER ARGUE: 'I CAN'T GIVE YOU A GUARANTEE, but I'VE LOOKED SPECIFICALLY FOR EVERY SIGN OF ABUSE AND FOUND NONE, and she's happy in herself. IF YOU STILL HAVE CONCERNS, WE CAN INVOLVE THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM at the Women's and Children's FOR A MORE COMPLETE ASSESSMENT. I EXPECT THEY'LL SAY THE SAME, BUT I'D RATHER YOU FELT SURE. WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO MAKE THAT CALL?' THE VARIANT — THE CARD SHOWS BLISTERS AND INNER-THIGH BRUISING: 'Jenny, WHAT I FOUND ON EXAMINATION CONCERNS ME. THERE ARE BLISTERS AND BRUISING, AND I'M NOT ABLE TO CALL THIS A SIMPLE SKIN IRRITATION. I NEED TO INVOLVE THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM at the Women's and Children's TODAY so Mia is properly assessed and kept safe. I AM REQUIRED TO REPORT THIS, AND I WILL SUPPORT YOU THROUGH EVERY STEP. PLEASE DON'T QUESTION MIA ABOUT IT YOURSELF — THE TEAM ARE TRAINED TO DO THAT GENTLY.' Notify CARL on 13 14 78, involve the Women's and Children's child protection service, DOCUMENT VERBATIM, and DO NOT PERFORM A FORENSIC EXAMINATION IN GENERAL PRACTICE.
plan: OPEN SLOWLY — THERE IS A COMMUNICATION MARK AND YOU EARN IT IN THIRTY SECONDS: 'you're Mia's mum — Jenny? How can I help you today?' → the opening line about abuse. → 'I UNDERSTAND HOW CONCERNING THIS IS, JENNY. LET ME ASK YOU A FEW QUESTIONS TO GET TO THE BOTTOM OF IT, AND I PROMISE I'LL PROVIDE THE BEST CARE FOR YOU AND MIA. CAN YOU TELL ME WHY YOU SUSPECT SEXUAL ABUSE? HAS THERE BEEN ANY RECENT UNUSUAL INCIDENT, OR HAS SHE SAID ANYTHING?' → just the rash, and she was at her father's last week; no incident, no disclosure. (Rushing the acknowledgement is the first trap — and if you dismiss it early with 'it's just a rash', she goes cold.)

HOME, AND EACH ADULT GETS HIS OWN QUESTIONS: 'how are things at home? Who do you live with?' → divorced, living with her boyfriend Dave for six months. Then THE BOYFRIEND: 'how is your relationship with Dave? Is he supportive? DO YOU HAVE ANY CONCERNS ABOUT HIM WITH MIA — ANYTHING THAT HAS MADE YOU UNEASY?' Then THE FATHER: 'and Mia's father — how is your relationship with him? Does she see him — how often, WHO ELSE IS THERE? How is her relationship with him — IS SHE KEEN TO GO?' Then: 'any stressors at home? Money worries? DO YOU, YOUR BOYFRIEND OR HER FATHER DRINK HEAVILY OR USE DRUGS? HOW HAS YOUR MOOD BEEN?' (Stopping after 'who do you live with' loses TWO required items — and the role-player is briefed to say later 'YOU DIDN'T REALLY ASK ABOUT DAVE'.)

THE RASH: 'where exactly is the rash? IS IT RED SKIN, OR DOES IT LOOK LIKE A BRUISE? Any discharge? Itchy? Sore? Fever?' → around the outside, both sides, red not a bruise, no discharge, she scratches and it stings, no fever.

THE DIRECT ABUSE-SIGN QUESTIONS, ASKED AS A NAMED SET — a required item: 'some specific things I always check. HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY BRUISES ON HER PRIVATE PARTS OR ANYWHERE ELSE? ANY ULCERS, BLISTERS OR SORES? ANY YELLOWISH SMELLY DISCHARGE? ANY BLEEDING?' → all negative.

THE DERMATITIS HISTORY — where the actual diagnosis is: 'does it burn when she passes urine? Any constipation? Tight underwear, leggings, tights? NEW SOAPS, BODY WASH, BUBBLE BATH, WIPES, MOISTURISER? Swimming? WHO WIPES AFTER THE TOILET, AND WHICH WAY? Eczema in her or the family? Itchy and restless at night?' → cries when she wees, a bit constipated, LEGGINGS MOST DAYS, BUBBLE BATH EVERY NIGHT, weekly swimming, wipes herself with direction unknown, mother has eczema. (DYSURIA HERE IS NOT A UTI — IT IS SKIN, AND SAY SO.)

THE CHILD'S BEHAVIOUR — AND DO NOT SKIP IT BECAUSE THE SOCIAL ANSWERS WERE REASSURING, BECAUSE THE SYMPTOMS OF ABUSE ARE BEHAVIOURAL: 'how is she behaving these days? Withdrawn, clingy, angry? Does she seem sad? Sleeping well — NIGHTMARES, WETTING THE BED AGAIN? ANY NEW FEARS OF A PERSON OR PLACE, OR PLAY THAT SEEMS SEXUAL FOR HER AGE? DOES SHE LOOK FORWARD TO SEEING HER FATHER? How is kindy?' Then alert, eating, drinking, immunisations, growth and development.

THE CARD — AND USE IT AS IT IS: well, happy child, NON-SPECIFIC VULVAL ERYTHEMA, no discharge, vesicles, ulcers, bruising, tears or bleeding, anal region normal, no bruises elsewhere. (Asking to examine internally, or to swab 'for STIs to be safe', is the trap.)

EXPLAIN VULVOVAGINITIS, THEN GIVE THE REASONING BEFORE SHE ASKS FOR IT (see dx) → 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE IT'S NOT ABUSE?' → re-explain once. → 'I'M STILL WORRIED, DOCTOR.' → OFFER THE CHILD PROTECTION PATHWAY CALMLY. (Arguing, or refusing the pathway, is the fail — re-explain once, then offer it.)

THE HYGIENE PLAN AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx): no tests in mild cases, front to back, soap-free cleanser, STOP THE BUBBLE BATH, the vinegar bath, cotton underwear and no leggings, barrier cream, hydrocortisone if itchy, the constipation, review in one to two weeks, and 'if anything changes — bruising, discharge, bleeding, OR A CHANGE IN HOW SHE'S BEHAVING — I want to see her straight away.'

You have lived with your boyfriend DAVE, A FARM WORKER, FOR SIX MONTHS. OPENING LINE: 'SHE HAS A RASH IN HER PRIVATE PARTS AND I'M WORRIED SHE'S BEEN SEXUALLY ABUSED.' WHY: ONLY THE RASH, plus the fact she was at Ben's last week — NO INCIDENT, NO DISCLOSURE.

HIDDEN DYNAMICS: YOU HAVE NO SPECIFIC CONCERN ABOUT DAVE OR BEN — REVEAL THAT ONLY WHEN ASKED DIRECTLY ABOUT EACH OF THEM. ONCE after the explanation, and 'I'M STILL WORRIED' ONCE MORE; ACCEPT IF THE REASONING IS CLEAR AND THE CHILD PROTECTION OPTION IS OFFERED. BECOME COLD IF DISMISSED EARLY WITH 'IT'S JUST A RASH'. back.dx: BALANITIS — INFLAMMATION OF THE SKIN AT THE TIP OF THE PENIS AND THE FORESKIN, WITH A NON-RETRACTILE FORESKIN THAT IS NORMAL FOR AGE AND A NEGATIVE DIPSTICK. EXPLAIN IT: 'Liam has a condition called BALANITIS. In plain words, IT'S INFLAMMATION OF THE SKIN AT THE TIP OF THE PENIS AND THE FORESKIN. THAT SKIN IS THIN AND SENSITIVE, AND UNDER A NAPPY IT SITS IN MOISTURE AND URINE; BUBBLE BATH AND WIPES IRRITATE IT FURTHER, AND SOMETIMES A YEAST JOINS IN. IT'S THE BOY'S VERSION OF NAPPY RASH, AND VERY COMMON.' THEN KILL THE UTI IDEA EXPLICITLY: 'IT HURTS WHEN HE WEES BECAUSE URINE STINGS THE IRRITATED SKIN — IT DOESN'T MEAN HE HAS A URINE INFECTION, AND HIS DIPSTICK IS CLEAR.' THEN THE FORESKIN: 'HIS FORESKIN NOT PULLING BACK IS NORMAL AT HIS AGE — PLEASE DON'T FORCE IT; IT LOOSENS BY ITSELF OVER THE NEXT FEW YEARS.' MANAGEMENT, CONSERVATIVE AND SPECIFIC: KEEP IT CLEAN AND DRY — CHANGE NAPPIES OFTEN, NAPPY-FREE TIME, WASH WITH WATER OR A SOAP-FREE CLEANSER, AND STOP THE BUBBLE BATH AND SCENTED WIPES; A WARM SALT-WATER BATH ONCE OR TWICE A DAY, THEN PAT DRY; A MILD STEROID CREAM WITH AN ANTIFUNGAL — HYDROZOLE FROM THE PHARMACY — A THIN LAYER TWO OR THREE TIMES A DAY FOR UP TO A WEEK; AND PARACETAMOL IF HE'S SORE. REVIEW IN THREE TO FIVE DAYS. THE RED-FLAG SAFETY-NET, WHICH IS A REQUIRED ITEM: 'COME BACK STRAIGHT AWAY IF HE CAN'T PASS URINE, IF THE TIP SWELLS OR GOES DARK, IF THE REDNESS SPREADS UP THE SHAFT WITH FEVER, OR IF HE BECOMES UNWELL.' THE THREE QUESTIONS HE WILL ASK: 'IS IT BECAUSE I PULLED IT BACK?' → 'THAT MAY HAVE ADDED A LITTLE IRRITATION, BUT THIS HAPPENS IN BOYS WHO'VE NEVER BEEN TOUCHED — PLEASE JUST DON'T FORCE IT AGAIN.' 'DOES HE NEED ANTIBIOTICS?' → 'NO — ANTIBIOTICS DON'T HELP SKIN INFLAMMATION; THE CREAM DOES.' 'SHOULD HE BE CIRCUMCISED?' → 'NO. CIRCUMCISION IS ONLY CONSIDERED FOR REPEATED PROBLEMS OR A SCARRED, TIGHT FORESKIN THAT DOESN'T RESPOND TO CREAM.' VARIANTS: FEBRILE AT 38.8 WITH REDNESS ONTO THE SHAFT, WARMTH AND PUS AT THE MEATUS — 'THIS IS MORE THAN BALANITIS — A CELLULITIS, AND I MUST EXCLUDE A URINE INFECTION. URINE CULTURE FIRST, ORAL ANTIBIOTICS TODAY, REVIEW IN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS; DROWSY, VOMITING OR NOT IMPROVING MEANS THE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL.' VERIFY THE FORESKIN STUCK BACK WITH A PURPLE TIP — 'THAT'S PARAPHIMOSIS AND IT'S URGENT — THE FORESKIN IS ACTING LIKE A TIGHT RING AND CUTTING OFF THE BLOOD SUPPLY. I'LL GIVE HIM PAIN RELIEF AND TRY TO REDUCE IT NOW; IF I CAN'T, HE GOES TO THE CHILDREN'S SURGEONS TODAY.' THE CHANGED SOCIAL HISTORY — a new partner, weekends with his mother, BEDWETTING AGAIN AND NIGHTMARES: go deeper on supervision, WHO BATHES HIM, bruising and disclosures, then 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME. I'D LIKE ADVICE FROM THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM AT THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S — A ROUTINE STEP TO MAKE SURE LIAM IS SAFE.'
plan: OPEN AND ADDRESS THE CONCERN, THEN SITE AND MORPHOLOGY BOTH: 'you're Liam's dad? I can see you're concerned about his penis — TELL ME MORE... I understand the worry. Let me ask a few questions, then examine him, then explain. WHERE EXACTLY IS THE REDNESS — TIP, FORESKIN, SHAFT, OR THE GROIN CREASES? JUST RED SKIN, OR BLISTERS, SPOTS OR SORES? Painful? Itchy? ANY DISCHARGE FROM THE TIP? Other rashes anywhere?' (Site and morphology are what separate dermatitis from herpes and cellulitis — ASK BOTH.)

TIMING, TRIGGERS AND DERMATITIS RISK FACTORS: 'when did you first notice it? First time? Getting worse? Anything making it better or worse — BATHS, BUBBLE BATH, MOISTURISER? STILL IN NAPPIES? Any NEW SOAP, BODY WASH, WIPES? ECZEMA IN HIM OR THE FAMILY? AND HAS ANYONE BEEN PULLING THE FORESKIN BACK TO CLEAN IT?' → worse after the bubble bath, still in nappies, new wipes last month, and 'I TRIED TO PULL IT BACK ONCE TO CLEAN UNDERNEATH AND HE SCREAMED, SO I STOPPED.'

INFECTION, AND THE REAL UTI QUESTIONS — a required item: 'any fever or chills? Drowsy or off his food? DOES IT HURT WHEN HE PASSES URINE?' → 'yes — he cries when he wees. IS IT A URINE INFECTION?' → SAY IT OUT LOUD: 'IT CAN BE, BUT IRRITATED SKIN AT THE TIP STINGS WHENEVER URINE TOUCHES IT, SO I'LL CHECK PROPERLY.' Then: 'ANY DIFFICULTY PASSING URINE — STRAINING, DRIBBLING, A POOR STREAM, OR THE FORESKIN BALLOONING? FOUL-SMELLING URINE? VOMITING?' → good stream, no smell, no vomiting. (Answering 'yes, a urine infection' and reaching for antibiotics is the fail the father is briefed to mark.)

THE FORESKIN QUESTION, ASKED AS ROUTINE — the second required item: 'ONE QUESTION I ASK EVERY DAD: ARE YOU ABLE TO GENTLY PULL HIS FORESKIN BACK, AND HAS IT EVER GOT STUCK?' → 'it doesn't really go back — IT NEVER HAS. NEVER STUCK.'

THE SOCIAL AND ABUSE SCREEN, FRAMED AS ROUTINE: 'some routine questions I ask FOR EVERY CHILD WITH A PROBLEM IN THIS AREA. How are things at home? Who lives with you? Any stressors? ANY BRUISES ON HIS PRIVATE PARTS OR ELSEWHERE? ANY CHANGE IN HIS BEHAVIOUR — SAD, WITHDRAWN, NOT SLEEPING, NEW FEARS? How are things at childcare?' Then well-child and BINDSMA: alert and active, eating, drinking, wet nappies, term, immunisations, development and toilet training, medicines, allergies.

CONSENT AND CHAPERONE, THEN THE EXAMINATION REQUEST WITH RETRACTABILITY AND THE DIPSTICK NAMED: 'WITH DAD'S CONSENT AND A CHAPERONE PRESENT, I'd examine Liam. General appearance — alert or drowsy, hydration, any other rash? Temperature and heart rate? Inspecting the penis: WHERE IS THE REDNESS — foreskin, glans, shaft, groin? Blisters, ulcers, discharge, bruising, swelling? On palpation — warm, tender, fluctuant? INGUINAL LYMPH NODES? IS THE FORESKIN RETRACTABLE, WITHOUT FORCING, AND IS THERE ANY SCARRING OR A TRAPPED RING? Scrotum and testes? AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' (Forgetting consent and chaperone, or forgetting retractability, are the two traps here.)
EXPLAIN BALANITIS IN PLAIN WORDS, KILL THE UTI IDEA WITH THE DIPSTICK, AND SAY THE FORESKIN IS NORMAL FOR AGE (see dx) → 'IS IT BECAUSE I PULLED IT BACK?' → answer it without blame.

back.dx: VERSION A — ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA in a 9-month-old, and the station is about EXCLUDING THE OTHERS ALOUD. NAME IT WITH REASONS: 'your son has a condition called OTITIS MEDIA — AN INFECTION IN THE MIDDLE EAR, BEHIND THE EARDRUM. He has a fever, HE'S PULLING HIS EARS, and when I looked in, THE EARDRUM IS RED AND BULGING.' THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS BY GROUP, QUICKLY, WITH COLIC LAST — never a fifteen-item list: 'I was also thinking about OTHER INFECTIONS — a urine infection, a joint infection, a chest infection; PROBLEMS IN THE TUMMY — reflux, A HERNIA IN THE GROIN, INTUSSUSCEPTION, constipation; INJURIES, INCLUDING BLEEDING INSIDE THE HEAD; and things like A SCRATCH ON THE EYE OR A HAIR WRAPPED ROUND A TOE. NORMAL EXCESSIVE CRYING — COLIC — IS AT THE BOTTOM OF MY LIST, AND I ONLY CONSIDER IT ONCE EVERYTHING ELSE IS EXCLUDED.' MANAGEMENT, VERSION-SPECIFIC: OTITIS MEDIA — 'PAIN RELIEF FIRST, paracetamol or ibuprofen AT THE RIGHT DOSE FOR HIS WEIGHT. BECAUSE HE IS UNDER TWO AND QUITE UNWELL, I'll start AMOXICILLIN FOR FIVE DAYS. Most ear infections settle on their own; the antibiotic shortens it and reduces complications.' UTI — 'I'll collect A CLEAN URINE SAMPLE TO SEND TO THE LAB BEFORE STARTING THE ANTIBIOTIC, start ORAL CEFALEXIN today, and arrange A KIDNEY ULTRASOUND AFTER THIS FIRST INFECTION.' INTUSSUSCEPTION, HERNIA, SEPTIC JOINT OR NAI — 'THIS NEEDS THE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TODAY. I'm arranging transfer BY AMBULANCE, NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK, and I'll speak to the surgeons now.' THE SAFETY-NET, EVERY VERSION: 'come back or go to the emergency department straight away if he becomes DROWSY OR FLOPPY, has FEWER WET NAPPIES, VOMITS REPEATEDLY OR GREEN VOMIT, PASSES BLOOD, DEVELOPS A LUMP, STOPS MOVING AN ARM OR LEG, or you're worried. I'll see you in 48 HOURS. AND IF YOU EVER FEEL YOU CAN'T COPE, PUT HIM SAFELY IN THE COT AND WALK AWAY FOR A FEW MINUTES — and call the Parent Helpline or me.' AND NAME THE PATHWAY, BECAUSE 'REFER TO HOSPITAL' WITHOUT A ROUTE LOSES MARKS: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval, the Women's and Children's for surgery, CARL 13 14 78 for a child-protection notification. THE NAI VERSION, AFTER THE DISCLOSURE: 'THANK YOU FOR BEING HONEST WITH ME — THAT TOOK COURAGE. BABIES' HEADS ARE FRAGILE AND SHAKING CAN CAUSE BLEEDING AROUND THE BRAIN, so he needs to be CHECKED IN HOSPITAL TODAY — A SCAN AND X-RAYS. I AM REQUIRED BY LAW TO NOTIFY THE CHILD PROTECTION SERVICE; THAT IS NOT ABOUT PUNISHING YOU, IT'S ABOUT KEEPING HIM SAFE AND GETTING YOU SUPPORT. I'LL STAY WITH YOU THROUGH THIS.' To the examiner: ADMIT VIA MedSTAR, DO NOT DISCHARGE, DOCUMENT VERBATIM, NOTIFY CARL, involve the paediatric team and social work, AND SCREEN THE MOTHER FOR DEPRESSION AND DOMESTIC VIOLENCE. THE COLIC VERSION: 'everything is normal. This is INFANT COLIC — EXCESSIVE CRYING WITHOUT A CAUSE. It peaks around two months and settles by three to four. IT'S NOT YOUR FAULT.' Feed on demand, rocking, white noise or a carrier, the safe-cot line, the child health nurse, review in two weeks, sooner for fever, drowsiness, vomiting, fewer wet nappies or blood.
plan: VITALS AND TEMPERATURE, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE BEFORE THE FIRST CLOSED QUESTION: 'may I have the vital signs, INCLUDING THE TEMPERATURE?' Then: 'how can I help you today?' → 'he's been crying for four hours and NOTHING SETTLES HIM. I'm exhausted.' → 'I CAN HEAR HOW STRESSFUL AND OVERWHELMING THIS IS. Let me ask you some questions so we can find out what's going on, and then we'll make a plan together.' (Opening with 'babies cry at this age' signals premature closure in the first twenty seconds, and she answers 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK HIM?')

EXPLORE THE CRYING — INCLUDING THE QUESTION THAT OPENS EVERY DOOR: 'when did it start? IS IT ON AND OFF, OR CONTINUOUS? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse — feeding, nappy changes, picking him up? AND WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED TO CALM HIM DOWN?' (That last one is what produces GRIPE WATER in the colic version and 'WE SHOOK HIM' in the NAI version — ask it every time and LISTEN TO THE ANSWER.)

THE INFECTION BLOCK: 'any fever? PULLING HIS EARS? Discharge? Vomiting? Diarrhoea? Anyone else unwell? Travel? ANY RASH, REDNESS, OR A RED SWOLLEN JOINT? CRYING WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY? SMELLY URINE? Nappy rash? Runny nose, cough, DROOLING?' Then THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS: 'is he ALERT AND ACTIVE, OR DROWSY? Eating and drinking as usual? FEWER WET NAPPIES?'

THE GASTROINTESTINAL BLOCK: 'ANY LUMP OR SWELLING IN THE GROIN? DOES HE GO PALE WHEN HE CRIES? ANY RED, JELLY-LIKE STOOL? Recent viral illness or vaccination? Refusing feeds? ARCHING HIS BACK? Constipation or blood in the stool?' → 'I HAVEN'T LOOKED IN THE GROIN — HE'S HAD THE NAPPY ON.' (A 'no' to the groin question DOES NOT RULE OUT A HERNIA — the mother has not looked, so THE EXAMINATION REQUEST MUST NAME THE INGUINAL AREA.)

INJURY AND THE SEVEN SOCIAL QUESTIONS — asked even in the versions where nothing is planted: 'any falls or bumps to the head? Any bruises? IS HE MOVING BOTH ARMS AND LEGS? HOW HAVE YOU BEEN COPING WITH THE CRYING? How are things at home — who do you live with, IS YOUR PARTNER SUPPORTIVE? How has your mood been? Any financial worries? Do you or your partner use drugs or alcohol?' AND IF THE VIBE IS THERE, THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION: 'SOME PARENTS GET SO FRUSTRATED THEY SHAKE OR HURT THE BABY — HAS THAT HAPPENED WITH YOU OR YOUR PARTNER?' THEN SILENCE. (Asking 'do you hit him?' closes the parent. And if you never ask it in the NAI version, YOU FAIL THE STATION. If you never ask about coping at all, she becomes tearful at the end and says 'I FEEL LIKE A BAD MOTHER'.)

THE REST: red eyes or discharge; breast or formula, how much and how often, solids, rash after solids; immunisations; development and growth; medical problems, medicines, allergies; AND 'DID ANYONE IN THE FAMILY CRY A LOT AS A BABY?'

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, HEAD TO TOE AND UNDRESSED, NAMING WHAT THE EXAMINER WILL OTHERWISE WITHHOLD: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? FONTANELLE? Any rash or bruising ANYWHERE? Temperature? EYES — red, discharge, FLUORESCEIN? EARS — tympanic membranes? Throat? Chest — air entry, added sounds? ABDOMEN — distension, masses, tenderness, rigidity, bowel sounds? INGUINAL AREA — ANY LUMP? IF SO, IS IT REDUCIBLE AND IS IT TENDER? JOINTS AND LIMBS — swelling, redness, warmth, IS HE MOVING ALL FOUR LIMBS? FINGERS, TOES AND GENITALIA — ANY HAIR TOURNIQUET? Nappy area? AND A URINE DIPSTICK, PLEASE.'
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS, THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS BY GROUP WITH COLIC LAST (see dx) → 'SO IT'S NOT SERIOUS?' / 'DOES HE NEED ANTIBIOTICS?' / 'IS IT SOMETHING I DID?'
VERSION-SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT, THEN THE SAFETY-NET, THE 48-HOUR REVIEW AND THE PARENT-COPING LINE (see dx), naming MedSTAR, the Women's and Children's or CARL as the route.

pefe: Role-player (Version A): Sarah, 26, mother of Liam, 9 months; part-time barista, lives with her husband Tom who is supportive, and her mother helps. LIAM: formula 200 mL five times a day, solids since six months, immunisations up to date, thriving; RUNNY NOSE LAST WEEK. TODAY: crying since about 10 am, FELT HOT LAST NIGHT, GRABBING HIS RIGHT EAR, off solids, still taking bottles, normal nappies, alert. GAVE PARACETAMOL AN HOUR AGO. No falls, no bruises, moving all limbs, no groin lump noticed, no pale spells, no jelly stool. REGISTER: exhausted, close to tears, WANTS REASSURANCE QUICKLY. HIDDEN AGENDA: 'IS IT SOMETHING I DID? DOES HE NEED ANTIBIOTICS?' — volunteered only if asked about concerns, or late.

HOW TO PLAY IT: OPEN WITH FRUSTRATION — 'he's been crying four hours and nothing works'. ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED; DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE EAR-PULLING UNTIL ASKED ABOUT EARS OR FEVER. IF THE DOCTOR SAYS 'BABIES CRY AT THIS AGE' BEFORE EXAMINING: 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK HIM?' If asked what you have tried: paracetamol, nothing else. IF THE DOCTOR NEVER ASKS ABOUT COPING OR HOME, BECOME TEARFUL AT THE END AND SAY 'I FEEL LIKE A BAD MOTHER' — AND MARK THEM DOWN. NAI VARIANT: 'HE FELL WHILE MY BOYFRIEND WAS CHANGING HIM' — AND GIVE THE SHAKING DISCLOSURE ONLY AFTER THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION, AFTER A LONG PAUSE.

Score them on: asked vitals AND temperature; acknowledged your distress; onset, pattern, triggers AND what you tried; the infection block; the four well-baby questions; THE GI BLOCK INCLUDING GROIN, PALLOR AND JELLY STOOL; injury and bruises; SEVEN SOCIAL QUESTIONS; A HEAD-TO-TOE EXAMINATION NAMING THE INGUINAL AREA, JOINTS AND DIGITS; named the diagnosis with reasons; DIFFERENTIALS BY GROUP WITH COLIC LAST; analgesia first with the antibiotic criteria; and a safety-net, a review and the 'safe to walk away' line. FAIL IF: COLIC BEFORE EXAMINATION, NO TEMPERATURE, NO ABDOMEN AND GROIN EXAMINATION, OR THE DISCLOSURE MISSED.

Take a focused history from the father, ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings, explain your diagnosis, and explain your management plan. 8 minutes. VARIANTS: IT BECOMES ANAPHYLAXIS; A LARGE LOCAL REACTION AT 24 HOURS; THE FATHER WILL NOT LET THE PEN GO; and IT WAS A WASP OR AN ANT.

back.dx: A MILD LOCAL REACTION TO A BEE STING — NOT ANAPHYLAXIS. NAME IT: 'Liam has had A MILD LOCAL REACTION TO A BEE STING. That means HIS BODY HAS REACTED TO THE VENOM ONLY WHERE THE STING WENT IN — the redness, the swelling and the pain are all in that one spot.' THEN THE NEGATIVES, SAID OUT LOUD, WHICH IS WHAT TURNS A LABEL INTO REASONING: 'I say that because I'VE SPECIFICALLY CHECKED FOR THE THINGS THAT WOULD MAKE THIS A SEVERE REACTION, AND HE HAS NONE OF THEM: NO RASH ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY, NO SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE, NO CHANGE IN HIS VOICE, NO NOISY BREATHING OR WHEEZE, NO VOMITING OR TUMMY PAIN, AND HE HASN'T BEEN DROWSY, FLOPPY OR FAINT. His breathing, his heart rate and his blood pressure are ALL NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.' WHEN HE ASKS 'SO HE'S NOT ALLERGIC TO BEES?': 'NOT IN THE DANGEROUS SENSE. ALMOST EVERYONE SWELLS AND GOES RED WHERE A BEE STINGS THEM — THAT'S THE VENOM, AND IT'S NORMAL. A DANGEROUS ALLERGY IS WHEN THE REACTION SPREADS BEYOND THE STING. ONE LOCAL REACTION LIKE THIS DOESN'T TELL US HE HAS THAT.' THE PLAN: the sting already removed BY SCRAPING SIDEWAYS — 'I'M SCRAPING IT OUT RATHER THAN SQUEEZING IT, BECAUSE THE VENOM SAC KEEPS EMPTYING WHILE IT'S IN'; wash it; A COLD PACK FOR TEN TO FIFTEEN MINUTES; PARACETAMOL FOR THE PAIN, because a sting hurts more than it itches; A NON-DROWSY ANTIHISTAMINE for the itch and swelling; and a period of observation before home. NO ADRENALINE, NO STEROIDS, NO ANTIBIOTICS — 'the redness today is the venom, not an infection.' AND DO NOT INVENT AN OBSERVATION RULE: 'THERE'S NO FIXED NUMBER OF HOURS FOR A REACTION LIKE THIS' — four hours is the ANAPHYLAXIS observation, not this. THE PEN QUESTION, WHICH IS THE AUTO-FAIL: 'it's a fair question, AND THE HONEST ANSWER IS NO — AND I WANT TO EXPLAIN WHY RATHER THAN JUST SAY IT. AN ADRENALINE PEN IS FOR A CHILD WHOSE REACTION GOES BEYOND THE STING SITE: breathing trouble, swelling of the tongue or throat, a rash all over, collapse. LIAM'S REACTION STAYED EXACTLY WHERE THE STING WAS. CARRYING A PEN WOULDN'T MAKE HIM SAFER, AND IT WOULD MEAN LABELLING HIM WITH A SEVERE ALLERGY HE HASN'T SHOWN ANY SIGN OF.' THEN GIVE HIM THE TRIGGER, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE REFUSAL SAFE: 'WHAT MATTERS FAR MORE IS THAT YOU KNOW WHAT TO WATCH FOR. IF HE IS EVER STUNG AGAIN AND REACTS AWAY FROM THE STING — A RASH ON HIS BODY, SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE, NOISY BREATHING, VOMITING — THAT IS A DIFFERENT SITUATION. CALL AN AMBULANCE, AND HE'LL THEN NEED AN ALLERGY SPECIALIST AND VERY LIKELY A PEN.' SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE: six red flags — lip or tongue swelling, voice change, noisy breathing or wheeze, a rash anywhere else, vomiting, or going pale, floppy or faint — plus 'if in two days the redness is spreading AND he has a fever, that would be an infection'; then avoidance advice, a written sheet, AND TEACH-BACK: 'CAN YOU TELL ME TWO OF THE THINGS THAT WOULD BRING YOU BACK?' And speak to Liam: 'you were very brave.' THE FOUR SENTENCES THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR: those observations are normal for a five-year-old; there is nothing away from the sting site and no airway, breathing or circulation involvement; this is a mild local reaction, not anaphylaxis; and he does not need adrenaline or a pen — AND HERE IS EXACTLY WHEN HE WOULD. IF YOU RUN SHORT OF TIME, drop the avoidance advice and the immunisation question — NEVER DROP THE SYSTEMIC SCREEN, THE STING REMOVAL, OR THE RED FLAGS.
plan: VITALS FIRST, BECAUSE THE STEM OMITS THEM ON PURPOSE — THEN INTERPRET THEM: 'examiner, could I have his vital signs, please: heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, saturations and temperature?' → 90/60, 125, 26, 98%, 36.9. → 'thank you — THOSE ARE ALL NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD, SO HE'S STABLE, and I'll take a history. THANK YOU FOR BRINGING HIM STRAIGHT IN. Tell me what happened.' (The examiner is marking THE INTERPRETATION, not the request.)

THE STING AND THE SITE: 'when exactly did it happen, and WHERE ON HIS BODY? Do you know WHAT STUNG HIM — A BEE, A WASP, AN ANT? WAS HE STUNG MORE THAN ONCE? Is there swelling or redness around the sting? IS IT GETTING BIGGER? Is it painful or itchy? And has anything been done to it already?' (Stopping here and giving a diagnosis is THE COMMONEST FAIL — the marks are in the next block.)

THE ANAPHYLAXIS SCREEN, AS A BLOCK: 'I need to run through some specific things. HAS HE COME UP IN ANY RASH, HIVES OR WELTS ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY? ANY SWELLING OF HIS FACE OR EYES? ANY SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE? ANY DROOLING? HAS HIS VOICE OR HIS CRY SOUNDED DIFFERENT? HAS HE SAID HIS THROAT FEELS TIGHT? ANY NOISY BREATHING, WHEEZE, COUGH OR TROUBLE GETTING HIS BREATH? ANY VOMITING OR TUMMY PAIN? HAS HE BEEN DROWSY, FLOPPY OR PALE AT ANY POINT? DID HE FAINT OR GO BLANK?' (SKIPPING THE GUT IS THE NAMED TRAP: after an insect sting, PERSISTENT VOMITING OR ABDOMINAL PAIN IS ANAPHYLAXIS, not an upset tummy — and it is the feature examiners add to turn this into Version B.)

BACKGROUND, ATOPY AND FAMILY: 'any new food or new medicine today? HAS HE EVER BEEN STUNG BEFORE, AND WHAT HAPPENED THAT TIME? Does he have any known allergies, or has he ever had a severe allergic reaction? Does he have ASTHMA, ECZEMA OR HAY FEVER? Any regular medicines? Immunisations up to date? ANY FAMILY HISTORY OF ALLERGY OR ANAPHYLAXIS? And has he been eating, drinking and passing urine normally?' → 'MY SISTER CARRIES ONE OF THOSE PENS FOR BEES, ACTUALLY.' (If he says Liam has asthma, SAY OUT LOUD THAT THIS RAISES THE STAKES IF HE EVER REACTS SYSTEMICALLY.)

WHAT WAS WORRYING YOU MOST? → 'HONESTLY — THAT HE'D STOP BREATHING. MY SISTER ENDED UP IN INTENSIVE CARE.' → ACKNOWLEDGE IT WITHOUT LETTING IT BECOME LIAM'S DIAGNOSIS: 'I can hear how frightening that is with your sister's history behind it. Let me go through it carefully and then I'll tell you exactly where Liam stands.'

THE EXAMINATION, NAMING THE AIRWAY STRUCTURES AND THE STING SITE: 'general appearance and conscious state; the observations again INCLUDING CAPILLARY REFILL; THE LIPS AND TONGUE, ANY DROOLING, THE VOICE, AND ANY STRIDOR; THE WHOLE SKIN for hives or swelling AWAY FROM THE SITE; THE STING SITE — the size of the erythema and swelling, warmth and tenderness, AND IS THE STING STILL VISIBLE, AND MAY I REMOVE IT? The chest for work of breathing and wheeze; heart sounds and peripheral perfusion; and the abdomen.' THEN REMOVE IT: 'I'M SCRAPING IT OUT SIDEWAYS RATHER THAN SQUEEZING IT, BECAUSE THE VENOM SAC KEEPS EMPTYING WHILE IT'S IN.' (Asking for 'a general examination' gets you a general answer and no marks — and the sting removal is THE ONE PROCEDURAL MARK IN THE STATION.)
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH THE NEGATIVES SAID OUT LOUD (see dx) → 'SO IT'S NOT AN ALLERGY?' / 'SO IT'S NOT LIKE MY SISTER?'

THE PLAN, THEN THE PEN DECLINED WITH THE FUTURE TRIGGER (see dx) → 'MY SISTER CARRIES AN EPIPEN. SHOULDN'T WE HAVE ONE FOR LIAM?' — asked at least once, and AGAIN IF FOBBED OFF. Then the six red flags, the infection line at 48 hours, avoidance advice, a written sheet, AND TEACH-BACK: 'CAN YOU TELL ME TWO OF THE THINGS THAT WOULD BRING YOU BACK?' Then a one-paragraph summary, and a word to Liam.
