'IS THE STING STILL VISIBLE — MAY I REMOVE IT?' / 'I'M SCRAPING IT OUT RATHER THAN SQUEEZING, BECAUSE THE VENOM SAC KEEPS EMPTYING.' / 'This is A MILD LOCAL REACTION TO A BEE STING.' / 'His body has reacted ONLY WHERE THE STING WENT IN.' / 'I'VE CHECKED FOR THE FEATURES OF A SEVERE REACTION AND HE HAS NONE OF THEM.'

'AN ADRENALINE PEN IS FOR A REACTION THAT GOES BEYOND THE STING SITE.' / 'IF HE EVER REACTS AWAY FROM THE STING, THAT IS DIFFERENT — CALL AN AMBULANCE.' / 'There's no fixed number of hours for a reaction like this.' / 'CAN YOU TELL ME TWO OF THE THINGS THAT WOULD BRING YOU BACK?'

VERSION B — IT BECOMES ANAPHYLAXIS: 'HE'S JUST BEEN SICK TWICE AND THERE ARE BLOTCHES COMING UP ON HIS TUMMY — AND HE'S GONE QUIET.' → STOP THE HISTORY: 'thank you — THAT CHANGES THINGS AND I NEED TO ACT NOW. Examiner: THIS IS ANAPHYLAXIS. I'm giving INTRAMUSCULAR ADRENALINE INTO THE LATERAL THIGH, 0.01 mg PER KILOGRAM TO A MAXIMUM OF 0.5 mg, LAYING HIM FLAT WITH HIS LEGS RAISED, calling for senior help, giving HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN and getting IV access.' To the father: 'the injection I've just given IS EXACTLY THE RIGHT TREATMENT and it usually works within minutes. I can repeat it after five minutes. HE'LL NEED TO STAY AT LEAST FOUR HOURS because occasionally these reactions come back.' At discharge: 'NOW he does need TWO ADRENALINE AUTOINJECTORS, AN ASCIA ACTION PLAN, TRAINING FOR YOU AND THE SCHOOL, AND AN ALLERGY REFERRAL — VENOM IMMUNOTHERAPY SUBSTANTIALLY REDUCES THE RISK.' VERIFY

VERSION C — LARGE LOCAL REACTION AT 24 HOURS: 'the swelling has spread past his elbow BUT EVERYTHING IS STILL CONFINED TO THE ARM and he's well. This is A LARGE LOCAL REACTION — uncomfortable and slow, BUT NOT DANGEROUS AND NOT THE SAME AS AN ALLERGY THAT AFFECTS THE WHOLE BODY. It PEAKS AT ONE TO TWO DAYS and settles over about a week.' Plan: regular non-sedating antihistamine, elevate the arm, cold packs, analgesia, AND DRAW AROUND THE EDGE so you can see whether it is still moving; a short oral steroid course is sometimes used for very large reactions VERIFY. HE STILL DOESN'T NEED A PEN. / VERSION D — HE WILL NOT LET IT GO, 'I'M NOT LEAVING WITHOUT ONE': 'I hear you, AND I'M NOT BRUSHING YOU OFF. I won't prescribe something that isn't indicated, BECAUSE IT WOULD GIVE YOU FALSE CONFIDENCE ABOUT THE WRONG THINGS. What I WILL do is give you the written warning signs, book you with your GP this week, and WRITE ASKING FOR AN ALLERGY OPINION so you can hear it from a specialist. If he ever reacts beyond the sting site, THAT DECISION CHANGES IMMEDIATELY.' / VERSION E — A WASP OR AN ANT: 'wasps and ants DON'T LEAVE A STING BEHIND, so there's nothing to remove — and A WASP CAN STING MORE THAN ONCE, so I'll check him for other sites. The reaction itself, and how I judge it, IS EXACTLY THE SAME.' JACK JUMPER ANTS in South Australia can cause severe reactions and have A DESENSITISATION PROGRAMME — but that is a specialist referral AFTER a generalised reaction. VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: Shane, 34, A SHEARER FROM THE YORKE PENINSULA, Liam's father. Liam, 5, was stung ON THE RIGHT FOREARM ABOUT THIRTY MINUTES AGO near the clover. HE SCREAMED, CRIED FOR TWO MINUTES, AND HAS BEEN COMPLETELY HIMSELF SINCE — talking, complaining, CROSS ABOUT MISSING HIS TELEVISION PROGRAMME. The site is red and puffy, ABOUT A FIFTY-CENT PIECE, MORE PAINFUL THAN ITCHY; you put a cold flannel on it. NOTHING ELSE HAS HAPPENED: no rash elsewhere, no lip or tongue swelling, no voice change, no noisy breathing or wheeze, NO VOMITING OR TUMMY PAIN, no drowsiness, no faint. Stung once as a toddler AND IT JUST WENT RED. No known allergies; ECZEMA AS A BABY; no medicines; immunisations up to date.

HIDDEN AGENDA: YOUR SISTER HAD A BEE-STING REACTION YEARS AGO, SPENT A NIGHT IN INTENSIVE CARE AND NOW CARRIES AN ADRENALINE PEN. YOU ARE FRIGHTENED LIAM WILL STOP BREATHING, AND YOU WANT A PEN FOR HIM. YOU WILL NOT SAY THIS UNTIL THE DOCTOR ASKS WHAT WORRIES YOU — or, if they never ask, RAISE IT YOURSELF ONCE THEY START EXPLAINING THE PLAN. REGISTER: anxious and slightly embarrassed at first, SETTLING IF THE DOCTOR EXPLAINS RATHER THAN DISMISSES. BECOME TENSE AGAIN IF THEY SAY 'IT'S ONLY A BEE STING' OR REFUSE THE PEN WITHOUT A REASON.

HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE SYSTEMIC NEGATIVES AS A LIST — MAKE THE DOCTOR ASK EACH ONE. PUSH ONCE AT MINUTE SIX: 'SHOULDN'T YOU GIVE US ONE OF THOSE PENS?' IF THE DOCTOR REFUSES WITHOUT EXPLAINING, GET UPSET: 'SO YOU'RE JUST SENDING HIM HOME? MY SISTER NEARLY DIED.' If the doctor explains the reasoning AND GIVES YOU THE FUTURE TRIGGER, settle and accept. If asked to repeat the red flags, give two, correctly, ONLY IF THEY WERE CLEARLY TOLD TO YOU. Score them on: asked for vital signs before starting; SAID OUT LOUD THAT THE OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL FOR AGE; introduced, gained permission AND SPOKE TO LIAM DIRECTLY; timing, site, number of stings and the culprit; RASH AWAY FROM THE SITE; lips, tongue, drooling and voice; noisy breathing, wheeze, shortness of breath; VOMITING AND ABDOMINAL PAIN; drowsiness, floppiness, pallor, fainting; previous stings, atopy and family history; ASKED WHAT WORRIED YOU MOST; a targeted examination NAMING LIPS, TONGUE, VOICE, WHOLE SKIN AND THE STING SITE; ASKED TO REMOVE THE STING AND DESCRIBED SCRAPING NOT SQUEEZING; named it A MILD LOCAL REACTION WITH THE NEGATIVES; AVOIDED ADRENALINE, STEROIDS AND ANTIBIOTICS; DECLINED THE AUTOINJECTOR AND GAVE THE FUTURE TRIGGER — AUTO-FAIL IF NOT; at least four specific red flags with a check of understanding; and a one-paragraph summary.
fails: ★ Treating a local reaction as anaphylaxis — and above all, promising an adrenaline pen for the future
★ Reading 90/60 with a pulse of 125 as shock, when both are normal at five — and not saying the interpretation aloud
Stopping after a tidy site history and giving the diagnosis, when the marks are in the systemic screen
Skipping the gut questions — after an insect sting, persistent vomiting or abdominal pain IS anaphylaxis, and it is the feature that turns this into Version B

Asking for 'a general examination' instead of naming lips, tongue, voice, the whole skin and the sting site; forgetting to remove the sting, which is the one procedural mark; inventing an observation rule like four hours, which belongs to anaphylaxis; and caving when the father asks the second time

setting: A PURE EXAMINATION-REQUEST AND COUNSELLING STATION — THE CHILD IS NOT PRESENT, THERE IS AN ABDOMINAL MANNEQUIN IN THE ROOM, AND EVERY FINDING IS GIVEN ONLY IF ASKED FOR BY NAME. THE MARKS ARE IN THE GRANULARITY: 'YES THERE IS A RASH' IS NOT AN ANSWER — ask the FIVE INSPECTION AND FOUR PALPATION ITEMS, AND SURFACE IS THE ONE THAT REMOVES SCARLET FEVER. 'YES THERE ARE NODES' IS NOT AN ANSWER EITHER — ASK THE CHAIN, because POSTERIOR TRIANGLE IS THE EBV CHAIN and the examiner is waiting for it. AND HALF OF CHILDREN WITH EBV HAVE NO PALPABLE SPLEEN, SO KEEP THE DIAGNOSIS WHEN THE MANNEQUIN GIVES YOU NOTHING.
stem: General practice. NOAH, 4 YEARS. TWO DAYS AGO he presented with A SORE THROAT; on examination he had ENLARGED TONSILS AND WAS PRESCRIBED AMOXICILLIN. HE HAS PRESENTED AGAIN TODAY, brought by his father, WITH A RASH. Alert, drinking, low-grade fever.

THERE IS AN ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION MANNEQUIN IN THE ROOM AND THE CHILD IS NOT PRESENT. 8 minutes: ask the examiner for a COMPLETE physical examination, PERFORM AN ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION ON THE MANNEQUIN talking the examiner through it, then explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the father, with reasons.

GENERALISED PINK MACULOPAPULAR on the TRUNK AND LIMBS — no discharge, no scratch marks — NOT WARM, NOT TENDER, BLANCHING, AND SMOOTH

back.dx: INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS — EBV — WITH THE AMINOPENICILLIN RASH; the second differential is AMOXICILLIN HYPERSENSITIVITY and the third is SCARLET FEVER. TO THE FATHER: 'Noah most likely has GLANDULAR FEVER — an infection with a virus called EPSTEIN-BARR, EBV. It causes exactly this: A VERY SORE THROAT WITH WHITE PATCHES, GLANDS AT THE BACK OF THE NECK, TINY RED SPOTS ON THE ROOF OF THE MOUTH, and it can make THE SPLEEN — an organ under the left ribs — SWELL. THE RASH IS THE IMPORTANT PART: WHEN SOMEONE WITH THIS VIRUS TAKES AMOXICILLIN, MOST OF THEM COME OUT IN EXACTLY THIS KIND OF RASH. SO IT IS THE VIRUS AND THE ANTIBIOTIC TOGETHER, which is why I am confident about the diagnosis.' THEN THE TWO DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ITS REASON: 'A GENUINE ALLERGY TO THE AMOXICILLIN — less likely because THE RASH ISN'T HIVES, IT CAME ON DAYS IN, AND THERE'S NO SWELLING OR WHEEZE; and SCARLET FEVER — less likely because HIS RASH IS SMOOTH RATHER THAN ROUGH AND HIS TONGUE IS NORMAL.' THE ALLERGY QUESTION, ANSWERED PROPERLY: 'a TRUE ALLERGY GIVES HIVES, SWELLING OF THE LIPS OR FACE, SOMETIMES WHEEZE, USUALLY WITHIN AN HOUR OF A DOSE. Noah's rash is FLAT AND SMOOTH, CAME ON TWO DAYS IN, no swelling, no breathing trouble. I'LL RECORD IT AS A RASH WITH AMOXICILLIN DURING GLANDULAR FEVER, SO NOBODY WRONGLY LABELS HIM ALLERGIC.' THEN THE THREE THINGS THE TASK DOES NOT ASK FOR BUT THE MARK SHEET CONTAINS: STOP THE AMOXICILLIN TODAY — 'it isn't treating a virus and it's driving the rash'; THE SPLEEN RULE — 'it can swell with this virus AND A KNOCK CAN TEAR IT, so NO FOOTBALL, RUGBY, TRAMPOLINES OR ROUGH PLAY FOR AT LEAST FOUR WEEKS AND UNTIL HE IS COMPLETELY WELL. IF HE GETS PAIN UNDER THE LEFT RIBS OR IN THE LEFT SHOULDER, OR GOES FLOPPY OR PALE, THAT IS AN AMBULANCE'; and THE RED FLAGS — 'bring him straight back if he CAN'T SWALLOW HIS OWN SALIVA, BREATHES NOISILY, STOPS DRINKING, GOES YELLOW, or gets A RASH THAT DOESN'T FADE WHEN YOU PRESS A GLASS ON IT.' Then a blood test to confirm, review in two days, AND TEACH-BACK: 'CAN YOU TELL ME THE TWO THINGS YOU'LL WATCH FOR?'
plan: HAND HYGIENE STATED, AND THE FATHER ADDRESSED FIRST: 'I've read that Noah was here two days ago with a sore throat and started amoxicillin, and now he has a rash. I'm going to go through his examination with the examiner, examine his tummy, and then explain what I think is going on.' → 'IT'S EVERYWHERE — IT CAME UP OVERNIGHT. IS IT THE ANTIBIOTIC?' → 'THAT'S A VERY SENSIBLE QUESTION AND I'LL ANSWER IT PROPERLY ONCE I'VE EXAMINED HIM.'

GENERAL APPEARANCE — and the airway words are what make it a paediatric assessment: 'is Noah alert or drowsy? Any signs of dehydration — sunken eyes, dry mouth? IS HE DROOLING? ANY STRIDOR OR NOISY BREATHING? HAS HIS VOICE CHANGED? Is he toxic-looking? IS THERE A RASH?'

THE RASH IN NINE PARTS — and stopping at 'yes there is a rash' is the first trap: 'ON INSPECTION: what is the PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY — macular, papular, petechial, purpuric, urticarial? WHERE is it and WHAT COLOUR? Any discharge or scratch marks? ON PALPATION: is it WARM, TENDER, BLANCHING OR NON-BLANCHING, AND WHAT IS THE SURFACE LIKE?' (SURFACE IS THE ONE THAT REMOVES SCARLET FEVER.)

VITALS, ENT AND NODES: 'temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations, capillary refill. Ears — red or bulging drums? Nose — discharge? Mouth and throat — are the TONSILS swollen, red, WITH EXUDATE? IS THERE A STRAWBERRY TONGUE? ANY PETECHIAE ON THE PALATE? Any PERIORAL PALLOR? Sinus tenderness? CERVICAL NODES — WHICH CHAIN, tender, mobile, how big? Neck stiffness?' ('Yes there are nodes' then 'thank you' loses it — POSTERIOR TRIANGLE IS THE EBV CHAIN, and the examiner has it on the card waiting for you.)

THE FULL CHEST AND HEART — not a two-second version because 'it's EBV': 'respiratory — symmetrical movements, trachea central, percussion note, air entry, added sounds, vocal resonance? Cardiovascular — S1 and S2, any murmur? ANY PALLOR, BRUISING OR JAUNDICE ELSEWHERE?' (You have five minutes to spare; a brief chest reads as a candidate who has stopped thinking.)

THE MANNEQUIN, EXAMINED AS A CHILD: 'I'd wash my hands, EXPLAIN TO NOAH AND DAD, expose from nipples to groin and have him flat. INSPECTING FROM THE LEVEL OF THE ABDOMEN for symmetrical movement, distension, scars, masses, bruising — AND I'M NOTING NO BRUISING IN THE FLANKS OR AROUND THE UMBILICUS. SUPERFICIAL PALPATION OF ALL NINE REGIONS, WATCHING HIS FACE for tenderness, guarding or rigidity. DEEP PALPATION OF ALL NINE REGIONS.' (Announcing that the mannequin is not breathing, or doing nothing but the left upper quadrant, are the two traps — SAY WHAT YOU SKIP AND WHY.)

LIVER, THEN SPLEEN, WITH THE TECHNIQUE NARRATED: 'the LIVER: from the right iliac fossa up to the costal margin WITH EACH BREATH IN, feeling for an edge. The SPLEEN: MY LEFT HAND BEHIND HIS LEFT LOWER RIBS, RIGHT HAND FROM THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA MOVING DIAGONALLY to the left costal margin with each inspiration, FEELING FOR A NOTCHED EDGE... not felt — I'D ROLL HIM ONTO HIS RIGHT SIDE AND REPEAT. I'd PERCUSS TRAUBE'S SPACE AND CASTELL'S POINT ON INSPIRATION. Auscultating for bowel sounds. I WOULD NOT PERFORM A RECTAL EXAMINATION — NOT INDICATED IN THIS CHILD. And I'd finish the LYMPH NODE SURVEY: axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal, supraclavicular.'

TURN FULLY TO THE FATHER, GIVE THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS THREE REASONS AND THE TWO DIFFERENTIALS (see dx) — AND KEEP EBV DESPITE THE ABSENT SPLEEN: 'HALF OF CHILDREN WITH GLANDULAR FEVER HAVE NO PALPABLE SPLEEN.' → 'SO IS HE ALLERGIC TO PENICILLIN?'

THE ALLERGY ANSWER, STOPPING THE AMOXICILLIN, THE SPLEEN AND SPORT RULE, THE RED FLAGS, THE BLOOD TEST, REVIEW AND TEACH-BACK (see dx) → 'HE'S GOT FOOTBALL ON SATURDAY' — held until the end. (The task says DIAGNOSIS — but leaving without stopping the amoxicillin, answering the allergy question and giving the spleen rule leaves marks on the table.)

VARIANT A — URTICARIAL WITHIN THE HOUR: 'urticarial, itchy, lip swelling, forty minutes after a dose — THIS IS A TRUE HYPERSENSITIVITY UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Any wheeze, stridor, hypotension? Then STOP THE AMOXICILLIN, oral antihistamine, observe, ADRENALINE 10 MICROGRAM/KG IM if any airway, breathing or circulation involvement. I'll DOCUMENT A PENICILLIN ALLERGY and refer for allergy assessment. HE MAY STILL HAVE GLANDULAR FEVER UNDERNEATH — the examination for that continues.' VERIFY / VARIANT B — SCARLET FEVER: 'a ROUGH, SANDPAPER-TEXTURED blanching rash with A STRAWBERRY TONGUE and PERIORAL PALLOR — this is scarlet fever, streptococcal. The amoxicillin will be covering it, BUT THE RECOMMENDED DRUG IS PHENOXYMETHYLPENICILLIN FOR TEN FULL DAYS, and he's excluded from childcare UNTIL 24 HOURS AFTER THE FIRST DOSE. I'd still check for a spleen.'

VARIANT C — DROOLING AND A MUFFLED VOICE: 'drooling with a muffled voice in a child with huge tonsils IS AN AIRWAY EMERGENCY. I'll stop the routine examination, keep him UPRIGHT ON DAD'S LAP, give oxygen, NOT EXAMINE THE THROAT WITH A SPATULA, and call MedSTAR Kids on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the Women's and Children's. Steroids for tonsillar airway compromise on specialist advice.' VERIFY / VARIANT D — THE SPLEEN IS 3 cm BELOW THE COSTAL MARGIN: 'thank you — A PALPABLE SPLEEN SUPPORTS EBV. I'd confirm with percussion, check for tenderness, AND THE ADVICE BECOMES STRICTER: no contact sport, NO HEAVY LIFTING, seat-belt and rough-play warnings, and I'd RE-EXAMINE AT EACH REVIEW UNTIL IT HAS GONE DOWN. Sudden left-sided pain or faintness is an emergency.'
pefe: Role-player: Mark, 36, A MECHANIC IN KADINA, father of Noah, 4, his only child. Two days ago the practice saw A SORE THROAT WITH BIG TONSILS and prescribed AMOXICILLIN LIQUID; NOAH HAS HAD EVERY DOSE — FOUR SO FAR. THIS MORNING HE WOKE COVERED IN A PINK RASH that came up overnight, ABOUT TWO DAYS AFTER STARTING. He is grizzly but playing, EATING LITTLE, DRINKING OKAY, weeing normally, VERY TIRED — SLEPT FOURTEEN HOURS. Fever 38 this morning, paracetamol helps. The rash is A LITTLE ITCHY but he is not scratching much; NO lip or face swelling, no wheeze, no vomiting, no tummy pain. No known allergies; immunisations up to date; A CHILD AT KINDY HAD 'TONSILLITIS'.

REGISTER: worried, HOLDING THE MEDICINE BOX, AND SLIGHTLY ANNOYED THAT 'THE ANTIBIOTIC MADE HIM WORSE'. HIDDEN AGENDA, THREE QUESTIONS: (1) IS HE ALLERGIC TO PENICILLIN — RAISE THIS AS SOON AS THE DOCTOR PAUSES, AND AGAIN IF NOT ANSWERED; (2) SHOULD HE KEEP TAKING IT; (3) CAN HE PLAY UNDER-6s FOOTBALL ON SATURDAY — HOLD THIS UNTIL THE END. BECOME SHARPER IF THE DOCTOR RUSHES THE EXAMINATION OR BRUSHES OFF THE ALLERGY QUESTION. SOFTEN WHEN THEY EXPLAIN THE VIRUS-PLUS-DRUG RASH CLEARLY.

EXAMINER CARD — ONLY GIVE A FINDING IF IT IS ASKED FOR BY NAME. General: alert, lips dry, no drooling or stridor, voice normal, not toxic. Rash: PINK MACULOPAPULAR, trunk and limbs, no discharge, no excoriation; not warm, not tender, BLANCHING, SMOOTH. Vitals: T 38.1, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 98%, CRT under 2 s. Ears and nose normal. TONSILS ENLARGED, RED, WHITE EXUDATE; NO STRAWBERRY TONGUE; PALATAL PETECHIAE PRESENT; no perioral pallor. Sinuses non-tender. POSTERIOR TRIANGLE NODES 1-2 cm, mildly tender, mobile. No neck stiffness. Chest and heart normal. No pallor, bruising or jaundice. MANNEQUIN: GIVE 'NOTHING PALPABLE' WHATEVER THEY DO; allow them to skip percussion and the rectal examination. SCORE: hand hygiene; introduced to the father; general appearance INCLUDING DROOLING, STRIDOR AND VOICE; FIVE RASH INSPECTION ITEMS; FOUR PALPATION ITEMS INCLUDING SURFACE; vitals; ears and nose; TONSILS, TONGUE AND PALATE; sinuses; NODES WITH THE CHAIN; neck stiffness; FULL CHEST; heart; abdomen — inspect, superficial, deep, liver, BIMANUAL SPLEEN FROM THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA, ROLL RIGHT, percussion stated, bowel sounds, RECTAL DECLINED WITH A REASON; node survey; EBV WITH THREE REASONS; DRUG REACTION NAMED; SCARLET FEVER NAMED; KEPT EBV DESPITE NO SPLEEN; STOP THE AMOXICILLIN; ALLERGY QUESTION ANSWERED CORRECTLY; SPLEEN AND SPORT RULE; red flags; review and teach-back.
fails: ★ Stopping at 'yes there is a rash' — the five inspection and four palpation questions are the marks, and SURFACE is what removes scarlet fever
★ Accepting 'yes there are nodes' without asking the chain — posterior triangle is the EBV chain and the examiner is waiting for it
Dropping EBV because the mannequin gives nothing — about half of children with EBV have no palpable spleen
Leaving without stopping the amoxicillin, answering the allergy question, or giving the spleen and sport rule

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST AND EXPLANATION — general practice, AND THE RECALL NOTES SAY 'PRECOCIOUS PUBERTY'. back.dx: NORMAL PUBERTY — NOT PRECOCIOUS. GIVE IT WITH THREE REASONS: 'the most likely cause of the new smell is NORMAL PUBERTY. My reasons: Ella has EARLY BREAST DEVELOPMENT AND THE BEGINNINGS OF HAIR GROWTH, which are exactly the first normal signs of puberty at her age; HER GROWTH CHART IS NORMAL; and I HAVE CHECKED FOR THE OTHER CAUSES — thyroid, diabetes, rare inherited conditions, skin problems and diet — AND FOUND NOTHING. PUBERTY STARTING AT NINE IS NOT EARLY; WE ONLY CALL IT EARLY IF IT BEGINS BEFORE EIGHT.' THEN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS: 'in puberty the body starts making NEW HORMONES. They SWITCH ON A SECOND TYPE OF SWEAT GLAND in the armpits and groin, and THE BACTERIA THAT NORMALLY LIVE ON OUR SKIN ACT ON THAT SWEAT and produce the adult-type smell. IT IS THE SAME SWEAT EVERYONE GETS — IT'S JUST NEW FOR ELLA.' THEN SIX DIFFERENTIALS NAMED: 'whether it was MAINLY ELLA who felt she smelled, WHICH CAN HAPPEN WITH ANXIETY — but you and Dad noticed it; AN OVERACTIVE THYROID; DIABETES; BEING OVERWEIGHT; RARE CONDITIONS LIKE PKU, CYSTIC FIBROSIS OR COELIAC DISEASE that change the smell of sweat; SKIN INFECTIONS; and SPICY FOODS OR MEDICINES. NONE OF THOSE FIT.' MANAGEMENT AND SAFETY-NET: 'NO TESTS ARE NEEDED. Practical things: A DAILY WASH WITH SOAP, DRYING WELL, BREATHABLE COTTON CLOTHES, SPORTS GEAR WASHED AFTER EACH USE, AND A MILD DEODORANT OR ANTIPERSPIRANT — THEY'RE SAFE AT HER AGE. I'll give Ella A GOOD BOOK ON PUBERTY AND THE ROYAL CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL FACT SHEET so she knows what's coming. About the comment at school — if it happens again, LET THE TEACHER OR WELLBEING LEADER KNOW. I'd like to see Ella in THREE TO SIX MONTHS to check that puberty is progressing normally, and SOONER IF SHE GROWS VERY QUICKLY, GETS ACNE OR A DEEP VOICE, DRINKS OR WEES MUCH MORE, OR SEEMS LOW OR WORRIED.' THEN TURN TO THE CHILD: 'Ella — any questions for me?' → 'CAN I STILL PLAY NETBALL?' → 'ABSOLUTELY. Just wash the uniform.' THE VARIANTS. THE MOTHER INSISTS ON HORMONE TESTS AND A SPECIALIST: 'I understand — you want to be certain. HORMONE TESTS AND BONE-AGE X-RAYS ARE FOR CHILDREN WHO START PUBERTY BEFORE EIGHT, or who are growing unusually fast or have signs like a deep voice or severe acne. Ella has none of those, SO THE TESTS WOULD NOT CHANGE ANYTHING AND WOULD ONLY WORRY HER. What I WILL do is see her again in three months and measure her; IF ANYTHING CHANGES, I'LL REFER HER TO THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S THAT DAY.' 'NOBODY ELSE CAN SMELL IT — SHE SHOWERS FIVE TIMES A DAY AND WON'T GO TO SCHOOL': 'THAT TELLS ME THE WORRY ITSELF IS THE PROBLEM, NOT THE SMELL. Ella, can I ask you a few questions on your own for a minute?' — then a HEADS assessment with a mood and self-harm screen. 'This is a recognised kind of anxiety; it responds well to talking therapy, and I'd like to involve a psychologist and the school wellbeing leader.' A SEVEN-YEAR-OLD WITH THE SAME FINDINGS: 'at seven, breast development IS EARLIER THAN WE EXPECT, so I DO want tests: A BONE-AGE X-RAY, HORMONE BLOODS, A PELVIC ULTRASOUND, and a PAEDIATRIC ENDOCRINOLOGIST at the Women's and Children's. Most causes are benign, and early puberty is treatable if needed.'
plan: GREET ELLA FIRST AND GET HER PERMISSION, THEN NORMALISE WITHOUT REASSURING: 'you must be Ella — hi. Mum, what's brought you both in?' → 'about two months ago we noticed SHE SMELLS — LIKE AN ADULT. She showers every day. I'm worried something's wrong, OR THAT IT'S PUBERTY FAR TOO EARLY.' → 'that's VERY COMMON FOR PARENTS TO NOTICE AROUND THIS AGE AND IT'S SENSIBLE TO CHECK. I'll ask some questions that may seem unrelated so we can be sure about the cause. ELLA, OKAY IF I ASK MUM ABOUT YOU? JUMP IN ANY TIME.' (Saying 'smelly' or 'body odour problem' with Ella in the room is an automatic fail — SAY 'THE NEW SMELL MUM HAS NOTICED'. And reassuring before any screen earns 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW WITHOUT CHECKING?')

THE COMPLAINT, WITH TWO DISCRIMINATING QUESTIONS: 'when did you first notice it? All the time or on and off? Worse? Anything that makes it worse — sport, hot days, foods? IS SHE SWEATING MORE THAN BEFORE, OR A NORMAL AMOUNT THAT SMELLS DIFFERENT? Where — armpits, feet, everywhere? AND HAVE OTHER PEOPLE NOTICED IT, OR IS IT MAINLY ELLA WHO SAYS SO?' → normal sweat, new smell, armpits, and BOTH PARENTS NOTICED WHILE ELLA IS NOT FUSSED.

IMPACT AND MIND, INCLUDING ONE DIRECT QUESTION TO THE CHILD: 'has anyone at school said anything — teasing, bullying? How is her mood? Sleep? How are things at home, school, friends?' Then: 'ELLA — ANYTHING BOTHERING YOU?' → 'I don't care. Mum does.'

THE ORGANIC SCREEN — ONE PLAIN QUESTION EACH, NO EXPLANATIONS, KEEP MOVING: washing and clothes, and is the netball gear washed each time; 'does she prefer heat or cold — HEAT INTOLERANCE, SHAKY HANDS, RACING HEART, WEIGHT LOSS? PASSING LOTS OF URINE, DRINKING LOTS, LOSING WEIGHT? Any recent WEIGHT GAIN? WAS HER NEWBORN HEEL-PRICK TEST NORMAL? Ongoing DIARRHOEA, GREASY POO, TUMMY PAIN, CHESTY COUGH, SALTY SKIN? YELLOW EYES, ITCH, DARK URINE, SWELLING? Rash in the armpits or groin, any discharge?' (Asking these as a lecture — 'I need to exclude phenylketonuria' — is the trap.)

PUBERTY LAST, DELIBERATELY: 'may I ask about puberty changes? ANY BREAST DEVELOPMENT? HAIR UNDER THE ARMS OR IN THE PRIVATE AREA? ANY BLEEDING?' → 'BREAST BUDS FOR ABOUT SIX MONTHS — I THOUGHT THAT WAS TOO EARLY TOO. A little hair under the arms and down below. No bleeding.' (THE LECTURER WANTS THIS ASKED LAST SO THE EXAMINER SEES THE EXCLUSION PROCESS BEFORE THE ANSWER.)

DIET, DRUGS, FAMILY AND WELL-CHILD: 'any medicines or supplements? Lots of GARLIC, ONION, CURRY OR SPICES? HOW OLD WERE YOU WHEN YOUR PERIODS STARTED? Anyone in the family with thyroid problems, diabetes OR VERY EARLY PUBERTY? Is she alert and active, eating and drinking normally? Born at term, immunised, developing normally?'

THE EXAMINATION, ASKED BY NAME: 'general appearance — sweaty, flushed, dressed appropriately? Vitals. THE GROWTH CHART — height, weight, BMI, ANY CENTILE CROSSING? TANNER STAGING — BREAST STAGE, PUBIC HAIR STAGE, AXILLARY HAIR. THYROID — goitre, tremor, eye signs. SKIN — intertrigo, acne, hirsutism, acanthosis. Chest, heart, abdomen for masses. BLOOD GLUCOSE AND URINE DIPSTICK.'
THE DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS AND THE 'NOT EARLY' SENTENCE, THEN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS (see dx) → 'SO IT'S NORMAL? I REALLY THOUGHT NINE WAS TOO YOUNG.'

SIX DIFFERENTIALS, THEN MANAGEMENT WITH NO TESTS, THE SCHOOL COMMENT, REVIEW AT THREE TO SIX MONTHS AND THE RED FLAGS (see dx) → 'DO WE NEED BLOOD TESTS?' — and if you never mention tests, she asks it late. Then turn to Ella for her question.

REGISTER: slightly embarrassed, protective, CONVINCED NINE IS 'WAY TOO EARLY' — and you relax when the doctor gives reasons. HIDDEN AGENDA: you have READ ABOUT PRECOCIOUS PUBERTY and want to ask 'DOES SHE NEED HORMONE TESTS?' — VOLUNTEER IT LATE IF NOT ADDRESSED. PLAY ELLA TOO: shrug, 'I DON'T CARE, MUM DOES', and at the end 'CAN I STILL PLAY NETBALL?' IF THE DOCTOR SAYS 'PRECOCIOUS PUBERTY' OR ORDERS HORMONE TESTS: 'SO IT IS EARLY? IS SOMETHING WRONG WITH HER?' — AND MARK IT A FAIL. IF THEY SAY 'SMELLY' OR 'BODY ODOUR PROBLEM' IN FRONT OF ELLA, GLANCE AT HER AND LOOK UNCOMFORTABLE. IF THEY REASSURE BEFORE ASKING ANYTHING: 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW WITHOUT CHECKING?'

SCORE — ONE POINT EACH, 12 OF 17 TO PASS: greeted Ella and asked permission; normalised WITHOUT reassuring prematurely; timing, pattern and triggers; SWEAT VOLUME VERSUS SMELL; DO OTHERS NOTICE IT; impact — teasing, mood, sleep, home, school; ONE DIRECT QUESTION TO ELLA; hygiene; thyroid, diabetes, weight, heel-prick, gut and cystic fibrosis, liver, skin — one each; PUBERTY ASKED LAST; diet and drugs; maternal menarche and family history; ASKED FOR THE GROWTH CHART AND TANNER STAGING BY NAME plus thyroid, skin, systems and BSL; DIAGNOSIS = NORMAL PUBERTY WITH THREE REASONS AND 'NOT EARLY — BEFORE EIGHT IS EARLY'; the mechanism in plain words; SIX DIFFERENTIALS NAMED; management — hygiene, antiperspirant, a resource, the school, review at 3-6 months with red flags; and NO UNNECESSARY TESTS.

setting: HISTORY, DIAGNOSIS AND COUNSELLING — rural hospital, AND SHE IS CRYING WHEN YOU WALK IN. FOUR EMPATHY POINTS ARE SCORED SEPARATELY: AT THE OPENING, BEFORE THE DIAGNOSIS, BEFORE MANAGEMENT, AND AT THE END — so it is not one warm sentence, it is four. AND THERE ARE THREE FORGOTTEN MANAGEMENT POINTS THAT DECIDE THE STATION: INVESTIGATIONS THEN ANTIBIOTICS, SURFACTANT AS AN OPTION, AND TRANSFER TO A TERTIARY NICU BECAUSE A RURAL HOSPITAL CANNOT PROVIDE THE CARE. 'HE IS STABLE AND THIS IS A CONDITION WE TREAT' IS HONEST — 'HE'LL BE FINE' IS NOT.
stem: You are the HOSPITAL MEDICAL OFFICER at a rural hospital in Wallaroo. JANE, 26, HAS JUST DELIVERED A BABY BOY AT 32 WEEKS. Delivery was uncomplicated, but IMMEDIATELY AFTER BIRTH HE DEVELOPED RESPIRATORY DISTRESS and was placed IN A HEADBOX WITH 40% OXYGEN; HE IS NOW STABLE. THIS IS HER SECOND PREGNANCY — THE FIRST ENDED IN MISCARRIAGE. SHE IS CRYING AND ASKING TO SPEAK TO A DOCTOR.

8 minutes: take a focused history from the mother (3 minutes), explain the most likely diagnosis, then explain your immediate management AND COUNSEL HER, ADDRESSING HER CONCERNS. VERSION B: COUNSELLING ONLY, NO HISTORY. VERSION C: she volunteers AN E. COLI URINARY INFECTION AT 14 WEEKS and RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES EIGHT HOURS BEFORE DELIVERY.

What she asks if you omit it
No transfer mentioned: 'SO HE'LL STAY HERE WITH ME?' — no antibiotics: 'COULD THE INFECTION I HAD HAVE GOT INTO HIM?' — no surfactant: 'IS THERE ANY MEDICINE FOR HIS LUNGS?'

back.dx: NEONATAL RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME — SURFACTANT DEFICIENCY OF PREMATURITY at 32 weeks. NAME IT AND EXPLAIN SURFACTANT CORRECTLY: 'your son most likely has a condition called RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME — it's VERY COMMON IN PREMATURE BABIES. INSIDE THE LUNGS ARE MILLIONS OF TINY AIR SACS, AND THEY'RE COATED WITH A SOAPY SUBSTANCE CALLED SURFACTANT THAT STOPS THEM STICKING SHUT AT THE END OF EACH BREATH. BABIES MAKE MOST OF THEIR SURFACTANT IN THE LAST FEW WEEKS OF PREGNANCY, so a baby born at 32 weeks DOESN'T HAVE ENOUGH YET; the air sacs PARTLY COLLAPSE WITH EVERY BREATH and he has to work hard to breathe — THAT'S THE GRUNTING AND THE PULLING-IN OF HIS CHEST.' The 'chest-wall lubricant' explanation is wrong and is a named trap. THEN REMOVE THE BLAME AND REASSURE AGAIN: 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS, AND THE MISCARRIAGE ISN'T CONNECTED. BEING BORN EARLY IS THE REASON — and that happens to many women who did everything right. We can treat this, AND MOST PREMATURE BABIES WITH IT DO WELL.' THEN THE MANAGEMENT, AND THE THREE FORGOTTEN POINTS ARE THE STATION. ONE — INVESTIGATIONS, THEN ANTIBIOTICS: 'first, some tests — blood tests INCLUDING A BLOOD CULTURE, a check of his oxygen and sugar levels, and A CHEST X-RAY. THE MAIN REASON FOR THE TESTS IS TO MAKE SURE THERE'S NO INFECTION, BECAUSE INFECTION CAN LOOK EXACTLY LIKE THIS — and given the urine infection and your waters breaking early, WE TAKE THAT SERIOUSLY. SO AS SOON AS THE SAMPLES ARE TAKEN, WE'LL START HIM ON ANTIBIOTICS THROUGH A DRIP, AS A PRECAUTION, AND STOP THEM IF THE TESTS COME BACK CLEAR.' TWO — RESPIRATORY SUPPORT AND FLUIDS, WITH SURFACTANT NAMED AS AN OPTION: continuous oxygen monitoring; 'if his breathing gets harder we can help him in two ways: A SMALL MASK THAT GIVES A GENTLE CONTINUOUS FLOW OF AIR TO HOLD THE AIR SACS OPEN — CALLED CPAP — or, if needed, A TUBE INTO HIS WINDPIPE with a machine to breathe for him. Because breathing is hard work, HE WON'T FEED BY MOUTH YET — fluids and sugar through the drip, AND I'D ENCOURAGE YOU TO START EXPRESSING MILK so it's ready when he can take it. THERE IS ALSO A TREATMENT WHERE THE SPECIALISTS GIVE HIM SURFACTANT — THE VERY SUBSTANCE HE'S SHORT OF — DOWN A THIN TUBE INTO THE LUNGS. It's an option they'll consider, and OFTEN THE TRANSPORT TEAM GIVES IT BEFORE HE TRAVELS.' THREE — TRANSFER, FRAMED AS BEST CARE: 'THE MOST IMPORTANT THING I NEED TO TELL YOU: this condition needs CLOSE, CONTINUOUS MONITORING IN A NEONATAL INTENSIVE CARE UNIT, and it usually takes DAYS TO WEEKS to improve. WE DON'T HAVE THAT UNIT HERE IN WALLAROO. So I'm arranging for the specialist neonatal retrieval team — MedSTAR — to take him to the Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide. THAT IS NOT BECAUSE HE'S GETTING WORSE; IT'S SO HE GETS THE BEST POSSIBLE CARE.' THEN HER: 'we'll do everything to keep you together' — travel with him where possible, otherwise as soon as she is fit, with PATS TRAVEL AND ACCOMMODATION SUPPORT for her and Sam; CHECK HER OWN BLEEDING AND BLOOD PRESSURE so she is well enough to go; WRITTEN INFORMATION from the Women's and Children's; A FAMILY MEETING WITH SAM BEFORE THE TEAM ARRIVES; and 'any question, at any hour, ask the nurses to get me.' CLOSE WITH THE SUMMARY AND THE FOURTH EMPATHY POINT: 'a treatable lung condition of prematurity; he's stable; tests, antibiotics as a precaution, support for his breathing, and the specialists may give surfactant; and he's going to the intensive care nursery in Adelaide for the best care, with you close by. I'M SO SORRY YOU'RE GOING THROUGH THIS — YOU'VE DONE NOTHING WRONG.'
plan: EMPATHY, REASSURANCE, PERMISSION — THE FIRST OF FOUR SCORED EMPATHY POINTS: [sit close, hand the tissues] 'Jane, I'm Dr -, the doctor looking after you and your son. I'M SO SORRY THIS IS HAPPENING — IT MUST BE TERRIFYING SO SOON AFTER THE BIRTH.' → [crying] 'he can't breathe properly. WHY IS THIS HAPPENING? I LOST THE FIRST ONE — IS HE GOING TO DIE?' → 'I can only imagine what you're going through. I want you to know first that HE IS STABLE RIGHT NOW, HE'S IN SAFE HANDS, and we're giving him the very best care. May I ask a few questions, and then I'll explain exactly what's happening and what we're doing?' (Launching into questions without empathy, or answering 'HE'LL BE FINE', are the two traps — 'HE IS STABLE AND THIS IS A CONDITION WE TREAT' is the honest version.)

THE BREATHING: 'when you say he's having trouble — IS HE COUGHING, IS IT NOISY, OR IS HE WORKING HARD, STRUGGLING? Did it start STRAIGHT AFTER BIRTH or was he fine at first? Constant, or on and off? Worse with anything — feeding, lying a certain way?'

PREGNANCY — AND THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT CARRY MARKS: 'any infections or fevers in the pregnancy — URINE INFECTIONS? High blood sugar or blood pressure? DID YOUR WATERS BREAK EARLY — HOW LONG BEFORE HE WAS BORN? Any medicines, alcohol or drugs? Were your tests and scans normal? WERE YOU GIVEN STEROID INJECTIONS BEFORE THE BIRTH?' → an E. coli urine infection at 14 weeks, WATERS BROKE ABOUT EIGHT HOURS BEFORE, and NO STEROIDS BECAUSE THERE WASN'T TIME. (Not asking about antenatal steroids, or not linking the UTI and early rupture to infection risk, are both named traps.)

DELIVERY AND AFTER: 'how many weeks were you? Vaginal or caesarean, any complications? DID HE CRY STRAIGHT AWAY — DID THEY NEED TO HELP HIM BREATHE? Did they mention HE'D PASSED A BOWEL MOTION INSIDE THE WOMB? Has he had VITAMIN K? Any DROOLING OR FROTHY SALIVA, any TURNING BLUE? Is he alert or sleepy? HAS HE PASSED URINE OR A BOWEL MOTION YET?'

THE MOTHER HERSELF — a scored item candidates drop: 'and HOW ARE YOU FEELING RIGHT NOW, Jane? IS ANYONE HERE WITH YOU? How are you physically — bleeding, pain?' → 'terrified. My partner Sam is parking the car. I'm sore but OK.'

THE DIAGNOSIS — EMPATHY AGAIN FIRST, THEN SURFACTANT IN PLAIN WORDS (see dx) → 'IS IT BECAUSE OF THE INFECTION I HAD? BECAUSE I LOST THE FIRST ONE?' / 'DID I DO SOMETHING WRONG?' → 'NO. Nothing you did caused this, AND THE MISCARRIAGE ISN'T CONNECTED.' Then REASSURE AGAIN — the second scored empathy point sits right here.

MANAGEMENT, POINT ONE AND TWO: TESTS THEN ANTIBIOTICS, then oxygen, CPAP, intubation, fluids, expressing, AND SURFACTANT NAMED AS AN OPTION (see dx) → 'CAN'T YOU JUST GIVE THE SURFACTANT NOW?' / 'WILL HE BE ON THE MACHINE FOR LONG?'

MANAGEMENT, POINT THREE — THE TRANSFER, FRAMED AS BEST CARE (see dx) → [panicking] 'TRAVELS? WHERE?' / 'WHY ADELAIDE — IS IT THAT BAD?' / 'CAN I GO WITH HIM?' → 'we'll do everything to keep you together' — then PATS, and checking she is well enough to travel. ('We'll keep him here and see' is the fail, and if you never mention transfer she asks 'SO HE'LL STAY HERE WITH ME?')

SUPPORT, SUMMARY AND THE FOURTH EMPATHY POINT (see dx): written information, a family meeting with Sam before the team arrives, 'any question at any hour', then the five-part summary ending 'I'M SO SORRY YOU'RE GOING THROUGH THIS — YOU'VE DONE NOTHING WRONG.'

ask: 'I'M SO SORRY THIS IS HAPPENING — I CAN ONLY IMAGINE HOW FRIGHTENING THIS IS.' / 'HE IS STABLE, HE'S IN SAFE HANDS, AND WE'RE GIVING HIM THE BEST CARE.' / 'Is he coughing, is it noisy, OR IS HE WORKING HARD TO BREATHE?' / 'DID YOUR WATERS BREAK EARLY — HOW LONG BEFORE THE BIRTH?' / 'Did he cry straight away — did they need to help him breathe?' / 'WERE YOU GIVEN STEROID INJECTIONS BEFORE THE BIRTH?' / 'And how are YOU feeling?'

'A SOAPY SUBSTANCE CALLED SURFACTANT THAT STOPS THE AIR SACS STICKING SHUT.' / 'Babies make most of it in the last few weeks — at 32 weeks he doesn't have enough yet.' / 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS — BEING BORN EARLY IS THE REASON.' / 'The miscarriage isn't connected.'

'AS SOON AS THE SAMPLES ARE TAKEN WE'LL START ANTIBIOTICS AS A PRECAUTION.' / 'CPAP — A GENTLE CONTINUOUS FLOW OF AIR TO HOLD THE AIR SACS OPEN.' / 'SURFACTANT IS AN OPTION THE SPECIALISTS WILL CONSIDER.' / 'WE DON'T HAVE A NEONATAL INTENSIVE CARE UNIT HERE — SO HE'S GOING TO THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S, NOT BECAUSE HE'S WORSE, BUT FOR THE BEST CARE.' / 'We'll arrange travel and accommodation for you both.' / 'I'd encourage you to start expressing milk.'

VERSION B — COUNSELLING ONLY, NO HISTORY: open with empathy and stability, THEN THE AGENDA QUESTION, WHICH IS WHAT THIS VERSION SCORES: 'before I explain, CAN I CHECK WHAT YOU'VE BEEN TOLD SO FAR, AND IS THERE ANYTHING YOU'RE MOST WORRIED ABOUT?' → 'nobody's told me anything. IS HE GOING TO DIE? IS IT MY FAULT?' Then the diagnosis and surfactant as above, then: 'THREE THINGS WE DO NOW, AND ONE BIG THING. Tests then antibiotics as a precaution; oxygen, with CPAP or a breathing tube if he needs it, and fluids through a drip; and the specialists may give him surfactant into the lungs. THE BIG THING: he needs an intensive care nursery, WHICH WE DON'T HAVE HERE, so the retrieval team will take him to the Women's and Children's — FOR THE BEST CARE, NOT BECAUSE HE'S WORSE.'

VERSION C — THE POSITIVE FINDINGS: 'I had a urine infection at 14 weeks — E. coli — and my waters broke eight hours before he came. DID THAT CAUSE THIS?' → 'thank you for telling me — BOTH ARE IMPORTANT. The infection was treated, and eight hours is not a long time for the waters to be broken, SO NEITHER OF THESE CAUSED HIS LUNGS TO BE SHORT OF SURFACTANT; BEING BORN AT 32 WEEKS DID. BUT BOTH MAKE INFECTION SOMETHING WE TAKE EVEN MORE SERIOUSLY — which is exactly why we'll take blood tests and start antibiotics straight away, rather than waiting for results.' And to the examiner, if asked whether it changes management: 'NO — IT STRENGTHENS THE CASE FOR EMPIRICAL ANTIBIOTICS AFTER CULTURES, and I would ADD A LUMBAR PUNCTURE IF HE SHOWED ANY SIGNS OF SEPSIS; the diagnosis, respiratory support, surfactant option and transfer are unchanged.' (Saying the findings 'DON'T MATTER' is the trap — they do not change the plan, but they MUST be acknowledged and linked to sepsis risk.)
pefe: Role-player: JANE, 26, A SCHOOLTEACHER IN WALLAROO. You have just delivered your son AT 32 WEEKS after a quick labour; YOUR WATERS BROKE ABOUT EIGHT HOURS BEFORE. YOUR FIRST PREGNANCY ENDED IN MISCARRIAGE AT 10 WEEKS LAST YEAR. You had AN E. COLI URINARY INFECTION AT 14 WEEKS, treated with antibiotics. No diabetes, no blood pressure problems, normal scans, NO STEROID INJECTIONS — NO TIME. The baby CRIED BRIEFLY, THEN GRUNTED; the midwives rubbed him and gave oxygen through a headbox; NO TUBE. HE HAS NOT FED. Your partner SAM IS PARKING THE CAR.

EMOTIONAL REGISTER: CRYING, FRIGHTENED, GUILTY. ASK EARLY: 'IS HE GOING TO DIE?' and 'IS IT MY FAULT — THE INFECTION? I LOST THE FIRST ONE.' WHEN TRANSFER IS MENTIONED, PANIC: 'WHY ADELAIDE? IS IT THAT BAD? CAN I GO WITH HIM?' IF THE DOCTOR NEVER MENTIONS TRANSFER, ASK AT THE END: 'SO HE'LL STAY HERE WITH ME?' IF THEY NEVER MENTION ANTIBIOTICS OR INFECTION, ASK: 'COULD THE INFECTION I HAD HAVE GOT INTO HIM?' IF THEY NEVER MENTION SURFACTANT, ASK: 'IS THERE ANY MEDICINE FOR HIS LUNGS?'

Saying 'he'll be fine' instead of 'he is stable and this is a condition we treat'
The 'chest-wall lubricant' explanation of surfactant, or blaming the mother for the infection or the miscarriage

back.dx: VERSION A — VARICELLA (CHICKENPOX). 'A common virus that causes A FEVER AND THEN VERY ITCHY SPOTS that turn into little blisters and then scabs — THE MIX OF NEW SPOTS, BLISTERS AND SCABS TOGETHER IS WHAT MAKES ME CONFIDENT. His cousin's illness two weeks ago fits exactly.' DIFFERENTIALS NAMED: a cold-sore-type virus (HSV), HAND-FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE, and SCHOOL SORES (impetigo) — 'the pattern and the sites don't fit those. And importantly, HE'S ALERT, DRINKING, THE SPOTS FADE WHEN PRESSED AND HE HAS NO BRUISING, so I'm not worried about the serious rashes.' MANAGEMENT: no specific medicine in a healthy child; PARACETAMOL, AND AVOID IBUPROFEN AND ASPIRIN IN CHICKENPOX; cool baths, calamine, SHORT NAILS, loose cotton clothes; EXCLUSION FROM CHILDCARE UNTIL EVERY BLISTER HAS SCABBED, ABOUT FIVE DAYS. THEN THE QUESTION THAT MUST BE ASKED: 'IS ANYONE PREGNANT, A NEWBORN, OR ON TREATMENT THAT WEAKENS THE IMMUNE SYSTEM IN YOUR CIRCLE? THEY SHOULD RING THEIR DOCTOR TODAY' — and if she is not immune, ZOSTER IMMUNOGLOBULIN CAN PROTECT HER IF GIVEN EARLY, WITHIN 96 HOURS AND UP TO 10 DAYS. SAFETY-NET: come straight back or call 000 if he becomes DROWSY, STOPS DRINKING, HAS TROUBLE BREATHING, or ANY SPOT BECOMES RED, SWOLLEN AND PAINFUL, or THE FEVER RETURNS AFTER A FEW DAYS. Give it in writing, and notify SA Health as routine. VERSION B — HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA: 'inflammation of small blood vessels after a viral infection. IT USUALLY SETTLES, but I need A BLOOD COUNT TODAY to be sure her platelets are normal, and because IT CAN AFFECT THE KIDNEYS we'll CHECK HER URINE AND BLOOD PRESSURE REGULARLY FOR SIX MONTHS.' Emergency return for SEVERE TUMMY PAIN, BLOOD IN THE STOOL, OR A SWOLLEN PAINFUL TESTICLE. Ask: does it blanch, blood in the urine, nosebleeds or bleeding gums, pale or tired, any lumps — and request BLOOD PRESSURE AND A URINE DIPSTICK FOR BLOOD AND PROTEIN by name. VERSION C — ROSEOLA INFANTUM (HHV-6): 'THE TELL-TALE SIGN IS THE FEVER BREAKING JUST AS THE RASH APPEARS.' No treatment, childcare when well — and the one thing to add: THE HIGH FEVER CAN OCCASIONALLY TRIGGER A BRIEF FEBRILE SEIZURE, so lie him on his side, nothing in the mouth, and call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes. THE TRAP IN VERSION C IS CALLING IT MEASLES — he is immunised, there is no cough, coryza or conjunctivitis, AND THE FEVER HAS GONE — or ordering tests on a well, blanching child.
plan: VITALS FIRST, THEN OPEN AND SIGNPOST — skipping the observations because the child 'looks well' is the first trap, and the examiner marks whether you asked. 'A few rashes can look alike early on and ONE OR TWO ARE SERIOUS, so I'm going to ask a set of questions, some about things that may seem unrelated, then examine Liam and tell you what I think.' (Jumping to 'it's chickenpox' in the first minute earns 'ARE YOU SURE? HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING WORSE?')

THE RASH: onset, WHERE IT STARTED AND WHERE IT IS NOW, spreading, colour, RAISED OR FLAT, ARE SOME OF THEM BLISTERS, pus or weeping, warm or painful, itchy and worse at night or after a bath. (NOT ASKING ABOUT BLISTERS AND STAGES IS THE TRAP — THE MULTIPLE-STAGE DESCRIPTION IS THE DIAGNOSIS.)

GROUP 1, INFECTIVE — with the two marked items: 'HAS HE HAD A FEVER? WHEN, IN RELATION TO THE RASH?' then immunisations, CONTACTS INCLUDING CHICKENPOX, travel, coryza, vomiting or diarrhoea, recent antibiotics, AND 'IS HE ALERT, DRINKING NORMALLY, NORMAL WET NAPPIES?' (Both the fever-rash timing and the drowsy/drinking/nappy questions are separately marked.)

GROUPS 2, 3 AND 4, RUN AS BLOCKS: AUTOIMMUNE — blood in the poo, greasy poo, sore joints, sore or red eyes, mouth ulcers, cracked lips. ALLERGIC — family atopy, NEW SOAPS, CREAMS, SUNSCREEN, FOODS, MEDICINES OR BITES, NOISY BREATHING OR LIP SWELLING. PURPURIC — EASY BRUISING, NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, pale, tired, weight loss, lumps.

BINDSMA AND THE SOCIAL HISTORY — and omitting it because the diagnosis is obvious is a named trap, because IT IS THE NAI SCREEN AND IS SCORED IN EVERY RASH STATION: 'born at term, any problems? Growing and developing well? Regular medicines or allergies? AND I ASK EVERY FAMILY THIS — who's at home with you, how are things going, any stresses? How is childcare — any concerns?'

THE EXAMINATION, IN STRUCTURE AND ENDING WITH THE LAST TWO BOXES: 'general appearance and hydration; THE RASH — distribution, whether the lesions are MACULES, PAPULES OR VESICLES, WHETHER THEY ARE AT DIFFERENT STAGES, any crusting or discharge; WHETHER THEY BLANCH; warmth and tenderness; the throat and mouth, ears, chest, heart, ABDOMEN FOR LIVER AND SPLEEN, joints, AND A FULL LYMPH NODE EXAMINATION.' (Stopping after the rash is the trap — LYMPH NODES AND SPLEEN ARE THE LAST TWO BOXES.)
DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS WITH THE STAGES AS THE REASON, THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS AND THE REASSURING NEGATIVES (see dx).

MANAGEMENT, THE PREGNANT-CONTACT QUESTION AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'MY SISTER'S 30 WEEKS PREGNANT AND SHE WAS HERE YESTERDAY.' Then written information, notification, and a summary. (Ibuprofen, the wrong exclusion period, no pregnant-contact question, or reassurance without safety-netting are the four management traps.)

'New spots, blisters and scabs together is what confirms chickenpox.' / 'PLEASE AVOID IBUPROFEN AND ASPIRIN WITH CHICKENPOX.' / 'HOME UNTIL EVERY BLISTER HAS SCABBED — ABOUT FIVE DAYS.' / 'IS ANYONE PREGNANT, NEWBORN OR ON IMMUNE-WEAKENING TREATMENT?' / 'Come straight back or call 000 if he is drowsy, not drinking, or breathing hard — or a spot becomes red, swollen and painful.'

VERSION B — HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA: ask 'DO THE SPOTS FADE WHEN YOU PRESS A GLASS ON THEM? Any blood in her wee? Nosebleeds or bleeding gums? Is she pale or tired, any lumps?' Then request BLOOD PRESSURE, A URINE DIPSTICK FOR BLOOD AND PROTEIN, abdomen, joints, nodes, liver and spleen. Explain: 'inflammation of small blood vessels after a viral infection. It usually settles, BUT I NEED A BLOOD COUNT TODAY to be sure her platelets are normal, and BECAUSE IT CAN AFFECT THE KIDNEYS we'll check her urine and blood pressure REGULARLY FOR SIX MONTHS. SEVERE TUMMY PAIN, BLOOD IN THE POO, OR A SWOLLEN PAINFUL TESTICLE needs the emergency department.'

VERSION C — ROSEOLA: the winning question is 'SO THE RASH APPEARED AS THE FEVER DISAPPEARED?' Then alert and drinking, does it blanch, immunisations. 'This is ROSEOLA — a common, harmless virus in toddlers. THE TELL-TALE SIGN IS THE FEVER BREAKING JUST AS THE RASH APPEARS. No treatment, childcare when he feels well. The one thing to know is that THE HIGH FEVER CAN OCCASIONALLY TRIGGER A BRIEF FEBRILE SEIZURE — lie him on his side, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH, and call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes.' (Calling it measles in an immunised child with no cough, coryza or conjunctivitis and a settled fever, or ordering tests on a well blanching child, are the two traps.)

THE FOUR GROUPS, AS A CHECKLIST FOR ANY PAEDIATRIC RASH: INFECTIVE — fever and its timing, immunisations, contacts, travel, coryza, gut symptoms, antibiotics, and the well-baby questions. AUTOIMMUNE — bowel, joints, eyes, mouth and lips. ALLERGIC — atopy, new exposures, and the anaphylaxis screen. PURPURIC — bruising, bleeding, pallor, fatigue, weight loss and lumps. THEN BINDSMA AND THE SOCIAL SCREEN.
pefe: Role-player: Kate, 29, a hairdresser in Wallaroo; LIAM, 3, born at term, healthy, IMMUNISED. He came out in spots yesterday; YOU HAVE SEEN CHICKENPOX IN YOUR NEPHEW TWO WEEKS AGO AND SUSPECT IT, but you are tired and want certainty. Partner Josh works FIFO. REGISTER: anxious and tired, NOT ANGRY. IF THE DOCTOR JUMPS TO 'IT'S CHICKENPOX' IN THE FIRST MINUTE: 'ARE YOU SURE? HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING WORSE?'

THE HIDDEN CONTACT: YOUR SISTER BEC IS 30 WEEKS PREGNANT AND VISITED YESTERDAY — MENTION IT ONLY IF THE DOCTOR ASKS ABOUT PREGNANT CONTACTS, or volunteer it at the very end: 'OH — SHOULD I BE WORRIED ABOUT MY SISTER?' Also ask 'WHEN CAN HE GO BACK TO CHILDCARE? I HAVE TO WORK', and ask 'IS IT MY FAULT?' if the doctor sounds judgemental.

Score them on: ASKED FOR VITALS FIRST; addressed your worry; explored timing, site, BLISTERS and itch; FEVER-RASH TIMING; immunisation; contacts; ALERT, DRINKING AND NAPPIES; the bowel-joints-eyes group; atopy, new products and breathing; THE BRUISING-BLEEDING GROUP; SOCIAL HISTORY WITHOUT JUDGEMENT; an examination request ENDING WITH LYMPH NODES; said chickenpox in plain words; NAMED TWO OR MORE DIFFERENTIALS; paracetamol with NO IBUPROFEN OR ASPIRIN; EXCLUSION UNTIL CRUSTED; ASKED ABOUT PREGNANT OR IMMUNOCOMPROMISED CONTACTS; safety-net for drowsy, not drinking, breathing and secondary infection; and summarised.

back.dx: IRRITANT NAPPY DERMATITIS — IRRITANT CONTACT DERMATITIS — triggered by the diarrhoea three weeks ago, WITH A MOTHER WHO IS NOT COPING. EXPLAIN IT: 'when WEE AND POO SIT AGAINST THE SKIN for a while, ESPECIALLY AFTER DIARRHOEA, the skin gets OVER-WET AND INFLAMED, and wiping makes it sting. SOMETIMES A YEAST CALLED CANDIDA GROWS ON TOP; I DON'T SEE SIGNS OF THAT TODAY, but it's common and easy to treat if it appears.' THE FOUR-PART PLAN, GIVEN AS A TEAM PLAN: CHANGE — every two hours by day, AT EVERY NIGHT FEED, and straight after every poo; CLEAN — warm water and a soft cloth or fragrance-free wipes, PAT DRY, NO SOAP; BARRIER — A THICK ZINC CREAM AT EVERY SINGLE CHANGE, THICK ENOUGH THAT YOU CAN'T SEE SKIN THROUGH IT, AND LEAVE THE OLD LAYER ON; AIR — nappy off on a towel a few times a day. THEN THE ESCALATION RULE: 'IF THE REDNESS SPREADS INTO THE CREASES OR YOU SEE LITTLE RED DOTS AROUND THE EDGE, WE ADD AN ANTIFUNGAL CREAM UNDERNEATH.' WHEN SHE ASKS 'IS IT MY FAULT? BECAUSE I DON'T CHANGE HIM ENOUGH?' — NEVER SAY YES: 'RASHES LIKE THIS HAPPEN TO LOTS OF BABIES AFTER DIARRHOEA. MORE FREQUENT CHANGES WILL HELP IT HEAL — AND I WANT TO MAKE THAT EASIER FOR YOU, NOT JUST TELL YOU TO DO IT.' THEN THE SUPPORT, WHICH IS THE PART THAT PASSES THE STATION: a HOME VISIT FROM THE CHILD AND FAMILY HEALTH NURSE this week; THE PANDA LINE for parents feeling overwhelmed; 'could your mum come up for a week?'; when the partner is home, HE DOES THE NIGHT CHANGES; and THE 6-WEEK CHECK AND IMMUNISATIONS booked for next week so the rash, the weight and the mother are all reviewed together. SAFETY-NET: come straight back if he has A FEVER, IS SLEEPY OR FEEDING POORLY, or the rash develops SORES, PUS OR BLISTERS, or HASN'T IMPROVED IN A WEEK — and write it all down. VERSION B — ECZEMA: 'the skin barrier is leaky and the immune system over-reacts, so it's dry, inflamed and itchy in cycles; it runs with asthma and hay fever.' TWO THINGS WORK: A THICK MOISTURISER OVER THE WHOLE BODY AT LEAST TWICE A DAY, EVERY DAY, FLARING OR NOT; and A STEROID CREAM — hydrocortisone on the face, slightly stronger on the body — ONCE OR TWICE DAILY UNTIL THE FLARE IS COMPLETELY CLEAR, usually one to two weeks, THEN STOP. ANTIHISTAMINES DON'T HELP THIS ITCH. Soap-free wash, short lukewarm baths, cotton clothes, a WRITTEN ACTION PLAN, review in two weeks — sooner if it WEEPS, CRUSTS, or he has COLD-SORE-LIKE BLISTERS AND IS UNWELL. (The traps are 'steroids are dangerous, use for a week only', prescribing an antihistamine, and not specifying moisturiser frequency.) VERSION C — SEBORRHOEIC DERMATITIS: 'the oil glands are over-active and inflamed, producing GREASY YELLOW SCALE ON A PINK BASE. IT ISN'T ITCHY, ISN'T INFECTIOUS AND ISN'T CAUSED BY ANYTHING YOU'VE DONE; it settles by itself, USUALLY BY SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS.' Soften with baby oil or white soft paraffin, leave an hour, mild shampoo, lift gently with a soft brush; 1% HYDROCORTISONE for a few days if the skin underneath is red and sore; an antifungal shampoo if it persists. THE DIFFERENCE FROM ECZEMA: ECZEMA IS ITCHY, COMES AND GOES, AND RUNS IN FAMILIES. VERSION D — ERYTHEMA INFECTIOSUM: take the abuse concern seriously and DO THE SOCIAL AND NAI SCREEN AND THE INJURY EXAMINATION FIRST — 'any concern that a child has been hurt is something I take seriously and will look into properly.' Ask about fever and coryza this week, alertness, immunisations, OTHER RASH ON THE ARMS OR TRUNK, sick contacts at daycare, home and daycare history. Then: 'BRIGHT SYMMETRICAL ERYTHEMA OF BOTH CHEEKS SPARING THE MOUTH, a RETICULAR RASH ON THE ARMS, NO BRUISING, NO FINGER MARKS, no other injuries' — 'this is SLAPPED CHEEK DISEASE, PARVOVIRUS: a few days of fever and a runny nose, THEN BRIGHT RED CHEEKS — THERE ARE NO MARKS OF A HAND. No treatment; HE CAN GO BACK TO DAYCARE BECAUSE HE'S NO LONGER INFECTIOUS ONCE THE RASH IS OUT. ONE IMPORTANT THING: IS ANYONE IN YOUR FAMILY OR CLOSE CONTACTS PREGNANT? THEY SHOULD SEE THEIR DOCTOR FOR A BLOOD TEST.'
plan: VITALS, OPEN, AND CATCH THE TIREDNESS: 'may I have Oscar's observations — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, and is he alert and feeding?' Then: 'Emma, tell me what's been happening.' → 'he's had this rash for three weeks. IT'S NOT GOING AWAY WHATEVER I PUT ON IT. I'M JUST SO TIRED — HE DOESN'T LET ME SLEEP.' → 'THAT SOUNDS EXHAUSTING — a rash that won't settle plus broken nights, six weeks in. Let me work out what's driving this rash, AND WE'LL SORT IT OUT TOGETHER.' (Ignoring the tiredness comment is the first trap — NOTE IT NOW AND RETURN TO IT.)

THE RASH: 'where exactly is it — IS IT ANYWHERE ELSE, LIKE HIS SCALP, FACE OR NECK FOLDS? When did it start, is it spreading? Just redness, or any BLISTERS, RAW AREAS OR SORES? Any discharge or WHITE MATERIAL? Warm to touch? Is he more irritable, ESPECIALLY AT CHANGES? First time? What have you tried?' ('Anywhere else?' is a marked question even though the photograph shows the site.)

THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS — and the second one is where the station turns: 'HAS HE HAD ANY DIARRHOEA RECENTLY? HOW OFTEN DO YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY — DURING THE DAY, AND OVERNIGHT? ANY NEW WIPES, BODY WASH, CREAM, OR A NEW BRAND OF NAPPY?' → 'three or four times a day. At night, ONCE, WHEN I REMEMBER — I'M SO TIRED.' → NO CHANGE IN TONE: 'THANK YOU FOR BEING HONEST WITH ME — THAT REALLY HELPS.' (Reacting with a lecture here loses the station; come back to it in the social history.)

THE OTHER GROUPS: other rashes — scalp, behind the ears, neck; FAMILY ATOPY; fever, alert or sleepier, feeding and wet nappies; sick contacts; IMMUNISATIONS; AND 'ANY WHITE PATCHES IN HIS MOUTH OR ON HIS TONGUE?' Then feeding, weight gain, blood or greasy stools, rash after feeds, vomiting, birth, heel-prick, medicines and allergies.

THE SOCIAL AND MOOD BLOCK — THE DISCRIMINATING ONE, ASKED WARMLY AND NOT AS AN ACCUSATION: 'Emma, you've mentioned a couple of times HOW TIRED YOU ARE. Who's at home with you? HOW MUCH SLEEP ARE YOU GETTING? OVER THE LAST TWO WEEKS, HAVE YOU OFTEN FELT DOWN, DEPRESSED OR HOPELESS — OR HAD LITTLE INTEREST OR PLEASURE IN THINGS? DO YOU HAVE ANYONE WHO CAN HELP WITH NIGHT CHANGES AND FEEDS?' → tearful: 'not depressed exactly. FLAT. OVERWHELMED. Some days I don't know if I'm doing any of it right.' → 'THAT IS A VERY NORMAL THING TO FEEL SIX WEEKS IN WITH NO SLEEP AND NO HELP — AND IT'S SOMETHING I CAN ACTUALLY DO SOMETHING ABOUT.' (TWO SCREENING QUESTIONS PLUS A SUPPORT QUESTION, WARMLY, IS THE PASS.)

THE EXAMINATION, WITH THE TWO DECIDING ITEMS NAMED: 'general appearance, hydration and temperature, AND HIS WEIGHT ON THE GROWTH CHART. The rash: DISTRIBUTION — CONVEX SURFACES OR INTO THE FOLDS — ANY SATELLITE SPOTS, PUSTULES, EROSIONS OR DISCHARGE. THE MOUTH FOR THRUSH. Scalp, face, neck folds and behind the ears, and the rest of the skin. Abdomen for liver and spleen, and lymph nodes.' (Not asking about the folds and satellites is the trap — THAT IS WHAT DECIDES WHETHER YOU ADD AN ANTIFUNGAL.)
THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS AND THE FOUR-PART PLAN — CHANGE, CLEAN, BARRIER, AIR — WITH THE ESCALATION RULE (see dx) → 'IS IT BECAUSE I DON'T CHANGE HIM ENOUGH? IS IT MY FAULT?' → never yes.

THE SUPPORT, THE 6-WEEK CHECK AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx): the child health nurse home visit, PANDA, asking about her mother coming up, the partner doing night changes when home, immunisations next week, and the return criteria — written down. Then summarise.

Then fever and coryza this week, alertness, immunisations, ANY OTHER RASH ON THE ARMS OR TRUNK, sick contacts at daycare, home and stresses, how long at daycare and any previous concerns. pefe: Role-player: EMMA, 24, FIRST-TIME MOTHER of Oscar, 6 weeks, in Wallaroo. PARTNER JAKE IS FIFO AT A MINE, AWAY TWO WEEKS IN THREE. YOUR MUM IS IN ADELAIDE AND YOU HAVEN'T ASKED FOR HELP. Normal pregnancy and birth; Oscar is breastfed and gaining weight. HE HAD DIARRHOEA THREE WEEKS AGO AND THE RASH STARTED THEN. YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY 3-4 TIMES BY DAY AND ONCE AT NIGHT. YOU ARE GETTING ABOUT FOUR BROKEN HOURS OF SLEEP.

HIDDEN AGENDA: YOU FEEL FLAT AND OVERWHELMED AND SECRETLY WONDER WHETHER YOU ARE A BAD MOTHER. REGISTER: tired, flat, EYES DOWN; BECOME TEARFUL WHEN SOMEONE ASKS KINDLY HOW YOU ARE. IF THE DOCTOR LECTURES YOU OR SAYS ANYTHING LIKE 'YOU NEED TO CHANGE HIM MORE', GO QUIET AND SAY 'I KNOW. I'M DOING MY BEST.' IF THE DOCTOR NEVER ASKS ABOUT YOUR SLEEP, MOOD OR SUPPORT, VOLUNTEER AT THE END: 'SORRY — I'M JUST SO TIRED ALL THE TIME. IS THAT NORMAL?' And ask 'IS IT MY FAULT?' after the diagnosis.

Score them on: vitals first; ACKNOWLEDGED YOUR TIREDNESS AT THE START; asked 'ANYWHERE ELSE?'; onset, colour, blisters, discharge, irritability; DIARRHOEA; CHANGE FREQUENCY WITHOUT JUDGEMENT; NEW PRODUCTS; other rashes and family atopy; fever, alertness, feeding, wet nappies; THE THRUSH QUESTION; feeding and weight; stools; SLEEP, MOOD WITH TWO SCREENING QUESTIONS, AND SUPPORT; an examination request INCLUDING FOLDS, SATELLITES, MOUTH, OTHER SKIN AND ABDOMEN; a plain-words diagnosis; CHANGE-CLEAN-BARRIER-AIR; the antifungal plan if folds or satellites; DID NOT BLAME YOU; ARRANGED SUPPORT — CaFHS, PANDA, family; THE 6-WEEK CHECK AND IMMUNISATIONS; a safety-net for fever, sleepiness, feeding and sores; and a summary.

back.dx: INFANTILE HYPERTROPHIC PYLORIC STENOSIS. EXPLAIN IT AS A GATEWAY: 'at the bottom of the stomach there's A RING OF MUSCLE — A GATEWAY — that lets milk into the bowel. In this condition THAT MUSCLE GETS THICK AND THE GATEWAY NARROWS, so milk can't get through. THE STOMACH SQUEEZES HARD AGAINST IT and the milk comes back up with force.' THEN FOUR REASONS: 'ONE, HIS AGE — IT SHOWS UP AT TWO TO EIGHT WEEKS, AND HE'S THREE WEEKS. TWO, THE VOMITING IS FORCEFUL. THREE, HE'S HUNGRY STRAIGHT AFTER AND TAKES ANOTHER FEED. FOUR, THE VOMIT IS MILKY, NOT GREEN, WHICH TELLS ME THE BLOCKAGE IS AT THE STOMACH EXIT, NOT LOWER DOWN. And when I examined him I FELT THE THICKENED MUSCLE AS A SMALL LUMP AND SAW THE STOMACH SQUEEZING' — plus the family history, because IT RUNS IN FAMILIES. THEN THE TWO THINGS SHE IS WAITING FOR: 'NOTHING YOU'VE DONE — THE FORMULA, THE FEEDING — CAUSED THIS' and 'REFLUX IS A FAIR THOUGHT, BUT REFLUX BABIES DRIBBLE MILK WITHOUT FORCE AND OFTEN GO OFF THEIR FEEDS; OLIVER IS THE OPPOSITE.' DIFFERENTIALS: REFLUX; A BLOCKAGE OR TWIST LOWER IN THE BOWEL, WHICH USUALLY GIVES GREEN VOMIT; A TRAPPED HERNIA IN THE GROIN; AN INFECTION — URINE, CHEST OR BLOOD; A KNOCK TO THE HEAD; and A RARE SALT-LOSING GLAND CONDITION — congenital adrenal hyperplasia — THAT WE CHECK FOR ON HIS BLOODS. MANAGEMENT, IN ORDER, AND NEVER 'SURGERY TONIGHT': STOP THE FEEDS; A DRIP TO REHYDRATE AND REPLACE THE SALTS HE'S LOST, WITH BLOODS TO CHECK THEM; AN ULTRASOUND TO CONFIRM; THEN THE CHILDREN'S SURGEONS. 'The treatment is A SMALL OPERATION THAT OPENS UP THE GATEWAY — IT'S CURATIVE, and most babies FEED WITHIN HOURS AND GO HOME IN A DAY OR TWO. IT ISN'T DONE TONIGHT: WE GET HIS SALTS RIGHT FIRST BECAUSE THAT MAKES THE ANAESTHETIC SAFER.' SAFETY-NET: tell the nurse straight away if he VOMITS GREEN, BECOMES FLOPPY OR DROWSY, OR STOPS WEEING. VERSION B — THE BLOODS: 'these show what the vomiting has done. HE HAS LOST A LOT OF THE ACID AND SALT FROM HIS STOMACH, so HIS CHLORIDE AND POTASSIUM ARE LOW AND HIS BLOOD HAS BECOME SLIGHTLY ALKALINE. He's also dry — that's the raised urea. THIS PATTERN ACTUALLY SUPPORTS THE DIAGNOSIS. We correct it BEFORE any operation: a drip with salt water, sugar and potassium, RECHECK EVERY FEW HOURS, and the surgeons operate once the numbers are back in range — usually within a day or two.' And if the examiner asks why not operate now: 'UNCORRECTED ALKALOSIS IS ASSOCIATED WITH POST-OPERATIVE APNOEA; CORRECTION TO A CHLORIDE ABOVE 100 AND BICARBONATE BELOW 30 IS STANDARD BEFORE ANAESTHESIA.' VERSION C — THE GREEN VOMIT: 'GREEN VOMIT CHANGES THINGS — it means the blockage may be BELOW the stomach, and one cause is A TWIST OF THE BOWEL THAT NEEDS THE SURGEONS URGENTLY. Is his tummy swollen or sore? Any blood in the nappy? I'm going to examine him now AND CALL THE SURGICAL TEAM STRAIGHT AWAY.' DO NOT CONTINUE DOWN THE HPS PATHWAY ONCE THE VOMIT IS BILIOUS — MALROTATION WITH VOLVULUS IS THE DIAGNOSIS TO EXCLUDE FIRST.
plan: VITALS AND HYDRATION BEFORE YOU SIT, THEN OPEN: 'could I have the vital signs AND HYDRATION STATUS, please?' Then introduce, signpost, and 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'he keeps throwing up his feeds. It started two days ago and IT'S GETTING WORSE — IT COMES FLYING OUT OF HIM. MY MATERNAL NURSE SAID IT'S PROBABLY REFLUX but he's not keeping anything down.' → 'that sounds frightening, AND YOU'VE DONE THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN.' (She has handed you 'reflux' — TAKE IT AS A HIDDEN AGENDA TO ADDRESS LATER, NOT AS THE DIAGNOSIS.)

THE VOMIT: 'how many times a day? EVERY FEED? Getting worse? WHAT COLOUR — MILKY, YELLOW, GREEN — ANY BLOOD? How much — a mouthful, or the whole feed? DOES IT COME OUT WITH FORCE, UNDER PRESSURE? How soon after the feed? Does lying him down or his position change it?' (Do not accept 'a small amount' as reassurance, and DO NOT SKIP FORCE BECAUSE SHE SAID REFLUX.)

THE HUNGRY QUESTION — the one that separates it from reflux: 'AFTER HE VOMITS, IS HE STILL HUNGRY? DOES HE TAKE ANOTHER FULL FEED?' → 'HE'S STARVING.' Then: 'HAVE YOU EVER FELT A LUMP IN HIS TUMMY, OR SEEN A RIPPLING MOVEMENT ACROSS IT AFTER A FEED?'

THE GI BLOCK: last bowel motion, wind, diarrhoea, BLOOD IN THE NAPPY, distension; ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN WHEN HE CRIES; SCREAMING EPISODES WITH LEGS DRAWN UP, GOING PALE, RED-JELLY STOOL; then the GORD block — refuses feeds, ARCHES HIS BACK, laid flat after feeds, burping; AND IS HE GAINING WEIGHT? → he had STOPPED GAINING at the last weigh.

INFECTION, WELL-BABY AND NEURO: fever, contacts, travel, cough, runny nose, DROOLING, crying on weeing or smelly urine, rash; ALERT OR DROWSY; feeding as usual; HOW MANY WET NAPPIES TODAY → 'ONLY THREE — USUALLY SIX OR SEVEN' → SAY IT OUT LOUD: 'THAT'S FEWER THAN I'D LIKE — IT TELLS ME HE'S GETTING DRY.' Then falls or knocks to the head, and who else looks after him.

BIRTH AND FAMILY — AND LEAVE TWENTY SECONDS FOR THE LAST QUESTION, WHICH IS THE FINAL MARK: pregnancy complications, medicines, alcohol, smoking; delivery; FIRST BOWEL MOTION, HEEL-PRICK, JAUNDICE; breast or formula and how much; antibiotics; AND 'ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WHO VOMITED A LOT AS A BABY OR HAD A TUMMY OPERATION AS A BABY?' → THE BROTHER. Then: 'is there anything you're particularly worried about?' → 'IS IT MY FORMULA? IS IT REFLUX LIKE THEY SAID? WILL HE NEED SURGERY?'

THE EXAMINATION, AND YOU MUST ASK FOR THE MASS: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, DEHYDRATION, rash, jaundice? Vital signs? Throat and ears? Chest — air entry, added sounds? ABDOMEN: DISTENSION, SCARS, VISIBLE PERISTALSIS? ON PALPATION — ANY MASS, WHERE, TENDERNESS, GUARDING? Bowel sounds? GROIN AND SCROTUM? Urine dipstick and glucose?' — and INTERPRET THE DEHYDRATION ALOUD as about five per cent.
NAME IT, THE GATEWAY EXPLANATION, THEN THE FOUR REASONS (see dx) → 'WHY DO YOU THINK IT'S THAT AND NOT REFLUX?' → the four reasons plus the family history.
THE TWO ANSWERS SHE NEEDS AND THE DIFFERENTIALS (see dx) → 'DID I CAUSE IT WITH THE FORMULA?' → 'NO. Nothing you've done caused this.' Then the six differentials, each dismissed against the findings.

MANAGEMENT IN ORDER AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → yes, curative, feeds within hours, home in a day or two — BUT NOT TONIGHT, AND SAY WHY. Then summarise. (She becomes tearful at the word OPERATION and settles once you say it is curative and not tonight.)

back.dx: VERSION A — GASTRO-OESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE. 'In babies, THE GATEWAY AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FOOD PIPE IS IMMATURE AND DOESN'T CLOSE PROPERLY, so some of the stomach contents come back up and he brings up his milk — THAT'S REFLUX. WHEN IT STARTS TO CAUSE PROBLEMS — INFLAMMATION IN THE FOOD PIPE, ARCHING AND DISTRESS, AND MOST IMPORTANTLY TROUBLE GAINING WEIGHT, WHICH HIS CHART SHOWS — WE CALL IT REFLUX DISEASE.' VERSION B — PHYSIOLOGICAL GOR: 'the good news is THIS IS REFLUX — PHYSIOLOGICAL REFLUX — NOT A DISEASE. I'm confident because IT'S ONLY MILK, IT'S EFFORTLESS, IT'S ALWAYS AFTER FEEDS, and most importantly HE'S HAPPY, WELL HYDRATED AND GROWING BEAUTIFULLY ON HIS CHART. IT SETTLES AS THE GATEWAY MATURES — MOST BABIES BY THEIR FIRST BIRTHDAY.' THE DIFFERENTIALS, LONG AND SPECIFIC IN BOTH VERSIONS: COW'S MILK PROTEIN ALLERGY; A NARROWING AT THE STOMACH OUTLET — pyloric stenosis; A BOWEL BLOCKAGE OR HERNIA; INFECTIONS INCLUDING A URINE INFECTION; A METABOLIC CONDITION; AND PRESSURE INSIDE THE HEAD — 'nothing points to those.' MANAGEMENT, FOUR THINGS, AND EDUCATION COMES BEFORE ANY DRUG: ONE — POSITIONING: 'after each feed HOLD HIM UPRIGHT AGAINST YOUR SHOULDER FOR TWENTY TO THIRTY MINUTES AND BURP HIM BEFORE YOU LIE HIM DOWN; HE STILL SLEEPS FLAT ON HIS BACK.' TWO — THICKENING: 'express some milk and add a feed thickener from the pharmacy; KEEP BREASTFEEDING, THERE'S NO NEED FOR A SPECIAL FORMULA.' THREE — SMALLER FEEDS MORE OFTEN, with a LACTATION CONSULTANT OR CHILD HEALTH NURSE REVIEW of how he feeds. FOUR — RED FLAGS: 'if he starts REFUSING FEEDS, ARCHING AND SCREAMING, STOPS GAINING WEIGHT, or the vomit is ever GREEN OR HAS BLOOD IN IT, or he's FEVERISH OR DROWSY, come straight back.' REVIEW IN TWO WEEKS WITH A WEIGHT. IN VERSION A ONLY, THE DRUG COMES AFTER THE EDUCATION IN THE SAME BREATH: 'first we change how we feed him, AND I'LL ALSO START A FOUR-WEEK TRIAL OF AN ACID-SUPPRESSING MEDICINE, OMEPRAZOLE, TO LET THE FOOD PIPE HEAL' — plus referral to the paediatrician and consideration of cow's milk protein in the mother's diet. 'It's safe as a short course; WE AVOID LONG-TERM USE BECAUSE OF SIDE EFFECTS, WHICH IS WHY THE FEEDING CHANGES COME FIRST.' IN VERSION B, WHEN SHE PUSHES FOR MEDICINE: 'I understand why you'd want that. MEDICINE DOESN'T FIX AN IMMATURE GATEWAY AND HAS SIDE EFFECTS, so for a baby who's growing well WE DON'T USE IT. The feeding changes work — and IF HE EVER STOPS GAINING OR STARTS REFUSING FEEDS, I'LL SEE HIM STRAIGHT AWAY and refer him to the paediatrician, and we'd talk about medication then.' THE OTHER VARIANTS: BLOOD OR MUCUS IN THE STOOL WITH ECZEMA — 'this makes me think of AN ALLERGY TO COW'S MILK PROTEIN, WHICH CAN COME THROUGH BREAST MILK. CUT ALL DAIRY FROM YOUR DIET FOR TWO WEEKS and we'll see whether the vomiting and the stools settle; THEN WE REINTRODUCE IT TO CHECK' — with a paediatrician and DIETITIAN to keep her diet safe. A 2-MONTH-OLD WITH FORCEFUL VOMITING — ask 'IS IT PROJECTILE? IS HE HUNGRY STRAIGHT AFTER? LOSING WEIGHT?' and if the examiner gives an olive and visible peristalsis, IT IS PYLORIC STENOSIS and he goes to the Women's and Children's TODAY. GREEN VOMIT ON A REFLUX BACKGROUND — 'GREEN MEANS BILE, WHICH MEANS A BLOCKAGE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — THIS IS NOT HIS REFLUX', emergency department now, ring ahead, MedSTAR Kids. HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE CROSSING UPWARD — ask about A BULGING FONTANELLE AND PROMINENT SCALP VEINS, and arrange AN URGENT SCAN AND PAEDIATRIC REVIEW TODAY.
plan: VITALS, THEN THE EMPATHY STATEMENT — A MARKED BOX, DONE ONCE AND PROPERLY: 'Examiner, the vital signs please.' Then: 'tell me what's been going on.' → 'he's been vomiting for two months. I'VE SEEN THREE DOCTORS AND THEY ALL SAY IT'S NOTHING. I'm exhausted and I'M SICK OF BEING TOLD IT'S NOTHING SERIOUS.' → 'I'M REALLY SORRY YOU'VE HAD THAT EXPERIENCE. Two months of this is exhausting, and IT'S ABSOLUTELY RIGHT TO WANT IT LOOKED AT PROPERLY. Let's go through it carefully together.' (Launching into 'how many times?' costs the communication mark — and if you never acknowledge it, SHE CUTS IN AT MINUTE TWO WITH 'YOU'RE JUST LIKE THE OTHERS'. Do it once, then move on.)

THE VOMIT: how long, how many a day, most days, worse; WHAT COLOUR, ANY BLOOD, IS IT JUST THE MILK HE'S HAD; how much; DOES IT SHOOT OUT WITH FORCE; smell; better or worse; ANY POSITION; related to feeds or food. (You now know it is reflux — THE MARK IS IN CONTINUING THE STRUCTURE ANYWAY.)

THE GI BUCKET AND THE REFLUX BLOCK: last bowel motion, wind, diarrhoea, BLOOD OR MUCUS IN THE NAPPY, bloated. Then: 'does it ALWAYS happen after a feed? DO YOU LIE HIM DOWN STRAIGHT AFTER FEEDING? DO YOU BURP HIM? DOES HE ARCH HIS BACK? DOES HE REFUSE FEEDS? IS HE GAINING WEIGHT AS EXPECTED ON HIS GROWTH CHART? Does he sleep well? How much and how often is he feeding?' (ASK THE GROWTH QUESTION IN THOSE WORDS — 'ANY CONCERNS ABOUT HIS GROWTH?' GETS 'NOT REALLY'.)
THE THREE EXCLUSIONS: 'ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN? SCREAMING EPISODES — DOES HE GO PALE? EVER A FORCEFUL, PROJECTILE VOMIT?'

INFECTION, WELL-BABY, NEURO, ALLERGY, BIRTH AND IMMUNISATION, run fast: fever, travel, contacts, coryza, cough, DROOLING, ear-pulling, crying with nappy changes, smelly urine, rash; alert or drowsy, drinking, WET NAPPIES; falls or head knocks; how are things at home; solids started, RASH ROUND THE MOUTH WITH A FOOD; pregnancy and birth, HEEL-PRICK, FIRST POO, immunisations.

THE EXAMINATION, WITH THE CHART REQUESTED BY NAME: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? Dehydration? Rash? COULD I SEE HIS GROWTH CHART — WEIGHT, LENGTH AND HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE? ENT: throat, drums? Chest: air entry, added sounds? Abdomen: distension or visible mass, then mass, tenderness, rigidity or organomegaly, and bowel sounds. INGUINAL REGION — ANY LUMP? FONTANELLE — BULGING? AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' THEN READ THE TREND ALOUD: 'his weight HAS CROSSED TWO CENTILE LINES DOWNWARD while his head and length are tracking — THAT IS FALTERING GROWTH' or 'weight, length and head circumference are ALL TRACKING NORMALLY.'
THE LABEL WITH ITS REASON, THE GATEWAY EXPLANATION, AND THE LONG SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIAL LIST (see dx) → 'SO IT IS SOMETHING. WHY DID NOBODY SAY?' / 'IS IT SERIOUS?'

MANAGEMENT — EDUCATION FIRST, ALWAYS (see dx): positioning with the twenty to thirty minutes upright and STILL FLAT ON HIS BACK TO SLEEP; thickening with breastfeeding continued; smaller feeds more often with a lactation review; then in Version A only, THE FOUR-WEEK OMEPRAZOLE TRIAL IN THE SAME BREATH AS THE FEEDING CHANGES, plus paediatrician referral. → 'CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING TO STOP IT?' / 'SHOULD I STOP BREASTFEEDING AND TRY A SPECIAL FORMULA?'

RED FLAGS AND REVIEW: refusing feeds, arching and screaming, stopping gaining, GREEN OR BLOODY VOMIT, fever or drowsiness — and REVIEW IN TWO WEEKS WITH A WEIGHT. Then check the plan feels right to her.

His head is growing faster than the rest of him — I'm concerned about PRESSURE INSIDE THE HEAD and he needs AN URGENT SCAN AND PAEDIATRIC REVIEW TODAY.'

VERSION A ONLY: HE SOMETIMES ARCHES AND CRIES AFTER FEEDS, WAKES OFTEN, AND THE CHILD HEALTH NURSE SAID HE HAS 'SLIPPED DOWN THE CHART'. back.dx: VERSION A — FEBRILE URINARY TRACT INFECTION in a 9-month-old. GIVE IT WITH THREE REASONS: 'most likely David has A URINARY TRACT INFECTION — AN INFECTION IN THE BLADDER AND THE URINARY TUBES. I'm saying that because HE HAS A FEVER AND VOMITING, WHICH TELL ME THERE'S AN INFECTION; HE CRIES WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY AND HIS URINE SMELLS STRONG; and WHEN I EXAMINED HIM I COULDN'T FIND ANOTHER SOURCE — HIS THROAT, EARS AND CHEST ARE CLEAR — BUT THE URINE TEST SHOWS SIGNS OF INFECTION.' THEN A FIVE-SECOND DIFFERENTIAL LIST: a blockage in the bowel, reflux, a hernia, a tummy bug, other infections — throat, ears, chest — AND A SERIOUS BLOOD INFECTION — 'none of those fit.' DO NOT SAY CYSTITIS OR PYELONEPHRITIS: THEY ARE NOT SEPARABLE CLINICALLY IN INFANTS, AND A FEBRILE INFANT UTI IS TREATED AS UPPER TRACT. TASK 4, AND THE FIRST WORDS MATTER: 'TO CONFIRM IT I NEED TO SEND A URINE SAMPLE FOR MICROSCOPY, CULTURE AND SENSITIVITY. We'll collect it BY CLEAN CATCH — clean his genitals and catch the urine in a sterile jar as it comes. THE MOST RELIABLE WAY, WHICH WE USE IF A BABY IS UNWELL OR IN HOSPITAL, IS A SUPRAPUBIC ASPIRATE — drawing urine directly from the bladder with a fine needle — OR A SMALL CATHETER.' ANY ANSWER THAT STARTS WITH 'FBE, CRP, ULTRASOUND' HAS SPENT THE MARK. THEN: oral antibiotics for SEVEN DAYS once the sample is taken, small frequent fluids, KEEP BREASTFEEDING, and REVIEW IN 48 HOURS WITH THE RESULT. 'HE DOESN'T NEED AN ULTRASOUND FOR A FIRST INFECTION unless it's severe, doesn't respond in two days, or comes back.' SAFETY-NET: come straight back or call 000 if he becomes DROWSY, WON'T DRINK, HAS NO WET NAPPY FOR SIX HOURS, GETS A RASH, OR KEEPS VOMITING THE MEDICINE. VERSION B — VIRAL PHARYNGITIS: 'most likely he has PHARYNGITIS — an infection in the throat. He has fever, he's vomiting, YOU TOLD ME HE'S DROOLING, and when I examined him HIS THROAT IS RED.' Then the same broad differential list — bowel obstruction such as intussusception or a hernia, reflux, gastroenteritis, pneumonia, middle-ear infection, urine infection, SEPSIS, and problems in the head. 'URTI' IS NOT SPECIFIC ENOUGH WHEN YOU HAVE BEEN HANDED A RED PHARYNX. AND WHEN DROOLING IS REVEALED, CLEAR THE AIRWAY FIRST: 'is he BREATHING NOISILY OR WORKING HARD TO BREATHE? CAN HE SWALLOW HIS SALIVA? IS HE SITTING FORWARD OR HOLDING HIS NECK STILL?' — 'good, that fits A SORE THROAT RATHER THAN ANYTHING BLOCKING HIS AIRWAY.' MANAGEMENT, FOUR THINGS: PARACETAMOL, and ibuprofen with food if he's drinking well; ONDANSETRON — A WAFER THAT MELTS UNDER THE TONGUE — as a SINGLE DOSE; PUSH FLUIDS in small sips, Hydralyte or Gastrolyte, icy poles fine; and RED FLAGS — if he keeps vomiting, the fever climbs, he becomes DROWSY, has TROUBLE BREATHING OR SWALLOWING, or gets A RASH, come straight to hospital. NO BLOOD TESTS. Home from childcare until well. STARTING WITH 'I WOULD DO SOME BLOOD TESTS' FAILS A VIRAL PHARYNGITIS. THE OTHER VARIANTS: A CLEAR OTHER FOCUS — exudative tonsils or a red drum — means 'BECAUSE I'VE FOUND THE SOURCE OF THE FEVER, I DON'T NEED TO COLLECT URINE TODAY; if the fever hasn't settled in 48 hours we'll re-look and test the urine.' AN INFANT UNDER 3 MONTHS WITH A FEBRILE UTI: 'AT THIS AGE A URINE INFECTION CAN SPREAD TO THE BLOOD, so he needs HOSPITAL FOR INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS and a full check including A SUPRAPUBIC SAMPLE AND AN ULTRASOUND' — call the Women's and Children's and MedSTAR Kids. MODERATE DEHYDRATION OR NOT TOLERATING ORAL: nasogastric or intravenous fluids and IV antibiotics until he keeps them down. RECURRENT UTI: a KIDNEY ULTRASOUND — not urgent — and a paediatrician referral; PREVENTIVE ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT ROUTINE.
plan: VITALS AT THE DOOR, THEN ONE OPEN QUESTION AND THE CONCERN STATEMENT: 'Examiner, before I begin, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' Then: 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'he's been vomiting for two days and he's really hot. I'M WORRIED, DOCTOR.' → 'I can see how worrying this is. Let's work through it together — I'll ask some specific questions and then we'll examine him.' (Asking three open questions in a row is the trap — THE ROLE-PLAYER ANSWERS ONE, THEN WAITS FOR SPECIFICS.)

THE VOMIT AND THE FEVER: when it started, how many times since, on and off or continuous, getting worse, WHAT COLOUR, ANY BLOOD, large or small, IS IT FORCEFUL, any foul smell, anything better or worse, any position, related to feeds or a food. Then: 'HAVE YOU MEASURED THE FEVER? GIVEN ANYTHING? DOES IT WORK?'
THE GI BUCKET: last bowel motion, passing wind, DIARRHOEA, BLOOD IN THE STOOL, bloated tummy, ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN, ANY EPISODES OF SCREAMING.

EVERY INFECTION — AND TWO QUESTIONS HERE ARE THE DIAGNOSIS: travel; SICK CONTACTS; runny nose, DROOLING, cough; PULLING AT HIS EARS; 'DOES HE CRY OR SEEM IRRITABLE WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY OR HE PASSES URINE? DOES THE URINE SMELL UNUSUAL?'; any rash. → 'HE SCREAMS EVERY TIME I CHANGE HIS NAPPY' and 'IT DOES SMELL STRONG.' (The cousin's cold or the brother's tummy bug is BAIT — NO DIARRHOEA PLUS NAPPY-CHANGE CRYING KEEPS YOU ON UTI.)

WELL-BABY, NEURO AND BINDSMA: alert or drowsy, drinking as usual, FEWER WET NAPPIES, falls or knocks to the head, how are things at home, immunisations, gaining weight as expected. → SLEEPIER, A BIT FLOPPY, DRINKING LESS, TWO FEWER AND DARKER NAPPIES.

THE EXAMINATION, HEADLINED, WITH DEHYDRATION FIRST AND THE DIPSTICK REQUESTED WITHOUT DEBATE: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? ANY SIGN OF DEHYDRATION — capillary refill, mucous membranes, skin turgor, sunken eyes? Any rash? ENT — throat red, any exudate, tympanic membranes red or bulging? Respiratory — air entry equal, added sounds? Abdomen — distension or visible mass, then mass, tenderness or rigidity, and bowel sounds. INGUINAL REGION — ANY LUMP OR SWELLING? A URINE DIPSTICK PLEASE — AND IS THE ANTERIOR FONTANELLE BULGING?' (Do NOT ask for cervical nodes, hepatosplenomegaly or a full neurological examination — there is no time and no marks.)

THE DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS, THEN THE FIVE-SECOND DIFFERENTIAL LIST (see dx) → 'A URINE INFECTION? HE DOESN'T SEEM TO HAVE TROUBLE WEEING.' / 'COULD IT BE MENINGITIS?' if you never asked what worries her.

TASK 4 IN ONE SENTENCE, STARTING WITH THE RIGHT WORDS: 'TO CONFIRM IT I NEED TO SEND A URINE SAMPLE FOR MICROSCOPY, CULTURE AND SENSITIVITY' — then clean catch, and the suprapubic aspirate or catheter as the reliable method in an unwell baby. Then oral antibiotics for seven days, fluids, KEEP BREASTFEEDING, review at 48 hours, and no ultrasound for a first infection. → 'DOES HE NEED A SCAN OF HIS KIDNEYS?'
THE SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE: drowsy, won't drink, NO WET NAPPY FOR SIX HOURS, a rash, or vomiting the medicine — come back or call 000. Then invite questions.

DOES THE URINE SMELL?' / 'Is he alert and active, or drowsy? Drinking as usual? FEWER WET NAPPIES?'
'Examiner, IS THERE ANY SIGN OF DEHYDRATION?' / 'I'd like to examine THE INGUINAL REGION — any lump or swelling?' / 'A URINE DIPSTICK, PLEASE.' / 'Is the anterior fontanelle bulging?'

VERSION B — DROOLING REVEALED, CLEAR THE AIRWAY FIRST: 'IS HE BREATHING NOISILY OR WORKING HARD TO BREATHE? CAN HE SWALLOW HIS SALIVA? IS HE SITTING FORWARD OR HOLDING HIS NECK STILL?' → 'no, he's just dribbly and grizzly.' → 'good — THAT FITS A SORE THROAT RATHER THAN ANYTHING BLOCKING HIS AIRWAY.' Then PHARYNGITIS, not 'URTI', and the management: PARACETAMOL, ibuprofen with food if drinking well; ONDANSETRON — A WAFER THAT MELTS UNDER THE TONGUE — AS A SINGLE DOSE; PUSH FLUIDS, small sips, Hydralyte or Gastrolyte, icy poles fine; and RED FLAGS — keeps vomiting, fever climbing, DROWSY, TROUBLE BREATHING OR SWALLOWING, or a RASH. NO BLOOD TESTS.

OTHER VARIANTS: A CLEAR OTHER FOCUS — exudative tonsils or a red drum: 'because I've found the source of the fever in his throat or ear, I DON'T NEED TO COLLECT URINE TODAY. I'll treat that, and if the fever hasn't settled in 48 hours we'll re-look and test the urine.' / UNDER 3 MONTHS WITH A FEBRILE UTI: 'AT THIS AGE A URINE INFECTION CAN SPREAD TO THE BLOOD, so he needs to be in hospital for INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS and a full check including A SUPRAPUBIC URINE SAMPLE AND AN ULTRASOUND' — ring the Women's and Children's and arrange MedSTAR Kids. / MODERATE DEHYDRATION OR NOT TOLERATING ORAL: fluids by nasogastric tube or drip and IV antibiotics until he can keep them down. / RECURRENT UTI: 'this is his second infection, so this time I'll arrange A KIDNEY ULTRASOUND — NOT URGENT — and refer him to the paediatrician. WE DON'T USE PREVENTIVE ANTIBIOTICS ROUTINELY.'
